Although his rejection of conjunction elimination might on first acquaintance give an observer a defeasible reason to deny that he understood ‘and’, any such reason is defeated by closer observation of him. He genuinely doubts conjunction elimination as we use it. Nor is he a marginal case of understanding: his linguistic competence is far more secure than that of young children or native speakers of other languages who are in the process of learning English. If some participants in a debate have an imperfect linguistic understanding of one of the key words with which it is conducted, they need to have its meaning explained to them before the debate can properly continue. But to stop our logical debate with the imaginary speaker in order to explain to him what the word ‘and’ means in English would be irrelevant and gratuitously patronising. The understanding which he lacks is logical, is not semantic. His attitude to conjunction elimination manifests only some deviant patterns of belief and belief-formation. Since there clearly could have been, and perhaps are, people such as our imaginary speaker, we have a counterexample to the understanding-assent link for conjunction elimination9.

It is arguable that linguistically competent violations of conjunction elimination are actual, not just possible, in the Conjunction Fallacy, a much-studied psychological phenomenon in which subjects assign a higher probability to a conjunction than to one of its conjuncts10.

By tweaking the example, we can construct a counterexample to the original understanding-assent link UA, for ‘Every vixen is a female fox’. Imagine a speaker who uses the same weak Kleene three-valued tables, but treats only truth as a designated value. Furthermore, this speaker treats a universal generalization of the form ‘Every F is a G’ as true if and only if the conditional ‘x is an F → x is a G’ is true for every value of the variable ‘x’ in the contextually relevant domain. Thus he treats ‘Every vixen is a female fox’ as true if and only if the conditional ‘x is a vixen → x is a female fox’ is true for every such value of V. But there are borderline cases for ‘vixen’, for example when one retraces the maternal line of a fox back to an evolutionary ancestor that was borderline for membership of the current species. For that value of ‘x’, ‘x is a vixen’ is undefined on the envisaged account of vagueness (‘Every vixen is a female fox’ is intended to cover past animals as well as present ones), so, by the weak Kleene table for →, ‘x is a vixen → x is a female fox’ is also undefined. Consequently, ‘Every vixen is a female fox’ receives an undesignated value on the account with only one designated value. Thus our second imagined speaker does not assent to ‘Every vixen is a female fox’. Nevertheless, he understands it with its ordinary English sense, for reasons similar to those already sketched.

Our imaginary speakers are not so different from actual native speakers of English who deny that a man who has lived with a partner for several years without getting married is a bachelor, or assert that someone who underwent a sex-change operation after giving birth is a mother without being a female parent11. Suppose that they are in fact mistaken; ‘bachelor’ is synonymous in some sense that entails sameness of intension with ‘unmarried man’, and ‘mother’ with ‘female parent’. They falsely believe that ‘bachelor’ is not synonymous in that sense with ‘unmarried man’ or that ‘mother’ is not synonymous with ‘female parent’. Nevertheless, they fall well within the range of permissible variation for linguistically competent speakers. They are only giving more weight than others to an inclination that most speakers feel in some degree to classify the cases that way. Without regarding them as having spoken parrot-fashion, we report their beliefs using the words ‘bachelor’ and ‘unmarried’. We classify them as believing that some unmarried men are not bachelors and that some mothers are not female parents because we interpret them as having used the words with their normal English meanings, despite their errors. That is how they intend to be interpreted, not as using the words with idiosyncratic senses12. If we believe that all unmarried men are bachelors and all mothers are female parents, we therefore classify their beliefs in question as untrue, for the belief that some unmarried men are not bachelors is true if and only if some unmarried men are not bachelors, and the belief that some mothers are not female parents is true if and only if some mothers are not female parents. Given that we correctly interpret them as using the words with their normal English meanings, they understand the words in the relevant sense of ‘understand’. Although they are ignorant of some facts about the normal English meanings of the words, such ignorance is quite compatible with linguistic competence, which is why native speakers of English take university courses in the semantics of English. Arguably, their error is not primarily semantic: they have the semantic belief that the word ‘bachelor’ does not apply to all unmarried men because they have the non-semantic belief that some unmarried men are not bachelors and the semantic knowledge that ‘bachelor’ applies only to bachelors; they have the semantic belief that the word ‘mother’ does not apply only to female parents because they have the non-semantic belief that some mothers are not female parents and the semantic knowledge that the word ‘mother’ applies to all mothers.

Such cases also help answer the objection that, in such cases, the awkward subject who consciously denies that P also has unconscious, semantically derived knowledge (or belief) that P. When a competent native speaker denies that every unmarried man is a bachelor, the postulation of unconscious knowledge (or belief) that every unmarried man is a bachelor serves no good explanatory purpose. The speaker tends to apply ‘bachelor’ to something once they have applied ‘unmarried’ and ‘man’ to it, but the tendency is defeasible. Such defeasible connections can be explained without postulation of unconscious belief in a universal generalization. In such cases, there need be no hint of the cognitive dissonance or tension that one might expect from a direct contradiction between conscious and unconscious beliefs. Given that there is no contradicted unconscious knowledge in these simple cases, it is not clear what better reason there is supposed to be in postulating it for more complex cases either.

To try to save understanding-assent links by restricting them to rational agents would be pointless. By ordinary standards, our imagined speakers are rational agents. Although they fall short of some high standards of rationality, so do most humans. Understanding-assent links that do not apply to most humans would be of limited epistemological interest. The picture was that those who appear to reject sentences that are candidates for epistemological analyticity can be excluded from the discussion because they lack the linguistic competence to engage in it; but we cannot exclude humans who reject such sentences on those grounds if the connection between rejecting them and lacking competence holds only for super-humans, not for humans.

One might try to salvage something from understanding-assent links by weakening the putatively necessary condition for understanding from assent to a disposition to assent, with the thought that our imagined speakers understand ‘and’ and other logical words only because they have an unmanifested disposition to make the logically orthodox inferences, masked by a superficial overlay of unorthodox theorizing. Space does not permit detailed exploration of that proposal here. However, empirical evidence from the psychology of reasoning tells against the postulation of underlying classical logical dispositions of the required kind: humans have nothing like a deductive logic module isolated from the effects of unorthodox theorizing. The case for treating lack of a disposition to assent to a sentence such as ‘Every vixen is a vixen’ as lack of linguistic competence depends on the status of the sentence as an elementary truth of deductive logic. But human deductive competence is far more sensitive than linguistic competence to high intelligence and advanced education. Deductive competence is a reflective skill, often painfully acquired and under one’s personal control. It is not insulated from one’s conscious theorizing. Thus deductive proficiency is not a precondition of linguistic competence (Williamson 2006, 2007a).

No given argument or statement is immune from rejection by a linguistically competent speaker. Quine’s epistemological holism in ‘Two Dogmas of Empiricism’ undermines his later claim about the deviant logician’s predicament: ‘when he tries to deny the doctrine he only changes the subject’ (1970: 81).
Some special cases deserve separate discussion.

For example, some metalinguistic sentences look analytic for distinctive reasons. Consider theoretical terms. We can understand the word ‘phlogiston’ without believing phlogiston theory. Might we do so because we still believe that ‘phlogiston’ is generally associated with that theory, just as one can understand a natural kind such as ‘gorilla’ without believing the associated stereotype (‘Gorillas are ferocious’) because one still believes that ‘gorilla’ is generally associated with that stereotype? However, such sociolinguistic beliefs are no more immune than logical beliefs from the challenge of theoretical unorthodoxy without change of meaning. If T is any version of phlogiston theory, someone can understand ‘phlogiston’ and associate it with T without believing that it is generally associated with T, in the belief that ‘phlogiston’ is and was generally associated not with T but with somewhat different versions of phlogiston theory. This is clear if T is a strong version of the theory. Even if T is a weak version, they may believe that the word is generally associated with a stronger version, and deny that it is ipso facto associated with T. On such grounds, they may even disbelieve that they themselves associate the word with T. Let such sociolinguistic beliefs be false; nevertheless, holding them is quite consistent with understanding ‘phlogiston’. It is futile to multiply disjuncts and restrictive clauses in the hope of formulating a sociolinguistic claim so anodyne that anyone who understands ‘phlogiston’ must accept it. The result will just be a complex theoretical claim that ordinary speakers can legitimately doubt, on the grounds that such matters are hard to determine.
A more minimalist line of argument for metalinguistic analyticities appeals to the connection between understanding and knowledge of reference. Suppose that someone understands this sentence:
‘Tree’ applies to all and only trees.

Then they understand its constituent words, in particular ‘tree’ as used at the end of (1). So they know what ‘tree’ means. For common nouns, knowledge of meaning requires knowledge of application conditions. Consequently, they know that ‘tree’ applies to all and only trees. Moreover, since knowledge entails belief, they also believe that ‘tree’ applies to all and only trees. Since they understand (1), they know that it means that ‘tree’ applies to all and only trees. Thus, it seems, they should knowledgeably assent to (1). The argument generalizes to a large class of disquotational claims (disquotationality is crucial, since understanding of the expression used on the right-hand side would not imply knowledge of a truth about a distinct expression mentioned on the left-hand side).

Nevertheless, those who understand (1) may refuse assent to it. Our second imagined speaker is an example, since on his view a universally quantified biconditional with borderline cases for both sides is not definitely true. Indeed, some supervaluationists about vagueness even deny such disquotational principles for vague terms. However erroneous such theories of vagueness, holding them is consistent with ordinary linguistic understanding of (1). If understanding really does involve tacit propositional knowledge of meaning, that knowledge may contradict conscious beliefs.

Let us grant for the sake of argument that understanding (1) entails knowing both that ‘tree’ applies to all and only trees and that (1) means that ‘tree’ applies to all and only trees. How then can one understand (1) without assenting to it? We lack direct conscious access to whatever tacit knowledge linguistic understanding is supposed to consist in, otherwise semantics as a branch of empirical linguistics would be much easier than it actually is. We consciously entertain the proposition that ‘tree’ applies to all and only trees as presented by sentence (1). In tacitly knowing that ‘tree’ applies to all and only trees (if we do), we tacitly entertain that proposition under a quite different mode of presentation. Thus understanding-assent links such as UA* fail for sentences of natural language:
Necessarily, whoever understands the sentence ‘“Tree” applies to all and only trees’ assents to it.
For any tacit assent to the proposition that ‘tree’ applies to all and only trees is not to it under the modes of presentation that UA* requires13.

If linguistic understanding involves tacit propositional knowledge of meaning, it presumably involves tacit assent to the relevant propositions under modes of presentation of some sort. To determine in exactly what sense of ‘tacit’, if any, understanding does involve tacit propositional knowledge of meaning lies beyond the scope of this paper. Whatever the answer, no reflective intellectual discipline operates at the level of tacit assent and dissent, even if such a tacit level is necessary for its operation. For instance, linguists’ tacit knowledge of their native language does not satisfy the goal of linguistics.

One remaining concern is that logical skills must play some role in linguistic competence because logical features play a role in determining well-formedness. An example is the category of negative polarity items. Consider these sentences:
If she ate any of the cake, she was hungry.
If she was hungry, she ate any of the cake.

‘Any’ is a negative polarity item. To a first approximation, the reason why ‘she ate any of the cake’ is acceptable as the antecedent of the conditional but not as the consequent is that the antecedent is in a downward entailing (negative) context while the consequent is instead in an upward entailing (positive) context. A context C is upward entailing just in case whenever A entails B, C(A) entails C(B); C is downward entailing just in case whenever A entails B, C(B) entails C(A). Thus recognition of the logical features of contexts seems to be needed in order to distinguish between well-formed and ill-formed sentences. But things are not so simple. Consider these sentences:
Exactly four people in the room were of any help.
Few people in the room were of any help.

Logically, ‘few’ creates a downward entailing context; ‘exactly four’ does not. However, (4) is acceptable provided that in the context it is taken to imply (5), but not generally otherwise. Thus the phenomenon involves a significant pragmatic element: which contexts are suitable for ‘any’ cannot be determined on purely logico-linguistic grounds. If we disagree with the speaker of (4) about how many people were in the room or what proportion of them could have been expected to help, we may find her use of ‘any’ inappropriate without regarding her as linguistically incompetent. Similarly, if a speaker has deviant views as to which contexts are downward entailing, but uses ‘any’ in just those contexts which she regards as downward entailing, we can find her deviant use of ‘any’ inappropriate without regarding her as linguistically incompetent, precisely because the deviation is explained by logical rather than linguistic unorthodoxy. Thus the role of logical knowledge in such cases does not make it part of purely linguistic competence. All our knowledge is potentially relevant to judging the appropriateness of a given use of ‘any’14.

Understanding words in a natural language has much to do with the ability to use them in ways that facilitate smooth and fruitful interaction with other members of the community. That ability can be realized in indefinitely various forms. Speakers can compensate for their deviance on one point by their orthodoxy on others, their ability to predict the reactions of non-deviant speakers, their willingness in the long run to have their utterances evaluated by public standards. As we have seen, such compensation is often possible when the deviance results from localized interference in the normal practice of using a word by high-level theoretical concerns. Thus there is no litmus test for understanding. Whatever local test is proposed, someone could fail it and still do well enough elsewhere with the word to count as understanding it.

Could an inferentialist reply that such objections trade on a loose everyday sense of ‘understanding’ that must be replaced by something more precise for theoretical purposes? It is far from clear that a stricter sense would do a better job. The relevant features of the ordinary conception of understanding are not mere unreflective sloppiness. Rather, they are an appropriate response to an important constraint on a theory of linguistic meanings: that there is little point in talking about them unless they can be shared across significant differences in belief, between different individuals at the same time or the same individual at different times. They can survive factual learning and factual disagreement. Although inferentialist accounts respect the letter of that constraint, they violate its underlying spirit, by setting inflexible limits to the scope for genuine disagreement. The more holistic ordinary notion of understanding permits localized disagreement at virtually any point.

Cases of logical deviance hint at ways in which the failure of individualist accounts of meaning go deeper than the immediate lessons of the original anti-individualist arguments of Putnam (1975) and Burge (1979). Their cases are often analysed in terms of a distinction between experts with full understanding and lay-people with partial understanding who defer to the experts, in virtue of which one may correctly ascribe to them attitudes to the contents that experts determine15. Such asymmetries are postulated by Putnam’s Hypothesis of the Universality of the Division of Linguistic Labor:

But experts themselves can make deviant applications of words as a result of theoretical errors and still count as fully understanding their words. Although they defer to nobody on the matters at issue, they are more than adequately integrated members of the speech community with respect to those very words. Their assignments of meaning to those words are not parasitic on the assignments that more privileged individuals make. Rather, each individual uses words as words of a public language; their meanings are determined not individually but socially, through the spectrum of linguistic activity across the community as a whole. The social determination of meaning requires nothing like an exact match in use between different individuals; it requires only enough connection in use between them to form a social practice. Full participation in that practice constitutes full understanding. That is why there is no litmus test for understanding.

A complex web of interactions and dependences can hold a linguistic or conceptual practice together even in the absence of a common creed that all participants at all times are required to endorse. This more tolerant form of unity arguably serves our purposes better than would the use of platitudes as entrance examinations for linguistic practices.

Evidently, much of the practical value of a language consists in its capacity to facilitate communication between agents in epistemically asymmetric positions, when the speaker or writer knows about things about which the hearer or reader is ignorant, perhaps mistaken. Although disagreement is naturally easier to negotiate and usually more fruitful against a background of extensive agreement, it does not follow that any particular agreement is needed for disagreement to be expressed in given words. A practical constraint on useful communication should not be confused with a necessary condition for literal understanding. Moreover, the practical constraint is holistic; agreement on any given point can be traded for agreement on others. The same applies to principles of charity as putatively constitutive conditions on correct interpretation: imputed disagreement on any given point can be compensated for by imputed agreement on others16.

It is far easier and more rewarding to discuss the existence of true contradictions with a dialetheist such as Graham Priest than creationism with a Christian fundamentalist or Holocaust denial with a neo-Nazi17. The difficulty of engaging in fruitful debate with fundamentalists or neo-Nazis is not plausibly attributed to some failure of linguistic understanding on their part (or ours); it arises from their wilful disrespect for the evidence. Such difficulty as there is in engaging in fruitful debate with dialetheists provides no significant reason to attribute to them (or us) a failure of linguistic understanding. Competence with the English language no more requires acceptance of some law of non-contradiction or any other logical law than it requires acceptance of the theory of evolution or the historical reality of the Holocaust.

We cannot anticipate all our disagreements in advance. What strike us today as the best candidates for analytic or conceptual truth some innovative thinker may call into question tomorrow for intelligible reasons. Even when we hold fast to our original belief, we can usually find ways of engaging rationally with the doubter. If a language imposes conditions of understanding that exclude such a doubt in advance, as it were in ignorance of its grounds, it needlessly limits its speakers’ capacity to articulate and benefit from critical reflection on their ways of thinking. Such conditions are dysfunctional, and natural languages do not impose them18.

There is, of course, a distinction between understanding a word and not understanding it. One can lack understanding of a word through lack of causal interaction with the social practice of using that word, or through interaction too superficial to permit sufficiently fluent engagement in the practice. But sufficiently fluent engagement in the practice can take many forms, which have no single core of agreement19.

At this point, someone sympathetic to the spirit of epistemological analyticity may suspect that the mistake was to go for the idea that understanding is somehow psychologically sufficient for assent. Instead, the suggestion is, we should go for the idea that understanding is somehow epistemologically sufficient for assent20. Externally, logically deviant speakers are in a position to know (or to assent with justification). They seem to be willfully and perversely turning their backs on knowledge that is available to them. It is there for the taking, but they are psychologically blocked from taking it.

We must be careful about the source of the blockage. Suppose that it is lack of logical insight. Although our imagined speaker understands the word ‘and’, he lacks the logical insight competently to apply conjunction elimination. Other people just like him except for having more logical insight do competently apply conjunction elimination. Anyone who understands ‘and’ and has a modicum of logical insight can competently apply conjunction elimination. That story assigns no special role to linguistic understanding, beyond the usual role that it plays as a precondition for all intelligent discourse: the decisive role is assigned to logical competence, not semantic competence.
For semantic competence to play the decisive role, something like this is needed:
Whoever competently applies conjunction elimination for ‘and’ in the normal way does so simply on the basis of their understanding of ‘and’.

(Treat ‘on the basis of’ more like ‘by an exercise of’ than like ‘by inference from’.) KU may be plausible at first sight. It does not imply that whoever understands ‘and’ applies conjunction elimination for ‘and’ or even has a disposition to do so, competently or otherwise.

What does the definite description ‘their understanding of “and”’ in KU denote? There are thick and thin candidates. The thin candidate is the mere fact that they understand ‘and’. The thick candidate is the body of underlying facts that constitute the thin candidate, the facts that realize this particular subject’s understanding of ‘and’ at this particular time. The thin candidate is exactly similar for any two people who understand ‘and’, since they have the same property of understanding it. The thick candidate may differ between any two people who understand the word, since different underlying facts can constitute their doing so. These characterizations are schematic, but will do for present purposes.

Suppose that the definite description in KU denotes the thick candidate. KU remains plausible on this reading. Then, given the picture of linguistic understanding in previous sections, KU has much less epistemological significance than might have been hoped. The facts that constitute your understanding of a given word include various cognitive capacities that are not in general necessary for understanding that word, but help to make up your particular competence with it. For example, the facts that constitute the understanding of ‘and’ on the part of the imagined speaker who rejects conjunction elimination for ‘and’ include his logical capacities and dispositions. The basis cited in KU includes cognitive capacities that are not in general necessary for understanding the word. Thus the thick candidates are too thick to yield bases for analyticity; they involve knowledge that is not semantic in any relevant sense.

Suppose instead that the definite description in KU denotes the thin candidate. But it is not the basis in any useful sense for competently applying conjunction elimination for ‘and’ in the normal way, although confusion with the thick candidate may suggest otherwise. The thin candidate implies no specific logical capacity at all. It is not as though in such cases a subject’s understanding quietly tells them to make the inference but they override the advice; it is providing no such advice to be overridden. Consequently, understanding in the thin sense provides no basis for assent to anyone. Of course, understanding ‘and’ is a precondition for competently applying conjunction elimination for ‘and’, and in that sense may be part of the basis for so applying it, but that point is quite general; it is neutral between the analytic and the synthetic. Thus the thin candidate is too thin to be a basis for knowledge.
We could try eliminating the talk of bases, for instance in a formulation like this:
Whoever understands ‘and’ and applies conjunction elimination for ‘and’ does so with justification.

But such principles are false, since someone who understands ‘and’ but applies conjunction elimination for ‘and’ because his manifestly unreliable guru told him to does so without justification. The obvious way to avoid such counterexamples and make the connection with semantic competence is to qualify ‘applies conjunction elimination’ by ‘on the basis of that understanding’. But that returns us to the problems of KU.

The problem is general. The idea that, in the cases at issue, understanding is epistemologically sufficient for assent to the inference is the idea that assent on the basis of understanding has the desired positive epistemic status. But once we disambiguate ‘understanding’ between thick and thin candidates, we can see that the thin candidates are too thin to be bases for assent while the thick candidates are not purely semantic or conceptual. The attempt to base the epistemology of obviously valid inference rules such as conjunction elimination on preconditions for linguistic competence with them rests on a confusion between linguistic competence and logical competence. Similarly, dissent from the law of non-contradiction in its various forms is simply a logical failure; dialetheists such as Graham Priest manifest semantic competence with the logical particles of their native languages in their ordinary senses. Epistemological analyticity is an illusion.

works.title: Review of A.W. Moore, Points of View
passages: Review of A.W. Moore, Points of View

The Basic Argument of Points of View starts from the Basic Assumption that ‘‘Representations are representations of what is there anyway’’ (p. 68, following Bernard Williams) and reaches the conclusion that ‘‘Absolute representations are possible’’ (p. 74, capitals and italics Moore’s). What does Moore mean?
Review of A.W. Moore, Points of View

Moore conscientiously defines most of his terms. ‘‘A representation is anything which has content and which, because of its content, is either true or false’’ (p. 283). He does not define ‘‘anyway’’. If the Basic Assumption meant that representations are representations of what would have been there even if the representing had not occurred, it would succumb to obvious counterexamples (‘I am speaking’). Moore intends something else; the Assumption ‘‘involves a cluster of interrelated ideas about the unity, substantiality and autonomy of reality’’ (p. 74). Perhaps it just means whatever it has to mean in order to validate the Basic Argument. As for the Argument’s conclusion: ‘‘A representation is absolute iff it is from no point of view…. Equivalently, a representation is absolute iff it can be integrated by simple addition with any other possible representation’’ (p. 280). To integrate two representations by simple addition is to produce a conjunctive representation whose conjuncts match the originals in content and type, where ‘‘The content of a representation is how things must be if it is true’’ (p. 280) and ‘‘The type of a representation is the role it must play in the psychology of its producer if it expresses a belief of its producer’’ (p. 283). The model for an absolute representation is a non-indexical sentence, but for Moore indexicality is not the only way of being from a point of view. The definition of ‘type’ should clarify this metaphorical extension. Unfortunately, it does not work as intended unless representations are individuated by type in a prior sense of ‘type’; although the notion of linguistic meaning or character provides such a prior sense, it reintroduces the problem of extrapolation from a comparatively clear linguistic phenomenon to something more general and less clear.
Review of A.W. Moore, Points of View

The Basic Argument itself is disappointing. Someone who doubted its conclusion might think that sometimes two representations R and S are true, yet the points of view from which one can see the content of R do not overlap the points of view from which one can see the content of S. A way reality is—being both the way that makes R true and the way that makes S true—makes both R and S true, but this conjunctive way cannot be seen from any point of view. Moore’s response to such suggestions is that the conjunctive way ‘‘comes to nothing if it is not so much as possible to indicate what that way is’’ (p. 69). This is bluff. His opponent, who need not be any kind of verificationist, can reply that reality’s being a certain way comes to exactly the same thing whether or not it is possible to indicate what that way is. The Basic Assumption is too inchoate to help at this point.
Review of A.W. Moore, Points of View

Moore interprets Nietzsche, Goodman and Derrida as denying the Basic Assumption. He considers using transcendental idealism to reconcile their views with his by denying the Assumption only transcendentally. Moore rejects this on the plausible grounds that transcendental idealism is incoherent. But since its deep-sounding language continues to attract him, he finds an ingenious way to keep the words while admitting that they are nonsense. He defines ‘‘A is shown that x’’ as ‘‘A had ineffable [non-representational] knowledge, and when an attempt is made to put what A knows into words, the result is: x’’ (p. 157). Moore argues that what replaces ‘x’ is nonsense in this context, and that formulations of transcendental idealism are such nonsense.
Review of A.W. Moore, Points of View

Ineffable knowledge is knowledge that is not knowledge-that. Is there such knowledge? The cheap traditional way to argue that there is would be to argue that knowledge-how is not knowledge-that; knowing how to ϕ is just being able to ϕ. Moore rejects this way for good reasons, following Paul Snowdon. To lose one’s legs is not to forget how to swim; one might still use one’s knowledge how to swim in teaching others. Conversely, someone who does not know how to break bad news may be only too able to do so (he just does it very badly). Logically and linguistically, ‘know how’ belongs to the same general family as ‘know who/what/which/when/where/why/whether’, as Hintikka has emphasised. They are all ways of describing knowledge-that. To know when to ϕ is, roughly, to know of some time t that t is the time to ϕ, to know how to ϕ is, roughly, to know of some way w that w is the way to ϕ. No verbal description of t or w is needed; one’s grasp of the propositional content may be distinctively practical (‘ϕ now!’; ‘ϕ like this!’). Nevertheless, Moore argues that some practical knowlege is not knowledge-that. He frequently characterises this knowledge as knowledge-how: ‘‘our receiving the world as we do involves our knowing, ineffably, how to do so’’ (p. 210). This is a mistake. The logico-linguistic argument for assimilating knowing-how to knowing-that permits no such exceptions. Knowing how to receive the world (if there is such knowing) is knowing of some way w that w is the way to receive the world, and is therefore not ineffable in Moore’s sense.
Review of A.W. Moore, Points of View

Moore’s prime example of ineffable knowledge is one’s understanding of one’s own idiolect. He claims that it has nothing to answer to; ‘rabbit’ denotes hares in my idiolect if I think it does (p. 184). Work by Burge and others undermines this conception of an idiolect. One is fallible even about one’s own idiolect and one’s own concepts. Since grasping a concept C is knowing how to exercise C, it is knowing of some way w that w is the way to exercise C, which is effable. So is understanding one’s idiolect. Ineffable knowledge is an illusion. What may have misled Moore is that the knowledge in question is knowledge of necessary truths; noting that reality could not have falsified it, he concludes that it answers to nothing.
Review of A.W. Moore, Points of View

Moore finds further examples of ineffable knowledge in Dummettian anti-realism. His discussion depends on the inference from the denial of ‘‘There is at least one proposition whose truth or falsity we cannot determine’’ to ‘‘there cannot be any harm in assuming that every proposition is either true or false’’ (p. 242). Dummett’s anti-realist should reject this inference; intuitionistically, ¬∃P¬(P∨¬P) is consistent with ¬∀P(P∨¬P) and there are arguments for both.
Review of A.W. Moore, Points of View

Moore holds that ‘‘for any representation, there is a finite extension of our powers enabling us to know whether or not it is true’’; following Joseph Melia, he formulates his anti-realism this way and refuses to say that ‘‘for any true representation, there is a finite extension of our powers enabling us to know that it is true’’ (p. 139) in view of Fitch’s argument that if all truths are knowable then all truths are known. But what seems to motivate his anti-realism is a Dummettian argument which concludes ‘‘the proposition must not be true without our being able to tell that it is’’ (p. 242), the form of anti-realism previously rejected.
Review of A.W. Moore, Points of View

The book’s flaws contrast with very many shrewd and subtle points made in passing. If one must listen to the unfresh sirens of transcendental idealism, one should tie oneself to the mast rather more firmly than Moore has done.

works.title: Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth
passages: Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth

William Alston defends alethic realism, which he defines as the conjunction of two theses: (a) the realist conception of truth is the correct account of what it is for a proposition, statement, or belief to be true; (b) truth is important. The realist conception of truth is in turn summarized by a substitutionally quantified biconditional (28):
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth
(p) The proposition that p is true iff p.
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth
Alston is willing to go beyond RCT to a minimalist correspondence account (38):
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth
(p) If the proposition that p is true it is made true by the fact that p.
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth

He gives no account of facts, except to insist that they need not be mere shadows of propositions. He explains the application of ‘true’ to sentences as derivative from its application to the propositions that they express.
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth

Alston usefully distinguishes between the concept and the property of truth. He intends RCT and MCA as accounts of the ordinary concept of truth, not of the property that it picks out. He allows that another concept of truth might pick out the same property by specifying its hidden essence; for example, the concept might embody a rich theory of facts. In this sense, Alston is a minimalist about the concept of truth, but not about the property of truth.
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth

Does reference to the property of truth have explanatory value? In defending the importance of truth, the second conjunct of alethic realism, Alston uses considerations like this: when I act on a belief, I am more likely to achieve my goal if the belief is true. Minimalists about the property of truth object that the reference to truth is redundant, for it would have sufficed to say: when I act on a belief that p, I am more likely to achieve my goal if p. Alston replies that the disappearance of truth is only apparent. He claims that the generalizations in which ‘true’ does not occur are synonymous with generalizations in which it does, so the former employ the concept of truth just as the latter do (238). Thus, (1) must be equated in meaning with (2):
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth
(p) When I act on a belief that p, I am more likely to succeed if p.
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth
(p) When I act on a belief that p, I am more likely to succeed if that p is true.
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth

The quantifier ‘(p)’ in (1) is substitutional, so ‘(p)’ had better be substitutional in (2), too. The phrase ‘that p’ in (2) refers to a proposition; otherwise, ‘is true’ does not have the sense in which Alston is interested. Presumably, (1) and (2) are synonymous only if their corresponding substitution instances are synonymous, and those substitution instances are synonymous only if their corresponding constituents are synonymous. Thus, (1) and (2) are synonymous only if the result of substituting ‘Caesar was murdered’ for ‘p’ in the matrix of (1) is synonymous with the result of making the same substitution in (2), which is so only if the result of substituting ‘Caesar was murdered’ for ‘p’ in ‘p’ is synonymous with the result of making the same substitution in ‘that p is true’, that is, only if ‘Caesar was murdered’ is synonymous with ‘That Caesar was murdered is true’. But elsewhere in the book Alston denies that ‘Caesar was murdered’ has the same content as ‘The proposition that Caesar was murdered’, on the grounds that only the latter is about a proposition (47). By the same token, ‘Caesar was murdered’ is not synonymous with ‘That Caesar was murdered is true’; if they were synonymous, truth would not be a genuine property, which Alston insists that it is. Thus, (1) is not synonymous with (2). Although they are no doubt logically equivalent, that is not enough for Alston’s defense of the importance of truth. That (1) is logically equivalent to something that employs the concept of truth does not entail that (1) itself employs the concept of truth, any more than the fact that (1) is logically equivalent to something that employs the concept of butter entails that (1) itself employs the concept of butter.1 No alternative to (2) would do better for Alston; if any sentence in which truth is explicitly predicated of a proposition is synonymous with (1), (2) is.2 Thus, Alston’s defenses of the two conjuncts of alethic realism seem to conflict with each other.
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth

Truth is important in at least this sense: there is an important difference between cases of true belief and cases of false belief. But it does not follow that we can distinguish between the two kinds of case only by referring to the property of truth. There is an important difference between cases in which the set of one’s friends is the null set and cases in which it is not, but we can distinguish between the two kinds of case without referring to the null set.
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth

Much of the book is a response to Brand Blanshard, Michael Dummett, and Hilary Putnam, who proposed epistemic accounts of truth. Alston has many effective points to make. The main focus of his attack is on epistemic accounts of the ordinary concept of truth. Some verificationists might accept RCT as an account of the ordinary concept, but insist that for some epistemic concept E (for example, justifiability in ideal epistemic conditions) we can know a priori that the ordinary concept and E pick out the same property. Alston argues much more tentatively against such epistemic accounts of the property of truth, suggesting that some highly theoretical propositions may be true without falling under E (203). Surprisingly, he does not consider examples used by Frederic Fitch, Bill Hart, and others. Let p be the proposition expressed by the sentence ‘The number of hairs now on my head is even and no one will ever be justified in believing that the number of hairs now on my head is even’, and q the corresponding proposition when ‘odd’ replaces ‘even’. The number is either even or odd. Since no one will in fact bother to count, no one will ever be justified in having a belief either way. Thus, either p is true or q is. But no one could be justified in believing either proposition, even in ideal epistemic conditions: if someone were, the second conjunct would be false, so the whole proposition would be, contrary to the epistemic account of the property of truth.3
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth
There are some lapses. Alston argues that Dummett’s verification-conditional semantics cannot use defeasible verification conditions:
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth

the statement of a set of confirming conditions, C, for a putatively non-conclusively verifiable sentence, S, is itself conclusively verifiable. But by the terms of verificationist semantics the statement of C is synonymous with S, since C is what specifies S’s meaning. Therefore S is conclusively verifiable after all. Hence there can be no merely defeasibly verifiable meaningful sentences on this semantics. Q.E.D. (127).
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth
This confuses specifying the meaning of S with providing a synonym of S. The verificationist semantics might entail something of this form about S, where ‘c’ states C:
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth
S is confirmed when and only when c.
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth

Since Dummettian verificationists suppose verification conditions to be epistemically unproblematic, they will grant that when c, it is conclusively verifiable that c, as the first quoted sentence says. Since they will also grant that competent speakers of the language implicitly know VS, it is conclusively verifiable that S is confirmed when and only when it is conclusively verifiable that c. Putting these pieces together with VS, one concludes that when S is confirmed, it is conclusively verifiable that S is confirmed. What one cannot conclude is that when S is confirmed, S itself is conclusively verifiable. VS does not make S and ‘c’ synonymous. For example, it does not imply that they have the same disconfirmation conditions.
Review of W.P. Alston, A Realist Conception of Truth

I have concentrated on points of disagreement. Much in the book deserves agreement and applause; it is argued with care, subtlety, and good sense. If the ordinary concept of truth is not a very exciting one, that is not Alston’s fault; it is just part of what he is telling us.

If a substitutionally universal generalization is synonymous with the infinite conjunction of its instances, then (1) employs the concept of truth, because some of its instances do. For the same reason, (1) employs the concept of butter; such considerations do not show that truth is more important than butter.

In Alston’s own example, he claims synonymy between (3) ‘For any p if p is asserted in the book, p’ and (4) ‘Everything asserted in the book is true’. (3) is ill formed, since ‘p’ occurs in both name and sentence position; presumably ‘p is asserted’ should be ‘that p is asserted’ and ‘For any p’ is a substitutional quantifier. Alston does not say whether the quantification in (4) is substitutional, but a difference in type of quantification would be hard to reconcile with the claimed synonymy.

Such propositions are counterexamples to Alston’s claim that ‘The proposition that p would be known by an omniscient being iff p’ is analytically true (53), unless there actually is an omniscient being.

works.title: Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought
passages: Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought

Graham Priest is a dialetheist: he believes that some contradictions are true. It is notoriously hard to pin down a fallacy in the reasoning that yields the semantic and set-theoretic paradoxes; Priest’s explanation is that there is no fallacy. In classical logic, any proposition whatsoever can be deduced from a contradiction, so contradictions induce trivialization. Priest therefore rejects classical logic in favour of paraconsistent logic, in which a contradiction lacks such global consequences. This book, however, makes only passing mention of logical issues, for which Priest refers the reader to his In Contradiction (Dordrecht, Kluwer, 1987). Rather, it sets the paradoxes within a wider context. According to Priest, thought runs into true contradictions when it runs up against its own limits, and the book attempts to trace this pattern through the history of philosophy. Dialetheism must hope to gather from such an exercise support independent of that which it claims to receive from the semantic and set-theoretic paradoxes themselves.
Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought

Priest identifies four kinds of limit to thought: limits of expression (he discusses Plato on the need for something unchanging as a precondition of meaning; Aristotle on prime matter; Cusanus on the ineffability of God); limits of iteration (infinite regresses in Zeno, Aristotle, and Leibniz); limits of cognition (Sextus’ skepticism and Protagoras’ relativism); limits of conception (Anselm’s ontological argument and Berkeley’s inconceivability argument for idealism). Kant and Hegel are credited with having recognized the underlying pattern, although only Hegel regarded the contradictions as unavoidable. Hegel on the contradictory nature of the true infinite leads naturally to the paradoxes of set theory, and the analogous semantic paradoxes, the standard solutions to which Priest attacks. In particular, he accuses them of violating Cantor’s principle that for every potential infinity there is a corresponding actual infinity, a principle which he defends as a precondition for the meaningfulness of thought about the infinite. The final part of the book extends the argument to the limits of language: Frege’s claim that the concept horse is not a concept; the saying of what cannot be said in Wittgenstein’s Tractatus; Quine and Davidson’s application of the supposed indeterminacy of reference to the theorist’s own language; Kripke’s Wittgenstein and skepticism about meaning; Derrida’s use of ‘différance’ to express the inexpressible precondition of all expressing.
Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought

Unfortunately for dialetheism, Priest’s admirably eclectic survey does little to extend its evidential base. He is too good a logician to ignore the flaws in the paradoxical arguments he considers up to and including Kant’s antinomies. The nearest miss is Berkeley’s inconceivability argument. In response to the objection that ‘I can conceive that something is such that no one can conceive it’ does not entail ‘something is such that I can conceive that no one can conceive it’, Priest uses Hilbert’s ε-operator in an attempt to bridge the gap, via the intermediate step ‘I can conceive that no one can conceive ϵx (no one can conceive x)’. Edo Pivčević anticipated this line of thought in The Concept of Reality (London, Duckworth, 1986). Unlike Pivčević, Priest uses it for dialetheist rather than idealist ends because he thinks that we can conceive truly that something is such that no one can conceive it. The result of his modifications, although intriguing, is but a variation on König’s Paradox about the least undefinable ordinal (which has just been defined); as such, it lends no support to dialetheism independent of the semantic and set-theoretic paradoxes. As for the contradictions at the limits of language, they are too loosely presented to carry conviction. For example, the arguments about rule-following and the indeterminacy of reference appear to rest on reductionist assumptions about meaning for which Priest offers no support. The case for dialetheism has not been extended beyond the usual paradoxes.
Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought

Priest emphasizes the Principle of Uniform Solution: same kind of paradox, same kind of solution. Only dialetheism satisfies it, he claims. The Principle itself is hardly contentious: as he acknowledges, the difficulty is in knowing when two paradoxes are of the same kind. Priest classifies the central paradoxes in the book as of one kind by a formal criterion. They all instantiate his Inclosure Schema, a generalization of one stated by Russell in ‘On Some Difficulties in the Theory of Transfinite Numbers and Order Types’. An instance of Inclosure consists of properties ϕ and ψ and a function δ such that:
Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought
Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought
if x⊆Ω and ψ(x) then(a) δ(x)∉x(b) δ(x)∈Ω.
Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought

Substitution of ‘Ω’ for ‘x’ in (2) yields a contradiction with (1). For example, in König’s Paradox ϕ is the property of being a definable ordinal, ψ the property of being definable, and δ(x) the least ordinal not in x (given a reading of ‘definable’ on which not all ordinals are definable). Priest admits that any paradox whatsoever can be dressed up as an instance of Inclosure, but argues that only some paradoxes can be explained as instances of it; they are supposed to form the kind.
Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought
Priest may have drawn the boundaries of the kind too narrowly. Consider the Liar:
Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought
Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought

Following Curry, one can form a variant paradox by using a conditional → and an absurdity ⊥ that entails everything (e.g. ‘Everything is true’; Priest allows ⊥, merely denying that every contradiction behaves like it):
Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought
Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought

One half of a disquotational principle about truth gives True⁡(CL)→(True⁡(CL)→⊥); a principle of Absorption gives True⁡(CL)→⊥; the other half of the disquotational principle gives (True⁡(CL)→⊥)→True⁡(CL); two steps of detachment give True⁡(CL) and then ⊥; ⊥ gives everything. Is this an instance of Inclosure? According to Priest, it depends on what → is. If → is a material conditional, then True⁡(CL)→⊥ is equivalent to ¬True⁡(CL), the paradox is Liar-like and does instantiate Inclosure. On other readings of →, however, True⁡(CL)→⊥ is not equivalent to ¬True⁡(CL). For Priest, the paradox then belongs
Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought
to a quite different family. Such paradoxes do not involve negation and, a fortiori, contradiction. They therefore have nothing to do with contradictions at the limits of thought (p. 186).
Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought

This is dubious. Suppose, for example, that → is strict implication. Then CL is equivalent to something like ‘This statement is necessarily false’. A treatment of ‘This statement is false’ that does not generalize to ‘This statement is necessarily false’, and is forced to consign the latter to some quite different kind, appears to violate the Principle of Uniform Solution. Contradictions are a symptom of the underlying condition; they are not the condition itself.
Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought

Priest’s unconvincing discussion of Curry paradoxes hints at deeper problems for dialetheism. Its strength is supposed to be its ability to preserve intuitively compelling inferences in semantics and set theory, by preventing them from trivializing. Curry paradoxes show that this strategy does not generalize, because they trivialize even on dialetheist terms. Dialetheism must therefore reject those intuitively compelling arguments. For example, it rejects detachment for material conditionals (Priest sometimes uses detachment without comment; he must have some other reading of → in mind). These moves look as ad hoc, as lacking in independent motivation, as many of the proposed solutions to which Priest objects. The exposition largely obscures this point (there are occasional warning signs). Although the suppression of logical issues is supposed to make the book accessible to logically innocent readers, it prevents them from assessing the costs of dialetheism.
Review of G. Priest, Beyond the Limits of Thought

Nevertheless, the book has many virtues. It is clever, resourceful, undogmatic, unpretentious, often sensible and usually clear over a wide range of issues. If one abjures contradictions, it is certainly harder to think about the limits of thought; but that extra difficulty may in the end produce greater depth.

works.title: Review of R.B. Marcus, Modalities. Philosophical Essays
passages: Review of R.B. Marcus, Modalities. Philosophical Essays

The first systematic modern studies of quantified modal logic (QML) appeared in 1946: Carnap’s ‘Modalities and Quantification’ and ‘A Functional Calculus of First Order Based on Strict Implication’ by Ruth Barcan (as she then was). The following year, she published the first proof of the necessity of identity. QML was not universally welcomed. Its birth followed Quine’s early attempts to deny its right to life; he argued that quantification into modal contexts cannot be coherently interpreted because they are referentially opaque. Church and Smullyan soon pointed out the fallacy in Quine’s argument; its use of definite descriptions violated the scope distinctions emphasised in Russell’s theory of descriptions. Nevertheless, suspicion continued to hang over modal logic, especially QML (‘modal’ was fashionably pronounced to rhyme with ‘puddle’). The focus of Quine’s attack gradually shifted to the charge that QML commits one to obscurantist essentialism. Marcus replied that the commitment is to the intelligibility of non-trivial essentialist claims, not their truth, that they are intuitively intelligible, and that physical science sometimes gives us evidence for their truth (for causal modalities and properties essential to all members of a kind). Her reply, though forceful, challenged a deep-rooted conception of all necessity as verbal necessity. Only after Kripke and Putnam’s comprehensive attack on that conception and the former’s results in formal semantics did QML gain general acceptance.
Review of R.B. Marcus, Modalities. Philosophical Essays

Although the present collection omits Marcus’s early papers, it contains much philosophical reflection on their ideas. Deontic and doxastic modalities are also discussed; Marcus is sceptical about alleged inconsistencies in our moral principles or beliefs. There are fifteen papers, originally published between 1961 and 1990, two technical notes and the text of a 1962 debate between Marcus, Quine, Kripke, Føllesdal and McCarthy.
Review of R.B. Marcus, Modalities. Philosophical Essays

Marcus often anticipates later work. As early as 1962, she treated proper names as mere tags. This is not just to treat them as rigid designators, for such definite descriptions as ‘The square of 5’ and ‘The actual pope’ are rigid designators but not tags. Rather, it anticipates the more specific notion of direct reference.
Review of R.B. Marcus, Modalities. Philosophical Essays

Only one of the book’s many rewarding strands will be followed here. A theorem of its author’s systems is the Barcan formula (BF) ◇∃xϕ(x)⊃∃x◇ϕ(x) (for example, ‘If there could have been something divine, then there is something that could have been divine’). The converse (CBF) is also a theorem. On Kripke’s semantics, where each possible world has its own domain of quantification, BF is invalid unless one stipulates that, whenever a world x is accessible from a world w, the domain of w includes the domain of x. CBF is invalid unless one stipulates the converse inclusion. Together, the two formulas require a constant domain (as each does separately if accessibility is symmetric).
Review of R.B. Marcus, Modalities. Philosophical Essays

Marcus rejects variation between domains on the grounds that it amounts to the admission of (mere) possibilia; she argues that we cannot refer to possibilia. Kripke’s semantics with varying domains is indeed unsatisfying, for it treats quantifiers in the object-language but not in the meta-language as worldbound. If the domain of some world contains an element i not in the domain of the actual world, then the truth of ∀xϕ(x) requires i to satisfy ϕ(x) if the quantifier belongs to the meta-language but not if it belongs to the object-language. Why this discriminatory policy? After all, the meta-language can itself be treated as an object-language. However, merely to stipulate a constant domain is equally unsatisfying, for it deprives the formalism of its intuitive interpretation. We incline to believe that, although Queen Victoria and Cavour could have had a child, nothing that actually exists could have been their child. Given these beliefs, it is BF that commits us to possibilia, for instance, non-existent possible children. At least the following responses merit consideration:
Review of R.B. Marcus, Modalities. Philosophical Essays

(i) One rejects possibilia, BF and CBF, blaming the problem on the attempt to give the semantics of a modal object-language in a non-modal meta-language. In a modal meta-language (as used by Peacocke and others), one can describe putative counter-examples to BF without invoking possibilia. A non-modal meta-language is mathematically convenient but philosophically misleading.
Review of R.B. Marcus, Modalities. Philosophical Essays

(ii) One accepts possibilia, BF and CBF, holding that we can refer to possibilia. Marcus’s argument to the contrary assumes that we can refer only to what we have empirically encountered (p. 207). One might prefer Kripke’s suggestion that we can use a definite description to fix the reference of a proper name, and invoke descriptions such as ‘what would have resulted from the union of sperm s and egg e’. The name may still be directly referential, for the description does not give its meaning.
Review of R.B. Marcus, Modalities. Philosophical Essays
(iii) One accepts possibilia, BF and CBF, holding that, although we cannot refer to possibilia individually, we can quantify over them.
Review of R.B. Marcus, Modalities. Philosophical Essays

Both (ii) and (iii) involve a non-substitutional view of quantification: (iii) obviously, (ii) because a substitutional treatment of the quantification implicit in the description requires independent reference to the designated item. In several of the papers Marcus defends a substitutional account of quantification (this may have been an obstacle to acceptance of her work). Most recently, however, she argues that non-substitutional quantification is also required (p. 213), in which case (ii) and (iii) cannot be ruled out on substitutional grounds. We seem to quantify over space-time points without the physical possibility of encountering individual points empirically (at best we encounter very small regions); why should possibilia be different?
Review of R.B. Marcus, Modalities. Philosophical Essays

Of course, one can quantify substitutionally if one so wishes. As Copeland has pointed out, BF and CBF will then be valid only if the class of substituted terms is constant from world to world. Moreover, quantification just over what we happen to have named is of little interest. Marcus treats the substitutional account as easily extended to quantification over everything that we could name (pp. 119–124), but does not explain how to solve the implicit problems. For example, we should like to evaluate ‘Some star is unnamed’ as true. An actually unnamed star could have been named ‘S’, but to make ‘S is unnamed’ true the semantics must evaluate it under its merely possible meaning at the actual world. How is this to be done without possibilia in a way satisfactory for the nominalist to whom Marcus is recommending substitutional quantification? Again, if there are nondenumerably many objects, we may be able to name any of them, but cannot name all of them. Marcus replies that a first-order theory (interpreted non-substitutionally) with a nondenumerable model has a denumerable model (p. 124). She does not argue (for example, in Putnam’s style) that there is no sense in which the former might be the intended model and the latter unintended. Moreover, the implicitly invoked Löwenheim–Skolem theorem does not apply to second-order theories.
Review of R.B. Marcus, Modalities. Philosophical Essays

Although the book makes few concessions to the non-technical reader, it is of far more than technical significance. Marcus has participated in a critical turn of twentieth-century philosophy: not the linguistic turn, but that later turn by which a rigorous study of natural and artificial language uncovered a space of non-linguistic questions, answerable by logically disciplined metaphysics. To understand this turn one must understand Marcus’s achievement, and its temporary neglect.

works.title: Review of C.J.G. Wright, Truth and Objectivity
passages: Faced with a discourse, many philosophers begin with the question: does it involve the making of true or false statements? In trying to understand moral discourse, for example, they ask whether a sentence like ‘Rape is wrong’ is used to say, truly or falsely, that something is the case, or merely to express an emotional attitude, without propositional content, to rape. Moral realism, in one sense of the term, is the claim that moral discourse does involve the making of true or false statements. Parallel forms of realism can be identified with respect to other discourses. This use of the term ‘realism’ presents the applicability of the notions of truth and falsity as an issue central to the status of the discourses in question. In his new book, Crispin Wright argues that the issue does not deserve that central place, which he reassigns to a bundle of other issues. For Wright, the existence of moral truths should not be particularly contentious; what we ought to be arguing about is their objectivity. Not that he supposes the word ‘objectivity’ to stand for anything clear: the book works hard to construct various precise notions of objectivity with which to capture what should be at stake in the debates labelled ‘realism v. anti-realism’.

Wright’s earlier work proceeded from a conception of such debates due to Michael Dummett. That conception assigns the central place to the relation between truth and knowledge. Dummett’s realist asserts, while his anti-realist denies, that it is possible for a statement made within a discourse to be true yet incapable of being known to be true by participants in the discourse. A realist theory of meaning for the discourse explains statements by giving necessary and sufficient conditions for them to be true, without any reference to the cognitive capacities of participants as such. These conditions (it assumes) either obtain or fail to obtain, even if participants cannot recognize which. According to the realist about mathematical discourse, for example, a conjecture is bivalent (either true or false), even if we can neither prove nor refute it. In the latter case, either it is an unknowable truth or its negation is. By contrast, an anti-realist theory of meaning explains statements by giving necessary and sufficient conditions for us to be warranted in asserting them. These conditions (it assumes) are either recognizable by participants as obtaining or recognizable by them as failing to obtain. According to the anti-realist about mathematical discourse, our practice entitles us to regard a conjecture as bivalent only if we can in principle either prove or refute it.

Dummett’s conception does not always capture what is at stake in debates labelled ‘realism v. anti-realism’. For example, a moral realist in Dummett’s sense would be someone who thought that there could be unknowable moral truths. But that is not the point at issue in the dispute about moral discourse. Those who hold that ‘Rape is wrong’ expresses a moral truth are also likely to hold that it expresses moral knowledge. Although a willingness to assert that there are unknowable moral truths may be sufficient to qualify one as a moral realist in the original intuitive sense, it hardly seems necessary. A broader conception than Dummett’s is therefore required of the geography of possible realisms and anti-realisms. The book is intended as a contribution to the required broadening.

Wright surveys a labyrinth of positions, most of them occupied by at least one philosopher. The goal of the book is not primarily to adjudicate between them, but rather to clarify the issues that such an adjudication would need to address. Only a selection of these issues can be discussed here. §II argues that the notion of truth is not quite as minimal as Wright suggests. §III considers his notion of superassertibility. To hold that superassertibility plays the role of truth with respect to a discourse is to be one kind of anti-realist with respect to that discourse. A difficulty will be raised for this kind of anti-realism. §IV considers Wright’s notion of Cognitive Command. To hold that a discourse fails to exert Cognitive Command is to be a different kind of anti-realist with respect to that discourse (although someone might be an anti-realist of both kinds). It will be argued that Cognitive Command is not defined clearly enough to resist the charge that it is satisfied trivially. §V questions the notion of a discourse in terms of which Wright frames his discussion.

Wright conceives the notion of truth as a superficial one. Its applicability to a discourse requires, on his view, only that the latter possess certain manifest features: its sentences should have both the syntactic capacities of declaratives and accepted standards for their proper use. In moral discourse, for example, superficial linguistic appearances favour moral truth. ‘Rape is wrong’ is a well-formed declarative sentence, grammatically isomorphic to ‘Philately is laborious’. It has a negation, and occurs as the antecedent and as the consequent of conditionals.1 One can therefore state a truth-condition for it homophonically: ‘Rape is wrong’ is true if and only if rape is wrong. Moreover, there are public standards for the use of such sentences, according to which moral utterances may be warranted or unwarranted. Wright suggests that we should not argue with these appearances. If a discourse appears to permit the making of true or false statements, then it really does so: not because the appearances are an infallible sign of something deeper, but because they constitute the capacity of the discourse for truth or falsity. Indeed, since the language of the discourse contains negation and the negation of a falsehood is a truth, the discourse includes truths if it includes falsehoods, so the appearances constitute the capacity of the discourse for truth. Truth is not a deep notion. If we want to ask a deep question about moral discourse, then we should ask whether it is objective.

Wright’s argument may prompt some unease. Take a miniature case: ‘Eldorado’ appeared to name a city, but did not really name anything at all. On one respectable view, no statement is then made by use of a sentence like ‘Eldorado is crowded’; it says nothing that is even a candidate for truth or falsity. It has, in Wright’s phrase, no assertoric content. Nevertheless, it appears capable of truth and falsity. It is a well-formed declarative sentence, grammatically isomorphic to sentences that are used to make true or false statements. It has a negation, and occurs as the antecedent or consequent of conditionals. One can therefore appear to state its truth-condition homophonically, by saying ‘“Eldorado is crowded” is true if and only if Eldorado is crowded’. Moreover, there appear to be public standards for the use of such sentences, according to which ‘Eldorado’-utterances are warranted or unwarranted. Wright gives us no reason to argue with these appearances.2 Yet one does not really state a truth-condition by saying ‘“Eldorado is crowded” is true if and only if Eldorado is crowded’, for what follows ‘if and only if’ has no assertoric content. Why should moral discourse not be in the same plight?

Wright does allow that, in special circumstances, we might be mistaken in supposing a discourse to have assertoric content (pp. 140–1). However, this is not to concede that the linguistic appearances are insufficient for assertoric content; the cases envisaged are ones in which we are merely over-hasty in assessing the linguistic appearances. Now it could be denied that there really is a distinction between warranted and unwarranted ‘Eldorado’-utterances. But if that denial is right, then the linguistic appearances are insufficient for a genuine standard of warrant, and a fortiori insufficient for assertoric content.

The sentence ‘Eldorado is crowded’ aspires to assertoric content. That aspiration may be constituted more generally by the linguistic appearances to which Wright appeals; it does not follow that they constitute the achievement of assertoric content. Suppose that moral discourse aspires to assertoric content without achieving it, perhaps because moral terms fail to refer, there being no properties for them to refer to of the required sort. Then moral discourse rests on an error. Wright briefly discusses such a view, as held by John Mackie (pp. 9–10, 86–7). The situation once recognized, Wright plausibly suggests, one could engage in moral discourse only in bad faith. Although Mackie’s view may be implausible, it is not obviously incoherent. If moral discourse does achieve assertoric content, its doing so is not conceptually guaranteed by the linguistic appearances.

It might be claimed that the failed aspiration to assertoric content is essentially a local matter. It can vitiate discourse involving a particular would-be name, but not something on the scale of moral discourse. However, Wright does not make this claim, and there does not seem to be any good argument for it. We cannot rely on some general guarantee that we shall never have reason to give up an extensive discourse as vitiated by reference failure. Nevertheless, Wright may be correct to this extent: if a discourse displays the linguistic appearances to which he points, then we can engage in it in good faith only if we are prepared to regard it as achieving assertoric content, and therefore as permitting us to make true statements.

If a discourse aspires to truth in virtue of displaying the appropriate linguistic appearances, how substantial a notion of truth is at issue? On a deflationist view, it is very insubstantial. According to one form of deflationism, ‘true’ is simply a device for endorsing assertions. That cannot be quite right as it stands, for it neglects unasserted occurrences of ‘true’, as in the antecedent of a conditional. However, not all forms of deflationism make that mistake. The more general view is that the content of ‘true’ is exhausted by disquotational equivalences such as: ‘Grass is green’ is true if and only if grass is green.

Wright interprets the deflationist as denying that ‘true’ introduces a discourse-governing norm over and above the norm of warranted assertibility. He argues, against this, that the linguistic appearances manifest a norm of truth distinct from the norm of warranted assertibility (pp. 19–21).3 For if the norm of truth coincided with the norm of warranted assertibility, then to criticize the assertion ‘P’ as not warranted would be tantamount to criticizing it as not true, which would in turn be tantamount to asserting the negation of ‘P’, given the very disquotational equivalences on which the deflationist relies.4 Yet, by accepted standards of warrant, the former criticism is often apt when the latter is not. An assertion made on the basis of a lucky guess may be true but unwarranted. In almost any discourse there will be situations in which there is neither warrant to assert ‘P’ nor warrant to assert ‘It is not the case that P’; the speaker may be in the dark. If truth were equivalent to warranted assertibility, these would be situations in which neither ‘P’ nor ‘It is not the case that P’ was true. By the disquotational equivalences, these are situations in which it is not the case that P and it is not the case that it is not the case that P. But that is a contradiction; there are no such situations. Thus truth is not equivalent to warranted assertibility.

Wright is correct in arguing that, if there is a norm of truth, it is distinct from the norm of warranted assertibility. Will the deflationist concede that there is a norm of truth? Assertion of ‘Grass is green’ is governed by a norm that is satisfied if and only if grass is green, and assertion of ‘Snow is white’ is governed by a norm that is satisfied if and only if snow is white; why suppose these to be the same norm? Wright considers the question, and answers that the norm is the same because all the disquotational equivalences can be gathered into a single schema, giving a uniform account of ‘true’. An utterance u is true if and only if, for some P, u says that P and P (p. 31).5 This will not satisfy all deflationists. In effect, the truth of u is equated with an infinite disjunction: either u says that grass is green, and grass is green, or u says that snow is white, and snow is white, or . . . Some deflationists may deny that such a disjunction of norms is itself a further norm. After all, it would be a mistake to argue that all games have the same set of rules, given by the infinite disjunction: either one is playing cricket and [the rules of cricket], or one is playing chess and [the rules of chess], or . . . Each game is governed by its own rules; there is no need for an extra universal rule that one should obey the rules of the game one is playing (if such a meta-rule were needed to make one obey the specific rules, a meta-meta-rule would be needed to make one obey the meta-rule, and so ad infinitum). According to this deflationist, the notion of obedience to the rules simply collects together the norms specific to particular games, and the notion of truth simply collects together the norms specific to particular utterances.

The denial that any one norm is satisfied by all true utterances may be interpreted as a corollary of another denial, issued by many deflationists, that any one property is common to all true utterances (pp. 14–15). Their denial can seem utterly baffling, for the ascription of truth to all those utterances seems precisely to be the ascription of a common property. However, things are not so straightforward. There is a distinction between predicates and properties, and a sense in which not every predicate stands for a property. For example, one may predicate ‘is white or green’ of both snow and grass, but in doing so one does not ascribe a common property to them, in a rich sense of the word ‘property’. Snow and grass do not resemble each other in both being white or green. In this sense, to predicate ‘is true’ of various utterances is not automatically to ascribe a common property to them. If the predicate ‘is true’ does not stand for a property, that would give point to the denial that it stands for a separate norm. Of course, one would like some elucidation of this rich notion of a property. Must a predicate figure in a scientific theory in order to stand for a property? If so, what entitles science to this privileged status? The challenge to these deflationists is to say what it is that truth is not.

A further difficulty for the idea that ‘true’ expresses different norms for different sentences arises from the possibility of combining different sentences into more complex ones, whose truth-conditions are determined by the truth-conditions of their constituents. ‘Snow is white or grass is green’ is true if and only if ‘Snow is white’ is true or ‘Grass is green’ is true. This threatens the analogy between sentences and games. There is no game of which both chess and cricket are constituents. If we did have a systematic way of combining any two games into a third game, it might require us to think of winning in a more unitary way. This point will be extended in §V.

Wright’s argument has at least the merit of emphasizing that explanations of ‘true’ as merely a device for endorsing assertions make no sense of our use of ‘not true’. One may add that the problem is not solved by the amended explanation that ‘true’ is merely a device for endorsing or denying assertions. The amendment still makes no sense of occurrences of ‘true’ in forms such as ‘If u is true then Q’; the antecedent is neither asserted nor denied in the assertion of the conditional. ‘Speech act’ analyses of ‘true’ are best forgotten. What remains is disquotation.

The slogan ‘Truth is disquotational’ can mean many things. Suppose that we are interested in the truth or falsity of an utterance u.
