The disquotationality of truth amounts to at least the following pair of schemas, which formalize Aristotle’s dictum ‘To say of what is that it is not, or of what is not that it is, is false, while to say of what is that it is, or of what is not that it is not, is true’ (Metaphysics Γ 7.27):
If u says that P, then u is true if and only if P.
If u says that P, then u is false if and only if not P.

Strictly, ‘u says’ here abbreviates ‘the utterer of u says by uttering u’, and ‘not P’, ‘it is not the case that P’. ‘P’ is a schematic letter for which declarative sentences may be substituted. Of course, instances of (T) and (F) will say something (have assertoric content) in a given context only if the declarative sentence substituted for ‘P’ says something in that context; thus (T) and (F) rely on a pre-given standard of saying. Not even the most extreme realist need find anything to quarrel with in (T) and (F). They may be regarded as simply the most fundamental principles governing the concepts of truth and falsity.

The slogan ‘Truth is disquotational’ may also be read as claiming that there is nothing more to the notions of truth and falsity than (T) and (F). What does this claim amount to? It may simply be the claim that (T) and (F) uniquely characterize the notions of truth and falsity. This may be made precise, as follows. Suppose that ‘true1’ and ‘true2’ both express notions of truth. Each therefore obeys (T) in place of ‘true’. But then one can argue that ‘true1’ and ‘true2’ are equivalent. For suppose that an utterance u says that P. By (T) for ‘true1’, u is true1 if and only if P. By (T) for ‘true2’, u is true2 if and only if P. Since ‘if and only if’ is symmetric and transitive, u is true1 if and only if u is true2. The only remaining case is that in which for no possible value of ‘P’ does u say that P; but then u says nothing, and therefore satisfies no genuine notion of truth; once again, albeit vacuously, u is true1 if and only if u is true2. Thus ‘true1’ and ‘true2’ are equivalent. In exactly parallel fashion, one can argue by appeal to (F) that if ‘false1’ and ‘false2’ both express notions of falsity, then they are equivalent. In this sense, the notions of truth and falsity are uniquely characterized by (T) and (F).6 Again, there is nothing here with which the most extreme realist need quarrel.

There is a different way of understanding the claim that there is nothing more to the notions of truth and falsity than (T) and (F), on which it is inconsistent with some forms of realism. For it may be claimed that our grasp of the notions of truth and falsity extends only as far as our grasp of the relevant instances of (T) and (F).7 This claim affronts the realist thought that we can coherently suppose there to be creatures with conceptual capacities vastly more powerful than our own, some of whose utterances express truths untranslatable into any language that humans can learn.8 If u is such an utterance, u does not say that P for any value of ‘P’ intelligible to us. The realist will insist that we can coherently apply our notions of truth and falsity to u, because we grasp (T) and (F) as open-ended schemas; it is sufficient that they have instances whose antecedent is satisfied by u, and not necessary that we grasp those instances. This is just what is denied by the claim that our grasp of the notions of truth and falsity extends only as far as our grasp of the relevant instances of (T) and (F). On the latter view, no true or false utterance involves concepts unavailable in principle to us. One may suspect this claim of depending on a neglect of the open-ended nature of schemas. After all, when we appreciate the validity of a logical law such as modus ponens, it is natural to suppose that we do not simply appreciate that all its instances in the language we happen to speak are valid. We appreciate the validity of the form, and therefore of an indefinite variety of its instances in extensions of our language, irrespective of whether those extensions are humanly learnable. Be that as it may, the contested claim provides a way of understanding the disquotationality of truth with anti-realist consequences. However, it is not a way discussed by Wright.

What Wright emphasizes is the philosophical neutrality of principles such as (T) and (F). Taken by themselves, they neither entail that truth and falsity are mind-dependent nor entail that they are not (in any sense of ‘mind-dependent’). They constitute common knowledge for realists and anti-realists. Nevertheless, Wright takes the philosophical neutrality of the notion of truth to have a bias: truth should be assumed anti-realist until proved realist. More precisely, minimalism about a discourse is the anti-realist claim that its truth predicate has no intuitively realist features beyond those required for it to qualify as a truth predicate at all. ‘Because of its unassuming character, this minimalism’, Wright suggests, ‘should always be viewed as the “default” stance, from which we have to be shown that we ought to move’ (p. 174). Unfortunately, Wright does not make it clear why it is more ‘unassuming’ to assume that the truth predicate has no intuitively realist extra features than to assume that it has no intuitively anti-realist extra features (nor why we need make either assumption prior to investigation).9 Moreover, minimalism is supposed to be inappropriate to at least some discourses (e.g. astronomy), which have at least some intuitively realist extra features. The idea that minimalism remains the default option therefore rests on the problematic idea that different discourses are governed by nonequivalent truth predicates (see §V).

The concepts of truth and falsity may be very simple ones. To acquire them, one may need to learn little more than (T) or (F). That point gives no support to any kind of anti-realism. Realists of various kinds require truth and falsity to be mind-independent in various ways. They do not require mind-independence to be written into the concepts, to be read off by their possessors. Realist views merely require mind-dependence not to be written into the concepts. There is, quite generally, no presumption that we can think of something mind-independent only by thinking of it as mind-independent. Dogs who want water (if there are such dogs) think of a mind-independent natural substance, but are presumably incapable of thinking of it either as mind-independent or as mind-dependent. To say that truth is mind-independent is not to say that everyone who thinks of truth thinks of it as mind-independent.

The fundamental principle governing the notion of truth, (T), does not by itself make truth independent of the standards of warranted assertion operative in a discourse. No doubt truth cannot actually be warranted assertibility, for the reason rehearsed in §II, but, on the face of it, (T) permits truth to be a construction out of warranted assertibility. Wright introduces the notion of superassertibility as just such a construction. It is intended to be the nearest thing to warranted assertibility with a reasonable chance of satisfying (T). An item is superassertible if and only if:

it is, or can be, warranted and some warrant for it would survive arbitrarily close scrutiny of its pedigree and arbitrarily extensive increments to or other forms of improvement of our information (p. 48).10

Wright’s argument for distinguishing between truth and warranted assertibility does not automatically extend to an argument for distinguishing between truth and superassertibility. It is more obvious that we are actually in the dark on some matters than that we cannot escape from it however hard we try. An anti-realist interpretation of a discourse might therefore equate truth in it with superassertibility. The anti-realist thereby makes the large assumption that ‘superassertibility’ can be substituted for ‘true’ in (T), giving for all utterances u in the discourse:
If u says that P, then u is superassertible if and only if P.

As Wright admits, his definition of superassertibility is vague in a number of important respects. For example, over what possibilities does the word ‘can’ range in the phrase ‘is, or can be warranted’? They must not include possibilities in which ‘the facts are different’ (as to whether P), otherwise (S) will certainly fail, but these possibilities must be excluded without use of a truth predicate for the discourse, since that is what the anti-realist is trying to construct. However, such difficulties will not be pressed here. The notion of superassertibility is clear enough for a different problem to be raised, concerning the idea that truth might be equivalent to superassertibility in a discourse whose vocabulary is not tightly restricted.

Suppose that truth coincides with superassertibility in a discourse D. Let ‘Q’ go proxy for a declarative sentence in D that can be used to say something in this context. If D has enough vocabulary, the following conjunction should also be expressible in D:11
Q and no-one ever has a warrant to assert that Q.

Let u be an utterance expressive of (*) in D. Thus u says that: Q and no-one ever has a warrant to assert that Q. By substituting (*) for ‘P’ in (S) and using reasoning of a kind employed by Wright, we can deduce:
If u is not superassertible, then not: Q and no-one ever has a warrant to assert that Q.

Now u is superassertible only if some state of information provides a warrant to assert that: Q and no-one ever has a warrant to assert that Q. But a warrant to assert that conjunction is impossible, for it would involve a warrant to assert the first conjunct, that Q, and the existence of such a warrant is contradicted by the second conjunct, that no-one ever has a warrant to assert that Q. Thus u is not superassertible. Given (1), this follows:
Not: Q and no-one ever has a warrant to assert that Q.
If we use classical logic, from (2) we can deduce:
If Q then someone at some time has a warrant to assert that Q.

Now (2) and (3) speak not of the existence or availability in principle of a warrant, but of the actual possession of one by a particular person at a particular time. Wright’s argument for distinguishing between truth and warranted assertibility requires that conditionals of the form ‘If Q then I now have a warrant to assert that Q’ can fail in the discourse. (3) is of course a weaker conditional, but it looks open to the same sort of objection. If, given that Q, one has a warrant to assert that Q only if one gets into the right position, what guarantee is there that anyone will ever actually happen to get into the right position? The claim that Q only if someone at some time happens to get into the right position looks like an extreme form of subjective idealism. (2) and (3) can fail. Since they are the outcome of the assumed coincidence of truth and superassertibility in D, that coincidence can fail. Truth and superassertibility are not equivalent in D.

The argument leaves it open that superassertibility might be equivalent to truth in a discourse whose vocabulary is too limited to permit one to talk about warrants for assertion. If it is a moral question whether Q, for example, it does not immediately follow that it is a moral question whether anyone will ever have a warrant to assert that Q. Now there are general grounds for doubting the equivalence of truth and superassertibility even with respect to limited discourses.12 Suppose, however, that the two are equivalent within a discourse D. The significance of this point will depend on whether truth in D is simply the restriction of truth in general to D. If it is, then the point reveals something about the nature of D, not about the nature of truth; D is simply too limited to exemplify the general divergence between truth and superassertibility. If the point is to reveal more than that, truth in D must somehow be independent of truth in other discourses. §V will question the possibility of such independence.

If I think that rhubarb is disgusting and you think that it is delicious, the idea that one of us is right and the other wrong may seem unattractive to a third party. It is tempting to say that deliciousness and disgustingness are relative to the observer – whatever that means. Again, many have been tempted by the appearance of irresoluble moral disagreements between societies to say that moral goodness and badness are relative to the society – whatever that means. Such relativism is one kind of anti-realism. Philosophers have sometimes been reluctant to discuss it, for it is notoriously hard to formulate in coherent terms, but its wide appeal makes it hard to ignore.

Wright uses the concept of Cognitive Command to put relativism (although he does not call it that) on his map as a coherent option. According to his definition, a discourse exerts Cognitive Command if and only it is a priori that differences of opinion formulated within the discourse, unless excusable as a result of vagueness in a disputed statement, or in the standards of acceptability, or variation in personal evidence thresholds, will involve something which may properly be regarded as a cognitive shortcoming (p. 144). Relativism with respect to a discourse becomes the denial that it exerts Cognitive Command. For example, the relativist might insist that it is not ruled out a priori that, when I say that rhubarb is disgusting and you say that it is delicious, neither of us may properly be accused of a cognitive shortcoming, even though our difference of opinion is not a result of vagueness in our statements, or in our standards of acceptability, or variation in our personal evidence thresholds.

Wright’s relativist is willing to apply a minimal notion of truth to the utterances at issue, for they display the required linguistic appearances. This creates a prima facie problem for relativism. Suppose that my opinion ‘Rhubarb is disgusting’ and your opinion ‘Rhubarb is delicious’ are both true. Then, by the disquotational property of minimal truth, rhubarb is disgusting and rhubarb is delicious. That, however, is impossible; ‘disgusting’ and ‘delicious’ are contraries (the point is even more obvious in the case in which you merely opine ‘Rhubarb is not disgusting’). It follows that our opinions are not both true. Thus it seems to be a priori that our difference of opinion does involve something which may properly be regarded as a cognitive shortcoming. The threat is that every discourse to which a minimal notion of truth applies will trivially exert Cognitive Command, in which case Wright has failed to capture a coherent relativist option.

Much depends on what is meant by ‘cognitive shortcoming’. If the phrase refers to the operation of those faculties by which we gain and process information about the world, then it is not obvious that an untrue opinion need constitute a cognitive shortcoming. We have an adequate supply of information only because our methods of gathering information are fallible; they could be infallible only by being cautious to the point of uselessness. Thus the healthy operation of our faculties occasionally results in the acquisition of untrue opinions without cognitive shortcomings in a restricted sense, when external conditions are misleading. However, this restricted notion of cognitive shortcoming is unsuitable for Wright’s purposes. A strict realist may recognize differences of opinion in which one opinion is true and the other is false, but no cognitive shortcoming in the restricted sense is involved, nor is the difference excusable as a result of vagueness in a disputed statement, or in the standards of acceptability, or variation in personal evidence thresholds.

Wright takes the threatened trivialization seriously, and tries to ward it off. His strategy is to argue that those who think that the discourse exerts Cognitive Command must regard truth in the discourse either as always recognizable by the participants or as sometimes transcending their powers of recognition, and that each possibility can be substantiated only by hard philosophical work (pp. 148–56). However, this seems off the point. The objector did not claim that, once it was conceded that the discourse exerted Cognitive Command, there could be no further philosophical disputes about it, such as that between realists and anti-realists in Dummett’s sense. Cognitive Command alone is threatened with trivialization. What Wright needs to meet the threat is a way of blocking the original trivializing argument. The only promising way of doing so is by a clarification of the notion of a cognitive shortcoming suitable to his purposes that would enable him to deny that the holding of untrue opinions must involve a cognitive shortcoming. No such clarification is supplied by Wright’s complex argument. Without it, Cognitive Command is too obscure to do philosophical work. A coherent relativism remains an elusive option.

Wright treats discourse as divided into a variety of separate discourses. It is crucial to his argument that a notion of truth appropriate to one discourse may be inappropriate to another. There is moral discourse, mathematical discourse, discourse about the past, discourse about the funny, discourse about pain and so on. Wright is by no means the originator of this conception (Wittgenstein on language-games is one ancestor). At first sight it looks entirely natural. After all, we can separate the sentences in which a past tense is used from all others, and so on.

Doubt begins to seep in when one notes that the discourses are not disjoint from each other. The sentence ‘Yesterday only five of the twelve torturers inflicted pain, but the other seven who amused them with funny stories were equally bad’ concerns morality, mathematics, the past, the funny and pain together. More generally, suppose that the discourses D1 and D2 are both conducted in English, and meet Wright’s conditions for the applicability of a notion of truth. Let ‘A1’ and ‘A2’ be declarative sentences in D1 and D2 respectively. Thus ‘Either A1 or A2’ is also a declarative sentence of English. Some notion of truth is applicable to both the disjunction and its disjuncts, for otherwise the platitude that ‘Either A1 or A2’ is true if and only if either ‘A1’ is true or ‘A2’ is true would be vitiated by equivocation.13 Thus at least one notion of truth is applicable to both ‘A1’ and ‘A2’, and to longer sentences in which they are embedded. There is no need for a notion of truth applicable to ‘A1’ but not to ‘A2’, or vice versa. By the argument for unique characterization in §II, such a restricted notion would anyway be equivalent within its domain to the more general one.

Nothing just said militates against the possibility that interesting generalizations can be made about truth for restricted classes of utterances, generalizations not applicable to all utterances saying that something is so. The mistake is to claim that the generalizations involve different notions of truth, as though the word meant something different in the phrases ‘mathematical truth’ and ‘moral truth’. A natural language is strongly unified in syntax and semantics. Any finite set of its words can be combined within the unity of a sentence. The notion of truth must respect and reflect this integrity. Truths are many; truth is one.14

The unity of a natural language shows that we end with a single notion of truth for that language. It does not immediately show that we begin with one. Might we begin with many separate notions of truth, and gradually paste them together? Such an account corresponds to nothing in the process by which we learn the language. We do not first understand phrases such as ‘mathematical truth’ and ‘moral truth’ as unstructured idioms. We learn them in the obvious way, just as we learn the phrases ‘mathematical confusion’ and ‘moral confusion’, by first understanding their component words. ‘Truth’ comes before ‘mathematical truth’ and ‘moral truth’. The latter merely restrict the former to mathematical and moral discourse respectively. Our general notion of truth allows us to ask whether an utterance of an unfamiliar kind is true, without learning a new notion of truth for it. The existence of different notions of truth for different discourses is a myth.

The unity of truth threatens Wright’s piecemeal approach. He assumes that the central question at issue between realists and anti-realists with respect to a discourse D is ‘What is the appropriate notion of truth for D?’, and that the answer is likely to be quite different from one discourse to another. The aim is to construct a taxonomy of notions of truth, and therefore a taxonomy of discourses. If there is only one notion of truth, this divide-and-conquer strategy fails, for no genuine division is possible. The central question has the same answer in every case.

The unity of truth does not threaten all piecemeal approaches. It is not necessary to assume that every question at issue between realists and anti-realists does concern the appropriate notion of truth for a discourse. For example, we can ask whether the meaning of ‘wrong’ (or the property of wrongness) is such that something is wrong if and only if it is superassertible that it is wrong, and that is quite different from asking whether the meaning of ‘wet’ (or the property of wetness) is such that something is wet if and only if it is superassertible that it is wet. Some of Wright’s discussion could be recast in such terms. Even here, however, ‘wrong’ and ‘wet’ cannot be treated in isolation. Superassertibility that it is wrong or that it is wet depends on the available ways of referring to it; consideration of these ways will take one back towards the language as a whole. If one is to work with a single notion of truth, then sooner or later one must ask how far it is a realist one. For example: can there be unknowable truths? That question is not best approached piecemeal. Indeed, Wright sketches a perfectly general argument for a negative answer to it from Wittgenstein’s rule-following considerations, but does not press the matter (p. 228).15

Truth and Objectivity is a strikingly resourceful and serious book, imbued with respect for the difficulty of philosophical problems and a readiness to probe them with all the conceptual instruments of contemporary analytic philosophy. The richness of Wright’s discussion has only been hinted at in this review. What is less obvious is that the problems are best tackled by the proliferation of complexity. Some of the main issues are, after all, quite stark. The quality of the details in Truth and Objectivity is so high that one is ungratefully disappointed when one discovers that their sum is not a new or compelling vision of the issues as a whole. It is not obvious that such a vision is possible; it is not obvious that it is not.
Thanks to John Campbell for helpful discussion of this review.

To treat one utterance as the negation of another is already to classify them semantically, not just syntactically, and in ways that involve the application of the notions of truth and falsity; u′ is the negation of u only if u′ is true if u is false and false if u is true. However, it may be held that there are syntactic marks of negation, to which Wright’s criterion can appeal. Similar remarks apply to conditionals. ↩︎

Wright compares his account of truth to Frege’s Platonism about numbers, interpreted ‘as based on the view that an expression’s candidacy to refer to an object is a matter of its syntax’ (p. 28). However, even on this interpretation, syntax provides no sufficient condition for an expression to succeed in referring to an object, since it could meet all syntactic constraints without being a constituent of any sentence that expressed a truth, in which case it would not refer. Thus the analogy does not exhibit a case in which semantic facts are guaranteed by non-semantic facts. There is no clear sense in which the truth of ‘2 + 2 = 4’ (or even its bivalence) is internal to mathematical discourse. ↩︎

Wright claims that truth and warranted assertibility nevertheless coincide in positive normative force, on the grounds that ‘u is true’ is warrantedly assertible if and only if ‘u is warrantedly assertible’ is warrantedly assertible (p. 18). Since truth disquotes, this claim is only as plausible as the assumption that ‘It is warrantedly assertible that P’ is equivalent to ‘It is warrantedly assertible that it is warrantedly assertible that P’. Wright may assume this because he takes warranted assertibility to be a decidable matter (p. 56). Now it seems to be a feature of our ordinary practice of assertion that the only adequate warrant for assertion that P is knowledge that P (Peter Unger, Ignorance [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1975], pp. 252–65; Michael Slote, ‘Assertion and Belief’, in J. Dancy [ed.], Papers on Language and Logic [Keele: Keele University Library, 1979]; Vic Dudman, ‘Probability and Assertion’, Analysis, 52 [1992], pp. 204–11). The relevant assumption therefore becomes the equivalence of something like ‘One is in a position to know that P’ and ‘One is in a position to know that one is in a position to know that P’. However, the former does not entail the latter; one argument to this effect is given in my ‘Inexact Knowledge’, Mind, 101 (1992), pp. 217–42, and extended to notions such as rational belief that provide weaker warrants for assertion. Thus ‘It is warrantedly assertible that P’ does not entail ‘It is warrantedly assertible that it is warrantedly assertible that P’, and the warranted assertibility of ‘u is true’ does not entail the warranted assertibility of ‘u is warrantedly assertible’. In this sense, truth is weaker than warranted assertibility in positive normative force. ↩︎

The argument assumes that if ‘“P” is true’ is equivalent to ‘P’, then the negation of ‘“P” is true’ is equivalent to the negation of ‘P’ (p. 32). Wright is surely entitled to the latter equivalence in arguing against the deflationist, for how is the deflationist to deflate the occurrence of ‘true’ in ‘“P” is not true’ if not by using its equivalence to the negation of ‘P’? ↩︎

Wright requires there to be a unique P such that u says that P. This would naturally be expanded as ‘There is a P such that for all Q, u says that Q if and only if P=Q’. However, this expansion is ungrammatical, for P and Q are intended to be substitutional variables over declarative sentences, and the result of substituting declarative sentences for them in ‘P=Q’ is ill-formed. Something like ‘Necessarily, P if and only if Q’ should replace ‘P=Q’. ↩︎
If so desired, the argument can be relativized to truth and falsity for a particular discourse. ↩︎
The claim is hinted at on pp. 194–5 of D. Davidson, ‘On the Very Idea of a Conceptual Scheme’, in his Inquiries into Truth and Interpretation (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1984). ↩︎
See pp. 90–109 of T. Nagel, The View from Nowhere (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1986), and my ‘Anthropocentrism and Truth’, Philosophia, 17 (1987), pp. 33–53. ↩︎
The point is amplified in ‘Unreflective Realism’, my contribution to a book symposium on Truth and Objectivity, forthcoming in Philosophy and Phenomenological Research. ↩︎
Wright defines superassertibility for statements rather than utterances. The difference is not crucial for present purposes. ↩︎

The use of sentences like (*) in such arguments goes back to F. B. Fitch, ‘A Logical Analysis of Some Value Concepts’, Journal of Symbolic Logic, 28 (1963), pp. 135–42. It is discussed in a different context by Wright in his Realism, Meaning and Truth (Oxford: Blackwell, 1987), pp. 309–16, where he rejects an attempt to deal with the problem by resort to intuitionistic logic, (on which the inference from (2) to (3) is invalid). ↩︎

For terminological uniformity with (T) and (F), the platitude should be read as predicating ‘true’ of utterances of the sentences types ‘A1’, ‘A2’ and ‘Either A1 or A2’, not of the sentence types themselves. ↩︎

Some – but not all – solutions to the Liar and other semantic paradoxes require the division of the truth predicate into a hierarchy. However, this point has nothing to do with its supposed division into a variety of predicates for separate discourses. The truth predicate at the lowest level of the hierarchy already applies over a huge range of non-semantic utterances, and the levels are cumulative rather than disjoint. In terms of (T) and (F), the hierarchy may be conceived as a series of increasingly inclusive notions of saying. ↩︎

Wright asks: ‘what conception of such matters [the proper application of rules] can both allow them to be determinate in ways which human beings cannot, perhaps in principle, acknowledge and yet leave space for the idea that their very constitution somehow depends on contingencies of human subcognitive propensity?’. For the beginnings of an answer see my ‘Vagueness and Ignorance’, Aristotelian Society supp. 66 (1992), pp. 145–62. ↩︎

works.title: Review of G. Vision, Modern Anti-Realism and Manufactured Truth
passages: Review of G. Vision, Modern Anti-Realism and Manufactured Truth

Gerald Vision makes the Correspondence theory of truth the core of global realism. On his first shot, the theory says that “what is true is so by virtue of its correspondence with something in the not-essentially-mind-dependent world” (25). This is later replaced by a revision of J. L. Austin’s account.
Review of G. Vision, Modern Anti-Realism and Manufactured Truth
Correspondence: A statement made with sentence S is made true by the specific state of affairs which S-as-used demonstrates being of a type discriminated by the type of S, qua sentence. (128)
Review of G. Vision, Modern Anti-Realism and Manufactured Truth

The denial of essential mind-dependence has dropped out in the official version. However, what matters to Vision is just that Correspondence should be consistent with mind-independence; it is then up to a local realism to assert “that a certain fragment of language has truth-values founded in a distinctive sort of cognition-independent fact” (139). The second half of his book attacks globally antirealist views which rule out all such local realisms by injecting cognition-dependence into the very nature of truth. Michael Dummett, Thomas Kuhn and some readings of Wittgenstein receive special attention.
Review of G. Vision, Modern Anti-Realism and Manufactured Truth

One antirealist strategy would concede Vision’s Correspondence, but argue that only cognition-dependent types of states of affairs can be discriminated. It may claim, for example, that a sentence type discriminates a state of affairs type only in virtue of its use by speakers of the language, and that their use must be insensitive to states of affairs whose obtaining they cannot recognize. Vision makes some telling points against arguments of this kind. However, antirealists may be motivated by a failure to find any mechanism for discriminating unrecognizable states of affairs. Vision does not attempt to supply such a mechanism, and gives no substantive account of discrimination. “Not much can be said to elucidate further what it is for a sentence-type to discriminate a type of situation” (129; Vision identifies situations and states of affairs). The antirealists’ suspicions are unlikely to be allayed, even though their arguments do not compel realists to share their suspicions.
Review of G. Vision, Modern Anti-Realism and Manufactured Truth

A distinction can be drawn between recognition-independent and recognition-transcendent types of states of affairs. X is recognition-immanent iff necessarily, X obtains only if it can be recognized to obtain; otherwise, X is recognition-transcendent. X is recognition-dependent iff necessarily, X obtains only if it does so because it can be recognized to obtain; otherwise, X is recognition-independent. Recognition-dependence entails recognition-immanence but not vice versa, so recognition-transcendence entails recognition-independence but not vice versa. Vision could thus claim that Correspondence secures at least recognition-independence, on the simple grounds that it does not include recognition of the token state of affairs as belonging to the type in what makes the statement true (‘X is made true by ---’ is a hyperintensional context for ---), while the antirealist suspicions point at most to recognition-immanence. Recognition-independence might then be offered to the intuitions of the realist, even if recognition-transcendence must be sacrificed to those of the antirealist (cf. 15–17). However, few realists will be satisfied with a point of such slight metaphysical consequence. The point of substance is that truth has been restricted to recognizable truth, whether or not the restriction is written into the official account of truth-making.
Review of G. Vision, Modern Anti-Realism and Manufactured Truth

A more promising strategy would use recognition-independence as a base from which to argue for recognition-transcendence, no doubt by consideration of specific kinds of statement (cf. 18–20). Unfortunately, Correspondence is ill fitted to play a role in such an argument. It is embedded in neither systematic theory nor familiar usage; one can give a clear sense to its explanans only through one’s independent understanding of its explanandum; it is not far short of useless.
Review of G. Vision, Modern Anti-Realism and Manufactured Truth

One problem may be allowed to stand for many. The sentence type ‘This is longer than that’ might be expected to discriminate the type of situation in which something is longer than something else. By ordinary lights, that type of situation is the type of situation in which something is shorter than something else. Given parity of treatment, the sentence types ‘This is longer than that’ and ‘This is shorter than that’ then discriminate the same situation type. But tokens of these types will demonstrate the same situation token, if uttered in the same context with no change in the reference of ‘this’ or of ‘that’. Thus one statement is made true if and only if the other is, according to Correspondence. In order to avoid this result, the concept of a situation must be refined. The realist should not say that the sentence type ‘This is longer than that’ discriminates the type of situation in which something referred to by ‘this’ is longer than something referred to by ‘that’, for this situation type obtains only if someone uses the words ‘this’ and ‘that’, whereas what makes the statement true is intended (here at least) not to involve minds at all. Rather, a situation should be taken as something like an ordered sequence; ‘This is long than that’ could discriminate the type of situation in which the first member is longer than the second—or it could discriminate the type of situation in which the second member is longer than the first. One must choose between these equally good alternatives. The point is that even very simple sentences force the defender of Correspondence not so much to expound the concepts of discrimination and situation as to construct them. Correspondence is not an account of truth; it is a vague gesture in the direction of one.
Review of G. Vision, Modern Anti-Realism and Manufactured Truth

Modern Anti-Realism and Manufactured Truth has many worthwhile things to say about important and difficult issues. Unfortunately, it is written in so turgid a style that only the most determined reader will find out what they are.

works.title: Review of R. Sorensen, Blindspots
passages: You are reading this review without my supposing that you are; the number of books now in the Bodleian is even and no one will ever know it; some of my beliefs are not true; there are no beliefs. Each of these propositions is true or could have been. Yet each evades cognition in some way. I cannot truly suppose the first and no one can ever know the second (if supposition and knowledge distribute over conjunction); my belief in the third ensures that some of my beliefs are not true; eliminativists’ belief in the fourth ensures its falsity. All are blindspots in Roy Sorensen’s sense: consistent propositions to which certain individuals cannot take certain propositional attitudes, perhaps relative to certain norms or other constraints. The book overflows with examples and classifications of blindspots. Sorensen displays their potential as a rich source of objections to philosophical theories, particularly to those of an anti-realist cast. His main purpose, however, is to argue that blindspots are the common root of many philosophical paradoxes, notable the sorites, the prediction (or surprise examination) paradox and a group of decision-theoretic problems such as iterated prisoners’ dilemma. His characteristic method is to assemble a wide range of variant paradoxes and rival and preliminary solutions, in an attempt to show that only his final view solves the problem at the requisite level of generality. His positive account is sometimes hard to find in the cornucopia of argument, example and theory. One can browse through the useful and curious information as in Brewer’s Dictionary of Phrase and Fable. Nevertheless, a central thread of argument is there.

Sorensen’s response to sorites arguments, following James Cargile and Richmond Campbell, is the epistemic theory of vagueness. On this view some proposition of the form ‘n+1 grains make a heap and n grains do not make a heap’ is true but unknowable; it is a blindspot. Thus the major premiss of the paradoxical argument is false. Sorensen claims ‘Resistance to the epistemic theory of vagueness can only be motivated by a prior resolve to allow no unknowable truths’ (p. 245). The present reviewer is a counter-example, resistant to the theory but well-disposed to unknowable truths. One does not need to be an anti-realist to believe that predicates do not acquire their satisfaction-conditions by magic. Sorensen betrays no curiosity as to how our word ‘heap’ has acquired the determinate extension he claims for it, or as to why we cannot know what that extension is. It is not just our dispositions to apply or withhold the word that fail to specify boundaries; one can be quite prepared to invoke causal relations to natural kinds in explaining the realist satisfaction-conditions of some predicates without supposing that heaps form a natural kind. Even if the epistemic theory of vagueness is correct, it cannot claim to have solved sorites paradoxes until it has dispelled these mysteries. Sorensen neither argues that there cannot be a substantive theory of reference nor indicates a theory that might explain the nature of the link between ‘heap’ and its extension compatibly with his account of vagueness. No doubt our understanding of reference is poor, but the issues need to be addressed. Sorensen’s insensitivity to them is manifest in his handling of Benacerraf’s argument that no identification of numbers with sets is correct, since there is no reason to prefer one identification to its rivals; this too is treated as a crude move from unknowability to untruth. Are we to suppose that Shakespeare may have used ‘seven’ to refer to the corresponding Zermelo set rather than the von Neumann one? Sorensen’s arguments risk proving too much, by ruling out semantic indeterminacy altogether. Surely it can occur, as when I define the term ‘cammal’ only by the stipulations: (1) all cats are cammals; (2) all cammals are mammals. He would need to provide a positive account of this fairly unproblematic kind of semantic indeterminacy to show that vague predicates do not manifest a subtler form of the same phenomenon.

Blindspots provide a more plausible account of the prediction paradox and its relatives. When the famously reliable teacher tells her pupils that there will be a surprise test next week, they know that her announcement will be fulfilled. However, when they argue that the test cannot be on the last day, because by then it would not be a surprise, they assume that if there is no test by the eve of the last day then they will still know at that later time that her announcement will be fulfilled: but the assumption is false, for otherwise they would in effect know ‘There will be a test tomorrow and we do not know it’, which is a blindspot for them. Thus their original argument that there will be no test does not get started. As given, the diagnosis turns on ‘the existential premiss’: if the announcement is fulfilled, there will be a test. Sorensen argues that it is inessential to the underlying problem by considering puzzles without it in decision theory. His response is to suggest a way in which an existential premiss, and therefore blindspots, may be introduced by the actions of rational agents rather than by the original announcement.

Sorensen does not mention a closer variant of the surprise examination without an existential premiss. A test is conditionally predictable if the pupils know the night before ‘If there is a test this week, it will be tomorrow’. The teacher announces just that there will be no conditionally predictable test the following week. If there is no test at all, the announcement is fulfilled. Thus not only can the pupils know at the time of the announcement that it will be fulfilled, they can continue to know it when no test has occurred by the eve of the last day; at that time they will be able to work out that no test will be given. So what is to stop them from working that out at the start of the week? Sorensen himself provides the materials to fill the apparent lacunae in the pupils’ argument. Yet a conditionally unpredictable test on Tuesday is clearly possible. It is not clear that Sorensen’s blindspot analysis of the decision-theoretic cases extends to this one. Even if Sorensen’s account of the prediction paradox is insufficiently general, his criticisms of rival approaches are generally effective, and he provides a splendid variety of data against which all future work on the topic should be tested. Historians of philosophy should also enjoy his account of the paradox’s development. It seems to have begun in about 1943, when the Swedish mathematician Lennart Ekbom reflected on a radio announcement that there would be a surprise civil defence exercise in the following week. Sorensen traces the way in which journal discussion of the issue gradually revealed its depth, partly through dubious assimilation to recognized paradoxes (such as the Liar), after some early responses of delightful superficiality. It may provide a paradigm of one kind of progress in analytic philosophy.

Sorensen’s long book contains so many arguments that even its unusually high ratio of valid to invalid ones leaves far more of the latter than can be mentioned here. Just one further issue will be raised. Individual blindspots such as ‘It is raining and I do not believe it’—in contrast to universal blindspots such as ‘It is raining and no one believes it’—seem to have a special connection with the first person. The irrationality or impossibility of my believing ‘It is raining and TW does not believe it’ or ‘It is raining and the man who left his manuscript in his garden does not believe it’ seems to depend on my belief that I am TW or the man who left his manuscript in his garden; the irrationality or impossibility of my believing ‘It is raining and I do not believe it’ is not derivative in this way. Sorensen denies the contrast. He argues that (A) ‘I’ is not referentially transparent and asserts that (B) there is no other reason to postulate the contrast (p. 32). (B) is false; Sorensen does not eliminate the possibility of basing the contrast on the point that a belief expressible by its subject as ‘It is raining and I do not believe it’ gets its subject into trouble no matter who he or she is, which is not the case for ‘It is raining and TW does not believe it’. As for (A), ‘suppose the evil demon sends a signal that will later produce the thought “I am now thinking” in Descartes. By the time Descartes thinks the thought, the evil demon has committed suicide. Since “I” was produced by the evil demon, it refers to him’ (p. 31; this is not the whole of Sorensen’s argument). If the evil demon has simply caused Descartes to think a certain thought, there is no reason to suppose that the ‘I’ of the thought refers to the demon rather than to Descartes. The more interesting suggestion is that the demon is using Descartes’ consciousness as a surface on which to scrawl token thoughts of which Descartes is not the thinker. Descartes will be aware of the thoughts, and wrongly believe himself to be their thinker. However, this is no counter-example to the claim that the reference of ‘I’ in a thought is transparent to its thinker, for Descartes is by hypothesis not the thinker of the demon-inscribed token (the point is more obvious for belief in place of thought). Sorensen may have confused this token with Descartes’ (mis)understanding of it, for in being aware of it he may (falsely) think ‘That is a token of the thought: I am now thinking’ and thereby produce a token of ‘I am now thinking’ whose ‘I’ does refer to him, but it is quite distinct from the former token. Could Descartes think a token of ‘I am now thinking’ under the misapprehension that its thinker was the demon? He might have the thought ‘I am now thinking’ and later or elsewhere in his mind think ‘The demon is the thinker of that thought’ about it; I can write ‘I am now thinking’ on a piece of paper and come to believe that it was written by someone else. If Sorensen is to undermine the apparent link between blindspots and ‘I’, he needs to attack not the infallibility of my thoughts about my ‘I’-thoughts but my self-acquaintance as the referent of ‘I’ in my thinking of the ‘I’-thought itself.
I recommend watching this book snap at the heels of philosophical dignitaries; its teeth sometimes close on clay.

works.title: Review of A. Appiah, For Truth in Semantics
passages: Review of A. Appiah, For Truth in Semantics

For Truth in Semantics is in the same sense against justified assertion in semantics. Anthony Appiah’s polemic (his word) in Blackwell’s new series Philosophical Theory argues that realist theories of meaning should be preferred to anti-realist ones, in Michael Dummett’s terminology: the key semantic notion should be that of the condition for a declarative sentence to be true, not for its assertion to be justified by evidence. The book should be read by anyone at graduate level or above who is inclined to favour anti-realist semantics; it is not guaranteed to reduce that inclination, but it does present a formidable array of difficulties for the anti-realist to overcome.
Review of A. Appiah, For Truth in Semantics

Appiah begins by sketching his preferred form of realism, on which sentences have the truth-conditions of the beliefs they express. Conventions linking sentences and beliefs are roughly sketched. As stated (pp. 10–12), they run foul of irony and perhaps metaphor, seeming to require me (as an English speaker) to use the English sentence ‘Brutus is an honourable man’ with its normal truth-conditions only if I intend thereby to give other English speakers who hear me reason to believe that I believe that Brutus is an honourable man. The reader is referred for more details to Appiah’s other book Assertion and Conditionals (Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, 1985), where at p. 150 special provision is made for utterances with an ironic intonation: but only the crassest forms of irony (e.g., sarcasm) require special intonation (one can be ironic in writing). No doubt these cases are difficult for any theorist. There is also a problem about self-contradictory and Moore-paradoxical sentences; they have truth-conditions, but there do not seem to be regularities linking their assertion to the appropriate beliefs. An appeal to the compositional structure of the sentences might help, but its evaluation would require more theoretical context than Appiah provides (there is a similar difficulty on p. 148, where an account of the functionalist individuation of belief uses in effect the simplifying assumption that beliefs are finite in number and unstructured: structure is crucial to the individuation of belief, and the reader needs a more detailed picture of Appiah’s envisaged treatment). It is assumed (p. 17) that competent speakers must actually recognize the conventions of their language as conventions; this ignores Tyler Burge’s plausible argument to the contrary (‘On Knowledge and Convention’, The Philosophical Review, 84 (1975), pp. 249–55).
Review of A. Appiah, For Truth in Semantics

Appiah divides anti-realism into a negative programme – the critique of realist semantics – and a positive one – the development of anti-realist semantics; his main targets for both are Dummett and Crispin Wright. The negative programme turns on the idea that speakers can associate sentences only with such states of affairs as they can recognise to obtain. E. J. Craig is said to have shown that anti-realists have no argument for this verificationist constraint. However, Appiah goes on to distinguish between two forms of it: strong verificationism requires speakers of a language to be able to verify its true sentences as true in their current circumstances; weak verificationism only requires them to be able to verify those sentences in appropriate, perhaps counterfactual circumstances. He then argues that only weak verificationism is plausible, whilst only strong verificationism threatens realist semantics. The latter contention is doubtful. For example, no sentence of the form ‘P and it is never verified that P’ can be verified as true; nevertheless, for a realist some sentences of that form are true, since there are many unimportant facts that nobody will ever bother to ascertain. I have argued elsewhere that Dorothy Edgington’s attempt to resolve this problem, which Appiah endorses (p. 86), by using the idea of knowledge in one situation of what is the case in another yields a form of verificationism too weak to be relevant. Let ‘weakish verificationism’ mean a weak verificationism without Edgington’s modifications. Thus realism is incompatible with weakish verificationism. Conversely, those who find weakish verificationism compelling have reason to avoid realism. I have also argued elsewhere that the case of sentences of the above form can be reconciled with weakish verificationism in the context of an anti-realist theory of meaning that yields a non-classical logic. At this point Appiah may reply that he is free to allow exceptions to weakish verificationism. However, those with anti-realist sympathies may suspect that Appiah’s functionalist theory of belief ultimately commits him to weakish verificationism, on the grounds that absolutely unverifiable states of affairs would have no functional role with respect to belief. Appiah has not yet shown that suspicion to be misplaced.
Review of A. Appiah, For Truth in Semantics

Appiah usefully emphasizes the fact that many (if not all) empirical claims are to be justified by defeasible evidence, in contrast to Dummett’s paradigm of mathematical proof. Anti-realists cannot easily transfer accounts of the logical constants from mathematical to empirical language. There are, however, at least two senses of ‘defeasible’. An assertion is defeasible1 just in case evidence for it is always consistent with its falsity; it is defeasible2 just in case evidence for it is always controvertible by further evidence. Appiah does not clearly distinguish between these two notions (p. 41). Neither obviously implies the other. On an externalist view of evidence, the fact that I remember eating truffles is evidence for my assertion ‘I have eaten truffles’; since the evidence entails the truth of the assertion, the latter is not defeasible1, but it is defeasible2, since any evidence for it could be controverted by misleading further evidence that what I ate were not truffles. Conversely, on an internalist view of evidence, the assertion ‘We are not brains in vats having experience as though we were not brains in vats’ may be defeasible1 without being defeasible2, if no evidence can either entail or controvert it. The latter case is of course a very special one: an internalist view of evidence would entitle Appiah to assume that almost all empirical assertions are defeasible in both senses, and his anti-realist opponents to seem to have chosen to use such a view in their theorizing. Nevertheless, one might wonder about the prospects for anti-realism based on an externalist view of evidence. The contrast with mathematical language would then be less thorough-going, for although almost all empirical assertions would be defeasible2, the same could be said of mathematical assertions, for even if I have seen a valid proof of a theorem, I should believe the opposite if mathematicians whom I know to be better than I tell me that it has been discovered to contain a subtle fallacy; as already noted, some empirical assertions would be like mathematical ones in not being defeasible1. Appiah is hardly to be blamed for not going into this under-explored territory.
Review of A. Appiah, For Truth in Semantics

The attack on the positive programme begins with an argument that an anti-realist semantics for a past language will violate the strong verificationism on which the negative programme is supposed to be premissed. The point is roughly that the anti-realist will state our twentieth century AD understanding of first century BC Latin in biconditionals such as:
Review of A. Appiah, For Truth in Semantics
‘Alea iacta est’ was assertible for Caesar […] iff Caesar had evidence that the die was cast. (p. 93)
Review of A. Appiah, For Truth in Semantics

Pretend, for the sake of argument, that neither ‘“Alea iacta est” was assertible for Caesar’ nor ‘Caesar had evidence that the die was cast’ is currently verifiable as true or as false. Then ASS1 itself is supposed to be a currently unverifiable anti-realist claim, so that strong verificationism would make as much trouble for anti-realism as for realism. The argument assumes that if ‘P iff Q’ is currently verifiable then so are P and Q. This requirement is implausible (put P=Q). The anti-realist could allow a current verification of ASS1 to consist in evidence justifying the assertion that if in the future we have evidence justifying the assertion that ‘Alea iacta est’ was assertible for Caesar then we shall have evidence justifying the assertion that Caesar had evidence that the die was cast, and vice versa; this would be quite in the spirit of the intuitionist semantics for mathematical language. Appiah’s objections to such replies (pp. 103–4) depend on his assumption that the anti-realist believes the two halves of ASS1 (or other sentences like them, p. 94) to be verification-transcendent. Perhaps a better view for the anti-realist is that no sentences are verification-transcendent, but that some would be were the realist correct.
Review of A. Appiah, For Truth in Semantics

Appiah goes on to argue that, whatever the status of strong verificationism, anti-realist theories of meaning are unacceptable, whether they follow a Davidsonian truth theory, but with ‘true’ replaced by ‘assertible’ (as Wright has suggested), or take some other form (Wright has replied in ‘Can a Davidsonian Meaning-theory be Construed in Terms of Assertibility?’, at pp. 287–316 of Realism, Meaning and Truth, Blackwell, Oxford, 1987). The key idea, following Robert Brandom, is that for many sentential operators O the assertibility-condition for OP is not a function of the assertibility-condition for P, since there are co-assertible sentences P and Q (i.e., it is necessary that P is assertible iff Q is assertible) such that OP and OQ are not co-assertible; thus an assertibility-conditional theory could not make sense of the compositionality of meaning. For instance, ‘It is assertible that Caesar cast the die’ and ‘Caesar cast the die’ seem to be co-assertible, but, if we have no evidence as to whether Caesar cast the die or not, ‘It is not the case that it is assertible that Caesar cast the die’ is assertible while ‘It is not the case that Caesar cast the die’ is not. Appiah considers the suggestion that the anti-realist might distinguish between the meanings of P and Q in such cases by working with deniability- as well as assertibility-conditions; he objects that treating P and its negation independently would also violate compositionality (pp. 135–7). This reply assumes that the denial of a sentence is conceived simply as the assertion of its negation, but the anti-realist might conceive it as a separate speech act (compare the Quinean scheme of assent, dissent and abstention): the equivalence of the denial of P with the assertion of its negation would be thought of as defining negation, not denial. Appiah’s discussion of such a possibility assumes that deniability-conditions are still to be explained in terms of assertibility-conditions (p. 121); this leaves open a modified anti-realism on which speakers must know both conditions in order to understand a sentence, neither needing to be explained in terms of the other. However, it can be argued on Appiah’s behalf that ‘It is assertible that P’ and ‘P and it is assertible that P’ are both co-assertible and co-deniable; then if O…=‘It is possible that (… and it is not the case that P)’, ‘It is possible that (it is assertible that P and it is not the case that P)’ and ‘It is possible that ((P and it is assertible that P) and it is not the case that P)’ should be co-deniable: but the latter is deniable and the former is not, when the assertibility of P does not guarantee its truth. Another line for the anti-realist is to argue that the realist has a parallel difficulty in explaining how ‘John believes that P’ and ‘John believes that Q’ can have different truth-conditions even when P and Q do not; since realists may distinguish at this point between P and Q on the basis of their internal structure, why may anti-realists not do the same? Appiah objects (pp. 143–4) that it makes sense to think of O as structure-sensitive only if O itself has to do with states, as of a computational agent, which may depend on structured representations (e.g., ‘John believes that…’), and that many of the operators which give anti-realists this problem are not of that kind (e.g., ‘It is not the case that…’). The point is not decisive, for anti-realists can reply that they are concerned to explain how the assertibility of OP depends on the assertibility of P, and assertibility does have to do with states, as of a computational agent, which may depend on structured representations. Since they have not actually provided such an explanation, however, the reply is a somewhat hollow one.
Review of A. Appiah, For Truth in Semantics

Appiah offers an explanation for the anti-realists’ difficulties. It is that they seek to individuate beliefs (as expressed by sentences) solely in terms of ‘input claims’ about the internal states of the individual and the causal impact of the environment on them, whereas a correct functionalist account must individuate beliefs in terms of both input claims and output claims about the causal impact of the internal states on the environment; beliefs have effects on action as well as causes in perception (pp. 152–3; note that the anti-realist does make claims about actions of a special kind, assertions; ‘output claim’ should exclude these). Now, schematically, it is plausible that a belief-individuating functionalist theory must contain output claims as theorems, and it is plausible that assertibility-conditional theories of meaning do not contain output claims as axioms, but what Appiah does not show is that input claims together with some a priori truths linking the concepts of belief, desire, intention and action cannot entail output claims. Some of Dummett’s remarks about the need for harmony between the conditions for an utterance and the consequences of it are suggestive in this respect. It might be objected that no relation between inputs and apparently assertoric noises would suffice to show that one was dealing with a mind at all: but that is not obviously correct where those noises are of sufficiently complex apparent structure, and sensitive to sufficiently complex conditions. Appiah’s diagnosis remains unproven, though promising.
Review of A. Appiah, For Truth in Semantics

For Truth in Semantics is clearly and unpretentiously written and full of interesting detail. Unfortunately, it is marred by what seems to be over-hasty composition; the reader is often having to work out how much the correction of some oversight would damage Appiah’s overall argument. Many slips are incidental. The negation of a sentence is defined as the result of negating its main verb (p. xiii; consider ‘Some dogs like cats’ and ‘Either he goes or I go’); the phrase ‘We have seen already’ (p. 13) refers to no preceding passage; a quotation is misinterpreted (p. 120); some arguments are confusingly expressed (e.g., at pp. 150–1, 155). The reader may also be confused by statements such as ‘For the realist, however, the beliefs we ascribe are not instrumentalist hypotheses but real states of persons’ (p. 6), where ‘the realist’ refers not to everyone who accepts a realist (i.e., truth-conditional) theory of meaning but only to those who think like Appiah. Other problems are more serious. Intuitionism in mathematics is said to demand that ‘there should actually be some procedure that guarantees that we should eventually come to confirm (or disconfirm) each sentence’ (p. 44); intuitionists reject the Law of Excluded Middle precisely because they do not regard this demand as reasonable. It is assumed that a theory with an unverifiable consequence cannot be confirmed (p. 67); why should it not be confirmed by an inference to the best explanation of some of its verifiable consequences, since confirmation does not entail truth? The reader is informed that ‘the conjunction of all (finitely statable) truths is itself a (finitely statable) truth’ (p. 86); what if there are infinitely many finitely statable truths? Realists are told to acknowledge without controversy that those who understand a sentence know when evidence justifies its assertion and when not (p. 145); since I do not know whether my evidence justifies the assertion ‘Mallory and Irvine died without reaching the summit of Everest’, I presumably do not know what it means. It is said that ‘what we should believe in the face of external evidence, is what we would believe if we were CPAs’ (computationally perfect agents, p. 154); what I should believe when I look at my logic notebook is that I have no idea whether A is a theorem of arithmetic, but is that what I would believe if I were a CPA?
Review of A. Appiah, For Truth in Semantics
Anthony Appiah has written a useful book. With more care, it would have merited the phrase ‘state of the art’.
I thank Anthony Appiah for comments on a draft of this review.

works.title: Review of P. Simons, Parts: A Study in Ontology
passages: Some writers take the relation of limb to body as paradigmatic for that of part to whole, regarding talk of non-spatial parts as shaky metaphor. Others take the notion of a part to be as formal as the notion of a subclass. But on either view there is room for both a formal theory of parts and wholes – mereology – and an informal account of its application. Peter Simons provides both in his authoritative study.

Mereology has lived as the poor relation of set theory. In the earliest systems, developed by Lesniewski and, somewhat later, by Leonard and Goodman, the algebraic structure of the part-whole relation was that of the subset-set relation made ugly by the omission of the null set.1 Complete assimilation was impossible, given that ordinary individuals are not sets; indeed, the motivation for mereology was often the nominalist hope of substituting it for set theory, in order to avoid the latter’s commitment to abstract objects. But this seemed to require mereology to mirror characteristic features of set theory. Sets are extensional; they are identical if and only if they have the same members. Similarly, mereology took wholes to be identical if and only if they have the same parts. Both principles were applied even to identity over time or across different possibilities, if only by default; change or contingency were not contemplated in either the members of a set or the parts of a whole. Sets are also promiscuous; any random individuals are collected by some set as its members. Similarly, mereology summed any random individuals into a whole. Simons uses the phrase ‘extensional mereology’ broadly to describe approaches of this kind. His opening chapters are a valuable guide through the maze of systems into which they have proliferated.

Extensional mereology had a place within a certain metaphysical picture. To simplify, there was a primal medium, sometimes the four-dimensional space-time continuum, sometimes the private world of phenomenal experience. Individual objects were carved out of this medium. Since the medium could be treated as though it were composed of points, each object corresponded to a unique non-empty set of points and each non-empty set of points corresponded to a unique object. On this conception, mereological relations between objects are isomorphic to set-theoretic relations between non-empty sets of points in the medium. The picture was always at odds with the everyday ontology of three-dimensional continuants having spatial but not temporal parts, on which arbitrary mereological sums are not permitted. Still, it could represent itself as the scientific world-view. It had a perspicuous simplicity; the absence of a distinction between essential and accidental properties made reputable truth-functional logic sufficient for its needs; the four-dimensional view gained prestige from its association with Einstein.

Things have changed. A revival of Aristotelian metaphysics and a better understanding of the semantics of modal logic have combined to make a distinction between essential and accidental properties seem both necessary and possible. The restriction to truth-functional logic feels correspondingly oppressive. The supposed inconsistency between the four-dimensional space-time continuum of relativistic physics and the three-dimensional objects of common sense has proved elusive. Perspicuous simplicity is not far from simple-mindedness. This metaphysical turn leaves the natural habitat of extensional mereology behind.2 Yet it does not diminish the need for a systematic theory of part and whole. The chief aim of Simons’s book is to develop a mereology in tune with, and contributory to, neo-Aristotelian metaphysics. Such a theory will distinguish between essential and accidental parts, making the appropriate background logic a modal one; it will assign ordinary things spatial parts at times but not spatio-temporal parts; it will not permit arbitrary mereological sums.

Although Simons criticizes extensional mereology as inadequate for continuants, he allows that some form of it may apply to certain other categories. He considers the cases of occurrents, classes and masses, arguing in Aristotelian tenor that the terms ‘part’ and ‘whole’ have a variety of analogous senses, related but distinct.

(a) Occurrents. These include events, processes, activities and performances. Unlike continuants, they have temporal as well as spatial parts. Since the metaphysical picture behind extensional mereology assimilates continuants to occurrents, it might be expected to fit the latter reasonably well.3

Simons associates the possession of temporal parts with an incapacity for change. We may say that a sea battle moved from the Channel to the Atlantic, but that is because one phase (temporal part) was in the Channel and a later one in the Atlantic; unlike a continuant, it is not the whole battle that had first one property and then a contrary one (p. 135). Simons follows tradition in using italicization of ‘whole’ to make the point, but ordinary language can be slippery: someone might say that the whole battle had moved because all the ships had. This may be to treat the battle as a kind of continuant (metaphysical error or stylistic variation?); in any case, the line between continuants and occurrents is not always easy to draw.

Having developed a mereology for occurrents, Simons uses it to distinguish between activity verbs and performance verbs. ‘Laugh’ is an activity verb; if one is laughing then one has laughed. ‘Dress’ is a performance verbs; if one is dressing then one has not yet dressed. Simons argues that the nominals of activity verbs are phase-dissective; any reasonably long phase of a laughing is itself a laughing. In contrast, the nominals of performance verbs are phase anti-dissective; no phase of a dressing less than the whole is itself a dressing. The relation between continuous and perfective aspects of the verbs is then explained in terms of this contrast.

Simons presents the distinction as an ontological one between two kinds of occurrent, activities and performances (pp. 137-8). That is dubious. By the tests on which he relies, ‘sail from Ireland’ is an activity verb phrase; ‘sail to Byzantium’ is a performance verb phrase. If single words are required, we could introduce the verbs ‘sailfromireland’ and ‘sailtobyzantium’ with corresponding senses. Now if a man has sailed from Ireland to Byzantium, are there two occurrents, his activity of sailing from Ireland and his performance of sailing to Byzantium? Of course, his leaving Ireland was not his arriving at Byzantium, and the property of sailing from Ireland is not the property of sailing to Byzantium, and the fact that he sailed from Ireland is not the fact that he sailed to Byzantium. Nevertheless, there seems to be a perfectly good sense in which just one sailing from Ireland to Byzantium occurred, a voyage which began and ended on specifiable dates. It might be objected that a strong wind could cause his sailing to Byzantium without causing his sailing from Ireland. In the same sense, a famine could cause his sailing from Ireland without causing his sailing slowly from Ireland, where both ‘sail from Ireland’ and ‘sail slowly from Ireland’ are activity verb phrases. Similarly, curiosity could cause his sailing to Byzantium without causing his sailing slowly to Byzantium, where both ‘sail to Byzantium’ and ‘sail slowly to Byzantium’ are performance verb phrases. Thus the objection requires a sense in which his sailing from Ireland was not his sailing slowly from Ireland, and his sailing to Byzantium was not his sailing slowly to Byzantium. But, so taken, the gerunds do not seem to deliver what Simons’s explanation requires, occurrents with genuine mereological structure. In the needed sense, the man’s sailing from Ireland was his sailing slowly from Ireland, and his sailing to Byzantium was his sailing slowly to Byzantium; but in a corresponding sense his sailing from Ireland was his sailing to Byzantium. The logical differences between activity and performance expressions do not prevent them from picking out the same occurrent. This point is quite compatible with the rest of Simons’s discussion, for ‘phase-dissective’ and ‘phase anti-dissective’ are defined for predicates of occurrents, not for occurrents themselves.4

(b) Classes. Simons distinguishes between high-brow and low-brow classes. A high-brow class is one abstract individual, such as the set of Danes; a low-brow class is many concrete individuals, such as the Danes. Low-brow class theory makes no provision for classes of classes; ‘the Danes and the Norwegians’ refers to a class whose members are people, not classes. May one say that the low-brow class of Danes is not the high-brow class? The singular is misleading. The claim is simply that the Danes are not the high-brow class: indeed, they are not any one thing, and no one thing is the Danes. For classes, ‘part of’ may be read as ‘some of’ or ‘a subclass of’: the Danes are some of the Europeans, a subclass of them, and in that sense part of them. Not surprisingly, extensional mereology suffices. But it would be wrong to suppose that parthood or anything else is a two-place relation on low-brow classes; if there is a relation between the Danes and the Europeans, it has several million terms.

(c) Masses. ‘Part of’ should be read as ‘some of’ for mass terms too: in Richard Sharvy’s example, some of my whisky-and-water is the water (although it is not some whisky-and-water). Like Sharvy, Simons resists the assimilation of masses to individuals. Mass terms cannot be analysed as class terms; ‘Most of the world’s gold is under water’ is not equivalent to ‘Most of the world’s portions of gold are under water’. What this argument does not close off is the possibility that ‘the world’s gold’ denotes a single scattered Quinean individual, the terrestrial part of the single individual denoted by ‘gold’. ‘Most of the world’s gold is under water’ might then be compared to ‘Most of Krakatoa is under water’, with ‘most’ meaning ‘the greater part’.

For Simons, masses stand to individuals in the relation of constitution, and thereby play a fundamental role in his neo-Aristotelian metaphysics. Nevertheless, extensional mereology may apply to masses. Indeed, he follows Sharvy in suggesting that they may provide its most plausible, if unintended, interpretation.

According to extensional mereology, objects are determined by their parts, for they are identical if they have the same parts. According to Simons, individual continuants are not determined by their parts. The issue is subtler than it looks, for the operative part-whole relation is reflexive. Each object is quite legitimately taken as a limiting case to be part of itself. Thus objects with the same parts are parts of each other: Simons argues that, if continuants, they may nevertheless be distinct. Some clarification is required.

A directed relation R may be said to yield extensionality just in case no two things have R from exactly the same things in the domain (∀x∀y(∀z(zRx↔zRy)→x=y)); the converse holds for every relation by Leibniz’s Law. Thus the relation of element to set yields extensionality on the domain of pure sets; so does its converse. It is easy to show that if R is reflexive and anti-symmetric (∀x∀y((xRy&yRx)→x=y)) then it yields extensionality. Conversely, if R is transitive and yields extensionality then R is anti-symmetric. Thus a reflexive transitive relation yields extensionality if and only if it is anti-symmetric. The part-whole relation is reflexive and transitive, making it closer to the relation of subset to set than that of element to set. Simons deals convincingly with objections to its reflexivity and transitivity. So the part-whole relation yields extensionality if and only if it is anti-symmetric. By contraposition, two objects have exactly the same parts if and only if each is part of the other.

How could two objects each be part of the other? For Simons, the basic notion is that of a proper part (≪; pp. 9-10). A proper part of a whole is in some sense less than the whole. ≪ is a transitive and asymmetric relation; it is therefore also irreflexive. From ≪, a reflexive notion of part is to be defined. The simplest definition is:

The reflexivity, anti-symmetry and transitivity of < follows from its definition and the asymmetry and transitivity of ≪. Thus < uncontroversially yields extensionality. No two objects have < to exactly the same objects (p. 11). However, < is not the only reflexive notion of part definable from ≪. Another is:

The reflexivity and transitivity of ≤ follows from its definition and the transitivity of ≪, but ≤ cannot be shown to be anti-symmetric without the use of special assumptions. Thus it is ≤ which does not yield extensionality, according to Simons. For him, it is a weaker relation than <; x<y entails x≤y but not conversely (pp. 112, 248).5

It can be shown that where distinct objects have < to each other, the second conjunct of the definition of ≤ drops out as irrelevant. That is, both objects have proper parts, and every proper part of one is a proper part of the other. Simons argues that two continuants can stand in this relation.

Some more terminology will help. Objects coincide if they have exactly the same parts (in the sense of ≤), and are superposed if they occupy exactly the same place. Both notions are relative to a time.6 Given that the location of an object is determined by the locations of its parts, coincidence entails superposition. Thus Simons argues for coincidence and superposition without identity. He appeals to three cases:

(A) The cat Tibbles consists of her tail, Tail, and the rest of her body, Tib. Tibbles is nevertheless distinct from the sum Tib + Tail, for she but not it is capable of Tail-less existence. According to Simons, Tibbles and Tib + Tail coincide and are superposed when Tail is in place.7

(B) The ship of Theseus is continually repaired, until none of the original material is left. However, someone collects the original material and makes it into a ship of exactly the original form. Which of the two ships is the original? Simons divides the original ship into two, a form-constant ship under continual repair and a matter-constant ship that is taken to pieces and reassembled. According to Simons, the two ships coincide and are superposed when first built.8
(C) I am not my body, since the latter will be in a coffin when I am not. According to Simons, I and my body coincide and are superposed when I am alive.9

It may be granted, at least for the sake of argument, that each case involves superposition without identity. For there is reason to doubt that any involves coincidence. In each case, one continuant seems to have a proper part the other lacks.

(A) One proper part of Tibbles is her nervous system. Is it a proper part of Tib + Tail? It is natural to suppose that any part of Tib + Tail consists of the sum of that part of it (if any) in Tib and that part of it (if any) in Tail. Thus Tibbles’s nervous system is part of Tib + Tail only if it is the nervous system in Tib + the nervous system in Tail. But these are distinct for the same sort of reason that Tibbles and Tib + Tail are distinct; the former but not the latter is capable of nervous-system-in-Tail-less existence. Thus Tibbles’s nervous system is not part of Tib + Tail. By transitivity, Tibbles too is not part of Tib + Tail.

(B) The form-constant ship has a form-constant hull and the matter-constant ship has a matter-constant hull. The hulls are distinct for the same reason as the ships: they will later be in different places. Since neither ship ever has more than one hull, the form-constant hull is a proper part of the form-constant ship but not of the matter-constant one and the matter-constant hull is a proper part of the matter-constant ship but not of the form-constant one. By transitivity, neither the form-constant ship nor the matter-constant ship is part of the other.

(C) My mind is not my brain, for the same reason that I am not my body: the latter will be in a coffin when the former is not. This no more makes my mind a Cartesian spirit than it does me. I exist in virtue of the functioning of my body; my mind exists in virtue of the functioning of my brain. My mind is a proper part of me, but not of my body. By transitivity, I too am not part of my body.
