None of the above is a knockdown objection, but each has some plausibility. No answer to any of them is discernible in Simons’s discussion. Thus he has not refuted the principle that coincident continuants are identical. The examples may instead refute the principle that superposed continuants coincide. Simons himself rejects this principle, for independent and admittedly inconclusive reasons (pp. 248-9). As a substitute for it, he suggests that superposed continuants weakly coincide, in the sense that they overlap the same individuals (p. 250). The objections to (A)-(C) seem to leave this weaker principle standing.

Simons uses modal mereology to define an impressive variety of concepts and principles for metaphysical theorizing. They cover amongst much else normal and essential parts, different kinds of dependence and integrity, and the distinction between substance and accident. Only the latter will be discussed here.

A substance is anything of which something is an accident but which is not itself an accident of anything. Simons defines x to be an accident of y if and only if (i) it is necessarily always necessary that if x exists then y exists without being part (≤) of x and (ii) y does not necessarily sometimes exist (p. 306).

Are persons substances? Simons wants his definitions to have them so, but considers the objection that they make persons accidents of the Universe, and therefore not substances. He replies that ‘the Universe’ either names a necessary existent or describes different things in different possible situations. The former case is ruled out by clause (ii) of the definition of accident; the latter leaves it open that, in some possible situation in which this person would exist, this Universe would not exist, contrary to clause (i) (p. 309). However, the example can be varied. ‘Space’ may rigidly designate a container capable of existing with different contents. It is necessarily always necessary that if I exist then space (this space) exists, certainly without being part of me. Moreover, space does not necessarily sometimes exist. There could have been nothing at all, and there could have been a space of a different number of dimensions, in which case this space would not have existed. Thus the definitions make me an accident of space, and therefore not a substance. Again, ‘the human race’ may rigidly designate our species, homo sapiens (not to be confused with the class or sum of its actually existing members). It is necessarily always necessary that if I exist then the human race exists, certainly without being part of me. Moreover, the human race does not necessarily sometimes exist. It might never have evolved at all. Thus the definitions make me an accident of the human race, and again not a substance. Yet the cited considerations just do not seem enough to make me an accident of space or the human race, let alone both.

The definition of ‘accident’ is defective. Can it be repaired? It is not obvious how. Even if an extra clause could be found to rule out the examples above, it risks being ad hoc. Indeed, clause (ii) is already ad hoc; the intention is to prevent ordinary substances from being counted as accidents of all necessary existents, but the effect is to prevent necessary existents from having any accidents at all. Gods would have no accidents, and would therefore not be substances. The relation of substance to accident may be simply too close to be captured by considerations of the sort used in Simons’s definition.

By the end of the book, Simons has reduced mereological theory to a core of four principles about ≪, the relation of a proper part to a whole. Three say that ≪ is an asymmetric transitive relation holding only between existents. Simons calls the fourth the Weak Supplementation Principle: if x is a proper part of y then y has a proper part z disjoint from x (i.e. x and z have no proper part in common, they are distinct, and neither is a proper part of the other; p. 362). Objects of special kinds may satisfy stronger principles, but only these four are formally or topic-neutrally valid.

Simons expresses the hope that his account will enable parthood to take a central place in ontology beside identity and existence (p. 363). That seems too much to ask. It is arguable that identity and existence are uniquely characterized by the logical principles which govern them.10 Thus any relation identity* governed by Leibniz’s Law and the principle of reflexivity is logically equivalent to identity. Nothing similar is true of parthood. For example, let p be any permutation of existents, and let x have ≪* to y just in case p(x) has ≪ to p(y). ≪* will satisfy exactly the same logical principles as ≪; in particular, it should satisfy Simons’s core mereological theory. Nevertheless, ≪* is not equivalent to ≪; the moon may have ≪* to my nose. Parthood is not a logical notion in the way identity and existence are, for its logic does not determine its content in the way theirs do. This can hardly be irrelevant to their role in ontology. However, parthood does have more of a logic than, say, the notion of gold has. In this respect one might compare parthood to similarity, causal necessity and temporal order. If it matters to ontology as much as they do, that is importance enough.

For the sake of interest, this article has concentrated on points of disagreement. These points are isolated ones. Simons’s discussion is almost always marked by fair-mindedness, formal rigour and subtle common sense. Parts could easily be the standard book on mereology for the next twenty or thirty years. It puts previous work in manageable order, purges it of unwanted assumptions, extends it, and points the way to further extensions. Metaphysics may be in danger of becoming a sober science.
I am grateful to David Wiggins for comments on an earlier version of this review.
Some writers even completed the analogy by postulating a null individual. ↩︎

Why not accommodate modality by adding it as a fifth dimension? Simons says that the move has not been seriously contemplated (p. 361 – all references to Parts unless otherwise specified). See now Andrew Brennan, ‘Best candidates and theories of identity’, Inquiry 29 (1986), pp. 429-38, at p. 434. ↩︎

In the absence of convincing counter-examples Simons allows the principle that occurrents with exactly the same parts are identical (p. 133). He denies that disparate occurrents must have a sum, although they will all be parts of the history of the Universe (p. 134); the history is not the sum of the occurrents, for something may overlap the history without overlapping any of the occurrents. ↩︎

The qualification ‘from Ireland’ is introduced for the sake of symmetry. The point could be made in terms of ‘sail’ and ‘sail to Byzantium’. ‘Read’ and ‘read War and Peace’ differ similarly. Consider also the activity verb ‘browse in’ and the performance verb ‘browse through’; my browsing in a magazine could be my browsing through it. ↩︎
The notational distinction between < and ≤ is unfortunately not used in much of the discussion. ↩︎
Simons argues persuasively against Roderick Chisholm’s mereological essentialism, on which there is no change or contingency in the parts of a genuine continuant. ↩︎

Simons draws on David Wiggins, ‘Mereological essentialism: asymmetrical essential dependence and the nature of continuants’, in E. Sosa (ed.), Essays on the Philosophy of Roderick M. Chisholm (Amsterdam: Rodopi, 1979). Wiggins slightly modifies his position at p. 93 n. 16 of his Sameness and Substance (Oxford, Blackwell, 1980). ↩︎

One may worry about the multiplication of ships. With sufficient ingenuity one could construct a continuum of persistence conditions for ships from the purely formal to the purely material. Is there a corresponding continuum of ships in every harbour? ↩︎
Simons draws on Frederick Doepke, ‘Spatially coinciding objects’, Ratio 24 (1982), pp. 45-60. ↩︎

See my ‘Equivocation and existence’, Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society 88 (1987/8), pp. 109-27. Compare Joseph Almog, ‘Logic and the world’, Journal of Philosophical Logic 18 (1989), pp. 197-220, on permutation-invariance as the mark of the logical. ↩︎

works.title: Review of R. Hale, Abstract Objects
passages: Review of R. Hale, Abstract Objects

Bob Hale’s monograph continues the tradition of Fregean thought about abstract objects to be found in Michael Dummett’s Frege, Philosophy of Language and Crispin Wright’s Frege’s Conception of Numbers as Objects. All those should enjoy it who finished Wright’s book asking for more. The reader is required to take little on trust except the general Frege/Dummett framework (for example, the murky notion of a criterion of identity is used without defence enough to impress its critics). My comments will focus on points of criticism rather than praise, for the usual reasons; those who have read the author’s earlier work will not be surprised to learn that Abstract Objects is a thoughtful and sophisticated performance, in argument fair-minded, patient, and often acute, in style pleasantly concise. Much recent work in its area is put under sharp scrutiny: Field on nominalism, Maddy on mathematical intuition, Kitcher and Edidin on the a priori, Hodes on arithmetic, McIntosh on Skolem. There is a welcome preparedness to follow the argument where it leads without claiming for the point of arrival any more permanent status than it deserves.
Review of R. Hale, Abstract Objects

Hale undertakes to defend a version of platonism, which he characterizes as the view that there are mind-independent abstract objects. His main argument for platonism is the Fregean one, that some true assertions contain singular terms which denote abstract objects if they denote anything; since the assertions are true, the singular terms denote. Mind-independence is a further issue; Hale takes it to mean that truths about the abstract objects hold independently of us; since its subsequent appearances are brief, it will not be discussed here. The relevant notions of singular term and abstract object are carefully examined in a chapter each. Both are given complicated, ad hoc analyses of the kind to which many of us react with the thought ‘Only lack of ingenuity will prevent me from finding an intuitive counter-example to this’. Hale’s analyses do indeed have counter-intuitive consequences, but there is a more serious point. We have no prior reason to suppose that philosophically significant concepts have interesting analyses into necessary and sufficient conditions. Our track record in finding them is poor. Hale follows the usual method of adding epicycles to a proposed analysis in the face of counter-examples until no more of the latter come to mind. What confidence is it rational to have in the result? One’s assurance that e (2.718…) is an abstract object if anything, and ‘e’ a singular term, will not be greatly increased if one learns that they fall under extremely tentative analyses of these notions. Even if one believed some messy analysis to be correct, the obvious conclusion to draw would be that the notion so defined had turned out to be unsuitable for systematic theorizing. It is true that, if the Fregean argument is not to beg the question, we must be able to recognize an expression as a singular term without first accepting that it denotes, and Hale’s modification of Dummett’s inferential criterion for singular termhood is intended to serve this purpose. However, platonists seem to have some other way of recognizing ‘7’ as a singular term—they are unlikely to have been using Hale’s criterion prior to reading his book—and this way will not presuppose that ‘7’ denotes 7, since they can recognize ‘7’ as a singular term in the same way as they can recognize ‘G’ as one, where G is defined to be the least even number greater than 2 which is not the sum of two primes; sensible platonists lack the belief that ‘G’ denotes G. Since the cues platonists tacitly but actually use carry more conviction than do recherché analyses, it might be worth finding out what they are. They seem to be linguistic rather than logical in character.
Review of R. Hale, Abstract Objects

Hale’s criterion for singular termhood leads him into difficulty with candidates such as ‘the age of the Queen’. He is driven to the implausible view that it has quite different meanings in ‘The age of the Queen is less than that of the Poet Laureate’, where it refers to a quantity, and ‘The age of the Queen is known only by her closest associates’, where it refers to a proposition stating her age (p. 29; what does it refer to in ‘The age of the Queen is rising’?). Hale’s treatment of abstract nouns such as ‘wisdom’ and ‘sliminess’ is disappointing. The possibility that they denote what the corresponding adjectives express in some other way is dismissed by the invocation of Frege’s name (pp. 4, 33). Universals are claimed to lack general criteria of identity, without any consideration of the obvious candidate: necessary co-instantiation (e.g. p. 40). It is strangely assumed that one can recognize cases of the quality of mercy as such only if one has a description approximately synonymous with ‘merciful’ (ibid.). The analysis of the abstract/concrete distinction (pp. 59–63) seems to imply that the time but not the place of an event is abstract.
Review of R. Hale, Abstract Objects

The middle chapters of the book contain useful treatments of knowledge and identifying thought about abstract objects, but I shall discuss only the long final chapter, on indeterminacy of reference as a threat to platonism. Hale takes the heroic course of defending a particular identification of numbers with sets as the correct one against Benacerraf’s familiar argument in ‘What Numbers Could Not Be’. He argues that numbers are equivalence classes of concepts under the relation of 1–1 correlation between their extensions—call these cardinality classes—on the grounds that these are the classes grasp of whose membership condition is in effect grasp of the Fregean criterion of identity for numbers (I omit much detail). Several things seem to have gone wrong. For instance, classes have many membership conditions (by extensionality); some membership conditions for cardinality classes do not involve 1–1 correlation (the Schröder–Bernstein theorem gives one example) and some membership conditions for non-cardinality classes do involve 1–1 correlation. So far as I can see, Hale says nothing to rule out alternative identifications of numbers with unions of cardinality classes or with their intersections with some class containing concepts with extensions of the relevant cardinalities. Although the issue is supposed to be the identity of the natural numbers, the argument would at most show that the cardinal numbers (including infinite ones) are the cardinality classes: but from this it would by no means follow that the finite cardinal numbers are the cardinality classes of finitely instantiated concepts, as Hale requires. Other difficulties could be mentioned.
Review of R. Hale, Abstract Objects

If Hale’s identification is not necessary, is it at least possible? He discusses the question of its consistency against the background of standard set-theoretic axioms (pp. 217–19). An argument for inconsistency not considered is the following. Consider the set of singly instantiated concepts, a cardinality class. With each singly instantiated concept can be associated its single instance. Therefore the set of all things which uniquely instantiate some concept exists, by the Replacement Axiom of ZF set theory. Now every set x uniquely instantiates some concept, if only the concept of being identical with x (we need to be able to specify concepts by means of parameters in this way, since we need to be able to count classes specified by means of parameters and on Hale’s view ‘the number of’ applies in the first instance to concepts). Thus we have a set containing all sets, which leads to the usual contradiction. Hale does have a defence against this argument, since his official view (p. 269 n. 23) is that abstract objects form a hierarchy such that cardinality classes do not exist, and numbers are really classes all of whose elements have less than a given rank; however, he suggests that contradiction might be avoided without appeal to this point (p. 269 n. 25). The official view raises further questions. Is there such a thing as the number of objects falling under a given concept (e.g. being self-identical, being a set) when those objects do not form a set? If so, how are considerations of rank to be accommodated? If not, it looks as though the primary application of ‘the number of’ is to sets, not—as Hale would have it—to classes. A better-defined theory of concepts and classes is required.
Review of R. Hale, Abstract Objects

Hale considers Harold Hodes’s argument that the platonist cannot say what the microstructure of reference is in virtue of which the standard numberer (taking each concept to the number of its instances) rather than some variant of it (for which the numbers have been permuted) is what we mean by ‘the number of’. He replies that Hodes can specify the non-standard numberers only in terms of the standard numberer, which suggests that the standard numberer is special after all (p. 223). This seems just to restate the difficulty. If there is a standard numberer then of course it is privileged, but Hodes is suggesting that since the platonist cannot explain why or how one particular function from concepts to numbers should get to have this privilege, one should conclude that there is no standard numberer. As an additional argument, Hale claims that only the standard numberer respects all equivalences of the type ‘The number of Fs = 4 iff there are exactly 4 Fs’ (pp. 223–4). However, although the right-hand side is equivalent to an unambiguous formula of quantification theory with identity, ‘4’ is not thereby disambiguated; non-standard numberers merely correspond to non-standard functions from numerical quantifiers to numbers. Finally, Hale suggests that Hodes’s argument is merely a special case of a general permutation argument used by Wallace, Davidson, and Putnam from Frege’s Context Principle to the indeterminacy of all reference; abstract objects would then be no worse off than concrete ones. The idea is that the reference of singular terms depends only on the truth-conditions of sentences (by the Context Principle); since permutations of reference can leave the truth-conditions fixed, reference is indeterminate. Much depends on how truth-conditions are individuated. If logical equivalence is sufficient for sameness of truth-conditions, the argument may be valid but the Context Principle is quite implausible; if truth-conditions are individuated in a way sensitive to sub-sentential structure, the permutations will not preserve truth-conditions. In particular, there would be room for independent causal constraints on reference which might determine it for concrete but not for abstract objects.
Review of R. Hale, Abstract Objects

A few minor grumbles. There is some confusion between ‘All mental events are abstract’ and ‘All abstract objects are mental’ (pp. 49–50, my formulations). A principle of extensionality for concepts is presupposed without argument (p. 71). Hale argues in effect that any apriority-preserving inference rule will allow us to construct arbitrarily long deductions from a given piece of a priori knowledge (p. 139); this does not seem to apply to elimination rules. Hale dismisses mathematical intuition, but speaks of ‘direct discernment of fundamental conceptual relationships’ (p. 142) without much explanation. There is some discussion of whether ‘each abstract object is the value of some function for some suitable argument’ (pp. 184, 190); so stated the answer is trivially positive; needed refinements are introduced only much later. The putative indeterminacy of reference to sets is discussed under the assumption that the mapping from {x:Fx} to {x:Fx∨Hx} (H fixed) is 1–1 (pp. 199, 225); consider the null set and {x:Hx}. There is a quantifier-shift fallacy from ‘All F-identity involves some criterion of identity’ to ‘Some criterion of identity is involved in all F-identity’ (pp. 213–14, my formulations). Many formulae lack essential logical symbols (pp. 71–2, 99, 119, 203, 246–7) as a result of proof-reading oversights.
Review of R. Hale, Abstract Objects
It is easy to stand on the sidelines and berate the players. Bob Hale is to be applauded for the seriousness and intelligence with which he has grappled with appallingly difficult issues.

works.title: Review of T.E. Burke, The Philosophy of Popper
passages: Review of T.E. Burke, The Philosophy of Popper

Sir Karl Popper holds that no aspect of human theory or practice is above criticism. Dr Burke is more concerned with this fallibilist principle as such than with the details of its application to politics or science. He offers a thoughtful critique of the canon, thorough, untechnical, unfussy and wisely free from paraphrase, since Popper is an easy philosopher to read. Burke argues the plausible case that, whatever Popper says, his fallibilism is ill-placed to withstand two of its intended victims, relativism and scepticism. In effect, Popper tries to leave criticism above criticism: he writes as though falsification, but not verification, were conclusive. Given that criticisms too can be mistaken, he cannot explain where our admittedly tenuous grip on reality comes from. However, Burke accepts Popper’s dilemma, either complete certainty for some statements or complete uncertainty for all; neither properly considers the alternative, that all statements are more or less probable or improbable. Some assumptions are in more urgent need of criticism than others; it does not follow that some are in no need of criticism at all.
Review of T.E. Burke, The Philosophy of Popper

Dr Burke thinks that, to avoid relativism, he must rule that any difference in how we investigate makes a difference in what we investigate (p. 103). Thus if a table looks perfectly smooth, physics cannot tell us that it is not (p. 111); my dream-thought ‘I am not dreaming’ is not falsified when I wake up (p. 113); what I praise as ‘killing for the sake of honour’ cannot be what you condemn as ‘murder’ (p. 200). Burke does not mention that the main detailed semantics based on these verificationist principles is the intuitionist one for mathematics; it rejects the law of excluded middle and revises classical theorems wholesale. Such a cure (an ‘innocuous relativism’, p. 119) is as painful as the disease. Fortunately, we need not choose between Burke’s alternatives, since we can reject his assumption, for which I could find no support, that unargued choices cannot be erroneous (p. 86). Indeed, they need not even be unjustified: he points out that we cannot adopt our first criteria for valid arguments on the basis of argument, but ignores Quine’s point that these criteria have evolved under the demands of an inhospitable environment. Nor does Burke consider the standard charge that relativism is self-refuting: it claims that all criteria are equally good because there is no neutral standpoint from which to judge them, yet this claim itself seems to presuppose a neutral standpoint, for without one, as Quine argues, we must judge from our own standpoint, which rejects many criteria as worse than ours and may be able to accept others as improvements.
Review of T.E. Burke, The Philosophy of Popper

Dr Burke concedes less to scepticism than to relativism. He says that if we always miscounted, ‘count’ would be meaningless; could not the sceptic agree, happy to throw his language into question along with everything else? Against Popper’s final defence, from the concept of approximation to the truth, Burke understates his case: Popper has had to abandon both the quoted definition (p. 127), for its untoward technical consequences, and his well-publicized abstention from inductive inference, a feat on which the fallibilism had been supposed to depend. These facts, however, will not surprise the reader of this unfashionable but attractively serious work.

works.title: Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics
passages: Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics
Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics (Oxford University Press, 2025), 280 pp., $35.00 (hbk), ISBN 9780197787809.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

Amie Thomasson is a leader of a programme for deflating the pretensions of metaphysics and finding something better for philosophers to do. She locates this programme within a broad neo-pragmatist tradition. Her latest book is a further contribution to the overall project and updates it by reference to recent trends in metaphysics.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

The first half of the book tries to show that there are no deep metaphysical truths out there to be discovered. This enterprise risks self-defeat, for if there are no deep metaphysical truths out there, that itself looks suspiciously like a deep metaphysical truth discovered by Thomasson and her allies, if their arguments work.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

Thomasson starts by emphasizing the lack of agreement in contemporary metaphysics, and the dim prospects for achieving it. This heightens the risk of self-defeat, for there is just as little agreement in her own line of work, contemporary metametaphysics, and the prospects for achieving it are equally dim. Indeed, metametaphysics is hard to separate from metaphysics, as just seen. The book will persuade few contemporary metaphysicians of the error of their ways; this review will no doubt leave neo-pragmatists feeling equally untroubled.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

According to Thomasson, the epistemology of contemporary metaphysics is irredeemably mysterious, and so, conducive to scepticism. That will be news to many who work in metaphysics and take its epistemology to be broadly abductive, like that of other highly theoretical sciences. On one version of this view, metaphysics works by inference to the best explanation; its explanations are constitutive rather than causal. For Thomasson, a metaphysical theory does not do the right sort of work in explanations to be confirmed if the explanations succeed; some other metaphysical theory could be substituted for it without explanatory loss. As she puts it, the metaphysical theory does not ‘fuel’ the explanations.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

The book’s dismissal of inference to the best explanation in metaphysics is too cursory to be convincing. More specifically, its picture of explanation is too closely modelled on causal explanation to give explanation in metaphysics a fair chance. A more sensitive approach would have spent more time on the varieties of non-causal explanation in the natural sciences before making comparisons with metaphysics. For example, theoretical unification is a form of non-causal scientific explanation, as in Newton’s unification of terrestrial and celestial mechanics. As that example suggests, unifying explanations can confirm the unifying theory. Metaphysical theories, with their great generality, are often intended to play a unifying role; if they succeed, why should they not be confirmed thereby?
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

On an increasingly widespread view, which this book ignores, abduction plays a central role in the epistemology of logic and mathematics too. Axioms and first principles of logic or set theory are not self-evident, nor are they conventional stipulations; genuine non-verbal disputes rage as to whether they are true or truth-preserving. Their theoretical standing depends on their abductive virtues—simplicity, strength, and fit with evidence, including the capacity to unify what is already known in the field without collapsing into absurdity—or lack of them. The theorems of such an abductively confirmed logical theory are good candidates for principles of a structural core of metaphysics.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

As it happens, I am no enthusiast for most of the specific metaphysical approaches criticized in the book. But they are serious attempts at systematic theorizing, which deserve a more discriminating and careful treatment. Arguably, their main problem is not that they are scientistic, but that they are not scientific enough—they are under-constrained and overfitted.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

In calling metaphysics a science, still immature if not still young, I do not restrict the term ‘science’ to the natural sciences, such as physics and biology, in which experimentation, observation, and measurement play so large a role. I use the term ‘science’ broadly, for any form of systematic, critical, evidence-based inquiry. In that sense, both mathematics and scholarly history are non-natural sciences. So is metaphysics, and philosophy more generally.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

By contrast, Thomasson leaves no room for metaphysics as a science. In particular, she reduces ontology to ‘easy ontology’, which merely expresses trivial conceptual or linguistic rules. The book repeatedly adverts to such rules en masse but does not articulate them with the clarity or generality a linguist might expect.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

A main example running through the book is how nominalisation introduces talk of properties by taking us from ‘That house is red’ to ‘That house has the property of being red’, for example. Thomasson treats such equivalences as trivially valid instances of a linguistic rule, making the existence of properties a case of epistemologically unproblematic easy ontology. She fails to note that the underlying rule is a naïve comprehension principle for properties, which is notoriously inconsistent by a variant of Russell’s paradox, since it makes ‘The property of not self-having has itself’ equivalent to its own negation. The outputs of a logically inconsistent rule are hardly epistemologically unproblematic.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

Of course, one can try to restore consistency by revising the original comprehension principle without dropping its most everyday instances, but historically, that has involved an arduous process of logical investigation and discovery quite unlike Thomasson’s image of easy ontology. Indeed, it has led to higher-order metaphysics, a rapidly emerging branch of metaphysics not mentioned in the book. Higher-order metaphysics uses the rigorous methods of type theory and higher-order logic, with quantification into predicate and sentence position; theorems are proved and discoveries made, as elsewhere in logic and mathematics. Higher-order theorizing is not just niche metaphysics. On its intended interpretation, second-order logic is arguably the best available framework for Peano arithmetic as a branch of mathematics since second-order arithmetic is categorical, in the sense that all its models are isomorphic to each other, whereas first-order arithmetic allows models of different non-standard structures and thereby fails to capture mathematicians’ intentions. For related reasons, higher-order logic is arguably the best available framework for set theory too. By contrast, in what the book presents by omission as an attitude of complacent incuriosity, easy ontologists leave underlying contradictions unidentified, rich logical structures unexplored, and deep structural connections with other disciplines unmade.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

For Thomasson, attempts at scientific metaphysics are worse than futile. They depend on an underlying error: the misconception that all discourse has a single function, to ‘track’ features of reality. They ignore the diversity of other functions served by language. When the book turns to another form of contemporary metaphysics, the reader can already predict that its failure will be blamed on this misconception. It is like a doctor who diagnoses all patients with the same disease, whatever symptoms they present with.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

Probably, all the metaphysicians whom Thomasson criticizes for treating language as though it served only a single function would happily agree with her that it serves many. Not only are there multiple forms of non-declarative sentence, such as the imperative and the interrogative, and multiple forms of verbal but non-sentential utterances, such as greetings and exclamations, but uttering a given declarative sentence can also serve many different functions. One can say ‘It’s cold outside’ to start a conversation with a stranger, to get someone to close the window, to parody British conversation, to display one’s competence in English, or whatever. So much is uncontroversial. What non-easy metaphysicians may add is that the sentence still expresses the proposition that it’s cold outside, even if the utterance’s primary purpose is not to communicate its truth. Which proposition it expresses is determined by the compositional semantics of the language, applied to the given context. Normally, achieving the other purposes depends on expressing the proposition, unless the speaker just wants to make a noise or create a diversion. Non-easy metaphysicians focus on the proposition expressed.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

As the book goes on, it encourages the reader to expect much-needed support for its deflationary treatment of metaphysics from functionally oriented linguistics. When it finally arrives, in Chapter 7, in the form of Michael Halliday’s Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL), it proves a dampish squib. Thomasson’s exposition focuses on three ubiquitous aspects of mature language: the ‘ideational metafunction’ concerns informational content, the ‘interpersonal metafunction’ the negotiation of social relations, and the ‘textual metafunction’ the organization of discourse. Of these, non-easy metaphysicians will acknowledge the obvious importance of the interpersonal and textual metafunctions for communication but deny them any distinctive role in metaphysics.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

That leaves the ideational. On Thomasson’s account, SFL has nothing very helpful to offer on how exactly a given sentence encodes some given informational content. There, by default, it hands over to more standard theories of compositional semantics. Although Thomasson evinces some sympathy for old-fashioned expressivist theories about various kinds of sentence, she is well aware of the notorious Frege-Geach problem concerning the need to explain embedded occurrences of such sentences under negation and other operators. She does not reject compositional semantics outright, though her instinct may be to deflate it, whatever exactly that involves.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

Thomasson takes modality as a case study of her approach in practice. According to her, the primary function of the modal verb system is interpersonal in the SFL sense. For example, we use deontic modals in applying social norms, and metaphysical modality is associated with the application of semantic norms.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

There is a large hole in Thomasson’s account of modal verbs: restricted circumstantial modals. Very young children grasp the difference between ‘I can reach it!’ and ‘I can’t reach it!’. ‘That could easily fall over’ is only slightly more sophisticated. Such non-normative distinctions have clear practical utility. Light has been cast on their epistemology by the work of Sonia Roca-Royes on modal induction, Margot Strohminger on modal perception, and Barbara Vetter on ability modals, amongst others. Again, uses of the contextually restricted modal verbs ‘would’ and ‘might’ in everyday counterfactual conditionals and elsewhere typically arise from offline applications of our capacity for predictive updating, calibrated by past experience, to hypothetical inputs in the imagination.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

Thomasson tries to marginalize such work by claiming that it concerns only ‘empirical modalities’, and so is irrelevant to metaphysical modality, which is what metaphysicians care about. For instance, she claims, empirical modalities cannot distinguish the statue from the clay (190-1). That is a mistake. I know in a very ordinary way that I could destroy the statue without destroying the clay by dropping the statue down the stairwell.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

Metaphysical modality is best understood as the limiting case of circumstantial modalities. Whatever is restrictedly objectively possible is also unrestrictedly objectively possible. Such an approach to metaphysical modality makes far better sense of Kripke’s cases of the necessary a posteriori and the contingent a priori than does Thomasson’s strained attempt to link metaphysical modality to semantic norms. She also misses the connection between metaphysical modality and various kinds of non-epistemic, non-deontic modality in natural science, such as the possible states in phase spaces and dynamical systems and the possible outcomes in probability spaces. According to Kripke, such scientific examples inspired his possible worlds semantics for modal logic.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

Thomasson’s reliance on FSL has misled her into seriously misrepresenting the modal verb system. A more standard compositional semantics for modal discourse, such as Angelika Kratzer’s, is both much more fruitful linguistically and much more friendly to modal metaphysics. As a test case for the neo-pragmatist approach, modality gives a negative verdict.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

In the final chapters, Thomasson recommends metaphysicians to find more humble and more useful employment as conceptual or linguistic engineers. If they are not to do more harm than good, they will need to understand the conceptual or linguistic systems they are re-engineering considerably better than Thomasson’s FSL approach understands the modal verb system.
Review of Amie L. Thomasson, Rethinking Metaphysics

The book presents engineers as making practical decisions, but of course, such decisions are not epistemologically unconstrained. They should know that the bridge will not fall down if built according to their plan, or at least that its probability of falling down is acceptably low. Thomasson puts the epistemological standard for respectable employment very high: the work must be done ‘in an epistemologically transparent way’ (97). What is epistemological transparency? Having wrestled with the nature of knowledge by perception, memory, testimony, and inference, it is hard to find any of them epistemologically transparent. No good evidence is provided that conceptual or linguistic engineering is any more epistemologically transparent than contemporary metaphysics. As a sample of neo-pragmatism at its best, the book left me with a strong sense of a degenerating research programme.

works.title: Essences, heuristics, and metaphysical illusions
passages: The paper is a critique of Kit Fine’s central argument in ‘Essence and Modality’ for the hyperintensionality of essence-attributing operators, from the premise that it is essential to Socrates that he is Socrates but not that he belongs to {Socrates}. Similar arguments can be given about what is essential to natural numbers, but are provably unsound. The proof of unsoundness exploits the category of singular terms with a compositionally complex semantics that are nevertheless directly referential, such as ‘7 + 1’; they must not be confused with definite descriptions. The proof depends on the standard logic of identity, not on any intensionalist assumption. The errors in our pre-theoretic essentialists judgments are explained by our reliance on an efficient but fallible heuristic. The analogous premises of Fine’s argument are generated by the same heuristic and so are untrustworthy. More generally, it is suggested, hyperintensionalist theorizing is guilty of overfitting dodgy data. The paper also notes a strand of Fine’s original article that restricts its claims to the intelligibility rather than truth of hyperintensional essentialism; its intelligibility is not contested.

I first encountered a version of Kit Fine’s seminal paper ‘Essence and Modality’ in 1992, when he presented it to an informal discussion group hosted by David Charles in his rooms at Oriel College, Oxford. It made a powerful impact. We came away with the impression that Fine was offering potentially devastating counterexamples to a widely held, Kripke-inspired modal approach to understanding essence, cases where one proposition but not another is essential to an object, even though the two propositions are necessarily equivalent. In particular, it is essential to Socrates that he is Socrates but inessential to him that he belongs to singleton Socrates, the set {Socrates}, even though, necessarily, he is Socrates if and only if he belongs to singleton Socrates. Thus, since essence cuts finer than modality, the first is irreducible to the second. That is how the paper has generally been received since it was published (Fine 1994). As a result, it has inspired the subsequent more general search for finer-grained, hyperintensional, metaphysical structure, which has clearly been one of the most significant trends in metaphysics over the past thirty years. There is even talk of a ‘hyperintensional revolution’ to match the ‘intensional revolution’ of the 1960s (Nolan 2014).

Rereading ‘Essence and Modality’ in 2024, I was surprised to find that its official claims are much more cautious than I had remembered, and than the received interpretation implies. For instance, we read:

Nor is it critical to the example [about Socrates and singleton Socrates] that the reader actually endorse the particular modal and essentialist claims to which I have made appeal. All that is necessary is that he should recognize the intelligibility of a position which makes such claims. For any reasonable account of essence should not be biased towards one metaphysical view rather than the other. It should not settle, as a matter of definition, any issue which we are inclined to regard as a matter of substance. (Fine 1994: 5)

On this conciliatory interpretation, the point of the example is not to show that modal accounts of essence are false, but merely to show that they are synthetic rather than analytic, in some relevant sense.1
A similar point may be intended in this passage:

For it seems to be possible to agree on all of the modal facts and yet disagree on the essentialist facts. But if any modal criterion of essence were correct, such a situation would be impossible. (Fine 1994: 8)

Of course, if two people agree on all modal facts but not on some essentialist facts, it follows trivially that some essentialist facts are not modal facts. But that argument is dialectically ineffective unless one has already ruled out the view that essentialist facts are modal facts ‘in disguise’. But the passage avoids such question-begging when read as suggesting that philosophers can agree in all explicitly modal discourse while disagreeing in some explicitly essentialist discourse. One might conclude that explicitly essentializing terms are not synonymous with explicitly modal alleged analyses.

Given the insensitivity of the concept of necessity to variations in source [whose essence yields necessity], it is hardly surprising that it is incapable of capturing a concept which is sensitive to such variation. (Fine 1994: 9)

Such a difference between the two concepts does not by itself force a difference between what they are concepts of. A theorist could in principle concede that the concept ‘essential’ involves a source parameter, which the concept ‘necessary’ lacks, while still arguing that the parameter is a redundancy in thought that makes no difference in reality.2 Not all differences between concepts project onto differences between what they are concepts of.

On the envisaged concessive view that ‘Essence and Modality’ in this mood permits (but does not endorse), essentiality is in fact necessity, even though the concept ‘essential’ is not the concept ‘necessary’; the genuine cognitive differences in our uses of the two words need not reflect differences in what they refer to. Likewise, gold is in fact the element with atomic number 79, even though the concept ‘gold’ is not the concept ‘the element with atomic number 79’; the genuine cognitive differences in our uses of the word and phrase need not reflect differences in what they refer to. Again, on the pretence that the good is in fact what maximises utility, the concept ‘good’ is still not the concept ‘what maximises utility’; the genuine cognitive differences in our uses of the word and the phrase do not prove a difference in what they refer to, whatever G.E. Moore’s ‘open question argument’ may be intended to show.

A similar caution appears in the paper’s treatment of a subsidiary theme: the analogy between essence and necessity, on one side, and definition and analyticity, on the other. Just as an essence is overtly the essence of something, so too a definition is overtly the definition of something. By contrast, neither necessity nor analyticity is overtly so sourced in anything, though there is the metaphysical theory that all necessity is sourced in essences of things, and the analogous theory that all analyticity is sourced in definitions of things; Fine calls the denial of the latter theory ‘holism’. Here too, he is surprisingly concessive:

However, just as in the essentialist case, the important issue concerns intelligibility rather than truth. We want to know if there could be a genuine difference of opinion as to whether ‘man’ is correctly definable as ‘bachelor or husband’ or as to whether some form of holism is correct; and when the point is put in this way, it seems hard to see how it could be denied. (Fine 1994: 11)
He also echoes the discussion of agreement and disagreement:

For just as it appeared to be possible to agree on the modal facts and yet disagree on the essentialist facts, so it appears to be possible to agree on the facts of analyticity and yet disagree on the facts of meaning. (Fine 1994: 11)

As before, some interpretation is required. If two people agree on all facts about analyticity but not on some facts about definitions, it follows trivially that some facts about definitions are not facts about analyticity. But that argument is dialectically ineffective unless one has already ruled out the view that facts about definitions are facts about analyticity ‘in disguise’. The passage avoids such question-begging when read as suggesting that philosophers can agree in all discourse explicitly about analyticity while disagreeing in some discourse explicitly about definitions. One might conclude that some terms of the latter discourse are not synonymous with alleged analyses in terms of the former discourse.

In such passages, ‘Essence and Modality’ presents itself as unambitiously defending just the intelligibility of the striking metaphysical claims for whose truth the paper is standardly read as providing robust arguments. That the paper achieves the modest goal of vindicating the intelligibility of those metaphysical claims is hardly in doubt. Obviously, by ordinary standards, many competent, reasonable, unconfused speakers of English—for instance, Kit Fine—can understand and even assent to statements like ‘Socrates is necessarily but not essentially a member of the set whose only member is Socrates’. The question is whether the metaphysical claims are true, not whether they are so much as intelligible.
Confusingly, in other passages, the paper is much less inhibited, and does address the question of truth:
But, intuitively, this [that Socrates essentially belongs to singleton Socrates] is not so. It is no part of the essence of Socrates to belong to the singleton. (Fine 1994: 4–5)

This is an outright claim about what is in the essence of Socrates, not just a claim about what is in our concept ‘essence of Socrates’. It corresponds to the claim that hydrogen is no part of gold, not to the mere claim that our concept ‘hydrogen’ is no part of our concept ‘gold’. The paper contains many more passages like that:

There is nothing in the nature of a person, if I may put it this way, which demands that he belongs to this or that set or which demands, given that the person exists, that there even be any sets. (Fine 1994: 5)
But it is not essential to Socrates that he be distinct from the [Eiffel] Tower, for there is nothing in his nature which connects him in any special way to it. (Fine 1994: 5)
But it is no part of Socrates’ essence that there be infinitely many prime numbers or that the abstract world of numbers, sets, or what have you, be just as it is. (Fine 1994: 5)

In these passages, Fine directly tells the reader what is in the essence of Socrates, though he does not explain how he knows. Thus, the usual metaphysical reading of ‘Essence and Modality’ also has clear textual support.

This paper concerns the metaphysical view for which ‘Essence and Modality’ is famous, irrespective of Fine’s intentions in writing it. Given uncontested background assumptions, do the proposed counterexamples indeed refute modal characterizations of essence? I will argue that although the key judgments about the examples may feel compellingly natural, they issue from a way of thinking whose outputs in similar cases are provably false; thus, the key judgments are unsafe and not to be relied on. More generally, all the extra theoretical complications incurred by the hyperintensionality of an anti-modalist theory of essence are likely to be artefacts of overfitting error-infected data. In other words, it results from a methodological pathology well-known in the natural and social sciences, whereby theories are made more and more complicated to achieve an exact fit with data, undermining theorists’ ability to spot outlying, potentially erroneous data points.3
It is essential to Socrates that he is Socrates.
It is essential to Socrates that he belongs to {Socrates}.
It is essential to {Socrates} that Socrates belongs to it.

On a Finean view, (1) is true and (2) false. For the set {Socrates} is in some sense extraneous to the man Socrates, while Socrates is trivially not extraneous to himself. In the same sense, Socrates is not extraneous to {Socrates}, for sets as normally understood are somehow constituted from their members (if any); in particular, {Socrates} is constituted from its only member, Socrates. Thus, (3) is presumably true, on the Finean view. The difference in truth-value between (2) and (3) reflects an asymmetry in constitution between sets and their members.

The Finean denial of (2) is not neutral on the metaphysics of sets. It coheres with a broadly iterative conception of sets, on which they are built up from their members stage by stage. In particular, {Socrates} is built up from Socrates, while Socrates is not built up from {Socrates}, so Socrates and {Socrates} are distinct. More generally, by the foundation (or regularity) axiom of standard Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory, every non-empty set is disjoint from at least one of its members; so, always, x≠{x}, otherwise {x} would not be disjoint from x. However, there are also well-developed alternative theories of non-wellfounded sets, which drop the foundation axiom and allow cases where x={x}; such an x is called a Quine atom. If Socrates is a Quine atom, then he is the set {Socrates} and belongs to it just by belonging to himself.4 In that case, the Finean objection to (2) might well lapse. This paper does not press such concerns. A background iterative conception of sets for the denial of (2) is plausible and widely held, independently of issues about hyperintensionality; it can reasonably be conceded, at least for the sake of argument.

Natural numbers are often, and very naturally, understood as metaphorically constructed in a similarly iterative way: a natural number is the result of starting from 0 and adding 1 as many times as needed. Such an iterative conception of natural numbers, although not uncontested, is plausible and widely held, independently of issues about hyperintensionality; it too can reasonably be conceded, at least for the sake of argument.
Given the iterative conception of natural numbers, consider these three statements:
It is essential to 8 that it is 8.
It is essential to 8 that it is 9 – 1.
It is essential to 8 that it is 7 + 1.

On a Fine-inspired view, (4) is true and (5) false. For, in the relevant sense, the natural number 9 is extraneous to the natural number 8, while 8 is trivially not extraneous to itself. In the same sense, 7 is not extraneous to 8. On the iterative conception, 8 is somehow built up from 7, and 9 from 8; 8 is not built up from 9. Presumably, (6) is true, on this Fine-inspired view. The difference in truth-value between (5) and (6) reflects an asymmetry in constitution between natural numbers and their predecessors.

Since 1 is itself one of the natural numbers to be constructed, we can enhance fidelity to the underlying vision by substituting the successor operation s for adding 1 and the predecessor operation p for subtracting 1, so that (5) and (6) become (5*) and (6*) respectively:
It is essential to 8 that it is p(9).
It is essential to 8 that it is s(7).
Given the iterative conception of natural numbers, one may naturally judge that (5*) is false, just like (2) and (5), while (6*) is true, just like (3) and (6).

One might worry that p is undefined on 0, since we are concerned with operations on natural numbers, not on positive and negative integers. Similarly, one might worry that the result of subtracting a larger natural number from a smaller one is undefined. One can easily solve these difficulties by stipulating that p(0)=0 and that m−n=0 for m<n. The artificiality of such stipulations only strengthens the impression that (5) and (5*) are false.

One can strengthen the analogy between the iterative conception of sets and the iterative conception of natural numbers, and subsume the latter under the former as a special case, by adopting one of the standard ways of identifying natural numbers with pure sets. On Zermelo’s way, 0 is the empty set {} and, for any natural number n, s(n) is {n}. On von Neumann’s way, 0 is again the empty set and for any natural number n, s(n) is n∪{n}. Both ways preserve the desired order of constitution, which is part of their appeal. However, no such identification of natural numbers with sets is assumed in what follows.

So far, apparently, so good. But something is wrong. For 9−1 and 7+1, and p(9) and s(7), are all just natural numbers, indeed, they are all the same natural number, 8. All five of these numerical terms coincide in reference, so substituting them for each other in (4), (5), (6), (5*), and (6*) should make no difference to their truth-value, contrary to the Fine-inspired judgments that (4), (6), and (6*) are true while (5) and (5*) are false. What is going on?

An initial reaction might be that the semantically complex expressions ‘9−1’, ‘7+1’, ‘p(9)’, and ‘s(7)’ are not names but definite descriptions. After all, they are naturally paraphrased in ordinary English by definite descriptions such as ‘the result of subtracting one from nine’, ‘the sum of seven and one’, ‘the predecessor of nine’, and ‘the successor of seven’. Such analyses of functional expressions in terms of predicates and definite descriptions were commonplace in logicist formalizations of mathematics. If one treats definite descriptions as quantifier phrases, one might then suspect that inter-substituting co-denoting definite descriptions within the scope of operators such as ‘it is essential to 8 that’ can fail to preserve the truth-value of sentences in which they occur, and so induce fallacies analogous to those in early critiques of quantified modal logic.

On further reflection, however, such reliance on definite descriptions represents a failure to take seriously a distinctive feature of standard mathematical notation. Mathematicians often achieve an elegantly streamlined notation by treating functional expressions as basic, for example, in both algebra and analysis. A notable case in point is primitive recursive arithmetic, whose theoretical significance depends on its elementary character. That is achieved in part by formulating it in a quantifier-free language, where no definite description operator is available, and formulas are read as implicit generalizations over arbitrary natural numbers. Psychologically, the use of function symbols such as ‘+’ in mathematics feels entirely natural; what feels unnatural and clunky is to use predicates and definite descriptions instead.

There is no semantic obstacle to treating functional expressions as primitive. In particular, we can give a quasi-homophonic recursive semantics for a functional expression in a metalanguage that extends the mathematical object-language, using the same functional expression to state the relevant semantic clause, just as we might expect for a primitive expression. Informally, for example, the reference of ‘7 plus 5’ is the reference of ‘7’ plus the reference of ‘5’, which is 7 plus 5, which is 12.

More formally and generally, we consider a formal language with both constant and variable atomic singular terms, and complex singular terms built up with function symbols. For any singular term t and assignment a_ of values to all variables, ref⁡a_(t) is the referent of t under a_. The case of ‘+’ is exemplary. Syntactically, whenever t1 and t2 are singular terms, so is ‘(’^t1^‘+’^t2^‘)’, where ^ is concatenation of syntactic strings. Semantically, we assume for simplicity that the domain is just the set of natural numbers. Then the natural semantic clause for ‘+’ says, for any singular terms t1 and t2:

The relativization to the assignment a_ enables us to bind variables in the scope of ‘+’, if we so wish, as in ‘For all natural numbers m and n, m+n=n+m’. Analogous syntactic and semantic treatments apply to the function symbols for subtraction, the successor and predecessor operations (totally defined as above), multiplication, exponentiation, and so on. Together, these clauses recursively determine the referent (under an assignment) of arbitrarily complex singular terms in a language for arithmetic, built up using functional symbols. Such terms are semantically complex, because their semantic evaluation is non-trivially compositional. But that semantic complexity does not imply any complexity in the corresponding referents or semantic values, which are (in this case) simply natural numbers. After all, by elementary arithmetic, equations such as ‘7+5=12’ are true, where ‘=’ means strict identity.5,6

Philosophers tend to think of all semantically complex singular terms on the model of definite descriptions, and therefore as not directly referential, as not contributing only their referent to the compositional semantic evaluation of the larger expressions in which they occur. But that is a mistake. On the natural semantics for functional expressions just sketched, what they contribute to compositional semantic evaluation is of exactly the same type as what atomic singular terms contribute, their referent—in this case, a number. Despite their semantic complexity, such functional expressions are directly referential. We have learnt from Kripke, Kaplan, and others not to assimilate individual constants to definite descriptions; the underlying lesson applies to semantically complex functional expressions too. In particular, unlike definite descriptions, functional expressions are scopeless, so the inter-substitution of the coreferential directly referential functional expressions ‘8’, ‘9−1’, ‘7+1’, ‘p(9)’, and ‘s(7)’ in (4), (5), (6), (5*), and (6*) preserves truth, without risking some sort of scope fallacy. Thus, all those sentences have the same truth-value. Since (4) is trivially true, (5), (6), (5*), and (6*) are true too. That (5) and (5*) are false is an illusion.

The claim is not that the singular terms ‘8’, ‘9−1’, ‘7+1’, ‘p(9)’, and ‘s(7)’ are all synonymous. They all differ from each other in semantic structure, as represented by a syntactic tree where each node is labelled with the semantic value of the corresponding constituent, so in a natural fine-grained sense they are not synonymous. Rather, the point is just that they all have the same final semantic value, the number 8, which is their input to the compositional semantic evaluation of the sentences in which they occur. For the same reason, the sentences (4), (5), (6), (5*), and (6*) are not synonymous in the fine-grained sense either; nevertheless, since they differ only in those singular terms, they all have the same compositionally derived semantic value, and so the same truth-value.

We can extend the argument to examples much closer to (1), (2), and (3), Fine’s case of Socrates and {Socrates}. In effect, the curly brackets ‘{’ and ‘}’ constitute a function symbol with a variable number of places: applied to a list (possibly empty) of singular terms, they result in a semantically complex term whose referent is the set of referents of the singular terms on the list. In particular, for singletons, ref⁡a_(‘{’∧t∧‘}’)={ref⁡a_(t)} for any singular term t and assignment a_. Just as addition has subtraction as a one-sided inverse, so singleton formation has a one-sided inverse: we can define a function symbol, ‘||’, by stipulating that |x|=y if x={y} and |x|=x if x is not a singleton set. In particular, |{Socrates}|=Socrates (though, since he is not a singleton, {|Socrates|}={Socrates}≠Socrates). Now consider:
It is essential to Socrates that he is |{Socrates}|.

This feels similar to ‘It is essential to Socrates that he is a member of singleton Socrates’. There is a natural temptation to judge (7) false, just like (2). After all, {Socrates} is supposed to be extraneous to Socrates himself. But ‘|{Socrates}|’ is simply a functional expression whose referent is Socrates, so replacing ‘|{Socrates}|’ by ‘Socrates’ in (7) should preserve its truth-value. But the result of the replacement is just the trivially true (1). Thus, the judgment that (7) is false was itself incorrect.

Again, the point is not that the singular terms ‘Socrates’ and ‘|{Socrates}|’ are synonymous. They differ in semantic structure and so, in the fine-grained sense, are not synonymous. Rather, the point is just that they have the same final semantic value, the man Socrates, which is their input to the compositional semantic evaluation of the sentences in which they occur. For the same reason, the sentences (1) and (7) are not synonymous in the fine-grained sense either; nevertheless, since they differ only in those singular terms, they have the same compositionally derived semantic value, and so the same truth-value.

At this point, hyperintensionalists about essence may start trying to construct an alternative semantics for functional expressions, one which avoids treating them as directly referential, and gives them complex enough semantic values to generate differences of truth-value under the relevant replacements—without giving the game away by treating the operator ‘It is essential to Socrates that’ as creating a merely quotational, metalinguistic context and thereby undermining its pretensions to reveal deep metaphysical structure. Such a reaction runs an obvious risk of overfitting the data. It is also quite unmotivated by anything about the standard mathematical notation to which the functional expressions belong. The simple, natural, homophonic semantics just sketched is linguistically far more natural.

A subsidiary point is that we can use functional expressions with the semantics above; stipulating that we will use them so does not remove the temptation to make logically untenable assignments of truth-values like those on which the alleged counterexamples to modal theories of essence rely. In such cases, our judgments of essence are liable to error; our reliance on them is misplaced. In any case, the reasonable assumption is that the straightforward semantics is indeed correct.

This argument from functional expressions does not involve any comparison between intensional and hyperintensional semantic frameworks. Possible worlds or the like were not mentioned. No appeal was made to necessary equivalence, only to simple identity, for instance of natural numbers by ordinary mathematical standards. Merely ‘going hyperintensional’ would be irrelevant to the challenge.

A better response to the cases is to learn from our mistakes, by trying to understand how elementary truths such as (5), (5*), and (7) can look false. Once we have diagnosed the mistake, we can ask whether it is also at work in our assessments of Fine’s examples, and in particular (2). That is the business of the next section.

Given an iterative conception of natural numbers, what may first strike one as off about (5) and (5*) in relation to the essence of 8 is the very mention of 9: it looks irrelevant. Similarly, given an iterative conception of sets, what may first strike one as off about (7) in relation to the essence of Socrates is the very mention of {Socrates}: it looks irrelevant. Fine’s own descriptions of his examples strongly evokes such reactions, for example when he says that it is not essential to Socrates that he be distinct from the Eiffel Tower because ‘there is nothing in his nature which connects him in any special way to it’ and that ‘it is no part of Socrates’ essence that there be infinitely many prime numbers or that the abstract world of numbers, sets, or what have you, be just as it is’ (Fine 1994: 5). Correspondingly, what may first strike one as off about (2), like (7), in relation to the essence of Socrates is the very mention of {Socrates}.

Such reactions to the examples are naturally explained by the operation of a crude relevance filter, which monitors the complement sentence ‘A’ in ‘It is essential to X that A’ for material irrelevant to answering the question ‘What is X?’, and rejects the whole statement if such material is found. Thus, it rejects (5) and (5*) because the complement has the constituent ‘9’, deemed irrelevant to answering the question ‘What is 8?’, and it rejects (2) and (7) because the complement has the constituent ‘{Socrates}’, deemed irrelevant to answering the question ‘What is Socrates?’ That happens even though the constituent occurs in the complement as part of a more complex expression which in effect ‘neutralizes’ the offending material. Such a mechanism explains the illusion of differences in truth-value amongst (4), (5), (5*), (6), and (6*), and between (1) and (7). By treating semantic constituents in isolation, the relevance filter is sensitive to differences in semantic structure between complex expressions whose overall semantic value is nevertheless the same. Thus, the relevance filter is fine-grained because it is superficial: it stays on the linguistic surface.

Once we have identified such a mechanism at work, we should also lose confidence in the key Finean judgment that (1) and (2) differ in truth-value, even though we lack the straightforward logical reason for holding it to be mistaken that we have in the other cases. The relevance filter will automatically reject (2) but not (1), without any attempt to determine whether the complement sentences ‘He is a member of {Socrates}’ and ‘He is Socrates’ express the same proposition, just as it automatically rejects (7) but not (1), without any attempt to determine whether the complement sentences ‘He is |{Socrates}|’ and ‘He is Socrates’ express the same proposition (as they do). Similarly, in the arithmetical case, the filter will automatically reject (5) and (5*) but not (4), without any attempt to determine whether the respective complement sentences ‘It is 9−1’, ‘It is p(9)’, and ‘It is 8’ express the same proposition (as they do).

The filter does not reject (3), (6), and (6*). Thus, with (3), it does not deem ‘Socrates’ irrelevant to answering the question ‘What is {Socrates}?’, although it deems ‘{Socrates}’ irrelevant to answering the question ‘What is Socrates?’, and with (6) and (6*), it does not deem ‘7’ irrelevant to answering the question ‘What is 8?’, although it deems ‘9’ irrelevant to answering the same question. These asymmetries are sensitive to our understanding of ‘What is’ questions about people, sets, and natural numbers. There is surely much more to be said about that, but it is not to our present purpose. The aim is not to give a positive metaphysical account of the examples, but rather to identify a specific cognitive mechanism that induces mistakes in our thinking, mistakes which may have widespread repercussions across much of our metaphysical theorizing.

Of course, irrelevance is one thing, falsity another. Ordinarily, we can handle the category ‘true, but irrelevant’ without too much difficulty. Why should a relevance filter induce us to categorize some statements about essence as false, not merely as irrelevant?

Such transitions from alleged irrelevance to alleged falsity tend to occur in broadly explanatory contexts, where the aim is to help someone understand something. For instance, you ask ‘How did Tom get injured?’ and I answer ‘He was knocked down by a yellow truck’. My statement is true, but the truck’s yellowness was irrelevant to Tom’s injury (we may assume). However, when we come to assess the statement ‘John got injured because he was hit by a yellow truck’, ‘because’ raises the stakes; we may suspect that, strictly speaking, including the word ‘yellow’ in the clause after ‘because’ falsifies the whole statement, by semantically requiring the yellowness to play some role in answering the question, by explaining John’s injury, which it does not. The suspicion may or may not be correct; what matters here is that it is naturally felt.

Something similar may be going on in our talk of essences. We may understand a statement of the form ‘It is essential to X that A’ as requiring ‘A’ to be a good answer to the question ‘What is X?’, one which at least partially explains what X is and excludes material irrelevant to the question, so ‘It is essential to X that A’ is false when ‘A’ includes explanatorily irrelevant material. Such connections between essence and explanation may indeed be congenial to Fine’s own metaphysics of essence, which is often interpreted as reviving a more Aristotelian form of essentialism, contrasted with Kripke’s austerely modal account (Kripke 1980). Aristotle offers a unified, richly interconnected account of essence, explanation, and definition (see Charles 2000 for a book-length treatment). Adding an irrelevant conjunct to a correct definition of something can easily yield an extensionally incorrect definition, and adding an irrelevant conjunct to a good explanation of something can easily yield a worse explanation.

Of course, just saying ‘He is Socrates’ by itself does not explain much, except perhaps by implication to an audience already well-informed about Socrates, but it could at least form the start of a good explanation. By contrast, starting an explanation with ‘He belongs to {Socrates}’ would typically introduce unhelpful, pointless clutter; unlike ‘He is Socrates’, it has already gone wrong as a response to the question ‘What is Socrates?’ We prefer explanations to begin at the beginning, to start simple, and to build up complexity as needed. A more natural contrast is between ‘He is a human’ and ‘He belongs to the set of humans’. The former could easily figure in a good explanation, while the latter introduces the same kind of unhelpful, pointless clutter as before. Correspondingly, many will be tempted to judge (8) true and (9) false:
It is essential to Socrates that he is a human.
It is essential to Socrates that he belongs to the set of humans.7
Nevertheless, on reasonable assumptions about the modal metaphysics of sets, necessarily, he is a human if and only if he belongs to the sets of humans.
Just as for (2) and (9), the relevance filter also explains our tendency to deny other claims rejected by Fine, such as (10) and (11):
It is essential to Socrates that he is not identical with the Eiffel Tower.
It is essential to Socrates that he is such that there are infinitely many primes.
The relevance filter picks up ‘Eiffel Tower’ and ‘infinitely many primes’, with the same results as for (2) and (9).

Those sketchy remarks indicate how irrelevance can easily be taken as a mark of error in explanatory and essentializing contexts. But that does not fully vindicate the relevance filter, since it is still predicted to generate logical errors like those identified above, given the superficial level at which it operates.

At best, such a relevance filter is a useful heuristic for testing essentialist claims, and other proto-explanatory claims. Such a heuristic is quick and easy to use, and often correct, but far from infallible. Psychologists have long studied the major role of heuristics in human cognition. The tradition associated with Gerd Gigerenzer characterizes them positively as ‘fast and frugal’ methods, boundedly rational, efficient, and surprisingly reliable (e.g., Gigerenzer, Hertwig, and Pachur 2011). The tradition associated with Daniel Kahneman characterizes them more negatively as ‘cheap and dirty’ methods, irrational and only of limited reliability (e.g., Kahneman, Slovic, and Tversky 1982). The two traditions agree that heuristics play a key role in human cognition, and that they are far from perfectly reliable. Such reliance on heuristic methods may be unavoidable for finite agents.

Heuristics do not wear their merely heuristic status on their sleeve. Many heuristics are embedded in our perceptual systems; we are alerted to our reliance on them by perceptual illusions. For example, our visual system uses colour boundaries in the visual field as a heuristic for the edges of three-dimensional physical objects in the environment, with no overt warning that we are relying on a mere heuristic. We may find out that we have been relying on such a heuristic when we discover that we have been deceived by camouflage. In a similar way, philosophical paradoxes may warn us of our reliance on general but fallible cognitive heuristics (Williamson 2024). When the heuristic works smoothly, the judgments may feel very clearly correct, but that does not guarantee that they are correct.

A relevance filter bears the marks of a typical heuristic. It requires only shallow processing, and so can be applied quickly, easily, and unreflectively. It often helps us focus on what matters, but sometimes sends us astray. It carries no distractingly salient cognitive health warning to give us pause, for instance when we use it to assess essentialist or explanatory claims. The relevance filter is efficient; no wonder we use it, despite its fallibility.
Unsurprisingly, the danger of heuristic-generated error is not confined to essentialist discourse. Even within metaphysics, explanatory heuristics may play a wider role.

Here is an example. The word ‘because’ is often regarded as hyperintensional, sensitive to differences between necessary equivalents (Schnieder 2011). Aristotle already observed the apparent asymmetry between pairs like (12) and (13) (where ‘because’ takes wide scope):
It is true that grass is green because grass is green.
Grass is green because it is true that grass is green.

It is natural to judge (12) true and (13) false: (12) gets the explanatory priority the right way round; (13) gets it the wrong way round. Nevertheless, necessarily, it is true that grass is green if and only if grass is green.
A square with sides 17 metres long has an area of 289 metres² because 17² = 289.
A square with sides 17 metres long has an area of 289 metres² because 17² = 17².

It is natural to judge (14) true and (15) false: in (14), the explanans ‘17² = 289’ makes the required connection between ‘17²’ and ‘289’, and is explanatorily relevant; in (15), the explanans ‘17² = 17²’ fails to make the connection, and is explanatorily irrelevant. But there is an illusion. For, on the natural semantics for functional expressions above, ‘17²’, though semantically complex, is nevertheless directly referential. It has the same semantic value as the numeral ‘289’, the number 289, which is their input to the compositional semantic evaluation of sentences in which they occur. Since (14) and (15) differ only in the substitution of ‘17²’ for ‘289’, they must have the same semantic value and so the same truth-value. Of course, as proposed explanations, sentence (14) is genuinely more helpful than sentence (15), but that turns out to be a matter of how perspicuously it presents things, not of which things it presents. The truth-value of (14) and (15) is insensitive to such presentational differences, except on a reading of ‘because’ as implicitly metalinguistic, which is not what friends of hyperintensional metaphysics want.

Once we have identified the illusion of hyperintensionality in (14) and (15), we should be very wary of assuming that the apparent hyperintensionality in pairs such as (12) and (13) is genuine. The difference between ‘It is true that grass is green’ and ‘Grass is green’ may turn out to be merely presentational, like that between ‘17²’ and ‘289’, and to make no difference to their semantic value, their input to the compositional semantic evaluation of sentences in which they occur. Thus, (12) and (13) may turn out to have the same truth-value after all. Elsewhere, I have explored in more depth the heuristic that arguably generates such illusions of hyperintensionality (Williamson 2024: chapter 3). The general mechanism is to use degree of explanatory helpfulness to assess the truth-value of sentences with trigger words such as ‘because’ or ‘essential’, which seem to invite such assessment. Since explanatory helpfulness is sensitive to all sorts of presentational differences between words and sentences not registered by their semantic values, which can be presented clearly or obscurely, perspicuously organized or all muddled up, illusions of hyperintensionality inevitably result. Thus, the evidence for hyperintensionality in metaphysics is much weaker than is usually assumed.

Intensionalism has obvious abductive advantages over hyperintensionalism in the simplicity and strength of its theoretical framework. The compensating advantage of hyperintensionalism was supposed to be its better fit with the evidence, mainly in the form of examples, especially the alleged counterexamples to intensionalism. That apparent evidential advantage is now dissolving under scrutiny. Metaphysicians need to reconsider a wide range of examples that have been taken to favour hyperintensionalism, and how they look from an intensionalist perspective.

Within a framework of intensional semantics, one can reinterpret the defining equations of a Boolean algebra as expressing identities between propositions, just as arithmetical equations express identities between natural numbers, in both cases with functional expressions interpreted as above.
