Of course, even if a philosophical intuition is humanly universal, it still does not follow that it is true – it might be a mere glitch in a humanly universal cognitive system. In any case, a metaphilosophical upshot of the negative program was a rejection of the case method in philosophy. The preferred alternative method of answering philosophical questions was less clear, but threatened to involve a reduction of philosophy to psychology (for a more recent general survey of experimental philosophy see Sytsma and Buckwalter (2016); my critical discussions of experimental philosophy are all reprinted in Williamson 2021; see also Nagel 2012 and Machery et al. 2017).
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

Early in the debate, both proponents and opponents of the case method characterized it as involving reliance on intuition – as many still do. When I was invited to give a talk at a workshop on intuition and epistemology at the University of Fribourg, Switzerland, in 2002, I accepted, in order to force myself to think more seriously about the issue. In my talk, I tried to fit intuition into my knowledge–first epistemology (Williamson 2000) by treating intuiting as a factive mental attitude, one which can be had only to true contents. My plan was to treat intuiting that P, like seeing that P, as a specific way of knowing that P. In apparent cases of intuiting a falsehood, one is not really in the mental state of intuiting, even if it feels just as if one were in it.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

However, when I started to write up the talk more carefully for publication as part of the workshop proceedings in an issue of the journal Dialectica, I ran into an obstacle. I wanted some clear, simple, non–philosophical examples of the putative mental attitude of intuiting, to illustrate the proposed epistemological structure, to which I could then compare standard cases of philosophical intuiting. Postulating a distinctive kind of mental attitude exclusive to philosophizing struck me, then and now, as grossly implausible – from an evolutionary perspective, extra cognitive structure is costly, and unlikely to confer much compensating benefit if it is useful only in philosophy. But when I tried to specify the content of such paradigmatically intuitive knowledge, complexity proliferated, unlike the simplicity of much ordinary perceptual knowledge.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

More specifically: Philosophers generally understood intuition and perception as mutually exclusive, by contrast with a widespread use of the terms in psychology, on which ordinary perceptual judgments count as ‘intuitive’ in the sense of not involving conscious reflection. Indeed, philosophers find the epistemology of intuition puzzling because they take intuition to be non–perceptual. They understand intuitions as relevantly like verdicts on hypothetical cases. But articulating such verdicts on hypothetical cases takes significant linguistic complexity, if the verdicts are to be apt for truth.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

For example, take a hypothetical case in moral philosophy on which you could express your verdict by saying ‘I am morally obliged to jump into the pond to save the drowning child’. What is actually true, I presume, is not the categorical claim that you are morally obliged to jump into the pond to save the drowning child. I trust that you are not reading this chapter by the side of a pond in which a child is drowning. Rather, what is actually true is something more like the counterfactual conditional that if you were in the relevant hypothetical scenario, you would be morally obliged to jump into the pond to save the drowning child – a conditional whose antecedent characterizes the hypothetical circumstances and whose consequent is the verdict conditional on the antecedent.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

Again and again, as I thought through candidate instances of intuitions, they turned out to have something like this complex conditional structure, sometimes explicit, sometimes implicit in a universal generalization. Treating the postulated special attitude of intuition as the distinctive feature of the example, while ignoring the complex structure of the sentence used to articulate the content to which the attitude was being taken, seemed quite premature. At the very least, one should take into account the contribution of linguistic structure to the distinctiveness of the examples before starting to postulate special attitudes. My paper in the workshop proceedings took a very different line from my talk at the workshop itself, and distanced itself from the postulated category of intuition; I put the word ‘intuitions’ in its title in ironic quotation marks (Williamson 2004).
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

A prototype of philosophical ‘intuition’ is the verdict on a Gettier case that the protagonist does not know. To adapt an example from Bertrand Russell, she forms a belief about the time by consulting a clock which, unbeknownst to her, had stopped exactly 48 hours earlier. Thanks to that coincidence, her belief that it is 3 o’clock is true. In the operative sense of ‘justified’, her belief is also justified, since she has no reason to suspect that the clock is not working. But, according to the standard verdict, she does not know that it is 3 o’clock. Thus, justified true belief is insufficient for knowledge, and the once–popular ‘jtb’ analysis of knowledge is mistaken. In imagining the scenario, one judges ‘She does not know that it is 3 o’clock’, which is just the ‘offline’ analogue of the ‘online’ judgment a third party in the scenario might make, observing people set their watches by the stopped clock.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

When giving talks on philosophical thought experiments, I sometimes explained at the start of the talk that I was not using power–point because the only time I had given a power–point presentation it was a complete disaster. Later in the talk, I revealed that I had been lying: there had been no disaster, because I had never given a power–point presentation at all (I have done so subsequently, including one at the Antwerp conference). Thus, their justified belief early in the lecture that I had never given a successful power–point presentation was true, but based on a false premise, and so had not amounted to knowledge. I had made the audience experience a real–life Gettier case from the inside. The point of the exercise was to emphasize how little difference it makes evidentially whether one uses a thought experiment or a real–life experiment; working offline or online, the upshot is the same: either way, the jtb analysis is refuted. The offline aspect of thought experiments makes them seem much more distinctive cognitively than they really are.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

Counterfactual conditionals in ordinary life are often easy to know: ‘If I’d dropped the soup bowl, there would’ve been a mess’, ‘If you hadn’t told me, I’d not have known it was painted by a ten–year old’. They often have practical or moral significance: ‘If I’d turned left instead of right, I’d have got there in half the time’, ‘If he hadn’t driven through the red light, there would’ve been no accident’. General scepticism about their cognitive utility is extravagant. Indeed, given the close connection between online and offline judgments, scepticism about the offline judgments infects the online judgments too. The counterfactual conditionals relevant to philosophical thought experiments are not exceptional in these respects: doubting ‘If that happened to someone, they wouldn’t know it was 3 o’clock’ about the offline case can easily lead to doubting ‘She doesn’t know it is 3 o’clock’ about the online case. We often learn counterfactual conditionals by making the counterfactual supposition and imaginatively drawing out its consequences in a way constrained by our background experientially–based expectations about how the world works. Philosophers’ use of hypothetical cases just recruits our ordinary capacity to know counterfactual conditions. It requires no mysterious capacity of ‘intuition’ (see Boghossian and Williamson 2020 for a debate on the role of intuitions in philosophy).
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

These ideas about the epistemology of counterfactual conditionals and their application to philosophers’ use of thought experiments were articulated in The Philosophy of Philosophy (Williamson 2007). Later, I developed them further, into a more general account of the cognitive function of the imagination (Williamson 2016). But they were provoked by the more specific debate in metaphilosophy, and my reflection on my own philosophical practice, and the practice of many philosophers like me, in using thought experiments. This extension from metaphilosophy to general epistemology and philosophy of mind is itself an instance of anti–exceptionalism about philosophy. It works because philosophical thinking uses the same general cognitive capacities as non–philosophical thinking.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

That is not the end of the story. In The Philosophy of Philosophy, I also applied my general account of the epistemology of counterfactual conditionals for another metaphilosophical purpose: to explain philosophers’ knowledge of metaphysical modality. Kripke had identified such necessity in Naming and Necessity as ‘necessity in the highest degree’, objective, non–epistemic, real rather than nominal, as his famous examples of the necessary a posteriori and the contingent a priori demonstrated (Kripke 1972; 1980). Predictably, he faced the neo–Humean challenge to explain how we can know, given that something is actual, whether it is necessary or contingent, and given that something is non–actual, whether it is possible or impossible. My strategy was to use counterfactual conditionals as the thin end of the wedge for metaphysical modality, by showing that anyone with the cognitive capacity to handle counterfactual conditionals already has the cognitive capacity to handle metaphysical modalities. This was a promising line of argument because in standard combined logics for counterfactual conditionals and modal operators (read metaphysically), the modal operators are equivalent to constructions built out of counterfactual conditionals. In particular, something is impossible if and only if it counterfactually implies a contradiction, something is necessary if and only if its negation is impossible, and so on. Thus, if you can assess sentences or thoughts involving counterfactual conditionals, you can also assess sentences or thoughts involving modal operators (read metaphysically) in the same way as you assess their counterfactual conditional equivalents. This does not require you to define the modal operators in terms of counterfactual conditionals; you just need to treat the corresponding sentences or thoughts alike.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

The equivalences are validated by standard semantic accounts of modal operators and counterfactual conditionals in a framework of possible worlds. They can also be derived by standard modal logic from two plausible and more general linking principles: first, an antecedent necessarily implies a consequent only if the former counterfactually implies the latter too; second, no possibility counterfactually implies an impossibility. So far, everything fits nicely together. Integral to this picture is the vacuous truth of counterpossibles: any counterfactual conditional with an impossible antecedent is true. That follows from the first linking principle by standard modal logic, for an impossibility necessarily implies anything, and so counterfactually implies anything. Semantically, no world is a counter – instance to a counterfactual conditional whose antecedent is false at every world.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

Around 2004, in the run–up to The Philosophy of Philosophy, I started presenting this material in talks on the epistemology of modality. One feature of the reactions slightly took me aback: the vehemence with which many able philosophers rejected the vacuous truth of counterpossibles, on the basis of what they took to be decisive counterexamples: obviously false counterpossibles. The alleged counterexamples themselves did not surprise me. Of course, pre–reflectively, some counterpossibles – such as ‘If there were a largest prime, it would make no difference to mathematics’ – are repugnant at first sight. What I found naïve or frivolous was the confidence with which carefully developed, elegant and powerful logical and semantical theories were thrown out on the basis of uncritically accepted first impressions. It only got worse when cumbersome, feeble, and unexplanatory semantic alternatives such as frameworks of impossible worlds were invoked as substitutes to vindicate whatever the first impressions happened to be (see Williamson 2024 for the methodological issues here). In teaching logic to clever students, one spends much of one’s time explaining how plausible–sounding objections to standard theorems are subtly mistaken. Why think that anything more is going on when clever philosophers make plausible–sounding objections to the vacuous truth of counterpossibles?
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

Still, an explanatory task remains. Why do the ‘counterexamples’ seem so compelling? It is surely not just a brute psychological fact. I noticed two features of typical alleged examples of false counterpossibles. First, they are rejected on the basis of what seems to be very shallow cognitive processing: the judgment is immediate, and the antecedent’s impossibility plays no apparent role. After all, they are presented as obvious counterexamples. Second, the opposite counterpossible is found obvious (opposite counterfactuals have the same antecedent and mutually contradictory consequents, as in ‘If I were talking to the King now, my clothes would be appropriate’ and ‘If I were talking to the King now, my clothes would not be appropriate’). For example, we accept the counterpossible ‘If there were a largest prime, it would make a difference to mathematics’ without bothering to consider whether its antecedent is impossible or contingently false. We just think how much actual mathematics involves the infinity of primes. That also seems to be the basis on which we reject the counterpossible ‘If there were a largest prime, it would make no difference to mathematics’. This suggests the hypothesis that we treat opposite counterfactuals as mutually inconsistent, so, having accepted one, we immediately reject the other.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

Can opponents of the vacuous truth of counterpossibles respond that we treat opposite counterfactuals as mutually inconsistent because they are mutually inconsistent, so opposite counterpossibles cannot both be true? The trouble is that the inconsistency principle does not fit other parts of our practice. For, on the equally obvious–seeming principle that a conjunction counterfactually implies its conjuncts, we accept both ‘If the Russell set were a member of itself and not a member of itself, it would be a member of itself’ and ‘If the Russell set were a member of itself and not a member of itself, it would be not a member of itself’, which are opposite counterfactuals. The mutual inconsistency of opposite counterfactuals is also hard to reconcile with their natural use to articulate arguments by reductio ad absurdum, when we refute a mathematical hypothesis H by proving (for some R) both ‘If H were so, R would be so’ and ‘If H were so, R would not be so’.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

I therefore proposed treating the mutual inconsistency of opposite counterfactuals as a heuristic in the psychologists’ sense: a cognitive shortcut, reliable in most but not all cases. Psychologists have studied many such heuristics intensively. Sometimes they characterize them negatively, as ‘cheap and dirty’, in the tradition of Daniel Kahneman (Kahneman, Slovic, and Tversky 1982), sometimes more positively, as ‘fast and frugal’, in the tradition of Gerd Gigerenzer (Gigerenzer, Hertwig, and Pachur 2011). At worst, heuristic–based cognition is regarded as a form of irrationality, at best, as a form of bounded rationality. Some heuristics are doubtless better than others, at least for a given purpose under given conditions. We might be better off avoiding some heuristics, but the nature of human cognition – perhaps of finite cognition in general – precludes avoiding them all. Many important heuristics are virtually universal to humans. For example, visual illusions are probably by–products of such heuristics built into the visual systems of humans and other animals (Fleming 2012, Gigerenzer 2021). We often rely on heuristics without realizing that we are doing so, often when they are built into our unconscious perceptual processing.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

I argued that apparent examples of false counterpossibles are artefacts of our unconscious reliance on the heuristic for mutual inconsistency of counterfactuals. Arguably, it fails only for counterpossibles; since most counterfactuals are not counterpossibles, it is quite reliable. Those who take themselves to be refuting the vacuous truth of counterpossibles are arguably the victims of their own heuristics (Williamson 2017, 2018).
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

The heuristic that opposite counterfactuals are mutually inconsistent is easily generalized to one which treats as mutually inconsistent counterfactuals with the same antecedent and contrary consequents, which need not be contradictory. Thus, ‘If Maria were in Europe, she would be in Italy’ is treated as inconsistent with ‘If Maria were in Europe, she would be in Spain’, not just with ‘If Maria were in Europe, she would not be in Italy’. However, that generalization does not go very far.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

Postulating a heuristic just for handling the special case of counterfactuals with the same antecedent and contrary consequents left me in an unstable position. The heuristic leads you, having accepted one counterfactual, to reject other counterfactuals related to it in the specified way, but not to accepting any counterfactuals in the first place. It is useful only if you already have some other way of cognitively assessing counterfactuals and sometimes accepting them. But if you have that other way, why do you need the heuristic for the special case?
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

Fortunately, the special heuristic hinted towards a much broader generalization. For simplicity, take the analogous case for plain conditionals without ‘would’. Grant, for the sake of argument, both ‘If Maria is in Europe, she is in Italy’ and ‘If Maria is in Europe, she is in Spain’. Suppose that Maria is Europe. On that supposition, we have both ‘She is in Italy’ and ‘She is in Spain’ about Maria, an inconsistency. By the analogous special heuristic for plain conditionals, we project that inconsistency conditional on ‘Maria is in Europe’ onto an unconditional inconsistency between the two original conditionals with antecedent ‘Maria is in Europe’. The underlying general rule is to project a joint assessment of a set of statements on a given supposition onto the same assessment outright of the set of conditionals with that supposition as their shared antecedent and the statements in the original set as their consequents. In particular, when the original set has just one member statement, the conditional with that member statement as its consequent and the supposition as its antecedent is assessed outright as the member statement is assessed on the supposition. For example, we accept the conditional ‘If Maria is in Europe, she is in Italy’ outright when we accept ‘She is in Italy’ under the supposition ‘Maria is in Europe’, we reject the conditional outright when we reject ‘She is in Italy’ under the same supposition, and we suspend judgment on the conditional when we suspend judgment on ‘She is in Italy’ under the supposition.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

A similar pattern applies to counterfactual conditionals, with a slightly different style of assessment appropriate to counterfactual suppositions, which are more ‘distanced’ from reality, by ‘would’, than plain conditionals. From this general heuristic, one can then recover the original principle that opposite counterfactuals are mutually inconsistent as a special case.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

This large step of generalization was not meant as a compelling argument. It just explains how natural it was for me to reach the hypothesis of a simple, general, supposition–based heuristic for assessing conditionals. The hard work was then to show in detail how postulating such a heuristic explains our assessment of conditionals in general. I did that work in my book Suppose and Tell: The Semantics and Heuristics of Conditionals (Williamson 2020). Once I had the central idea, writing the book went quickly, because everything fell into place much more smoothly and neatly than I had anticipated.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

The suppositional heuristic was by no means a completely new idea. It is closely related to a seminal suggestion by Frank Ramsey about how we assess conditionals, known as the ‘Ramsey test’. The heuristic also subsumes both the standard introduction and elimination rules for the conditional (conditional proof and modus ponens) in systems of natural deduction and the attractive, much–discussed, but problematic idea that the probability of a conditional should be the conditional probability of its consequent on its antecedent (see Williamson 2020 for discussion and references). It also harmonizes with the picture of the cognitive assessment of counterfactual conditionals in The Philosophy of Philosophy, and the central role of the imagination there. In turn, that role enables us to use conditional words like ‘if’ in extracting, articulating, and communicating informative connections embedded in our experientially informed ways of developing suppositions, the offline analogues of our capacities for online updating of our expectations about the future.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

Attempts to build such ideas about conditionals directly into their semantics had led to disaster, as shown by various impossibility theorems proved by David Lewis and others. In brief, the general suppositional heuristic is inconsistent in various ways, both in itself and with uncontentious background knowledge. From my perspective, those results showed, not that the ideas should be abandoned, but that their plausibility comes from their match to our heuristics, not to our semantics. An inconsistent test can give correct results most of the time, but it cannot be logically valid.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

The need for hypothetical thinking is deeply rooted in intelligent life. For example, when one has to decide between several possible actions, one must compare what would or might happen if one took this action with what would or might happen if one took another action. Thus, our primary way of assessing conditionals – the imaginative use of the suppositional heuristic – is a good candidate for a human universal. Since it is fallible, it also constitutes a potential source of error in our case judgments of conditionals. The usual methods of experimental philosophy will not pick it up, for the consequent errors may not show up in divergence between judgments made by different demographic groups or under different environmental conditions.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

In postulating a fallible general heuristic for conditionals, I have encountered far more resistance from semanticists in both philosophy and linguistics than I have from psychologists and psychologically–informed philosophers. The latter groups’ reaction seems to be: ‘Of course we rely on heuristics in assessing conditionals, just as we do in other cognitive tasks – how else would we do it? The question is which heuristics we use.’ By contrast, semanticists are more likely to question the need for an intermediate level of heuristics between the semantics and our assessments of particular conditionals in particular contexts. It is as if the semantic evaluation of the conditional in the context were transparent to competent speakers and hearers; as if they could read off its semantic status directly, without cognitive effort. Although it would be uncharitable to accuse semanticists of really believing that, I often find them reluctant to admit that the cognitive task might be hard enough to require heuristics. They seem understandably afraid that admitting the role of heuristics risks losing them their data, their empirical constraints, since common native speaker assessments of sample sentences will no longer be reliable.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

Such fears are over–pessimistic. The natural sciences have operated for centuries with less than fully reliable data, and have found ways to manage the risks. One such way is an aversion to what natural and social scientists call ‘overfitting’: profligacy with theoretical complexity, especially in multiplying the number of independent parameters in the model (‘degrees of freedom’), which enables them to fit current data closely – including any erroneous data points! – but also leads to predictive failures and theoretical instability. Significantly, contemporary semantics shows increasing signs of overfitting, with very complicated semantic clauses for common words (such as ‘if’), and little sense that adding new parameters of semantic evaluation might have a cost in degrees of freedom (see Williamson 2024 for more discussion). I have seen simplicity as a criterion of theory choice incredulously rejected as quite alien to semantics.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

The ‘paradoxes’ of material (truth–functional) implication constitute a case in point. By the usual truth–table, ‘If A, C’ is true on the material reading of ‘if’ whenever A is false or C is true. It is therefore easy to manufacture apparent counterexamples to the material reading of natural language conditionals. For example, ‘If my lottery ticket won, it lost’ seems obviously false, but on the material reading it is almost certainly true, since its antecedent is almost certainly false. The suppositional heuristic predicts our negative judgment: we reject ‘If my lottery ticket won, it lost’ unconditionally because we reject ‘It lost’ conditionally on ‘My lottery ticket won’. Nevertheless, in Suppose and Tell, I argue that the material interpretation of ‘if’ makes the best overall sense of our total practice of using conditionals to extract, store, and communicate information, and that the rejection of some true conditionals turns out to be a small price to pay for its overall utility. That account can be extended to counterfactual conditionals, and in particular to the vacuous truth of counterpossibles. The apparent falsity of some counterpossibles is an artefact of the corresponding heuristic.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

When writing the conditionals book, I naturally wondered what role heuristics might be playing in other philosophical problems. Unsurprisingly, my thoughts turned to the problem of vagueness. Many philosophers understand sorites paradoxes as generated by ‘tolerance principles’ for vague terms, such as ‘A heap minus one grain is still a heap’. Iterating its application takes one from the obviously true ‘Then thousand grains make a heap’ to the obviously false ‘One grain makes a heap’. Some philosophers even classify tolerance principles as ‘analytic’ or ‘conceptual connections’. But the attraction of assigning them such semantic dignities just indicates the poverty of available options for general principles in philosophers’ toolbox. Once one has the category of heuristics, a much more natural and plausible option becomes available. Tolerance principles are just labour–saving devices by which we ignore small differences and so avoid the expense in time and energy that would otherwise be spent on continually reassessing our classifications when updating on titbits of new information. To emphasize that invoking heuristics was not just an ad hoc move for handling conditionals, I added a few pages on tolerance principles as heuristics to Suppose and Tell. I even showed how to estimate their reliability in some cases: although tolerance principles generate paradoxes, in almost all instances they preserve truth. Since then, I have realized that tolerance principles are just special cases of a much more general principle, the ‘persistence heuristic’, on which ignoring small differences is the default: it is neither specific to vague terms nor just labour–saving, but practically indispensable for any data base.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

This approach can be taken more generally to philosophical paradoxes (Williamson 2024). For example, the Liar paradox and other semantic paradoxes depend on disquotational principles for truth and falsity, on which ‘“Snow is white” is true’ is equivalent to plain ‘Snow is white’ and “Snow is white” is false’ to ‘Snow is not white’. Such principles are needed, and almost always unproblematic, but have rare pathological instances. They can be understood as heuristics for truth and falsity. Again, Kripke’s puzzle about belief can be read, against his intentions, as showing how Frege puzzles for belief like ‘Hesperus’/‘Phosphorus’ depend on heuristics for determining what people believe from their linguistic behaviour (Kripke 1979). Heuristics for ascribing knowledge and belief can in turn cast light on the nature of knowledge and belief themselves.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

In brief, the links of the chain connected like this. In response to a metaphilosophical challenge to philosophers’ putative knowledge of metaphysical modality, standard logical equivalences were invoked between metaphysical modalities and counterfactual conditionals. Those equivalences require the vacuous truth of counterpossibles, to which counterexamples were proposed – a niche dispute in philosophical logic rather than metaphilosophy. Scrutiny of the allegedly false counterpossibles indicated that what makes them look false is a form of reasoning which usually preserves truth but is untrustworthy for counterpossibles, so the alleged counterexamples were not probative. The role of that plausible but fallible form of reasoning can be explained as an application of a psychological heuristic. It is a special case of a general heuristic for assessing conditionals, the suppositional heuristic. The hypothesis that this heuristic is our primary way of assessing conditionals is central to an explanation of our practice of using conditionals, how we manage it cognitively, why it is so useful for us in extracting and communicating information, but also why the semantics of conditionals has baffled philosophers and logicians for over two thousand years – because our heuristic for conditionals is implicitly inconsistent, so no semantics validates all our assessments. In particular, when philosophers talk of conditional ‘paradoxes’, the air of paradoxicality is an artefact of their reliance on the suppositional heuristic.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

That account of conditionals in turn suggests a more general hypothesis about philosophical paradoxes. They are artefacts of fallible but useful heuristics on which we unreflectively rely because they are built into our general cognitive systems, just as visual illusions are artefacts of fallible but useful heuristics on which we unreflectively rely because they are built into our visual systems. In both cases, the heuristics may be human universals.
5 From Metaphilosophy to the Nature of Conditionals: One Philosopher’s Experience

The general hypothesis about the origin and nature of philosophical paradoxes presumably belongs to metaphilosophy. But its consequences for specific paradoxes belong to more general philosophy – topics such as conditionals, vagueness, truth and falsity, knowledge, and belief are not in themselves metaphilosophical. These interconnections exemplify the intricate relations between philosophy and metaphilosophy.

Reflecting on one’s own practice can prompt one to modify that practice. Although metaphilosophy is just one small part of philosophy, it can sometimes command the rest. Through self–criticism, one may learn to do philosophy differently, perhaps even to do it better. Reflection on one’s own philosophical practice can also alert one to cognitive phenomena of wider interest: one can see a world in a grain of sand. The epistemology, metaphysics, or semantics of a philosophical statement is a sample of general epistemology, metaphysics, or semantics.

Of course, the relation of one’s philosophy to one’s metaphilosophy varies from philosopher to philosopher, and from tradition to tradition. It partly depends on the content of one’s metaphilosophy – for example, on whether one inclines to philosophical exceptionalism or anti–exceptionalism. And some philosophers are much more prone to metaphilosophical reflection than others are. On such a matter, one should aim not to draw up general rules, but to appreciate the range of possibilities. This paper has illustrated how complex and indirect the dialectic between philosophy and metaphilosophy can be. Surely many other episodes in the history of philosophy illustrate the same point.

Thanks are due to audiences for my remote presentation of this material at the 2022 conference on ‘Metaphilosophy in History’ at the University of Antwerp and my live presentation of it at Yale University for helpful discussion, and to the conference organizers, Catherine Dromelet, Willem Lemmens, and Tamas Demeter, for taking the risk of inviting a metaphilosopher who is very much not a historian of philosophy to speak at such an event.

works.title: Menzel on pure logic and higher-order metaphysics
passages: Menzel on pure logic and higher-order metaphysics

In ‘Pure Logic and Higher-Order Metaphysics’ (this volume), Christopher Menzel presents and defends a type-free theory of structured propositions and of properties, based on first-order logic. He contrasts it favourably with the higher-order intensional approach I take in Modal Logic as Metaphysics (Williamson 2013). In this chapter, I will discuss some distinctive aspects of Menzel’s account, and explain problems for them, problems that do not arise for the higher-order intensional approach.

From his title on, Menzel emphasizes a distinction between ‘pure logic’ and other kinds of abstract theorizing. His initial characterization is that pure logic ‘should be universal and topic neutral’ (§1.1; such references are to his chapter sections). However, the purity of pure logic turns out to be a vague matter of degree. Universality is the idea that ‘the general patterns of representation and reasoning that a logic is capable of expressing should be applicable to most any conceivable domain’ (§1.1). Menzel finds topic neutrality more elusive, but suggests glossing it as the constraint that ‘a logic shouldn’t of itself entail the existence of any particular things or particular properties; it should be indifferent to the particular identities and natures of things’, though he admits that this needs ‘a bit of qualification’ (§1.1, his italics).

Menzel’s account of ‘pure logic’ is no mere stipulation as to what he will mean by the word ‘logic’. It does methodological work for him, because he treats revision of pure logic as more disruptive and costly than revision of other theories. This is reminiscent of Quine’s attitude that we should keep revision as close to the periphery of the web of belief as we can (Quine 1951, 1970). For example, in Menzel’s assessment of the Prior-Kaplan paradox, he treats it as an advantage of his first-order account that he can treat it as a local problem, ‘specifically a paradox of truth […] as opposed to a paradox of pure logic’ (§3.1, his italics); by contrast, for me the paradox relies only on pure logic, as he notes, citing my brief discussion of it (Williamson 2016b). However, he omits my tentative conclusion there: that the paradox requires no revision of logic at all, but instead a deeper understanding of the non-transparency of our attitudes to externalist contents. I will return to that issue in the second part of these comments.

The ‘bit of qualification’ Menzel gives to his provisional gloss on topic neutrality comes in his discussion of identity. He reasonably decides that, even though the logic of identity is committed to a particular relation, identity, excluding it from pure logic would be too Draconian. Rather, he suggests, the commitments of pure logic ‘should not extend beyond those needed to think and reason within any conceivable domain’ (§1.5, his italics), which is in line with the methodological point that revising pure logic has global repercussions. Since he judges that commitment to identity passes the test of being needed to think and reason within any conceivable domain, he decides that pure logic should include the logic of identity.

Menzel takes the opposite attitude to the exemplification relation between things and properties (where properties count as things too). He judges that exemplification’s ‘properties are largely irrelevant to most areas of inquiry’ and so, by the same criterion, excludes the theory of exemplification from pure logic (§1.4). Consequently, on his view, the revision of the unrestricted comprehension principle needed to avoid the property version of Russell’s paradox counts as a revision to the local theory of property exemplification rather than to global pure logic, and so is much less disturbing.
Can identity and exemplification be kept so easily apart? In Menzel’s setting of first-order property theory, here is a natural formulation of Leibniz’s Law, the indiscernibility of identicals:
For any things x and y and property p, if x = y then x exemplifies p if and only if y exemplifies p.

But if pure logic includes the theory of identity, which includes LL, won’t pure logic also need to include the theory of exemplification, to handle its role in LL? Thus Menzel’s differential treatment of the theory of identity and the theory of exemplification threatens to be unstable.

Formally, Menzel can confine ‘pure logic’ to standard first-order logic with identity, which has no logical constant for exemplification and replaces the universal generalization LL with a schema LL∗ of the usual sort, which does not mention properties; roughly:
If x = y then φ(x) if and only if φ(y).

(I omit technical details.) However, that is less than satisfying. From the standpoint of first-order property theory, LL provides the unifying rationale for LL*’s infinitely many instances. After all, LL* is meant to be open-ended. The lack of counterexamples to it is no mere artefact of the accidentally limited expressive power of the language. As we add new atomic predicates to the language, we automatically add corresponding instances of LL*. LL is part of the rationale for doing so, since the new predicates are meant to express properties. If someone wanted to add a new predicate to be read ‘is so-called because of his size’ and then use LL* to argue that Giorgione ≠ Barbarelli, we could respond that no property has been specified for the predicate to express (the example is from Quine 1953). Of course, Quine himself would object to LL, because he regards properties as creatures of darkness. But Menzel posits properties and presumably accepts LL; he just wants to keep it out of pure logic, which will contain only LL*.

Obviously, in most domains of inquiry, non-logicians do not focus on principles like LL. But they also do not focus on principles like LL*. They just reason about cases of identity, more or less in conformity with both LL and LL*. More generally, explicit logical principles rarely figure in most domains of inquiry. They make patterns of reasoning explicit which are normally left implicit. LL takes that a step further than LL*. From this perspective, Menzel’s claim that the properties of exemplification ‘are largely irrelevant to most areas of inquiry’ looks quite dubious. Even though they are rarely the focus of inquiry, they are still relevant because they underpin patterns of reasoning employed in most areas of inquiry. Thus Menzel’s grounds for excluding the theory of exemplification from pure logic are unconvincing.

As a corollary, Menzel may be premature in his satisfaction at keeping pure logic untouched by the revisions required by various paradoxes he considers. Revisions to the theory of exemplification may be revisions to pure logic. In that respect, the advantages he claims over higher-order approaches may well be illusory. Indeed, his position is worse than that. For the restrictions on his comprehension principle for properties (§1.4) might compromise the use of LL to rationalize LL*, when no property p is exemplified by all and only those things which satisfy the predicate substituted for the schematic letter ‘φ’, though perhaps LL* could still be derived from LL in some less straightforward way—for example, by induction on the complexity of the predicate, if his property comprehension principle holds at least for the atomic predicates (but why should it?). By contrast, the higher-order approach supports an unrestricted second-order comprehension principle in place of Menzel’s restricted first-order comprehension principle for properties, which enables all instances of LL* to be smoothly derived from a second-order analogue of LL in a uniform way. Thus the higher-order perspective affords a more perspicuous view of the logic of identity.

A second distinctive feature of Menzel’s approach is its hyperintensionality: he denies that strictly equivalent propositions and properties are always identical. For example, while agreeing that, necessarily, whatever exemplifies triangularity exemplifies trilaterality and vice versa, Menzel denies that triangularity is trilaterality: ‘they are intuitively distinct, as one concerns the number of angles of a geometric figure and the other the number of sides’ (§1.3). Perhaps in support of this, he adds that (13) ‘doesn’t seem to follow’ from (12) (his numbering):

Of course, if one already regards triangularity and trilaterality as distinct, one will naturally take (13) not to follow from (12). But if one is still wondering whether ‘triangularity’ and ‘trilaterality’ refer to the same property, one should not allow the apparent gap between (12) and (13) to settle the issue. After all, to many people, (13!) doesn’t seem to follow from (12!) and the astronomical facts (which Chelsea may not know):

But, for all that, Hesperus is Phosphorus. As for Menzel’s first argument, that triangularity concerns the number of angles while trilaterality does not, we should wonder what is meant by saying that a property ‘concerns’ something. ‘Concerning’ sounds suspiciously like a semantic relation of aboutness. But properties are normally assumed to be worldly items; like planets and unlike concepts, they are not about anything. We do not want to fall into a trap analogous to arguing that since Hesperus concerns the evening while Phosphorus does not, Hesperus is not Phosphorus. Thus Menzel’s opening case for hyperintensionalism should not satisfy the antecedent doubts we might have on the matter.

Admittedly, the terms ‘triangular’ and ‘trilateral’ are not always interchangeable in explanatory contexts without loss. But that is only to be expected, because explanations should be as perspicuous as possible. Substituting co-referential terms can make an explanation harder or easier to follow, and so yield explanatory loss or gain. If we have been talking about angles, the transition to using the word ‘triangular’ may be cognitively smoother than the transition to using the word ‘trilateral’, just as, if we have been talking about the evening, the transition to using the name ‘Hesperus’ may be cognitively smoother than the transition to using the name ‘Phosphorus’. In both cases, to infer a difference in reference incurs the suspicion of projecting the structure of our cognition onto the structure of the world.

To argue for the hyperintensionality of propositions, Menzel takes the example of the proposition that alligators don’t exist and the proposition that, if alligators exist, there is a largest prime, which are necessarily equivalent in truth-value (§1.6). He then asserts that ‘intuitively’, from (22) ‘we cannot reasonably infer’ (23):
Sasha believes that alligators don’t exist.
Sasha believes that, if alligators exist, there is a largest prime.

Thus, Menzel concludes, the proposition that alligators don’t exist is distinct from the proposition that, if alligators exist, there is a largest prime, because Sasha can believe the former without believing the latter.
We should be wary of that argument too. Consider the similar argument that ‘intuitively’, from (22!) and the astronomical facts (which Sasha may not know), we cannot reasonably infer (23!):
Sasha believes that Hesperus is bright.
Sasha believes that Phosphorus is bright.

Thus, the argument concludes, the proposition that Hesperus is bright is distinct from the proposition that Phosphorus is bright, because Sasha can believe the former without believing the latter. As Kripke has forcefully explained, the conclusion is not safe, because our practices of belief ascription are not fully consistent; they can lead us into inconsistency through over-sensitivity to the subject’s linguistic utterances (Kripke 1979). This can happen even in cases of generally accepted synonymy, as with the words ‘furze’ and ‘gorse’, which are simply two words for the same shrub, and are associated with the same non-metalinguistic descriptions. Nevertheless, if we are not sure whether Sasha is aware of the co-reference, from (22!!) and our awareness of the linguistic facts, we may feel that we cannot reasonably infer (23!!):
Sasha believes that furze has yellow flowers.
Sasha believes that gorse has yellow flowers.

Thus, the analogous argument concludes, the proposition that furze has yellow flowers is distinct from the proposition that gorse has yellow flowers, because Sasha can believe the former without believing the latter. But the conclusion is hopeless: the proposition that furze has yellow flowers is the proposition that gorse has yellow flowers, for we use the words ‘furze’ and ‘gorse’ synonymously, we use the sentences ‘Furze has yellow flowers’ and ‘Gorse has yellow flowers’ to express the same proposition, and we are the people discussing whether the proposition that furze has yellow flowers is the proposition that gorse has yellow flowers. Elsewhere, I have discussed such cases in much greater detail, and shown how the potentially inconsistent rules for belief ascription identified by Kripke can be understood as heuristics, quick and easy ways of meeting cognitive challenges which usually but not always give the correct answer (Williamson 2021b). We rely on heuristics in many different areas of cognition. On the emerging picture, the truth-conditions of propositional attitude ascriptions are much less transparent to us than they seem, and we are much less reliable in recognizing whether they obtain than we assume ourselves to be. The convoluted and inconclusive literature published over the past seventy years on the semantics of attitude ascriptions is a manifestation of the difficulties.

In the case of Menzel’s example, Sasha may of course assent to the sentence ‘Alligators don’t exist’ while too uncertain to assent to ‘If alligators exist, there is a largest prime’, but if so it does not follow that (22) is true and (23) false. Similarly, if Sasha assents to ‘Hesperus is bright’ but not to ‘Phosphorus is bright’, it does not follow that (22!) is true and (23!) false, and if Sasha assents to ‘Furze has yellow flowers’ but not to ‘Gorse has yellow flowers’, it does not follow that (22!!) is true and (23!!) false. Nothing was stipulated as to how much English (if any) Sasha knows. Of course, with the pair (22) and (23), unlike the pairs (22!) and (23!) and (22!!) and (23!!), the two embedded sentences also differ in structure and subject matter. But just what those differences imply for belief is not obvious, given the lack of consensus in the literature. We may end up having to say that Sasha believes a proposition p under the guise of the sentence ‘Alligators don’t exist’ but does not believe p under the guise of the sentence ‘If alligators exist, there is a largest prime’, even though both sentences express p. A cautious moral is that, in the present state of understanding of the semantics and heuristics of propositional attitude ascriptions, our ‘intuitive’ judgements about them are not a safe guide to the individuation of propositions. In particular, they are not decisive against a coarse-grained intensional account of propositions like that of Stalnaker (1984, 1999; see also Williamson 2021a,b, 2022).

None of this by itself constitutes an argument against hyperintensionalism about propositions and properties. It just shows that the case for hyperintensionalism is much weaker than its proponents assume. ‘Intuitively’ appealing examples are not enough. The issue will eventually have to be determined on more theoretically informed grounds. In what follows, I will make some comments towards an assessment of Menzel’s specific hyperintensional theory of propositions in its own right, putting aside his inconclusive case for hyperintensionalism in general.

According to Menzel, ‘propositions exhibit a fine-grained structure similar to (but by no means isomorphic to) the grammatical structure of the sentences that express them’ (§1.6). For some, this remark will set off alarm bells: it sounds as though the structure of language is being projected onto the structure of reality. In Modal Logic as Metaphysics, I summarily wrote: ‘Hyperintensionality arises at the level of thought and linguistic meaning, and should be explained at that level, not at the level of anything like a general theory of properties and relations’ (2013: 266). Menzel responds:

contrary to what Williamson appears to imply, ontological commitments that arise “at the level of thought and linguistic meaning” are entirely pertinent to the logic of metaphysical modality. On a realist view of thought and meaning, there are the things thought and meant. [§1.4, his italics]

Neither in the passage to which Menzel objects nor now do I disagree with the realist claim that there are the things thought and meant (though I prefer to give it a higher-order inflection). If some mental or semantic phenomenon is a counterexample to a putative law of logic, then of course that law is false. My point was quite different: although mental or linguistic representations (such as predicates) can be necessarily co-extensive yet cognitively different, we should not project that feature onto the properties or relations to which they refer.

To illustrate the point for properties, we should first note that Menzel sketches the familiar treatment of sentences and propositions as a special case of n-place predicates and n-place properties respectively, for n = 0. Thus, having introduced notation for nominalizing complex sentences and so referring to propositions in his formal object language, he writes ‘The framework developed here generalizes quite naturally to one that contains complex n-place predicates’ (footnote 24), by introducing notation for nominalizing complex predicates and so referring to properties in the object language. He later supplies some of the logical details, treating the propositional case as that for n = 0 (footnote 27). We have already seen how he carefully argues in parallel for the hyperintensional individuation of properties and the hyperintensional individuation of propositions.

If we generalize Mendel’s hyperintensional approach to the individuation of propositions to properties in the natural way, we obtain the result that being both square and square is a distinct property from being either square or square, because conjunction and disjunction are distinct operations on properties—because, in effect, being both square and square is treated as a conjunctive property, not a disjunctive one, while being either square or square is treated as a disjunctive property, not a conjunctive one. Such results might be acceptable in a theory of Fregean senses, modes of presentation of their referents. But that is not what Menzel is offering, as can be seen from his claim that the proposition that Bernie Sanders is a Democrat is determined by the property of being a Democrat and Bernie Sanders himself—not by a sense which presents Bernie Sanders (§2.2). In that respect, Menzel’s propositions and properties are worldly; his theory abstracts away from differences at the level of modes of presentation. Yet in distinguishing being both green and green or being either green or green from simply being green, his theory refuses to abstract away from other differences which to many philosophers (including me) seem blatantly to belong at the level of modes of presentation: redundant applications of a logical operator. Imagine a medical scientist discovering that what really causes lung cancer is not smoking but instead either smoking or smoking. Numerous similar examples would make the same point. By contrast, natural science robustly investigates modal distinctions: in their intended applications, dynamical systems and other mathematical structures based on phase spaces are interpreted as modelling the physically possible states of a physical system (Williamson 2016a). In short, Menzel’s rules for individuating propositions and properties have no clear unified motivation.

The implausibility of Menzel’s account is somewhat disguised in his paper because he develops it explicitly only for propositions, despite apparently regarding them as a special case of properties. But that assimilation does not fit some standard ways of thinking about propositions. In particular, propositions are often characterized as the objects of belief. In other words, they are defined by their role in mental life. That introduces a link to modes of presentation and makes the hyperintensional way in which Menzel individuates propositions much less surprising. By contrast, properties and relations are not usually defined by their role in mental life. More often, they are associated with ways in which objects resemble or differ from each other, irrespective of anyone’s mental life. That cuts the link to modes of presentation and makes the analogous hyperintensional way of individuating properties and relations much more surprising. If one wants a term for a 0-place property, ‘state of affairs’ is preferable to ‘proposition’, since the phrase ‘state of affairs’ lacks the associations with mental life which confuse the issue with the word ‘proposition’. Some states of affairs obtain, for instance Rome’s being the capital of Italy, while others do not, for instance Milan’s being the capital of Italy (for those uncomfortable with this terminology, the phrase ‘way for things to be’ may work better than ‘state of affairs’). Menzel’s approach would then imply that x’s being both square and square is a different state of affairs from x’s being either square or square, and both from x’s being square. Again, to many philosophers (including me) the differences seem blatantly to belong at the level of modes of presentation. Imagine a seismologist discovering that Taiwan has so many earthquakes not because two tectonic plates converge nearby but instead because either two tectonic plates converge nearby or two tectonic plates converge nearby. Again, the contrast with the robust role of modality in natural science is striking.

Menzel does not seem oblivious to this tension. Of the system as developed in the paper, with no complex predicates, he writes: ‘Intuitively, propositions, so represented, exhibit a level of richness and complexity that, in the framework at hand, properties do not; the latter are taken to be structurally simple’ (§1.5). After noting that ‘The framework developed here generalizes quite naturally to one that contains complex n-place predicates’, he expresses doubts as to whether the generalization would be semantically warranted (footnote 24). Yet he argues for hyperintensionalism in the two cases in parallel ways, and he does not suggest withdrawing those arguments. Presumably, unpacking ‘triangular’ and ‘trilateral’ by the complex predicates they definitionally abbreviate would make no crucial difference.

If a natural generalization of Menzel’s framework is indeed illegitimate, that hints that something may be wrong with the original framework too. His ambivalence could be interpreted as responsive to the instability of the underlying conception.

Hyperintensionalists more full-hearted than Menzel have an easier time, blithely distinguishing the property of smoking from the property of smoking or smoking because (supposedly) the former grounds the latter and not vice versa (or whatever). They treat their proliferating distinctions as a methodological benefit, giving greater flexibility, more degrees of freedom in modelling examples. Their attitude contrasts strikingly with that of modellers in the natural and social sciences, who regard increasing a model’s degree of freedom (roughly, the number of independent parameters) as a methodological cost, not a benefit, because it makes fitting the data too easy, thereby reducing explanatory power. I have developed this critique of hyperintensionalism elsewhere (Williamson 2021a), and plan to extend it further. Rather than pursue the issues here, I will briefly discuss a problem that depends only on Menzel’s fine-grained way of individuating propositions, whether or not he individuates his properties and relations in an analogously fine-grained way.

A notorious challenge faces theories such as Menzel’s, which individuate propositions in line with the syntactic structure of the sentences that express them: the Russell-Myhill paradox. It comes in various forms. I will focus on the one which most worries Menzel, because he regards it as the closest to a paradox of pure logic.

Menzel’s plural Russell-Myhill paradox starts from a standard comprehension principle PC for plurals, which says roughly that if something meets a condition, then there are the things that meet the condition (where ‘meets the condition’ is to be replaced by any open formula of the object language). Menzel describes PC as ‘arguably both ontologically innocuous and logically self-evident’, and is inclined to count it and the rest of a standard theory of plurals as ‘pure logic’ (§3.2)—though those grounds do not quite match his original criteria of universality and topic neutrality. Given his plural logic, including PC, and his fine-grained account of propositions, Menzel can then show that there are the propositions 𝗋𝗋 of the form [𝗓𝗓=𝗓𝗓] that are not among the things 𝗓𝗓 they are about (where ‘𝗋𝗋’ and ‘𝗓𝗓’ are plural terms), and from there derive a contradiction in a quasi-Russellian way; 𝗋𝗋 is of course the analogue of the Russell set, the set of the sets which are not members of themselves.

Menzel considers two strategies for blocking the paradox. The first is to restrict the plural comprehension principle PC, as some others have done. Menzel would then sugar the pill by also denying that plural comprehension principles belong to ‘pure logic’ (contrary to his initial inclination), though quite what would be at stake in doing so is not very clear. One problem for this strategy is that the original interest of plurals was that, apparently, they satisfied the unrestricted comprehension principle PC (with the trivial exception of the empty case) without introducing any ontological mysteries, so that interpreting second-order quantification in plural terms would legitimize second-order logic with its unrestricted comprehension principle as a framework for mathematical theories (Boolos 1984). But once PC is restricted, plurals no longer properly serve that purpose. They still have some interest for the semantics of natural languages, but for mathematical purposes they are in danger of becoming useless middlemen between predicates and sets. That would deprive plurals of much of their apparent interest.

Menzel’s second strategy, which he seems to prefer to the first, is to reject the assumption that every sentence of his formal object language expresses a proposition. He sketches a hierarchical conception of propositions on which they are built up in stages from below. At no stage have all the propositions in the Russell plurality 𝗋𝗋 been formed, so 𝗋𝗋 themselves are never collectively available to be put into a proposition. The upshot is that although ‘there is the plurality 𝗋𝗋’, ‘there are no propositions about 𝗋𝗋’, as Menzel puts it (§3.2, his italics). That blocks the final stage of the paradoxical derivation by restricting propositional comprehension.

There is a problem. In stating his solution, Menzel asserts ‘there is the plurality 𝗋𝗋’ and ‘there are no propositions about 𝗋𝗋’. Do those sentences, in that context, express propositions? If they do, they express propositions about 𝗋𝗋, in Menzel’s sense; that is how his theory of propositions works. But then his account is wrong, because it implies that there are no propositions about 𝗋𝗋. So, on Menzel’s view, neither of those sentences should express a proposition. But then his attempt to state a solution to the plural Russell-Myhill paradox fails, because at the crucial point no proposition was expressed—he was just uttering empty words.

Someone might try to tell a story in which Menzel somehow gets his point across non-propositionally. But what is his point, if not a proposition? Presumably, according to him, his point is both believable and true, but how can it be believable or true if his best attempt to express it fails to express a proposition? Menzel’s propositions are in danger of becoming redundant, if everything works fine without them. What are Menzel-propositions supposed to be needed for? Just as Menzel’s contemplated restriction on plural comprehension undermines the utility of plurals, so his contemplated restriction on propositional comprehension undermines the utility of propositions.

The case is worth comparing with Menzel’s argument that ‘the entire framework of type theory teeters rather perilously on the edge of self-refutation’ (§1.3), since both concern expressive limitations. To illustrate his claim, he considers sentence (11), which he describes as ‘a metatheoretic truth of the semantics of higher-order logic’:
Every property belongs to some type.

According to Menzel, ‘It is difficult to see any other way of understanding (11) than as a general, untyped proposition […] whose quantifiers range unrestrictedly over a universe that contains all properties and all types’. Naturally, type-theorists deny that such untyped quantification is possible. They need not deny that (11) is meaningful; they can understand the quantifiers ‘every property’ and ‘some type’ as ordinary first-order quantifiers, so that (11) may have a meaning, just not one that connects with the intended semantics of higher-order logic in any useful way. Contrary to Menzel’s claim, (11) is not a metatheoretic truth of the semantics of higher-order logic; it is a Trojan horse, an unwanted gift he offers to type-theorists, who must learn from the Trojans’ example. By contrast, the sentences about 𝗋𝗋 above were written by Menzel, not pressed on him by his opponents; they are his statement of his tentative answer to an objection to his view of plural logic. In committing itself to their not expressing propositions, the answer is not so much teetering on the edge of self-refutation as marching right over it.

In a footnote at the end of his paper, Menzel mentions with apparent sympathy the attempted potentialist solution in Yu (2017) to the Russell-Myhill paradox for plural propositions. Since he does not elaborate on the idea, nor will I.
In support of his type-free approach, Menzel also offers a variety of more everyday sentences of English involving nominalizations (§ 1.2–3), such as his (6) and (7):

As Russellian paradoxes teach us, nominalization cannot in general work as we want it to. An unrestricted first-order comprehension principle for properties is inconsistent. That does not imply that nominalization is meaningless, but for many theoretical purposes we do better to avoid its combinatorial limitations by working in a typed language and using type-raising rather than type-lowering devices. For example, rather than applying a type-lowering device to the predicate ‘is wise’ to get ‘wisdom’, as in (7), we can apply a suitable type-raising device to the two-place predicate ‘loves’ to get a new two-place predicate, higher-order in its second argument place, which can combine with ‘Charles’ and ‘is wise’ to make a meaningful sentence.

If we are condemned to work in an untyped framework, we can learn to live with its problems, under some or other ad hoc restrictions to maintain consistency. But we are not so condemned. We can work in higher-order intensional logic with its unrestricted comprehension principles, if we like both for plurals and for propositions. Menzel’s troubles stem from his ultra-fine-grained hyperintensional approach. His initial case against intensionalism turned out to be flimsy. That would not have mattered too much if his positive theory had proved to be explanatorily powerful. But it did not. In its struggle for consistency, it had drastically to restrict the comprehension principles needed for explanatory power. By any reasonable abductive criteria of simplicity, strength, elegance, and capacity to unify, higher-order intensional logic is by far the better theory.
