Of course, some people claim that vagueness shows that not all trivial theorems of classical mathematics are true. That claim is usually premised on many-valued logic, which has already been rejected. Of course, it might have some other premise. Nevertheless, the aim in the remainder of this paper will be to explore issues of vague identity under the assumption that classical reasoning may be used in the metalanguage.

Let us apply (CLL) to the claim that it is sometimes neither true nor false to say of given objects that they are identical. Suppose that the assignment A assigns the object o to the variable x and the object o* to the variable y. If it is neither true nor false to say of o and o* that they are identical, then the formula x=y is neither true nor false relative to A, when = means identity. Let 𝐀* be the assignment that differs from A at most in assigning o to y; since 𝐀* assigns o to x too, x=y is true relative to 𝐀*. Since x=y is by hypothesis not true relative to A, by (CLL) o and o* are not identical. But then if = really means identity, x=y should be false relative to A, contrary to hypothesis. Thus the supposition that it is neither true nor false to say of o and o* that they are identical is incoherent.
Someone might object that in a context in which we are contemplating truth-value gaps for identity statements with uniquely denoting terms, ‘not true’ in (CLL) must be replaced by ‘false’:

Let an assignment A assign an object o to a variable v, an assignment 𝐀* assign an object o* to v, and 𝐀* be exactly like A in every other way. Suppose that a sentence α is true relative to A and false relative to 𝐀*. Then o and o* are not identical.

But this modification gets things back to front. Entertain for a moment the dialetheist idea that a sentence can be both true and false relative to the very same assignment 𝐀#. Let 𝐀# assign the object o# to a variable v. When we take both A and 𝐀* to be 𝐀#, and both o and o* to be o#, (CLL–) delivers the absurd result that o# is distinct from itself. If one accepts (CLL–), one does so on the basis of the anti-dialetheist assumption that if α is false relative to 𝐀* then it is not also true relative to 𝐀*. That is, the reason for accepting (CLL–) is that it follows by the mutual exclusiveness of truth and falsity from (CLL), which is a special case of a theorem of classical mathematics. (CLL–) is not a special case of a theorem of classical mathematics; unlike (CLL), it depends on something specifically semantic, the mutual exclusiveness of truth and falsity. To endorse (CLL–) without (CLL) is confused. Furthermore, no good reason has been provided to reject (CLL). Of course, someone who clings on at all costs to the claim that identity statements with uniquely denoting terms can have truth-value gaps might mechanically reject (CLL) simply on the grounds that it is the key premise of an argument against the claim. Any error can be protected like that. The point is that nothing has been done to explain how (CLL) could fail.

We should not take it for granted that indeterminate identity is to be understood in terms of truth-value gaps. Once we have Δ in the object-language, we can apply (CLL) to the earlier formulation ¬Δx=y∧¬Δ¬x=y. Suppose that it is indeterminate whether the objects o and o* are identical. Let A be an assignment that assigns o to the variable x and o* to the variable y. By hypothesis, the formula ¬Δx=y is true relative to A. Let 𝐀* be the assignment that differs from A at most in assigning o to y. Since 𝐀* also assigns o to x, ¬Δx=y is not true relative to 𝐀*. Consequently, by (CLL), o and o* are not identical. The result would be the same even if one used (CLL–) rather than (CLL) here, for ¬Δx=y is false as well as not true relative to 𝐀*. Thus it is indeterminate whether objects are identical only if they are not identical. Although this is of course a variation on the original Evans argument, it uses no substitution principle for the object-language.

It would be misconceived to object that the notion of truth relative to an assignment of objects to variables in the scope of the determinacy operator Δ is problematic. For unless we can apply that notion to the formula ¬Δx=y, we cannot locate the indeterminacy in the relation between the objects themselves. The application is licensed by the hypothesis of indeterminate identity itself (see also Heck [1998], pp.278-81).

What exactly has the argument shown? If it is indeterminate whether o and o* are identical, then o and o* are distinct. Is this a reductio ad absurdum of the supposition that it is indeterminate whether o and o* are identical? Not straightforwardly. In object-language terms, ¬Δx=y entails ¬x=y. But ¬x=y is not immediately inconsistent with ¬Δx=y∧¬Δ¬x=y. What is wrong with the hypothesis that although it is indeterminate whether o and o* are identical, they are in fact not identical? The flavour of absurdity comes from the idea that, once we have worked out that o and o* are not identical, it follows that it is determinate that they are not identical. If ¬x=y entails Δ¬x=y then ¬Δx=y∧¬Δ¬x=y is inconsistent, because ¬Δx=y entails ¬x=y. The question is whether to accept the form of inference from α to Δα.

Recall the kind of situation which the notion of indeterminacy was introduced to describe. Supposedly, the grounds for asserting something and the grounds for asserting its negation are evenly balanced, and there is no room for further considerations to decide the matter. If the relation between o and o* conforms to this pattern, then the grounds for asserting that they are identical and the grounds for asserting that they are not identical should be evenly balanced, and there should be no room for further considerations to decide the matter. But, if it is indeterminate whether they are identical, then the argument above does decide the matter, in favour of asserting that they are not identical. The grounds are after all not evenly balanced. Thus the hypothesis that it is indeterminate whether they are identical looks inconsistent with what indeterminacy is supposed to be.

As we might expect, the argument leaves it open that for some relation of coincidence, similar but not strictly equivalent to identity, certain objects neither determinately coincide nor determinately fail to coincide (Akiba [2000] elaborates such a possibility within a quasi-supervaluationist framework). But vague coincidence is not vague identity.

A more formal point can be developed. Those who defend the verdict of indeterminacy in some particular case of o and o* presumably hold that it is determinate that it is indeterminate whether o and o* are identical. In symbols, they defend Δ(¬Δx=y∧¬Δ¬x=y) relative to an appropriate assignment.
We can formulate two plausible principles about the logic of Δ, using the symbol ⊨ for semantic consequence:

(RK) says that determinacy is closed under semantic consequence; if there are decisive grounds for the premises of a semantically valid argument, they combine with that semantic connection to constitute decisive grounds for its conclusion. We allow n to take the value 0, in which case (RK) boils down to the ‘determination’ rule that ⊨β implies ⊨Δβ, but only the case when n takes the value 1 is used in what follows. (RT) is the uncontentious principle that whatever is determinately so is so.

Granted the semantic relation ¬Δx=y⊨¬x=y already argued for by appeal to (CLL), we can use (RK) and (RT) to argue by reductio ad absurdum against the supposition Δ(¬Δx=y∧¬Δ¬x=y) of determinately indeterminate identity, thus:
Thus Δ(¬Δx=y∧¬Δ¬x=y) is an inconsistent hypothesis (see also McGee and McLaughlin [1995], p.232). It cannot be determinate that it is indeterminate whether objects are identical.

For some but not all supervaluationists the discharge of a premise in the use of reductio ad absurdum at line 9 would be problematic (Williamson [1994], p.151-2). However, they could reformulate the argument in terms of the unconditional semantic validity of conditional statements; for example, line 1 would become ⊨¬Δx=y→¬x=y. Under corresponding reformulations of (RK) and (RT), the revised argument would be acceptable to those supervaluationists too, and its bottom line would still be 9. Anyway, line 8 is already bad news for determinately indeterminate identity.

Evans envisaged a related argument that would reduce the original indeterminacy hypothesis ¬Δx=y∧¬Δ¬x=y itself to absurdity within an analogue of the strong modal system S5. In addition to (RK) and (RT), such a system would have the S5 rule ¬Δα⊨Δ¬Δα, and therefore in particular ¬Δx=y⊨Δ¬Δx=y. That would combine with line 2 above to yield ¬Δx=y⊨Δ¬x=y and therefore ¬Δx=y∧¬Δ¬x=y⊨Δ¬x=y∧¬Δ¬x=y, which gives ⊨¬(¬Δx=y∧¬Δ¬x=y). The hypothesis that it is indeterminate whether objects are identical is incoherent. However, the S5 rule is suspiciously strong. In combination with (RK), (RT) and classical logic, it generates the conclusion ⊨ΔΔα∨Δ¬Δα, which excludes indeterminacy in Δα. But any case for first-order indeterminacy corresponds to a case for such second-order indeterminacy. If it is indeterminate when there ceased to be a heap, it is equally indeterminate when it ceased to be indeterminate when there ceased to be a heap. Consequently, we should not rely on S5 reasoning.

We should however note that ¬Δx=y∧¬Δ¬x=y can be reduced to absurdity on assumptions weaker than the S5 rule. For example, the so-called Brouwerian rule ¬α⊨Δ¬Δα is quite consistent with higher-order vagueness (Williamson [1999] has more discussion); one instance is ¬x=y⊨Δ¬Δx=y. But we have ¬Δx=y⊨¬x=y by assumption, so transitivity gives ¬Δx=y⊨Δ¬Δx=y, exactly the special case of the S5 rule that excluded indeterminate identity. Other rules short of S5 have a similar effect (McGee and McLaughlin [1995], p.250). But whether the Brouwerian rule or another of those rules holds on a reading of Δ as ‘determinately’ is far from clear (see also Williamson [1996], p.12-13). Let us therefore concentrate on the inconsistency of Δ(¬Δx=y∧¬Δ¬x=y), which does not depend on such controversial reasoning.

Even if for no objects is it determinate that it is indeterminate whether they are identical, it does not immediately follow that it is not determinate that for some objects it is indeterminate whether they are identical, for Δ∃x∃y(¬Δx=y∧¬Δ¬x=y)∧¬∃x∃yΔ(¬Δx=y∧¬Δ¬x=y) is not an immediately inconsistent combination. Perhaps it is determinate that there are cases of indeterminate identity even though there are no determinate cases of indeterminate identity. Nevertheless, on a non-epistemic understanding of indeterminacy, the impossibility of determinate cases of indeterminate identity does seem to detract from the reality of indeterminate identity. Consider a formally similar case. According to supervaluationists, it is determinate that some number n is a sharp cut-off point for baldness, in the sense that having just n hairs on one’s head implies baldness but having just n+1 hairs on one’s head does not (Δ∃n(Bn∧¬Bn+1)), for each sharpening of ‘bald’ provides such a cut-off point. However, supervaluationists regard this as somehow not a serious commitment to a cut-off point, for they also hold that for no number n is it determinate that n is a cut-off point for baldness (¬∃nΔ(Bn∧¬Bn+1)); the cut-off point varies across sharpenings. If ¬∃nΔ(Bn∧¬Bn+1) undermines the apparent commitment in Δ∃n(Bn∧¬Bn+1) to a sharp cut-off point, then by parity of reasoning ¬∃x∃yΔ(¬Δx=y∧¬Δ¬x=y) should undermine the apparent commitment in Δ∃x∃y(¬Δx=y∧¬Δ¬x=y) to an indeterminate identity.

The previous result that any case of indeterminate identity is a case of non-identity makes the supposedly non-epistemic nature of the indeterminacy quite hard to grasp (for the general difficulty of elucidating a non-epistemic conception of indeterminacy see also Williamson [1995], [1997], pp.216-17). On an epistemicist conception, we are irremediably ignorant in borderline cases. Since there is a truth of the matter, however unknowable, vagueness does not invalidate classical logic. Let us explore questions of vague identity within such an epistemicist framework.

The Evans argument, once modified to rely on (CLL), involves assignments of objects to the variables in the formula Δx=y, that is, on an epistemicist reading, to variables within the scope of an epistemic operator. Such assignments are notoriously problematic. If John knows that Hesperus is Hesperus but does not know that Hesperus is Phosphorus, what is the truth-value of the formula ‘John knows that x is y’ when that planet is assigned to both variables? Not everyone accepts that the substitution of coreferring singular terms in propositional attitude contexts does affect truth-value (Salmon [1986]). But since it certainly appears to, we must proceed with great caution.

We can express the epistemicist reading of Δ by using ‘clear’ in place of ‘determinate’. The simple reading of Δ as ‘it is knowable’ is inadequate, for it would make the formula ¬Δα∧¬Δ¬α true whenever the truth-value of the proposition expressed by α could not be known; but our current interest is not in cases in which the source of the unknowability has nothing to do with vagueness (undecidable propositions of mathematics may provide examples; see Williamson [1995]). The intended epistemicist reading of Δ prescinds from such irrelevant obstacles to knowledge. The relevant obstacle is, very roughly, that a vague sentence might express a true proposition on its actual interpretation I while expressing a false proposition on some close counterfactual interpretation 𝐈*, where speakers’ insensitivity to the difference between I and 𝐈* makes any belief they express by uttering the sentence too unreliable to constitute knowledge (Williamson [1994], pp.230-4 has more details). In such circumstances we may describe 𝐈* as indiscriminable from I. The natural proposal is therefore that Δα is true on an interpretation I if α is true on every interpretation 𝐈* indiscriminable from I. On such a semantics, what kind of context does Δ create? We can answer the question by examining the simplest interesting case.

Consider a propositional language with just two singular terms, the constants a and b, in which the only atomic sentences are a=a, a=b, b=a and b=b. There are just three primitive sentence operators, Δ, ¬ and ∧. Other operators are introduced as metalinguistic abbreviations. A model is an ordered pair of a class of interpretations and a reflexive symmetric relation of indiscriminability defined over them. A sentence is valid in a model if and only if it is true on every interpretation in the model. For most purposes reference to the model can be left tacit. An interpretation I assigns a denotation to each constant. The sentence t1=t2 is true on I if and only if I assigns the same denotation to the constants t1 and t2. As usual, ¬α is true on I if and only if α is not true on I, and α∧β is true on I if and only if α is true on I and β is true on I. Finally, Δα is true on I if and only if α is true on every interpretation indiscriminable from I.

On this semantics, = is treated as a logical constant; it is always interpreted as identity, just as ¬ and ∧ are always interpreted as negation and conjunction respectively. The logical constants are treated as precise. In the case of identity, this assumption has been challenged (Hirsch [1999]). However, identity is a logically salient relation, the narrowest necessarily reflexive relation. It is implausible that an unnoticeable shift in our use of = would make it refer to some other relation. The assumption is therefore reasonable.

Consider a model with just two interpretations, 𝐈1 and 𝐈2, each indiscriminable from the other. 𝐈1 assigns a and b the same denotation; 𝐈2 assigns them different denotations. Since a=b is true on 𝐈1, ¬Δ¬a=b is valid; since a=b is not true on 𝐈2, ¬Δa=b is valid. Since a=a and b=b are valid, so are Δa=a and Δb=b. In this model, indiscriminability is transitive as well as reflexive and symmetric; consequently, Δ has an S5-like logic. In particular, all sentences of the forms ¬Δα→Δ¬Δα, Δα→α and (Δα∧Δ(α→β))→Δβ are valid, and whenever α is valid, so is Δα. We could easily complicate the model to invalidate S5 while retaining the features of current interest.

On this semantics, Δ creates an opaque context, in the sense that not every instance of the substitution principle t=t*→(α→α*) is valid in every model, where α* differs from α at most in having some occurrences of the constant t* where α has occurrences of t. For example, a=b and Δa=a are true on 𝐈1 but Δa=b is not. Consequently, we should not regard a sentence of the form Δt1=t2 on an interpretation I as expressing a proposition about the objects that t1 and t2 do in fact denote on I to the effect just that they are clearly identical. For otherwise Δa=a and Δa=b would express the same proposition on 𝐈1, and would therefore have the same truth-value. Thus ¬Δa=b∧¬Δ¬a=b on a given interpretation does not express a proposition about the objects that a and b do in fact denote on that interpretation to the effect just that it is unclear whether they are identical. It would be less inaccurate to regard Δα as quoting α, and ¬Δa=b∧¬Δ¬a=b in particular as expressing a proposition about the names a and b themselves to the effect that it is unclear whether they denote the same object. That is vagueness in language, not in the objects to which it refers.

We can introduce variables and quantifiers into the language with an auxiliary notion of truth on an interpretation relativized to assignments of values to variables. These assignments should be independent of the interpretations. For otherwise a single assignment A could assign to the variable n relative to each interpretation I the cut-off point for ‘bald’ on I; thus Bn∧¬Bn+1 would be true on every interpretation relative to A, so Δ(Bn∧¬Bn+1) would be true relative to A, so ∃nΔ(Bn∧¬Bn+1) would be true. Intuitively, that is the wrong result, for the formula says that some number is the clear cut-off point for baldness. Thus assignments should be independent of interpretations. But then relative to any given assignment either x=y is true on every interpretation or ¬x=y is true on every interpretation, depending on the identity or non-identity of the objects assigned to the variables x and y by that assignment. Thus relative to any assignment either Δx=y is true or Δ¬x=y is true. Consequently, the formula ∀x∀y(Δx=y∨Δ¬x=y) is valid. It does not follow that the schema Δt1=t2∨Δ¬t1=t2 is valid for closed singular terms, which it certainly is not; since closed singular terms can be vague in a way in which variables cannot be, they cannot be substituted for variables within the scope of Δ to instantiate a universal geneneralization, just as nonrigid designators cannot be substituted for variables in modal contexts.

Thus epistemicism validates the natural formalization of the claim that it is never vague whether objects are identical: ¬∃x∃y(¬Δx=y∧¬Δ¬x=y). In that sense, it excludes vague identity (Williamson forthcoming has more details). That is hardly surprising. Nevertheless, we want more. For some identity statements constitute borderline cases while others do not: the relevant singular terms refer to objects. Surely we can say something about the objects themselves on that basis.

We can say more by exploiting the expressive resources of the metalanguage. Given epistemicism, one interpretation is correct; it maps expressions to their actual referents. We can therefore use a notion of absolute truth, truth on the correct interpretation. We can then define some binary relations between objects o1 and o2 thus:
o1 and o2 are presentable as clearly identical ⇔
Δt1=t2 is true for some constants t1 and t2 denoting o1 and o2 respectively.
o1 and o2 are presentable as clearly distinct ⇔
Δ¬t1=t2 is true for some constants t1 and t2 denoting o1 and o2 respectively.
o1 and o2 are presentable as either clearly identical or clearly distinct ⇔
Δt1=t2∨Δ¬t1=t2 is true for some constants t1 and t2 denoting o1 and o2 respectively.
o1 and o2 are presentable as not clearly identical ⇔
¬Δt1=t2 is true for some constants t1 and t2 denoting o1 and o2 respectively.
o1 and o2 are presentable as not clearly distinct ⇔
¬Δ¬t1=t2 is true for some constants t1 and t2 denoting o1 and o2 respectively.
o1 and o2 are presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct ⇔
¬Δt1=t2∧¬Δ¬t1=t2 is true for some constants t1 and t2 denoting o1 and o2 respectively.

These equivalences define genuine relations; in these contexts the substitution of coreferring terms for o1 and o2 is legitimate. We could define corresponding ternary relations by relativizing the binary relations to interpretations in the obvious way.

Here are some elementary logical features of the relations. Since indiscriminability is reflexive, t1=t2 is true whenever Δt1=t2 is, so objects are presentable as clearly identical only if they are indeed identical. Similarly, since ¬t1=t2 is true whenever Δ¬t1=t2 is, objects are presentable as clearly distinct only if they are indeed distinct. Obviously, objects are presentable as either clearly identical or clearly distinct if and only if they are either presentable as clearly identical or presentable as clearly distinct. Less obviously, they are presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct if and only if they are both presentable as not clearly identical and presentable as not clearly distinct. One half is obvious: if they are presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct then they are both presentable as not clearly identical and presentable as not clearly distinct. For the converse, suppose that o1 and o2 are both presentable as not clearly identical and presentable as not clearly distinct. There are two cases. First, suppose that o1 and o2 are identical. Since they are presentable as not clearly identical, ¬Δt1=t2 is true for some constants t1 and t2 denoting o1 and o2 respectively. But since o1 and o2 are identical, ¬Δ¬t1=t2 is also true. Thus ¬Δt1=t2∧¬Δ¬t1=t2 is true, so o1 and o2 are presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct. Similarly, suppose that o1 and o2 are distinct. Since they are presentable as not clearly distinct, ¬Δ¬t1=t2 is true for some constants t1 and t2 denoting o1 and o2 respectively. But since o1 and o2 are distinct, ¬Δt1=t2 is also true. Thus ¬Δt1=t2∧¬Δ¬t1=t2 is true, so o1 and o2 are again presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct. QED.

If t1=t2 is any borderline identity statement, and t1 and t2 denote the objects o1 and o2 respectively, then o1 and o2 are ipso facto presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct. Of course, the reason may be that t1 or t2 happens to be vague. For, in virtue of more precise names, o1 and o2 may also be presentable as either clearly identical or clearly distinct. Indeed, if they are identical, then they are presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly identical only if they are also presentable as clearly identical. For by hypothesis some constant t1 denotes o1; but Δt1=t1 is true, and t1 denotes both o1 and o2 (this point is of course related to the Evans argument). Even if o1 and o2 are distinct, they may be both presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct and presentable as clearly distinct. For example, fix the reference of the name s by stipulating that it is to denote the highest small natural number. Suppose that in fact s denotes 17, although for all we can know it denotes another number; in particular, on some interpretations indiscriminable from the right one it denotes 16. But the numerals ‘16’ and ‘17’ precisely denote 16 and 17. Since Δ17=17 is true, 17 is presentable as clearly identical with 17 (that is, 17 and 17 are presentable as clearly identical). Since ¬Δs=17∧¬Δ¬s=17 is true, 17 is also presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct from 17 (that is, 17 and 17 are presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct). Since Δ¬16=17 is true, 16 and 17 are presentable as clearly distinct. Since ¬Δs=16∧¬Δ¬s=16 is true, 16 and 17 are also presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct. Thus presentability as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct, although a genuine relation, is a rather trivial one. It gives little information about its relata.

A more revealing relation is non-presentability as either clearly identical or clearly distinct. There are two cases in which o1 and o2 fail to be presentable as either clearly identical or clearly distinct. In the first case, no constants denote o1 and o2 respectively. Thus o1 and o2 will not be presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct. The issues raised by nameless objects will not be discussed here; although significant, they would take us out of our way. They arise in acute form only for essentially nameless objects, if such exist (see Williamson [1994], p.262). In the second case, some constants t1 and t2 denote o1 and o2 respectively, but Δt1=t2∨Δ¬t1=t2 is false for all of them. Since ¬Δt1=t2∧¬Δ¬t1=t2 is true if Δt1=t2∨Δ¬t1=t2 is false, o1 and o2 will be presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct. Conversely, if they are presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct then some pair of constants denotes them. Thus for our purposes the interesting case is that in which objects are presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct without being presentable as either clearly identical or clearly distinct. We noted above that if o1 and o2 are identical, they are presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly identical only if they are also presentable as clearly identical. Thus the interesting case always involves distinct objects.

We can illustrate the interesting case in the simple model sketched above, with just two interpretations 𝐈1 and 𝐈2, indiscriminable from each other, and two constants a and b. Let a denote o1 on both 𝐈1 and 𝐈2; let b denote o1 on 𝐈1 but the distinct object o2 on 𝐈2. Suppose that 𝐈2 is in fact the correct interpretation. Since ¬Δa=b∧¬Δ¬a=b is true and a and b denote o1 and o2 respectively (on the correct interpretation), o1 and o2 are presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct. Since no other constants denote o1 and o2 respectively, they are not presentable as either clearly identical or clearly distinct.

Of course, such a case might simply manifest the expressive limitations of the language. Perhaps it is sheerly accidental that the language does not contain more precise constants t1 and t2 denoting o1 and o2 for which Δ¬t1=t2 is true. To define more satisfying notions, we should generalize over potential as well as actual ways of denoting the objects. If the language contains demonstratives, we must at least consider various contexts of their utterance. Since similar issues arise for vague thought about objects as well as for vague talk, we must consider guises, modes of presentation or individual concepts of the objects, and elucidate those notions. But there is an opposite risk: if we generalize too far, we may make all pairs of objects both presentable as either clearly identical or clearly distinct and presentable as neither clearly identical nor clearly distinct, so that the interesting case never arises. Perhaps we can avoid that result by restricting ourselves to cognitively accessible ways of denoting objects in some sense. If so, in the interesting case the non-presentability of the objects as either clearly identical or clearly distinct will manifest the cognitive inaccessibility of all ways of denoting them on which their distinctness is clear. Although that would reflect some cognitive limitation on the thinkers, it would also reflect something about the objects too, because it would distinguish them non-accidentally from other pairs of distinct objects. The task of specifying the appropriate notion of cognitive accessibility will not be attempted here; the suggestion is left as programmatic. What has been specified is the overall structure of such an account.

We cannot know of any particular objects that they are not presentable as either clearly identical or clearly distinct. For otherwise we could deduce that they were distinct and thereby come to know that they were distinct, in which case they would be presentable as clearly distinct, in virtue of whatever ways of denoting them we used; we are in a position to know only what is clear. Such ignorance will not surprise the epistemicist. We may know that some pairs of objects exemplify the interesting case, even if we cannot know which objects they are. We might even know of particular objects that, unless they are identical, they are not presentable as either clearly identical or clearly distinct.

The technique used to define relations between objects from opaque occurrences of their names can obviously be generalized. For example, we could substitute mereological relations for identity and distinctness; o1 might be presentable as neither clearly part nor clearly not part of o2 without being presentable as either clearly part or clearly not part of o2. Any closed sentence ϕ(t1,t2) could be substituted for t1=t2, although any vagueness in ϕ(t1,t2) not derivative from vagueness in t1 or t2 is liable to diminish the interest of the corresponding relation between objects. The logic of the resulting notions will be quite complex. For instance, although Δ(α∧β) is equivalent to Δα∧Δβ, objects may be both presentable as clearly R and presentable as clearly S without being presentable as clearly both R and S, for the constants needed to present them as clearly R may differ from those needed to present them as clearly S.

The relations between objects are defined in the metalanguage. The move from object-language to metalanguage is usually conceived as a move from talk about things to talk about words. That conception is too simple when the metalanguage has the resources for referential semantics. In the present case, the move from use of object-language sentences of the forms Δt1=t2 and Δ¬t1=t2 to mention of them in the metalanguage is exactly what enables us to define an identity-involving relation between things rather than a relation of vague coreference between their names. A fuller exploration of these points can be set in a framework for discussing wider issues about vagueness in reality (see Williamson forthcoming for such a framework).

Which of those relations objects have to each other depends on epistemic factors. In that sense, the relations do not concern only the mind-independent environment, even when the objects so related belong to that environment. Perhaps the relations are extrinsic. Nevertheless, they relate the objects themselves, not linguistic or conceptual representations of them. Nothing in the borderline cases that inspire talk of vague identity requires more than epistemicism provides. It can do justice to those modest phenomena. We have seen reason to doubt that other views can.

Thanks to audiences at Edinburgh, St Andrews, Bergamo and Syracuse for helpful comments on earlier versions of this material, and in particular to Dorothy Edgington for her reply at Bergamo, to Brian Weatherson for his reply at Syracuse, and to Kit Fine, Richard Holton and Graham Priest for further discussion.

works.title: Soames on vagueness
passages: Scott Soames has a justly high reputation for the precision and rigour of his work in the philosophy of language. It is therefore with considerable interest that one turns to the chapter of Understanding Truth on vagueness and the sorites paradox to see what he has to say.

Soames’s account is based on the old idea that borderline cases involve truth-value gaps. He says rather little in justification of this idea, merely that it seems arbitrary where to locate the cut-off point for a vague term and that it is unclear what semantic mechanism could determine that point. The book shows no awareness of work on the epistemicist alternative that borderline cases involve irremediable ignorance of truth-values. Since I have defended that alternative at length elsewhere, I will not labour the point here.
Surprisingly, Soames combines his anti-epistemicist commitments with the following two claims (216-17):
Often there will be a sharp line separating things that are F, according to a given conversational standard, from things for which, according to the standard, the predicate is undefined.

Attempts to display that sharp dividing line for inspection will result in a change of standards, according to which the flanking adjacent items in the progression come to be characterized in the same way (with respect to the predicate).

The mechanism of contextual adjustment in (ii) is similar to one postulated by Hans Kamp in ‘The Paradox of the Heap’ in U. Mönnich (ed.), Aspects of Philosophical Logic (Dordrecht: Reidel, 1981). Soames uses it to explain how sharp semantic lines can be systematically elusive and therefore appear not to exist. But if he is willing to do that in defence of a hidden sharp boundary between truth and undefinedness, would it not be simpler to do it in defence of a hidden sharp boundary between truth and falsity? He could then drop all the complications introduced by the postulation of truth-value gaps (at least with respect to vagueness) and adopt a contextualist form of epistemicism. Soames can hardly take his generic objections to truth-values in borderline cases to be decisive, for they could also be made to the claim that a predicate is either true, false or undefined in a higher-order borderline case. Presumably Soames thinks that he can recognize cases in which it is plausible to postulate a hidden sharp boundary from cases in which it is not, but how he recognizes them I do not know.

Soames’s willingness to defend (i) might give the impression that he denies higher-order vagueness. In fact he acknowledges that there is higher-order vagueness (219-21). But that does not help to elucidate the supposed distinction between cases in which hidden semantic lines are allowed and cases in which they are not. Of course, a formal model can imply such a distinction; the issue is whether a model with that implication is well-motivated. The motivation which Soames supplies is inadequate.

One of the crucial tests for a theory of vagueness is its evaluation of complex sentences. To handle the postulated truth-value gaps, Soames uses the three-valued strong Kleene tables (207). In particular, he treats a conditional with an undefined antecedent and an undefined consequent as undefined. Consider, for example, ‘Small’ as a vague predicate of natural numbers. If it is undefined for both n and n+1, then according to Soames this conditional is neither true nor false:
This provides an undefined instance of the universally quantified major premise of the corresponding sorites paradox for ‘Small’ (Wang’s paradox):

On such grounds, Soames regards the major premise of a sorites paradox as not true, and therefore as deserving rejection. But since he believes that it has no false instances, he also regards it as not false; therefore, its negation also deserves rejection (207).
This account has highly counter-intuitive consequences unmentioned by Soames. Surely, if a number is small then any smaller number is small too. Thus the converses of (1) and (2) should be true:

But Soames’s account makes (1C) and (2C) undefined for exactly the same reason as before; if a conditional has an undefined antecedent and consequent, so has its converse. Thus Soames must reject the generalization ‘The predecessor of a small number is small’.

One might be tempted to suppose that Soames could avoid the problem at the meta-linguistic level. Surely it is at least true to say that if ‘Small’ is true of a number then it is true of any smaller number. Thus, using ‘True’ for the true-of relation, one might replace (1C) and (2C) by these meta-linguistic claims:

But a moment’s reflection on higher-order vagueness shows that (1CT) and (2CT) are no improvement on (1C) and (2C). As already noted, Soames allows that his semantic concepts may be vague. It is certainly no easier to say exactly which numbers ‘Small’ is true of than to say exactly which numbers are small. Just as there are successive numbers for which ‘Small’ is undefined, on Soames’s view, so there will be successive numbers for which ‘True’ is undefined when the term in its first argument-place designates ‘Small’. Thus, unless Soames treats higher-order vagueness in an implausibly different way from first-order vagueness, he will have to reject (1CT) (for some n) and (2CT) for the same reason as (1C) and (2C) and as (1) and (2).

Consider another example. Suppose that Barry and Harry are identical twins who are going bald in exactly the same way; their scalps match perfectly. Surely it follows that one twin is bald if and only if the other is. Thus we can assert:

But if the twins’ scalps are in an intermediate state for which ‘Bald’ is undefined, then the strong Kleene table makes (3) undefined. Thus Soames is committed to implausibly rejecting the claim ‘One twin is bald if and only if the other is’. Again, it would not help Soames to go meta-linguistic. Given higher-order vagueness, a parallel objection applies to the meta-linguistic biconditional:
These problems have serious consequences for Soames’s ability to state his account coherently. For example, at one point he says that the following principle ‘really is true’ (215):

For any two patches of color x and y that are perceptually indistinguishable to competent observers under normal conditions, if someone who is presented with x characterizes the predicate looks green as applying to it, then that person is thereby committed to a standard that counts the predicate as applying to y as well.

Consider a case in which two patches of colour x and y are perceptually indistinguishable to competent observers under normal conditions, and I am presented with x, but it is vague whether I have characterized looks green as applying to x; I assent to the application in a somewhat reluctant, hesitant or frivolous way. Thus, given the view expressed in (P2*), it is also vague whether I am thereby committed to a standard that counts the predicate as applying to y as well. Thus, on Soames’s view, the conditional in (P2*) has an undefined antecedent and consequent in this instance. Therefore, (P2*) is not true on Soames’s semantics, contrary to his claim.

Here is another example. Soames writes ‘The default determinate-extension of F is the set of things that the communitywide rules or conventions of the language (plus relevant nonlinguistic facts) determine that the predicate applies to’ (209). By the axiom of extensionality, this set-identity claim entails a universally quantified biconditional:
∀x(x is in the determinate-extension of F≡the communitywide rules or conventions of the language plusrelevant nonlinguistic facts determine that F applies to x)

But Soames admits that ‘is in the determinate extension of F’ (in a given context) may be vague (220). If so, (4) will have at least one undefined instance, for the strong Kleene table for ≡ makes any biconditional undefined if at least one of the flanking sentences is undefined. Consequently, (4) is not true. Thus higher-order vagueness commits Soames to rejecting (4). The problem is quite general. Suppose that Soames, in his theorizing, attempts to lay down a necessary and sufficient condition for a vague concept. That would require him to assert a universally quantified biconditional with at least one instance in which the left-hand side is undefined. But then on his view the universally quantified biconditional is not true, and the attempt to lay down a necessary and sufficient condition has failed. Even ∀x(Fx≡Fx) is not true on the Kleene semantics if F has borderline cases.

Since the Kleene semantics gets Soames into so much difficulty, I will ignore it for the remainder of this discussion. As is well known, a supervaluationist approach permits truth-value gaps while avoiding the kind of problem just considered. However, Soames explicitly rejects supervaluationism on the grounds that ‘it violates fundamental truths about the meanings of various logical terms’ (225).

It is integral to Soames’s account that borderline cases are in neither the default determinate-extension nor the default determinate-antiextension of a vague predicate; they are the cases for which speakers have contextual discretion. Suppose, for example, that Harry is borderline for ‘bald’. Then, according to Soames, the conventions of English (plus relevant non-linguistic facts) neither determine that ‘bald’ applies to Harry nor determine that ‘bald’ does not apply to Harry (209). What are these conventions of English?
One might initially suppose the most relevant convention to be this:
For all x, ‘bald’ applies to x if and only if x is bald.
But Soames cannot accept (C) as a convention of English. On his view, the reference of a vague predicate varies contextually. (C) is no more a convention of English than is this:
For all x, ‘belongs to me’ applies to x if and only if x belongs to me.

As uttered by me, (C*) is false of contexts in which I am not the speaker. Since linguistic conventions are general, they should apply to such contexts. Similarly, (C), as uttered by me, is false of contexts in which the reference of ‘bald’ differs from its reference in my present context. Thus the relevant conventions must be stated non-homophonically.
Soames explains how the default determinate-extension and determinate-antiextension of ‘bald’ are fixed (210):

(i) The predicate is applied to certain specific individuals who are taken as paradigmatic examples of baldness, and it is denied of other specific individuals who are taken as paradigmatic examples of people who are not bald. (ii) It is resolved that other individuals, y, are to be taken as determinate instances of baldness if they bear the relation Re — y has a perceptually equivalent amount of hair as x or less hair than x — to someone, x, in the initial sample of paradigmatically bald individuals. (iii) It is further resolved that still other individuals, z, are to be taken as determinate instances of individuals who are not bald if they bear the related relation Ra — z has a perceptually equivalent amount of hair as w or more hair than w — to someone, w, in the initial sample of individuals who are paradigmatically not bald.

Evidently this is a fantasy. There are no specific individuals who are semantically guaranteed to be bald. Although we can point to certain specific individuals as paradigms of baldness, no convention of English implies that they are not in the antiextension of ‘bald’ and wearing a tight skin-coloured cap. Similarly, there are no specific individuals who are semantically guaranteed not to be bald. Although we can point to certain specific individuals as paradigms of non-baldness, no convention of English implies that they are not in the extension of ‘bald’ and wearing a wig.

If there are semantic conventions of English about ‘bald’, their content is general; they make no reference to specific individuals. For example, it might be a convention of English that ‘bald’ applies to anyone who has no hair. But what of other numbers of hairs? Is there a number n for which it is a convention of English that anyone with at least n hairs is not bald? If so, for which values of n is that a convention? Clearly, it is no easy matter to state the supposed conventions. But the problem goes deeper than that. For, in view of higher-order vagueness, the conventions governing vague terms will themselves be vague. Since the homophonic approach to stating the conventions fails, for the reason noted above, a semantic convention about a vague term t will need to be stated by use of another vague term t*. Soames does not discuss the danger of an infinite regress. Nor would it be attractive to postulate unstatable conventions, for the most powerful accounts of conventions make them a matter of mutual knowledge or belief, as in David Lewis’s classic Convention (Oxford: Blackwell, 1969).

We can exemplify the problem. In stating what has been ‘resolved’, Soames uses the phrase ‘perceptually equivalent’. With little ingenuity, one can construct sorites series to show that it is vague. Of course, there are clear cases of perceptual equivalence and clear cases of perceptual inequivalence. But to put them in a story about ‘perceptually equivalent’ parallel to Soames’s story (i)-(iii) about ‘bald’ is, in addition to its implausibility, merely to postpone the moment at which one must explain how vagueness can occur without conventions or resolutions.

It is doubtful that there are any semantic conventions of the special kind that Soames postulates. The need to postulate conventions for which there is no independent evidence suggests that something is awry in Soames’s theory.

We can reach the same point by another route. Vagueness is not confined to public languages. Thought is vague too. Unless Soames wants to argue that thought is impossible without a public language, he will have to accept that there can be vagueness in the absence of a public language. But his account as given in the book does not apply to such vagueness. Even if there is a language of thought, it does not rely on conventions (see Roy Sorensen, ‘Vagueness within the language of thought’, Philosophical Quarterly 41 (1991): 389-413). One might attempt to construct an account structurally similar to Soames’s of vagueness in thought, but it does not look promising. Consider the most primitive concepts; some and perhaps all of them will be vague. From what source are they supposed to derive the elaborate structure Soames postulates of a default determinate-extension and a default determinate-antiextension?

Some of the conversational mechanisms postulated by Soames may well have a part to play in a full account of vagueness in natural languages. But contextual variation in reference is entirely consistent with epistemicism about vagueness. The parts of Soames’s account that get him into trouble are the parts inconsistent with epistemicism.

works.title: Reply to Machina and Deutsch on vagueness, ignorance, and margins for error
passages: Reply to Machina and Deutsch on vagueness, ignorance, and margins for error

In their paper “Vagueness, Ignorance, and Margins for Error” Kenton Machina and Harry Deutsch criticize the epistemic theory of vagueness. This paper answers their objections. The main issues discussed are: the relation between meaning and use; the principle of bivalence; the ontology of vaguely specified classes; the proper form of margin for error principles; iterations of epistemic operators and semantic compositionality; the relation or lack of it between quantum mechanics and theories of vagueness.
Reply to Machina and Deutsch on vagueness, ignorance, and margins for error
Keywords: Vagueness; epistemicism; bivalence; margin for error; coordinated attack; compositionality; quantum mechanics.
Reply to Machina and Deutsch on vagueness, ignorance, and margins for error

Kenton Machina and Harry Deutsch [2002] make several mutually independent criticisms of the epistemic theory of vagueness and the arguments for it advanced in my book [1994]. I will rebut their criticisms one by one.1 My sections follow theirs in the obvious way.

Machina and Deutsch are willing to agree with me that the extensions of typical vague predicates supervene on ‘a mishmash of linguistic conventions, overlapping linguistic communities, and changing linguistic patterns and community memberships, in interaction with a changing world’, where ‘No one in these communities knows exactly where the boundaries of the extensions are, and if forced to make a decision, they do not agree with one another’.2 Unlike me, they think that such a description ‘almost implies [sic] that precise extension boundaries do not exist’. Although they do not quite say that the description is inconsistent with epistemicism, they do present it as strong evidence against the view. But they do not explain why they count the description as any evidence at all against epistemicism. They do not even try to argue that epistemicism implies (or ‘almost implies’) some description of the use of vague predicates that is inconsistent with the one quoted above.

Machina and Deutsch may have been misled by their own terminology. They repeatedly characterise the epistemicist as holding that a vague predicate has precise boundaries. Since the terms ‘vague’ and ‘precise’ are normally used as a contrasting pair, that initial characterisation already presents epistemicism as committed to an internal incongruity. The description of the supervenience base for the extension of a vague predicate merely makes vivid what the use of a vague predicate is like. But what does it mean to call the boundaries of a vague predicate, rather than the vague predicate itself, ‘precise’? Presumably, Machina and Deutsch mean (on behalf of the epistemicist) that everything either falls within the boundaries or fails to do so. According to the epistemicist, it is a matter of logic that all boundaries are precise in that sense. Only an anti-epistemicist who already assumes that only precise predicates have such boundaries should regard the word ‘precise’ as an apt term for such boundaries themselves.3 Let us call them, more neutrally, ‘excluded middle boundaries’. Then the epistemicist holds that excluded middle boundaries can supervene on messy, fluctuating, heterogeneous, casual use. Since Machina and Deutsch do not claim that such use (described non-semantically) itself violates the law of excluded middle, it is quite unclear why they suppose it to constitute evidence that boundaries that supervene on it violate that law.
Someone might accept a pair of claims like these:
If an object o falls under a predicate P, then some local feature of the supervenience base makes o fall under P.
If an object o does not fall under a predicate P, then some local feature of the supervenience base makes o not fall under P.

To fall under a predicate here is to fall within the boundaries of its extension; to make o (not) fall under P is to be sufficient for o (not) to fall under P. The notion of a local feature of the supervenience base is intended to be quite informal; a local feature is relatively specific (not the whole supervenience base) and has obvious relevance to whether the object falls under the predicate. In a borderline case, we may suppose, no local feature makes o fall under P and no local feature makes o not fall under P. If we can contrapose on (Ia) and (Ib), then o does not fall under P and does not not fall under P, which is a contradiction. At any rate, someone who accepted (Ia) and (Ib) might well be suspicious of the claim that vague predicates have extensions with excluded middle boundaries. However, the epistemicist rejects (Ia) and (Ib). The extension of a vague predicate may depend on global features of the supervenience base. The supervenience relation may be governed by default principles: if the supervenience base is globally insufficient for o to fall under P, it is thereby globally sufficient for o not to fall under P.4

Machina and Deutsch do not commit themselves to (Ia) and (Ib), nor do they commit themselves to any other principles that would explain why they regard the nature of the supervenience base as any evidence at all that vague predicates lack excluded middle boundaries. They find the postulation of such boundaries implausible, but they provide no non-question-begging argument against it from the nature of the supervenience base.

That everything either falls under a predicate or fails to do so is an instance of the law of excluded middle, which is a theorem of classical logic. That logic has massive theoretical virtues such as simplicity, strength, entrenchment and success in applications. Machina and Deutsch insist that classical logic is not sacrosanct. They ‘urge a spirit of exploration and flexibility’; why not? But the epistemicist does not claim that classical logic is sacrosanct, in the sense that it is methodologically vicious to consider alternatives. In my book I consider various non-classical logics in detail and argue, independently of classical assumptions, that none of them provides an adequate explanation of vagueness (in particular, they all come to grief on higher-order vagueness). It would be methodological madness to abandon classical logic at the first sign of trouble, but if the phenomena of vagueness present sufficiently strong evidence against it, we might reasonably look for alternatives. Although Machina and Deutsch treat the nature of the supervenience base for vague predicates as strong evidence against classical logic, we saw in the previous section that they provide no justification for doing so. They fail to remove the initial presumption in favour of classical logic.5

The anti-epistemicist typically denies that vague predications are bivalent. The epistemicist replies by arguing that, under plausible assumptions, the denial of bivalence leads to contradiction. According to Machina and Deutsch, we can ‘see (without looking at its details) that [the epistemicist argument] must fail’ (their italics). Their argument is merely that if P is not bivalent, ‘nothing about this situation requires P to have more than one truth value’. But this claim takes for granted that the situation is indeed possible, which is just what the epistemicist’s argument calls into question. So we do better to ignore their attempt at a pre-emptive strike, and examine what they say when they do look at the details of the epistemicist argument.
The epistemicist aims to reduce the following supposition to absurdity:
It is not the case that either P is true or P is false.

Then the epistemicist invokes standard biconditionals that govern the notions of truth and falsity. Machina and Deutsch present them in somewhat nonstandard forms, but they will do for present purposes:
There exists some statement Q such that P is true if and only if Q.
For that very same Q, P is false if and only if not Q.
From (a), (b) and (c) a contradiction follows (compare Williamson [1994]: 188-98).
‘To make clear what goes wrong’, Machina and Deutsch tell us to ‘rewrite’ (a) along these lines:
It is not the case that either P is fully true or P is fully false.
Once that is done, (b) and (c) must also be rewritten to engage with (a′):
There exists some statement Q such that P is fully true if and only if Q.
For that very same Q, P is fully false if and only if not Q.

They argue that (b′) and (c′) form an uncompelling pair, because the standard principles for truth and falsity do not apply to full truth and full falsity. They are doubtless right about that, unless the word ‘fully’ is redundant in ‘fully true’ and ‘fully false’. Without (b′) and (c′), the argument against (a′) fails.

Why should we rewrite (a) as (a′)? According to Machina and Deutsch, we should do so in order ‘to not beg the question against degree [of truth] theories’; they add ‘Williamson should not object; this merely clarifies what (a) is saying’. But Williamson does object. Machina and Deutsch do not claim that predications of ‘true’ and ‘false’ are meaningless unless implicitly or explicitly qualified by ‘fully’. On the contrary, they say of what is in effect a particular instance of (b) that it ‘seems perfectly unexceptionable’, and that ‘both the degree theory and the lack of truth value theory can agree that [it] is completely true’, and contrast it with the corresponding instance of (b′), to which they object; thus ‘true’ unqualified is not equivalent to ‘fully true’.6 Their point is not that ‘true’ and ‘false’ can only mean ‘fully true’ and ‘fully false’; (a) can be read at face value, as not equivalent to (a′). Rather, their point must be that what the epistemicist needs to argue against is (a′), not (a).

The epistemicist can happily agree that the style of argument in question works against (a) and not against (a′). It was only ever intended to work against (a). Machina and Deutsch offer no objection to the argument against (a). In their terminology of statements, the natural understanding of bivalence is as the principle that every statement is either true or false. Thus they offer no objection to the epistemicist argument against the denial of any particular instance of bivalence. Their point is just that the argument does not refute another claim, (a′), that some anti-epistemicists make. Exactly this point is made in the book ([1994]: 194-5) about the analogue of (a′) with ‘definitely’ in place of ‘fully’. As argued there, we need an explanation of the new operator (‘fully’ or ‘definitely’) before we can even judge whether (a′) or its analogue is inconsistent with epistemicism; if ‘fully’ meant something epistemic, the epistemicist might even accept (a′). Of course, many advocates of degrees of truth will try to explain ‘fully’ in non-epistemic terms; the book presents detailed arguments against anti-epistemic accounts of degrees of truth ([1994]: 113-38, 154-64), to which Machina and Deutsch offer no response. In brief, what they attack is not the epistemicist reductio ad absurdum of the denial of a particular instance of bivalence, construed as (a), but only an argument that I have never proposed.

Machina and Deutsch tack on a further objection to epistemicism, that ‘it yields an incredibly overgrown ontology’ because ‘We now not only have the class of even numbers or of odd numbers but also the class of small numbers and of numbers somewhat larger than 2!’. This argument confuses new ways of determining classes with new classes. We can form the description ‘class of natural numbers referred to on posters in London during the nineteenth century’, which is not synonymous with any class term in a purely mathematical language; nevertheless, using it clearly does not inflate our ontology, because we know that it designates a class that is also designated by some purely mathematical description, although for empirical reasons we do not know which one.7 Similarly, according to the epistemicist, since not all natural numbers are small and some are somewhat larger than 2, the least number principle assures us that some number m (we cannot know which one) is the least non-small natural numbers and some number n (again, we cannot know which one) is the least natural number somewhat larger than 2; since any natural number smaller than a small number is itself small and any natural number larger than a number somewhat larger than 2 is itself somewhat larger than 2, it follows that the class of small numbers and the class of numbers somewhat larger than 2 are simply {i:i<m} and {i:i≥n} respectively. For epistemicists, m and n are not new natural numbers, just old ones under new descriptions. Likewise, {i:i<m} and {i:i≥n} are not new classes, just old ones under new descriptions. Mathematicians were already committed to those old classes. Unless Machina and Deutsch are already assuming that epistemicism is false, they cannot complain of any ontological growth here.

Machina and Deutsch’s examples may be peculiarly ill-suited to their purpose. Perhaps some other vague terms (such as ‘religion’) do allow us to single out some other classes that we cannot in practice single out in precise terms. Even so, that would merely mitigate an expressive limitation of our precise vocabulary. The new classes would be of the same general kind as the old ones. Similarly, when we expand a standard language L1 for first-order set theory by adding precise predicates not coextensive with any predicate of L1 (such as a coded truth predicate for L1), we can formulate instances of set existence principles (such as the axiom schema of separation) for new sets, but that merely mitigates the expressive limitations of L1. Epistemicism does not crazily imply that a class with c members can have more than 2c subclasses. It does not inflate our ontology in any relevant sense. Interestingly, Machina and Deutsch make no attempt to explain how a non-epistemic theory of vagueness might handle vague class terms without ontologically inflationary consequences.
In [1994], I used principles about margins for error to explain our ignorance in borderline cases. Such principles can take this general form:
If x is similar enough to y, and x is known to be F, then y is F.

The required degree of similarity depends on the circumstances; it is the margin for error. The intuitive idea is that if x is similar enough to y and y is not F then a judgement that x is F would not be reliable enough to count as knowledgeable. (W) implies a kind of inexactness in knowledge. Not all such inexactness flows from vagueness; the epistemicist proposes that vagueness is a distinctively conceptual source of inexactness. (W) explains our failure to know that x is F when x is a borderline case, and therefore similar enough to some y that is not F.
Machina and Deutsch argue that Type W principles fail in some examples, in which they must be replaced by principles of this form:
If x is similar enough to y, and x is known to be F, then y is not known not to be F.8

By itself, (D) is too weak to explain all our ignorance in borderline cases, for if x is F and similar enough to y, which is not F, although (D) implies that we do not both know that x is F and know that y is not F, it does not imply that we neither know that x is F nor know that y is not F.

Many details of Machina and Deutsch’s argument in relation to (W) and (D) are puzzling. They characterize Type W principles in terms of the notion of being “right on the borderline” [between F things and non-F ones] and insist that ‘The notion of being “right on the borderline” makes sense only when there is an ordering scheme for the relevant cases’. The formulations in the text show that neither (W) nor (D) relies on any notion of being “right on the borderline” that would require a [relevant linear?] ordering of cases (yet Machina and Deutsch are aware that similarity does not require a linear ordering of cases). Rather than trying to sort out the details of this part of their argument, and make them relevant to what epistemicists actually say, let us consider an example that appears to make trouble even for Type D principles.

Define a natural number n to be effish if and only if n is either even or much greater than 100. The second disjunct makes ‘effish’ vague; it has borderline cases, numbers that are neither clearly effish nor clearly not effish. Nevertheless, we know that 0 is effish (since it is even) and that 1 is not effish (since it is neither even nor greater than 100); between 0 and 1 ‘effish’ has a known sharp cut-off. If 0 and 1 are sufficiently similar, both (W) and (D) fail for ‘effish’ in place of ‘F’. Intuitively, what such examples show is that a predicate can be vague in some regions of conceptual space and precise in others. The epistemicist would therefore expect the required margins for error to be wide in the former regions and to shrink to nothing or almost nothing in the latter regions. On this understanding, Machina and Deutsch’s examples are quite consistent with (W). Replacing (W) by (D) achieves nothing; what matters is to interpret ‘sufficiently similar’ with sufficient flexibility. (W) itself is only a schema: it gets its bite only in specific instantiations. The epistemicist always acknowledged that in complex cases the width of the margin would vary in complex ways ([1992]: 225-6; [1994]: 226-30). Nevertheless, (W) is not trivial, for it gives a general form for explaining our ignorance in borderline cases.

The complexities in such examples are not specific to epistemicism. Any theory of vagueness must account for them. The identifiable cut-off point for the vague term ‘effish’ is a prima facie counter-example to many claims made by non-epistemic theorists of vagueness. Like epistemicists, they must formulate their theories in sufficiently flexible ways.
‘A technical difficulty for Williamson’s margin for error principles’
A simple margin for error principle about a sorites series is this (for each natural number n):
‘A technical difficulty for Williamson’s margin for error principles’
If C(n grains make a heap) then n−1 grains make a heap.
‘A technical difficulty for Williamson’s margin for error principles’

‘C’ here abbreviates ‘clearly’, where a borderline heap is one that is neither clearly a heap nor clearly not a heap. As Machina and Deutsch acknowledge, we could also read ‘C’ as ‘it is known that’ without materially affecting the argument. (MFE) is not the margin for error principle most directly related to the vagueness of the word ‘heap’, for (MFE) is not even meta-linguistic ([1994]: 232). Nevertheless, (MFE) is derivable from a simple model of what is clear or unclear in the sorites series, a model that I am willing to endorse at least as a first approximation. Machina and Deutsch claim to reduce (MFE) to absurdity. What they do not emphasize is that the derivation on which they rely was in effect already presented and analysed in my original discussion ([1992]: 240-1).
‘A technical difficulty for Williamson’s margin for error principles’

Let us first get a comparatively minor point out of the way. Machina and Deutsch assume that for each natural number m I accept Cm(MFE), the result of prefixing (MFE) by m iterations of the ‘clearly’ operator C. ‘It would be quite mysterious if he didn’t’, they say. In support, they argue that since I hold that one arrives at (MFE) by philosophical reflection, I must assign it a priori status, and therefore treat it as an informal theorem, consequently subject to the analogue for C of the necessitation rule in modal logic: if A is a theorem, then so too is CA. I do regard (MFE) as broadly a priori, but fear that it lacks the informal logical status of a theorem. The argument for (MFE) is unfortunately neither as general nor quite as compelling as those for basic structural principles about clarity, such as that it implies truth (CA→A; what is clearly the case is the case). Some uncertainty attends any substantive philosophical reflection. Thus, quite unmysteriously, I am not committed in the way that they propose to Cm(MFE). Indeed, I am inclined to think that Cm(MFE) is false for large values of ‘m’, although true for small values. Strictly speaking, this is already enough to block their attempted reductio as they present it. However, it does not yet speak to their underlying worry, which concerns the existence of large but finite bounds on the iteration of the ‘clearly’ operator C. A large bound on m in Cm(MFE) would presumably puzzle Machina and Deutsch as much as does the bound that they discuss. The argument for their bound depends on the non-existence of a bound on m in Cm(MFE).9 To simplify the argument, I therefore grant them for present purposes Cm(MFE) for all natural numbers m and n.
‘A technical difficulty for Williamson’s margin for error principles’

Given the assumptions now in play, and the epistemicist’s logic for the operator C, Machina and Deutsch point out that if for some natural number n Cm(n grains make a heap) holds for every natural number m, then it follows that 0 grains make a heap. Since 0 grains do not make a heap, for every natural number n there is a bound k such that Cm(n grains make a heap) fails for every natural number m≥k. Machina and Deutsch find this result absurd. Why?
‘A technical difficulty for Williamson’s margin for error principles’

Our authors are particularly surprised that the upper bound established on m in Cm(n grains make a heap) depends on n. The larger n is, the larger the upper bound on m. They call this ‘a very bizarre result, one without any intuitive content that we can discern’. Rhetorically, they ask ‘Why should more C’s […] be allowed to prefix “20,000 grains make a heap” than “10,000 grains make a heap”?’. But their question has an easy answer. It is even more thoroughly obvious that 20,000 grains make a heap than that 10,000 grains make a heap. Our use of ‘heap’ would have to be even more different in the relevant respects to falsify ‘20,000 grains make a heap’ than to falsify ‘10,000 grains make a heap’. On the margin for error model, each iteration of C slightly reduces the range of cases in which Cm(n grains make a heap) holds, by eroding away an outer margin of cases. In general, CA holds only in those cases in which A holds that are not too close for clarity to cases in which A fails. After enough iterations, nothing is left (on the simple model). Since ‘20,000 grains make a heap’ holds in a wider range of cases than does ‘10,000 grains make a heap’, more iterations are needed to reduce the former range than the latter to nothing. Thus the dependence of the bound on m in Cm(n grains make a heap) has a clear intuitive content.
‘A technical difficulty for Williamson’s margin for error principles’

Machina and Deutsch offer another objection to the existence of a large bound on m. They claim that, ‘for ordinary cognitive agents’, iterations of C after some point become semantically redundant. According to them, ‘such iterations, beyond some intuitive number, do not have distinct meanings’. To put it in terms of knowledge, as they are willing to do, they hold that for some natural number m, the operators Km and Km+1 are synonymous, where K abbreviates ‘it is known that’ and the exponent indicates the number of iterations. If we understand ‘it is known that’ as ‘everyone knows that’, with reference to the people in a given group, then Machina and Deutsch’s claim appears to be contradicted by standard examples in epistemic logic, independently of vagueness. Consider, for example, the coordinated attack problem:
‘A technical difficulty for Williamson’s margin for error principles’

Two divisions of an army, each commanded by a general, are camped on two hilltops overlooking a valley. In the valley awaits the enemy. It is clear that if both divisions attack the enemy simultaneously they win the battle, while if only one division attacks it will be defeated. As a result, neither general will attack unless he is absolutely sure that the other will attack with him. In particular, a general will not attack if he receives no messages. The commanding general of the first division wishes to coordinate a simultaneous attack (at some time the next day). The generals can communicate only by means of messengers. Normally it takes a messenger one hour to get from one encampment to the other. However, it is possible that he will get lost in the dark or, worse yet, be captured by the enemy. Fortunately, on this particular night, everything goes smoothly. How long will it take them to coordinate an attack?10
‘A technical difficulty for Williamson’s margin for error principles’

The problem is that the first general does not know that the second general has received the message to attack until he receives the second general’s acknowledgement, and the second general does not know that the first general knows that he (the second general) has received the original message until the second general receives the first general’s acknowledgement of the first acknowledgement, and the first general does not know that the second general knows that the first general knows that the second general has received the original message until the first general receives the second general’s acknowledgement of the first general’s first acknowledgement, and so on. Consequently, no member of the following series entails any later member: ‘The original message was received’, ‘Both generals know that the original message was received’, ‘Both generals know that both generals know that the original message was received’, ‘Both generals know that both generals know that both generals know that the original message was received’, … Moderately intelligent human cognitive agents can appreciate the failure of such entailments, even though they have computational difficulties in intuitively grasping all but the first few members of the series (and the generals might somehow muddle through). Obviously, the argument does not depend on vagueness. Thus the iteration of epistemic operators does not in general reach a point after which further iteration is semantically redundant. Do Machina and Deutsch suppose that ‘clearly’ and ‘it is known that’ (not now understood as ‘everyone knows that’) are somehow exceptional in this respect? If so, they do not explain why.
‘A technical difficulty for Williamson’s margin for error principles’
Machina and Deutsch’s claim of semantic redundancy is in any case inconsistent with highly plausible principles of compositional semantics, such as this:
‘A technical difficulty for Williamson’s margin for error principles’
For any declarative English sentences S1 and S2, ‘It is known that’^S1 is synonymous with ‘It is known that’^S2 only if S1 is synonymous with S2.11
‘A technical difficulty for Williamson’s margin for error principles’

Equivalently, any difference in meaning between S1 and S2 implies a difference in meaning between KS1 and KS2. For example, let S be the sentence ‘It is raining’. According to Machina and Deutsch, for some number m, Km is synonymous with Km+1. Therefore, KmS is synonymous with Km+1S. Therefore, by (COMP), Km−1S is synonymous with KmS. By another m−1 applications of (COMP), they will eventually reach the conclusion that S is synonymous with KS: ‘It is raining’ is synonymous with ‘It is known that it is raining’. But that conclusion is patently false; when there is ignorance about the weather, S can be true while KS is false. Thus Machina and Deutsch are presumably committed to denying (COMP). Yet (COMP) has an obvious semantic motivation, one that is quite independent of vagueness, indeed quite independent of the specifically epistemic meaning of ‘It is known that’. The meaning of ‘It is known that’^S is a structured whole composed from the meanings of its constituents, in the first instance the operator ‘It is known that’ and the sentence S. Unless S1 and S2 are synonymous, ‘It is known that’^S1 and ‘It is known that’^S2 have different meanings in structurally the same argument place, and therefore themselves fail of synonymy. Hence a premise of Machina and Deutsch’s second argument against bounds on the iteration of the relevant epistemic operators violates compelling principles of compositional semantics. Consequently, both their arguments fail to show that the consequences extracted from (MFE) are absurd.12

In a brief final section, Machina and Deutsch propose Heisenberg’s Uncertainty Principle, non-epistemically interpreted, as an alternative model of vagueness and inexact knowledge. How do they apply the quantum mechanical model to these new cases? Unfortunately, their sketchy remarks leave that unclear. Of course, if epistemicists went to great lengths to preserve bivalence and classical logic in the face of vagueness, only to give them up when confronted by quantum phenomena, then epistemicism would lose much of its attraction. But Machina and Deutsch do not begin to establish that quantum mechanics, non-epistemically interpreted, rules out the combination of bivalence and classical logic. They do not discuss non-classical quantum logic, whose heyday seems in any case to be long past. Nor do they suggest that quantum mechanics excludes semantic principles such as (a) and (b) from which bivalence follows by classical logic. After all, quantum mechanics is not even about semantics. Accepting classical logic and bivalence, one could still consistently hold that a particle is located in a region without being located at any point in that region; that is just a claim about the nature of the location relation, and it is independent of epistemicism about vagueness. Machina and Deutsch neither propose a deviant quantum logic nor exhibit any inconsistency between epistemicism about vagueness and a non-epistemic interpretation of quantum mechanics without a deviant quantum logic. Thus they have not yet identified an anti-epistemicist model of inexact knowledge.

Machina and Deutsch’s invocation of quantum mechanics fails to address a more urgent problem for them: how to reconcile the ‘intuitive appeal’ that they concede to margin for error principles with their rejection of their consequences, the bounds on the iteration of epistemic operators. They never explain how to treat margin for error principles and the arguments for bounds on the model of quantum mechanics.

No theory of vagueness, epistemic or non-epistemic, has made any significant contribution that I know of to the understanding of the quantum world. That is not a criticism of theories of vagueness, for they deal with something different. To assimilate the baffling phenomena of the quantum world to mere vagueness is to miss what is most distinctive and peculiar about them, and thereby radically to underestimate the problems that they pose. By comparison, vagueness is an easy problem which, for all that Machina and Deutsch show, epistemicists have already solved.

I will not discuss Deutsch and Machina’s criticism of Roy Sorensen’s version of epistemicism, although some of what they say about him appears to be vulnerable to points similar to those in the text. ↩︎
All quotations are from Deutsch and Machina [2002] unless otherwise specified. ↩︎
In [1994] and elsewhere I specifically avoided using the word ‘precise’ in the way that Machina and Deutsch use it. ↩︎
Williamson [1997] explores possible default supervenience principles in more detail. ↩︎

Machina and Deutsch compare the epistemicist’s commitment to classical logic to Frege’s. However, whereas Frege used classical logic to exclude vague concepts, the epistemicist denies any incompatibility between classical logic and vague concepts. ↩︎
The relevant instances of (b) and (b′) are Machina and Deutsch’s (f) and (g) respectively. ↩︎
For the sake of the example, we may assume that the description has no actual borderline cases. ↩︎
Principle (!!) at my [1994]: 246 is similar in structure to (D). ↩︎
See Williamson [1992]: 240–1 for details of the trade-off between the two bounds. ↩︎
Quotation from Fagin, Halpern, Moses and Vardi [1995]: 176–7. The book is a very useful resource for more examples of related kinds and references to the earlier literature. ↩︎
