works.title: Tennant on knowable truth
passages: The paper responds to Neil Tennant’s recent discussion of Fitch’s so-called paradox of knowability in the context of intuitionistic logic. Tennant’s criticisms of the author’s earlier work on this topic are shown to rest on a principle about the assertibility of disjunctions with the absurd consequence that everything we could make true already is true. Tennant restricts the anti-realist principle that truth implies knowability in order to escape Fitch’s argument, but a more complex variant of the argument is shown to elicit from his restricted principle exactly the consequences which it was intended to avoid.

A diffuse philosophical tendency cannot be refuted once and for all by a single rigorous argument. Nevertheless, such an argument can severely constrain the forms in which the tendency is expressed. A case in point involves the tendency labelled ‘anti-realism’ and a now celebrated argument, sometimes known as the paradox of knowability, introduced into discussion by Frederick Fitch. In earlier work I sketched a form of anti-realism on which Fitch’s argument fails to reach its final conclusion. Naturally, my aim was not to endorse that form of anti-realism; I find it deeply implausible. But that does not distinguish it from other forms of anti-realism, and such dispositions are not invariant across persons. My aim was rather to see what forms of anti-realism must be argued against in some way beyond Fitch’s. Neil Tennant has recently criticized the envisaged anti-realist response to Fitch, and proposed an alternative anti-realist response of his own. In this paper I explain why both Tennant’s criticism and his alternative fail. His proposal collapses into the one he criticizes. The result illustrates a more general point: that moderate forms of anti-realism tend to be the least stable.

Anti-realists argue that truth is epistemically constrained. Their arguments are too complex, elusive and at least vaguely familiar to formulate here; we can gesture at them thus: a sentence s as uttered in some context expresses the content that P only if the link between s and the condition that P is made by the way speakers of the language use s; their use must be sensitive to whether the condition obtains; that requires of them the capacity in principle to recognize that it obtains, when it does so; thus P only if speakers of the language can in principle recognize that P. In brief: all truths are knowable. We can formalize the anti-realist conclusion in a schema:

Here ◇ and K abbreviate ‘it is possible that’ and ‘someone sometime knows that’ respectively; ϕ is to be replaced by declarative sentences.1 The relevant sense of ‘possible’ is not merely epistemic, because the anti-realist takes sensitivity to whether a condition obtains to require a genuine recognitional capacity (an ‘ontic’ possibility of knowing), not a mere incapacity to recognize one’s ignorance (an epistemic possibility of knowing). According to (1), the truth really could have been known.

Much in the anti-realist arguments deserves to be questioned. Fitch (1963) introduced a direct objection to their conclusion with an apparent reductio ad absurdum of (1). It requires two highly plausible principles about knowledge: only truths are known, and known conjunctions have known conjuncts.2 Consequently:

(2) and (3) entail that nothing is ever known to be an always unknown truth. For (2) yields K(ϕ∧¬Kϕ)→(ϕ∧¬Kϕ) and therefore K(ϕ∧¬Kϕ→¬Kϕ) while (3) yields K(ϕ∧¬Kϕ)→(Kϕ∧K¬Kϕ) and therefore K(ϕ∧¬Kϕ)→Kϕ, so together they give:

(2) and (3) are intended as necessary constraints on knowledge, and the propositional logic used to derive (4) from (2) and (3) is necessarily truth-preserving, so by a variant of the rule of necessitation in modal logic we can conclude that what (4) says is not could not have been:
Consider the special case of (1) with ϕ∧¬Kϕ in place of ϕ:
In classical logic, (7) is equivalent to:

(8) is deeply implausible. In effect, it says that any truth is known. As one instance, it says that there is a fragment of Roman pottery at a certain spot only if someone sometime knows that there is a fragment of Roman pottery there. The corresponding instance of (1) for the same value of ϕ is quite plausible: there is a fragment of Roman pottery there only if it is possible that someone sometime knows that there is a fragment of Roman pottery there. But according to (8), there is a fragment of Roman pottery there only if the possibility of knowing is actualized; that claim seems quite unwarranted. Although (by (4)) the attempt to identify a particular example of an unknown truth would be self-defeating, we surely have ample indirect evidence for the general claim that not all truths are ever known. Of course, some believe that an omniscient god makes (8) true, but that debate is not very pertinent here. For if we restrict the substitutions for ϕ to sentences of our language, the anti-realist motivation for (1) allows us to read ‘someone’ in the definition of K as ‘some member of our speech community’; the links between sentences of English and their contents are made by human speakers of English without divine aid. ‘There is a fragment of Roman pottery at that spot’ is a sentence of our language; surely not all truths expressible in our language will at some time be known by some member of our speech community. K will henceforth be understood with that restricted reading. We should therefore reject schema (8). Given that (8) was derived from (1) using uncontentious principles, we should reject (1).

The seminal presentation of the case for (1) is Michael Dummett’s. Notoriously, he integrates it with a case for a comprehensive anti-realist reconception of meaning in terms of verification-conditions rather than truth-conditions, which, he argues, will invalidate classical logic, in particular the law of excluded middle, and justify its replacement by something like intuitionistic logic. The latter was originally proposed as the logic of intuitionistic mathematics, and its intended semantics reflects that role, being formulated in terms of the notion of proof. Since the notion of proof is inappropriate to empirical statements, Dummett envisages a generalized intuitionistic semantics in which a broader notion of verification plays the key role. Whether or not his argument is compelling, it is pertinent to ask how the attempted reductio ad absurdum of (1) fares under intuitionistic logic, which we may provisionally suppose the anti-realist defender of (1) to have adopted.
The argument from (1) to (7) is intuitionistically acceptable, but the step from (7) to (8) is not. (7) is intuitionistically equivalent to:

Intuitionistically, we cannot delete the negations in contraposing (9) to reach (8).3 Intuitionists can consistently accept (9) while denying that all truths are known. Since (7) generalizes, they must deny that there is an unknown truth: on their constructivist understanding of the existential quantifier, one could in any case verify that one could never verify that existential claim, because (by (4)) one could never verify a particular instance of it. Intuitionistically, to verify that one could never verify ψ is to verify ¬ψ. Denying that there is an unknown truth does not commit one intuitionistically to asserting that all truths are known. Given (9), the intuitionist can consistently deny the universal generalization of (8) but cannot consistently deny any particular instance of (8), for (9) is intuitionistically equivalent to the double negation of (8). In this respect, the intuitionistic status of ϕ→Kϕ given (9) is exactly like that of the law of excluded middle. For the intuitionist can consistently deny the universal generalization of ϕ∨¬ϕ but cannot consistently deny any particular instance of it, because ¬¬(ϕ∨¬ϕ) is intuitionistically valid.4 Call an anti-realist position on which (7) is valid and (8) invalid moderately hard anti-realism. It is opposed to very hard anti-realism, on which both (7) and (8) are valid, and soft anti-realism, on which both (7) and (8) are invalid.5 A consistent moderately hard anti-realist view can be worked out in some detail within the framework of intuitionistic logic (Williamson 1982, 1988, 1992). Moderately hard anti-realists may regard the Fitch problem as a further reason for anti-realists in general to adopt intuitionistic rather than classical logic, since their response to the problem depends on a distinction available within intuitionistic but not classical logic.

Of course, (9) itself is a deeply problematic consequence of (1). According to (9), what is never known is not true: thus if no one ever knows that there is a fragment of Roman pottery at a certain spot, there is no fragment of Roman pottery there. That sounds as bad as (8). But there are differences. (8) eliminates the distinction between ϕ and Kϕ, for (8) and its uncontentious converse (2) yield ϕ↔Kϕ, and therefore Σ(ϕ)↔Σ(Kϕ) for any sentential context Σ() defined with the standard intuitionistic connectives (in particular, of course, ¬ϕ↔¬Kϕ). Although (9) eliminates the distinction between ¬ϕ and ¬Kϕ, since (9) and (2) yield ¬ϕ↔¬Kϕ, and therefore Σ(¬ϕ)↔Σ(¬Kϕ), it does not eliminate the distinction between ϕ and Kϕ, as the underivability of (8) from (9) shows. The moderately hard anti-realist loses fewer distinctions than does the very hard anti-realist. Indeed, the former can deny the universal generalization of (8), while the latter must assert it. Thus the moderately hard anti-realist, unlike the very hard anti-realist, can assert a gap between what is true and what is ever known. It is just that the acknowledgement of the gap is essentially general; it cannot be made at the level of an individual sentence.

But how can the moderately hard anti-realist mitigate the implausibility of particular instances of (9)? If one knew that human life was about to be eliminated by a huge meteorite, might one not be entitled to assert that no one will ever know that there is a fragment of Roman pottery at that spot without being entitled to assert that there is no fragment of Roman pottery there?6 Such examples suggest that intuitionistic ¬ does not correctly formalize the negation that we apply to empirical sentences, such as those of the form Kϕ. Dummett distinguishes the negation of intuitionistic mathematics from empirical negation (1977: 337). That is not to say that intuitionistic negation cannot meaningfully be applied to empirical sentences; rather, another negation operator may be needed as well to interpret ‘not’ in empirical discourse. Empirical negation must itself behave non-classically if moderately hard anti-realism is not to collapse into very hard anti-realism, for otherwise it could be substituted for ¬ in the derivation of (8), but it must not behave non-classically in exactly the same ways as ¬, otherwise it would offer no advantage. Major difficulties face the attempt to add such an operator (Williamson 1994). In what follows, I continue to assume that the anti-realist employs intuitionistic negation, without seeking to minimize the associated problems. Moderately hard anti-realism remains a deeply problematic position. Nevertheless, it avoids the most drastic consequences of very hard anti-realism, and an adequate critique of it will not simply cite Fitch.

Of those engaged in the refinement of Dummett’s programme and the generalization of intuitionistic semantics to empirical language, one of the most active has been Neil Tennant (1987, 1997). In his recent analysis of the Fitch problem, he argues that moderately hard anti-realism is an unstable position, and proposes an alternative soft anti-realist strategy based on restricting the knowability principle (1) (1997: 245–279).7 §2 below shows that his objection to moderately hard anti-realism is fallacious. §3 shows that under rather general conditions his restricted version of (1) still implies (7), so that his would-be soft anti-realism collapses into the moderately or very hard view.

Tennant objects to moderately hard anti-realism that it is unstable because in the crucial test cases for the Fitch argument the distinction between (7) and (8) collapses. He correctly points out that in the examples I use to illustrate the argument, I instantiate ‘ϕ’ with a decidable sentence: we have a decision procedure whose application would result in a verification or falsification of ϕ. This is the simplest and most vivid form of the problem that Fitch raises, and a crucial test for any adequate treatment. Tennant also correctly points out that (7) is intuitionistically equivalent to (8) when Kϕ is decidable. He then attempts to argue that Kϕ is decidable if and only if ϕ is decidable. If he is right, moderately hard anti-realism fails the crucial test.

Tennant’s objection is sustained if he can demonstrate that Kϕ is decidable whenever ϕ is; the converse does not concern us here. I will argue that his supposed demonstration that the decidability of ϕ implies that of Kϕ is fallacious. Here it is:

Suppose that ϕ is decidable. Then here is a decision method for Kϕ: apply the given decision method for ϕ. If you thereby determine that ϕ is true, then you know that ϕ. So you have determined that Kϕ is true. If, on the other hand, you determine that ϕ is false, then you have determined that Kϕ is false, because no one could ever know a falsehood. So if ϕ is decidable, then so is Kϕ. (1997: 262)
Our possession of a decision procedure for Kϕ entitles us to assert:8
Intuitionistically, (7) and (10) entail (8). If Tennant is right, the distinction between moderately and very hard anti-realism collapses in paradigms of the cases where it was supposed to help.
Why does Tennant suppose that our possession of a decision procedure for Kϕ entitles us to assert (10)? He is relying on a principle about the assertibility of disjunctions:
Our possession of a method whose application will either verify ϕ or verify ψ entitles us to assert ϕ∨ψ.

(DIS) allows us to assert the disjunction in advance of actually applying the method.9 Since the application of Tennant’s decision procedure will either verify Kϕ or verify ¬Kϕ, by (DIS) our mere possession of the decision procedure, in advance of actually applying it, entitles us to assert Kϕ∨¬Kϕ. (DIS) sounds very plausible. It is surely correct when ϕ and ψ are mathematical.

Nevertheless, we can easily see that Tennant’s argument must be unsound. For if it were sound, there would also be a sound argument for a much stronger conclusion, namely, that our possession of a decision procedure for ϕ entitles us to assert this:
We can argue for this conclusion in Tennant’s style:

Suppose that ϕ is decidable. Then apply the given decision method for ϕ. If you thereby determine that ϕ is true, then you know that ϕ. So you have determined that Kϕ is true. If, on the other hand, you determine that ϕ is false, then you know that ¬ϕ. So you have determined that K¬ϕ is true.

The reasoning for the case where ϕ is true is Tennant’s own; the reasoning for the case where ϕ is false in effect substitutes ¬ϕ for ϕ in that reasoning. By (DIS), we can conclude that our mere possession of the decision procedure for ϕ entitles us to assert (11). Now (11) is equivalent to the proposition that someone sometime will know whether ϕ holds, for each disjunct entails that proposition, which in turn entails (11). But only very hard anti-realists claim that whenever ϕ is decidable, someone sometime will know whether ϕ holds. Mere possession of the decision procedure does not entitle us to assert that anyone will ever have that knowledge. For in advance of applying the procedure, we may have no reason to think that it will ever be applied; indeed, we may have reason to think that it will never be applied. Perhaps its application is costly in time and other scarce cognitive resources and ϕ is a proposition whose truth-value is unlikely ever to be of interest to anyone. Moreover, it may be unlikely that anyone will ever come to know whether ϕ holds without applying such a decision procedure.

We can accept the Tennant-style argument for the proposition that if ϕ is decidable then we have a method whose application will either verify Kϕ or verify K¬ϕ. Nevertheless, our mere possession of that method does not entitle us to assert Kϕ∨K¬ϕ. Thus the problem lies with (DIS). What has gone wrong is that the application of the decision procedure for ϕ brings about the state of affairs expressed by (11). That is why our mere possession of the method is not enough. To assert (11), we need some reason to think that someone sometime will apply the method. Exactly the same problem affects Tennant’s assumption that we are entitled to assert (10) whenever ϕ is decidable. For, if ϕ is true, the application of the decision method for ϕ brings about the state of affairs expressed by Kϕ. Our mere possession of the method, in advance of actually applying it, does not entitle us to assert (10). If our possession of a decision method for α entitles us to assert α∨¬α, then Tennant is mistaken in claiming that our possession of a decision method for ϕ puts us in possession of a decision method for Kϕ. Alternatively, if we did count his procedure as a decision method for Kϕ, then mere possession of a decision method in that weak sense for Kϕ would not entitle us to assert Kϕ∨¬Kϕ, and his argument would still fail because we could not bridge the gap from (7) to (8).10

For a more dramatic example of the fallacy, consider a paradigm of a potentially undecidable sentence, ‘A city was, is or will be built on this spot’ (compare Dummett 1959). Assume that no city has ever been built on the spot, and there is no present plan to build one, but equally no special reason why one should never be built there. For the Dummettian anti-realist, we are not entitled to assert ‘Either a city was, is or will be built on this spot or no city was, is or will be built on this spot’, for we have no procedure for determining which disjunct holds. Now imagine someone claiming:
We do have a decision method for the sentence. For you can in principle build a city on this spot. Having done so, you will have determined that a city was, is or will be built on this spot.

Although we have the capacity in principle to build a city on the spot, it does not put us in possession of a decision procedure in the relevant sense, for by intuitionistic standards it does not entitle us to assert ‘Either a city was, is or will be built on this spot or no city was, is or will be built on this spot’ in advance of exercising the capacity. Indeed, the problem for (DIS) is even worse, for we can take both ϕ and ψ in it to be ‘A city was, is or will be built on this spot’. We possess a method (building a city) whose application will verify ‘A city was, is or will be built on this spot’. Therefore, by (DIS) we are now entitled to assert ‘Either a city was, is or will be built on this spot or a city was, is or will be built on this spot’. Since even in intuitionistic logic ϕ∨ϕ is trivially equivalent to ϕ, we are now entitled to assert ‘A city was, is, or will be built on this spot’, in advance of building one or even planning to do so. That is absurd. More generally, such an argument would conclude that whenever one has the power in principle to make ϕ true, one is entitled to assert ϕ in advance of exercising that power. That conclusion involves one in contradictions, since one often has both the power to make ϕ true and the power to make ¬ϕ true, for example when ϕ is ‘I will count to a thousand by midnight’.11 By (DIS), one is now both entitled to assert ϕ and entitled to assert ¬ϕ, irrespective of one’s intentions. Evidently (DIS) can fail for sentences whose truth-values depend on our will; more specifically, it fails when the truth-value of ϕ or of ψ depends on whether the method is actually applied. Of course this problem does not arise when ϕ and ψ are mathematical.

If (DIS) does not govern the assertibility of disjunctions, what does? Intuitionistic semantics relies on some notion of canonical verification (Dummett 1977: 389–403). One is entitled to make an assertion for which one lacks a canonical verification, if one knows that such a verification exists. The existence of the verification does not consist in its being possessed by anyone; nevertheless, since the intuitionist conceives it as essentially capable of being possessed by someone, it does not import any sort of platonism inconsistent with the intuitionistic view.12 The natural suggestion is then that a canonical verification of a disjunction consists of a canonical verification of a disjunct. We may be entitled to assert a disjunction without being entitled to assert any disjunct, because we know that a canonical verification exists for some disjunct without knowing which. We are in that position with respect to ϕ∨¬ϕ when we have a genuine decision procedure for ϕ but have not yet applied it. But if we possess Tennant’s purported decision procedure for Kϕ without having applied it, we do not thereby know that a canonical verification for Kϕ or a canonical verification for ¬Kϕ exists, even though we know how to bring such a canonical verification into existence. Consequently, we do not know that a canonical verification for Kϕ∨¬Kϕ exists; so we are not entitled to assert the disjunction.

On an adequate understanding of intuitionistic semantics, the decidability of ϕ does not imply the decidability of Kϕ in any sense conducive to (10). Tennant fails in his attempt to collapse (7) into (8) for decidable ϕ. He has located no instability in moderately hard anti-realism.

Tennant’s positive response to Fitch’s argument is to construct and defend a modified knowability principle. Having defined a sentence ϕ to be Cartesian if and only if the contradiction ⊥ does not follow from Kϕ, he endorses this restricted variant of (1), formulated as a rule of inference:
ϕ; ergo ◇Kϕ, where ϕ is Cartesian.13

Intuitively: (◇KC) says that truth entails knowability except when Fitch’s problem occurs. Tennant admits that it may be undecidable whether a given step is an instance of a rule like (◇KC), because it is undecidable whether ⊥ follows from Kϕ. He claims that this does not matter, on the grounds that we will apply it only when we do know that the condition is met. Since (◇KC) is intended for use only in a few philosophical arguments, not for systematic application in mathematics or science, the undecidability does not defeat its purpose.

Tennant’s rule looks desperately ad hoc. But that is not the worst of its problems. The point of restricting (◇KC) to Cartesian cases is to enable the soft anti-realist to avoid asserting (8), that something is true only if known. Since Tennant holds that (7) collapses into (8) when ϕ is decidable, his soft anti-realist rejects (7) too. The restriction on (◇KC) blocks the original derivation of (7) from (1). But Tennant has overlooked a more complex derivation of (7) from (◇KC) and some plausible assumptions.

The argument will be conducted in Tennant’s preferred background logic, which is not the standard intuitionistic one but his weaker system IR of intuitionistic relevance logic (Tennant 1997: 343-4). The differences do not affect the argument below. For definiteness, let ϕ be the decidable sentence ‘There is a fragment of Roman pottery at that spot’ (we assume a suitable context). Introduce a name ‘n’ by the stipulation that it is to designate (rigidly) the number of books actually now on my table. Let E be the predicate ‘is even’.
We first argue that the conjunction ϕ∧(Kϕ→En) is Cartesian. For suppose that K(ϕ∧(Kϕ→En)) is inconsistent. Then this story contains an inconsistency:

I find a fragment of Roman pottery at this spot and identify it correctly; I thereby come to know that there is a fragment of Roman pottery there. I also count the books actually now on my table and discover that the number is even; I deduce that if someone sometime knows that there is a fragment of Roman pottery at that spot then n is even.14 By putting the two pieces of knowledge together, I acquire the knowledge expressed by the conjunction ϕ∧(Kϕ→En). Thus K(ϕ∧(Kϕ→En)) is true.

But the story is obviously consistent. Of course, n may in fact be odd, in which case, since that number could not have been even, the story expresses an impossible state of affairs. Nevertheless, the story itself is still consistent; one cannot discern by reason alone that the description which fixes the reference of ‘n’ picks out an odd number. Someone who asserts En because he failed to see one of the books is not guilty of an inconsistency. A more liberal interpretation of inconsistency might trivialize ◇KC; it is not what Tennant intends. Thus ⊥ does not follow from K(ϕ∧(Kϕ→En)), so ϕ∧(Kϕ→En) is Cartesian.
Let ⊢ be the consequence relation of a system of epistemic logic based on IR with the additional rule (◇KC) and the axiom schemas (2) and (3).15 Since its condition is met in this case, (◇KC) gives:
For ¬α⊢α→β holds even in IR (Tennant 1997: 344); from ¬Kϕ⊢Kϕ→En we can derive (13) by the rules for ∧. (12) and (13) yield:
The next step is an argument following Fitch for:

Now (3) and ∧-elimination yield K(ϕ∧(Kϕ→En))⊢Kϕ, while (2) and ∧-elimination yield K(ϕ∧(Kϕ→En))⊢Kϕ→En), and even in IR we can then move to (15).16 Since the rules used to derive (15) are truth-preserving in all possible situations, not just the actual one, if the premise of (15) expresses a possibility, so does its conclusion (if α→β is a theorem of a normal modal logic, so is ◇α→◇β):

For it is not contingent whether n is even. Since I can count the books on my table, it is decidable whether n is even; hence n is either odd or even; but if n is odd, it could not have been even, for the mathematical properties of numbers are not contingent; thus n could have been even only if it is even (En∨¬En, ¬En→¬◇En, ◇En⊢En).17 We can now repeat the argument for (18) with ‘odd’ in place of ‘even’ to derive:

(20) makes (7) a theorem. But the point of Tennant’s restricted knowability principle (◇KC) was precisely to enable the soft anti-realist not to assert (7), which on Tennant’s view collapses into (8), the principle definitive of hard anti-realism. Thus Tennant’s restriction is futile.

Should Tennant’s anti-realist seek a knowability principle with a stronger restriction to avoid (7)? The natural suspicion is that such a restriction would have to be very draconian indeed. But the search is in any case ill-motivated. The original knowability principle (1) was the outcome of an anti-realist argument (albeit a very dubious argument). If (1) has false consequences, then something must be wrong with the argument. If the argument is irreparably fallacious, one has lost one’s reason for postulating any knowability principle at all, restricted or unrestricted. If the argument can be repaired, the nature of the repairs should dictate the nature of the restrictions on the resultant knowability principle.18 Tennant does not indicate any form of anti-realist argument that would motivate the restriction in (◇KC). To say that ϕ is Cartesian is not to explain on anti-realist terms how ϕ could be unknowably true, how speakers’ use of ϕ could be sensitive to a condition they could not in principle recognize to obtain or how ϕ could express its content without such sensitivity; it is merely to say that broadly logical considerations rule out knowledge of its truth. Without such an explanation, from the perspective of principled anti-realism it is quite premature to endorse (◇KC) or anything like it.
If Fitch’s argument does not refute all forms of anti-realism, it certainly shows how much remains to be done before there is a working anti-realist semantics for empirical language.
Thanks to Peter Milne and Peter Pagin for comments on a draft of this paper.

He has overlooked the discussions of such readings of the argument at Williamson 1982: 204, 1988: 425–8 and 1994: 141, 144. It is unnecessary to add to them here. ↩︎

See Williamson 1982: 206. The objection rests on an error. Intuitionistically, ¬Kϕ and ¬¬ϕ imply ¬(¬Kϕ→¬ϕ), the negation of (9); thus ¬(ϕ→Kϕ) is intuitionistically inconsistent given (1) (and the other principles used to derive (9)) although it does not intuitionistically imply ϕ. ↩︎

Nevertheless his discussion makes clear that we can reasonably treat instances of (2) and (3) as theorems of epistemic logic. ↩︎

(◇KC) is in any case unpromising on an epistemic reading of ◇. If ◇ is read as ‘for all we know’, we can choose an example in which it is in fact known whether n is even, on which assumption ◇En is true only if En is, and a form of the problem in the text can still be raised. A reading of ◇ as ‘for all we know a priori’ tends to trivialize (◇KC) by making ◇Kϕ say little more than that ϕ is Cartesian. ↩︎

The proposal is grounded in Usberti’s anti-Dummettian analysis of the arguments for an intuitionistic approach (see also Williamson 1998). works.title: Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom
passages: Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

A canonical argument for skepticism about our ordinary knowledge of the external world is this: we have ordinary knowledge of the external world only if we know that we are not brains-in-vats (BIVs); we do not know that we are not BIVs; therefore, we do not have ordinary knowledge of the external world. Hilary Putnam (1981) famously suggested that semantic externalism undermines the skeptical argument. The semantic externalist postulates necessary connections between the content of our thinking and the external world. According to Putnam, those necessary connections preclude BIVs from entertaining the proposition that they are BIVs. If so, there is a valid argument from semantic externalism and the plausible premise that we do entertain the proposition that we are BIVs to the conclusion that we are not BIVs.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

One standard objection to Putnam’s argument is that for some of the less radical BIV scenarios, no plausible form of semantic externalism precludes BIVs from entertaining the proposition that they are BIVs. Perhaps you lack the requisite connections with the external world if you have always been a BIV, but surely you still have them if you were envatted only last night. Thus, as Keith DeRose notes in his illuminating paper, the semantic externalist argument against skepticism looks insufficiently general. DeRose also raises a new problem for the semantic externalist strategy. That is the main topic of this response.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

Consider senses of “semantic externalism” and “BIV” in which semantic externalism does entail that BIVs cannot entertain the proposition that they are BIVs. Suppose that semantic externalism is true and that we do entertain the proposition that we are BIVs. Then the argument from semantic externalism and the auxiliary premise that we entertain the proposition that we are BIVs to the conclusion that we are not BIVs is not just valid but sound; its premises and conclusion are true. We might be tempted to assume that a sound argument to the conclusion that we are not BIVs constitutes an effective reply to the skeptic who denies that we know that we are not BIVs. As DeRose shows, that assumption is unwarranted. He forcefully presses the question: even if the argument is sound, how would it support our putative knowledge that we are not BIVs? After all, if we are not in fact BIVs, then the argument “We are not BIVs; therefore we are not BIVs” is a sound argument to the conclusion that we are not BIVs, but no one supposes that it would support our knowledge that we are not BIVs.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

The obvious way for a valid argument to help us know its conclusion is this: we start by knowing its premises, and then by following the argument, come to know its conclusion. For that way to work, deduction must be a way to extend one’s knowledge, a closure assumption denied by some epistemologists, such as Robert Nozick (1981). However, both DeRose and I endorse the closure assumption. DeRose has argued elsewhere (1995) that apparent counterexamples to it cheat by changing the context in which the word “know” is used halfway through. However, DeRose points out, to come to know that one is not a BIV in the obvious way, by following the argument to the conclusion that one is not a BIV from semantic externalism and the premise that one entertains the proposition that one is a BIV, one must first know the premises of the argument. If one is indeed entertaining the proposition that one is a BIV, then it is perhaps not very difficult to know that one is, but one must also know the truth of semantic externalism. If, although semantic externalism is true, one does not know that it is, then the obvious way of using the argument to come to know that one is not a BIV is not open to one. DeRose notes that since most people in the world have never even heard of semantic externalism, they have no chance of coming to know in that way that they are not BIVs, even if they have heard of BIVs. Should we make the teaching of semantic externalism compulsory in schools, to enable future generations to know that they are not BIVs? If DeRose is correct in claiming that his Mom has not encountered Putnam’s argument, and she knows that she is not a BIV, then she knows it in some other way.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

As DeRose argues, a further problem faces those of us who have heard of semantic externalism, for its epistemic status is far from secure. Although thought experiments provide strong support for the minimal claim that the content of one’s thinking does not supervene on one’s internal physical states, that minimal form of semantic externalism by itself has little impact on problems of skepticism, for it is not strong enough to preclude BIVs from entertaining the proposition that they are BIVs. Precluding that requires a specific kind of causal constraint on reference. Since we find it very hard to state such a constraint without immediate confrontation by counterexamples, probably no one yet knows the truth of any such constraint. Probably, therefore, no one has ever come to know that he or she is not a BIV in the “obvious” way, by following the semantic externalist argument to the conclusion that he or she is not a BIV.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

Suppose that although the semantic externalist argument is sound, semantic externalism is not known to be true. Is there some less obvious way in which the argument would support our putative knowledge that we are not BIVs—even if we have never heard of semantic externalism? I will suggest that the semantic externalist has more scope for maneuver than DeRose is inclined to allow, and that DeRose’s own work provides such scope. I will show how semantic externalism is relevant to skeptical issues in a way quite different from the one DeRose considers, on at least some conceptions of knowledge. I will begin with a drastically oversimplified form of reliabilism, and then allow it to become more sophisticated in the direction of DeRose’s own account of knowledge attributions.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

One infallibly believes p if and only if one believes p and, necessarily, if one believes p then p is true. All infallible belief is of course true belief. A drastically oversimplified form of reliablism says that knowledge is infallible belief:
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom
For all p, one knows p if and only if one infallibly believes p.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

Now suppose that semantic externalism entails that, necessarily, no BIV entertains the proposition that it is a BIV (for given senses of “semantic externalism” and “BIV”). But, necessarily, in believing that one is not a BIV, one thereby entertains the proposition that one is a BIV, in order to deny it. Hence, necessarily, if one believes that one is not a BIV, then one is not a BIV, so one’s belief is true. That yields this principle:
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom
If one believes that one is not a BIV, then one infallibly believes that one is not a BIV.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom
Given the right-to-left direction of (1), (2) entails:
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom
If one believes that one is not a BIV, then one knows that one is not a BIV.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

Thus semantic externalism and simpleminded reliablism entail that one knows that one is not a BIV, provided that one believes that one is not a BIV, even if one has never heard of semantic externalism, and a fortiori even if one does not know the truth of semantic externalism. The argument does not even require one to know that one entertains the proposition that one is a BIV.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

The obvious objection to (1) is that, although it may permit one to know that one is not a BIV (courtesy of semantic externalism), it permits one to know very little else. For almost every proposition p such that one is ordinarily said to know p (for example, that one had breakfast), one can believe p falsely. Thus, granted semantic externalism, (1) has the opposite effect to that of Nozick’s account of knowledge: (1) gives one knowledge that one is not a BIV but not ordinary knowledge, whereas Nozick’s account gives one ordinary knowledge but not knowledge that one is not a BIV.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

The skeptical consequences of (1) just noted flow from its left-to-right direction; its antiskeptical consequences such as (3)—given semantic externalism—flow from its right-to-left direction. Thus if we replace “infallibly believes” in (1) by one of its weaker consequences, we might avoid the skeptical consequences while preserving the argument to (3). The simplest way of doing that would be to weaken the interpretation of “necessarily” in the definition of “infallibly believes.” In the new sense, “S infallibly believes p” is true as uttered in a context c if and only if in every possible world relevant to c in which S believes p, p is true. Not every metaphysically possible world is relevant to every context. “S knows that she has had breakfast” is true as uttered in c if every world in which S believes falsely that she has had breakfast is irrelevant to c. Since contextually relevant possible worlds are still possible worlds, this reinterpretation of (1) preserves the argument to (3).
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

An alternative weakening of “believes infallibly” replaces the strict conditional by a counterfactual conditional. One sensitively believes p if and only if one believes p and if p were not true one would not believe p. All sensitive belief is true belief, because a counterfactual conditional entails the corresponding material conditional. In particular, “If p were not true, S would not believe p” entails the truth-functional “If p is not true then S does not believe p.” Moreover, all infallible belief is sensitive belief (on the strict original reading of “infallible”), for a strict conditional entails the corresponding counterfactual conditional. In particular, “Necessarily, if S believes p, then p is true” entails “If p were not true, S would not believe p” because it entails “Necessarily, if p is not true, then S does not believe p.” But not all sensitive belief is infallible belief, for one can believe sensitively but not infallibly that one has had breakfast. Thus we may consider this form of reliabilism:
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom
For all p, one knows p if and only if one sensitively believes p.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom
Unlike (1) (on the original strict reading), (1*) does not imply that we lack ordinary knowledge. Now, since infallible belief entails sensitive belief, (2) entails:
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom
If one believes that one is not a BIV, then one sensitively believes that one is not a BIV.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

Given the right-to-left direction of (1*), (2*) entails the original (3). Since the source of (2) and therefore of (2*) was semantic externalism, (1*) preserves the relevance of semantic externalism to BIV skepticism.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

Nozick’s initial analysis of knowledge, before he introduces the complications of method, is close to (1*). He conjoins sensitive belief with the fourth condition “If p were true, S would believe p,” interpreted to mean that if p were true but things were slightly different in some other way, S would still believe p. The fourth condition interferes with the argument to (3), because it does not follow from infallible belief. Nevertheless, it is independently plausible that the fourth condition holds in ordinary cases when p is the proposition that one is not a BIV, so the argument to (3) can go through with that extra premise. Nozick’s account preserves the relevance of semantic externalism to BIV skepticism, even when the complications of method are introduced.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

DeRose’s account (1995, 1996) contains elements both of the contextualized (1) and of (1*). He does not accept (1*) as a true generalization. It conflicts with the reasonable closure principle that if one knows p and believes q on the basis of competent deduction from p then one knows q. For example, if b is the proposition that I had breakfast this morning and f is the proposition that I falsely believe that I had breakfast this morning as a result of confusing memories of today and yesterday, then I sensitively believe b, and I believe ∼f on the basis of competent deduction from b, but I do not sensitively believe ∼f. For DeRose, closure holds within contexts but not across them. He treats the truth-condition for knowledge ascriptions as similar in spirit to the contextualized version of (1), but postulates a conversational effect by which utterances of the form “S knows p” tend to make the closest worlds in which p is false contextually relevant, so that instances of (1) for contextually salient ascriptions of “knowledge” tend to be true. My utterance “I know that I had breakfast this morning” makes contextually relevant the closest worlds in which I did not have breakfast this morning; in those worlds my memory is not confused and I do not falsely believe that I had breakfast this morning. I sensitively believe b and in an ordinary context “I know b” expresses a truth. But when I deduce ∼f, my utterance “I know that I do not falsely believe that I had breakfast this morning as a result of confusing memories of today and yesterday” adds to the contextually relevant worlds the closest worlds in which I do falsely believe that I had breakfast this morning as a result of confusing memories of yesterday and today. I do not sensitively believe ∼f and “I know ∼f” expresses a falsehood. But in this new context “I know b” expresses a different and false proposition. My belief in b may be sensitive, but it is not infallible, even in the contextualized sense; I falsely believe b in some contextually relevant worlds. The details of the conversational mechanisms do not concern us here. What matters is that, on DeRose’s account, the truth of the proposition expressed by the skeptic’s utterance “S does not know p” in its context typically depends on the skeptic’s ability to make worlds in which S falsely believes p contextually relevant. But if one infallibly believes p, then there are no such worlds, and a version of the argument to (3) still goes through. Thus DeRose’s own account appears to suggest that at least some forms of semantic externalism falsify at least some forms of BIV skepticism.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

At this point DeRose is entitled to remind us that, in many less radical senses of “BIV,” no plausible form of semantic externalism precludes BIVs from entertaining the proposition that they are BIVs. But if we do not know that we are not BIVs in one of those less radical senses, and the closure principle holds, then the skeptical consequences are still devastating. However, the picture changes when we consider a modification of the account forced on DeRose by some recalcitrant examples.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

Let p be the proposition that I don’t falsely believe that I have hands. If p were false, I would falsely believe that I have hands, and would therefore believe something from which p follows, and would therefore believe p (we may assume). Thus my belief in p is not sensitive. Intuitively, however, this example hardly threatens my knowledge that I don’t falsely believe that I have hands. In this case, the left-to-right direction of (1*) fails. The same goes for my knowledge that I’m not an intelligent dog who’s always incorrectly thinking that it has hands (1995, 22).
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom
In response, DeRose proposes a rough qualification of (1):
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

We don’t … judge ourselves ignorant of p where ∼p implies something we take ourselves to know to be false, without providing an explanation of how we came to falsely believe this thing we think we know. Thus, I falsely believe that I have hands implies that I don’t have hands. Since I do take myself to know that I have hands (this belief isn’t insensitive), and since the above italicized proposition doesn’t explain how I went wrong with respect to my having hands, I’ll judge that I do know that proposition to be false. (1995, 23; symbolism altered).
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

The passage suggests that the consequence of ∼p we take ourselves to know to be false (“I don’t have hands”) is falsely believed to be false if p is false, and that ∼p does not explain why. From a third-personal perspective, we presumably judge S to know p in these cases only if S believes p at least in part because ∼p has the consequence we take S to know to be false; S does not know p if S believes p only on different and bad grounds. This reference to the grounds on which S believes is a step in the direction of Nozick’s methods, but not far enough to block the account’s partially skeptical consequences. The negation of the proposition that I am not a BIV induced to appear to itself to have hands does explain how I could falsely believe that I have hands, because that skeptical scenario has enough detail to be explanatory.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

DeRose’s account as just stated is insufficiently general. For example, let A be a case in which I am climbing a mountain and appear to myself to be climbing a mountain; things appear to me as they are. In case B, I am a BIV, but things appear to me just as they do in A. If I were in B, I would believe that I was not in B. If p is the proposition that I am not in B, then I do not sensitively believe p. Nevertheless, in my actual present case, I know that I am not in B, because I am in neither A nor B; things do not appear to me at all as they would in B. I appear to myself to be sitting in front of a computer screen in my office. I do not appear to myself to be climbing a mountain, as I would in B.1 No matter what my situation, I cannot sensitively believe p. This is a counterexample to (1*). Moreover, my false beliefs when I am in B are just as explicable as in other skeptical scenarios, while the example does not involve false beliefs when I am in either A or my actual case. Thus the example does not involve unexplained false belief at all, unlike the apparent suggestion in the quoted passage.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

A small modification of DeRose’s suggestion does handle the example. Let q be the proposition that I do not appear to myself to be climbing a mountain. Thus q entails p (that I am not in B), so ∼p entails ∼q; if I am in B, then I appear to myself to be climbing a mountain. I take myself to know q; it is a belief about how things appear to me. I am mistaken about q in none of the relevant cases. I sensitively believe q, for if I appeared to myself to be climbing a mountain I would not believe that I did not appear to myself to be climbing a mountain. Moreover, in B I do not falsely believe q; I believe ∼q, truly. Thus ∼p does not explain how I could falsely believe q. One might, therefore, modify DeRose’s suggestion thus: when we judge that S knows p without sensitively believing p, we do so because S sensitively believes a proposition q that entails p, and ∼p does not explain how S could falsely believe q. When S does sensitively believe p, p is itself such a proposition q, granted that ∼p does not explain how one could falsely believe p when one would not believe p if p were false. We might therefore consider the following modification of (1*):
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom
For all propositions p, one knows p if and only if for some proposition q: q entails p, one sensitively believes q and ∼p does not explain how one could falsely believe q.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

Further modifications could be made. We might require that S believes p because S believes q. We might allow the link between q and p to be looser than entailment. The discussion below will not depend on these details.2 The contextualist motivation for replacing (1*) by (1**) is that when we evaluate “S knows p” we need not consider cases in which S falsely believes q, because we have no contextually relevant explanation of how S could do so. Of course, DeRose is not committed to (1**) as a true universal generalization about knowledge but as a principle contextually salient instances of which tend to express truths. But let us consider the effect of (1**) on skeptical claims in those cases in which it does hold.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

We are interested in the skeptical hypothesis that I am a BIV in a less radical sense of “BIV” in which no plausible form of semantic externalism precludes a BIV from entertaining the proposition that it is a BIV. Let the good case be one in which everything appears to me just as it actually does, and as far as possible is that way. Let the bad case be one in which I am a brain in a vat and everything appears to me as far as possible as it actually does. Let us reserve the term “BIV” for a brain in a vat in that bad case and assume that, semantic externalism notwithstanding, if I were a BIV, I would believe that I was not a BIV. If p is the proposition that I am not a BIV, then I do not sensitively believe p, although I may believe p truly. According to (1**), do I know p? Trivially, if I am a BIV, then I do not know p, because p is false. The question is whether I know p in the good case, when I believe p truly.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

In the good case I may believe sensitively a proposition q from which I deduce p, and semantic externalism may prevent the BIV from entertaining q, even though it does not prevent the BIV from entertaining the proposition that it is a BIV. For example, in the good case I am looking at a cloud in the sky. If I were a BIV, I could not see this cloud and would never have had any contact with it, however indirect. In the bad case, the BIV does not think about this cloud, although the BIV might think about clouds in general, and perhaps even about a cloud-image. In the bad case, I might understand the linguistic meaning of the words “I see this cloud,” but they would not express the proposition that I see this cloud, and I would be unable to entertain that proposition. Even if the BIV could have designated the cloud by some elaborate description, it does not do so, because I deploy no such description in the good case, and the bad case is relevantly similar. Let p be the proposition that I am not a BIV, and q the proposition that I see this cloud. Given what has been built into the current definition of “BIV,” q entails p. Since I cannot believe q when p is false, ∼p does not explain how I could falsely believe q. In the good case, I sensitively believe that I see this cloud. If I did not see it, I would presumably be in some other ordinary situation and would not believe that I saw it. Even if I would or might be a BIV if q were false, I would still not believe q. In the good case, I competently deduce p from q, and believe p on that basis. If I were a BIV, I would still have the premise token “I see this cloud,” and go through a process superficially like deduction, but my premise token would lack content. Thus, in the good case, the right-hand-side of (1**) is verified for the specified value of “p” by the specified value of “q.” Consequently, the effect of (1**) is that I know that I am not a BIV, even in a sense of “BIV” in which a BIV can entertain the proposition that it is a BIV. The result depends on semantic externalism, but not on the very strong causal constraints on reference that Putnam’s argument requires. Rather, it depends on a less contentious externalist conception of singular propositions on which one cannot think about a particular without some kind of special link to it, a link which I have to the cloud in the good case but not in the bad case.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

In his earlier work, DeRose aimed to explain the appeal of skepticism by showing how skeptical claims express truths in the contexts in which they are made. Once his account is modified in the direction of (1**), semantic externalism jeopardizes that explanation.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

Could DeRose handle the problem by modifying (1**) to speak of quasi-propositions rather than propositions, where quasi-propositions are like propositions except for being individuated in a semantically internalist manner? That is easier said than done, for we need to be told which narrow criterion is to individuate quasi-propositions; which internal differences are consistent with thinking the same quasi-proposition? Furthermore, the appeal to quasi-propositions looks suspiciously ad hoc. It needs some independent motivation if it is not to be a mere device for rigging (1**) in favor of the skeptic. Such a regression to internalist modes of thought also looks foreign to the otherwise externalist spirit of DeRose’s account.
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

A more general concern is that the simple forms of reliabilism considered have all been proposition-specific, in that they imply that infallibly believing p is sufficient for knowing p. That implication is false, of course. If one believes a mathematical truth, for example, then one believes it infallibly, for all mathematical truths are necessary truths, but one can believe a mathematical truth without knowing it, if one believes it on the basis of a thoroughly fallacious proof.3
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

It has become clear that on at least some accounts of knowledge, including versions of DeRose’s own account, there is a way of drawing antiskeptical consequences from semantic externalism not closed off by the arguments of DeRose’s paper. The crucial questions are left open here. Is one of those accounts of knowledge correct? Are the antiskeptical consequences as extensive as we desire? Could they be derived in no other way?
Skepticism, semantic externalism, and Keith's Mom

One methodological point is worth making. Semantic externalism is a doctrine whose implications are often surprising at first sight, although satisfying on further thought. We should not expect them to be intuitively obvious. Therefore, we should not revise our account of knowledge merely so that semantic externalism does not generate antiskeptical consequences that sound overweening when we first hear them. They might be true.
I thank DeRose for helpful discussion. Some of the issues raised in this response are discussed further in my forthcoming book (Williamson, 2000).
Stephen Schiffer raises a similar problem for the skeptical hypothesis that I’m a BIV′, which is just like a BIV except for lacking auditory sensations (1996, 331). ↩︎
(1**) is based on a suggestion made by Keith DeRose, although he is not responsible for the details of my formulation. ↩︎
The willingness of Lewis (1996) to countenance such consequences of his account is one of the factors that makes it hard to compare with the ordinary conception of knowledge. ↩︎
DeRose, K. 1995. Solving the skeptical problem. Philosophical Review 104: 1–52.
DeRose, K. 1996. Knowledge, assertion and lotteries. Australasian Journal of Philosophy 74: 568–580.
Lewis, D. K. 1996. Elusive knowledge. Australasian Journal of Philosophy 74: 549–567.
Nozick, R. 1981. Philosophical explanations. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
Putnam, H. 1981. Reason, truth and history. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
Schiffer, S. 1996. Contextualist solutions to scepticism. Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society 96: 317–333.
Williamson, T. 2000. Knowledge and its limits. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

works.title: Semantic paradox and semantic change
passages: If semantic paradoxes such as the Liar arise because ‘true’ and other metalinguistic expressions can change their reference with changes of linguistic context, is that due to indexicality (they have the same linguistic meaning as reference changes) or ambiguity (their linguistic meaning itself changes)? An argument from communication that appears to favour the indexicality interpretation is not compelling. This paper defends the ambiguity interpretation. It is left open whether its considerations generalize to other kinds of paradox.

One standard philosophical response to a paradox is to postulate non-obvious contextual shifting in some key term. The technique has been applied to sceptical paradoxes, sorites paradoxes, and semantic paradoxes, with varying degrees of plausibility. ‘Know’, ‘heap’, and ‘true’ are said to change their reference according to the context in which they are uttered. The propounding of the paradoxes is supposed to induce critical changes of context.

A general question arises for this approach. Does the change in the reference of the term reflect a change in its linguistic meaning? If linguistic meaning by itself determined reference, the answer would have to be positive. But for indexical terms linguistic meaning determines reference only relative to the context of utterance, sometimes determining different references relative to different contexts. For example, the linguistic meaning of ‘I’ consists in something like the rule that as used in any context c it refers to the speaker in c. In virtue of this unchanging rule, the reference of ‘I’ varies from context to context. For a given paradox, is the diagnosis that the key term has an unchanging indexical meaning, or that it has a changing meaning and is therefore ambiguous? Of course, the answer may depend on which paradox we are talking about, but the question arises in every case.

To the extent that the question has a received answer, it is that the key term is indexical rather than ambiguous. The obvious argument for this answer appeals to our success in communication. If the statement of the paradox changed the meaning of ‘know’, ‘heap’, or ‘true’, how could we recognize the new sense of the term? Such changes in meaning would apparently undermine the possibility of mutual understanding, perhaps even of self-understanding. Yet we do succeed in communicating with each other, even about the paradoxes. Our reactions to them are not merely idiosyncratic. A single, unchanging indexical meaning, by contrast, would nicely explain our ability to communicate in these cases, just as our grasp of the unchanging meaning of ‘I’ enables us to understand strangers when they refer to themselves as ‘I’.

It is worth remarking that the argument from communication requires the indexical meaning to consist in more than an arbitrary association of contexts with references. If it were merely such an association, the problem of learning the meaning of the indexical term in the first place would be just as hard as the problem of communication facing the alternative claim of semantic change, for the reference of the indexical term in those contexts in which the learner had heard it uttered would give no clue as to its reference in other contexts. Rather, the indexical meaning should consist in a unitary rule, like that for ‘I’, which enables speakers to grasp on the basis of limited experience a general rule by which the reference of the term depends on its context of utterance. Such a rule of reference is also needed to state a correct generalization about its reference. Notoriously, even homophonic generalizations about reference across contexts are false (not trivial) for indexical terms. ‘Now’ as uttered at past or future times does not refer to now; it refers to then. The non-trivial non-homophonic rule that ‘now’ refers to the time of utterance is needed to generalize correctly about its reference. Without such a rule, the indexicality diagnosis of a paradox cannot be fully articulated.

This paper concerns the specific case of the semantic paradoxes. It argues against the indexicality interpretation of reference change; it interprets that change as reflecting a change in meaning. The argument does not immediately generalize to the other paradoxes; their proper treatment will be left as an open question. But the paper will at least show that the general argument from communication for the indexicality approach is much less compelling than it first appears.

To fix ideas, Tyler Burge will be taken as a leading example of the indexicality approach to the semantic paradoxes. Burge diagnoses the semantic paradoxes as illicitly exploiting shifts of context. He postulates a system of levels; for each level i, there is a set of truei sentences and a set of pathologicali sentences, and the Tarskian disquotational T-schema holds with respect to ‘true’ for all non-pathologicali sentences. The level of ‘true’ is determined contextually; as Kripke emphasized, the level cannot be determined just by the sentence-type in which ‘true’ occurs. To validate individual steps in the paradoxical derivations, one must assign different levels to different occurrences of ‘true’, and the contradictions vanish. On Burge’s view, classical logic is valid.1
That the semantic paradoxes involve context-shifting has some plausibility, as Burge shows. Consider a simple formal version of the Liar. Let ‘L1’ name the sentence ∼True(L1) (‘L1 is not true’), so:
The Tarskian disquotational equivalence for ∼True(L1) is:
Using (1), we substitute its left-hand side for its right-hand side in (2):

When we reflect on the paradox, it seems right to assert ‘Whatever the semantic status of L1, it cannot be true, given this paradox’, and therefore ‘L1 is not true’, i.e., L1. But in originally propounding the paradox, it was not right to assert L1, because it was paradoxical. Indexicality in ‘true’ would explain L1’s change in assertibility.

Context-shifting is particularly vivid in a variant of König and Berry’s paradoxes. Only finitely many natural numbers will ever be named by me. Thus some natural numbers will never be named by me. By the least number principle, there is the least natural number I shall never name; name it ‘Minimus’. I have just named Minimus; contradiction. This is no a priori proof that I shall eventually name all natural numbers. Rather, reflection on an initial use of ‘name’ seems to yield a more inclusive use of the term, and a correspondingly higher value of ‘Minimus’, a process which can be iterated indefinitely. A semantic account of ‘name’ and ‘Minimus’ should not ignore such contextual effects.
Unfortunately, a Strengthened Liar Paradox appears to infects Burge’s approach. He replies to the objection thus:

one might suggest a sentence like (a), ‘(a) is not true at any level’. But this is not an English reading of any sentence in our formalization. Our theory is a theory of ‘true,’ not ‘true at a level’. From our viewpoint, the latter phrase represents a misguided attempt to quantify out the indexical character of ‘true’; it has some of the incongruity of ‘here at some place’. No relativization will “deindexicalize” ‘true’.2

This is unsatisfying. To try to deindexicalize ‘here’ by saying ‘here at some place’ is indeed confused, but English has a perfectly good word for what it is an attempt to say: ‘somewhere’. Quantification over levels certainly appears to make sense; if it does, we can give Burge’s sentence (a) a paradoxical reading, even if that is not the reading it receives in current English, and we must confront that paradox. If that reading is non-indexical, as it apparently is, the Strengthened Liar requires a different solution, which suggests that Burge’s diagnosis does not go deep enough. Burge contests these appearances. In his meta-language, the subscript in ‘truei’ is not a variable of quantification but a schematic letter; if we say that every instance of a schema is true, that use of ‘true’ is itself either indexical or schematic over indexical uses, and a version of Burge’s original diagnosis applies.3

We can consider the problem within a rigorous framework for treating indexicality, provided by David Kaplan. On Kaplan’s account, “If c is a context, then an occurrence of [a sentence] ϕ in c is true iff the content [proposition] expressed by ϕ in this context is true when evaluated with respect to the circumstances of the context.”4 An appropriate level for ‘true’ would constitute one aspect of the context. For Kaplan, the contextual variable ‘c’ is open to quantification; he quantifies on it in defining logical truth as truth in every context.5 How else could we generalize about indexicality? We can therefore construct a paradox about logical truth.
Let True(s,c) say that the sentence s is true as uttered (with its present meaning) in the context c. Let ‘L2’ name the sentence ∀c∼True(L2,c) (‘L2 is true in no context’), so:

Let c0 be a context. We cannot generally assert homophonic Tarskian disquotational equivalences for truth in c0; unless c0 is the very context of our theorizing, an indexical sentence may express a different content in c0 from the one it expresses in the context of our theorizing, so the two sides of the biconditional may differ in truth-value. Thus I do not assert: ‘I live in Edinburgh’ is true as uttered by you if and only if I live in Edinburgh. However, let us assume that L2 expresses the same content in every context, as it appears to do. Then we have the homophonic equivalence:

The left-to-right direction of (3*) and universal instantiation give:
