works.title: Sense, validity and context
passages: How does Frege’s distinction between sense and reference apply to terms whose reference depends on context? The stakes are high; a good account of the sense of ‘I’ might constitute an analysis of self-consciousness. Frege’s own remarks on this matter are notoriously unsatisfactory. In Past, Space, and Self, John Campbell does better. The depth and freshness of his investigations are outstanding. He uncovers a wide variety of evidence, both logical and psychological, to which any account must do justice.
For Campbell, our primary fix on the notion of sense is by the logical notion of valid inference. Suppose that I argue thus:
This is rough. This is red. Something is rough and red.

The two tokens of ‘this’ express the same sense if and only if my argument is valid. Since the identity in linguistic type of the two tokens does not settle the question of validity either way, Campbell treats arguments as constituted of token sentences or acts of judgement; I will follow him in this for the moment. Since the identity in reference of the two tokens seems not to guarantee validity either, even granted the identity in linguistic type—the first demonstration might be tactile, the second visual—identity in reference seems to be insufficient for identity in sense (reference does not determine sense). But if the two tokens refer to different objects, then the argument is invalid, for the truth of the premises does not imply the truth of the conclusion; so the senses are distinct. In this case at least, identity in reference is necessary for identity in sense (sense determines reference).

On Campbell’s account, the question ‘What is the sense of “I”?’ becomes ‘Which arguments involving “I” are valid?’. If you say ‘I am hungry’ and I say ‘I am sleepy’, there is no valid argument to the conclusion ‘Someone is hungry and sleepy’ in anyone’s mouth. Thus the two tokens of ‘I’ cannot be said to have the same sense. Since we both used ‘I’ with its standard linguistic meaning, that shared meaning is not the sense of tokens of ‘I’. One can specify the shared linguistic meaning by stating the reference rule for ‘I’:
Token-reflexive rule Any token of ‘I’ refers to whoever produced it.

The rule explains why your token of ‘I’ refers to you and mine refers to me. Campbell rightly puts the token-reflexive rule at the centre of his account. He combines it with the assumption that the premises and conclusion of a genuine inference must be produced by a single subject (p. 105). Thus all tokens of ‘I’ in an inference are guaranteed coreference, and have the same sense. Any genuine inference of this form is valid:
I am hungry. I am sleepy. Someone is hungry and sleepy.

Campbell’s account undermines the Fregean claim that senses are public, even for context-independent expressions. There is no valid inference from your token of ‘37 is prime’ to mine, for they were produced by different subjects; thus there is no basis for assigning them the same sense. Equally, there is no invalid inference from your token to mine; thus there is no basis for assigning them different senses. The account seems to make all your senses incommensurable with mine.

How persuasive is Campbell’s assumption that the premises and conclusion of an inference must be produced by a single subject? Imagine a logic class in which one pupil produces a premise, another produces a second premise, a third produces a conclusion, and the teacher asks the others ‘Was that a valid argument?’. The blanket answer ‘It wasn’t an argument at all’ does not seem compelling. Even if the act of inferring a conclusion must always be performed by a single subject (which is doubtful), it does not follow that the question of validity arises only when the premises were produced by the same subject. Why can’t I validly infer my token of ‘37 is prime’ from yours? One might instead try to preserve the connection between validity and sense by allowing multi-subject arguments.

In other respects, Campbell allows valid inferences to straddle contexts. For example, he takes his earlier token of ‘I am F’ to be logically related to his later token of ‘I was F’ (p. 84). He does not assume that the premises and conclusion of an inference must be produced at a single time (the word ‘simultaneously’ on p. 105 obscures this). He allows ‘now’, unlike ‘I’, to change its reference in the course of an inference. If ‘I’ were allowed to change its reference in the course of an inference too, the asymmetry would disappear.

By what principle is the argument from Campbell’s earlier token of ‘I am F’ to his later token of ‘I was F’ valid? The obvious proposal is to combine a token-reflexive account of ‘I’ and tense with context-independent information about the tokens to generate context-independent truth-conditions for them, then apply a standard account of validity for context-independent arguments. Thus a token of ‘I am F’ uttered by J. C. at noon on 29 July 1996 is true if and only if J. C. is [tenselessly] F at noon on 29 July 1996; a token of ‘I was F’ uttered by J. C. at noon on 30 July 1996 is true if and only if J. C. is [tenselessly] F before noon on 30 July 1996; the inference from ‘J. C. is F at noon on 29 July 1996’ to ‘J. C. is F before noon on 30 July 1996’ is context-independently valid. Unfortunately, this account makes too much information accessible to pure reason. The inference from the earlier token of ‘I am F’ uttered by J. C. to a later token of ‘J. C. was F’ comes out valid by the same standard; Campbell denies its validity (p. 84). Similarly, a token of ‘Now = noon on 29 July 1996’ uttered at noon on 29 July 1996 becomes a logical truth (logically valid); but logic should not tell us the time. It would not help Campbell to bite the bullet, accept these inferences and argue that we are not always in a position to recognize validity when we see it; for then there would be no good reason to make validity sensitive to anything more fine-grained than reference; the distinction between sense and reference would disappear. The notion of validity is hard to apply directly to inferences between token-reflexive tokens in different contexts.

The original reason for not applying the notion of validity to arguments constituted of sentence types was that an argument type involving demonstratives, such as (I), has both valid and invalid instances. But that point does not force one all the way to applying the notion of validity to arguments constituted of sentence tokens. One could handle it by subscripting demonstratives within sentence types under a convention of coreference for identically subscripted demonstratives; thus (I) becomes valid when and only when the two occurrences of ‘this’ receive the same subscript (compare David Kaplan, ‘Afterthoughts’, in Joseph Almog, John Perry and Howard Wettstein, eds., Themes from Kaplan (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1989), at p. 587). Validity could then be explained as truth-preservation with respect to each context of utterance. The context must not vary from premises to conclusion, otherwise even the argument from ‘It is dark here’ to ‘It is dark here’ would count as invalid (of course, our ability to understand the premises and conclusion may depend on experience in other contexts, but that does not imply variation in the context of utterance within the argument itself). Since the token-reflexive rule fixes the reference of ‘I’ in any context, ‘I’ will not be subscripted.

There is a problem. On this account, the validity of an argument tells us nothing about truth-preservation when the premises and conclusion are instantiated in different contexts. But inference takes time; we judge the premises and conclusion successively. Thus the account of validity looks irrelevant to the inferences we actually make. Consider this argument:
Judy is dancing. Judy is singing. Someone is both dancing and singing.

If names need to be subscripted, assign the two occurrences of ‘Judy’ the same subscript, so that coreference is not in doubt. Thus (III) is valid: at any one context of utterance, its conclusion is true if its premises are. But if the premises and conclusion of (III) are judged in that chronological order, then the three tokens of the present-tense ‘is’ occur at three successive times; the tokens of the premises might be true and the token of the conclusion false. Intuitively, the problem is rather trivial; (III) could represent a cognitively praiseworthy piece of reasoning. How can that be?

Throughout an extended period of time, you might have a belief that Judy is dancing, a belief that Judy is singing, and a derived belief that someone is both dancing and singing. At each moment in that interval, your beliefs can be expressed by the premises and conclusion of (III); they instantiate a valid argument. Things go deductively wrong only when the premises and conclusion of (III) are realized as a series of occurrent judgements. In the circumstances, this realization may be psychologically necessary for the production of the inferred belief. We sometimes need to be in conscious control of our inferences, which requires their premises and conclusions to be realized successively as conscious judgements. We are psychologically capable of being in many simultaneous belief states; we are not psychologically capable of performing many simultaneous acts of conscious judgement. The single context of utterance is a context of purely notional utterance. But the function of this process is mainly instrumental; what matters is the deductive relation between the beliefs at any one time, in the interval, not the deductively invalid relation between the judgements at successive times in the interval. The simultaneous states of belief constitute a proper application of (III); the successive acts of judgement do not.

Our inferential practice exploits a convenient insensitivity to the specific context of our judgements. As a result, we sometimes run into trouble. One example may be the philosophical tendency to suppose that change is contradictory: the disposition to connect judgements inferentially as in (III) might overspill into the inference from the true judgement ‘Judy is dancing’ and the true judgement made a second later ‘Judy is not dancing’ to the self-contradictory judgement ‘Someone is both dancing and not dancing’.

An epistemological objection remains. If there are no logical relations over time between tensed judgements, how can we retain tensed knowledge? Suppose that I judge ‘It is raining’, and on that basis later judge ‘It was raining’. If the latter judgement is supposed to derive its epistemic status from the former, but the two are logically independent, how can the latter express knowledge?

The objection overplays the role of logic in extending our knowledge. Consider my knowledge that Paris is on the Seine. My current present-tense belief ‘Paris is on the Seine’ was caused by my present-tense belief a minute ago ‘Paris is on the Seine’; I have received no independent confirmation. There is no deductive connection between the two beliefs; it is logically possible for the earlier belief to be true and the later belief false, the Seine having cataclysmically altered its course. Nevertheless, if no such cataclysm has been a serious possibility, my later belief that Paris is on the Seine does constitute knowledge. The present fact that Paris is on the Seine and my present belief that it is are connected, in a way sufficient for knowledge, with their common cause in the past fact that Paris was on the Seine some time ago. This is not to assume that knowledge is definable in causal terms; what is plausible is that the common cause plays a central role in these specific cases of knowledge.

Recall (III). No doubt my belief at time τ that someone is both dancing and singing is caused by my beliefs at τ−∂ that Judy is dancing and that Judy is singing, not by the corresponding beliefs at τ itself; causation is not instantaneous. The truth of the cause beliefs does not strictly imply the truth of the effect belief. Nevertheless, in most circumstances in which the present-tensed beliefs at τ that Judy is dancing and that Judy is singing would constitute knowledge, even if they were caused by the corresponding present tensed beliefs at τ−∂, rather than by subsequent perception of Judy, the inferred belief at τ that someone is both dancing and singing also constitutes knowledge. Although the time-specific belief states by which it was caused are not those to which it is deductively related, this mismatch does not undermine knowledge in favourable circumstances.

Where does all this leave the notion of sense? Valid arguments are constituted of sentence types. If one explained sense in terms of validity as Campbell does, then sense would become a property of sentence types, not tokens. ‘I am hungry’ would express a single sense, irrespective of the speaker. If the sentence expresses different beliefs when uttered at different times or by different speakers, then senses would not be the objects of belief (compare Kaplan’s claim at p. 539 of ‘Demonstratives’ in Themes from Kaplan, op. cit., that characters, not contents, are the bearers of logical truth). Sense would no longer determine reference. That notion of sense is blind to the preservation of reference across context, the object of Campbell’s study.

Has too much been expected of the notion of validity? We lack clear intuitions about the validity of inferences involving context-dependent expressions in different contexts. This is not to deny all connection between validity and sense. Since any reasonable notion of sense should determine a reasonable notion of validity, constraints on validity imply constraints on sense. If the notion of sense is required to invalidate the inference from ‘Hesperus is bright’ to ‘Phosphorus is bright’, then ‘Hesperus’ and ‘Phosphorus’ must be assigned different senses. It often seems clear that the questions ‘Does this logically follow from that?’ and ‘Does this have the same sense as that?’ should have the same answer, but in many of those cases it is unclear what that answer should be. Similarly, considerations of validity give no easy answer to the question whether ‘I’ as used by the same subject at different times expresses the same sense. Logic does not need a general notion of sense.

The felt need for a distinction between sense and reference is connected with a felt need for a distinction between a priori and a posteriori knowledge. The dependence of reasoning on memory points up obscurities in both distinctions.
Thanks to John Campbell, Jason Stanley and a Cornell discussion group for helpful comments on an earlier version of this material.

works.title: Reply to commentators
passages: In their intriguing comments, Paul Horwich and Stephen Schiffer accept one main thesis of Vagueness, that vague sentences express true or false propositions in borderline cases. Neither of them denies the further thesis that we cannot know which truth-values those propositions have. Of course I will concentrate on their objections to more specific features of my view, hoping that this will not obscure the many points of agreement.

Vagueness is the capacity for borderline cases. On my view, the mark of a borderline case is a distinctive kind of obstacle to knowledge. Although we understand the word ‘bald’ and know the exact distribution of hairs on Jack’s scalp, we are not in a position to know whether Jack is bald. We can usually recognize whether the obstacle to knowledge is of the kind that constitutes vagueness; I discuss the underlying nature of this kind below. Horwich disputes this epistemic characterization of borderline cases:

[T]he essence of this phenomenon is not that borderline predications cannot be known to be correct. The essence of it […] is that in certain cases we are normally unwilling to apply the predicate, unwilling to deny that it applies, and confident that no further investigation could yield a decision. The problem of knowledge in such circumstances is a result of this paralysis of judgement.

Horwich notwithstanding, paralysis of judgement is quite unnecessary for vagueness. Consider an opinionated macho community, in which everyone applies the term ‘bald’ or its negation confidently and unhesitatingly on the basis of impressions gained from casual observation whenever the issue arises. There is no appeal to precise necessary and sufficient conditions. Speakers accept that the application of ‘bald’ depends only on the exact distribution of hairs on someone’s scalp, but vagaries of mood and perception cause them often to apply the term ‘bald’ when the distribution is exactly the same as in a previous case which they classified as ‘not bald’. When they disagree, each dogmatically insists that the other is clearly wrong. When inconsistencies are pointed out in a single speaker’s application of the term, they are denied ad hoc (‘I never said that!’, ‘His hair has grown since then!’). On Horwich’s account, ‘bald’ is not vague in the language of this community, because there are no cases in which speakers ‘are normally unwilling to apply the predicate, unwilling to deny that it applies, and confident that no further investigation could yield a decision’. But ‘bald’ is vague in the language of this community. If every speaker has about a 50% chance of dogmatically applying the term ‘bald’ to Jack and about a 50% chance of dogmatically applying the term ‘not bald’, then in the envisaged circumstances Jack is a borderline case for ‘bald’, even though no speaker recognizes him as such. Neither ‘Jack is bald’ nor ‘Jack is not bald’ is clearly true. Neither those who say ‘Jack is bald’ nor those who say ‘Jack is not bald’ know the truth of what they are saying. That is the point of characterizing borderline cases epistemically; Horwich’s non-epistemic characterization fastens onto an inessential accompaniment of vagueness.1

The members of the imagined community lack self-knowledge. They are spectacularly bad at knowing that they do not know. We are somewhat better in this respect, although obviously, inevitably and massively fallible. When one does not know whether something is the case, knowing that one does not know has survival value; it prevents rash action. The macho community may suffer for its epistemic overconfidence. In a borderline case, we know that we are not in a position to know whether Jack is bald, and do not waste time in sterile debate. Sometimes we know that we do not know whether Jack is bald because we know that we are not inclined to make a judgement either way; sometimes we are inclined to make such a judgement, but still know that we do not know, because we know that the inclination is too shaky for knowledge. We can recognize our ignorance in this way without conscious epistemological theorizing. Likewise, if one is inclined to judge that a passer-by is an Italian on the basis of her appearance, one need not be an epistemologist to reflect that, since judgements on such a basis are highly unreliable, one does not know whether she is an Italian. But the explanation of our knowledge that we do not know in borderline cases is in any case a secondary issue; they remain borderline even if we believe that we do know, for our belief is false.

On the epistemic view, we can suppose that baldness is the property of having fewer than 3,832 hairs on one’s scalp.2 Furthermore, reference supervenes on nonintentional use-and-environment properties, so for some such property π:
Necessarily, whatever has π refers to the property of having fewer than 3,832 hairs on one’s scalp;

As Schiffer notes, if we could know both (1) and (2), we could deduce that ‘bald’ refers to the property of having fewer than 3,832 hairs on one’s scalp.3 Since we already know that what ‘bald’ refers to is baldness, we could come to know that baldness is the property of having 3,832 hairs on one’s scalp, contrary to the epistemic view. Thus the view implies that we cannot know the conjunction of (1) and (2).4 What explains our ignorance? It is not the vagueness of ‘bald’, for that word is used in neither (1) nor (2); although it is mentioned in (2), that does not make (2) vague.5 In effect, I gave a brief account of our ignorance of (1) and (2) in an article. Schiffer objects on two grounds. First, that account is independent of my general theory of the ignorance that constitutes vagueness, and must be so because our ignorance of (1) and (2) does not involve vagueness, so the general theory is inadequate. Second, he finds the account of our ignorance of (1) and (2) unconvincing in itself.

Schiffer is right to be dissatisfied with the account in the article of our ignorance of (1) and (2). Although it is not false as far as it goes, it does not go far enough. For our ignorance of (1) does depend on vagueness: not vagueness in ‘bald’, of course, but vagueness in ‘refer’. It is vague whether having π is sufficient for referring to the property of having fewer than 3,832 hairs on one’s scalp. Having π is neither clearly sufficient nor clearly insufficient for having that property. The word ‘bald’ is a borderline case for the predicate ‘refers to the property of having fewer than 3,832 hairs on one’s scalp’. More generally, semantic ascent preserves vagueness. For example, since it is clear that something is bald if and only if it is in the extension of ‘bald’, ‘bald’ has the same borderline cases as ‘in the extension of “bald”’.

My general explanation of the ignorance that constitutes vagueness extends to semantic terms. Although someone may judge truly ‘Baldness is the property of having fewer than 3,832 hairs on one’s scalp’, the judgement does not express knowledge, for whatever produced a judgement in those words could very easily have done so even if the overall use of ‘bald’ had been very slightly shifted (as it could very easily have been) in such a way that it referred to the property of having fewer than 3,831 hairs on one’s scalp, in which case the judgement then made in those words would have been false. What produces the judgement does not produce true judgements reliably enough to produce knowledge. Thus we are not in a position to know that baldness is the property of having fewer than 3,832 hairs on one’s scalp.6 To extend this explanation of our non-semantic ignorance to an explanation of our semantic ignorance, note that in the envisaged counterfactual circumstances the sentence “‘Bald” refers to baldness’ naturally still commands assent (clearly, ‘bald’ refers to baldness). In those circumstances, the false judgement in the words ‘Baldness is the property of having fewer than 3,832 hairs on one’s scalp’ goes with a false judgement in the words “‘Baldness” refers to the property of having fewer than 3,832 hairs on one’s scalp’. Although someone may use the latter words to make a true judgement in the actual circumstances, the judgement does not express knowledge, for what produces it does not produce true judgements reliably enough to produce knowledge. Thus the account explains equally why we are not in a position to know that ‘baldness’ refers to the property of having fewer than 3,832 hairs on one’s scalp.
The effect of Schiffer’s challenge is to confirm the book’s original explanation of our ignorance. Horwich is sceptical about two aspects of that explanation.

First, Horwich does not see why small shifts in use should induce corresponding small shifts in reference. He is right that the postulated correspondence, although simple, natural and plausible, is not indubitable. But why should it be indubitable? In science, when we want to explain some effect, we look for simple, natural and plausible assumptions that would explain it; we do not require them to be indubitable. Their ability to explain the effect is itself a further reason to believe them, by inference to the best explanation. And what is the alternative to the postulated correspondence between shifts in use and shifts in reference? The reference of a vague term would be insensitive to most small shifts in use, but would change in large jerks as the pattern of use shifted across critical boundaries. The privileged extensions would mark out something like hidden natural kinds. Situations like the following would obtain. ‘Bald’ actually refers to the property of having fewer than 3,832 hairs on one’s scalp. If we had been as likely to apply ‘bald’ to someone with n hairs as we actually are to apply it to someone with n+100 hairs (for all n), then ‘bald’ would still have referred to the property of having fewer than 3,832 hairs on one’s scalp. But if we had been as likely to apply ‘bald’ to someone with n hairs as we actually are to apply it to someone with n+1,000 hairs (for all n), then ‘bald’ would have referred to the property of having fewer than 2,832 hairs on one’s scalp. 3,832 and 2,832 are natural boundaries of a sort; 3,732 is not. That is implausible, although not incoherent. What is implausible is the supposed naturalness of the boundaries, not their hiddenness. Of course, Horwich may offer an explanation of our ignorance compatible with the jerky hypothesis, but I argue below that he has not done so. If the only available explanation of our ignorance assumes the smooth hypothesis, that strengthens the case by inference to the best explanation for accepting the smooth hypothesis.

Second, Horwich asks why someone who makes a judgement in vague words might very easily still have made a judgement in those words even if the overall pattern of use had been slightly different. The book gives an answer to his question (p. 231). The overall use of a vague term has a sprawling quality: it involves dispositions to use the term in a wide variety of contexts. A change in my dispositions with respect to some contexts does not imply a change with respect to all. For example, if malevolent moods had made me more willing to call people ‘bald’ than they actually do, benevolent moods might not have made me less willing to call people ‘bald’ than they actually do. Moreover, interpersonal meaning supervenes on interpersonal use (and the environment); my use of a word might have been the same as my actual use even if other speakers’ use of it had been slightly different from their actual use. When I make a judgement in a given context, I might very easily still have made a judgement in the same words in that context even if other speakers’ use had been slightly different in ways such that my reference would have been different. That the overall use of a vague term has this sprawling quality is also not indubitable, but it is plausible, and we have further reason to accept it when it enables us to explain our ignorance in borderline cases, and other explanations fail.
Horwich purports to give an alternative explanation of our ignorance in borderline cases. He encodes the use of a predicate “H” in a function A(H).

[T]here are cases in which we are unwilling to confidently apply either “H” or “-H”. Moreover, since the regularity A(H) gives the full, basic explanation of the use of “H”, any decision about these borderline objects would have to be a consequence of it. But […] there appear to be no plausible auxiliary facts which don’t concern “H” but which, in conjunction with A(H), would explain such a decision. Therefore, insofar as A(H) is really the complete articulation of the basic regularity governing our use of “H”, then no matter what else is discovered, it cannot imply a confident application of either “H” or “-H” to the borderline objects. Thus we have explained our conviction that further information about the borderline objects will not help us to reach a decision about which are the ones that “H” applies to.

Of course, the further information that “H” applies to a particular borderline case or the further information that it does not would enable us to reach a decision in that case, and on Horwich’s view there is such a fact to be informed of. What is to be explained is our inability to be informed of it.

Does Horwich mean to explain our failure to decide the borderline cases at time t by the assumption that our use of “H” at t falls under the regularity A(H)? The explanation would be trivial, for the assumption includes what has to be explained; A(H) simply records our failure to decide the borderline cases, which is part of our use. Perhaps Horwich means to explain why A(H) is an equilibrium in use: if our use of “H” at t falls under A(H), then further reflection and investigation will not cause our use of “H” at a slightly later time t* to fall under a different regularity A*(H), on which “H” or “-H” would be confidently applied in the cases that were borderline at t. But Horwich has not explained even that. Whether “H” applies in a borderline case supervenes on A(H) and auxiliary facts not concerning “H”. If we could know the relevant supervenience conditional and A(H) (compare Schiffer’s (1) and (2)), we could work out whether “H” applies. On Horwich’s view, what we can’t know is the supervenience conditional (he does not deny that we can know A(H)). Why can’t we know the supervenience conditional? Horwich says only that ‘there appear to be no plausible auxiliary facts which don’t concern “H” but which, in conjunction with A(H), would explain such a decision’. But if we could know the supervenience conditional, that knowledge would explain such a decision. Presumably, Horwich counts the truth of the conditional as a fact but not a ‘plausible’ fact. That is merely to restate what has to be explained. He has not produced an alternative non-trivial explanation of our ignorance in borderline cases.

Our ignorance is not just a failure to decide. Although many speakers do not confidently apply “H” or “-H” in a given borderline case, some do. An eccentric speaker who confidently applies “H” to a borderline case that is H has a true belief; why does it not constitute knowledge? Horwich’s discussion suggests no answer.

As Horwich notes, my explanation of our ignorance does not extend automatically to cases not covered by the stipulations that wholly determine the meaning of an artificially introduced term. They are not paradigmatic borderline cases, not least because in principle they need not involve higher-order vagueness. They have a kind of cognitive transparency which might conceivably enable us to overcome the usual obstacles to knowledge. The epistemic view is not committed to the inevitability of ignorance in these special cases.
In the book (p. 213) and elsewhere, I consider default principles that might settle truth-values in such cases. Here are two simple possibilities:
When everything else is equal, an atomic predication is true.
When everything else is equal, an atomic predication is false.

Horwich agrees that “a is H” is true or false even when our attitudes to “a is H” and to “a is -H” are perfectly symmetrical. Thus default principles of some kind operate on his view too. They might be less general than DEFAULT-T and DEFAULT-F, each perhaps applicable only to a single predicate, although he offers no reason to think that there is such variation from case to case. At their most specific, default principles are simply supervenience conditionals. Presumably what Horwich finds ‘far-fetched’ is the idea that we might learn the default principles, although he offers no non-trivial explanation of our inability to learn them. I too am unsure that we can come to know them. Equally, we do not know that DEFAULT-T is false, and we do not know that DEFAULT-F is false. The epistemic view is consistent with each, and entails neither.7

If we cannot know the default principles, the problem may be that the default is truth in some kinds of case and falsity in others, cases of each kind being too close to cases of the other to enable us to discriminate between them. The explanation of our ignorance of the default principles would follow the same lines as the explanation of our ignorance in borderline cases.

Alternatively, perhaps we can know general default principles, by reflection on the concepts of truth and falsity. Even so, we may still be unable to know truth-values in particular cases. In order to apply the principles, we should need to know that everything else was equal, and we might be unable to know that. Cases of perfect symmetry might be too close to cases of slight asymmetry. Even when we make explicit stipulations, slight asymmetries in the use those stipulations caused us to make of the defined terms would tip the balance. Again, the explanation of our ignorance in these cases could be subsumed under my general explanation of our ignorance in borderline cases.
I see no special problem for the epistemic view here, but plenty of scope for further inquiry into the nature of stipulation.

Schiffer raises a problem about communication. On my view, slight differences in the use of a vague term typically make slight differences in its meaning. But different speakers use a vague term in slightly different ways. We may therefore expect what they mean by it to be slightly different too. Moreover, the principles underlying my explanation of ignorance in borderline cases seem to imply that one speaker’s belief about what another means by the vague term would not count as knowledge, even if it happened to be true. Thus one speaker could not know what another meant by a vague term, and communication would break down.
Schiffer’s worry is addressed in the book (p. 211):

Perhaps no two speakers of English match exactly in their dispositions to use ‘thin’. It does not follow that no two speakers of English mean exactly the same by ‘thin’. For what individual speakers mean by a word can be parasitic on its meaning in a public language. The dispositions of all practitioners collectively determine a sense that is available to each.8

In a footnote, Schiffer expresses scepticism about a similar line, but gives no reason for his scepticism. Does he doubt that meaning can be socially determined? I do not say that all meaning is socially determined. Schiffer’s problem is solved if, in clear cases of successful communication, meaning is determined by use (and the environment) at the level of a community that includes both the speaker and the hearer.

The notion of a speech community is itself vague. What are the spatial and temporal boundaries of my present speech community? Some words differ in meaning between Britain and America; some words have changed in meaning over the last thirty years. A sorites paradox threatens the idea that meaning is determined by use in a community that extends over both space and time. But the paradox can be solved. Consider a particular episode of successful communication. The speaker says ‘Jack is bald’. The hearer thinks to himself ‘She said that Jack is bald’. ‘Say’ and ‘speech community’ vary slightly in content from context to context. In the context of the hearer’s thought, the speaker at the time of speaking and the hearer at the time of hearing count as members of the same community; what people count as saying in this context depends on which speech community they count as members of in this context. In this context, the hearer’s thought is true, and can even constitute an expression of knowledge. Of course, if the speaker and hearer used ‘bald’ in radically different ways, they might not count as members of the same speech community for the purpose of determining its meaning; but they can count as members of the same speech community for this purpose even if they use it in slightly different ways. The sorites paradox does not arise, because in a given context not all slight differences in use imply sameness in speech community: the implication holds only for some slight differences that are salient in that context.

The issue of communication arises equally for non-epistemic views of vagueness. Typically, they claim that the connection between meaning and use is cognitively more transparent than it is on the epistemic view; they have even more reason than the epistemic view has to accept that slight differences in the use of a vague term make slight differences in its meaning. For example, suppose that the meaning of ‘bald’ were given by a function B from natural numbers to real numbers in the interval [0,1], where B(n) is the degree to which ‘bald’ applies to someone with n hairs, conceived as something like the probability that a normal speaker would be willing to apply the term ‘bald’ to someone with n hairs in normal conditions of observation. Then a slight difference in these probabilities would constitute a slight difference in use; it would change B to a slightly different function B*. That would constitute a slight difference in meaning. How then is communication possible? Non-epistemic views of vagueness too could answer the question by appeal to the social determination of meaning.

Is communication possible when speaker and hearer do not belong to the same speech community? They can still know that they mean at least roughly the same by a word. That is enough for most practical purposes. Again, this answer is independent of the epistemic view of vagueness.
Schiffer’s final objection is that the epistemic account conflicts with the role of intention in demonstrative reference:

my intentions in uttering ‘she’ determine the person to whom I’m referring. In this case, of course, I must have some way of thinking of that person other than as “she”. I must, it would seem, have some way of identifying my referent, some way of picking her out.

Schiffer objects that when one uses the demonstrative ‘here’ with ordinary vagueness, one has no way of identifying or picking out the sharply demarcated region to which one is referring, on the epistemic view. I am not sure what Schiffer means by a way of ‘identifying’ or ‘picking out’ the referent. It would be unreasonable to require the speaker to be able to refer non-demonstratively to the thing in question. Nor need the speaker know how to trace its boundaries in practice (consider ‘this galaxy’). We should like an answer to the question ‘Why does the demonstrative refer to x?’. Presumably, a central part of the answer will often be that the speaker is perceptually attending to x. But Schiffer gives no reason to suppose that one can perceptually attend to x only if one can locate the exact boundaries of x. ‘Perceptually attend’ is a vague expression; it is vague just what information link is needed between me and a point of space for that point to be part of the region to which I am perceptually attending. The epistemic view applies to the vagueness of ‘perceptually attend’. I can perceptually attend to the region with exact boundaries b even if no one is in a position to know that I am perceptually attending to the region with exact boundaries b; what I know is that I am looking at this region here. The epistemic view is consistent with all reasonable constraints on the role of intention in demonstrative reference.

Some writers on vagueness, such as C. S. Peirce and Crispin Wright, characterize borderline cases in terms of the conflict rather than absence of opinion. Neither is essential; what matters is the absence of knowledge. ↩︎

Schiffer says ‘Williamson recognizes that there is no such thing as the property of being bald, for occurrences of “bald” can express different properties in different contexts of utterance’. I recognize the point about contextual variation, but the definite description ‘the property of being bald’ as used in a particular context of utterance can still denote a unique property. ↩︎

Schiffer formulates (1) and (2) in terms of the inner representations of a single subject. This makes no difference for present purposes. I use ‘refers to’ where Schiffer uses ‘means’ because there is a salient sense of the latter in which: (a) the reference of ‘bald’ varies contextually while its linguistic meaning remains fixed; (b) ‘means’ creates an intensional context unsuited to Schiffer’s argument. ↩︎

If we can refer to a property in one way, we can refer to it in many cognitively inequivalent ways. ‘π’ should be read as though it abbreviated a specification in nonintentional use-and-environment terms of the relevant property. ↩︎
For simplicity, I assume that words are not individuated semantically. ↩︎
See R. M. Sainsbury, ‘Easy Possibilities’, Philosophy and Phenomenological Research 57 (1997): 907–19, for further discussion of this proposal. ↩︎
In the book (p. 208) and elsewhere I have expressed a tentative preference for DEFAULT-F, for admittedly inconclusive reasons. That preference is unimportant here. ↩︎
See Sainsbury, op. cit., for a development of this thought. ↩︎

works.title: Replies to Commentators
passages: Terry Horgan argues that the epistemic view of vagueness implies that some facts about supervenience have no imaginable explanation, a consequence which he rejects as intolerably mysterious. On closer inspection, his objection turns out to threaten the epistemic view only to the extent to which it threatens the view that there are semantic facts. Not only epistemicists should reject his assumptions.

It is intuitively plausible that there is no semantic difference without a non-semantic difference. If two possible situations are the same in all non-semantic respects, then they are the same in all semantic respects too.1 Why the supervenience claim should be so plausible is by no means obvious. But it is plausible; I will grant its truth. On which aspects of the non-semantic does the semantic depend? In [1994] I proposed the following as a first approximation (p. 206):
If an expression e is used in a possible situation s in the same way as an expression f is used in a possible situation t, then e has the same meaning in s as f has in t.

I noted that # needs refinement, for instance to take account of the environment as a constitutive factor in meaning and to clarify the notion ‘used in the same way’; ignore such refinements for present purposes. Let an expression e be used in a way W with meaning M in our present situation; W is maximally specific and specifiable in non-semantic terms. Then # implies this:
Necessarily, any expression used in way W has meaning M.

What kind of meaning does the epistemic view attribute to vague expressions? Horgan’s assumption that the postulated meanings embody sharp boundaries is over-simple, for on the epistemic view a vague expression can express different boundaries in different contexts of utterance while its linguistic meaning remains fixed; ‘here’ is an obvious example (Williamson [1994]: 215).2 The number of grains needed for ‘heap’ to apply may likewise vary with context. However, this misinterpretation is not the focus of Horgan’s argument. For simplicity, treat the relevant contextual features as part of the way in which an expression is used on that occasion. On that understanding, the epistemic view postulates truths of this form:
Necessarily, any expression used in vague way W has sharp boundary B.

Horgan objects that we cannot imagine what could explain #b; either it has no explanation, or its explanation is unimaginable. Regarding both alternatives as repugnant to good sense, he denies the postulated sharp boundary.

To say that an expression e has a sharp boundary is just to say picturesquely that e is true or false of each thing.3 Thus #b in effect conjoins many more specific supervenience theses of these two forms:
Necessarily, any expression used in vague way W is true of everything of type T.
Necessarily, any expression used in vague way W is true of nothing of type T.

‘Type T’ summarizes the precisely described non-semantic features relevant to expressions used in way W: for example, the precisely described state of a candidate bald man’s scalp. To explain #b is to explain a vast conjunction whose conjuncts are the appropriate instances of #c and #d. What Horgan finds puzzling is less the conjunction as a whole than some particular conjuncts of it: those for which type T constitutes a borderline case. For definiteness, we may therefore assume that the explanandum is such a borderline instance of #c (#d raises exactly parallel problems).

Many other instances of #c are usually taken to be unproblematic: those for which type T constitutes a clear case. For example, W is the way in which we actually use ‘heap’, and objects of type T are paradigmatic heaps. Such clear instances of #c are common ground between the epistemic view and most of its rivals. What explains the clear instances of #c? Horgan gives no hint of an answer. If every sentence to which 90% of speakers of the language assent were true, then perhaps we could provide such an explanation; but the generalization is obviously false. What law of semantics could do the explanatory work? Horgan’s considerations are quite insensitive to the difference between the borderline instances of #c and the clear ones. Any doubt which they cast on the former they cast on the latter too. Suppose that an unknown law of semantics does explain the clear instances of #c; why think that it could not also explain borderline instances of #c, unless one already thinks on independent grounds that they are not true?4

Horgan’s argument does not tell specifically against the epistemic view of vagueness; it tells quite generally against any reasonable version of the view that there are semantic facts which supervene on non-semantic facts.5 Indirectly, it tells against the view that there are any semantic facts. Indeed, Horgan’s own view of vagueness in his [1995] implies that really there are no semantic facts.

How strong is Horgan’s argument from supervenience? Why shouldn’t the regress of explanations end in instances of #c and #d? On Horgan’s view, we should expect the regress to end in a tightly knit bundle of fundamental laws, in which such instances have no place. The fundamental laws will be framed in a restricted theoretical vocabulary. How can such laws explain anything framed in a less restricted vocabulary? Bridge laws will be needed to connect the two vocabularies. Instances of #c and #d are embryonic bridge laws, connecting the non-semantic notion of way W with the semantic notions of truth and falsity. The variety of ordinary notions absent from the postulated fundamental laws implies a corresponding variety of bridge laws.6 To deem such a variety implausible, and yet to demand explanations of ordinary truths, is to prejudge the issue in favour of Horgan’s eliminativist metaphysics. Anyone inclined to think that there are semantic facts has reason to reject Horgan’s explanatory demands.

Can we know bridge laws of the forms #c and #d? If we could, and we could also in principle survey the way in which a vague expression is used, then we could in principle find out whether it applied to things of a given type. The trouble is that #c and #d employ a vague notion of truth for linguistic items, ‘true of’. It is vague whether ‘heap’ is true of a borderline candidate. This notion satisfies the principle that if a predicate e refers to a property π, then e is true of a thing x if and only if x has π; but ‘refers’ is vague too. We can know that ‘is a heap’ refers to a property π only under a vague description of π, such as ‘heaphood’. That will not help us to know an instance of #c or #d in a borderline case. The obstacle to knowing such an instance is simply a special case of the general obstacle to vague knowledge in a borderline case (Williamson [1994]: 230-234). The appeal to use is an attempt to circumvent first-order ignorance by semantic ascent; it is blocked by second-order vagueness.
Mario Gomez-Torrente raises three difficulties for my epistemic account. I deal with each in turn.

If vagueness does not essentially depend on ignorance, then it should be harmless to imagine a speaker who is omniscient in all relevant vague respects. I argued that ‘The hypothesis of an omniscient speaker gives us a [… ] way to appreciate the difficulty of thinking through a non-epistemic view of vagueness’ ([1994]: 199). The thought experiment was not presented or intended as a knockdown refutation of the non-epistemic view; nevertheless, I continue to think that it has some weight. It involves continually asking a series of cooperative non-colluding omniscient speakers ‘Is this a heap?’ as one removes grain after grain. Each time, they can answer ‘Yes’, ‘No’ or anything else. In the relevant version of the experiment, they are instructed to be conservative, i.e. to use any discretion they have to minimize the number of times they answer ‘Yes’. I argued that they would all stop answering ‘Yes’ at the same point, since otherwise at least one of them would not have been conservative. Even if the point at which they all stop answering ‘Yes’ is not the point at which they all start answering ‘No’, it is just the kind of hidden boundary (perhaps a higher-order boundary) which the non-epistemic view will not countenance.

Gomez-Torrente objects that the term ‘conservative’ is itself vague: ‘if there are no hidden boundaries of conservativeness, they [the omniscient speakers] may set the boundaries at many different points, within some limits’. If so, they may use their discretion to set the boundaries of ‘conservative’ in a way which does not minimize the number of times they answer ‘Yes’. Would that violate the instruction ‘Be conservative’? Gomez-Torrente argues that it would not, on the grounds that to make the instruction self-applicable is to make it unintelligible: ‘they cannot be expected, any more than we can, to understand an instruction in a particular way before they have understood it in some way’. But to know the linguistic meaning of an expression is not to set its boundary on a particular occasion; a sentence with a given vague meaning can express different propositions on different occasions. The omniscient speakers certainly know the linguistic meaning of the sentence ‘Use any discretion you have to minimize the number of times you answer “Yes”’. They still have to set boundaries to ‘discretion’, but if ‘they may set the boundaries at many different points, within some limits’, then to do so in a way which would not minimize the number of times they answer ‘Yes’ would clearly violate the instruction, given the linguistic meaning of the sentence by which it was expressed. Thus the challenge to think through a coherent non-epistemic view of the thought experiment has not been met.

If one prefers, one can dispense with notions like ‘conservative’ in an alternative version of the thought experiment. Let the omniscient speakers use their discretion as they wish. Suppose that they do not all stop answering ‘Yes’ at the same point. Nevertheless, on reasonable non-epistemic views all omniscient speakers will answer ‘Yes’ at some early stages when a paradigm heap is present, however many one asks. Consider the first point at which some omniscient speakers stop answering ‘Yes’, as the number of speakers asked goes to infinity. It is just the kind of hidden boundary (perhaps a higher-order boundary) which the non-epistemic view will not countenance.
Gomez-Torrente discusses the relation between ordinary vague terms and the terms of natural science. He pretends that we have empirical evidence for the following pair of hypotheses:
For all x, if x is a bald man by age a, then x has gene G.
For all x, if x is not a bald man by age a, then x does not have gene G.

Now a man who does not have gene G can shave all his hair off by age a. If (A) is a serious scientific hypothesis, he would not thereby refute (A). Thus ‘bald’ in (A) and (B) should be understood dispositionally; one is bald if one is predisposed to have one’s hair fall out. The number of hairs on one’s head does not determine whether one is bald in this sense. We might even decide that baldness is essentially possession of gene G. ‘Bald’ in this sense is a natural kind term.7 It poses no more difficulty to the epistemic view than does ‘water’ or ‘gold’. Most of our ignorance of baldness would be ordinary scientific ignorance.8 None of this implies that we can find out whether a borderline case is bald in the ordinary sense.

In general, a vague term can unexpectedly pick up the boundaries of a natural kind. Our ignorance may then be remediable by ordinary scientific means. No scientific remedy is available in the central cases of vagueness. The epistemic account does not entail that such a remedy is absolutely impossible; it says that we have no idea how to find one, and no reason to think that one exists.9

Our ignorance in borderline cases can be explained by appeal to margin for error principles (Williamson [1994]: 216–247). For example, when ‘bald’ is understood in the ordinary way, not as in the previous section, we have for all n:
If it is known that a man with n hairs is bald, then a man with n+1 hairs is bald (for all n).

The idea behind (1) is this. When I assert ‘A man with n hairs is bald’, my assertion is knowledgeable only if my disposition to utter the sentence would not easily be manifested in contexts in which it would express a false proposition. But if ‘bald’ does not apply to a man with n+1 hairs, then I might easily have uttered the sentence even if ‘bald’ had meant something very slightly different and did not apply to a man with n hairs, so that the sentence did express a false proposition, for the vagueness of ‘bald’ implies that particular utterances of the sentence are not perfectly sensitive to the whole pattern of use in virtue of which ‘bald’ means what it does. Hence my assertion is knowledgeable only if ‘bald’ does apply to a man with n+1 hairs. Thus if a man with n hairs is bald and one with n+1 hairs is not, I am not in a position to know that a man with n hairs is bald.

The argument turns on the vagueness of ‘bald’. But ‘known to be bald’, ‘known to be known to be bald’, … are also vague, so they should saistfy margin for error principles too. Gomez-Torrente suggests that this generates a new sorites paradox. His argument can be symbolized as follows. Let ‘B(n)’ and ‘Kn’ abbreviate ‘A man with n hairs is bald’ and a sequence of n occurrences of ‘it is known that’ respectively. A margin for error principle for the predicate KmB(x) says this:
According to Gomez-Torrente, a man with no hairs is not only bald but known to be bald, known to be known to be bald, …. Hence:

Given (1(m)) for all m and (2(k)) for fixed k, one can prove B(k+1). For one can prove Kk+1−jB(j) for 0≤j≤k+1 by mathematical induction on j. The basis (j=0) is simply (2(k)). The induction hypothesis is Kk+1−jB(j). It combines with (1(k−j+1)) for n=j to give Kk−jB(j+1), as required to complete the induction. Now put j=k+1. Thus the assumptions imply that a man with k+1 hairs is bald, whatever k is.

What is Gomez-Torrente’s argument for (2(k))? He calls the proposition that a man with no hairs is bald an ‘especially transparent proposition that we might even be tempted to call analytic’. This might explain how it is known that a man with no hairs is bald, but does not directly explain how it is known that it is known that a man with no hairs is bald. After all, it is not analytic that it is known that a man with no hairs is bald. It is far from obvious that (2(k)) is actually true for all k, for it is far from obvious that all the iterations of knowledge have actually been realized. If a proposition is known only if it is thought, and (2(k−1)) has not been thought, then (2(k)) is not true. Gomez-Torrente might reply that we can make (2(k)) true for any particular k just by thinking the relevant propositions: that would not make a man with k hairs bald. But merely thinking a true proposition is not in general sufficient for knowing it; if (2(k−1)) is true, why should thinking so make (2(k)) true? To make (2(k)) true for large k, we must know (2(k−1)), which is to know that the complex empirical proposition (2(k−2)) is known. If each stage in this process involves a slight loss of transparency, we may be unable to make (2(k)) true for large k. Gomez-Torrente has not provided a compelling argument for (2(k)).

Consider a formal model. For each natural number i, let si be a situation in which B(n) is true just in case n<i; i is the cut-off point for baldness. Let sj be accessible from si (epistemically possible from the standpoint of si) just in case |i−j|≤1. Treat K like □ in possible-worlds semantics: KA is true in a situation si if and only if A is true in every situation accessible from si. Thus the accessibility relation specifies the margin for error. Our actual situation is si for some fairly large i; no situation other than si−1, si and si+1 is actually epistemically possible. One easily shows by induction on m that KmB(n) is true in si if and only if m+n<i. Thus every instance of (1(m)) is true in every situation, and (2(k)) is true in si if and only if k+1<i. Whatever the cut-off point for baldness, (2(k)) fails for some k. If one doubts that this does justice to the special paradigmatic status of the proposition that a man with no hairs is bald, one can delete s0 (the situation in which not even a man with no hairs is bald) from the model. B(0) is then true in every situation in the new model; consequently, so is (2(k)) for each k. Nevertheless, when n>0, KmB(n) is true in si if and only if m+n<i. Thus an instance of (1(m)) is true in every situation when n>0, but fails in si when n=0 and m+1<i.

The failure of (1(m)) in the cropped model does not undermine the idea of margins for error, which is built into the accessibility relation of the model even without s0. In both models, this margin for error principle holds for all situations si and sj and all replacements for ‘A’:
If KA is true in si and |i−j|≤1 then A is true in sj.

(3) is more fundamental than (1). What fails in the cropped model is only the deduction of (1) from (3). But (3) is sufficient to explain our ignorance of cut-off points. If the cut-off point for baldness were known, K[B(n)&∼B(n+1)] would be true. But (3) implies that K[B(n)&∼B(n+1)] is true in si only if B(n)&∼B(n+1) is true in both si and si+1, which is impossible, for B(n) is true in si only if n<i, in which case n+1<i+1, so B(n+1) is true in si+1, so ∼B(n+1) is not true in si+1. What (3) illustrates is that the margins for error primarily relevant to vagueness are on a semantic dimension; si and si+1 differ in the cut-off point for baldness. The argument for (1) reflected this by appealing to small differences in the meaning of ‘bald’, not to small differences in the scalp of the person in view. If one wanted to accept (2(k)) for all k, one could do so on the cropped model, deny (1(k)) and still retain the margin for error principle (3) in the underlying epistemic explanation of our ignorance.10
Michael Tye worries that the epistemicist explanation of our ignorance

seems to threaten our knowledge of the meanings of vague terms. How can I know the meaning of the word ‘thin’, if there is a relevantly similar situation in which the word has a slightly different meaning even though I do not recognize that any shift in meaning has occurred?

We know that ‘thin’ means thin. If our dispositions to use ‘thin’ had been very slightly different, it would have meant something very slightly different, say thin*. But if ‘thin’ had meant thin*, we should not have believed falsely that it meant thin; we should have believed truly that it meant thin*. The same factors would determine both its meaning and the content of our belief as to its meaning. Such a counterfactual situation does not threaten our knowledge that ‘thin’ means thin.

Does the argument trivialize knowledge of meaning? Consider an analogy. A shape is projected onto a screen. I can point and say ‘The screen shows that shape’. By ordinary standards, I know the proposition expressed. If I know that the same slide is also being projected onto another screen, I know that the second screen shows that shape [pointing at the shape on the first screen]; it is no harder to know that the first screen shows that shape. Nevertheless, in some sense I know only roughly what shape the screen shows. My eyesight is far from perfect, and I should not notice if a slightly different shape were substituted. In a similar sense we know only roughly what our words mean. We should not notice if the meaning changed very slightly.

The point is independent of the epistemic view of vagueness. On any reasonable view, gradual changes in meaning can occur. Suppose that for all n ‘n grains make a heap’ has the semantic status which ‘n+1 grains make a heap’ had last century, whatever that status is. The assumption that no semantic change had occurred would imply that for all n ‘n grains make a heap’ has the same semantic status as ‘n+1 grains make a heap’, which generates a sorites paradox. An undetectable semantic change has occurred. In this harmless sense, we know only roughly what ‘heap’ means; still we know that it means heap. Likewise, we know only roughly what shape the screen shows; still we know that it shows that shape [pointing].

Perhaps I can discriminate the present shape S from the shapes on all the other slides in the projectionist’s box when they are projected. I may even have looked at the slides in advance, and checked that no other slide has a shape on it anything like S. If so, I have a local capacity to recognize S, which I shall lose as soon as he acquires a slide with a shape on it indiscriminably different from S. But the mere possibility of such a slide is compatible with my local capacity to recognize S. Similarly, we have a local capacity to recognize the meaning M of a vague word ‘M’ if our language does not in fact contain a word with a meaning indiscriminably different from M, even though it could have contained such a term (Williamson [1994]: 234-237). Tye asks:

Why should our ability to know where the precise boundaries lie in borderline cases (given arguendo that there are such boundaries) be undermined by the mere possibility of slight shifts in meaning in vague terms?

There is a subtle difference. The possibility that does not undermine our local capacity to recognize M is the possibility of a word other than ‘M’ having a meaning indiscriminably different from M. The possibility that does undermine our knowledge of the boundary of ‘M’ is the possibility of ‘M’ itself having a meaning indiscriminably different from M. The difference is like that between the possibility of a new slide showing a shape indiscriminably different from S and the possibility of the original slide showing such a shape. Why should the difference matter? If our language does not in fact contain a word with a meaning very similar to M, then there is a straightforwardly detectable difference between our language as it actually is and our language as it would have been had it contained a word other than ‘M’ with a meaning indiscriminably different from M. The latter either has a new word not in our language as it actually is or assigns an old word a meaning quite different from its actual one. That counterfactual situation is not epistemically possible. In contrast, there is no detectable difference between our language as it actually is and our language as it would have been if ‘M’ had had a meaning indiscriminably different from M. That counterfactual situation is epistemically possible. It undermines our knowledge of the boundary of ‘M’. It does not undermine our local capacity to recognize M, for in it we do not misattribute M to ‘M’; we do not attribute M at all, just because ‘M’ does not mean M.

The epistemic view is consistent with the knowledge that ‘thin’ means thin. It is not consistent with a capacity to discriminate the meaning of ‘thin’ from every other possible meaning. Just in that sense it implies that we do not know exactly what ‘thin’ means; but it was never plausible to attribute such a capacity to ourselves.
I thank all three commentators for their remarks, which raise a variety of significant issues about the epistemic view of vagueness.

The semantic here includes intentional psychology: the difference between having a belief and lacking it counts as a semantic difference. Thus if ‘possible’ in the supervenience claim means metaphysically possible, then the claim implies (given the modal logic S5 that an extreme Cartesian view on which differences in thought content do not supervene on anything non-semantic is metaphysically impossible, not just false. To avoid this consequence, a more restrictive notion of possibility (e.g. nomological possibility) might be employed. My reply to Horgan does not depend on a particular resolution of this issue. ↩︎

Gomez-Torrente’s attribution to the epistemicist of the view that ‘given any scale of precision relevant to the question whether it applies or not, every predicate has associated with it a sharp cut-off point in that scale between cases in which it applies and cases in which it does not apply’ would involve a similar misinterpretation if the association between predicate and cut-off point were supposed to be context-independent. ↩︎
Variants on ‘true of’ and ‘false of’ are needed for some grammatical categories, but the underlying point is the same. ↩︎
This kind of argument is elaborated in Williamson 1996. ↩︎
An unreasonable version of the view against which Horgan’s argument may not tell is one which embodies a crude consensus theory of truth. ↩︎

In his paper, Horgan imagines an explanation of the exact moment of onset of an avalanche on the basis of the laws of physics, which he regards as unproblematic even though in practice we cannot know the initial conditions in sufficient detail. Since ‘moment of onset of the avalanche’ is itself vague, the explanation would involve bridge laws of the kind he finds unproblematic. ↩︎

See Hart [1991–2] (discussed in Williamson [1994]: 213) for an ingenious argument that ‘heap’ is a natural kind term whose boundary we can identify. The argument does not generalize to ‘large heap’. ↩︎
Even ‘has gene G’ is vague in principle (imagine someone whose genetic structure has been massively disrupted by radiation). Such vagueness will transfer across (A) and (B) to ‘is a bald man’. ↩︎
Williamson [1996] discusses the relation between vague predicates and (less vague) scientific ones in more detail. ↩︎
I discuss examples in which margin for error principles like (1) fail but those like (3) still hold in [1994]: 233–234. For more on formal models like those in the text see [1994]: 270–275. ↩︎
For other points raised by Tye’s reply see footnote 2 and the text to footnote 11 of Williamson [1997]. ↩︎
