Then it might be a convention in a particular community that in normal contexts one should utter s only if one knows £(s). Such a convention of knowledgeableness in £ might even be part of what it is for £ to be the language of that community. This convention in £ is an obvious variant on the convention of truthfulness in £ used by David Lewis to define what it is for £ to be the language of a community: “To be truthful in £ is to act in a certain way: to try never to utter any sentences of £ that are not true in £. Thus it is to avoid uttering any sentence of £ unless one believes it to be true in £” (1983, 167, from Lewis 1970). Of course, the account of what it is for £ to be the language of a community must somehow take into account the possibility that speech acts other than assertion can be performed in £ (Lewis 1983, 172). The shift from conventions of truthfulness to conventions of knowledgeableness also has repercussions in the methodology of interpretation. The appropriate principle of charity will give high marks to interpretations on which speakers tend to assert what they know, rather than to those on which they tend to assert what is true, or even what is reasonable for them to believe. ↩︎

Brandom 1983 gives an interesting account of the role of testimony and inference in the social practice of assertion; however, it is based on a notion of justification too generic to distinguish assertion from the other speech acts envisaged in the text. Craig 1990 attempts to explain the concept of knowledge in terms of the need for such a practice, but the knowledge account is not an immediate consequence. ↩︎

“[T]he essential character of the assertoric use of language lies in its availability for communicating, in the sense of transmitting knowledge about the subject matter of assertions” (McDowell 1980, 128; compare Evans 1982, 310). ↩︎
‘Normal circumstances’ adverts to the hearer’s knowledge that the speaker asserted that P, the speaker’s lack of a reputation for unreliability, and so on. ↩︎

Obedience to a command may also require an appropriate causal connection between the command and the action; if I do not hear the command to halt, but halt anyway, there is a sense in which I have not obeyed the command. Similarly, if I know that P and assert that P, but the asserting is causally independent of the knowing, then something is wrong with the asserting. Perhaps what is wrong can be derived from the knowledge account. ↩︎

works.title: How much common belief is necessary for a convention?
passages: How much common belief is necessary for a convention?

We study Bayesian coordination games in which players choose actions conditional on the realization of their respective signals. Due to differential information, the players do not have common knowledge that a particular game is being played. However, they do have common beliefs with specified probabilities concerning their environment. In our framework, any equilibrium set of rules must be simple enough so that the actions of all players are common belief with probability 1 at every state. Common belief with probability close to 1 will not do. Journal of Economic Literature Classification Numbers: C72, D82.

Coordination problems come in many forms. A case of particular interest to students of norms and conventions is that in which the payoff function of the coordination game depends on the state of Nature. In such an environment, the possibility of conditioning one’s actions on some signal of the state of Nature adds an extra dimension to the coordination problem and makes it a more accurate representation of the problem of day-to-day interaction in which individuals face a variety of coordination problems determined by the state of Nature. In such an environment, the problem becomes one of coordinating on the most advantageous set of rules of action, where each player’s rule of action maps a possible realization of his signal to an action.

If the players have perfect information, the problem can be reduced to the solution of each one-shot coordination game for each realization of the state of Nature. Since in general the payoffs vary across states, the players will be made better off by coordinating on strategies which utilize their information concerning the true state. However, if the players have imperfect information, constraints will be placed on the rules of action which can be sustained as an equilibrium. We shall examine how much of the information of the individual players may be utilized in the equilibrium of a Bayesian coordination game. If the players, taken individually, are capable of making fine distinctions across the states of the world, and an equilibrium prescribes strategies which depend on such fine distinctions, we can regard such an equilibrium as being “intricate” relative to the information of individual players. In contrast, if an equilibrium involves strategies which do not utilize to any great extent the private information of individual players, then we may informally dub such an equilibrium “simple” relative to the information of individual players.

This question is of more than just passing interest, since many of the conventions around us tend to be simple relative to the set of signals on which we could condition our actions. For example, it could be argued that our conventions concerning appropriate dress are too rigid relative to rules which are Pareto superior. Why isn’t there a convention that jackets and ties should be worn by men to dinner unless the temperature is above a threshold level, in which case all the men turn up in T-shirts?

On a less frivolous note, the archetypal convention is that of language and the meaning we associate with sentences. Lewis’ (1969) account of the use of language as an equilibrium in a coordination game has been very influential among philosophers. In this context, it is an intuitively appealing principle that the meaning of sentences should not vary with, say, the season or day of the week. For example, it is difficult for us to picture a language in which the sentence “the cat is on the mat” means that the cat is on the mat, on weekdays, but means that the cherry is on the tree, on weekends. However, if we take at face value the claim that language is merely a coordination device, we are hard put to give a quick rebuttal to such oddities. Why are such perverse languages not observed in practice?

We provide one possible answer. We show that for a wide class of coordination problems with smooth action sets, the optimizing behavior of individuals eliminates all rules of action except those which are “very simple” relative to the information of individual players, in the sense that only the public signals matter for equilibrium, and any equilibrium action is common belief with probability 1 at every state. Common belief with probability close to 1 will not do. Formally, a convention can be sustained only if it prescribes actions which are measurable on the meet of the individuals’ information partitions.

In pointing to this connection between common belief and equilibrium, our result has some bearing on the debate on the robustness of equilibrium to small departures from common knowledge. Rubinstein’s (1989) example of the electronics mail game demonstrates in a striking way how equilibrium may change when the hierarchy of iterated knowledge is truncated at some high, but finite degree. For Rubinstein, iterated knowledge of high degree constitutes a situation “close” to common knowledge.

An alternative dimension in which to relax common knowledge is to replace knowledge by belief and to restore the unbounded hierarchy. In an important contribution, Monderer and Samet (1989) explore this approach and note its implications for game theory. In particular, they show that if players are ϵ-optimizers, then for most states, equilibrium behavior implied by common belief with high probability approximates behavior implied by common knowledge. Our contribution to this debate is to strike a cautionary note for the program of supplanting common knowledge by common belief. For the coordination games in this paper, if the players are fully rational, then no amount of common belief (short of the maximum) will do as a substitute for common knowledge.

This conclusion places our result on the simplicity of equilibria under sharper focus. On the face of it, we have the somewhat paradoxical result that full rationality leads to simple rules, while ϵ-rationality admits complex ones. As for the question of how reasonable ϵ-rationality is in this context, the answer must depend on the particular game under scrutiny. However, if behavior motivated by ϵ-rationality differs radically from the behavior motivated by full rationality, then the reasons for this difference ought to be of interest to game theorists. Thus, we may be justified in regarding Monderer and Samet’s result as a starting point in the investigation of the role of common belief in games rather than the last word on this subject.

Our discussion is also closely related to the question of when a correlated equilibrium in a convex combination of Nash equilibria (Forges, 1990; Cripps, 1993). This is so, since in the special case of our framework when the payoffs do not depend on the state, an equilibrium of the Bayesian game corresponds to a correlated equilibrium of the one-shot game with the same payoffs. If every Bayesian equilibrium involves constant (i.e., state-independent) strategies, then every correlated equilibrium must be a Nash equilibrium. Neyman (1991) has used the notion of a potential of a game (introduced by Monderer and Shapley, 1988) to show that if a game has a smooth and strictly concave potential, then there is a unique correlated equilibrium. Among other things, this implies that Bayesian equilibrium strategies of such games must be constant.

Neyman’s argument is of interest to us, since for the standard examples of our framework, developments of Neyman’s result could be used as an alternative to our argument to derive the results reported here. We find this a very interesting and satisfying coincidence, since the two arguments rest on very different constructions. We shall return to this point later in the paper. For now, it suffices to say that, although it is an open question as to whether Neyman’s result can be used to prove our main theorem, the typical cases dealt with in our framework can be tackled by a suitable modification of Neyman’s result. Accordingly, the emphasis in our discussion will be on the insights and interpretations offered by our argument for the simplicity of equilibria.

The setting for our general argument is a coordination game with n players, each with action set A where A is a closed interval of the real numbers. We denote by ai the action of player i, and by a the vector of actions (a1,a2,…,an). Associated with this game is a state space Ω, with a typical element ω. We shall assume that Ω has a countable number of elements. There is a probability distribution ϕ over Ω which assigns positive weight to all states. Each player has an information partition over Ω. We denote by 𝒫i the partition of player i, and by Pi(ω) the element of 𝒫i containing ω.

In what follows, it will be useful to draw on the terminology of types (Harsanyi, 1967). Each element of 𝒫i indexed by i has the interpretation of a type of player i. We define the set of types of player i to consist of ordered pairs (P,i), where P∈𝒫i. Let Ti denote the set of types of player i. Since Ω is countable, each player has a countable number of possible types.
The strategy of player i is a function

which maps each type of player i to an action. Alternatively, we could define a strategy to be a function mapping each state ω to an action, with the proviso that the strategy be measurable on the partition 𝒫i. It will be convenient to use both notions of a strategy below. We denote by si(ω) the action of player i at ω, and by si(t) the action of type t of player i.

We now turn to the payoffs. We will denote by ui(a,ω) the payoff of player i at state ω given actions a. Rather than tying down ui to any specific functional form, we will impose a general condition on these payoffs, consonant with our aim of investigating coordination problems. For this purpose, define

In other words, Mi(ω) is the least upper bound on the actions of i’s opponents which player i believes possible at state ω. The greatest lower bound mi(ω) is defined analogously. Thus, at state ω, player i believes that other players have chosen actions in the interval [mi(ω),Mi(ω)]. We consider payoff functions which satisfy the following condition on the best reply of player i at state ω.
(CC) If ai is optimal at ω and mi(ω)=Mi(ω), then ai=mi(ω)=Mi(ω). If ai is optimal at ω and mi(ω)<Mi(ω), then mi(ω)<ai<Mi(ω).

The “CC” stands for “convex combination.” This condition stipulates that a player choose a strict convex combination of the actions of his opponents that he believes to be possible given his information. The force of condition (CC) is that this convex combination be strict. No player wants to be an “outlier,” and there is an incentive to conform to some nontrivial average. Our example in Section 2 exhibits payoffs which are instances of (CC). As mentioned earlier, it is not known at the time of this writing what relation holds between condition (CC) and the existence of a smooth and strictly concave potential. This question would be of independent interest and deserves further investigation.

The partition generated by this relation is the coarsest partition on which player i’s strategy can be defined. If this partition is fine relative to 𝒫i, player i’s strategy is utilizing much of i’s private information. If this partition is coarse relative to 𝒫i, the equilibrium is a simple one in which player i’s private information is not being used in equilibrium. Let us have the following definition.
Definition. An element C is a conditioning event for player i in the equilibrium (s1,s2,…,sn) if C is an element of the partition generated by ≡i.

We shall also carry over the formal definitions of belief and common belief given in the previous section. Bri(E) is the event that player i believes E with degree r, and common belief of event C is defined in terms of the sequence C0,C1,C2,…, suitably modified to include n players (see Monderer and Samet, 1989). Since the prior distribution ϕ assigns positive weight to all states, belief with probability 1 coincides with knowledge in our framework. Accordingly, common belief with probability 1 coincides with common knowledge. We will appeal to the following well-known sufficient condition for common knowledge. Recall that the meet of a set of partitions is the finest partition which is at least as coarse as all the partitions in the set.
Lemma 1. Event E is common belief with degree 1 at ω if there is an event C in the meet of the partitions {𝒫i} such that ω∈C⊆E.

Aumann (1976) and Bacharach (1985) provide proofs of this result. Brandenburger and Dekel (1987) examine common belief with probability 1 in a more general setting. Following Monderer and Samet (1989), we say that an event E is evident if E is common belief with degree 1 whenever the true state is in E. We can then state the main result of this paper.
Theorem 3. If C is a conditioning event for some player, then C is evident.
In other words, if si is an equilibrium strategy for player i, then si is constant on each element of the meet. This theorem has the following immediate corollary.
Corollary. At any state, the equilibrium action of any player is common belief with probability 1.

Theorem 3 and its corollary provide a precise answer to the question of how intricate a convention can be. Conventions must be simple enough so that the actions of all players are common belief with probability 1. Common belief with probability close to 1 will not do. An alternative interpretation of Theorem 3 is in terms of the distinction between private and public signals. If the players’ information partitions are generated by a set of signals, the subset of these signals which generate the meet of the player’s partitions could be seen as the “public” signals, observed by all. All other signals are classified as being private. Then, Theorem 3 implies that only the public signals have any bearing on equilibrium. Private signals are irrelevant. Notice that the notion of a private signal is a wide one. It encompasses those signals which are observed by “most” of the players, but not by all. Equilibrium strategies must be coarse enough to accommodate players with the worst information. This suggests that the number of players in the game is an important determinant of how fine an equilibrium can be.

Proof of Theorem 3 for Countable T. Consider an element E from the meet of the partitions and the associated irreducible persistent subchain of the Markov chain. Denote by T∧ the set of types for this subchain, and denote by {Xn} the subchain taking values in T∧. Lemma 3. {s(Xn)} is a Martingale with respect to {Xn}.

Since s(⋅) takes values in a fixed interval of the reals, s(⋅) is bounded. Hence, we can appeal to one of the standard convergence theorems for martingales (for example, Feller, 1968, p. 242), which states that {s(Xn)} converges almost surely to some random variable Z. But then, since {s(Xn)} converges almost surely to Z, it must be that Z takes the value s(t) with probability 1. However, t was chosen arbitrarily from T∧. Hence, Z=s(t) a.s. for all t∈T∧. Since all types receive positive probability, s(t)=s(t′) for any pair of types t and t′ in T∧. This proves Theorem 3. ◼

The kinds of coordination problems for which our framework is best suited are those in which the players are choosing from a continuum. The framework has little to say concerning coordination games with a small number of actions. For these games, rather different arguments are required. Morris et al. (1995) tackle this issue for general, finite Bayesian games.

However, subject to these qualifications, our argument may have explanatory value. Norms and conventions around us tend to be simple relative to the range of possible “sunspots” on which actions can be conditioned. It is perhaps an indication of this simplicity that most discussions of conventions outside the formal game-theoretic literature concentrate on one-shot coordination games. Since Lewis’ (1969) seminal work on the subject, Ullman-Margalit (1977), Gilbert (1990), Miller (1990), and others have developed the theme of conventions as being equilibrium strategies in coordination games. In the light of our discussion, this may not be unduly restrictive.

is such that L(k)(P)⊆L(k+1)(P). Now, if L(k)(P)=L(k+1)(P) for some k, then L(k)(P)=E, so that t and t′ communicate. Hence, suppose that L(k)(P)≠L(k+1)(P) for all k. Since there are countably many states in Ω, the sequence (A.4) converges to E in the sense that, for any state ω∈E, there is some k such that ω∈L(k)(P). Since P′⊆E, there is some k such that P′⊆L(k)(P), so that t and t′ communicate. ◼

works.title: Cognitive homelessness
passages: There is a constant temptation in philosophy to postulate a realm of phenomena in which nothing is hidden from us. René Descartes thought that one’s own mind is such a realm. Ludwig Wittgenstein1 enlarged the realm to everything that is of interest to philosophy. That they explained this special feature in very different ways hardly needs to be said; what is remarkable is their agreement on our possession of a cognitive home in which everything lies open to our view. Much of our thinking—for example, in the physical sciences—must operate outside this home, in alien circumstances. The claim is that not all our thinking could be like that.

To deny that something is hidden is not to assert that we are infallible about it. Mistakes are always possible. There is no limit to the conclusions into which fallacious reasoning can lure us. The point is that, in our cognitive home, such mistakes are always rectifiable. Similarly, we are not omniscient about our cognitive home. We may not know the answer to a question simply because the question has never occurred to us. Even if something is open to view, we may not have glanced in that direction. Again, the point is that such ignorance is always removable.

My aim is to argue that we are cognitively homeless. Although much is, in fact, accessible to our knowledge, nothing of interest is inherently accessible to it. It is first necessary to sharpen the issue, however, to make it more susceptible to argument.

It is convenient to frame the discussion in terms of conditions that obtain or fail to obtain in various contexts. Most conditions obtain in some contexts and not in others. For example, the condition that one is hungry obtains in the context of a particular person at a particular time, but a change of either person or time produces a new context in which the same condition may not obtain. The pronoun ‘one’ will be used for the subject of a context, to whom reference is made by use of the first person in that context, as in ‘the condition that one is hungry’. Although conditions are expressed by sentential clauses, they are not propositions as the latter are usually conceived, just because they are open with respect to person, place, and other contextual features. We often use clauses like that, as in ‘When it rains, it pours’. The domain of contexts will be taken to include counterfactual as well as actual circumstances. Since the circumstances on which the arguments below rely are physically and psychologically feasible, issues about the bounds of possibility are not pressing.

The next notion to be introduced is that of being in a position to know. To be in a position to know that P, it is neither necessary to know that P nor sufficient to be physically and psychologically capable of knowing that P. No obstacle must block one’s path to knowing that P. If one is in a position to know that P, and has done what one is in a position to do to decide whether P, then one does know that P. The fact is open to one’s view, unhidden, even if one does not yet see it. Thus, being in a position to know, like knowing and unlike being physically and psychologically capable of knowing, is factive: if one is in a position to know that P, then P. Although the notion of being in a position to know is obviously somewhat vague, it is clear enough for present purposes.
A special kind of condition can now be defined. If C is the condition that P, call C luminous just in case (L) holds:2
For every context α, if in α P, then in α one is in a position to know that P.

Since being in a position to know is factive, the converse of (L) holds for any value of ‘P’, so the conditional in (L) could just as well be a biconditional. The picture is that a luminous condition always shines brightly enough to make its presence visible. But (L) does not say that the condition that P must obtain independently of our dispositions to judge that P; for all (L) says, the condition might obtain in virtue of those dispositions. Now, a realm in which nothing is hidden is a realm in which all conditions are luminous. The question is: What conditions, if any, are in fact luminous?

Some examples will help. Pain is often conceived as a luminous condition, in the sense that, if one is in pain, then one is in a position to know that one is in pain.3 The definition of luminosity gives scope to finesse some of the more obvious objections to claims of this kind. Thus, people who lack the concept of pain (perhaps because their concepts carve up the space of possible sensations in an alternative way), and so never know that they are in pain, may still count as being in a position to know that they are in pain. Perhaps more primitive creatures are sometimes in pain without possessing any concepts at all; if they count as not even being in a position to know that they are in pain, a counterexample to luminosity might still be avoided by the ruling that the subject of a context must be a possessor of concepts. These rulings are not endorsed here, but they demonstrate the kinds of consideration to which the notion of luminosity can be made sensitive.
Two claims of luminosity are implicit in the following passage from Michael Dummett:4

It is an undeniable feature of the notion of meaning—obscure as that notion is—that meaning is transparent in the sense that, if someone attaches a meaning to each of two words, he must know whether these meanings are the same (ibid., p. 131).5

Thus, if two words have the same meaning in the context of a given subject (it is meaning for this subject which is in question), then that subject is in a position to know that they have the same meaning, and if the words have different meanings, then the subject is in a position to know that they have different meanings.6 The two claims of luminosity are genuinely distinct, for the premise that whenever P one is in a position to know that P does not entail the conclusion that whenever not-P one is in a position to know that not-P. If whenever one is awake one is in a position to know that one is awake, it does not follow that whenever one is not awake one is in a position to know that one is not awake.7

Other conditions for which luminosity is often claimed are those of the form ‘it appears to one that P’. When there really is an oasis ahead, one may not be in a position to know that there really is an oasis ahead, but, it is supposed, when there at least appears to be an oasis ahead, one must be in a position to know that there at least appears to be an oasis ahead.

I shall not dispute here that there are luminous conditions. An inconsistent condition is luminous because (L) holds vacuously; for it, the antecedent ‘in α P’ cannot obtain in any context. It is less obvious that a tautological condition is luminous, because it is less obvious that every context must have a subject who is in a position to possess the concepts that occur in the relevant tautology. I shall concede the point for the sake of argument, however, so that tautological conditions are luminous, too. The question thus becomes: Are there nontrivial luminous conditions? In the next section, I present a paradigmatic instance of a general form of argument against the luminosity of a given nontrivial condition.

For definiteness, I shall first present the argument for the particular case of the condition that one feels hot. To facilitate generalization, no special features of this case will be exploited. The argument proceeds by reductio ad absurdum on the relevant instance of (L), which claims that whenever one feels hot, one is in a position to know that one feels hot.

Suppose that the condition that one feels hot is luminous. Consider a morning on which one feels chilly at dawn, very slowly warms up, and feels much too hot by noon. One changes from not feeling hot to feeling hot, and from not being in a position to know that one feels hot to being in a position to know that one feels hot. If the condition that one feels hot is luminous, these changes are exactly simultaneous. Suppose that one’s feelings of heat and cold change so slowly during this process that one is not aware of any change in them over one second. Suppose, also, that throughout the process one thoroughly considers how hot or cold one feels. One’s confidence that one feels hot gradually increases. One’s initial answers to the question ‘Do you feel hot?’ are firmly negative; then hesitations and qualifications creep in, until one gives neutral answers, such as ‘It is hard to say’; then one begins to assent, with gradually decreasing hesitations and qualifications; one’s final answers are firmly positive.

Let t0,t1,…,tn be a series of times at one second intervals from dawn to noon. Let αi be the context at ti (0≤i≤n). Consider a time ti between t0 and tn, and suppose that at ti one is in a position to know that one feels hot. By hypothesis, at ti one has done what one is in a position to do to decide whether one feels hot, by thoroughly considering the matter, so one does know that one feels hot. Thus, one is at least reasonably confident that one feels hot, for otherwise one would not know. Moreover, this confidence must be reliably based, for otherwise one would still not know that one feels hot. This is not to assume that the concept of knowledge can be analyzed in terms of the concept of reliability: it is just to assume that reliability is necessary for knowledge (which is hard to deny), but not that other necessary conditions can be framed (without use of the concept of knowledge) whose conjunction with reliability is a necessary and sufficient condition for knowledge. Nor does the invocation of reliability presuppose that the condition obtains independently of one’s dispositions to judge that it does; a constitutive connection between them is often supposed to underpin luminosity, but its effect is to make reliability less contingent, not to make unreliability consistent with being in a position to know. Now, at ti−1 one is almost equally confident that one feels hot, by the description of the case. So if one does not feel hot at ti−1, one’s confidence at ti that one feels hot is not reliably based, for one’s almost equal confidence on a similar basis a second earlier that one felt hot was mistaken. In picturesque terms, that large proportion of one’s confidence at ti which one already had at ti−1 is misplaced. Even if one’s confidence at ti is just enough to count as belief, while one’s confidence at ti−1 fell just short of belief, what constitutes that belief at ti is largely misplaced confidence; the belief falls short of knowledge. One’s confidence at ti is reliably based in the way required for knowledge only if one feels hot at ti−1. Since, as already argued, one’s confidence at ti is so reliably based, one does feel hot at ti−1. In the terminology of contexts, this conditional has been upheld:
If in αi one is in a position to know that one feels hot, then in αi−1 one feels hot.

Note that (1) is merely a description of a specific process; it does not purport to be a general principle about feeling hot. It is asserted for each i from 1 to n, but it says nothing about contexts other than α0,…,αn.
The argument can now be completed. The supposed luminosity of the condition that one feels hot yields this conditional:
If in αi one feels hot, then in αi one is in a position to know that one feels hot.
By modus ponens, (2) and (3) yield this:
In αi one is in a position to know that one feels hot.
By modus ponens, (1) and (4) yield this:
The following is certainly true, for αn is the context at noon, when one feels very hot:
By repeating the argument from (4) to (5) n times, for descending values of i from n to 1, we reach the following from (6):

But (7) is certainly false, for α0 is the context at dawn, when one feels chilly. Thus, not all instances of (1) and (2) are true. But it has just been argued that all instances of (1) are true. Thus, not all instances of (2) are true. Since (2) expresses the luminosity of the condition that one feels hot, that condition is not luminous. Feeling hot does not imply being in a position to know that one feels hot.

An obvious doubt arises about the argument of section II. The reasoning is very reminiscent of that in sorites paradoxes (How can i grains make a heap unless i−1 do?). It may therefore be suspected of concealing a fallacy just like the concealed fallacy in sorites reasoning, whatever that is. May it not be illicitly exploiting the vagueness of ‘feels hot’ or ‘in a position to know’?

The doubt can be made more specific. If the conclusion of the argument is false, then either not all the premises are true or the reasoning is invalid. Given instances of (1) and the straightforwardly true (6) as premises, the argument derives instances of (2) from the supposed luminosity of the condition at issue, and then uses modus ponens to reach the straightforwardly false (7); by reductio ad absurdum, luminosity is rejected. On any reasonable view of vagueness, this reasoning shows that the luminosity claim is less than perfectly true, given that all instances of (1) are perfectly true. On some accounts, modus ponens fails to preserve less than perfect truth, but it should still preserve perfect truth. On other accounts, reductio ad absurdum is problematic because an assumption can have perfectly false consequences without itself being perfectly false, and therefore without having a perfectly true negation; nevertheless, it does still follow that the assumption is less than perfectly true. Moreover, it is arguable that vagueness requires no revision of classical logic at all.8 For my purposes here, it would suffice to argue that the luminosity claim is less than perfectly true, for then it will have perfectly false consequences, which should discourage its application to philosophy. Thus, the way for the defender of (perfect) luminosity to use the connection with sorites paradoxes is by arguing that not all instances of (1) are perfectly true, and using the vagueness of some relevant term to explain away their plausibility. Of course, the argument for (1) would remain to be addressed. Fortunately, however, the strategy can be tested more directly. For if (1) is, in effect, the major premise of a sorites paradox, then sharpening the relevantly vague expressions should give (1) a clearly false instance, just as sharpening the term ‘heap’ by stipulating a cut-off point gives the conditional ‘If i grains make a heap, then i−1 grains make a heap’ a clearly false instance. Does it?

The relevantly vague expressions in (1) are ‘feels hot’ and ‘in a position to know’. Sharpen ‘feels hot’ by using a physiological condition to resolve borderline cases. Assume that the subject of the process has no access to the technology needed to determine whether the physiological condition obtains, and so is not in a position to know whether it does. These stipulations in no way weaken the argument for (1). The considerations about reliability remain as cogent as before, for they were based on our limited powers of discrimination among our own sensations, not on the vagueness of ‘feels hot’. It might be objected that the sharpening violates the intended meaning of ‘feels hot’. But that would not undermine the contrast between (1) and the major premise of a sorites paradox. For any complete sharpening of ‘heap’ yields a clearly false instance of the principle ‘If i grains make a heap, then i−1 grains make a heap’, even if it violates the intended meaning of ‘heap’ by, for example, falsifying the converse upward principle ‘If i−1 grains make a heap, then i grains make a heap’. By definition, the sharpened term applies wherever the unsharpened term clearly applied and fails to apply wherever the unsharpened term clearly failed to apply; thus, on any sharpening, ‘10,000 (optimally arranged) grains make a heap’ is true and ‘0 grains make a heap’ false, so the major premise has a false instance. Even the truth of (1) on a sharpening of its vague terms that violates their intended meaning is enough to differentiate (1) from the major premise of a sorites paradox.

The vague expression ‘in a position to know’ remains. Sharpen it by tightening up its conditions of application: it is not to apply in borderline cases of being in a position to know (in the old sense). If anything, this strengthens the argument for (1), by building more into its antecedent. It does not help one to know whether one feels hot; indeed, one need not even be aware of the stipulation about ‘in a position to know’, for it is made by the theorist, not by the subject. The stipulations will not make ‘feels hot’ and ‘in a position to know’ perfectly precise; no feasible sharpening could do that. Fortunately, perfect precision is not necessary. It is sufficient to sharpen those expressions to a point at which the finitely many borderline cases that actually arise in the argument are resolved. Such sharpening has the opposite effect to that predicted by the assimilation of the argument against luminosity to sorites reasoning; (1) becomes more not less plausible. The argument is not just another sorites paradox.

Nevertheless, the argument against (2) might be thought to commit a subtler fallacy of vagueness. A defender of (2) might take the vagueness of its constituent terms to be essential to its truth, and explain the plausibility of (1) by assigning it a status short of perfect truth, while conceding that all instances of (1) are true on some sharpenings, such as those considered above. All sharpenings that falsify an instance of (2) might be held to violate the intended meanings of the vague terms, on the grounds that those meanings make (2) analytic. On such a view, the unsharpened (1) would be almost but not quite perfectly true in some instances, because its consequent would be almost but not quite as true as its antecedent. The reliability conditions adduced in favor of (1) would be treated as almost but not quite perfectly correct. No justification has been provided for not treating them as perfectly correct, but let that pass; for the concession is in any case inadequate. The view must reject the following variation on (1):
If it is perfectly true that in αi one is in a position to know that one feels hot, then it is perfectly true that in αi−1 one feels hot.
For if (2) is perfectly true, then the perfect truth of its antecedent implies the perfect truth of its consequent:
If it is perfectly true that in αi one feels hot, then it is perfectly true that in αi one is in a position to know that one feels hot.

(1P) and (2P) give an argument from the perfect truth of (3) to the perfect truth of (5), and therefore from the perfect truth of (6) (which is uncontested) to the perfect truth of (7); but the falsity of (7) is uncontested. The objector will treat (1P) like (1), claiming that for some i, it is perfectly true that in αi one is in a position to know that one feels hot, but slightly less than perfectly true that in αi−1 one feels hot. But can there be such an i? If it is less than perfectly true that in αi−1 one feels hot, then there is a strict standard by which it is false in αi−1 that one feels hot; so by that standard, in αi−1 one is fairly confident of what is false, that one feels hot (by the argument in section II), in which case it is less than perfectly true that in αi one is in a position to know that one feels hot, if the reliability considerations are to be assigned any positive weight at all. To put the argument more directly, if it is perfectly true that in αi one is in a position to know that one feels hot, then it is perfectly true that the reliability requirement is met, and therefore perfectly true that in αi−1 one feels hot. Thus, the objection to (1P) fails, and (1P) suffices for an argument against the perfect truth of (2). Invoking degrees of truth will not protect luminosity claims.9

The point is reinforced by the observation that, once the luminosity assumption is dropped, (7) does not follow in classical logic from (6) and all instances of (1). To see this, pick j and k such that n≥k>j>0; for each i, evaluate ‘one feels hot’ as true in αi if and only if i≥j, and otherwise as false; evaluate ‘one is in a position to know that one feels hot’ as true in αi if and only if i≥k, and otherwise as false. On this evaluation, each instance of (1) is true, for if the antecedent is true, then i≥k>j, so i−1≥j, so the consequent is true. (6) is true because n≥j. (7) is false because j>0. One can elaborate this evaluation in the manner of the standard semantics for modal logic by treating contexts like possible worlds and ‘one is in a position to know that…’ like ‘it is necessary that…’. The foregoing evaluation results if one defines αh to be accessible from αi just in case |h−i|≤k−j, evaluates ‘one is in a position to know that P’ as true at a context αi if and only if ‘P’ is true at all contexts accessible from αi, and evaluates ‘one feels hot’ as before. Since a classical evaluation makes (6) and all instances of (1) true and (7) false, the latter does not follow from the former in classical logic. Contrast the sorites paradox: ‘0 grains make a heap’ does follow in classical logic from ‘n grains make a heap’ and all instances of ‘If i grains make a heap, then i−1 grains make a heap’. Once luminosity is denied, (1) generates no paradox.

It is consistent with all this to postulate a more general phenomenon of which both the vagueness of ‘heap’ and the nonluminosity of the condition that one feels hot are instances. Inexact knowledge may be such a phenomenon. It is characterized by margin for error principles like (1), according to which, if in some context one is in a position to know that P, then in all sufficiently similar contexts it is true that P, whether or not one is in a position to know it, since otherwise one’s judgments would lack the margin for error that reliability requires, given one’s limited powers of discrimination; how much similarity suffices, and in what respects, depends on the details of the case.10 If vagueness is characterized by margin for error principles, however, their source will be of a peculiarly conceptual kind.11 On this view, the epistemological principles underlying (1) are important for vagueness, too, but it does not follow that all their manifestations involve vagueness. The argument against luminosity does not depend on any theory of vagueness.

How far does the argument against luminosity generalize? It assumes nothing specific about the condition of feeling hot. It extends to the examples of supposedly luminous conditions mentioned in section I. The onset of pain can be gradual, for example, as odd sensations merge into painful ones. An argument against the luminosity of the condition that one is in pain can be modeled on the argument against the luminosity of the condition that one feels hot, without any structural revisions. It is not perfectly true that in every context in which one is in pain, one is in a position to know that one is in pain. Being in pain does not imply being in a position to know that one is in pain.

Similarly, two words can gradually become synonymous, as a difference in application withers into a stylistic preference which slowly disappears altogether. The structure of the argument against luminosity is just as before. Assigning two words the same meaning does not imply being in a position to know that one assigns them the same meaning. Equally, assigning two words different meanings does not imply being in a position to know that one assigns them different meanings.

The argument also applies to conditions of the form ‘it appears to one that P’. A context in which it does not appear to one that P can gradually change into a context in which it does appear to one that P. Having it appear to one that P does not imply being in a position to know that it appears to one that P.12

Further applications of the argument involve conditions on what one is in a position to know. Since a context in which one is not in a position to know that P can gradually change into a context in which one is in a position to know that P, the argument shows that the condition that one is in a position to know that P is nonluminous (for most values of ‘P’).13 Being in a position to know that P does not imply being in a position to know that one is in a position to know that P. Thus, the operator ‘one is in a position to know that…’ does not satisfy the principle □p→□□p of the modal logic S4. Indeed, actually knowing that P does not imply being in a position to know that one knows that P. Equally, not being in a position to know that P does not imply being in a position to know that one is not in a position to know that P. Thus, the operator ‘one is in a position to know that…’ does not satisfy the principle ¬□p→□¬□p of the stronger modal logic S5. Indeed, not knowing that P does not imply being in a position to know that one does not know that P. These results can be extended. For example, there is no natural number n such that n iterations of ‘one is in a position to know that…’ imply n+1 iterations of it. The general absence of nontrivial luminous conditions can be represented in modal logic by the rule that A→□A is a theorem only if either A is a theorem or ¬A is.14

What are the general features of a condition on which the argument against luminosity depends? As it stands, it requires the condition to obtain in some contexts and not in others. Thus, it is ineffective against conditions that hold in all contexts or in none. Given a sufficiently restrictive understanding of what a context is, those might include some Cartesian conditions, such as that one exists and even that one thinks. They do not include the condition that one is thinking about one’s existence, however, since one is thinking about one’s existence in some contexts and not in others on any reasonable understanding of what a context is.

A condition that obtains in no context is automatically luminous. A condition that obtains in every context is not automatically luminous, for it is not automatic that in every context one is in a position to know that it obtains: perhaps it is an a posteriori necessity, or a mathematical theorem as yet unproved. But if one is not in every context in a position to know that the condition obtains, although the condition does obtain in every context, then it follows at once that the condition is not luminous. What is automatically luminous is a condition such that in every context one is in a position to know that it obtains.

The argument also requires the possibility of a change from a context in which the condition does not obtain to a context in which it does. Thus, the argument would not be effective against an eternal condition that always obtains if it ever obtains: for example, the condition that one felt hot at noon on midsummer’s day 1996. But an eternal condition often permits a change from a context in which one is not in a position to know that it obtains to a context in which one is in a position to know that it obtains; this certainly applies to the example just given. Such a condition cannot be luminous, for it obtains in the later context in which one is in a position to know that it obtains (because being in a position to know is factive), so it obtains in the earlier context in which one is not in a position to know that it obtains (because the condition is eternal). Thus, an eternal condition is luminous only if it is impossible to change from not being in a position to know that it obtains to being in such a position. No argument has been given against the luminosity of a condition such that, if one is ever in a position to know that it obtains, then one is always in a position to know that it obtains, even though some people are in a position to know that it obtains while others are not. There are candidates for such conditions. For example, if a subject S is always in a position to know that she is S (which is not to say that she must know her own name), then anyone who is ever in a position to know that the condition that one is S obtains is always in a position to know that it obtains, because the only such person is S herself. Perhaps the argument could be extended to show that not even this condition is luminous, by consideration of a science-fictional process of gradual change in which someone else becomes (is replaced by) S. But no such extension will be attempted here. Such examples do not seriously threaten the idea that only trivial conditions are luminous.

The argument depends on the gradualness of the change from contexts in which the condition does not obtain to contexts in which it does. The relevant kind of gradualness is epistemic, however. Even if there is a jump in conditions, the argument still applies, provided that there is no corresponding jump in our awareness of them. Such a jump in our awareness is never guaranteed to occur. Thus, the gradualness requirement does not obviously exclude any further conditions. We might therefore conjecture that no condition such that one can pass from not being in a position to know that it obtains to being in a position to know that it obtains is luminous.

A difficulty for the conjecture is raised by the notion of ancestrally knowing. One ancestrally knows that P just in case P, and one knows that P, and one knows that one knows that P, and so on ad infinitum. The condition that one ancestrally knows that P might seem to be luminous; for consider the following inference, with infinitely many premises:
P One knows that P. One knows that one knows that P. ⋮ One ancestrally knows that P.

The inference is deductively valid, by definition of ancestral knowledge. Now, anyone who ancestrally knows that P knows each premise of the argument, and so (it seems) is in a position to know the conclusion, for one should be in a position to know, even if one does not actually know, that which follows deductively from what one knows. Hence the condition that one ancestrally knows that P is luminous. Nevertheless, for most values of ‘P’, there seems to be no metaphysical impossibility in a change from not ancestrally knowing that P to ancestrally knowing that P, and so from not being in a position to know that one ancestrally knows that P to being in a position to know that one ancestrally knows that P. The condition that one ancestrally knows that P is therefore a prima facie counterexample to the conjecture.

The counterexample might be challenged on the grounds that we are not in a position to make infinitary inferences. Indeed, even when the inference is finitary, it is not obvious that one is in a position to know that which follows deductively from what one knows. Only in a rather attenuated sense are we in a position to know all the consequences of the axioms of Peano arithmetic. This response is not wholly satisfying, however, for the original argument against luminosity made no appeal to limits on powers of inference. If the condition that one ancestrally knows that P is luminous in the attenuated sense, why does the original argument fail to generalize to this case?

Ancestral knowing may fail the gradualness requirement. Although it is possible to change from not ancestrally knowing that P to ancestrally knowing that P, the change may necessarily be sudden. After all, it is the change from finitely many iterations of knowledge to infinitely many. How could it be gradual? Thus, ancestral knowing may provide a counterexample at least to the conjecture that no condition such that one can pass from not being in a position to know that it obtains to being in a position to know that it obtains is luminous in the attenuated sense.

If ancestral knowing does fail the gradualness requirement, it will be a hard state to enter. How is one to make the instantaneous jump from the finite to the infinite? The kind of common knowledge that we are supposed to have of conventions is usually defined in a way that requires us to know ancestrally; for example, if John knows that Jane knows that John knows that Jane knows that John knows that P, then John knows that John knows that John knows that P (at least in the attenuated sense). Common knowledge would therefore be a convenient idealization, like a frictionless plane.15 Thus, even if the conjecture is false, all luminous conditions may still be trivial in practice, for the condition that one ancestrally knows that P seems to be empty in practice. Similar remarks apply to being ancestrally in a position to know, which stands to being in a position to know as ancestrally knowing stands to knowing.

Luminous conditions are curiosities. Far from forming a cognitive home, they are remote from our ordinary interests. The conditions with which we engage in our everyday life are, from the start, nonluminous. Their obtaining does not wait for us to be in a position to know that they obtain.

To be physically and psychologically capable of knowing that P is not sufficient, even given that P, for being in a position to know that P; one may be in the wrong place. Thus, it does not follow from the nonluminosity of a condition that there are contexts in which, though it obtains, one is not physically and psychologically capable of knowing that it obtains. Nevertheless, it is natural to ask, if one is not in a position to know that one feels hot when one does feel hot, how is one to know it at all? Of course, in many other contexts one does know that one feels hot.16 The question is this: If in context α one feels hot, perhaps without being in a position to know that one feels hot, must or can there be another context β in which one knows that in α one feels hot? Analogous questions can be asked about other nonluminous conditions. The argument for nonluminosity leaves them open. It is consistent with, but does not entail, the possibility of a physiological technique by which one could subsequently discover that one had been feeling hot in α.

The hypothetical technique faces difficulties. Suppose that feelings of hot and cold are found generally to be correlated with a measurable physiological variable V. We must discover which values of V are associated with the condition that one feels hot. They include the values associated with the condition that one is in a position to know that one feels hot. But if they included only those values, the condition that one feels hot would be luminous, which it is not. We are not in a position to know which further values of V are associated with that condition. Our problem is that we cannot calibrate the physiological measurement of feeling hot. Even if measurements of V were perfectly precise—which they will not be—they would not answer the original question. Attempts to measure other ordinary conditions face similar problems.

It might still be held to be metaphysically possible to find out whether one feels hot by the testimony of a literal or metaphorical deus ex machina. But it certainly cannot be assumed without argument that, if an ordinary condition obtains in a context α, then in some possible context it is known that the condition obtains in α.

The failure of luminosity impinges on Dummett’s arguments for an antirealist theory of meaning. Of course, Dummett’s antirealist does not make the extreme claim that every condition is luminous. All parties can accept that stone-age people lived in contexts in which the moon caused the tides, although they were not in a position to know that the moon caused the tides. The connection between luminosity and antirealism is a subtler one.

Dummett objects to the realist’s truth-conditional theory of meaning that it violates a necessary connection between meaning and use. To understand a sentence is to know what it means; if, as Dummett’s realist holds, meanings are truth conditions, then speakers of a language know the truth conditions of its sentences.17 Knowing the truth condition of a sentence s cannot consist merely in being disposed to say something of the form ‘s is true if and only if P’; one must also understand the biconditional, and an infinite regress looms. If one could always recognize whether the truth condition obtained, then knowledge of the truth condition of s might consist in a willingness to assert s just when the truth condition obtains (it is assumed that dishonesty, shyness, and other complications can somehow be filtered out). But the realist insists that the truth conditions of some sentences obtain even though no speaker of the language can recognize that they obtain. Dummett argues that the realist has no substantial explanation of what knowing such truth conditions consists in. The proposed remedy is that the meaning of a sentence should be given by the condition for it to be warrantedly assertible, rather than by the condition for it to be true. Thus, to understand a sentence is to know its assertibility condition, and this knowledge can consist in a willingness to assert the sentence just when the assertibility condition obtains.18 The remedy would fail if the objection to truth-conditional theories of meaning applied equally to assertibility-conditional theories of meaning; thus, the argument requires that when an assertibility condition obtains, competent speakers of the language can recognize that it obtains. Dummett acknowledges this requirement: “The conditions under which a sentence is recognized as true or false […] have, by the nature of the case, to be conditions which we can recognize as obtaining when they obtain.”19 That is, when a recognition condition obtains, we can recognize that the recognition condition obtains. Dummett evidently intends the recognition condition for the truth of a sentence to be its assertibility condition, which yields the thesis that when an assertibility condition obtains, we can recognize that it obtains. But recognizing is coming to know, and Dummett’s ‘can’ may be glossed as ‘is in a position to’. Thus, Dummett requires assertibility conditions to be luminous.

The argument against luminosity in section II generalizes to assertibility conditions. For example, contexts in which it is not assertible that it is raining change gradually into contexts in which it is assertible that it is raining. By the argument, having it assertible that it is raining does not imply being in a position to know that it is assertible that it is raining. Even in the mathematical case, in which Dummett uses the proof-based intuitionistic semantics as a paradigm of an assertibility-conditional theory of meaning, proofs are acquired gradually; it takes time to understand and check them.20 By the argument, having a proof of a mathematical assertion does not imply being in a position to know that one has a proof of it. Thus, assertibility conditions have the very feature that is supposed to lay truth conditions open to Dummett’s attack.21

It might be replied that one’s antirealist understanding of a sentence can consist in the fact that one is willing to assert it when and only when its assertibility condition obtains, even if one does not know that it obtains. This reply concedes that assertibility conditions fail Dummett’s luminosity constraint; but then something is wrong with his argument for assertibility-conditional theories of meaning, which treats that constraint as binding.

A different reply is that, if Dummett intends recognizability to be assertibility, then what he requires is only that when it is assertible that P, it is assertible that it is assertible that P (the S4 principle for assertibility).22 If false assertions are sometimes warranted by misleading evidence, then it might be assertible that it is assertible that P even when one is not in a position to know that it is assertible that P; thus, Dummett would not require assertibility conditions to be luminous. This reply is open to objection. The argument that only trivial conditions are luminous can be generalized to an argument that only trivial conditions satisfy the requirement that whenever they obtain, it is assertible that they obtain: (1) is replaced by a conditional of the form ‘If in αi it is assertible that condition C obtains, then in αi−1 C obtains’. Of course, assertibility obeys a margin-for-error principle universally only if it is factive, for since any context α will be similar enough in relevant respects to itself, ‘In α it is assertible that C obtains’ would imply ‘In α C obtains’, given such a principle. Nevertheless, the analogue of (1) holds in particular examples, when the evidence may be inadequate but is not positively misleading, which is all that the argument requires.23 Moreover, appearances notwithstanding, having a warrant to assert that P arguably is being in a position to know that P. On this view, assertibility is factive but defeasible in the sense that it can be lost when further (misleading) evidence is gained, just as knowledge can be.24

The dialectical situation is further complicated by Dummett’s presentation of his argument as a challenge to the realist, to explain what knowledge of realist truth conditions consists in. He does not claim to prove that the realist cannot meet the challenge, although he certainly denies that it has been met so far. Nor does he rule out the possibility that it can be met in some areas and not in others. But Dummett does assume that the antirealist can easily meet the corresponding challenge, to explain what knowledge of assertibility conditions consists in. If the argument of this paper is correct, that assumption is false; the antirealist faces the same sort of difficulty as the realist does. The contrast between truth conditions and assertibility conditions may be off the point.

Both truth-conditional and assertibility-conditional theories of meaning find it hard to meet Dummett’s challenge because both truth conditions and assertibility conditions are nonluminous. They share this feature with every other kind of nontrivial condition that might be offered as the meaning of a sentence. Since trivial conditions are not serious candidates for the meanings of most sentences, a serious X-conditional theory of meaning will find it hard to meet Dummett’s challenge, for any X. If any systematic (contrast: skeptical) theory of meaning can be cast as X-conditional for some X, then any systematic theory of meaning will find it hard to meet Dummett’s challenge. If ‘hard’ turns out to be ‘impossible’, then failure to meet the challenge eliminates truth-conditional theories of meaning only if it eliminates all systematic theories of meaning. The challenge may be suspected of depending on excessive demands on a theory of meaning; in particular, the demand for an explanation of what knowledge of meaning ‘consists in’ seems to embody a dubious reductionism. That suspicion will not be investigated here.

On an antirealist picture, thought initially engages with conditions whose esse is their percipi; if it later finds its laborious way to conditions of greater depth, it must do so from the starting point of that cognitive home. Assertibility conditions are pictured as forming a linguistic version of the cognitive home. They do not. Thought engages with conditions whose esse is distinct from their percipi as soon as it engages with any conditions at all; even perception does. Trivialities aside, there is nothing else with which to engage. We have no cognitive home.

Earlier versions of this material were given in talks at the Universities of Edinburgh, Canterbury (Christchurch), Waikato, St. Andrews, Glasgow, and Sheffield, at Monash University, Oriel College/Oxford, and at the Instituto de Investigaciones Filosóficas of the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México. I thank the audiences there for helpful comments.

See Philosophical Investigations, G. E. M. Anscombe, trans. (New York: Macmillan, 1953), §126. Of course, Wittgenstein’s ‘we’, unlike Descartes’s, is collective. What is not hidden from each Cartesian subject is only its own thinking, not that of other Cartesian subjects. Wittgenstein is speaking of what is not hidden from any of us. The arguments below have not been, but could be, adjusted to Wittgenstein’s rejection in On Certainty—G. E. M. Anscombe and G. H. von Wright, eds.; Denis Paul and Anscombe, trans. (New York: Harper, 1969)—of claims to know that P when there is no question of doubting that P; conversational inappropriateness is compatible with truth. ↩︎

As formulated in the text, the definition embodies the assumption that, if the condition that P is the condition that Q, then (in every context, if P then one is in a position to know that P) if and only if (in every context, if Q then one is in a position to know that Q). If necessarily equivalent conditions had to be identical, this assumption might fail. For present purposes, conditions will therefore be so individuated that the condition that P is the condition that Q only if in every context (a) one is in a position to know that P if and only if one is in a position to know that Q; (b) P if and only if Q. Thus, the stated assumption holds. Conditions are individuated at least as finely as the objects of knowledge. ↩︎
For a recent discussion, see J. H. McDowell, “One Strand in the Private Language Argument,” Grazer Philosophische Studien, XXXIII/XXXIV (1989): 285–303. ↩︎

Compare Dummett’s Frege: Philosophy of Language (Cambridge: Harvard, 1981, 2nd ed.), p. 632, and The Seas of Language (New York: Oxford, 1993), p. 4. For a recent discussion, see Paul Boghossian, “The Transparency of Mental Content,” Philosophical Perspectives, VIII (1994): 33–50. ↩︎
Dummett does not make the qualification ‘in a position to’. What of a subject who has never compared the two words? ↩︎

See Bernard Williams, Descartes: The Project of Pure Enquiry (New York: Penguin, 1978), pp. 309–13. Lloyd Humberstone, “Some Epistemic Capacities,” Dialectica, XLII, 3 (1988): 183–200, discusses attempts to undermine such asymmetries. Strictly, having the same meaning and having different meanings are contraries, not contradictories, since both require the words to be meaningful. ↩︎

On logic for vague languages, see my Vagueness (New York: Routledge, 1994). The arguments of the present paper do not depend on the epistemic account of vagueness developed there, which requires no revision of classical logic. ↩︎
Thanks to Crispin Wright and Helen Beebee for discussion here. ↩︎
See my “Inexact Knowledge,” Mind, CI, 402 (1992): 217–42, and Vagueness, pp. 216–47. ↩︎

Such conditions are sometimes called “response dependent.” If the claim is just that they have some constitutive dependence on our dispositions to judge that they obtain, then it does not entail luminosity, although nonluminosity does constrain what forms of dependence they can exhibit. For related discussion in the case of color, see Vagueness, pp. 180–84. Many definitions of response dependence are conceivable. The failure of luminosity, however, may increase one’s skepticism about all claims of response dependence. ↩︎

The comparison with sorites paradoxes must be handled with particular care when the replacement for ‘feels hot’ itself involves ‘know’, for then the two expressions cannot be sharpened independently of each other. But (1) retains its plausibility on a restrictive sharpening of ‘in a position to know’ on any sharpening of the replacement for ‘feels hot’ on which it expresses a condition such that the subject’s confidence that it obtains change slowly. The relevant sharpenings of ‘one is in a position to know that P’ meet this requirement. Thanks to Kit Fine for discussion here. ↩︎
For more details, see my “An Alternative Rule of Disjunction in Modal Logic,” Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic, XXXIII, 1 (1992): 89–100. ↩︎

For a related discussion of iterated prisoner’s dilemma and the surprise examination paradox, see “Inexact Knowledge”; and for some weakenings of the notion of common knowledge, see R. Fagin, J. Y. Halpern, Y. Moses, and M. Y. Vardi, Reasoning about Knowledge (Cambridge: MIT, 1995), pp. 395–422. ↩︎
There are no contexts in which one knows the conjunction that the condition obtains and one is not in a position to know that it obtains. But that is another story. ↩︎

Provision must naturally be made for nondeclarative sentences, perhaps by a distinction between sense and force. Even for declaratives, knowledge of truth conditions may not suffice for understanding. More generally, knowledge of meaning may not suffice for understanding. A reliable informant tells me that a sentence of Hungarian written on the board means that the cat sat on the mat; I know by testimony that the sentence means that the cat sat on the mat, but arguably I do not understand it because I have no idea what each constituent word contributes to that meaning. Such complications will be ignored in what follows. ↩︎

Dummett says that “no difficulty can any longer arise over what such knowledge consists in”—Elements of Intuitionism (New York: Oxford, 1977), p. 375. Note that assertibility conditions are not truth conditions even on Dummett’s antirealist conception of truth (see footnote 21 below). ↩︎
Frege: Philosophy of Language, p. 586; see also The Logical Basis of Metaphysics (Cambridge: Harvard, 1991), p. 317, and The Seas of Language, pp. 45–46. ↩︎

On recognizing intuitionistic proofs as proofs, see S. Weinstein, “The Intended Interpretation of Intuitionistic Logic,” Journal of Philosophical Logic, XII (1983): 261–70; and Peter Pagin, “Knowledge of Proofs,” Topoi, XIII (1994): 93–100. An assertibility-conditional theory of meaning is likely to distinguish between canonical and noncanonical warrants for assertion—for example, between having a proof and having been told by a reliable informant that there is one. The recursive semantics will be formulated in terms of canonical warrants; a noncanonical warrant will be explained as an entitlement to believe that there is a canonical warrant. The argument in the text applies whether or not ‘warrant’ is qualified by ‘canonical’. ↩︎

In criticizing truth-conditional theories of meaning, Dummett often focuses on the undecidability of truth, that is, on the fact that speakers do not always have an effective procedure for coming to know whether a given truth condition obtains. When the argument takes this form, it threatens assertibility-conditional theories of meaning, too, unless assertibility is decidable, that is, unless speakers always have an effective procedure for coming to know whether a given assertibility condition obtains (Wright endorses the decidability of assertibility; see Truth and Objectivity (Cambridge: Harvard, 1992), p. 56). The decidability of assertibility does not entail the decidability of truth, even on most antirealist conceptions of truth, for the latter do not identify truth with assertibility in nonideal contexts. For example, intuitionists identify assertibility with possession of a proof and truth with the existence of one (that is, with the possibility of possessing it); they deny the law of excluded middle just because they take truth to be undecidable. Even if assertibility were luminous, its decidability would follow only on the additional assumption that unassertibility is luminous, too. Thus, what the antirealist requires of assertibility depends on whether what realist truth crucially lacks is luminosity or decidability, even though, given bivalence and the presence of classical negation in the object language—both assumptions acceptable to the realist—truth is decidable if and only if it is luminous (on an appropriate construal of ‘in a position to know’). But since any decidable condition is luminous (on that construal), the points in the text apply to both forms of antirealist argument. ↩︎
Wright seems to assume the S4 principle for assertibility in arguing that truth and assertibility coincide in “positive normative force” (op. cit., p. 18). ↩︎
See my “Does Assertibility Satisfy the S4 Axiom?” Crítica, XXVII, 81 (1995): 3–22. ↩︎

See my “Knowing and Asserting” (forthcoming). Dummett sometimes seems to lose sight of the distinction between defeasibility and nonfactiveness—for example, at Frege: Philosophy of Language, p. 355. ↩︎

works.title: Quantifiers and context-dependence
passages: Let DDQ be the thesis that definite descriptions are quantifiers. Philosophers often deny DDQ because they believe that quantifiers do not depend on context in certain ways, ways in which definite descriptions do depend on context. In this paper, we examine one such argument, which, if sound, would entail the negation of DDQ.1 We show that this argument fails, and draw some consequences from its failure.
As is familiar, the truth of an utterance of a sentence containing a quantified expression must be evaluated with respect to a contextually determined domain. An utterance of
Every bottle has been put on the shelf.

would not be true in an ordinary context in which a normal-sized shelf is at issue, unless the domain contained few of all the world’s bottles. Since there are clearly true utterances of (1) in ordinary contexts, it follows that utterances of sentences containing quantified expressions are evaluated with respect to contextually restricted domains.

Correct evaluation requires contextually determined variation in the domain between different utterances of the same sentence. Does it ever require contextually determined variation in the domain within a single utterance of a sentence? Utterances of sentences such as
Every bottle has been put on the shelf, but some bottles have not been put on the shelf.

sound paradoxical, indeed self-contradictory. One might therefore conclude that evaluation never requires contextually determined variation in the domain within a single utterance of a sentence. On this view, the evaluation of quantified expressions requires only utterances of whole sentences to be assigned to contexts; no such assignment to utterances of sub-sentential expressions is needed. Call this the Sentential Quantifier Thesis:
The context-dependence of quantifiers is captured by assigning utterances of sentences containing them to contexts.

SQT implies that domains for quantifiers can differ contextually only across sentential boundaries. Thus it implies that one can ascertain the truth-value of an utterance of a sentence containing two or more quantifiers by taking the domain of all quantifiers within the sentence to be the same.2

One who accepts SQT will conclude that DDQ is false, i.e. that definite descriptions are not quantifiers, for a reason now to be explained. Suppose that DDQ is true. Then the sentence ‘The F is G’ will be parsed as of something like the form ‘(The x: Fx)Gx’, and sentences of that form will be given something like the following semantics:
A sequence σ satisfies ‘(The x: Fx)Gx’ with respect to a domain D for that quantifier iff the sequence which
(i) assigns a member of D to ‘x’,
(ii) differs from σ at most in its assignment to ‘x’, and

What follows ‘iff’ is to be read as equivalent to the Russellian condition that one and only one sequence has the three properties (i) to (iii), and it satisfies ‘Gx’. Technicalities aside, THE implies that an utterance of ‘The F is G’ is true with respect to a domain just in case one and only one member of the domain is an F, and it is also G.
If definite descriptions are indeed quantifiers, then they pose a serious problem for SQT. Consider the following example, as in Lewis’s seminal ‘Score-keeping in a language game’:3
The dog bit the other dog.

Utterances of (3) do not sound paradoxical or self-contradictory; some are true. However, if DDQ is true, then, if SQT were true, (3) should sound paradoxical, even self-contradictory. For SQT requires evaluation to proceed with respect to the same domain for the two supposedly quantified expressions, ‘the dog’ and ‘the other dog’. (3) will be parsed as something like:
(The x: x is a dog)(The y: y is a dog and y≠x)x bit y.

For (3’) to be satisfied, the domain must contain exactly one dog; but ‘(The y: y is another dog) x bit y’ must also be satisfied, which requires another dog in the domain, for which there is no room. Thus SQT conspires with DDQ to prevent utterances of (3) from being true.

One might react to such examples by rejecting SQT, reasoning that since definite descriptions are quantifiers, they are counterexamples to SQT. On this view, (3) shows that the domain of quantification can shift within the utterance of a single sentence. However, in the absence of further support, this reaction involves a somewhat dogmatic adherence to DDQ. Alternatively, one could, of course, retain SQT and therefore reject DDQ.
However, SQT is false, and can be seen to be false quite independently of issues about descriptions. Consider this example:
A group of evangelists met in the square, whereupon everyone converted someone.

Clearly, the evangelists did not convert each other; they were already evangelists. An utterance of (4) is most naturally understood as asserting that every one of the evangelists converted someone who was not (yet) an evangelist. This reading requires the domain for ‘everyone’ to differ from the domain for ‘someone’. Since ‘everyone’ and ‘someone’ are clearly quantifiers, and occur within the same sentence, SQT is false.4
Examples such as (4) abound. Another is:
Someone angered everyone by being overly joyful.
An utterance of (5) is not naturally interpreted as implying that someone angered herself by her joyfulness.
There are also counterexamples to SQT in which different occurrences of the same quantified expression must be assigned different domains. A charming case, communicated to us by Peter Ludlow, is:
However, (6) would not be a counterexample to the following weakened version of SQT:
If no clausal boundaries appear between two occurrences Q and Q′ of quantified expressions, then Q and Q′ must be evaluated with respect to the same domain.
However, (4) and (5) are already counterexamples to CQT. A counterexample to CQT in which Q and Q′ are occurrences of the same quantified expression is this:
As the ship pulled away from the dock, every man waved to every woman, every woman waved to every man, and every child waved to every child.

It is natural to interpret (7) as not implying that if two children were both on the dock (or both on the ship) then they waved to each other, and as still less implying that they waved to themselves. Exercise: Is the following a counterexample to CQT?
When we looked out of the window, everyone saw everyone putting up their umbrellas.
(It is natural to interpret the first ‘everyone’ with respect to a domain of people inside looking out and the second with respect to a domain of people outside being looked at from within).

Several consequences flow from the failure of SQT/CQT. One such consequence is an argument that descriptions should be treated as unitary quantifier expressions, rather than analysed away in terms of their Russellian expansions. For consider (9), the English sentence expressing the Russellian expansion of (10):
There is exactly one bottle, and every bottle is in the refrigerator.
The bottle is in the refrigerator.

(9) could be uttered truly in a context in which there is exactly one coke bottle, and it is on the table, and all of the (many) beer bottles are in the refrigerator. (10), of course, has no such reading. Thus, the English sentence which expresses the Russellian expansion of a definite description is more context sensitive than the sentence which contains just the definite description. Since the failure of SQT/CQT shows that the domain can vary with each quantified expression, whereas only one domain is possible for utterances of (10), we can safely conclude that definite descriptions are not shorthand for English sentences containing multiple quantified expressions.

The failure of SQT/CQT also seems to us to provide evidence for DDQ. First of all, it demonstrates that examples such as (3) cannot be used as arguments against DDQ. But it also, arguably, shows something more. In the literature on incomplete descriptions, philosophers tend to assume that an account of the context-dependence of terms such as ‘every’ and ‘some’ is relatively easy to come by, but no such account will work for descriptions.
