Material in this paper was used in talks and classes at Oxford University, the Catholic University of Lublin, New York University, the University of New Mexico, Yale University, M.I.T., the University of St. Andrews, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, the Classical University of Lisbon and the University of Sussex; too many people improved it with their questions to be thanked individually. Peter Lipton, Roy Sorensen, Tim Cleveland, Pedro Hecht, Jonathan Dancy, Bill Brewer, Lloyd Humberstone, Mark Sainsbury, Scott Sturgeon and Mike Martin provided useful written comments. Discussions with John Campbell, Jonathan Dancy, Kit Fine, Elizabeth Fricker and James Higginbotham have also been very helpful.

Three clarifications: (a) only propositional knowledge will be considered; (b) the phrases “state of mind” and “mental state” will be used interchangeably; (c) the assumption that knowing entails believing will be examined in § VI. ↩︎
If our man has been convinced by the argument of Descartes’ Meditations, he will regard it as preserving him from philosophical scepticism. ↩︎
Hintikka (1962, p. 106) presents a similar case. ↩︎
Williamson (1992) argues on grounds compatible with the present account that one can know that P without being in a position to know that one knows that P. ↩︎

For the bearing of a similar view of knowledge on sceptical issues see McDowell (1982). The non-transitivity of indiscriminability between situations is another reason for not equating it with identity of mental state. ↩︎

On this kind of asymmetry of discrimination see Williams (1978, p. 309-313) and Humberstone (1988). Two further sceptical tactics are: (i) to consider a subject whose situation is oscillating over time between the good one and the bad one; (ii) to work with the relation of apparent identity rather than with that of indiscriminability. Ad (i): that subject may indeed be unable to discriminate between the good situation, presented indexically as “my present situation”, and the bad situation, presented indexically as “my situation five minutes ago”, and therefore lack the relevant knowledge. It does not follow that one lacks that knowledge even if one’s situation is not in fact oscillating. Ad (ii): apparent identity does differ from indiscriminability, for the two lines in the Müller-Lyer illusion are indiscriminable (because identical) in length, but do not look identical in length. However, an analogue of the point in the text about the modes of presentation of the two situations still makes difficulty for this version of the sceptic’s argument. Perhaps the subject has the same sensations in both cases, but so what? It should also be noted that anti-sceptical claims about the context-dependence of “know” are compatible with the present account, for “mental state” may be context-dependent too. ↩︎
In the relevant sense, a triangle is a physical shape of a particular size. Count all lines as indiscriminable in length to the naked human eye in situations in which there are no human eyes. ↩︎

From the perspective of a world w, a world w* is nomically possible just in case all the natural laws of w hold in w*. The use of nomic rather than metaphysical necessity is simply for commensurability with § IV, where the former is preferred in order not to make the internalist supervenience claim (5) stronger than it needs to be. As for the quantification over possible worlds, no objection is made here to reductionist accounts of it. ↩︎

See Shope (1983) for the history of a decade of research into the analysis of knowing after Gettier (1963); an equally complex book could be written on post-1983 developments. Not all this work aims to provide an analysis in the traditional sense; see Shope (1983, pp. 34–44). ↩︎

Craig (1990) interestingly attempts to explain the point of the concept of knowledge in the light of the failure of analyses of the standard kind. However, on the present view the approach remains too close to the traditional programme, for it takes as its starting our need for true beliefs about our environment (p. 11), as though this were somehow more basic than our need for knowledge of our environment. It is no reply that believing truly is as useful as knowing, for it is agreed that the starting point should be more specific than “useful mental state”; why should it be specific in the manner of “believing truly” rather than in that of “knowing”? ↩︎

For a sophisticated defence of conceptual analysis see Smith (1994, pp. 29–56, 161–4). However, the kind of non-reductive analysis that Smith defends constitutes little threat to the claim that knowing is a mental state in every reasonable sense of the latter term. Moreover, no positive reason is provided to suppose that a concept such as knowing can be non-trivially analysed even in the non-reductive sense. Much more needs to be said about the possible standards for conceptual analysis than can be said here. ↩︎
Russell (1910–11), Salmon and Soames (1988, p. 23); Russell calls it “The fundamental epistemological principle in the analysis of propositions containing descriptions”. ↩︎

In effect, Evans (1982) combines the Principle of Acquaintance with a conception of acquaintance much less extreme than Russell’s. Of course, Russell’s extreme empiricism on this point is not a mere extraneous dogma; it is an attempt to solve puzzles about identity and non-existence of denotation in intentional contexts. Unfortunately, the cure is worse than the disease. ↩︎

A further ground for suspicion of analyses of the concept of knowing in terms of the concept of believing is that they seem to imply that the latter concept is acquired before the former. Data on child development suggest, if anything, the reverse order (see Perner 1993, pp. 145–203 for discussion of relevant work). Crudely: children understand ignorance before they understand error. Naturally, the data can be interpreted in various ways, and their bearing on the order of analysis depends on subtle issues in the theory of concepts. ↩︎

The characterization of internalism in the text is not fully general, for it neglects radically dualist versions. The form of the argument would be little changed if “physical state” were replaced by “phenomenal state”, read internalistically. For simplicity, the text focuses on the currently most popular version of internalism. ↩︎
Whether, conversely, (4) entails (3) depends on whether what supervenes on one’s mental state is itself a mental state, a question not settled here. ↩︎

There is no corresponding sense in which something can be red, all but for being coloured; in this sense “know” is more complex than the example of “red” used in § III. But it does not follow that the distinction between what supervenes on internal physical state and what does not has any more significance for mental states than the distinction between what supervenes on weight and what does not. ↩︎
Stich (1978, p. 574), quoted in Kim (1993, p. 188). Kim (1993, pp. 175–93) is a clear statement of the kind of view opposed here. ↩︎
See Putnam (1973). The influence of Burge’s work, e.g. Burge (1986), will also be obvious. ↩︎
Predicates such as “loves Mary” and “hates Mary” are also wide, for their application depends on a relation to the particular individual named. ↩︎

The argument as stated assumes: (a) knowing entails believing; (b) the probability of his having entered the house not knowing that there was a diamond in it, conditional on his having entered it believing truly that there was a diamond in it, is non-zero. (a) may be an over-simplification (see § VI); if so, its restriction to the case at hand remains plausible and is all the argument requires. (b) is obvious in the relevant cases. The relevant fact about probability is that if Y entails X and Prob⁡(¬Y∣X)>0 then Prob⁡(Z∣X∧¬Y)<Prob⁡(Z∣Y) just in case Prob⁡(Z∣X)<Prob⁡(Z∣Y). ↩︎

It is not assumed that lowering the probability of the explanandum conditional on the explanans strictly entails loss of explanatory power: just that it results in such a loss when, as here, there are no compensating gains. ↩︎
See Pettit (1986) and Child (1994, pp. 204–16) for more discussion of related issues. ↩︎

A similar response can be made to the argument that knowing is not a mental state in the way that believing is because “know” is a normative term. Belief attributions have a normative element too, for to have any mental attitude to a content one must have some minimal ability to deal rationally with that content, and “rational” is at least as normative a term as “know”. ↩︎
The scrupulous will read quotation marks as corner quotes where appropriate. ↩︎
See Grice (1989, pp. 44–6, 279–80) for cancellability and the presuppositions of “know” respectively. ↩︎
See Vendler (1967, p. 104) for more on the linguistic marks of statives. ↩︎
See Unger (1975, pp. 158–83) for a good discussion. ↩︎
Steup (1992) is a recent example of such a view. ↩︎

The states in question are general: different people can be in them at different times. No claim is made about the essences of state tokens; indeed, the idea of a state token is of doubtful coherence. With respect to general states, the claims of necessity are de re, not just de dicto. Given (3) above, the de dicto claim “Necessarily for all x if x knows that P then P” implies the de re claim “There is a mental state S such that necessarily for all x if x is in S then P”. ↩︎
Someone who denies that the concept characterized in the text is our concept of knowing might think that it is more useful than the latter. ↩︎

The present account of knowing is consistent with the main features of a theory of concepts such as that in Peacocke (1992), on which an account of a concept gives necessary and sufficient conditions for possession of the concept without any need to decompose the concept itself. However, the account is not committed to any general programme of that kind. ↩︎
See Radford (1966), Armstrong (1973, pp. 138–149) and Shope (1983, pp. 178–87) for further discussion of such cases. ↩︎
See Austin (1946), Vendler (1972, pp. 89–119) and Shope (1983, pp. 171–8, 191–2) for further discussion of grammatical differences between “know” and “believe”. ↩︎

See Hinton (1967 and 1973), Snowdon (1980-81 and 1990), McDowell (1982) and Child (1994, pp. 143–64). That the disjuncts in a disjunctive account be mutually exclusive is not required by logic, although it may be by some philosophical applications (as it is by McDowell’s). ↩︎

Contrast: x opines that P if and only if x is in a state that x cannot discriminate from knowing that P, i.e. that is, for all x knows, knowing that P. The form in the text is preferable, for Twin Oscar is in a state that he cannot discriminate from knowing that water is wet, but does not believe, and therefore does not opine, that water is wet. ↩︎

One attraction of an explanation of believing to which the case of knowing is central is that it opens the prospect of explaining the impossibility, remarked by Hume, of believing that P at will in terms of the impossibility of knowing that P at will. ↩︎
Similar objections apply to disjunctive accounts of perception, appearance and experience. ↩︎

works.title: Does assertibility satisfy the S4 axiom?
passages: Many discussions of warranted assertibility take the following principle for granted:
If it is assertible that P, then it is assertible that it is assertible that P.

‘Assertible’ abbreviates ‘warrantedly assertible’ throughout. (AA) is the result of reading □ in the S4 axiom of modal logic □p→□□p as ‘it is assertible that’, or of substituting those words for ‘one knows that’ in the KK schema ‘If one knows that P, then one knows that one knows that P’. This paper argues that (AA) has false consequences.

Some clarifications: Assertibility depends on circumstances; it is gained or lost as the available evidence changes. Thus (AA) has implicit generality both over circumstances and in the schematic variable ‘P’. ‘P’ is replaceable by declarative sentences, which may have features sensitive to the circumstances, e.g. tense (as in the third occurrence of ‘is’ in (AA)). The circumstances are the context in which the assertion that P is envisaged as being made, which need not be the context in which (AA) itself is asserted. Although circumstances need not be actual, those considered below are physically possible and probably actual. It will be left open whether more than one person can be in the same circumstances; empirically, it may happen that only one person is in given circumstances. ‘Assertible’ will not be further defined, for the objection to (AA) is intended to apply over a wide range of readings.1

(AA) is particularly relevant to Michael Dummett’s arguments for an anti-realist theory of meaning. To summarize very roughly, Dummett objects to truth conditional theories of meaning that they violate a required connection between meaning and use: since the users of a sentence may be unable to recognize its truth condition as obtaining when it does obtain, its obtaining then would be a feature of its meaning not properly reflected in its use. The proposed remedy is that the meanings of sentences should be given by their assertibility conditions, not by their truth conditions. The remedy would fail if the objection to truth conditional theories of meaning applied equally to assertibility conditional theories of meaning; thus the argument requires that the users of a sentence must be able to recognize its assertibility condition as obtaining when it does obtain. Dummett endorses this requirement: ‘The conditions under which a sentence is recognized as true or false [. . .] have, by the nature of the case, to be conditions which we can recognize as obtaining when they obtain’ (Dummett 1981, p. 586); ‘according to a verificationist theory, [. . .] that in which an understanding of the sentence consists is an ability to recognize, whenever presented with it, whatever we take to count as establishing its truth’ (Dummett 1991, p. 317; see also Dummett 1993, pp. 45–46). That is, if one is in a position to recognize that the truth condition obtains, then one is in a position to recognize that one is in a position to recognize that it obtains. When the truth condition is that P, and ‘one is in a position to recognize’ is abbreviated by ‘it is assertible’ (as Dummett’s account permits), the result is (AA).2,3

Dummett treats (AA) as unproblematic (see also Dummett 1977, p. 375). It is not clear why. On the natural understanding of recognition as the acquisition of knowledge, (AA) is tantamount to the highly contentious principle that if one is in a position to know that P, then one is in a position to know that one is in a position to know that P: not something to be assumed without argument.4 Now both recognition and knowledge are factive attitudes; one is not even in a position to recognize or know that P unless P. If having a warrant to assert that P is equated with being in a position to know or recognize that P, then only truths are warrantedly assertible. Even if a falsehood is strongly supported by evidence, one is not warranted in asserting it. Perhaps surprisingly, there is much to be said for the principle that one has a warrant to assert that P if and only if one knows that P (Williamson 1995). However, this is not the place to say it, and the principle will not be assumed in what follows. The anti-realist may wish to adopt a conception of assertibility on which falsehoods are assertible when strongly supported by evidence, and may even suppose that such a conception makes (AA) more plausible. The arguments below are neutral towards the factiveness of assertibility; its denial does not help the anti-realist to defeat them.5

If the argument in III is correct, Dummett’s objection refutes truth conditional theories of meaning just in case it also refutes assertibility conditional theories of meaning. The point is not confined to assertibility as an alternative to truth in theories of meaning. If the generalized argument in VI is correct, nothing could have the characteristics that Dummett’s objection requires of the central notion in a theory of meaning. The moral presumably to be drawn is not that an adequate theory of meaning is impossible, but that something is wrong with Dummett’s objection. However, this is not the place to examine the grounds for Dummett’s objection. It will be more fruitful to consider what positive view of the relation between assertibility and truth is suggested by the arguments below. Some brief remarks to that effect will be made in conclusion.

Imagine an early navigator sailing unknown seas on a slowly moving boat. He wonders whether there is land ahead (at any distance: assume for simplicity that he does not know that the earth is round). Early in the morning, he has no idea; it is clear to him that no land is yet visible. Gradually something appears on the horizon. At first he is not sure whether he is imagining it; even after he is sure, he has at first no idea whether it is land or a mere bank of clouds. The former hypothesis slowly gains in probability over the latter. After several hours there is no doubt. By evening the boat is moored to land. The navigator is phlegmatic; his confidence that there is land ahead grows as slowly as the visible scene changes; he experiences no flash of conviction. The whole process is gradual.

Let t0 be a time early in the morning; for each natural number i, let ti be the time i seconds after t0; let tn be a time late in the evening. For each natural number i from 0 to n, let ci be the navigator’s circumstances at ti insofar as they are relevant to the assertibility of the claim that there is land ahead (this qualification will henceforth be understood). Although the navigator can easily discriminate between cn and c0, for no i can he discriminate between ci and ci−1 (indiscriminability is non-transitive). He cannot discriminate between his present circumstances and those in which he was a second ago; the change is too slow. For all that he has a warrant to assert in ci, he is in ci−1. Thus the following holds whenever a sentence concerning his circumstances replaces ‘P’:
If in ci it is assertible that P, then in ci−1 P.

(1≤i≤n, a qualification understood henceforth). ‘P’ should be read as expressing a condition on circumstances, not a fixed proposition: ‘In ci P’ does not entail ‘In cj P’ when i≠j. We often use declarative sentences like that in natural languages: ‘In Mexico it is raining’ does not entail ‘In Britain it is raining’.

(1) holds in virtue of the specific circumstances at issue; it does not purport to be a general truth. If (1) failed, something would be assertible in ci without being true in ci−1: but then the navigator would have a warrant to assert something in ci that was incompatible with being in ci−1. Moreover, ci−1 is a contextually relevant alternative to ci, for he was in it only a second earlier. The navigator has no such warrant; the difference between ci and ci−1 is far too small for him to detect. (1) would fail if he had misleading evidence that made some general falsehood assertible, but clearly the example can be so constructed that he has no such evidence. Although his evidence is inadequate at first to warrant a judgement whether there is land ahead, that does not make it positively misleading. Again, (1) might fail if he made a perceptual misjudgement, but the example can be so constructed that he makes no such misjudgement. If there is a warrant to assert that P, then it appears to be safe to assert that P, so, unless appearances are misleading, it is safe to assert that P. In ci appearances are not misleading, but it is not safe to assert that P, unless in ci−1 P, for otherwise the example can be so constructed that someone who asserted in ci might easily have asserted falsely in ci−1 that P (for relevant values of ‘P’, whether in ci−1 P does not depend on whether someone asserts that P). Thus if in ci there is a warrant to assert that P, then in ci−1 P.

The following objection to (1) might be made. In ci the navigator could introduce a name, e.g. ‘Kirk’, for his circumstances by ostension. Thus in ci it is trivially assertible that one is in Kirk. It would then follow by (1) that in ci−1 one is in Kirk: but that consequence is true only if ci and ci−1 are identical, which in general they are not. Although the distinctness of ci and ci−1 does not follow merely from the distinctness of i and i−1, since there might have been no change in circumstances from ti−1 to ti, ci and ci−1 must be distinct for many i, otherwise cn and c0 would not differ as much as they do. What the objection neglects is the significance of the qualification ‘in ci’ in the antecedent of (1). ‘In c Q’ on its intended reading is true only if it is necessary for the realization of c that Q. That condition is not met when c=ci and ‘Q’ = ‘It is assertible that one is in Kirk’. For ci can be realized again in the future, and it will not then be assertible that one is in Kirk; although one will in fact be in Kirk, one will be unable to discriminate finely enough to assert that one is in Kirk rather than a different but very similar set of circumstances in which one could easily be (since the introduction of the name ‘Kirk’ is not relevant to the assertibility of the claim that there is land ahead, it is not part of ci). Thus the antecedent of (1) is not true in the relevant case, and the objection fails.

A similar objection to (1) might exploit ostension of the time rather than of the circumstances. The suggestion would be that in ci it is assertible that the time is now, even though it is not the case that in ci−1 the time is now. The reply to the objection is also similar: the time is not essential to the circumstances, because it is not as such relevant to the assertibility of the claim that there is land ahead. Thus it is not the case that in ci it is assertible that the time is now.
One sentence concerning the navigator’s circumstances is ‘It is assertible that there is land ahead’. Thus the following holds as an instance of (1):
If in ci it is assertible that it is assertible that there is land ahead, then in ci−1 it is assertible that there is land ahead.

Note that, in the replacement for ‘P’, ‘assertible’ adverts to one set of circumstances in the antecedent of (2) and another in the consequent. That is quite consistent with the rationale for (1), for the navigator in ci has no warrant to assert a feature of his circumstances that would differentiate them from ci−1. The assertibility of the claim that there is land ahead is just such a feature of the circumstances.
Now assume (AA), for a reductio ad absurdum. Then the following instance of (AA) holds, with the circumstances made explicit:
If in ci it is assertible that there is land ahead, then in ci it is assertible that it is assertible that there is land ahead.
By the transitivity of the conditional (which may as well be material throughout), (2) and (3) yield:
If in ci it is assertible that there is land ahead, then in ci−1 it is assertible that there is land ahead.
So far, i has been arbitrary. Thus (4) has been derived for each i from n to 1. Given transitivity again, those n conditionals together yield:
If in cn it is assertible that there is land ahead, then in c0 it is assertible that there is land ahead.

(5) is false. The antecedent is true; in cn (late evening) it is manifestly assertible that there is land ahead. The consequent is false; in c0 (early morning) it is manifestly not assertible that there is land ahead (recall that assertibility varies with the evidence). Thus (AA) has false consequences. When the navigator is warranted in asserting ‘There is land ahead’, his warrant need not be transparent to him; he may have no warrant to assert ‘My last assertion was warranted’.

Could a rival case be made for blaming one of the other assumptions of the argument, (1) or the transitivity of the conditional? The best prospect for such a case is by appeal to the apparent affinity between the argument and sorites paradoxes. It might be suggested that the support for (1) is defective in whatever way the support for the major premise of a sorites paradox, e.g. ‘If i grains make a heap, then i−1 grains make a heap’, is defective. Alternatively, it might be suggested that, although (1) is true enough, the conditional is non-transitive, as some treatments of sorites paradoxes allege it to be.6 In either case, the problem will be traced to vagueness in some relevant term, and (AA) will be exonerated.

Treatments of the conditional on which vagueness makes it non-transitive are independently objectionable (Williamson 1994, pp. 123–138). They involve a problematic notion of degree of truth on which a conditional can be true enough to be true even though its consequent is slightly less true than its antecedent. In any case, one can shift the problem from the alleged non-transitivity of the conditional to the status of (1) by moving to a context in which only perfect truth counts as truth, so that a conditional is true enough to be true only if its consequent is at least as true as its antecedent. In this context, the transitivity of the conditional is unproblematic. Such a standard of truth is not unfair to (AA), whose proponents do not advance it as only roughly true.

The only serious candidate for the relevantly vague term is ‘assertible’. It is indeed vague; it has borderline cases. The question is whether its vagueness is the source of the present problem for (AA). If it is, then the problem would disappear if ‘assertible’ were made precise. That is, (1) would gain an obviously false instance, just as the schema ‘If i grains make a heap, then i−1 grains make a heap’ gains an obviously false instance when ‘heap’ is made precise enough by the stipulation of an arbitrary cut-off point. Suppose then that ‘assertible’ is sharpened, and in particular that this is done by tightening up the conditions for its application, so that borderline cases are resolved in favour of its non-application. ‘Assertible’ still applies in its new sense wherever it manifestly applied in its old sense; it still fails to apply in its new sense wherever it manifestly failed to apply in its old sense. For example, one might pick appropriate circumstances ci and stipulate that to be assertible is to be at least as assertible as it is assertible in ci that there is land ahead (for reasons connected with the discussion of the name ‘Kirk’ above, it would be misleading as well as unnecessary to imagine the navigator himself making the stipulation). Although the stipulation would not make ‘assertible’ perfectly precise, it would eliminate some vagueness. If the plausibility of (1) depends on the vagueness of ‘assertible’, then enough stipulation should give (1) an obviously false instance.

Does sharpening give (1) a false instance? On the contrary, (1) becomes more plausible, not less, for one only strengthens its antecedent by restricting the application of ‘assertible’. Such verbal stipulations do nothing to improve the navigator’s ability to discriminate between his successive circumstances. Note that, although the term ‘assertible’ may itself occur in substitutions for ‘P’ in (1), this does not matter, because (1) holds for any appropriate substitution for ‘P’, irrespective of whether ‘assertible’ in it has been sharpened. Moreover, (5) remains obviously false, for it involves only cases in which ‘assertible’ manifestly applies or manifestly fails to apply in its old sense. Thus the present problem for (AA) is merely exacerbated when ‘assertible’ is sharpened. The case for (1) does not depend on the vagueness of ‘assertible’. Vagueness is a red herring.7

Further to contrast (1) with the major premise of a sorites paradox, note that a classical semantics can make all instances of (1) true and (5) false. The following example uses some ideas from possible world semantics with a non-transitive relation of accessibility between worlds, corresponding to the failure of the S4 axiom. It is intended for illustrative purposes only. Treat truth-functional connectives classically. Evaluate ‘In ci it is assertible that P’ as true if and only if ‘In ci−1 P’ (for i≥1), ‘In ci P’ and ‘In ci+1 P’ (for i<n) are all true, and otherwise as false. Thus every instance of (1) is evaluated as true. Evaluate ‘In ci there is land ahead’ as true if and only if i≥n−1. Then (5) is evaluated as false, as is the instance (3) of (AA) for i=n.

Granted the failure of (AA), an attempt might be made to construct a new notion of assertibility, assertibility∗, that does satisfy the S4 axiom, out of the old one. Call circumstances c′ accessible from circumstances c if and only if everything assertible in c is true in c′. Let accessibility∗ be the (strong) ancestral of accessibility, i.e. c′ is accessible∗ from c if and only if for some sequence c0,…,cn (n>0), c0=c′, cn=c and each ci−1 is accessible from ci. Let it be assertible∗ in circumstances c that P if and only if in all circumstances c′ accessible∗ from c, P. Since accessibility∗ is automatically transitive, even though accessibility is non-transitive, assertibility∗ satisfies the S4 axiom.

The trouble with this construction is that assertibility∗ does not provide a reasonable standard of assertibility. Consider the navigator again. For each i, ci−1 is accessible from ci, by (1). Moreover, it is consistent with everything assertible in c0 that there is no land ahead, so circumstances d in which there is no land ahead are accessible from c0. Thus d is accessible∗ from cn. By definition of ‘assertible∗’, it is not assertible∗ in cn that there is land ahead. Yet it is quite obvious in cn that there is land ahead. The standard for assertibility∗ is too demanding to be of much interest.

A closely related point is this. For any i, let ‘it is assertiblei that’ abbreviate a string of i occurrences of ‘it is assertible that’. One can easily show by induction on i that in ci it is not assertiblei+1 that there is land ahead, using (1) and the fact that in c0 it is not assertible that there is land ahead. In particular, in cn it is not assertiblen+1 that there is land ahead. Warrants are not perfectly transparent even in cn. Although the navigator is warranted in asserting ‘There is land ahead’ in cn, and in adding several iterations of ‘it is assertible that’ to his assertion, he has no warrant to iterate indefinitely.

The argument of III generalizes. Nothing in it requires the replacement for ‘P’ in (1) to involve the notion of assertibility. Rather, an argument schema has been provided against any principle of the form:
If P, then it is assertible that P.

(AA*) is to be understood as advanced for all circumstances but a fixed ‘P’. Restrict circumstances to what is relevant to the assertibility of the claim that P. Suppose that circumstances c in which not P can change gradually into circumstances c′ in which P, without passing through circumstances in which one has misleading (as opposed to inadequate) evidence, makes perceptual misjudgements, etc. Since the subject’s powers of discrimination are limited, there is a series of successive circumstances, c0,…,cn between c (=c0) and c′ (=cn), each close enough to the next for (1) to hold (as reinterpreted for this case). Call such a series a fadeout for ‘P’. Thus (5*) is false:
If in cn P, then in c0 P.
Now assume (AA*), for a reductio ad absurdum. Then the following instance holds, with the circumstances made explicit:
If in ci P, then in ci it is assertible that P.
If in ci P, then in ci−1 P.

Since i was arbitrary, n instances of (4*) yield the false (5*). (AA*) is the culprit. As before, it would be a mistake to appeal to sorites paradoxes and blame (1) or the transitivity of the conditional.

(AA*) has false consequences whenever there is a fadeout for ‘P’. Most ordinary empirical claims have fadeouts. One can pass gradually from not being in pain to being in pain, from not seeing a red patch to seeing a red patch; things can change gradually from its not raining to its raining, from there not being humans to there being humans, and so on. Thus the principles ‘If one is in pain, then it is assertible that one is in pain’, ‘If one is seeing a red patch, then it is assertible that one is seeing a red patch’, ‘If it is raining, then it is assertible that it is raining’, ‘If there are humans, then it is assertible that there are humans’ and so on all have false consequences. Nor is the vagueness of the terms ‘pain’, ‘red’, ‘rain’ and ‘human’ crucial here; if they were sharpened by verbal stipulations, (AA*) would still fail under the relevant interpretations, for the subject’s powers of empirical discrimination would not have been improved.

The form of argument just considered does not apply when ‘P’ is an eternal sentence, always true if ever true, for no change would then take one from circumstances in which not P to circumstances in which P. If it is nevertheless contingent whether P, one might consider a revised version of the argument in which the series of circumstances c0,…,cn runs through different possible worlds rather than different times. However, a better revision is available, for even if ‘P’ is an eternal or non-contingent sentence, ‘It is assertible that P’ need not be.

Restrict circumstances to what is relevant to the assertibility of the claim that it is assertible that P. Suppose that circumstances c in which it is not assertible that P can change gradually into circumstances c′ in which it is assertible that P, without passing through circumstances in which one has misleading (as opposed to inadequate) evidence. Since the subject’s powers of discrimination are limited, there is a series of successive circumstances c0,…,cn between c (=c0) and c′ (=cn), each close enough to the next for (1) to hold (as reinterpreted for this case). Such a series is a fadeout for ‘It is assertible that P’. Thus (5**) is false:
If in cn it is assertible that P, then in c0 it is assertible that P.
Now assume (AA*), for a reductio ad absurdum. Then the following instance holds:
If in ci−1 P, then in ci−1 it is assertible that P.
If in ci it is assertible that P, then in ci−1 it is assertible that P.
Since i was arbitrary, n instances of (4**) yield the false (5**). As before, (AA*) is the culprit.8

(AA*) has false consequences whenever there is a fadeout for ‘It is assertible that P’. What correct principles of the form (AA*) does that leave? If in no circumstances P, then (AA*) is vacuously correct. If in all circumstances it is assertible that P, then (AA*) is again automatically correct, although an obvious question is whether this case can arise: is it assertible that P in circumstances incompatible with cognitive activity? However, no argument for a negative answer will be provided here.9 Suppose that in some circumstances P and in some circumstances it is not assertible that P. If (AA*) is correct for ‘P’, then the former conjunct implies that in some circumstances it is assertible that P. Thus it is assertible that P in some circumstances and not in others. What is to stop the construction of a fadeout from the former to the latter? Could there be an unbridgeable abyss between the circumstances in which it is assertible that P and all other circumstances, defeating the gradualness requirement? Could all the circumstances in which it is assertible that P involve misleading (as opposed to inadequate) evidence, perceptual misjudgements, etc., undermining (1)?10 An attractively simple conjecture is that such obstacles do not arise. More boldly, one may conjecture the following, for every claim that P:
It is assertible that P in all circumstances in which P if and only if there are no circumstances in which P.
The foregoing arguments do not establish (Conj), but they do suggest that, at worst, it fails only in a few marginal cases.11

The argument against (AA) is closely related to an argument against the KK principle that if one knows that P, then one knows that one knows that P (Williamson 1992). Indeed, the substitution of ‘known’ for ‘assertible’ turns the argument against (AA) into an argument against the KK principle. All the relevant assumptions retain their plausibility under this substitution. As already noted, nothing in the argument presupposes the general equivalence of ‘assertible’ and ‘known’; rather, its strategy is to exploit special cases in which any reasonable form of assertibility will behave in a knowledge-like way. This explains the need for assertibility not to depend on misleading evidence in the relevant cases. Indeed, since (1) relies on the similarity between the circumstances ci and ci−1, it is only as plausible as:
If in ci it is assertible that P, then in ci P.
Although the argument does not require assertibility to be factive in general, it does require it to behave factively in the special cases at issue.

When ‘known’ replaces ‘assertible’, (1) becomes a margin for error principle, according to which something is known in given circumstances c only if it is true in all circumstances within a margin for error of c.12 Such principles are motivated by reliability conditions on knowledge.13 Margin for error principles hold generally only of factive notions; (1) reflects the knowledge-like behaviour of assertibility in the chosen circumstances. (AA) fails in that case because its antecedent is true and its consequent false in circumstances that are within a margin for error of circumstances within a margin for error of circumstances in which not P but are not within a margin for error of circumstances in which not P. More generally, (AA*) fails in case assertibility behaves in a knowledge-like way because its antecedent is true and its consequent false in circumstances in which P that are within a margin for error of circumstances in which not P. Moral: the assertibility of something in one set of circumstances can depend on its truth in other circumstances in which it is not assertible.

Suppose that (AA) and its converse held generally.14 Then ‘P’ would have the same assertibility condition as ‘It is assertible that P’; moreover, the assertibility condition of ‘It is assertible that P’ would be the same as its truth condition. That ‘P’ had a given assertibility condition would never ground a distinction between its truth condition and its assertibility condition, for having that assertibility condition would be consistent with also having that condition as a truth condition (just as ‘It is assertible that P’ has). If one started with assertibility conditions, the distinction between truth and assertibility would therefore look problematic. It might still be made by appeal to the difference in assertibility conditions between ‘Not P’ and ‘It is not assertible that P’ (as in Wright 1992), but then issues about the identification of a genuine negation in the object language will arise. The distinction becomes at least difficult.

On the conception developed in this paper, by contrast, that ‘P’ has a given assertibility condition almost always grounds a distinction between its truth condition and its assertibility. For, given almost any condition C, if C is the truth condition of ‘P’ then (AA*) fails, so C is not the assertibility condition of ‘P’; thus if C is the assertibility condition of ‘P’, something other than C is its truth condition. No appeal to embedded occurrences of ‘P’ is needed to make the distinction. Of course, once the failure of (AA) is conceded, assertibility no longer appears to have the kind of Cartesian transparency that truth so signally lacks, and the idea that one should start with assertibility conditions rather than truth conditions loses much of its appeal.

That truth can exceed assertibility in given circumstances does not immediately imply that there can be truths not assertible in any circumstances at all. Many failures of (AA) and (AA*) are not of that kind. It is sometimes assertible that there is land ahead but not assertible that it is assertible that there is land ahead; nevertheless, at other times it is assertible that it is assertible that there is land ahead. Such contents are not essentially unassertible. Moreover, if ‘P’ is assertible in no circumstances, then an appeal to its assertibility condition will not distinguish ‘P’ from an obvious contradiction (although an appeal to the assertibility condition of ‘Not P’ might).

The arguments of this paper do nevertheless hint at essentially unassertible truths. If (AA) has false instances, then there are true conjunctions of the form ‘It is assertible that P and it is not assertible that it is assertible that P’. Surely one could never be warranted in asserting a conjunction of that form. But this is not the place to discuss the consequences of that fact.

Earlier versions of this material were given in talks at the Universities of Edinburgh, Canterbury (Christchurch) and Waikato, at Oriel College Oxford and at the Instituto de Investigaciones Filosóficas of the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México. I am grateful to the audiences there for helpful comments, to the University of Canterbury and the Research School of Social Sciences at the Australian National University for hospitality while the paper was written, and to the University of Edinburgh for leave that enabled me to accept that hospitality.

A comprehensive account of the topic would require a rigorous treatment of circumstances and of the semantics of circumstance-dependence. The arguments of this paper are not very sensitive to the details of such a treatment, whose development here would entail undue technicality. The use of quotation marks is casual for the same reason. ↩︎
Crispin Wright also seems to assume (AA) in arguing that truth and warranted assertibility coincide in positive normative force (Wright 1992, p. 18). ↩︎

The focus of Dummett’s critique of truth conditional theories of meaning is often on the undecidability of truth, i.e. on the fact that speakers sometimes lack an effective procedure for recognizing whether the truth condition of a sentence obtains (incidentally, this holds on both realist and anti-realist conceptions of truth; it is just because intuitionists take such procedures sometimes to be lacking that they reject the law of excluded middle). If the argument for an anti-realist theory of meaning takes this form, then it requires assertibility to be decidable, i.e. there must always be an effective procedure for recognizing whether a given sentence is assertible in a given context (a conclusion endorsed by Wright 1992, p. 56). This would not imply a procedure for recognizing whether it is true, even on an anti-realist conception of truth, which does not identify truth with assertibility in a given non-ideal context. For example, the intuitionist identifies assertibility with the subject’s possession of a proof and truth with the existence of a proof (i.e. the subject’s possible possession of one). The decidability of assertibility does not follow from (AA), since the former implies that if it is not assertible that P then, once the effective procedure has been applied, it is assertible that it is not assertible that P, a matter on which (AA) is silent (just as, in modal logic, the S5 axiom ¬□p→□¬□p does not follow from the S4 axiom). Thus it makes a significant difference to what the anti-realist requires of assertibility whether the objection to truth conditional theories of meaning is that truth is not always recognizable or that it is not always decidable, even though the two claims are equivalent given bivalence and the presence of classical negation in the object language. However, if assertibility is decidable then (AA) should hold, so the argument in the text applies to both forms of anti-realism. It could also be turned into a direct argument against decidability. ↩︎

In mathematics, knowing that P is to a first approximation having a proof that P (but see n. 5 for one necessary qualification), and (AA) becomes the principle that a proof that P is recognizable as a proof that P. For some questions about this principle see Weinstein 1983 and Stirton 1995. ↩︎

An anti-realist theory of meaning is likely to distinguish between canonical and non-canonical warrants for assertion, e.g. between having a proof and having been told by a reliable informant that there is one. The recursive semantics will be formulated in terms of canonical warrants, and non-canonical warrants are explained as warrants for supposing there to be canonical warrants. The argument in the text applies whether or not ‘assertible’ is understood as qualified by ‘canonically’. ↩︎
The argument can be reworked so that each step uses modus ponens rather than transitivity, but vagueness has sometimes been supposed to threaten even modus ponens. ↩︎
Nothing in the text presupposes the positive epistemic account of vagueness in Williamson 1994. ↩︎

The revised argument against (AA*) yields as a special case a revised argument against (AA), pushing ‘It is assertible that it is assertible that P’ rather than ‘It is assertible that P’ through the series of circumstances. ↩︎
A negative answer follows from the assumption that it is assertible that P only if it is known that P (Williamson 1995). ↩︎
Again, a negative answer seems to be required by the assumption that it is assertible that P only if it is known that P, since knowledge should not depend on misleading evidence. ↩︎
One consequence of (Conj) is that (AA) holds for a fixed claim that P only if it is in no circumstances assertible that P. ↩︎
For adaptations of margin for error principles to non-factive attitudes, see Williamson 1992, pp. 237–239 and 1994, pp. 244–247. ↩︎
It is consistent to accept reliability conditions on knowledge while rejecting reliability analyses of knowledge. ↩︎

The biconditional is endorsed by Wright 1992, p. 18. The converse of (AA) is much less contentious than (AA) itself. Nothing said here threatens it, and it would follow from the factiveness of assertibility. ↩︎
Dummett, M. A. E., 1977, Elements of Intuitionism, Clarendon Press, Oxford.
——, 1981, Frege: Philosophy of Language, 2nd. ed., London: Duckworth.
——, 1991, The Logical Basis of Metaphysics, London: Duckworth.
——, 1993, The Seas of Language, Oxford: Clarendon Press.
Stirton, W., 1995, ‘Anti-realism, truth-conditions and Verificationism’, Synthèse (typescript).
Weinstein, S., 1983, ‘The Intended Interpretation of Intuitionistic Logic’, Journal of Philosophical Logic, 12, pp. 261–270.
Wright, C. J. G., 1992, Truth and Objectivity, Cambridge (Mass.): Harvard University Press.
En este artículo se intenta mostrar que el principio (AA) tiene consecuencias falsas. Dicho principio es el siguiente (donde ‘ser afirmable’ abrevia ‘ser afirmable de manera justificada’):
(AA) Si es afirmable que P, entonces es afirmable que es afirmable que P.

(AA) está implícito en las objeciones de Dummett a las teorías del significado en términos de condiciones de verdad. Según Dummett dichas teorías violan la conexión necesaria entre uso y significado: dado que los usuarios exitosos de una oración pueden ser incapaces de reconocer que se dan las condiciones de verdad de la oración cuando éstas de hecho se dan, el que se den dichas condiciones es una característica del significado que no está reflejada adecuadamente en el uso de la oración. Dummett propone que los significados de las oraciones se den en términos no de sus condiciones de verdad, sino de sus condiciones de afirmabilidad. Para evitar que la objeción se aplique a la teoría del significado propuesta por Dummett, éste requiere que los usuarios de la oración puedan reconocer sus condiciones de afirmabilidad cuando éstas se dan.

El argumento en este trabajo intenta mostrar que la objeción de Dummett a las teorías veritativo condicionales del significado es exitosa sólo si es una objeción exitosa a las teorías del significado como las que él propone, a saber, basadas en las condiciones de afirmabilidad. De hecho, el argumento generalizado mostraría que nada podría tener las características que la objeción de Dummett requiere de la noción central dentro de una teoría del significado. A partir de esto, se concluye que algo está mal con la objeción de Dummett.

El argumento es por medio de un ejemplo y una reducción al absurdo. Supongamos que un marinero navega lentamente en un barco por mares desconocidos. Se pregunta todo el tiempo si hay tierra más adelante (ignorando que la Tierra es redonda). Temprano por la mañana le es claro que no hay tierra visible. Gradualmente algo aparece en el horizonte. Al principio el marinero no está seguro de si está imaginando lo que cree ver; pero aún después de estar seguro de no estar imaginándolo, no sabe en un principio si lo que ve es tierra o nubes. La primera hipótesis se vuelve gradualmente más probable que la segunda. Después de varias horas no tiene dudas y para la noche el barco está anclado en tierra. La seguridad en el marinero de que hay tierra más adelante se va incrementando gradualmente conforme la escena visual cambia.

Sea t0 un momento temprano por la mañana; sea ti, para cualquier número natural i, el tiempo que es i segundos posterior a t0; y sea tn un momento tarde por la noche. Sean ci (para cualquier número natural i de 0 a n) las circunstancias del navegante relevantes a la afirmación de que hay tierra adelante en ti. Aunque el navegante puede discriminar fácilmente entre c0 y cn, no puede discriminar fácilmente ci de ci−1 para cualquier ci. No puede discrimar entre sus circunstancias actuales y aquellas en las que se encontraba un segundo antes pues el cambio es demasiado lento. No importa la justificación que él tenga para afirmar ci, él está en ci−1. Así pues, (1) es cierto siempre y cuando una oración acerca de las circunstancias en las que está el marinero reemplaza a ‘P’ (donde dicho reemplazo expresa una condición en las circunstancias y no una proposición fija):
Si en ci es afirmable que P, entonces en ci−1 P.

(1) se sostiene en virtud de las circunstancias específicas en cuestión y no intenta ser una verdad general. Si (1) fuese falso, entonces algo sería afirmable en ci sin ser verdadero en ci−1; pero entonces el navegante tendría una justificación para afirmar algo en ci que fuese incompatible con estar en las circunstancias ci−1. Sin embargo, el navegante no tiene dicha justificación pues la diferencia entre ci y ci−1 es demasiado pequeña para que él la pueda detectar.
Una oración acerca de las circunstancias del marinero es ‘Es afirmable que hay tierra más adelante’. Luego, (2) es una instancia de (1):
Si en ci es afirmable que es afirmable que hay tierra más adelante, entonces en ci−1 es afirmable que hay tierra más adelante.
Asumiendo que (AA) es verdadero, (3) sería verdadero:
Si en ci es afirmable que hay tierra más adelante, entonces en ci−1 es afirmable que es afirmable que hay tierra más adelante.
Si en ci es afirmable que hay tierra más adelante, entonces en ci−1 es afirmable que hay tierra más adelante.
Dado que i es arbitrario (4) se puede derivar para cualquier i de n a 1. Nuevamente dada la transitividad los condicionales n juntos dan:
Si en cn es afirmable que es afirmable que hay tierra más adelante, entonces en c0 es afirmable que hay tierra más adelante.

(5) es falso, pues el antecedente es verdadero y el consecuente falso. En cn es afirmable que hay tierra adelante, pero en c0 no es afirmable que hay tierra más adelante. Luego (AA) tiene consecuencias falsas. Cuando el marinero está justificado en afirmar ‘Hay tierra más adelante’, su justificación no es necesariamente obvia o transparente a él, y puede entonces no estar justificado en afirmar ‘Mi última afirmación estaba justificada’. La afirmabilidad de que P no tiene pues la transparencia cartesiana que Dummett requiere (y que la verdad carece). Por esto la idea de que se debería construir una teoría del significado en términos de condiciones de afirmabilidad y no de condiciones de verdad pierde gran parte de su atractivo.

En el artículo se muestra cómo el argumento se generaliza para principios de la forma (AA*), donde no es necesario que la afirmabilidad de P esté presente en el antecedente y, no obstante, (AA*) tiene consecuencias falsas.
Si P, entonces es afirmable que P.
(AA*) falla pues su antecedente es verdadero y su consecuente falso en circunstancias en las que P está dentro de un margen de error de las circunstancias en las que no-P.

works.title: Definiteness and knowability
passages: Suppose that one uses classical logic and a disquotational principle for truth in a vague language. Must one then accept that vagueness is an epistemic phenomenon, a matter of unknowable truths as to the location of sharp cut-off points? The question is worth asking, for quite a few philosophers would like to use classical logic and a disquotational principle for truth in a vague language without accepting that vagueness is an epistemic phenomenon.1 This paper investigates the question. It finds no plausible way of substantiating that possibility. The final section sketches an epistemic account of vagueness, in order to refute the allegation made by some of those philosophers that such an account confuses vagueness with unrelated epistemic phenomena. The upshot is a disjunction: either classical logic fails, or the disquotational principle does, or vagueness is an epistemic phenomenon. To complete the argument for the third disjunct, one would need to argue against the first and second. That is done elsewhere.2

The claim that vagueness is an epistemic phenomenon will be taken to have some rough initial intelligibility. The development of the argument through the paper will elucidate it further. Of course, if vagueness were defined to be non-epistemic, then the claim would be self-contradictory. Such a definition is unhelpful, however, for it becomes controversial whether any expression generally classified as vague really is vague in the defined sense. It is better to define an expression as vague if and only if it is capable of yielding borderline cases, where the notion of a borderline case is introduced by examples. One can then go on to investigate the underlying nature of the phenomenon so identified, without having prejudged the issue by one’s choice of terminology. Vagueness is, for example, whatever it is that causes the trouble in the sorites paradox, which confronts one with borderline cases for ‘heap’.

Some initial remarks will help to clarify the assumptions that may or may not lead to an epistemic view of vagueness. Classical logic is to be understood as including not just standard theorems, such as the law of excluded middle, but also standard rules of inference, such as conditional proof, contraposition, reductio ad absurdum and argument by cases.3 It will be used in the metalanguage, not just in the object-language; the former is conceived as an extension of the latter. The disquotational principle for truth will be taken in the form:
‘P’ is true if and only if P.
The schema (T) is not claimed to be the whole truth about truth; it is merely claimed to be at least part of the truth. The combination of classical logic with (T) will be called ‘orthodoxy’.

The attribution of truth to declarative sentence types, as in (T), is not wholly felicitous. An indexical sentence type such as ‘I am hungry’ is used to say different things in different contexts. It is not usually the case that ‘I am hungry’ as uttered by you is true if and only if I am hungry. Utterances or the propositions they express may seem better suited to bear truth. However, (T) can be protected from the effects of indexicality by the understanding that truth is attributed on the left-hand side with respect to the very context in which the right-hand side is uttered (the bearing of context dependence on vagueness will be discussed later). Some restriction on (T) may also be needed to avoid Liar-like paradoxes. The attribution of truth to sentence types is convenient for bookkeeping purposes; handled with care, it should not distort the issues to be discussed.
On certain conditions, (T) follows from a more general quasi-Tarskian schema:
If in a context c a sentence s says that P, then s is true in c if and only if P.

What s says in c is the proposition that s in c is used to express. If one combines (T+) with the assumption that in the context in which the right-hand side of (T) is uttered the sentence ‘P’ says that P, one can derive (T) as understood above. The immediate rationale for (T+) is this: given that s says, e.g., that snow is white, what it is for s to be true is simply for grass to be green. This underwrites the biconditional ‘s is true if and only if P’, rather than some weakened principle, just as the fact that, given that b is 3 mm long, what it is for a to be longer than b is simply for a to be more than 3 mm long underwrites the biconditional ‘a is longer than b if and only if a is more than 3 mm long’, rather than some weakened principle.

(T+) also helps to explain why (T), if unrestricted, would fail for indexical sentences when the context shifts, for it may shift to a context in which ‘P’ does not say that P, either because it says that something else is the case or because it does not say that anything is the case. A shift of this kind may be occurring when (T) leads to trouble in Liar-like paradoxes; it is by no means obvious that they involve any violation of (T+).4

Both (T) and (T+) are subject to a further, informal constraint. The declarative sentence substituted for ‘P’ must say that something is the case, in that very context. For example, it should presumably not contain a demonstrative singular term that fails to pick anything out in the context, lest the relevant instances of (T) and (T+) fail to say that anything is the case. Optimists might suppose that possible substitutions for ‘P’ could be drawn from a language without context dependence in which such problems would not arise. Note that no such restrictions are needed on the sentence referred to by the singular term substituted for ‘s’ in (T+); at that point the sentence is mentioned rather than used, unlike the sentence substituted for ‘P’ on the right-hand sides of (T) and (T+), so failures in it do not infect the relevant instances of (T+).

At least one view does combine classical logic and (T+) with the denial that vagueness is an epistemic phenomenon in a way that seems at any rate not formally inconsistent. This is the view that vague sentences do not say that anything is the case, in borderline cases if not elsewhere. Thus, if ‘b’ is a borderline case for ‘bald’, to say ‘b is bald’ or ‘b is not bald’ is to make an utterance without propositional content. One says nothing by uttering either sentence, so neither is true. Thus, the corresponding antecedents of (T+), ‘in c “b is bald” says that P’ and ‘in c “b is not bald” says that P’, fail whatever legitimate substitution is made for ‘P’, and (T+) holds vacuously. The substitution of ‘b is bald’ or ‘b is not bald’ for ‘P’ in (T+) would not itself be legitimate on the view in question, for it would violate the informal constraint above that the substituted sentence should in context say that something is the case. For the same reason, (T) would have no relevant instance. Thus, there would be no relevant true sentence, and therefore nothing for speakers of the language to be ignorant of. On this view, vagueness is not an epistemic phenomenon.

No attempt will be made here to argue against that extreme view.5 Many of the philosophers who wish to accept orthodoxy while denying that vagueness is an epistemic phenomenon are willing to instantiate (T) with vague sentences even in borderline cases. They allow that ‘b is bald’ is true if and only if b is bald; ‘b is bald’ says that b is bald, even if b is borderline for ‘bald’.6 It is with this combination of views that the paper will be concerned. Such instances of (T) will therefore be taken as part of orthodoxy.
It can now be argued that, given orthodoxy, vagueness is an epistemic phenomenon in at least a minimal sense.

Let ‘P’ be a vague sentence in a paradigmatic borderline case, by which the notion of vagueness was defined above. If the language does not already include a negation sign, add one.7 Thus, ‘Not P’ is another vague sentence. The law of excluded middle tells us that either P or not P. By two instances of (T), ‘P’ is true if and only if P, and ‘Not P’ is true if and only if not P. By classical logic, one deduces:
Either ‘P’ is true or ‘Not P’ is true.

Since the truth of ‘Not P’ is equivalent to the falsity of ‘P’, this is just a form of the familiar entailment from the law of excluded middle and the disquotational principle to the principle of bivalence.

By hypothesis, the case is paradigmatically borderline, so there is no question of finding out whether P, of coming to know that P or to know that not P.8 Paradigmatic borderline cases are chosen for the peculiar way in which they throw competent speakers of the language into uncertainty. If a few assert that P, a few others deny that P. Many hesitate, or refuse to give a verdict. Speakers typically agree on reflection that the case is borderline, that it is unclear whether P, and that assertions and denials that P are not expressions of knowledge. In circumstances of explicit or implicit stipulation, the utterance of ‘P’ by x may bring it about that x must be interpreted as meaning something true by ‘P’, while the utterance of its negation by y brings it about that y must be interpreted as meaning something false by ‘P’, so that the apparent disagreement dissolves. However, even if x and y use assertion and denial of ‘P’ respectively to express knowledge, that is irrelevant, for the relevant senses of ‘P’ are the poststipulative ones, which are precise in relevant respects, whereas the sense of ‘P’ in which it has a borderline case is the vague prestipulative one, in which neither the assertion of ‘P’ nor its denial expresses knowledge.

Call a sentence s knowably true in a context c if and only if in c: s is true and, for some substitution for ‘P’, means are available to normal competent speakers of the language of s to come to know that P, where s says that P.9 A sentence is unknowably true in a context if and only if it is true but not knowably true in that context. A sentence might be unknowably true in this sense even if by extraordinary means (such as divine revelation) some normal competent speaker did acquire the relevant knowledge. What is obvious in the envisaged context, a paradigmatic borderline case, is just that normal competent speakers of the language have no means available to them to decide the matter, and the definitions were tailored accordingly. The unavailability of knowledge may now be stated metalinguistically:
‘P’ is not knowably true and ‘Not P’ is not knowably true.10

By itself, (2) does not assert that either ‘P’ or ‘Not P’ is unknowably true, for a sentence can fail to be knowably true without being unknowably true, by not being true at all. However, in combination with (1), (2) does yield:
Either ‘P’ is unknowably true or ‘Not P’ is unknowably true.
Either way, some sentence is unknowably true. The speakers’ ignorance has an object. The paradigmatic borderline cases used to define vagueness exemplify this epistemic phenomenon.

Does it follow that those who accept orthodoxy must regard vagueness as characterizable in epistemic terms? What has been shown is that they must regard it as involving the presence of unknowable truths, but it does not follow that they must regard it as constituted by that presence. Indeed, it is plausible that if some unknowable truths turn on vagueness, then many others do not (Goldbach’s Conjecture is an obvious candidate). If one thinks that (2) is a necessary condition for a case to be borderline, one should not also think that it is sufficient.

The point just made may seem to show that those who accept orthodoxy should not regard vagueness as an epistemic phenomenon. However, that would be too hasty. A particular epistemic condition, (2), has turned out not to be necessary and sufficient for a case to be borderline, but it does not follow that no epistemic condition is necessary and sufficient. For instance, vagueness might consist in a specific kind of unknowability. It could even be conceded that the vagueness explains the unknowability rather than vice versa, for a specific epistemic factor might explain the more general fact of unknowability in this case. These suggestions will be elaborated at the end of the paper. The question ‘Is vagueness an epistemic phenomenon?’ is in any case a vague one. What is needed is an investigation of the attempt, constrained by orthodoxy, to characterize vagueness in non-epistemic terms.

It is standardly suggested that borderline cases should be characterized in terms of a notion of indefiniteness, rather than unknowability. One introduces a notion of the definitely true on the understanding that a necessary and sufficient condition for the case to be borderline is:11
‘P’ is not definitely true and ‘Not P’ is not definitely true.

(4) differs from (2) only in having ‘definitely’ where (2) has ‘knowably’. Of course, if a sentence is definitely true, then it is true. If it is true but not definitely true, say that it is indefinitely true. Given orthodoxy, just as (2) entails (3), so (4) entails:
Either ‘P’ is indefinitely true or ‘Not P’ is indefinitely true.
Either way, some sentence is indefinitely true. On the envisaged view, it is the presence of indefinite truths that is distinctive of borderline cases, not the presence of unknowable truths.

As already seen, (2) is not sufficient for a case to be borderline. Since (4) is sufficient for that by hypothesis, (2) is not sufficient for (4). Thus, the following principle is not valid for every sentence s in every context:
If s is definitely true then s is knowably true.

For if (6) were valid, one could use it to argue contrapositively from (2) to (4), substituting ‘P’ and ‘Not P’ for ‘s’ in (6). The invalidity of (6) will presumably be part of the case for not regarding definiteness as an epistemic notion.

On the other hand, (2) is necessary for a case to be borderline; if the answer were known, the case would not be borderline. Since (4) is by hypothesis sufficient for the case to be borderline, (4) is sufficient for (2). It follows that the converse of (6) is valid:
If s is knowably true then s is definitely true.

One can argue for the validity of (7) as follows, taking s, without loss of generality, to be ‘P’ (which is not now assumed to be a borderline case). As before, add negation to the language if it is not already there. Suppose that ‘P’ is not definitely true. By excluded middle, ‘Not P’ is either definitely true or not definitely true. If ‘Not P’ is definitely true then it is true, so ‘P’ is not true (by (T) and classical logic), so ‘P’ is not knowably true. On the other hand, if ‘Not P’ is not definitely true then, since ‘P’ is by hypothesis not definitely true, (4) holds; since (4) has just been seen to be sufficient for (2) (for arbitrary ‘P’), (2) holds, so ‘P’ is again not knowably true. Thus, if ‘P’ is not definitely true then it is not knowably true; (7) follows. Knowable truth implies definite truth, but not vice versa.

One may add that definite truth implies truth, but not vice versa. If s is definitely true then it is true; the converse principle fails, for it would make (4) inconsistent with (1), and therefore with orthodoxy, whereas (4) was supposed to hold in borderline cases. Thus, definiteness lies strictly between knowability and truth in extension.

What, however, is definiteness? More specifically: can it be given a manifestly non-epistemic characterization that is consistent with orthodoxy? Attempts to do so will be examined, and found wanting. A manifestly epistemic characterization of definiteness will then be provided.

An initial attempt to give a non-epistemic characterization of definiteness consistent with orthodoxy might run as follows. Let a be an arrangement of grains such that neither ‘a is a heap’ nor ‘a is not a heap’ is definitely true. The case is borderline. The reason, it is suggested, is that ‘heap’ is not defined for this case. The semantic rules for ‘heap’ stipulate that it applies when a condition C+ holds and fails to apply when a disjoint condition C- applies, but make no stipulation either way for a case such as that of a in which neither C+ nor C- applies. ‘Heap’ is only partially defined. Speakers of English have had no practical need to make it precise.12

On a view of the kind envisaged, it is no wonder that knowable truth implies definite truth and not vice versa. Speakers cannot be expected to know the application of a term where that application has not even been defined. On the other hand, where the application has been defined, they might still be unable to know what it is, for they might be unable to know the relevant non-semantic facts. On this view, definiteness seems to be a semantic matter, not an epistemic one.

What is a wonder, on the proposed view, is that truth does not imply definiteness. Given orthodoxy, either ‘a is a heap’ or ‘a is not a heap’ is indefinitely true. Yet, if the indefinite is simply the undefined, what room is there for indefinite truth? Compare the perverse supposition that since ‘0/0’ is undefined, it refers to an indefinite object. How can an undefined question have a right answer?

To meet the difficulty, a more substantive account is needed of definite truth. One might start with the proposal that a sentence is definitely true just in case its truth follows from the semantic rules governing it and the facts (all relative to a context); the semantic rules alone would not suffice, of course, for many highly empirical sentences are definitely true. However, this proposal will not do in its present form, for it has no defense against the obvious objection that if s is true then it is a fact that s is true, so the truth of s follows from the facts (even without the semantic rules), which would imply that all true sentences are definitely true, contrary to the truth of (5) in borderline cases.

The obvious revision is the proposal that s is definitely true just in case its truth follows from semantic rules and the nonsemantic facts, or (since s might itself be metalinguistic) from semantic rules and the facts that s is about. Both the notion of a semantic rule and that of the facts that a sentence is about are hazy, but the revised proposal faces a more urgent problem.

Any adequate semantic account of the sentence ‘a is a heap’ as used here and now should imply at least this instance of (T): ‘a is a heap’ is true if and only if a is a heap. Thus, if ‘a is a heap’ is true, a is a heap, and the latter is a fact that the sentence is about. It follows from this fact and the biconditional, hence from this fact and semantic rules, that the sentence is true. In other words, the revised proposal still has the effect that ‘a is a heap’, if true, is definitely true, which is just what it was intended to avoid.

The spirit of the original proposal seems to be that, even if a is a heap, it is not a fact of the relevant kind that it is. Moreover, it is because ‘a is a heap’ is vague that it does not state a fact of the relevant kind. This suggests a third proposal: s is definitely true just in case its truth follows from semantic rules and precise facts or truths. Now one might well doubt that there could be the required precise truths, if that would imply the possibility of a perfectly precise language capable of describing the empirical world. But even if such a language were possible, the new proposal would do nothing to elucidate a way in which vagueness might be a non-epistemic phenomenon.

Vagueness was characterized in terms of definite truth, and definite truth in terms of precision, which is simply the contradictory of vagueness over the relevant class. Although this circularity may not void the account of all interest, it does mean that the account does not imply that vagueness is not an epistemic phenomenon. If the input notion of precision is nonepistemic, then the output notion of vagueness will also be non-epistemic, but if the input notion of precision is epistemic, then the output notion of vagueness will also be epistemic. The problem of elucidating a non-epistemic notion of precision (consistent with orthodoxy) is equivalent to the original problem of elucidating a non-epistemic notion of vagueness (consistent with orthodoxy). The new proposal makes no progress towards solving it.

The proposal in question leaves the point of the notion of vagueness quite mysterious. By the disquotational principle, vague truths as well as precise ones (if any) can be formulated in the metalanguage. Why should one be interested in what follows from a particular subclass of those truths, together with semantic rules? No explanation has been provided.

Since qualifications of the notion of a fact in the original proposal have been unavailing, one might try qualifying the notion of a semantic rule. More specifically, one might concentrate on rules of warranted assertion rather than on rules of truth. For even if either ‘a is a heap’ or ‘a is not a heap’ is true, it does not follow that either ‘a is a heap’ or ‘a is not a heap’ is warrantedly assertible. In a borderline case speakers may have no warrant either way; this is quite consistent with orthodoxy. One might therefore propose that a sentence is definitely true in just those contexts in which it is both true and warrantedly assertible. This proposal, however, is open to the objection sometimes made to epistemic accounts, that they fail to distinguish vagueness from unrelated kinds of unknowability. Goldbach’s Conjecture and its negation may simultaneously fail to be warrantedly assertible. It would not help to speak of warranted assertibility for hypothetical speakers who knew all the facts, for that would merely raise again the earlier problem: if a is a heap, why is that not itself a fact of the relevant kind?

A subtler suggestion is that the semantic rules governing assent to a sentence distinguish between what is permitted and what is mandatory.13 Might the characteristic of a borderline case be that assent is permitted without being mandatory? In contrast, assent to Goldbach’s Conjecture or to its negation would not even be permitted in the absence of a proof either way. This suggestion does better than the previous one, but it still fails to distinguish vagueness from some unrelated epistemic phenomena. For example, some speakers require more inductive evidence than others do before assenting to an empirical generalization. It does not follow that either the former group or the latter (perhaps both) is in breach of linguistic rules. The language does not specify a unique standard of inductive caution. If the gap between permitted and mandatory assent occurs anywhere, it occurs here. Yet, there need be no relevant vagueness in the empirical generalization. Thus, the gap between permitted and mandatory assent is not distinctive of vagueness.

To summarize the results so far: accounts of definiteness in terms of rules of truth leave no room for indefinite truth; accounts in terms of rules of assertion make no distinction between vagueness and unrelated epistemic phenomena. Either way, vagueness has not been adequately characterized.

At this point one might decide that one cannot make non-epistemic sense of vagueness by considering a sentence in a context in isolation from other sentences and contexts. One might therefore propose to bring other sentences or contexts into the analysis. That could be done in several ways. One could postulate that a vague utterance is an utterance of more than one sentence or has more than one context. Alternatively, one could allow that it is the utterance of a single sentence in a single context, but postulate that it is a vague matter which sentence has been uttered in which context.14 Such strategies will be briefly considered.

The utterance ‘a is a heap’ is by ordinary standards the utterance of a single sentence. If it is held that in reality many sentences were uttered, a special way of individuating sentences must be in play. For example, sentences might be regarded as abstract objects with precise truth conditions that contribute to their individuation. Say that a sentence s is co-uttered with a sentence s* in a context c just in case in c some utterance of s is also an utterance of s*. It might then be said: s is definitely true in c just in case in c every sentence co-uttered with s is true. The utterance of ‘a is a heap’ in a borderline case is supposed to instantiate many sentences with slightly different precise truth conditions, some true and some false in that context. Since the true sentences are co-uttered with false ones, they are indefinitely true.

Call the many nonstandardly individuated co-uttered sentences sharpened, and the original standardly individuated sentence unsharpened. One can still ask for the truth-value of unsharpened sentences. If the apparatus of sharpened sentences is to have explanatory value, truth for unsharpened sentences is presumably to be explained in terms of truth for sharpened ones. The only explanation to hand is that an unsharpened sentence is true just in case all the corresponding co-uttered sharpened sentences are true (in a given context). Thus, neither the unsharpened sentence ‘a is a heap’ nor its unsharpened negation will be true in a borderline case. Given classical logic, the disquotational principle must fail for unsharpened sentences. The envisaged view preserves orthodoxy for sharpened sentences, but not for unsharpened ones.15

The force of the disquotational principle does not depend on nonstandard forms of individuation. According to the original intuition, if a is a heap then the unsharpened ‘a is a heap’ is true; if a is not a heap then the unsharpened ‘a is not a heap’ is true, so the unsharpened ‘a is a heap’ is not true. For the unsharpened sentence ‘a is a heap’ says that a is a heap, and its unsharpened negation says that a is not a heap. The spirit of orthodoxy requires the disquotational principle for unsharpened sentences, not merely for sharpened ones, just as it requires classical logic for the former, not merely for the latter. Orthodoxy will henceforth be understood in that sense.

Truth for unsharpened sentences is thus not explicable in terms of truth for sharpened ones in any straightforward way. Indeed, an unsharpened sentence will be opposite in truth-value to many of the corresponding sharpened sentences. Some explanation is therefore needed of the relevance of the latter to the vagueness of the former. The intended connection seems to be a constraint on the correspondence relation: whenever an unsharpened sentence is definitely true, all the corresponding sharpened sentences are true. The problem, of course, is that the constraint uses the notion of definiteness. If this notion turns out to be epistemic, then so does the notion of vagueness that it generates. The original problem returns. The nonstandard individuation of sentences has not helped to elucidate a way, consistent with orthodoxy, for definiteness to be non-epistemic. The multiplication of sentences in a single utterance will therefore be abandoned.

Similar remarks apply to the multiplication of contexts of a single utterance. If contexts were individuated in a sharpened way, it might be claimed that speakers never single out a unique context.
