To argue from (2) to (3a), suppose that i are not clearly few. On Stoic principles, i are either clearly not few or not clearly not few. If i are clearly not few, they are clearly not clearly few, for since what is clear (i.e. the content of a cognitive impression) is true, if i were clearly few then i would be few, which they clearly are not. On the other hand, if i are not clearly not few, by supposition they are also not clearly few, so by (2) they are clearly neither clearly few nor clearly not few, so i are clearly not clearly few. Thus (2) implies (3a). (2) implies (3b) by a parallel argument. Conversely, (3a) and (3b) together imply (2), for if two propositions are clear, so is their conjunction. The notion of clarity validates the required assumptions that what is clear is true and that what follows from what is clear is itself clear. ↩︎

Barnes’s argument also assumes the S4 principle for clarity: what is clear is clearly clear. An argument that sorites series provide counterexamples to the S4 principle for clarity can be extracted from Section 8.4. It is worth noting that the Stoics themselves had the basis for a counterexample to the S4 principle for scientific knowledge. One might suppose that the wise man knows that he is wise, but a later variant on Eubulides’ puzzle of the Elusive Man suggests otherwise. ‘You say that the wise man is ignorant of nothing, and that nothing eludes him. How, then, can he ever have become wise? For at the instant at which a man becomes wise there is a fact of which he is ignorant, and which eludes him, namely the fact that he is now wise.’ Knowledge of the fact is subsequent to the fact. The case greatly troubled the Stoics, and Chrysippus wrote a book about it. It was held that it is possible to be wise and yet not know that one is (Sedley 1977: 94). The example can obviously be generalized. If one learns that i are few, there is an instant at which one knows that i are few but does not yet know that one knows that i are few. If the reason for the delay is that it takes time for a fact to become clear, there is an instant at which i are clearly few but not clearly clearly few. If what takes time is only assent, the case is not itself a counterexample to the S4 principle for clarity, but it is still very similar to the counterexample in Section 8.4, with temporal boundaries in place of conceptual ones. It cannot be taken for granted that Chrysippus would have accepted the S4 principle for clarity. ↩︎

works.title: Representing the knowledge of Turing machines
passages: Representing the knowledge of Turing machines

When each state of the world is a maximally specific, consistent description of the world, including the description of the knowledge and ignorance of all individuals, the standard partitional model of knowledge is inconsistent with the assumption that an individual’s powers are limited to that of a Turing machine. We show, however, that the epistemic logic S4 is consistent with computational constraints.
Representing the knowledge of Turing machines
In this paper, we shall follow the implications of the following pair of principles.
The state space should be construed as the set of all maximally specific descriptions of the world, including a complete specification of the knowledge (and ignorance) of all individuals.
An individual has exactly the reasoning ability of some computing machine.

Each of these principles, taken in isolation, have been enormously influential in decision theory and game theory, but relatively little attention has been devoted to the examination of the conjunction of these statements. Principle (i) has its historical roots in the theory of probability and in the identification of the state space with the sample space associated with a random variable, and in the logician’s idea of a ‘possible world’ as a maximally specific and consistent truth assignment to a set of sentences. Savage (1954) and Jeffrey (1983), among others, have developed this principle in decision theory, while Harsanyi (1967) has popularized this notion for the study of games. Bayesian game theory has now become one of the most important analytical tools in the economics of information, and has generated a huge literature. The work of Aumann (1976, 1987) is worthy of particular mention, and the reader is referred to the recent symposium and survey in the Journal of Economic Perspectives (Brandenburger 1992, Geanakoplos 1992, and Reny 1992).

The assertion that decision makers should be endowed with the abilities of a computing machine (and no more) can be seen as a response to the lacuna in conventional treatments of decision making which neglects the procedural aspects of rationality. This distinction between the substantive and procedural aspects of rationality as propounded, for example, by Simon (1976) takes on particular significance in game theory owing to the additional dimension of the problem posed by iterated knowledge, i.e., knowledge of what others know or don’t know. Binmore (1987) argues that the standard assumption in game theory that all players are “perfectly rational” becomes problematic when players are seen as computing machines. A related line of research, with similar methodological overtones, has been to examine the outcomes in specific games played between computing machines, both finite automata (as in Rubinstein 1986, and Abreu and Rubinstein 1988) and general Turing machines (as in Anderlini 1989, and Canning 1992). The motivation of these papers is to examine the extent to which the results of conventional game theory survive explicit incorporation of procedural rationality. In the case of the literature on finite automata, an additional motive is to explore the effects of bounded rationality on the outcomes of specific games.

In following up the consequences of the conjunction of principles (i) and (ii), we shall employ a framework which is as close as possible to the standard treatments of information and knowledge while being able to accommodate sufficient structure to formalize the notion that individuals are Turing machines. For a description of alternative approaches to modelling knowledge and of the current state of the art, the reader is referred to Lismont and Mongin (1994). In our paper, we start with a state space W each state of which describes the environment in which the individuals find themselves. In the case of Bayesian games, each state w will specify the game being played at that state. Since individuals’ knowledge depend on the environment, the knowledge of any individual will vary from state to state. More precisely, for each individual i, we associate with each state w a set of formulas, interpreted as those which i knows – that is, i’s theory at w.

We require that each individual’s theory include a version of arithmetic. In our case, the version of arithmetic employed is the theory Q, described in Boolos and Jeffrey (1980, p. 158). This requirement is permissible because the theorems of Q can be generated by a Turing machine. We do not want the reasoning abilities of individuals to be more limited than those of such a machine. The theory Q is a weaker theory than Peano Arithmetic, but has been shown to be sufficient to carry through the main results of Gödel (1931) and Rosser (1936). In particular, any consistent recursively axiomatized extension of Q is susceptible to the Gödel incompleteness theorems. We shall make essential use of this result ourselves.

In outline, our approach may be sketched as follows. The set of formulas Form in our framework is built up from two disjoint sets of atomic sentences. The first is a set of non-arithmetical sentences Π′, describing the environment in which the individuals find themselves. The second is a set of sentences Π in the language of arithmetic. Thus, a typical formula in Form will be a complex formula built up from arithmetical and nonarithmetical components, which are combined by means of logical connectives and the knowledge operators. The first question we address is whether the knowledge of these individuals can be represented in terms of the standard partitional information structures. In other words, whether we can define an equivalence relation of indistinguishability between states so that it is true that an individual knows A at w if and only if A is true at every state which is indistinguishable from w. Our first result is the negative one that, even if the knowledge of non-arithmetical formulas is governed by a partitional structure, the inclusion of arithmetical knowledge precludes a partitional structure over the knowledge of the set of all formulas. This is accomplished by demonstrating that the principle:

cannot hold for all formulas, A, even though (5) holds for all purely non-arithmetical formulas. This result rests on the observation that (5) implies (under soundness) that the set of formulas known by an individual at a state is not only recursively enumerable, but also recursive, thereby contradicting Rosser’s (1936) version of Gödel’s first incompleteness theorem. We will have a chance to review these concepts below.
Having established this negative result, we embark on our positive programme of seeing which principles of knowledge can be held consistently. The principle:
is shown to be consistent with computability in our framework. More importantly, our framework also satisfies the key principle:

This principle would seem to be an essential feature of knowledge, and yet, if the provability predicate of arithmetic is interpreted as the knowledge operator, (T) cannot hold in general, on pain of inconsistency. Boolos (1979) provides a detailed account of the modal logic of provability, and Binmore and Shin (1992) note some of the consequences of these results for game theory. In the following section, we rehearse some of the main results in this area.

We should state at the outset that our purpose is not define knowledge in terms of any specific logical system, but rather to show how an S4 logic of knowledge is consistent with computational constraints (and how S5 is not). Thus, the principle (T) is, in the first instance, an assumption which is then subsequently shown to be consistent with computational constraints. We do not believe that there is a unique “correct” system of logic for Turing machines which is waiting to be derived from first principles. There will be many logics which are consistent with machine knowledge, and the choice between them will be made on other grounds.

In short, our claim in this paper is twofold. Firstly, an S4 logic of knowledge is consistent with the limitations imposed by the fact that individuals are Turing machines, but secondly, the standard partitional representation of knowledge, i.e., the logic S5, is inconsistent with machine knowledge. We do not go much beyond making these two observations. Our motivation is to construct a model of knowledge for Turing machines which is as close as possible to the standard representation in economics and decision theory in terms of partitions over the state space. In this respect, our first (negative) result seems to be one which is insensitive to the details of the particular construction of the system.

Our result that the knowledge of Turing machines can satisfy S4 may have some bearing on decision theory, in particular on the idea of coherent belief revision in multiperiod settings. At a basic level, coherent belief change could be described as one which precludes the existence of “Dutch Books” against the decision maker. Although partitional information and Bayes updating from the true prior is sufficient for coherent belief revision, the results of Morris (1992) suggest that coherence can be maintained for more general information structures, provided that beliefs follow specified updating rules. In particular, S4 is shown to be adequate, provided that updated beliefs satisfy additional restrictions. The details of such arguments are beyond the scope of this paper, and we do not attempt to link our discussion to that of belief coherence. Indeed, we are keenly aware that the extension of our framework to settings which involve probabilistic beliefs is an important and potentially fruitful exercise.
Before proceeding with our construction, we sketch some of the background to our discussion by reviewing some earlier work in this area, and by stating some methodological preliminaries.

In this paper, it will be assumed without argument that a notion of knowledge can be applied to machines. We assume a fixed formal language, and treat the machine as knowing the truth of a formula A in it if and only if the machine eventually outputs “Yes” on input “A?”. It may be more accurate to view the output of “Yes” on input “A?” as the defining property of the machine’s belief of A rather than its knowledge, but we will not dwell on this distinction. Since our framework preserves the principle KA→A, no substantial issue will turn on the distinction between knowledge and belief.

What the machine knows will be considered as a formal system, with a recursively enumerable set of theorems. The machine’s knowledge is allowed to vary with the state of the world. Thus, each machine in each state of the world is associated with a formal system, whose theorems are what it knows in that state. The machine has some knowledge of its environment, which is incorporated in the axioms of its formal system. Thus a given machine is associated with different formal systems in different states of the world between which its knowledge of the environment differs. It will be assumed that the machines are numerate; in each state each machine’s formal system includes a basic system for arithmetic, Q (Boolos and Jeffrey 1980, p. 158). Moreover, it will be assumed that all the systems include truth-functional logic: all tautologies and modus ponens.

Treating knowledge as provability in arithmetic must be handled with some care, in view of Gödel’s incompleteness theorem. Gödel (1931) showed how one can compute, for each formula A in the language of arithmetic a numeral ⌈A⌉ and define a predicate Bew⁡(⋅) in that language which expresses the provability of A. If Bew⁡(⌈⋅⌉) is interpreted as the knowledge operator K, then the properties of K include that of the modal logic G. G is a normal system whose theorems include:
One can also show that, for any two formulas A and B,
If A and A→B are theorems of G, then so is B.
If A in a theorem of G, then so is KA.
From this, all instances of the following are theorems, too.
However, G does not include all instances of the following, on pain of inconsistency.

For let ⊥ be any contradiction. If K⊥→⊥ is a theorem, then so is K(K⊥→⊥) by (RN), so by (Löb) and (MP) K⊥, and hence ⊥, are theorems. This point is closely related to Gödel’s incompleteness theorem, for K⊥→⊥ is equivalent to ¬K⊥, a sentence expressing the consistency of the theory. No consistent extension of Q can prove its own consistency.

There is a way in which one can repair this particular difficulty. One might define KA not as “it is provable that A”, but as “it is provable and true that A”, i.e., formally by Bew⁡(⌈A⌉)∧A rather than by Bew⁡(⌈A⌉). This definition automatically secures (T). In this case the theory also includes the following class of (not very intuitive) formulas.

One also retains (K) and (RN). The system is axiomatized by (Taut), (K), (Grz), (MP) and (RN) is known as S4Grz (see Boolos 1979, pp. 159–167). All instances of (T) and (4) are derivable in it (van Benthem and Blok 1978).

However, this repair does not go to the heart of the problem. First, it makes KA express a condition one half of which (the truth of A) is independent of the activity of the machine. Second, in reasoning about its knowledge of the environment, a machine often needs to know that it is ignorant about some matter, e.g., that it does not know whether the coin will come up heads or tails at the next toss. Such ignorance is formalized as ¬KA∧¬K¬A. But if this is a theorem, so that the machine is aware of its ignorance, K(¬KA∧¬K¬A) is a theorem by (RN) and so is K¬KA∧K¬K¬A. However, S4Grz contains the following class of formulas.

If one knows that one doesn’t know that A is false, then one doesn’t know that one doesn’t know that A is true; thus one cannot know that one doesn’t know whether A is true. That is, K(¬KA∧¬K¬A) is inconsistent in S4Grz. One can prove this by using the fact that the theorems of S4Grz are exactly the formulas valid on all finite weak partial orderings, i.e., the accessibility relation is reflexive, transitive, and antisymmetric (Boolos 1979, p. 161). In such orderings, each world can access an end-point, i.e., a world that accesses only itself. Since ¬KA∧¬K¬A cannot be true at an end point (it is true only at worlds that can access at least two worlds), K(¬KA∧¬K¬A) is not true at any world. The problem is even worse in the original system G, for there if ¬KA, and KA→A, hence K(KA→A) is a theorem, then KA must be a theorem by (Löb), so that the system is inconsistent.

These problems require a fresh approach. It is intolerable to suppose that the numeracy of the machine prevents it from having knowledge of its own ignorance even in simple empirical situations. Our point of departure is to reinterpret the knowledge operator. The reinterpretation is quite subtle, for we retain the assumption that what an individual knows is precisely what is provable in that individual’s theory, where the axioms of that theory may include empirical information gathered from the environment about the state of the world. To abandon this assumption would be to refuse to take the computational constraint seriously. The assumption may appear to leave us no room for manoeuvre. However, interpretations of a knowledge operator can differ simply in the way they specify the knower. Although this difference seems trivial, it becomes crucial once the operator is iterated. To see this, consider the predicament of Oedipus, who is the son of Jocasta without knowing it. One might think that it makes no difference whether one interprets K as ‘Oedipus knows’ or ‘the son of Jocasta knows’. If Oedipus knows that it is hot, and knows that he, Oedipus, knows that it is hot, it follows that the son of Jocasta knows that it is hot, but it does not follow that the son of Jocasta knows that the son of Jocasta knows that it is hot. In fact, the son of Jocasta does not even know that she has a son. Thus, KKA is true under one interpretation of K and false under another. Turing machines are susceptible to a related phenomenon. Each type of machine is associated with a description #, listing outputs for each input and machine state. The Gödelian interpretation of KA as Bew⁡(⌈A⌉) interprets it as something like ‘The machine with description # knows’. But it cannot be assumed that the machine with description # knows that it is the machine with description #. If you ask it ‘Are you the machine with description #?’, it may not answer ‘Yes’. Machines of this kind are studied in Benacerraf (1967) and Reinhardt (1986). It follows that the Gödelian interpretation of K is not the one best suited to decision theory. Consider again the formula K(¬KA∧¬K¬A). We want it to express the agent’s knowledge that he does not know whether A, knowledge on which he might act, e.g. by seeking more information. On the Gödelian interpretation, the formula says that the machine with description # knows that the machine with description # does not know whether A. But if it does not know that it itself is the machine with description #, it may not know that it itself does not know whether A, and may therefore do nothing. To avoid this problem, we must interpret the knowledge operator with a specification of the machine under which the machine can recognize itself, just as Oedipus knows that he is Oedipus. We shall proceed on this understanding. Since our interpretation of K is not Gödelian, there is no reason to think that K must obey the principles of the system G. We now proceed to investigate some constraints on K.
3. The Framework and a Negative Result

Our construction is motivated by our goal of providing an account of the knowledge of a Turing machine which is as close as possible to the familiar partitional model of knowledge. We can think of our Turing machine as one which has access to empirical and factual knowledge, as well as to the theorems of arithmetic. Thus, the set of formulas over which the Turing machine has knowledge is of necessity a hybrid set consisting of arithmetical and non-arithmetical sentences, and complex formulas which combine both types by means of logical connectives and the knowledge operator. For our purposes, the extra structure offered by sentences of arithmetic will play no semantic role. Well formed formulas of arithmetic will be regarded as atomic propositions in our logic. However, the structure of arithmetic will play the key role of forcing the machine’s theory to be recursively enumerable, but not recursive. It is time that we reviewed some of these basic concepts.
3. The Framework and a Negative Result

First, recall the definitions of recursive and recursively enumerable sets. Informally, a set X of natural numbers is recursive if there is a Turing computable procedure that on input n gives output 1 if n∈X and output 0 if n∉X. The set x is recursively enumerable if there is a Turing computable procedure that on input n gives output 1 if n∈X, and either gives output 0 or never terminates when n∉X. Note that X is recursive if and only if it and its complement are recursively enumerable: a one-way positive test and a one-way negative test are jointly equivalent to a two-way test. We can extend these notions from natural numbers to formulas via the standard procedure for coding the latter by the former. A theory is said to be recursively axiomatized if the set of its axioms is recursive, i.e., it is computable whether or not something is an axiom. Now, if a theory is recursively axiomatized, the set of its theorems is recursively enumerable, because any theorem can be recognized as such via inspection of its proof. But the set of theorems need not be recursive, for there may be no algorithm for recognizing every non-theorem as such. Precisely this is the case with arithmetic.
3. The Framework and a Negative Result

With these preliminaries, we now proceed to describe our framework. For clarity, our construction will proceed in three steps. First, we define the basis for the empirical or factual knowledge of our individuals in terms of standard possible world semantics and partitional information structures. Next, we endow individuals with arithmetical knowledge by assuming that they know (at every state of the world) all the theorems of a version of arithmetic. Finally, we combine the two sources of knowledge, and construct the set of formulas known by an individual at each state of the world.

Proof. If w is i-sound, (5i)⊆Δi(w), then (5i) is valid in w, so Proposition 2 applies.

PROPOSITION 3. If (5i) is valid in w, Q⊆Δi(w) and Δi(w) is recursively enumerable, then w is not i-sound.
3. The Framework and a Negative Result
Proof. By Rosser’s (1936) strengthening of Gödel’s first incompleteness theorem, any recursive extension of Q is inconsistent. The result then follows by Proposition 2. □
3. The Framework and a Negative Result
COROLLARY 2. If (5i)⊆Δi(w), Q⊆Δi(w), and Δi(w) is recursively enumerable, then w is not i-sound.
3. The Framework and a Negative Result

Since the set of theorems generated by Turing machine i is recursively enumerable, Proposition 3 shows that (5i) makes a false claim about such a machine’s knowledge. The obvious corollary is that the machine itself cannot correctly make this claim.

One of the key hypotheses in showing that Turing machines cannot have partitional knowledge was that every state w is i-sound. In this section, we demonstrate that this is indeed the case, provided that the arithmetical theory used by the machines is correct. In so doing, we will be showing that every instance of

is true at every state. The statement of our result will be that if every element of Π is true in every state, then every element of Δi(w) is true in state w. Let us say that a state w is sound if it is i-sound for all i∈I.
PROPOSITION 4. If Π⊆𝐴𝑡(w), then w is sound.

The proof of this result requires more substantial groundwork as compared to our earlier results. The natural idea would be to prove that if A∈Δj(w) then w|=A by induction on the construction of Δj(w). However, the presence of the schema (T) blocks the basis of this induction, for in order to show that w|=KiA→A, one would have to show that if A∈Δj(w) then w|=A, which is just what we were trying to prove. A more indirect strategy is therefore needed. What we do is to transform each formula A into a formula ^A^ in such a way that instances of (T) are transformed into tautologies. We then perform the induction for ^A^ rather than A, and recover the result for A afterwards. ^A^ is defined recursively as follows.
The proof will proceed by a series of lemmas, each of which is stated under the hypothesis of Proposition 4. For ease of reference, the proofs of the individual lemmas are gathered in the appendix.
LEMMA 4.2. For w∈W and A∈Σ, w|=^A^.
LEMMA 4.3. For w∈W and A∈Σ, w*^A^.
LEMMA 4.4. For w∈W and A∈𝐹𝑜𝑟𝑚, w*^A^↔A.
LEMMA 4.5. For i∈I, w∈W and A∈Δi(w), w*A.
LEMMA 4.6. For w∈W and A∈𝐹𝑜𝑟𝑚(Π′), w|=A if and only if w*A.
LEMMA 4.7. For j∈I, w∈W and A∈Δj(w), w|=^A^.
LEMMA 4.8. For w∈W and A∈𝐹𝑜𝑟𝑚, w|=^A^↔A.
The proof of Proposition 4 can now be completed. For, by Lemmas 4.7 and 4.8, for all j∈I, w∈W and A∈Δj(w), we have w|=A. Thus, we can conclude that w is sound for all w∈W. □

It remains for us to note that the rule (RN) implies that instances of the formula KiA→KiKiA are true at every state. Together with Proposition 4, this tells us that our epistemic logic for Turing machines is S4. The most notable feature is that the principle KiA→A is consistent within our framework, thereby restoring the interpretation of Ki as a knowledge operator. This is in contrast to the modal logic G.

We do not claim that our construction is the only one available for Turing machines. Analogues of Proposition 4 could be proved for many different logics. However, the purpose of our exercise has been to present a construction which is designed to get as close to partitional knowledge as a Turing machine can. It is worth mentioning that our negative result does not make essential use of the construction of Δi(w). It is a very general result which relies on the fact that the set of formulas which a numerate Turing machine knows cannot be recursive, on pain of inconsistency.
Proof. By induction on the construction of A.
Basis. If P∈𝐴𝑡𝑜𝑚, ^P^=P, so ^P^↔P∈Taut, but 𝑇𝑎𝑢𝑡⊆Σ by construction of the latter, so ^P^↔P∈Σ.
Induction step. Suppose that A∉𝐴𝑡𝑜𝑚, and that the lemma holds for all formulas less complex than A.

Case (a): A is of the form ¬B. By induction hypothesis, ^B^↔B∈Σ. Now ^¬B^↔¬B=¬^B^↔¬B, and (^B^↔B)→(¬^B^↔¬B)∈𝑇𝑎𝑢𝑡, so (^B^B)→(¬^B^↔¬B)∈Σ. By construction, Σ is closed under MP, so ¬^B^↔¬B∈Σ, i.e. ^A^↔A∈Σ.
Case (b): A is of the form B∧C. Like case (a).

Case (c): A is of the form KjB. By induction hypothesis, ^B^↔B∈Σ. By reasoning as in case (a), ^B^→B∈Σ and B→^B^∈Σ. By construction, Σ is closed under RN⁡j. Hence Kj(^B^→B)∈Σ and Kj(B→^B^)∈Σ. Since (K)⊆Σ and Σ is closed under MP, Kj^B^→KjB∈Σ and KjB→Kj^B^∈Σ. Since (T)⊆Σ, KjB→B∈Σ. But (Kj^B^→KjB)→((KjB→Kj^B^)→((KjB→B)→((B→^B^)→((^B^∧Kj^B^)↔KjB))))∈𝑇𝑎𝑢𝑡, so (^B^∧Kj^B^)↔KjB∈Σ, i.e. ^A^↔A∈Σ.
LEMMA 4.2. For w∈W and A∈Σ, w|=^A^.
Proof. Fix w∈W. We show that for A∈Σn w|=^A^ by induction on n.
Case (a): A∈Π. Thus A∈𝐴𝑡𝑜𝑚, so ^A^=A. By hypothesis, Π⊆𝐴𝑡(w). Thus A∈𝐴𝑡(w). Hence w|=^A^.
Case (b): A∈𝑇𝑎𝑢𝑡. Since ^^ commutes with ¬ and ∧, ^A^∈𝑇𝑎𝑢𝑡. Since |= is defined so that w|=B for all B∈𝑇𝑎𝑢𝑡, w|=^A^.

Case (c): A∈(K). Thus for some B,C,j, A=Kj(B→C)→ (KjB→KjC). Now ^^ commutes with →, which is defined in terms of ¬ and ∧. Hence ^A^=((^B^→^C^)∧Kj(^B^→^C^))→((^B^∧Kj^B^)→(^C^∧Kj^C^)). Evidently, it suffices to show w|=Kj(^B^→^C^)→(Kj^B^→Kj^C^). Suppose w|=Kj(^B^→^C^) and w|=Kj^B^. Then ^B^→^C^∈Δj(w) and ^B^∈Δj(w). By construction, Δj(w) is closed under MP. Thus ^C^∈Δj(w). Hence w|=Kj^C^, as required.
Case (d): A∈(T). Thus for some B,j, A=KjB→B. Hence ^A^=(^B^∧Kj^B^)→^B^, so ^A^∈𝑇𝑎𝑢𝑡. Thus w|=^A^.

Case (e): A∈(4). Thus for some B,j, A=KjB→KjKjB. Hence ^A^=(^B^∧Kj^B^)→((^B^∧Kj^B^)∧Kj(^B^∧Kj^B^)). Evidently, it suffices to show w|=Kj^B^→Kj(^B^∧Kj^B^). Suppose w|=Kj^B^. Then ^B^∈Δj(w). By construction, Δj(w) is closed under RN⁡j. Thus Kj^B^∈Δj(w). Now ^B^→(Kj^B^→(^B^∧Kj^B^))∈𝑇𝑎𝑢𝑡, so ^B^→(Kj^B^→(^B^∧Kj^B^))∈Δj(w). Since Δj(w) is closed under MP, ^B^∧Kj^B^∈Δj(w). Thus w|=Kj(^B^∧Kj^B^), as required.
Induction step. Suppose that for all A∈Σn, w|=^A^. It suffices to show that if A∈MP⁡(Σn)∪RN⁡(Σn) then w|=^A^.
Case (a): A∈MP⁡(Σn). Thus for some B, B∈Σn and B→A∈Σn. By induction hypothesis w|=^B^ and w|=^B→A^. Since ^B→A^=^B^→^A^, w|=^A^.
Case (b): A∈RN⁡(Σn). Thus for some B,j, B∈Σn and A=KjB. By induction hypothesis, w|=^B^. By Lemma 4.1, ^B^↔B∈Σ. Since B∈Σn⊆Σ, ^B^∈Σ⊆Δj(w), so w|=Kj^B^. Thus w|=^B^∧Kj^B^, i.e. w|=^A^.
LEMMA 4.3. For w∈W and A∈Σ, w*^A^.
Proof. We show by induction on n that for all A∈Σn, w*^A^.
Case (a): A∈Π. A∈𝐴𝑡𝑜𝑚 and ^A^=A; since Π⊆𝐴𝑡(w), A∈𝐴𝑡(w), so w*^A^.
Case (b): A∈𝑇𝑎𝑢𝑡. As in (b) of the basis of Lemma 4.2, ^A^∈𝑇𝑎𝑢𝑡, so w*^A^.

Case (c): A∈(K). As in 4.2(c), ^A^ is of the form ((^B^→^C^)∧Kj(^B^→^C^))→((^B^∧Kj^B^)→(^C^∧Kj^C^)), which is a theorem of the modal system K and therefore valid in the possible worlds semantics for *.
Case (d): A∈(T). As in 4.2(d), ^A^∈𝑇𝑎𝑢𝑡, so w*^A^.

Case (e): A∈(4). As in 4.2(e), ^A^ is of the form (^B^∧Kj^B^)→((^B^∧Kj^B^)∧Kj(^B^∧Kj^B^)), which is a theorem of the modal system K4 and therefore valid in the possible worlds semantics for * given the transitivity of Rj.
Induction step. Suppose that for all A∈Σn and w∈W, w*^A^. It suffices to show that if A∈MP⁡(Σn)∪RN⁡(Σn) and w∈W then w*^A^.
Case (a): A∈MP⁡(Σn). Similar to (a) of the induction step of 4.2.
Case (b): A∈RN⁡(Σn). Thus, for some B∈Σn and i∈I, A=KiB. Pick w∈W. By induction hypothesis, w*^B^ and, for all x such that wRix, x*^B^. By definition of *, w*^B^∧Ki^B^, i.e. w*^A^.
LEMMA 4.4. For w∈W and A∈𝐹𝑜𝑟𝑚, w*^A^↔A.
Proof. By induction on the construction of A.
Basis. If P∈𝐴𝑡𝑜𝑚, ^P^=P, so ^P^↔P∈𝑇𝑎𝑢𝑡, so w*^P^↔P.
Induction step. Suppose that A∉𝐴𝑡𝑜𝑚, and that the lemma holds for all formulas less complex than A.
Case (a): A is of the form ¬B. By induction hypothesis, w*^B^↔B, so w*¬^B^↔¬B, i.e. w*^A^↔A.
Case (b): A is of the form A∧C. Similar to (a).

Case (c): A is of the form KjB. By induction hypothesis, for all w∈W, w*^B^↔B. By reasoning like that in 4.3, w*Kj^B^↔KjB. Since Rj is reflexive, w*KjB→B, so w*KjB→^B^. Thus w*(^B^∧Kj^B^)↔KjB, i.e. w*^A^→A.
LEMMA 4.5. For i∈I, w∈W and A∈Δi(w), w*A.
Proof. Fix i∈I and w∈W. We show by induction on n that for all x such that wRix and A∈Δi,n(w), x*A.
Basis. n=0. If A∈Δi,0(w) then A∈Σ∪Φi(w). Let wRix.
Case (a): A∈Σ. x*^A^ by 4.3, so x*A by 4.4.
Case (b): A∈Φi(w). By definition of Φi(w), w*KiA, so x*A since wRix.
Induction step. Suppose that for all x such that wRix, if A∈Δi,n(w) then x*A. It suffices to show that for all x such that wRix, if A∈MP⁡(Δi,n(w))∪RN⁡i(Δi,n(w)) then x*A.
Case (a): A∈MP⁡(Δi,n(w)). For some B, B∈Δi,n(w) and B→A∈Δi,n(w). By induction hypothesis, for all x such that wRix, x*B and x*B→A, so x*A.

Case (b): A∈RN⁡i(Δi,n(w)). For some B, B∈Δi,n(w) and A=KiB. By induction hypothesis, for all x such that wRix, x*B. Since Ri is transitive, for all x such that wRix, for all y such that xRiy, y*B. By definition of *, for all x such that wRix, x*KiB.
LEMMA 4.6. For w∈W and A∈𝐹𝑜𝑟𝑚(Π′), w|=A if and only if w*A.
Proof. By induction on the construction of A.
Basis. If P∈𝐴𝑡𝑜𝑚, w|=P iff P∈𝐴𝑡(w) iff w*P.

Induction step. Suppose that A∉𝐴𝑡𝑜𝑚, and that the lemma holds for all formulas less complex than A. If A is of the form ¬B or B∧C, the result is routine. Suppose that A∈𝐹𝑜𝑟𝑚(Π′) is of the form KjB. If w|=KjB, then B∈Δj(w), so KjB∈Δj(w) because Δj(w) is closed under RN⁡j, so w*KjB by 4.5. Conversely, if w*KjB then B∈Φj(w)⊆Δj(w) because B∈𝐹𝑜𝑟𝑚(Π′), so w|=KjB.
LEMMA 4.7. For j∈I, w∈W and A∈Δj(w), w|=^A^.
Proof. Fix j∈I and w∈W. We show by induction on n that for A∈Δj,n(w), w|=^A^.
Basis. n=0. If A∈Δi,0(w) then A∈Σ∪Φi(w).
Case (b): A∈Φj(w). A∈𝐹𝑜𝑟𝑚(Π′) and w*KjA, so by 4.4 w*^KjA^, i.e. w*^A^∧Kj^A^, so w*^A^, so w|=^A^ by 4.6.
Induction step. Suppose that for all A∈Δj,n(w) and w∈W, w|=^A^. It suffices to show that if A∈MP⁡(Δj,n(w))∪RN⁡j(Δj,n(w)) and w∈W then w|=^A^.
Case (a): A∈MP⁡(Δj,n(w)). Like (a) of the induction step of 4.2.
Case (b): A∈RN⁡j(Δj,n(w)). Thus for some B∈Δj,n(w), A=KjB. By induction hypothesis, w|=^B^. By Lemma 4.1, ^B^↔B∈Σ⊆Δj(w). Since B∈Δj,n(w), ^B^∈Δj(w), so w|=Kj^B^. Thus w|=^B^∧Kj^B^, i.e. w|=^A^.
LEMMA 4.8. For w∈W and A∈𝐹𝑜𝑟𝑚, w|=^A^↔A.

Proof. By induction on the construction of A. The only interesting case is the induction step for A=KjB. Suppose that w|=^B^↔B. If w|=^A^, i.e. w|=^B^∧Kj^B^, then w|=Kj^B^, so ^B^∈Δj(w), so B∈Δj(w) by 4.1, so w|=KjB. Conversely, if w|=KjB then B∈Δj(w), so ^B^∈Δj(w) by 4.1, so w|=Kj^B^; moreover, since B∈Δj(w), w|=^B^ by 4.7; thus w|=^B^∧Kj^B^. Hence w|=^A^↔A.

works.title: Non-genuine MacIntosh logics
passages: The aim of this paper is to extend recent work on admissible rules in modal logic. In the terminology of Chellas and Segerberg [2], the territory of a rule is the set of modal logics in which it is admissible. The structure of such a territory may be complex, not least because extensions of a logic do not in general preserve the admissibility of rules. It can also happen that two logics L and L′ admit a given rule, while L+L′, the smallest logic containing both of them, does not; thus the territory of the rule is not closed under +. Some results will be given of this kind (see 4.0–4.5 below).
Three rules will be investigated. A modal logic L provides the MacIntosh rule just in case for every formula A:
This is equivalent (in normal modal logics) to the principle: if A&◇¬A is consistent in L then ¬A&◇A is consistent in L. L provides the rule of margins just in case for every formula A:

This is equivalent to the principle: if A and ¬A are each consistent in L then A&◇¬A is consistent in L. Let □0A=A and □n+1A=□□nA. L provides the alternative rule of disjunction just in case for all formulas A0,…,An:

This is equivalent to the principle: if each Ai is consistent in L then A0&◇j(1)A1&⋯&◇j(n)An is consistent in L for some j(n),…,j(n). The relations between the rules are clarified in §1. The main results of the paper state sufficient conditions for a modal logic to provide all three rules.

Semantic methods are used. The main construction is of the stack of a model. If M! is the stack of M, every formula falsified at some world in M is falsified at some world in M!, and every world in M! has the ancestral of the accessibility relation to every world in M!. Hence if a logic L is characterized by a model M whose stack M! is also a model of L, L is characterized by a model M! in which every world has the ancestral of accessibility to every world. The proof of the main theorem (2.3) exploits this fact; most of the work involves showing that if L satisfies certain conditions then the stack of the canonical model of L is itself a model of L.

Some earlier results about the rule of margins and the alternative rule of disjunction were proved in [5]; [6] sketches a connection between the rule of margins and some issues in philosophy. Chellas and Segerberg introduce the MacIntosh rule in [2], where the origin of the name and the philosophical interest of the rule are explained. This paper answers some questions left open in [2].

Chellas and Segerberg investigate the class of MacIntosh logics, defined as the normal modal logics which provide the MacIntosh rule. ‘Normal’ is understood in this paper as in [3]. Thus a normal logic is closed under the rule of uniform substitution US; K4, for example, can be axiomatized by the addition of the single formula □p→□□p to the smallest normal logic K, with the same effect as the addition of the schema □A→□□A (‘p’ is always a propositional variable, ‘A’ and ‘B’ metalogical variables over all formulas). In contrast, [2] does not require normal logics to be closed under US.

K4 is not a MacIntosh logic, for it contains □p→□□p but not ◇□p→□p. But it is proved semantically in [2] that KD and KT, for example, are MacIntosh logics (Chellas and Segerberg ask for syntactic proofs of these results; they are given in [7]). It is also shown that any normal extension of KBn is a MacIntosh logic, where Bn is the formula p→□◇np (thus B0=p→□p and B1=B).

A MacIntosh logic is defined in [2] to be genuine just in case for some formula A it contains A→□A (and therefore ◇A→A) but neither □A nor ¬◇A. KB4 is genuine, for it contains □p→□□p but neither □□p nor ¬◇□p. KB0 is also genuine, for it contains p→□p but neither □p nor ¬◇p. But Chellas and Segerberg show that KD and KT are not genuine. They ask whether KBn is genuine for n>0. They also ask a question about the structure of the class of MacIntosh logics: if L and L′ are MacIntosh logics, does it follow that L+L′ (the smallest normal logic containing both L and L′) is also a MacIntosh logic? Both questions will be answered in the negative (for both senses of ‘normal’).
PROPOSITION 1.0. The alternative rule of disjunction is equivalent to its special case n=1.

Proof. It suffices to show that if L provides the rule for n=1 and n=k, L provides it for n=k+1. Fix j(1),…,j(k). If for all j(k+1) ⊢L(A0∨□j(1)A1∨⋯∨□j(k)Ak)∨□j(k+1)Ak+1, either ⊢LAk+1 or ⊢LA0∨□j(1)A1∨⋯∨□j(k)Ak by the rule for n=1. Thus if the premise of the rule holds for n=k+1, either ⊢LAk+1 or the premise of the rule holds for n=k.
PROPOSITION 1.1. If a normal logic provides the alternative rule of disjunction, it provides the rule of margins.
Proof. If ⊢LA→□A then ⊢L□jA→□j+1A for all j, so ⊢L¬A∨□jA for all j, so ⊢L¬A or ⊢LA by the alternative rule.
PROPOSITION 1.2. Not every normal logic providing the rule of margins provides the alternative rule of disjunction.
PROPOSITION 1.3. If a normal logic provides the rule of margins, it is a non-genuine MacIntosh logic.
Proof. Suppose that ⊢LA→□A. If ⊢LA then ⊢L□A and ⊢L◇A→A. If ⊢L¬A then ⊢L¬◇A and ⊢L◇A→A.
PROPOSITION 1.4. The smallest normal logic to provide the rule of margins is KD.

Proof. That any normal logic providing the rule extends KD is shown in [5]. For semantic proofs that KD provides the rule see [5] and, in effect, [2], or 2.4 below (since KD provides the Lemmon–Scott rule of disjunction); for a syntactic proof see [7].
PROPOSITION 1.5. Not every non-genuine MacIntosh logic provides the rule of margins.
Proof. K+□¬⊤ is a non-genuine MacIntosh logic (⊤ a tautology). Since it does not extend KD, by 1.4 it does not provide the rule of margins.
PROPOSITION 1.6. The smallest MacIntosh logic is K+□◇⊤.
PROPOSITION 1.7. If L is a normal logic, L+◇⊤ provides the rule of margins iff L+□◇⊤ is a non-genuine MacIntosh logic.

Proof. Write ⊢ for ⊢L+□◇⊤ and ⊢+ for ⊢L+◇⊤. Since ⊢+□◇⊤, L+◇⊤ extends L+□◇⊤. Left to right: Suppose that L+◇⊤ provides the rule of margins and ⊢A→□A. Thus ⊢+A→□A, so by the rule either ⊢+A or ⊢+¬A. If ⊢+A, ⊢◇⊤→A, so by normality ⊢□◇⊤→□A; since ⊢□◇⊤, ⊢□A; moreover, by normality ⊢◇A→◇⊤, so ⊢◇A→A. Similarly, if ⊢+¬A, ⊢¬◇A and ⊢◇A→A. Thus L+□◇⊤ is a non-genuine MacIntosh logic. Right to left: Suppose that L+□◇⊤ is a non-genuine MacIntosh logic and ⊢+A→□A. Hence ⊢◇⊤→(A→□A), so ⊢(◇⊤&A)→□(◇⊤&A). Since L+□◇⊤ is non-genuine, either ⊢□(◇⊤&A) or ⊢¬◇(◇⊤&A). In the former case, ⊢+□(◇⊤&A), so ⊢+◇(◇⊤&A) because ⊢+◇⊤. Since L+□◇⊤ is a MacIntosh logic, ⊢◇(◇⊤&A)→(◇⊤&A), so ⊢+◇(◇⊤&A)→(◇⊤&A), so ⊢+◇⊤&A, so ⊢+A. If ⊢¬◇(◇⊤&A), ⊢□(◇⊤→¬A), so ⊢□◇⊤→□¬A, so ⊢□¬A, so ⊢+□¬A, so ⊢+◇¬A. Moreover, ⊢¬A→□¬A; since L+□◇⊤ is a MacIntosh logic, ⊢◇¬A→¬A, so ⊢+◇¬A→¬A, so ⊢+¬A. Thus L+◇⊤ provides the rule of margins.
PROPOSITION 1.8. A normal extension of KD provides the rule of margins iff it is a non-genuine MacIntosh logic.
PROPOSITION 1.9. K+□◇⊤ is a non-genuine MacIntosh logic.
Proof. By 1.4, K+◇⊤ provides the rule of margins. The result follows by 1.7. Chellas and Segerberg subsequently gave a different proof of the non-genuineness of K+□◇⊤ (which they call DD‾).

Chellas and Segerberg prove that KBn is a MacIntosh logic, and ask whether it is genuine (n≥1). This section gives a negative answer. The strategy is to show that KBDn provides the alternative rule of disjunction, and then use 1.1 and 1.7 to show that KBn is non-genuine. KDB1 (= KDB) was already shown in [5] to provide the alternative rule, as were KD, KT, KTB and KTG1. Proposition 2.4 generalizes these results (this generalization does not cover all the normal logics proved in [5] to provide the alternative rule; KD! is an exception). It is proved by a simplification of the model-theoretic construction used in [5] (with notation as in [3]); however, the greater generality of the result requires a more complex argument.

The main construction is of the stack of a model. The stack of ⟨W,R,V⟩ is a new model ⟨W!,R!,V!⟩, defined as follows, where N is the set of natural numbers, p is any propositional variable and |i−j|=max⁡{i,j}−min⁡{i,j}.

⟨W!,R!,V!⟩ may be thought of as an infinite stack of copies of ⟨W,R,V⟩, with a warped copy at the bottom. Above the bottom, the accessibility relation is like R, but also projected up towards the next copy above and down towards the next copy below. At the bottom of the stack, the accessibility relation is warped; it holds everywhere. At the bottom, the valuation need coincide with V only on non-modal formulas. Each step up from one copy to the next guarantees the coincidence of the stack’s valuation with V for formulas with one more layer of modal operators. Thus each formula is evaluated as by V from some point up; this is the content of 2.0. Hence any formula true at some point in ⟨W,R,V⟩ is true at some point in ⟨W!,R!,V!⟩. Now suppose that R is serial; for every w∈W there is an x∈W such that wRx. Then any point not at the bottom of the stack has R! to some point in the copy below, and so has the ancestral of R! to some point in the bottom copy, and therefore to every point in the bottom copy. Similarly, suppose that R is backward-serial; for every w∈W there is an x∈W such that xRw. Then every point in the bottom copy has the ancestral of R! to any point in the stack. Thus if R is both serial and backward-serial, every point in the stack has the ancestral of R! to every point in the stack. In this case, suppose that the formula A holds somewhere in the original model, as does the formula B. By 2.0, A holds at some point in the stack and B holds at some point in the stack. Since the former point has the ancestral of R! to the latter, A&◇iB holds at the former point for some i. This property of the stack is crucial in the proof of 2.3.

Consider the case in which ⟨W,R,V⟩ is the canonical model of a logic L, and R is serial and backward-serial. If ⟨W!,R!,V!⟩ can be shown to be a model of L, it will have been shown that if A and B are each consistent in L then so is A&◇iB for some i. This is in effect what is needed to show that L provides the alternative rule of disjunction, from which it will follow by 1.1 and 1.3 that L provides the rule of margins and is a non-genuine MacIntosh logic. R will be serial if L is an extension of KD. R will be backward-serial if L provides denecessitation, in the sense that for every formula A, ⊢L□A implies ⊢LA. Thus the results below concern extensions of KD which provide denecessitation. It is also required that the stack of the canonical model of L be a model of L. Hence the interest is in properties of R that are preserved by R!. Such a property is m,n,j,k-incestuality for m+j≤n+k, where R is m,n,j,k-incestual just in case for all w,x and y, if wRmx and wRjy then, for some z, xRnz and yRkz; this is the content of 2.1. Now m,n,j,k-incestuality is known to be the semantic condition corresponding in the usual way to the formula Gm,n,j,k, ◇m□np→□j◇kp. The alternative rule of disjunction will therefore be established for extensions of KD which are axiomatized by such formulas and provide denecessitation. KDBn will emerge as a special case.
The modal depth #A of a formula A is defined as usual: #p=0 for each propositional variable p; #¬A=#A; #(A&B)=max⁡{#A,#B}; #□A=#A+1.
PROPOSITION 2.0. If ⟨W!,R!,V!⟩ is the stack of ⟨W,R,V⟩ and #A≤i, then V!(A,⟨u,i⟩)=V(A,u).

Proof. By induction on the complexity of A. The definition of V! gives the basis. The cases of ¬ and & are routine. Assume the claim is true for A, and #□A≤i. It suffices to show that V!(□A,⟨u,i⟩)=0 iff V(□A,u)=0. Suppose V!(□A,⟨u,i⟩)=0. Then for some v and j, ⟨u,i⟩R!⟨v,j⟩ and V!(A,⟨v,j⟩)=0. Since #A+1≤i, 1≤i. Thus, by definition of R!, |i−j|≤1 and uRv. Hence #A≤j, so by the induction hypothesis V(A,v)=V!(A,⟨v,j⟩)=0. Since uRv, V(□A,u)=0. Conversely, suppose V(□A,u)=0. Then for some v, uRv and V(A,v)=0. Now #A<i, so by hypothesis V!(A,⟨v,i⟩)=V(A,v). Moreover, ⟨u,i⟩R!⟨v,i⟩ by definition of R!. Thus V!(□A,⟨u,i⟩)=0. So V!(□A,⟨u,i⟩)=V(□A,u).
PROPOSITION 2.1. If ⟨W!,R!,V!⟩ is the stack of ⟨W,R,V⟩, m+j≤n+k and R is serial, backward-serial and m,n,j,k-incestual, then R! is m,n,j,k-incestual.
Proof. Suppose that ⟨w,g⟩R!m⟨x,h⟩ and ⟨w,g⟩R!j⟨y,i⟩. There are three cases.

Case (a): wRmx and wRjy. Since R is m,n,j,k-incestual, for some z, xRnz and yRkz. Thus there are x0,…,xn and y0,…,yk such that x=x0Rx1R…Rxn=z and y=y0Ry1R…Ryk=z. Assume h≤i (the argument is parallel if i≤h). By definition of R!, g≤h+m (because ⟨w,g⟩R!m⟨x,h⟩) and i≤g+j (because ⟨w,g⟩R!j⟨y,i⟩), so g+i≤h+g+m+j, so i−h≤m+j≤n+k. PROPOSITION 2.2. L provides denecessitation iff the canonical model of L is backward-serial.
Proof. A simple variation on the proof of Theorem 3.4 in [4].

for some g(1),…,g(h) such that #A0+#A1<g(1),…,#A0+#Ah<g(h), then ⊢KD+XAi for some i (0≤i≤h).

Proof. Let ⟨W,R,V⟩ be the canonical model of KD+X, and ⟨W!,R!,V!⟩ the stack of ⟨W,R,V⟩. Since KD+X extends KD, R is serial. Since KD+X admits denecessitation, R is backward-serial by 2.2. For Gm,n,j,k∈X, R is m,n,j,k-incestual by Theorem 4.2 of [4], so R! is m,n,j,k-incestual by 2.1 above, so ⟨W!,R!,V!⟩ is a model of Gm,n,j,k by Theorem 4.1 of [4]. Thus ⟨W!,R!,V!⟩ is a model of KD+X. Now suppose that ⊢KD+XAi for no i (0≤i≤h). Thus for 0≤i≤h there is a wi∈W such that V(Ai,wi)=0. Let f=#A0. It suffices to show that

COROLLARY 2.4. Under the conditions of Theorem 2.3, KD+X is a non-genuine MacIntosh logic and provides the alternative rule of disjunction and the rule of margins.
Proof. That KD+X provides the alternative rule of disjunction is immediate from 2.3. By 1.1, it provides the rule of margins. By 1.8, it is a non-genuine MacIntosh logic.

COROLLARY 2.5. Let X be a set of wff such that if A∈X, A=Gm,n,j,k for some m,n,j,k, where m+j≤n+k, and suppose that G0,0,0,k∈X for some k≥1. Then K+X is a non-genuine MacIntosh logic and provides the alternative rule of disjunction and the rule of margins.
Proof. G0,0,0,k=p→◇kp. Thus ⊢KD+X◇⊤, so K+X=KD+X. Moreover ⊢K+X□kA→A; thus K+X provides denecessitation, for if ⊢K+X□A, ⊢K+X□kA, so ⊢K+XA. The result follows by 2.4.

COROLLARY 2.6. Let X be a set of wff such that if A∈X, A=Gm,n,j,k for some m,n,j,k, where m+j≤n+k. Then KT+X is a non-genuine MacIntosh logic and provides the alternative rule of disjunction and the rule of margins.
COROLLARY 2.7. KDBk provides the rule of margins (k>0).
Proof. □p→◇p is G0,1,0,1 and p→□◇kp is G0,0,1,k. Together they yield p→◇k+1p, i.e. G0,0,0,k+1. Thus KDBk=K+{G0,1,0,1,G0,0,1,k,G0,0,0,k+1}. By 2.5, KDBk provides the rule of margins.
COROLLARY 2.8. KBk is a non-genuine MacIntosh logic (k>0).
Proof. By 1.7, KBk+□◇⊤ is a non-genuine MacIntosh logic iff KBDk provides the rule of margins, as it does by 2.7. But KBk+□◇⊤=KBk, for □◇k⊤, and so □◇⊤, is a theorem of KBk.

Why are the conditions of Theorem 2.3 needed? Proposition 3.1 below shows that the inequality m+j≤n+k is “the best possible” in the sense that for any m,n,j,k not satisfying the inequality, some normal logic satisfies the other conditions of Theorem 2.3 but not its conclusion. To see the point of the inequality, recall that Gm,n,j,k corresponds to m,n,j,k-incestuality: if wRmx and wRjy then, for some z, xRnz and yRkz. If R is symmetric, one can think of the minimum number of steps of R needed to get from x to y as the distance between them. Thus if the distance between x and y is m+j, there is a w such that wRmx and wRjy; but if yRnz and yRkz, the distance between x and y is at most n+k, so m+j≤n+k. So if n+k<m+j, m,n,j,k-incestuality limits the maximum distance between points (in symmetric models) to n+k. Thus if every point within a distance n+k has a certain property, so has every point within a distance n+k+1, which causes violations of the rule of margins. These remarks constitute a sketchy semantic equivalent of the proofs of 3.0 and 3.1. The need for the denecessitation condition in 2.3 is clear from 3.4. Proposition 3.6 gives an example of a logic meeting all the conditions for the proof of Theorem 2.3 except for denecessitation that does not provide the alternative rule of disjunction (note that the frame used to prove 3.6 is not backward-serial).
PROPOSITION 3.0. If L is a consistent normal logic and ⊢L□np→□jp where n<j, L provides neither the rule of margins nor the alternative rule of disjunction.

Proof. Let *(A)=A&□A&⋯&□j−1A. Since ⊢L□np→□jp and n<j, ⊢L*(p)→□jp. Since L is normal, ⊢L(*(p)&□jp)→□*(p). Thus ⊢L*(p)→□*(p). If L provides the rule of margins, either ⊢L*(p) or ⊢L¬*(p). If ⊢L*(p), ⊢Lp and L is inconsistent by US. If ⊢L¬*(p), ⊢L¬*(⊤) by US; but ⊢L*(⊤) by normality, and L is again inconsistent. Thus L does not provide the rule of margins. By 1.1, L does not provide the alternative rule of disjunction.
PROPOSITION 3.1. If n+k<m+j, no consistent normal extension of KBGm,n,j,k provides either the rule of margins or the alternative rule of disjunction.

Proof. Let L be a normal extension of KB+◇m□np→□j◇kp. Then ⊢L□m◇m□np→□m+j◇kp. Since L extends KB, ⊢Lp→□m◇mp; by US, ⊢L□np→□m◇m□np, so ⊢L□np→□m+j◇kp. By US, ⊢L□n+kp→□m+j◇k□kp. Since L extends KB, ⊢L◇k□kp→p and therefore ⊢L□m+j◇k□kp→□m+jp. Thus ⊢L□n+kp→□m+jp. Thus if L is consistent, by 3.0 it provides neither rule.
PROPOSITION 3.2. If n+k<m+j, any consistent normal extension of KDBGm,n,j,k is a genuine MacIntosh logic.
Proof. Such a logic is MacIntosh because it is a normal extension of KB. Were it non-genuine, by 1.8 it would provide the rule of margins, contrary to 3.1.
PROPOSITION 3.3. If n+k<m+j, KTBGm,n,j,k provides neither the rule of margins nor the alternative rule of disjunction.
Proof. The system is consistent because all its theorems become theorems of the propositional calculus on deletion of all occurrences of □ and ◇. The result follows by 3.1.
PROPOSITION 3.4. If L provides the rule of margins or the alternative rule of disjunction, L provides denecessitation.
Proof. If ⊢L□A, ⊢LA→□A. If L provides either rule, ⊢LA or ⊢L¬A. If ⊢L¬A, ⊢L□¬A, so ⊢L□(A&¬A); but by 1.4 L extends KD, so L is inconsistent, so ⊢LA.
PROPOSITION 3.5. If a MacIntosh logic extends KD, it provides denecessitation.
Proof. If ⊢L□A, ⊢LA→□A, so ⊢L◇A→A because L is a MacIntosh logic. But ⊢L◇A because L extends KD, so ⊢LA.
PROPOSITION 3.6. KDG2,2,2,2 provides none of: the MacIntosh rule, the rule of margins, the alternative rule of disjunction.
Proof. Call the logic L. Since L is normal, ⊢L□2◇2¬p∨□2◇2p, so ⊢L□(□◇2¬p∨□◇2p). If L provides one of the rules, it provides denecessitation by 3.4 and 3.5. Then ⊢L□◇2¬p∨□◇2p. Consider this frame:

The frame is clearly serial and 2,2,2,2-incestual, so L is valid on it. However, if V(p,x″)=1 and V(p,y″)=0, V(◇2¬p,x)=V(◇2p,y)=0, so V(□◇2¬p,w)=V(□◇2p,w)=0. Thus □◇2¬p∨□◇2p is not valid on the frame, and so is not a theorem of L. Thus L provides none of the rules.

The final topic is Chellas and Segerberg’s second question: if L and L′ are MacIntosh logics, does it follow that L+L′ is a MacIntosh logic too? Here L+L′ is defined as the intersection of all normal logics containing both L and L′. It turns out that KD! (KD+◇p→□p) and KD4c (KD+□2p→□p) are MacIntosh logics, but that their sum KD!4c is not. Moreover, KD! and KD4c both provide the alternative rule of disjunction and the rule of margins, while their sum provides neither. Thus MacIntosh logics do not form a lattice under + and ∩; similarly for the logics providing the alternative rule of disjunction, or the rule of margins.
PROPOSITION 4.0. KD! provides the alternative rule of disjunction and the rule of margins.
PROPOSITION 4.1. KD! is a non-genuine MacIntosh logic.
PROPOSITION 4.2. KD4c is sound and complete with respect to dense serial backward-serial models.

Proof. By Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 of [4], KD4c is sound and complete with respect to dense serial models. Thus it suffices to show that if a dense serial model invalidates A, so does a dense serial backward-serial model. Let ⟨W,R,V⟩ be dense and serial. Define a new model ⟨W*,R*,V*⟩ as follows (where Q+ is the set of non-negative rationals):

To see that R* is dense, suppose that ⟨u,r⟩R*⟨v,s⟩; if r=s=0 and uRv, then uRwRv for some w because R is dense, so

To see that R* is serial, consider ⟨u,r⟩; if r>0, ⟨u,r⟩R*⟨u,0⟩; if r=0, uRv for some v because R is serial, so ⟨u,0⟩R*⟨v,0⟩. R* is backward-serial because ⟨u,r+1⟩R*⟨u,r⟩. It is routine to show by induction on the complexity of A that V*(A,⟨u,0⟩)=V(A,u). Thus if ⟨W,R,V⟩ invalidates A, so does ⟨W*,R*,V*⟩.
Proof. By 4.2 and the proof of Theorem 3.4 in [4].
PROPOSITION 4.4. KD4c is a non-genuine MacIntosh logic and provides the alternative rule of disjunction and the rule of margins.
Proof. By 4.3, KD!4c=KDG0,2,1,0 meets the conditions of 2.4.
PROPOSITION 4.5. KD!4c provides none of: the MacIntosh rule, the rule of margins, the alternative rule of disjunction.
Proof. ⊢KD4c◇p→◇◇p, ⊢KD□p→◇p and ⊢KD!◇◇p→□□p, so ⊢KD!4c□p→□□p, so ⊢KD!4c(p&□p)→□(p&□p). Thus if KD!4c is a MacIntosh logic, ⊢KD!4c◇(p&□p)→(p&□p). However, consider this frame:

Since the frame is dense, serial and functional, KD!4c is valid on it. However, if V(p,w)=0 and V(p,x)=1, V(p&□p,w)=0 and V(p&□p,x)=1, so V(◇(p&□p),w)=1. Hence ◇(p&□p)→(p&□p) is not valid on the frame, and so is not a theorem of KD!4c. Thus KD!4c is not a MacIntosh logic. The result follows by 1.1 and 1.8.

works.title: Never Say Never
passages: I. An argument is presented for the conclusion that the hypothesis that no one will ever decide a given proposition is intuitionistically inconsistent. II. A distinction between sentences and statements blocks a similar argument for the stronger conclusion that the hypothesis that I have not yet decided a given proposition is intuitionistically inconsistent, but does not block the original argument. III. A distinction between empirical and mathematical negation might block the original argument, and empirical negation might be modelled on Nelson’s strong negation, but only on intuitionistically unacceptable assumptions. IV. Intuitionists may have to accept the original argument, and therefore be committed to a dubious view of time on which there cannot be merely inductive evidence for statements about the infinite future.

Consider any unsolved problem in mathematics: Goldbach’s Conjecture will do. We are strongly inclined to think that, for all we now know, the Conjecture will never be decided. This thought does not require it to be undecidable in principle, or even in practice. It may have a humanly feasible proof or counter-example that will never be discovered, because our species becomes prematurely extinct through nuclear war. Perhaps no other species capable of doing mathematics will happen ever to evolve anywhere in the universe. Such possibilities seem banal, if melancholy. Nevertheless, there are reasons to think that they must be denied by those who generalize intuitionism from mathematical to empirical thought. This paper states those reasons. In particular, it suggests that, so generalized, intuitionism embodies a conception of the infinite future radically at odds with our usual conception of it. On the intuitionistic conception, inductive evidence can support predictions about finite periods of the future, but not unrestricted generalizations over all future times. The reader is left to judge whether the result constitutes a reductio ad absurdum of intuitionism.

How is the intuitionist to acknowledge that Goldbach’s Conjecture may never be decided? There are two problems, one of expression and one of consistency. First, a way must be found to express, in terms that have been given an intuitionistic semantics, the claim that Goldbach’s Conjecture may never be decided. Second, that formula must be shown to be consistent with intuitionistic theory. These problems will be elaborated in turn.

The proposition that Goldbach’s Conjecture may never be decided seems to be constructed by the application of a possibility operator to the proposition that Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided. The latter proposition is empirical, not mathematical, in content. It concerns the constructions actually carried out by flesh and blood mathematicians in real time, not those notionally carried out by an idealized mathematician (the creative subject) in ideal time. What is at issue is therefore the extension of the language of intuitionistic mathematics by the addition of terms for empirical concepts. Such an extension raises large questions about the philosophy of intuitionism. On a narrow view, it is a philosophy of mathematics as a human construction of a very special kind, with no implications for the nature of human thought in general. If so, the language of intuitionistic mathematics may be sui generis; we simply step outside it, back into ordinary language as classically conceived, when we want to express an empirical proposition. On this view, there is no obstacle to acknowledging in so many words the empirical possibility that Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided. However, Brouwer did not always restrict his intuitionism to mathematics (1975, e.g. p. 488). Dummett (1975), Prawitz (1977) and others have argued systematically that the restricted view is too narrow. They conceive the intuitionistic account of the meanings of mathematical and logical symbols as a special case of a much broader constructivist approach to semantics in general. If they are right, a constructivist account must also be given of the meanings of empirical sentences, such as “Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided”. That is the issue discussed in this paper. Can the intuitionistic semantics for mathematical language be extended to a semantics for, in particular, the empirical tense operator “never”?

The problem is not simply a formal one. Formally, in the particular case at issue, the Kripke semantics for intuitionistic logic can indeed be extended to a Kripke semantics for intuitionistic tense logic (Ewald, 1986). But a Kripke semantics gives the meanings intended by the intuitionists only to the extent that it can be interpreted within their informal account of those meanings. That account explains the meaning of a mathematical sentence by the condition for something to count as a proof of it. The obvious difficulty in extending such an account to empirical sentences is that they do not have proofs. However, the notion of a proof may itself be taken as the specialization to mathematics of a more general notion of a warrant for assertion of some canonical kind, a notion applicable to empirical sentences as well as mathematical ones. The meaning of a sentence of either kind might then be explained by the condition for its assertive use to be warranted. The details of such an account remain to be worked out; indeed, it is not clear that they can be worked out. Nevertheless, the schematic generalization will tentatively be used as a background assumption in what follows, whose adequacy will be tested by the more specific discussion to come. The generalization will be assumed to be faithful enough to the original to validate intuitionistic logic; the problem concerns views with a serious right to be considered intuitionistic, not all those that take some vague inspiration from intuitionism.

Suppose that an intuitionistic semantics has been given for the sentence “Goldbach’s Conjecture may never be decided”. The second problem is to show that, so construed, it is intuitionistically consistent.

The consistency problem may be simplified slightly, by the removal of the modal element from the sentence. For the word “may” in this context expresses epistemic possibility; for all we know, Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided. Thus if the stronger non-modal claim “Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided” were intuitionistically inconsistent, then we could prove it to be inconsistent with what we know, thereby refuting the weaker modal claim “Goldbach’s Conjecture may never be decided”. Conversely, if the weaker claim is intuitionistically inconsistent, then so a fortiori is the stronger one. Thus the problem to be addressed is the intuitionistic consistency of the non-modal claim “Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided”. Of course, we have at present no positive reason to assert that Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided. For all we know, it will be decided tomorrow. The point is that we also seem to have no warrant to deny that it will never be decided. Thus there seems to be no warrant for a theory inconsistent with the supposition that Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided.

Let KA mean that at some past, present or future time someone possesses a warrant to assert A (in spite of the use of the letter “K”, it will not be taken for granted that such a warrant implies knowledge). Thus KA expresses an empirical proposition, even when A expresses a mathematical one. Suppose that intuitionistic negation ¬ may be applied to empirical as well as mathematical propositions, on some appropriate generalization of its usual semantics. Then, if p is Goldbach’s Conjecture, the sentence “Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided” may be formalized by ¬(Kp∨K¬p), which is equivalent in intuitionistic logic to ¬Kp∧¬K¬p. Why should there be any doubt as to the consistency of ¬Kp∧¬K¬p with intuitionistic theory?

The problem is that there seems to be an intuitionistically valid argument from ¬KA to ¬A. For consider the conjunction A∧¬KA. Could anyone ever possess a warrant to assert that conjunction? If so, K(A∧¬KA) would hold. Then KA would be true, for a warrant to assert a conjunction involves warrants to assert its conjuncts, so the second conjunct would be false, so the conjunction as a whole would be false. Thus one can possess a warrant to assert A∧¬KA only if what one asserts is false. Such a self-defeating warrant is evidently not a genuine warrant at all. Thus no one ever could possess a warrant to assert A∧¬KA, even in principle.1 Since a warrant is something that someone could in principle possess, there could not be a warrant to assert A∧¬KA. Now, intuitionistically, what proves ¬B is what proves that there could not be a proof of B. The obvious generalization of this from mathematical to empirical language is that what warrants the assertion of ¬B is what warrants the assertion that there could not be a warrant for asserting B. Now a warrant has just been displayed for the assertion that there could not be a warrant for asserting A∧¬KA; intuitionistically, it therefore warrants the assertion of ¬(A∧¬KA). But ¬(A∧¬KA) is intuitionistically equivalent to:

By substitution of p and then of ¬p for A in (1), the conjunction ¬Kp∧¬K¬p therefore entails ¬p∧¬¬p, a contradiction. The argument seems to have demonstrated the intuitionistic inconsistency of the hypothesis that a given proposition will never be decided.2

The argument is not restricted to the case in which p is a mathematical proposition, e.g. Goldbach’s Conjecture. Propositions about the past may never be decided, or so it seems, and the difficulty arises for them too (Percival, 1990). However, the semantics of the past tense raises a tangle of further difficulties for the intuitionist that cannot be addressed here (Dummett, 1969). For present purposes, p is best taken as a mathematical proposition whose intuitionistic semantics is clear, so that attention can be focussed on the problem raised by the foregoing argument. The considerations to follow should generalize to the other cases.

Intuitively, the point might be put like this. The intuitionist equates truth with the existence of a warrant. Since truth is closed under conjunction, warrants for asserting propositions separately must be combined into a warrant for asserting them together. Since there cannot be a warrant to assert Goldbach’s Conjecture together with the proposition that no one will ever have a warrant to assert Goldbach’s Conjecture, the existence of a warrant for the latter proposition entails the nonexistence of a warrant for the former, which is enough intuitionistically to make its negation true (Rabinowicz, 1985, p. 202).

In classical logic, the decisive conditional ¬KA→¬A is equivalent to A→KA. Although this form of contraposition is not generally valid in intuitionistic logic, it has been suggested that the intuitionistic semantics for → might validate A→KA directly (Hart, 1979, p. 165; Wright, 1987, p. 314). What proves A→B, according to the intuitionist, is an operation that provably transforms proofs of A into proofs of B. The obvious generalization of this clause to empirical sentences is that a warrant for A→B is an operation that is warranted to transform warrants for A into warrants for B. The argument is that if one possesses a warrant to assert A, then reflection on one’s possession of it immediately gives one a warrant to assert that someone at some time possesses a warrant to assert A, i.e. to assert KA; this reflection is warranted to transform warrants for A into warrants for KA, and therefore constitutes a warrant for A→KA. However, this argument neglects any distinction between the existence of a warrant and someone’s possession of it. What has to be transformed into a warrant for KA is a warrant for A; what the argument transformed into a warrant for KA was someone’s possession of a warrant for A. Intuitionists are not compelled to identify the existence of a warrant with someone’s possession of it. They will certainly regard a warrant as something that someone could possess, but it has not been shown that it exists only in actually being possessed. If the intuitionist makes this distinction, the operations on warrants for A to which the intuitionistic semantics of → appeals should not rely on someone’s possession of those warrants. Such a conception can be worked out in some detail, and does not require warrants to be treated platonistically in any intuitionistically unacceptable sense (Williamson, 1988). Thus the intuitionist need not assert A→KA. However, the argument for ¬KA→¬A remains, for it is not even possible to possess a warrant for A∧¬KA.

A striking feature of the argument for ¬KA→¬A is that it seems to go through even if KA is given the unintended reading “I now have a warrant to assert that A”. How could anyone ever have a warrant to assert “A and I do not now have a warrant to assert that A”? Yet if the intuitionist is forced to conclude “If I do not now have a warrant to assert that A, then it is not the case that A”, such a solipsism of the present moment surely is a reductio ad absurdum of intuitionism.

The nature of the problem may be clarified with a different example. Consider the sentence “On the next toss this fair coin will come up heads”. We may reasonably assume that there cannot be a warrant for using that sentence to make an assertion; one cannot know in advance how a fair coin will land. If the intuitionistic semantics for ¬ is taken at face value, it therefore seems to provide a warrant for using the negation of that sentence to make an assertion. That is absurd. One has no more warrant to assert “On the next toss this fair coin will not come up heads” than to assert “On the next toss this fair coin will come up heads”. For all one knows, in a few minutes one will have a warrant to assert “On the last toss this fair coin came up heads”.

The intuitionistic semantics for ¬ can be modified. What a warrant to use the sentence “¬A” assertively must exclude is a warrant to use some sentence or other to assert the statement that is expressed in the present context by the sentence “A”. The very statement that is expressed in the present context by the sentence “On the next toss this fair coin will come up heads” will be expressed in a few minutes by the sentence “On the last toss this fair coin came up heads”. A warrant to use the negation of the former sentence to deny the statement must exclude a warrant to use the latter sentence to assert it. This point does not depend on an ontology of statements as language-independent entities. The intuitionist who (unlike Brouwer) has taken the linguistic turn may regard sentences and statements as generated by two contrasting ways of classifying utterances into types. Utterances of “Today is fine” on Monday and Tuesday are tokens of the same sentence, of which an utterance of “Yesterday was fine” on Tuesday is not a token. Utterances of “Today is fine” on Monday and of “Yesterday was fine” on Tuesday are tokens of the same statement, of which an utterance of “Today is fine” on Tuesday is not a token. The intuitionist may then be regarded as giving a semantics of statements rather than sentences. The two kinds of semantics are prolegomena to the same end, the assignment of interpretations to individual utterances. An intuitionistic semantics must therefore include an account of the principles by which utterances are classified together as tokens of the same statement. To provide such an account is a non-trivial task.

The distinction between a semantics of statements and a semantics of sentences should not be pushed too far. A semantics of statements may be equivalent to a semantics in which a warrant to use a sentence in a context is explained in terms of warrants to use simpler sentences in related contexts. However, the simpler sentences will not all be constituents of the given sentence; “On the last toss this coin came up heads” is simpler than, but not a constituent of, “It is not the case that on the next toss this coin will come up heads”. Compositionality holds only for statements; a semantics of statements is therefore more perspicuous.

If the intuitionist can provide a semantics of statements, the argument for the conditional “If I do not now have a warrant to assert that A, then it is not the case that A” lapses. Someone better informed than I am now could very easily have a warrant now to assert the statement that A and I do not now have a warrant to assert that A; I could very easily become better informed and acquire a warrant a few minutes from now to assert the same statement. In neither case is it asserted by use of the sentence “A and I do not now know that A”, but that fact is irrelevant to a semantics of statements. Thus the intuitionist avoids the immediate threat of reductio ad absurdum.

A further question arises: can the notion of a statement also be used to block the argument for the crucial conditional ¬KA→¬A on its intended reading, “If no one ever has a warrant to assert that A, then it is not the case that A”? That would require warrant to assert the statement that A and no one ever has a warrant to assert that A by use of a sentence other than “A and no one ever has a warrant to assert that A”, indeed not even synonymous with it. The indexicality of “now” and “I” is not present to be exploited in the construction of such a sentence. Nevertheless, it has been suggested, although not in the context of intuitionism, that non-actual possible situations might play the role played above by future times and other persons (Edgington, 1985; Rabinowicz and Segerberg, 1994). In particular, it may be argued, the statement that is actually expressed by the sentence “C” could have been expressed in a non-actual situation by the sentence “If it had been that B, it would have been that C”, where, from the standpoint of that situation, what would have obtained had “B” as used there been true is the actual situation. For example, if “C” is “A and no one ever has a warrant to assert that A”, the non-actual situation might be one in which someone has a warrant to assert that A, but things are otherwise much as they are in the actual situation, and “B” might be “I did not acquire this warrant”. On this view, someone could have had a warrant to assert the statement that A and no one ever has a warrant to assert that A, by use of the sentence “If I had not acquired this warrant, it would have been that A and no one ever had a warrant to assert that A” rather than the sentence “A and no one ever has a warrant to assert that A”.

One difficulty for the foregoing proposal is that it is threatened by trivialization. If there is no restriction on the way in which the actual situation is described by “B”, the antecedent of the counterfactual, then “B” can be a conjunction of which one conjunct is “C”, the consequent of the counterfactual, whenever “C” as used in the relevant non-actual situation correctly describes the actual situation. In that case the counterfactual becomes a trivial logical truth (Williamson, 1987). This is particularly unfortunate for the intuitionist, since it removes the epistemological constraints on warrants; any true statement automatically acquires a trivial warrant when asserted under the guise of a suitably chosen counterfactual. Thus some restriction is needed on the way in which the actual situation is described by the antecedent of the counterfactual. No adequate restriction has been suggested.3

On the foregoing grounds, the proposal will be assumed to fail. An intuitionistic semantics of statements does not invalidate the conditional ¬KA→¬A. The formula ¬(Kp∨K¬p) therefore remains intuitionistically inconsistent. If intuitionistic theory is to be consistent with “Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided”, as it apparently should be, then that sentence must be formalized in some other way. Section III considers one such attempt.

A distinction is sometimes drawn between mathematical and empirical negation (Dummett, 1977, p. 337). One might therefore introduce a negation operator ∼ with a semantics quite different from that of ¬, and designed for empirical statements. If p is an empirical statement, there is still a statement ¬p, explained somewhat as above, but it is no longer regarded as the standard negation of p. It may also be assumed that there is a statement ∼p even if p is mathematical, for at worst we can make a special stipulation as to its significance in this case. In the previous formalization of “Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided”, ¬(Kp∨K¬p), the disjunction Kp∨K¬p is empirical, whereas p is mathematical. The proposal would therefore be to replace the outer but not the inner occurrence of ¬ by empirical negation, ∼. The new formalization of “Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided” is therefore ∼(Kp∨K¬p).

There is a difficulty. If ∼(Kp∨K¬p) is to be intuitionistically consistent when ¬(Kp∨K¬p) is not, the latter must not be an intuitionistic consequence of the former; yet there is reason to believe that any alternative negation must be at least as strong as ¬. For if ∼ is to count intuitionistically as any sort of negation at all, ∼A should at least be inconsistent with A in the ordinary intuitionistic sense. A warrant for A∧∼A should be impossible. That is, we should have ¬(A∧∼A). By the intuitionistically valid schema ¬(A∧B)→(B→¬A), this yields:
In particular, from ∼(Kp∨K¬p) one can derive ¬(Kp∨K¬p). Since the latter is intuitionistically inconsistent, so is the former. The appeal to empirical negation has achieved nothing.

That is not quite the end of the story. Suppose that we do after all replace the inner as well as the outer occurrence of ¬ in ¬(Kp∨K¬p) by ∼. From ∼(Kp∨K∼p) we can use (2) to derive ¬(Kp∨K∼p), which is equivalent to ¬Kp∧¬K∼p, from which ¬p∧¬∼p follows by (1). However, there is no reason to regard the last formula as a contradiction. We seem to have found a way of translating the sentence “Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided” into an intuitionistically consistent formula, by using the new negation throughout.

There is an obvious candidate for ∼: strong negation, as introduced by Nelson (1949) through the notion of constructible falsity. It is governed by the result of adding the following axiom schemas to intuitionistic propositional logic (axiomatized with modus ponens as the only rule of inference):4

One can adapt the Kripke semantics for intuitionistic logic to strong negation by adding to the idea of the verification of a formula at a node in the model a separate idea of its falsification there (Thomason, 1969; Rasiowa, 1974, pp. 276–310; van Dalen, 1986, pp. 301–303). Informally, the new semantics might be said to treat assertion and denial as autonomous but related speech acts.5 The condition for denial of a complex statement to have a warrant must be given in terms of warrants for its constituents, in parallel with the condition for its assertion. Formally, we start as usual with a set of nodes N and a reflexive partial order ≥ on N. α⊢A means that the node α verifies (provides a warrant to assert) the formula A; α⊣A means that α falsifies (provides a warrant to deny) A. If A is atomic, then we cannot have both α⊢A and α⊣A; if in addition α≤β, then α⊢A implies β⊢A and α⊣A implies β⊣A (monotonicity). Verification is incompatible with falsification; if something is verified, it stays verified under all enlargements of the state of information, and if it is falsified it stays falsified. Verification and falsification are extended to complex formulas as follows:

As usual, A↔B is defined as (A→B)∧(B→A). A is valid just in case α⊢A for every node α in every model. The axiom system is sound and complete with respect to this semantics. The deletion of the clauses for ⊣ and ∼ gives a Kripke model of the usual sort; conversely, any Kripke model of the usual sort can be extended to a strong negation model by setting α⊣A for no node α and atomic formula A at all. It follows that the axiom system is a conservative extension of intuitionistic propositional logic.

The point is rather that the proposed formalization of “Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided” can be shown to be consistent even in the presence of these very strong assumptions.

Consider a K model with just one node, α. Let no atomic formula be either verified or falsified at α. The proposed formalization, ∼(Kp∨K∼p), can be shown to be verified at α by the following argument:
