The critical feature of K models is that although verification of A is equivalent to verification of KA, falsification of A is not equivalent to falsification of KA. In the model above, for example, we have α⊣Kp but not α⊣p. If both equivalences held, K would be a redundant operator and ∼(Kp∨K∼p) would collapse into ∼(p∨∼p), which is equivalent to the contradiction ∼p∧p. The feature that prevents this collapse has an intuitive basis. The distinction between a warrant to assert A and a warrant to assert that A will be proved is a very subtle one. In contrast, the distinction between a warrant to deny A and a warrant to deny that A will be proved looks rather blatant. A collapse of the former distinction would not induce a collapse of the latter. If we knew that sentient life was about to be extinguished, we should have an empirical warrant to assert that various propositions would never be proved, because the requisite inquiries would never be completed, but that would not amount to a warrant to deny those propositions. The clause for α⊣KA in K models reflects this point by being as liberal as it can be, given the twin constraints of monotonicity and incompatibility with the clause for α⊢KA.

Since α⊢Kp is equivalent to α⊢p, Kp↔p is a theorem of the logic characteristic of K models. Since α⊣Kp is not equivalent to α⊣p, ∼Kp↔∼p is not a theorem of that logic. Thus the theoremhood of A↔B does not in general guarantee the theoremhood of Σ(A)↔Σ(B). This feature does not depend on the presence of K; for example, ∼¬p↔p is a theorem but ∼∼¬p↔∼p is not. The theoremhood of A↔B requires only that A and B be verified at the same nodes; the theoremhood of Σ(A)↔Σ(B) may require them to be falsified at the same nodes too. One can define a stronger conditional than → by equating A⇒B with (A→B)∧(∼B→∼A). If A⇔B is defined as (A⇒B)∧(B⇒A), then its theoremhood requires A and B to be both verified at the same nodes and falsified at the same nodes; it is therefore sufficient for the theoremhood of Σ(A)⇔Σ(B).

The use of strong negation may point the way towards a constructivist account of statements such as “Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided”. What is more doubtful is that this account is available to intuitionists. It involves the replacement of Kp∨K¬p by Kp∨K∼p as a formalization of “Goldbach’s Conjecture will one day be decided”. Thus K¬p is treated as insufficient for a negative solution to the problem, because the stronger K∼p is treated as necessary, even though p is mathematical rather than empirical.6 This seems tantamount to treating ¬ as not a genuine negation at all. The concomitant view of ¬p is one that a classical logician might take of it, as expressing the provable unprovability of Goldbach’s Conjecture but not its falsity. Only ∼p is viewed as expressing the latter. Although the resulting formal system is a conservative extension of intuitionistic logic, it is interpreted from a non-intuitionistic standpoint. Similarly, the classical modal logic S4 is a conservative extension of intuitionistic logic under a suitable mapping of formulas, but that does not make S4, as usually interpreted, available to the intuitionist. It may therefore be tentatively concluded that the strong negation account of sentences such as “Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided” is not available to intuitionists.

The objection generalizes from strong negation to anything recognizable as a negation operator within intuitionistic logic. Any such operator will satisfy (2), and will therefore need to replace ¬ within the scope of K in the formalization of “Goldbach’s Conjecture will one day be decided”. As before, K¬p will be treated as insufficient for a negative solution to the problem, and therefore ¬ as not a genuine negation; the account will not be available to intuitionists. On its intended interpretation, intuitionistic logic leaves no room for a nonstandard negation to solve the problem.7

In the light of section III, let us revert to the intuitionistic formalization of “Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided” as ¬(Kp∨K¬p). In the light of sections I and II, let us assume that this formula is indeed intuitionistically inconsistent. Thus the intuitionist denies that Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided. Is this denial well-motivated?

Intuitionistically, the denial that Goldbach’s Conjecture will never be decided would not commit us to the assertion that Goldbach’s Conjecture will one day be decided. Since we have no method for deciding the Conjecture, we have no intuitionistic warrant for the latter assertion. Thus the intuitionist can now assert “No one now possesses a warrant to assert that Goldbach’s Conjecture will one day be decided”. If we let KnA mean that someone now possesses a warrant to assert the statement that A, then the quoted assertion might be formalized by ¬Kn(Kp∨K¬p). It is critical that ¬ should not commute with Kn. ¬Kn(Kp∨K¬p) must not imply Kn¬(Kp∨K¬p), for the intuitionistic falsity of the latter formula follows from the assumed intuitionistic inconsistency of ¬(Kp∨K¬p).

The operator Kn can be given a crude semantics on Kripke trees by the condition that α⊢KnA if and only if α0⊢A, where α0 is the bottom node of the tree. Thus the schema KnA→A is valid (by monotonicity) but the schema A→KnA is not. Also, α⊢Kn¬A if and only if there is no node β such that β⊢A; α⊢¬KnA if and only if it is not the case that α0⊢A. It follows from the latter clause that present warrant is decidable, in the sense that KnA∨¬KnA is valid.8 Moreover, the schema Kn¬A→¬KnA is valid but the schema ¬KnA→Kn¬A is not. For example, if p is verified at some nodes on a tree but not at others, then both ¬Kn(p∨¬p) and ¬Kn¬(p∨¬p) are verified everywhere on the tree. If we make the simplifying assumption that KA is verified at exactly the same points on the tree as A, then ¬Kn(Kp∨K¬p) and ¬Kn¬(Kp∨K¬p) are verified together, as required. In this model, the warrant to assert that no one now possesses a warrant to assert that Goldbach’s Conjecture will one day be decided simply reflects the warrant to assert that no one now possesses a warrant to assert that Goldbach’s Conjecture is decidable.

Nevertheless, the assertibility of “No one now possesses a warrant to assert that Goldbach’s Conjecture will one day be decided” does not completely solve the problem, for it does nothing to explain the validity of the puzzling schema (1), ¬KA→¬A. How can the falsity of “Someone will one day prove Goldbach’s Conjecture” possibly be sufficient for the falsity of Goldbach’s Conjecture itself?

Clearly, no amount of evidence about the imminent extinction of life by nuclear war can warrant the denial of Goldbach’s Conjecture. Such evidence is simply irrelevant to the mathematical question. It does not even make the negation of Goldbach’s Conjecture probable. Now, given the a priori intuitionistic argument for (1), if such evidence made “No one will ever prove Goldbach’s Conjecture” probable, it would presumably make the negation of Goldbach’s Conjecture equally probable. If (1) is a priori, then it is a priori that the statement that no one will ever prove Goldbach’s Conjecture is equivalent to its conjunction with the negation of the Conjecture. Thus the view embodied in (1) (as the conclusion of an a priori argument) must be that evidence about (e.g.) the imminent extinction of life does not even make it probable that no one will ever prove Goldbach’s Conjecture. Is that not simply absurd?

Somehow, the intuitionist must deny that the statement that no one will ever prove Goldbach’s Conjecture can merely happen to be true, and insist that the statement is true only if made so by a disproof of the Conjecture. An initial thought is that such an insistence would have to derive from the view that future tense statements are true only if their truth is logically guaranteed by present facts. The only present fact (on an informal understanding of the phrase) that could logically guarantee the truth of the statement that no one will ever prove Goldbach’s Conjecture is the unprovability of the Conjecture. If it is unprovable, then by intuitionistic standards it certainly follows that it is false.

The view that future tense statements are true only if their truth is logically guaranteed by present facts goes naturally with the conception of the future as the realm of possibility. On this conception, there is such a thing as what will happen only to the extent that it is determined by the present; otherwise there is only what might happen. The present form of the conception is particularly extreme, for since the view requires present facts to guarantee the truth of future tense statements logically rather than causally, the future is conceived as the realm of logical rather than causal possibility. If a causal guarantee were enough, the truth of the statement that no one will ever prove the Conjecture might be guaranteed by all kinds of physical condition inconsistent with the provability of the Conjecture.

The appeal to the “present facts” view of future tense statements does not withstand further scrutiny. If it worked at all, it would work just as well for the future tense statement “No one will prove Goldbach’s Conjecture tomorrow”. The only present fact that could logically guarantee that no one will prove Goldbach’s Conjecture tomorrow is the unprovability of the Conjecture. The intuitionist does not want to endorse the validity of an argument from “No one will prove Goldbach’s Conjecture tomorrow” to the negation of the Conjecture. Indeed, the considerations of section II suggest that the very notion of a future tense statement is confused. The sentence “Tomorrow will be fine” is in the future tense, but the statement that it expresses will be expressed tomorrow by the present tense sentence “Today is fine”. Moreover, the absence of present facts that logically guarantee the truth of the statement that tomorrow will be fine in no way entitles one to deny that statement.

The intuitionist seems to need a rather different line of thought: that a statement is true only if its truth can be known at some time, and that one cannot know the future. This line of thought allows an empirical statement about a finite period of the future to be true, for it can be known once that period is past. In contrast, an empirical universal generalization over all future times concerns a period that will never be wholly past; such a generalization cannot be known in that way. Indeed, the point needs to be a priori, for the argument from “No one will ever prove Goldbach’s Conjecture” to the negation of the Conjecture is an a priori one. On this view, we can know that no one will ever prove Goldbach’s Conjecture only by having a proof of its unprovability, which amounts to a proof of its intuitionistic falsity.

For the intuitionist, the future is the realm of the possible, not because any finite stretch of it is a mere potentiality, but because its infinity is a potential infinity.9 Any finite stretch of the future will eventually be past; the whole infinite future never will be. There is not even any such thing as a definite course that the infinite future might take, for one could never be in a position to assert that it would take that course. There are only definite courses that it might take over finite periods. A universal generalization about all future times cannot merely happen to be true. For any finite period of future time, the supposition that Goldbach’s Conjecture will not be proved within that period has no mathematical implications, but the supposition that it will not be proved within an infinite period entails its falsity.

The intuitionistic conception of the future is embodied in the principle of open data for lawless sequences (Kreisel and Troelstra, 1970). If a lawless sequence ξ has a property ϕ, then there is a (finite) initial segment x of ξ such that every lawless sequence with x as an initial segment has ϕ. At any time, mathematical knowledge of ξ is confined to an initial segment of ξ, so such a segment must be sufficient for a proof that the sequence has ϕ. For example, although for any natural number n the denial that 0 occurs in the first n places of ξ is consistent, the denial that 0 occurs at all in ξ is inconsistent, for it cannot be warranted by any initial segment of ξ. We cannot assert that 0 occurs in ξ, but we can assert that it is not the case that it is not the case that 0 occurs in ξ. Similarly, for any natural number n the denial that a code for a disproof of Goldbach’s Conjecture occurs in the first n places of ξ is consistent with the Conjecture, but the denial that such a code occurs at all in ξ is inconsistent with the Conjecture, for it cannot be warranted by any initial segment of ξ in the absence of an intuitionistic disproof of the Conjecture.

Lawless sequences are usually conceived as occurring in the notional time of an ideal mathematician, not the historical time of real human mathematicians. Statements about them are supposed to be mathematical, not empirical. On the intuitionistic view just sketched, the distinction between the mathematical and the empirical begins to dissolve in the face of universal generalizations over all times. It does so because the use of inductive evidence has not been written into the semantics of such generalizations, which provides no shortcut to an analytic justification of induction. The content of the generalizations is fixed by the condition for knowledge of their truth, and possession of inductive evidence is conceived as falling short of knowledge. If we have inductive evidence, it is the condition for such knowledge that determines what it is that we have evidence for. In this sense, knowledge is privileged with respect to other cognitive states. Its privileged status combines with a specific conception of knowledge of infinite domains to give the envisaged view.10

The envisaged view makes no provision for truths to which our only conceivable access is through inductive generalization over all times. Causal laws seem to be just such truths. According to the view, the inductive evidence may confirm the generalization as restricted to any finite period, however long, for the possibility of knowing the truth of the restriction once that period is past gives it content. The unrestricted generalization cannot gain its content in this way. Its truth must be logically determined in advance. Since inductive evidence is not evidence for truth of that kind, it does not warrant the assertion of unrestricted generalizations over all times; it does not even constitute evidence for them. To misquote Wittgenstein, an infinite period is not like a finite period, only longer.

Consider Dummett’s example of an unrestricted generalization over all times, “A city will never be built on this spot” (1978, pp. 16–17). On the envisaged view, its assertion cannot be warranted inductively, and no other kind of warrant is in prospect. Its negation is therefore intuitionistically true: it is not the case that a city will never be built on this spot. Of course, it does not follow intuitionistically that a city will at some time be built on this spot, for we have no way of specifying such a time.

Dummett (1969) has emphasized the disturbing conception of the past embodied in anti-realist views modelled on mathematical intuitionism.11 The conception of the future just sketched is equally disturbing. The aim of this paper has been to suggest that it may nevertheless be forced on the intuitionist (perhaps not on all anti-realists). If so, the reader must judge whether it constitutes a reductio ad absurdum of intuitionism.

Some of the ideas in this paper were presented in a seminar at the University of Stockholm; several of those present – in particular Per Martin-Löf, Dag Prawitz and Peter Pagin – made helpful comments. Thanks also to Pagin and John Campbell for stimulating discussions, and to Philip Percival for detailed comments on an earlier draft.

The argument in the text draws on the argument in Fitch (1963) that if all truths are knowable then all truths are known, an argument discussed in the context of intuitionistic logic in Hart (1979); Williamson (1982, 1988, 1992); Wright (1987), pp. 312–316; Percival (1990). Melia (1991) claims that the argument raises no problem for anti-realism because, although A∧¬KA cannot be verified, it can be falsified (when A is false); this is simply irrelevant to intuitionistic forms of anti-realism, for they claim that all true propositions can be verified, not that all propositions can be either verified or falsified. ↩︎

Unlike Fitch’s original argument, the argument in the text does not rely on the schema KA→A, from which K(A∧¬KA)→¬KA would follow, combining with K(A∧¬KA)→KA to give ¬K(A∧¬KA); K(A∧¬KA) is absurd even without this mechanical reductio ad absurdum. For all the argument for ¬p∧¬¬p assumes, a warrant to assert ¬KA might consist of inductive evidence deductively consistent with KA. However, it should not be assumed that the generalization from mathematical to empirical language by itself forces abandonment of the schema KA→A. There are independent reasons for holding that one is warranted in asserting something only if one knows it to be true (Unger, 1975, pp. 252–265; Slote, 1979; cp. Dudman, 1992); this view of warranted assertion both applies to empirical statements and validates the schema. What is less clear is that an adequate semantics can be given for unrestricted generalizations about the future in terms of conditions for knowledge of their truth. ↩︎

Another difficulty for the proposal is that it requires statements to be individuated unnaturally (see Percival, 1991). We regard “Today is fine” as expressing different statements on different days. We do not regard it as expressing a different statement today, given the actual weather, from the statement that it would have expressed today if the weather had been different. The difference affects the truth-value of the statement expressed, not its identity. By treating situations on the model of times, the proposal obliterates this natural distinction. ↩︎
It is not difficult to add strong negation to intuitionistic predicate logic; details are omitted here for simplicity. ↩︎

The treatment of denial as an autonomous speech act does not require the treatment of negation as a sign for that speech act; the formal semantics treats neither ∼ nor ¬ in that way. As Frege pointed out, the latter treatment makes nonsense of occurrences of negation in the antecedents of conditionals (Dummett, 1973, pp. 316–326). One might think of assertion as the answer “Yes” to a question and denial as the answer “No”. ↩︎
The general problem can also be raised when p is empirical (e.g. “At some time a city will be built on this spot”); the argument requires only that it can be raised when p is mathematical. ↩︎
See Miglioli et al. (1989) for a development of constructivist systems related to, but not identical with, the strong negation system. ↩︎

Strictly, the decidability of KnA requires “here” as well as “now” to be built into its definition; quantification over all places for a given time raises many of the same problems for the intuitionist as quantification over all times for a given place. The semantics also validates the schema Kn(A∨B)→(KnA∨KnB), even though intuitionistically one can be entitled to assert a disjunction without being entitled to assert either disjunct, when one has a procedure for deciding between them that one has not carried out. Nevertheless, the schema remains acceptable provided that Kn is read as requiring a present warrant of canonical form. ↩︎

The text assumes that the future is infinite. Strictly, the argument for (1) relies on the quantification over all times in the definition of K, not on the infinity of the future. However, times figure in the argument as logically possible standpoints from which something might be asserted; in this sense the intuitionist will regard the future as infinite in extent. Empirical restrictions on the topology of time are not to the point. ↩︎
Some anti-realist accounts give induction a more central role (Dummett, 1978, pp. 161–162). ↩︎

For Dummett’s views on anti-realism about the future see Dummett (1978), pp. 16–17, 21–22, 152–153, 157, 161–162, 336, 339–340. For a defence of the view that we do not know the future see Dummett (1993), pp. 412–416. ↩︎

works.title: Verificationism and non-distributive knowledge
passages: There are unknown truths, but are there any unknowable ones? A negative answer may be called verificationism, for want of a better term. It is the direct outcome of some epistemic or pragmatist conceptions of truth, and the indirect outcome of some epistemic or pragmatist conceptions of meaning. All these conceptions are threatened by an argument against verificationism. The argument in question purports to show that if there are unknown truths (as there surely are), there are unknowable ones. Granted classical logic, the argument appears to stand or fall with a premise to the effect that knowledge distributes over conjunction; if one knows the truth of a conjunction, one knows the truth of its conjuncts. Verificationists may seek to escape the argument by denying the premise. One aim of this paper is to close that loophole. The plausibility of the premise is defended but, for safety’s sake, the argument is reconstructed without it.
The claim that every truth is knowable may be schematically formalized as:

A more precise claim is that, for any true proposition which humans can conceive, it is possible that the truth of that proposition was, is or will be known by some human. Thus ‘p’ is a propositional variable ranging over propositions which humans can conceive, ‘◊’ is to be read as ‘it is possible that’ (in the sense ‘it is or could have been the case that’) and ‘K’ as ‘it was, is or will be known by some human that’. The verificationist asserts (1) for all values of ‘p’.1
It is clear that not all truths conceivable by humans will ever be known by them. One does not want the principle:

For example, if p is the proposition that the number of tennis balls in NN’s garden on 7th November, 1991 is even, and q the proposition that it is odd, both propositions have been conceived by a human, but either p is a truth never known by any human or q is; one or the other is a counter-example to (2).
The relevant assumptions about knowledge can now be formulated. Knowledge is veridical; neither the actual world nor any possible one contains untrue knowledge. Thus the converse of (2) is necessary:

It is important here that the ‘was, is or will be’ in the definiens of ‘K’ does not act as a tense operator on the content clause following ‘known’, but only on ‘known’ itself. Thus K(it is raining) is evaluated as true with respect to a time t if there is knowledge at some time t# of rain at t; knowledge at t# of rain at t# is neither necessary nor sufficient. This is in fact a natural reading of the English ‘It was, is or will be known that it is raining’. On the other reading, Kp would entail ‘It was, is or will be the case that p’, but not p itself. The claim that knowledge distributes over conjunction can also be reflected in the language:
(4) is supposed to be non-contingently true.
The anti-verificationist argument is intended as a reductio ad absurdum of (1) to (2), by appeal to the necessity of (3) and (4). The first stage uses (3) and (4) to establish:
For, by substitution, (3) yields K(p&∼Kp)→∼Kp while (4) yields K(p&∼Kp)→Kp. Since (3) and (4) are assumed to be necessary, K(p&∼Kp) is impossible, not just false:
Now a special case of (1) is (p&∼Kp)→◊K(p&∼Kp); thus, by (6), (1) yields ∼(p&∼Kp), which is equivalent to (2) in classical logic. QED.2

If knowledge does not distribute over conjunction, (4) is not necessarily true and the argument against (1) breaks down.3 Indeed, there are systems based on the classical modal logic KT (also known as T, and as M) in which (1) and (3) are theorems, but (2) is not derivable. Can the verificationist plausibly deny that knowledge necessarily distributes over conjunction?

Many propositional attitudes distributes over conjunction. In conceiving that p and q, for example, one conceives that p and conceives that q; in saying that p and q, one says that p and says that q. Not all attitudes distribute. I disbelieve the conjunction that Edinburgh is in Scotland and Scotland is in Asia because I disbelieve the latter conjunct, but I do not disbelieve the former. However, that example leaves open the possibility that all positive propositional attitudes distribute over conjunction, in a sense of ‘positive’ that would need to be made precise.4

If a positive propositional attitude is closed under at least some forms of logical consequence, it is likely to be closed under a very obvious one such as &-Elimination. To investigate whether it distributes over conjunction would then be to test the null hypothesis that it satisfies no form of deductive closure at all. The null hypothesis in turn exemplifies a maximally liberal view of the extent to which rationality constrains the attribution of propositional attitudes.5

This paper concerns the special case of knowledge. We plainly do not know all the logical consequences of what we know; that is the point of mathematics. We do not even know all the obvious logical consequences of what we know, for what we know is linked to some of what we do not by chains of propositions each member of which is an obvious logical consequence of its predecessors. Thus a verificationist can deny that knowledge distributes over conjunction without denying that a conjunction obviously entails its conjuncts.

Two quite different kinds of counter-example might be offered against the claim that knowledge distributes over conjunction. For there are several logically independent necessary conditions for knowledge, and the nature of the putative counter-example will depend on which of them is supposed not to be transmitted from conjunction to conjuncts. Truth, of course, is one necessary condition for knowledge that cannot fail to be transmitted. It will simplify the classification to assume that belief is a necessary condition for knowledge; even if that principle is not quite correct when taken in its everyday sense, knowledge presumably does entail some sort of acceptance, for which the word ‘belief’ may be taken to stand in what follows.

Suppose that S knows that p and q, but S does not know that p. Thus S believes that p and q. Either S believes that p, or S fails to believe that p. If S fails to believe that p, that by itself accounts for S’s failure to know that p. Call such a case irrational; it would also be a counter-example to the principle that belief distributes over conjunction. If S does believe that p, S’s belief is true; S’s failure to know that p would need to be accounted for by the failure of some necessary condition for knowledge over and above that of true belief. Call such a case rational; with respect to the relevant propositions it would not violate the distribution of belief over conjunction.

The distribution of belief over conjunction seems to be neither necessary nor sufficient for the distribution of knowledge over conjunction. It seems to be unnecessary, because belief in the conjunct might follow from knowledge of the conjunction, although not from mere belief in it. Thus knowledge might distribute while belief failed to do so (perhaps failure to note certain immediate consequences is an obstacle to knowledge but not to belief). Conversely, the distribution of belief seems to be insufficient for the distribution of knowledge, since it rules out irrational counter-examples to the latter but not rational ones. Are there rational or irrational counter-examples to the claim that knowledge distributes over conjunction?

Robert Nozick’s theory of knowledge implies the possibility of rational counter-examples to the claim, as Nozick himself points out; it does not threaten the distribution of belief over conjunction in any way. According to Nozick, knowledge is a belief which tracks the truth. More precisely, S knows that p if and only if <1> it is true that p, <2> S believes that p, <3> if it were false that p then S would not believe that p and <4> if it were true that p then S would believe that p. On this analysis, belief in a conjunction may track the truth while belief in a conjunct does not because ‘We can satisfy condition 3 for a conjunction by satisfying it for its most vulnerable conjunct, the one that would be false if the conjunction were false; it does not follow that we satisfy condition 3 for the other conjunct as well’.6,7 Nozick sometimes knows that he is in Emerson Hall and not floating in an Earth-simulator on Alpha Centauri, for if the conjunction had been false it would have been because he was somewhere mundane other than Emerson Hall, not because he was floating in a tank on Alpha Centauri, and he would not have believed the conjunction. However, at those times he does not know that he is not floating in an Earth-simulator on Alpha Centauri, for if that conjunct had been false he would still have believed it. Less dramatic illustrations of the same point are also possible. A malicious man could determinedly adopt the following policy: if his wife has been moving and talking in her sleep, tell her the next morning that she has been, but in any other case tell her that she has been moving. If she believes what he tells her, then on an unfudged version of Nozick’s analysis she may know that she has been moving and talking in her sleep without knowing that she has been moving in her sleep.

What of irrational counter-examples? It is easy to find cases in which a man would assent to a conjunction if queried when he would have dissented from (and not assented to) one conjunct if queried on that alone. For example, a man might answer ‘Yes’ if asked ‘Is it true that a city other than Rome was once the capital of Italy and Turin was such a city?’ when he would have answered ‘No’ if asked ‘Is it true that a city other than Rome was once the capital of Italy?’. He might have forgotten that Turin was the capital of Italy from 1861 to 1864, and need mention of it to jog his memory. If a disposition to heartfelt assent on being asked whether p is sufficient for belief that p, and a disposition to heartfelt dissent incompatible with it, then (if neither question is in fact being asked) our man believes that a city other than Rome was once the capital of Italy and Turin was such a city without believing that a city other than Rome was once the capital of Italy. Moreover, he knows the conjunction, having learnt it at school from a reliable teacher in the usual way. Yet he does not know the conjunct, for he does not believe it.8

Neither kind of case is terribly convincing. The rational cases might well be taken as a reductio ad absurdum of Nozick’s theory of knowledge, the irrational ones as a reductio of too close a link between belief and speech dispositions.

Can it be argued that knowledge does distribute over conjunction? It would be insufficient to argue that a subject will always make the relevant inference, for making an inference takes time, so that the subject might violate the claim before the inference is completed. If knowledge of the conjuncts results from knowledge of the conjunction, and the cause is not simultaneous with the effect, then there would be a period during which the subject knew the conjunction without knowing its conjuncts; that period would constitute a counter-example. Moreover, there is no form of inference which people can be relied on to carry out; distraction or sudden death is always liable to intervene. The required premise is precisely not that deductive inference is a way of extending knowledge. Rather, what would need to be shown is that knowledge of a conjunction is already knowledge of its conjuncts.

It might be suggested that one can know a conjunction only by inferring it from its conjuncts, and that the output of the inference is knowledge only if the inputs are, so that in order to know a conjunction one must already know its conjuncts. However, although inference from the premises p and q may in some sense be the canonical way of coming to know the conjunction p&q, there are others: from testimony to the conjunction, or by inference from the premises (p&q)∨r and ∼r, and so on.

Nevertheless, &-Elimination has a rather special status. It may be brought out by a comparison with the ∨-Introduction inference from a disjunct p to the disjunction p∨q. Although the validity of the inference is fundamental to the meaning of inclusive disjunction, a perfect logician who knows that p may lack the concepts to grasp (understand) the other disjunct q. Since knowledge of a proposition requires grasp of it, and grasp of a complex proposition requires grasp of its components, the subject is in no position to grasp p∨q, and therefore does not know the disjunction. In contrast, those who know a conjunction grasp its conjuncts, for they grasp the conjunction.9 Moreover, they grasp the sense of its composition: they grasp the conjuncts as consequences of the conjunction. If they know the conjunction they grasp it, and in doing so grasp its conjuncts as its consequences. There is no obstacle here to the idea that knowledge of a conjunction constitutes knowledge of the conjuncts, just as, in mathematics, a proof of a conjunction counts as a proof of its conjuncts. If p&q is proved then p is proved, not just provable.

Someone might know a conjunction but believe one of its conjuncts for independent and bad reasons. The latter belief would not constitute knowledge. Nevertheless, the case is not a counter-example to what has just been said. For the person may be considered as having two beliefs in the conjunct, one constituted by their knowledge of (and therefore belief in) the conjunction, the other dependent on the bad reasons. The former counts as knowledge; the latter does not.

Unfortunately, no analysis of knowledge is well enough confirmed to act as an effective test of the claim that knowledge distributes over conjunction. In particular, any deduction of such a fine-grained principle is likely to be sensitive to small modifications of the analysis. The argument for distribution is suggestive, but no more. It is therefore prudent to seek ways of modifying the anti-verificationist argument so as to avoid commitment to the distribution of knowledge.

The anti-verificationist argument is a reductio of (1) to (2), given the necessity of (3) (knowledge implies truth) and (4) (distribution). There is no formal argument from (1) to (2) given only the necessity of (3). However, there are two obvious strategies for reconstructing an anti-verificationist argument without appeal to (4). (a) One might argue that verificationists are committed to something stronger than (1), and deduce the absurd (2) from it. (b) One might deduce something weaker than (2) from (1), but argue that it is still absurd. Both strategies look promising.
(a) Consider the principle that if a conjunction holds, it is possible that each conjunct is known to hold:

It is hard to see what reason someone could have to assert (1) that would not also be a reason to assert (1a). For example, verificationists who use meaning-theoretic considerations to motivate principles such as (1) often rely on some concept of canonical verification, where verification yields knowledge and canonically verifying a conjunction involves verifying its conjuncts. Someone who endorses (1) on the grounds that any truth can be canonically verified is equally committed to (1a). But an instance of (1a) is (p&∼Kp)→◊(Kp&K∼Kp). Given the necessity of (3), Kp&K∼Kp is impossible, and the argument proceeds as before. (1a) is reduced to the absurd (2); without (1a), (1) is unmotivated.

(b) Say that it is completely unknown that p if no one ever knows a conjunction of which it is a conjunct that p. No one can know that: p and it is completely unknown that p. For if someone did, it would not be completely unknown that p. This reasoning relies on the necessity of (3) but not on (4). Thus (1) implies that there are no completely unknown truths. But that is absurd, for no one will ever know a conjunction of which it is a conjunct that the number of tennis balls in NN’s garden on 7th November, 1991 is even and no one will ever know a conjunction of which it is a conjunct that the number is odd; since one of those propositions about the number of balls is true, one of them is a completely unknown truth.

Formal versions of (a) and (b) are given in the appendix. Even if knowledge does not distribute over conjunction, the anti-verificationist argument can be reconstructed in at least two ways. The verificationist cannot escape by denying distribution.

Other operators can be substituted for K in the reductio of (1) to (2). Any veridical attitude that distributes over conjunction will do, although it must be checked that the analogue of (2) is genuinely implausible. Consider, for example, T-conception. One T-conceives that p just in case p and one conceives (i.e., grasps the proposition) that p. T-conception is veridical by definition; it necessarily distributes over conjunction because both truth and conception do (if one conceives a conjunction, one conceives its conjuncts). The argument then shows that if all truths are T-conceivable, all truths are T-conceived. More specifically, if every truth conceivable by a human is T-conceivable at some time by a human, then every truth conceivable by a human is T-conceived at some time by a human. But surely not every truth conceivable by a human will ever be T-conceived by a human, just because not every truth conceivable by a human will ever be conceived by a human. Of course, I (being human) cannot give a counter-example; as soon as I gave it, it would be conceived, and therefore not a counter-example. I cannot even do what I could for (2): give a list of two or more propositions which I know to contain a counter-example. For no proposition I conceive is a counter-example to the principle that every truth conceivable by a human is at some time T-conceived by a human. Nevertheless, there are counter-examples, and I can gesture towards areas where some of them lie. For example, there are truths conceivable but never conceived by a human about the state of NN’s garden on 7th November, 1991; we all have better things to think about. By contraposition, there are truths that can be conceived by a human, but can never be true and conceived by one.

There are two obvious ways of trying to approximate an operator O which lacks a certain feature F by an operator with F. One is to seek the weakest operator O+ stronger than O which has F; the other is to seek the strongest operator O- weaker than O which has F. Of course, there is no general guarantee that either O+ or O- exists. However, when F is the feature of distributing over conjunction, both K+ and K- can now be defined in terms of K, granted a notion of propositions with conjunctive structure.
In what follows, every proposition is treated as a conjunct of itself, and every conjunct of a conjunct of a proposition as a conjunct of it. Put:
K+p= df For every conjunct q of p, Kq.
K-p= df For some q of which p is a conjunct, Kq.

K+p entails Kp, for p is a conjunct of itself. K+ also distributes over conjunction, since every conjunct of a conjunct is a conjunct of the conjunction. If (4) is not necessary, K+ is stronger than K. However, K+ is the weakest operator stronger than K to distribute over conjunction; i.e., K+ is entailed by any operator O which entails K and distributes over conjunction. For suppose Op; then Oq for every conjunct q of p, by the distributivity of O; since O entails K, Kq for every conjunct of p; i.e., K+p. Finally, K+ is veridical, since it entails the veridical K; its veridicality is necessary, for that of K is.

If K+ is substituted for K in the anti-verificationist argument, the result is a valid argument from the schema p→◊K+p to the schema p→K+p. Since the latter entails (2), it must be rejected. Thus p→◊K+p must be rejected too.

Now consider K-. Kp entails K-p, for p is a conjunct of itself. K- necessarily distributes over conjunction, just as K+ does. If (4) is not necessary, K- is weaker than K. However, K- is the strongest operator weaker than K to distribute over conjunction; i.e., K- entails any operator O which is entailed by K and distributes over conjunction. For suppose K-p; i.e., Kq for some q of which p is a conjunct; since K entails O, Oq; since p is a conjunct of q and O distributes, Op. Finally, K- is veridical, since if p is a conjunct of q, q entails p, so Kq also does by the veridicality of K; its veridicality is necessary, for that of K is.

If K- is substituted for K in the anti-verificationist argument, the result is a valid argument from the schema p→◊K-p to the schema p→K-p. Since (1) entails the former, it entails the latter. The latter is absurd, so (1) should be rejected.

The question is whether K+ and K- are well-defined. When p has only finitely many conjuncts, K+p can be defined without second-order quantification; the anti-verificationist argument does not require any proposition to have infinitely many conjuncts. In contrast, any proposition is a conjunct of infinitely many conjunctions, so the second-order quantification in the definition of K- is ineliminable. For some propositions p, a problem of circularity may arise for K-p. However, if K-p is not always well-defined, it does not follow that it never is. It seems quite easy to grasp in the cases relevant to the anti-verificationist argument. Not all impredicativity is vicious.
Thanks are due to Bill Brewer, Justin Broackes, John Campbell, Peter Carruthers, Bill Child, Philip Percival, Charles Travis and the referees for comments on earlier drafts of this paper.

Other readings of the symbolism are possible. (1) could be strengthened by contracting ‘was, is or will be known’ to ‘is known’, or weakened by enlarging ‘human’ to ‘being with an at most finite extension of human capacities’. The restriction on ‘p’ might be relaxed or dropped altogether; ‘◊’ could be interpreted in terms of different kinds of possibility. Different values of these parameters yield different forms of verificationism. However, we shall not be concerned with forms of verificationism in which ‘K’ is replaced by a non-veridical operator such as ‘there is good evidence that’, nor with those which introduce an ‘actually’ operator into (1); see Dorothy Edgington, ‘The Paradox of Knowability’, Mind 94 (1985) pp. 557-568; T. Williamson, ‘On the Paradox of Knowability’, Mind 96 (1987) pp. 256-261; P. Percival, ‘Knowability, Actuality and the Metaphysics of Context-Dependence’, Australasian Journal of Philosophy 69 (1991) pp. 82-97. The underlying propositional logic is assumed to be classical; for what happens when it is not see T. Williamson, ‘Knowability and Constructivism’, The Philosophical Quarterly 38 (1988) pp. 422-432 and ‘On intuitionistic modal epistemic logic’, Journal of Philosophical Logic 21 (1992) pp. 63-89. Subsequent arguments in the text might prompt a restriction of the possible values of ‘p’ to a proper subset of the propositions acknowledged as legitimate, e.g., excluding those about knowledge, or those which quantify unrestrictedly over times, or even all non-atomic propositions. Such weakened versions of (1) are not the concern of this paper; they look ad hoc, for verificationist arguments seem to support unrestricted (1) if they support anything. ↩︎

See F.B. Fitch, ‘A Logical Analysis of Some Value Concepts’, The Journal of Symbolic Logic 28 (1963) pp. 135-142, and W.D. Hart, ‘The Epistemology of Abstract Objects: Access and Inference’, The Aristotelian Society: Supplementary Volume 53 (1979) pp. 152-165. Note that the occurrence of one ‘K’ in the scope of another is syntactically and semantically well-formed; there is no more danger of vicious self-reference or the like than in ‘Someone knows that someone knows that the Emperor has no clothes’. ↩︎

Dorothy Edgington points out that the argument for (6) goes through if the assumption of the necessity of (4), i.e., □(K(p&q)→(Kp&Kq)), is weakened to its consequence ◊K(p&q)→◊(Kp&Kq). But what justifies the latter, if not the necessity of (4)? If the idea is that someone who knows the conjunction could have inferred the conjuncts, its natural expression is at most □(K(p&q)→◊(Kp&Kq)), which yields ◊K(p&q)→◊◊(Kp&Kq). A further inference in S4 style would be required, from ◊◊(Kp&Kq) to ◊(Kp&Kq); but the S4 principle is problematic for at least some kinds of verificationism (T. Williamson, ‘Two Incomplete Anti-Realist Modal Epistemic Logics’, The Journal of Symbolic Logic 55 (1990) pp. 297-314, at p. 301). Alternatively, one could use the double necessity of (3) to establish ∼◊◊(Kp&K∼Kp), and thence (6) by substitution in ◊K(p&q)→◊◊(Kp&Kq). This alternative has some plausibility. However, it does require the assumption that knowledge is transmitted across inference by &-Elimination, which a defender of (1) might deny in extremis. This paper explores versions of the argument that do not presume even a weakened form of distributivity. ↩︎
This generalization is suggested in J. Barwise and J. Perry, Situations and Attitudes (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press/Bradford Books, 1983), p. 205. ↩︎

It is obviously not suggested that deductive closure is even a rational ideal for propositional attitudes such as disbelief. In the case of belief, Brian Loar proposes distribution over conjunction as a perhaps dubious and approximate constraint on a functionalist attribution of beliefs in Mind and Meaning (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1981) p. 72. In contrast, Robert Stalnaker argues heroically that belief is closed under logical consequence, in Inquiry (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press/Bradford Books, 1984). See also Jaakko Hintikka, ‘Impossible Worlds Vindicated’, Journal of Philosophical Logic 4 (1975) pp. 475-484. In Topics in Philosophical Logic (Dordrecht: Reidel, 1968) pp. 46-47, Nicholas Rescher suggests that belief is closed under obvious consequence, and therefore distributes over conjunction; since obvious consequencehood is not transitive, he requires that the principle be used at most once in an argument: but this violates the transitivity of consequencehood; there is something wrong with a logic of belief which does not allow valid arguments to be chained together. ↩︎

See R. Nozick, Philosophical Explanations (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1981) p. 228. I follow Nozick in ignoring the effects of the epicycle about ways of knowing added to the analysis at pp. 182-185. Nozick rejects the claim that knowledge distributes over conjunction even when the subject knows the entailment from conjunction to conjunct. He also argues that the claim enables one to derive (i) knowledge is closed under known logical implication from (ii) knowledge is closed under known logical equivalence; since he accepts (ii) and rejects (i), he has another reason for rejecting the claim. However, the form of argument he uses (ibid., p. 692, fn.63), if valid, could be extended to show that if Nozick knows p to be logically equivalent to q, he also knows it to be equivalent to each member of the infinite series q&(q→p), (q&(q→p))&((q&(q→p))→p), …, which seems unlikely. ↩︎

Nozick’s objection to the distribution principle can be instantiated in the special case of (5). A naval historian knows that no one will ever know that it rained on Rockall on 1st January, 1800, but is convinced that it did. Indeed it did (p), but his belief that it did so does not constitute knowledge: had it not rained then, he would still have believed that it did. However, his true belief that ∼Kp does track the truth: had ∼Kp been false, a sailor would have noted that p in his diary, and the historian would not have believed ∼Kp. He truly believes the conjunction p&∼Kp; had it been false, Kp would have been true (voyages could more easily have been different than the weather), and he would not have believed the conjunction. Thus a simple-minded application of Nozick’s account seems to deliver K(p&∼Kp), and therefore ∼Kp. It may be felt that this result does more harm to Nozick than good to the verificationist. ↩︎

One might also consider a rather dim community whose members take several seconds to see the entailment from a given conjunction to one of its conjuncts; but do they know the conjunction before they know that it entails its conjuncts? Another objection, based on the idea that knowledge is implicitly typed according to a hierarchy of levels, is discussed at pp. 311-312 of ‘Two Incomplete Anti-Realist Modal Epistemic Logics’, op. cit. ↩︎

Fred Dretske’s endorsement, at p. 1009 of ‘Epistemic Operators’, The Journal of Philosophy 67 (1970) pp. 1007-1023, of the claim that knowledge of a conjunction entails knowledge of the conjuncts is compromised by his bracketing of it with the claim that knowledge of a disjunct entails knowledge of the disjunction. ↩︎

works.title: Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
passages: Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Abstract Epistemic logics for subjects of bounded rationality are in effect nonnormal modal logics. Admissible rules are of interest in such logics. However, the usual methods for establishing admissibility employ Kripke models and are therefore inappropriate for nonnormal logics. This paper extends syntactic methods for a variety of rules (e.g. the rule of disjunction) and nonnormal logics. In doing so it answers a question asked by Chellas and Segerberg.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

1 Introduction The admissibility of a rule by a logic depends only on the logic’s set of theorems. It does not depend on a choice of semantics or proof system (for which reason the phrase “rule of proof” is not ideal; but see Humberstone [4]). However, the usual methods of proving the admissibility of a rule in modal logic are semantic; they use standard “possible worlds” model theory. This semantic treatment is applicable only to normal model systems (see below). Thus the usual methods do not allow one to prove the admissibility of a rule in a nonnormal modal system. The aim of this paper is to extend the use of syntactic methods for proving admissibility, methods applicable to both normal and nonnormal systems.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
An important example is the rule of disjunction. A system S provides (admits) this rule just in case for all formulas A1,…,An:
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Lemmon and Scott established the rule of disjunction for a variety of modal systems by a model-theoretic technique that is now standard (Lemmon and Scott [9] pp. 44–46 and 79–81; Chellas [1] pp. 181–182; Hughes and Cresswell [3] pp. 96–100; see also Kripke [5], Lemmon [8], McKinsey and Tarski [10] and Segerberg [13]). Powerful though such techniques are, they are restricted to systems amenable to the model theory in question. Thus if a modal logic is nonnormal, because it lacks the rule of necessitation RN (if ⊢A then ⊢□A) or the K axiom schema (□(A→B)→(□A→□B)), it cannot be shown in the standard way to admit the rule of disjunction. Such a limitation is serious for two reasons.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

(a) If the admissibility of a rule is preserved when a normal system is weakened to a nonnormal one by the dropping of necessitation or the K schema (as is often the case), a model-theoretic technique obscures the generality of the phenomenon.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

(b) The formalism of modal logic is often applied to epistemic or doxastic issues, with □ read as “it is known that” or “it is believed that.” Normality is then equivalent to the closure of knowledge or belief under logical consequence: unbounded rationality. If one wishes to avoid this idealization, one will use a nonnormal logic. Even if one makes the idealization about individual subjects, but reads □ as “someone knows that” or “someone believes that,” one may reject the schema (□A∧□B)→□(A∧B) on the grounds that the perfect logicians who know or believe that A may not include any of the perfect logicians who know or believe that B, and normality is again lost. Yet one would still like to know what rules are admissible in the nonnormal epistemic or doxastic logic.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Standard “possible worlds” model theory can be generalized for systems without the rule of necessitation by the introduction of nonnormal worlds at which everything is possible. As a byproduct, Kripke showed that the nonnormal logics S2 and S3 admit the rule: if ⊢□A∨□B, then either ⊢□A or ⊢□B (Kripke [6], p. 220). However, this semantics still enforces the K schema and the rule RM that if ⊢A→B then ⊢□A→□B. A much wider generalization is to neighbourhood semantics or minimal models, but this still enforces the rule RE that if ⊢A≡B then ⊢□A≡□B ([1] pp. 207–210; by definition, the classical logics of [13] admit RE). Similar remarks apply to the use of algebraic semantics (for a recent example of its application to problems of admissibility in modal logic see Rybakov [12]). Even this form of deductive closure is too strong for many epistemic and doxastic applications. It is avoided in the impossible worlds semantics of Rantala [11], but there the K schema is valid; yet real knowledge or belief cannot be assumed to be closed under modus ponens.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

The proper response to the problem is not to seek further generalizations of the semantics, not least because anything general enough may be too trivial to be of use in establishing the admissibility of rules. It is more natural to develop a nonsemantic approach.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

2 Framework The language is standard, with a countably infinite class of propositional variables p0,p1,p2,…; the only primitive operators are the 0-place ⊥ (falsity), the 1-place □ and the 2-place → (material conditional). Other operators are treated as metalinguistic abbreviations, e.g. ¬A for A→⊥, ⊤ for ¬⊥, ◇A for ¬□¬A. □0A=A; □i+1A=□i□A. “A”, “B”, “C”, … are metalinguistic variables over all wff; “p”, “q” and “r” are metalinguistic variables over propositional variables. A function σ from wff to wff is a substitution iff σ⊥=⊥, σ□A=□σA and σ(A→B)=σA→σB for all A and B. If X is a set of wff, σX={σA:A∈X}. The modal degree #A of A is defined as usual: #p=#⊥=0; #(A→B)=𝑚𝑎𝑥{#A,#B}; #□A=#A+1.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

A theory is a set of wff containing all classical truth-functional tautologies and closed under modus ponens (MP). A logic is a theory closed under the rule of uniform substitution (US). A subtheory (sublogic) of a theory is a subset of it that is a theory (logic). PC, the set of all classical truth-functional tautologies, is the smallest theory and the smallest logic. If S is a theory, ⊢SA just in case A∈S. If X is a set of wff, X⊢SA just in case ⊢SB→A for some conjunction B of members of X. A logic is normal just in case it contains schema K and is closed under the rule of necessitation. The closure of a logic ℒ under a set of inference rules is the intersection of all logics containing ℒ that admit those rules.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
A rule is treated as a sequent X⊩Y, where X and Y are sets of wff (written without { and }).
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Definition 2.1 S admits the rule X⊩Y just in case for every substitution σ, if ⊢SσA for all A∈X then ⊢SσB for some B∈Y.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Thus the rule of necessitation RN is treated as a sequent p⊩□p, the rule RE as p≡q⊩□p≡□q, and Lemmon and Scott’s rule of disjunction (for fixed n) as the sequent
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
A special class of rules is of particular importance:
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Definition 2.2 X⊩Y is a □-introduction rule just in case for some wff G1,…,Gk and H, Y={(⋀i≤k□G1)→□h} and X⊢PC(⋀i≤kGi)→H, where X, Gi and H are nonmodal (i.e., #A=0 for A∈X∪{G1,…,Gk,H}).
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
The special case k=0 is allowed, where the rule is in effect X⊩□H, and X⊢PCH. Some □-introduction rules are:
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Note that a theory admits p≡q⊩□p→□q just in case it admits p≡q⊩□p≡□q. The rule of disjunction is obviously not a □-introduction rule, even for n=1; nor are p∨q⊩□p∨□q and ¬p⊩¬□p, for their conclusions are of the wrong form.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
The case X={} is also allowed, where ⊢PC(⋀i≤kGi)→H. □-introduction rules of this special kind will prove important, and deserve a special name:
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Definition 2.3 X⊩Y is an axiomatic □-introduction rule just in case it is a □-introduction rule and X={}.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
⊩□p is not an axiomatic □-introduction rule, since not ⊢PCp.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proposition 2.4 A logic ℒ is normal just in case ℒ admits all □-introduction rules.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Proof: If ℒ admits all □-introduction rules, it admits RN and the rule ⊩(□(p→q)∧□p)→□q, so every instance of the K schema is a theorem; thus ℒ is normal. Conversely, let ℒ be normal, X⊩(⋀i≤k□Gi)→□H a □-introduction rule, and σ a substitution. Suppose that ⊢ℒσA for all A∈X. By definition of a □-introduction rule, X⊢PC(⋀i≤kGi)→H, so σX⊢PCσ((⋀i≤kGi)→H). Hence ⊢ℒσ((⋀i≤kGi)→H), i.e. ⊢ℒ(⋀i≤kσGi)→σH. Since ℒ is normal, ⊢ℒ(⋀i≤k□σGi)→□σH, i.e. ⊢ℒσ((⋀i≤k□Gi)→□H). Thus ℒ admits the rule.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

3 Cancellation rules The aim is to find ways of establishing the admissibility of rules generalizable to theories in which not all □-introduction rules are admissible. Chellas gives an example of the kind of proof we are after ([1] pp. 124–125), in showing that the weakest normal logic K admits the rule
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

In other words, for any wff A and B, if ⊢𝐊□A→□B then ⊢𝐊A→B (on an epistemic reading, this rule has a constructivist flavor: if knowledge of A entails knowledge of B then A entails B). Chellas uses a mapping τ from wff to wff, defined as follows:
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Consider an axiomatization of K with all truth-functional tautologies and all wff of the form □(A→B)→(□A→□B) as the only axioms and MP and RN as the only primitive rules of inference (note that US is a derived rule). One can show by induction on n that if ⊢𝐊A with a proof of n lines then ⊢𝐊τA, as follows. If A is a truth-functional tautology, so is τA, for τ commutes with all truth-functional operators. τ(□(A→B)→(□A→□B))=(A→B)→(A→B), a truth-functional tautology. Thus τ maps axioms to axioms. Now assume the induction hypothesis for all proofs of less than n lines, and that ⊢𝐊A with a proof of n lines. If A is an axiom we are done. If A was derived by MP, then, for some B, ⊢𝐊B and ⊢𝐊B→A with proofs of less than n lines; by induction hypothesis, ⊢𝐊τB and ⊢𝐊τ(B→A), i.e. ⊢𝐊τB→τA; by MP, ⊢𝐊τA. If A was derived by RN, then A=□B for some B such that ⊢𝐊B; but τA=τ□B=B. This completes the induction. For any wff A, if ⊢𝐊A then ⊢𝐊τA; in brief, K is closed under τ. Thus if ⊢𝐊□A→□B then ⊢𝐊τ(□A→□B); but τ(□A→□B)=A→B. Hence K admits the rule □p→□q⊩p→q.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

The aim of this section is to make a detailed case study of the mapping τ and its use in proving results of this kind. Later sections study other mappings. Two kinds of generalization of the result just proved are possible. We can generalize on the rule □p→□q⊩p→q, and we can generalize on the system K. We begin with the former.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
The closure of K under τ implies that K also admits all of the following rules:
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
The same proof technique works, for τ◇A=τ¬□¬A=¬¬A, and it does not matter what truth-functional operator takes the place of →. Thus a general class of rules needs to be studied.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Definition 3.1 σ□ is the substitution such that σ□p=□p for every propositional variable p.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Definition 3.2 X⊩Y is a cancellation rule just in case X={σ□A} and Y={A} for some nonmodal wff A (#A=0).
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Thus the following are cancellation rules: □p→□q⊩p→q; □p≡□q⊩p≡q, and □p⊩p. □p→◇q⊩p→q, for example, is not a cancellation rule, but is admitted by a theory whenever the cancellation rule □p→¬□¬q⊩p→¬¬q is.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proposition 3.3 If a theory is closed under τ then it admits all cancellation rules.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Proof: Let S be a theory closed under τ, σ□A⊩A a cancellation rule and σ a substitution. What needs to be shown is that if ⊢Sσσ□A then ⊢SσA. Suppose ⊢Sσσ□A. By hypothesis, ⊢Sτσσ□A. Thus it suffices to show by induction on the complexity of A that τσσ□A=σA. Now τσσ□p=τσ□p=τ□σp=σp and τσσ□⊥=⊥=σ⊥. If τσσ□B=σB and τσσ□C=σC then τσσ□(B→C)=τσσ□B→τσσ□C=σB→σC=σ(B→C). This completes the induction; the case of □B does not arise, for #A=0 by definition of a cancellation rule.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

We shall be concerned with proofs that a system admits all cancellation rules. Proposition 3.5 shows that not every such result can be proved as for K, by means of τ. Proposition 3.4 is a lemma of general use, formulated relative to a particular choice of truth-functional primitives in the language.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proposition 3.4 If θ is a mapping from wff to wff such that θ⊥=⊥, and for all wff B and C, θ(B→C)=θB→θC, then PC is closed under θ.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Proof: If ⊢PCB then B=σA for some substitution σ and some wff A such that #A=0 and ⊢PCA. Define σθ as the substitution such that σθpi=θσpi for all i. One can then show that σθA=θσA by induction on the complexity of A. Since PC is closed under US, ⊢PCσθA, i.e. ⊢PCθσA, i.e. ⊢PCθB.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proposition 3.5 Not every normal logic that admits all cancellation rules is closed under τ.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Proof: Let ℒ be the smallest normal logic containing p≡□□p. ℒ admits all cancellation rules but is not closed under τ. A semantic proof of this uses standard correspondence theory: ℒ is the logic of a two-point frame in which each point is accessible from the other but not from itself, but τ(p≡□□p)=p≡□p, which is not valid on that frame. However, in the spirit of this paper a syntactic proof of the same result will be sketched. One first shows that ⊢ℒ□(p→q)≡(□p→□q) and ⊢ℒ□⊥≡⊥. Then let σ□A⊩A be a cancellation rule and σ a substitution. By induction on the complexity of A, ⊢ℒσ□A≡□A; hence ⊢ℒ□σσ□A≡σA. Thus if ⊢ℒσσ□A, by RN ⊢ℒ□σσ□A, so ⊢ℒσA. Thus ℒ admits the cancellation rule σ□A⊩A. To show that ℒ is not closed under τ, let σπ be the substitution such that σπp2i=p2i+1 and σπp2i+1=p2i for all i, and define a mapping π on wff by:
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Axiomatize ℒ with all theorems of PC and wff of the forms □(A→B)→(□A→□B) and A≡□□A as axioms and MP and RN as the only rules of inference. By induction on the length of proofs (using 3.4), if ⊢ℒA then ⊢PCπA (the converse also holds, but need not be proved). Finally, if ℒ is closed under τ, ⊢ℒτ(p0≡□□p0), i.e. ⊢ℒp0≡□p0, so ⊢PCπ(p0≡□p0), i.e. ⊢PCp0≡p1, which is absurd.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

In spite of 3.5, there is a close connection between the mapping τ and the admissibility of cancellation rules. A logic ℒ can admit all cancellation rules “because it is weak,” in the sense that every sublogic of ℒ (i.e. every logic all of whose theorems are theorems of ℒ) also admits all cancellation rules. This property of ℒ turns out to be equivalent to the property that τ maps every theorem of ℒ to a theorem of PC. A strongest logic with this “weakness property” will be identified. Normal logics, such as K, lack this weakness property, for □□⊤ is a theorem of K while τ□□⊤=□⊤ is not a theorem of PC; correspondingly, the weakest logic containing □□⊤ is included in K but does not admit the cancellation rule □p⊩p. However, it will be shown that if ℒ has the weakness property, then the closure of ℒ under any set of □-introduction rules is closed under τ and therefore admits all cancellation rules. K and a number of other normal logics are the closures of logics with the weakness property under the set of all □-introduction rules. In this way we can achieve a wide generalization of the result about K.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Some preliminary lemmas are needed for the proof of the results just mentioned. In particular, it helps to consider wff without propositional variables, for if A is any such wff, A is the premise and τA the conclusion of an instance of a cancellation rule (see 3.9). Wff with propositional variables do not in general have this feature: for example, the proof of 3.5 shows that no cancellation rule has an instance of which p≡□□p is the premise and τ(p≡□□p)=(p≡□p) the conclusion. 3.8 (for which 3.6 and 3.7 are preliminaries) shows that if τ maps a theorem of some logic to a nontheorem of PC, then it maps a theorem of that logic containing no propositional variables to a nontheorem of PC.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
For k≥0, let σk be the substitution such that for all i, σkpi=□(i+1)(k+2)⊥.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

4 Cancellation rules in systems with T axioms It is natural to study nonnormal logics with the T axiom □p→p. For example, if □ is read as “it is known that,” the T axiom should hold, since knowledge entails truth, yet ordinary knowledge is not closed under logical consequence. Logics with the T axiom are not in general closed under the mapping τ, for although τ maps the T axiom itself to the PC theorem p→p, τ maps its instance □¬□p→¬□p to ¬□p→¬p, whose addition to a logic with the T axiom yields modal collapse. Indeed, logics with the T axiom do not in general admit all cancellation rules. For example, we have ⊢𝐊𝐓¬□(p∧¬□p) but not ⊢𝐊𝐓¬(p∧¬□p), so that KT does not admit the cancellation rule ¬□p⊩¬p. Nevertheless, it is natural to ask whether logics with the T axiom admit modified forms of cancellation rules. This section gives a limited positive answer to that question.

Induction step: Suppose that (ii) holds for m. We conclude that it holds for m+1 by induction on the length of proofs in S. Given (i), the only interesting case concerns a □-introduction rule Y⊩(⋀i≤k□Gi)→□H used in the axiomatization of S. It suffices to show that if σ is a substitution, and ⊢SσB for all B∈Y, then ⊢SδS,m+1((⋀i≤k□σGi)→□σH). By induction hypothesis, ⊢SδS,mσB for all B∈Y. Let σ∧ be the substitution such that σ∧pi=δS,mσpi. By induction on the complexity of B, if #B=0 then σ∧B=δS,mσB. Now for all B∈Y, #B=0, so σ∧B=δS,mσB, so ⊢Sσ∧B by the above. Since S provides the rule, ⊢S(⋀i≤k□σ∧Gi)→□σ∧H. But #Gi=#H=0, so σ∧Gi=δS,mσGi and σ∧H=δS,mσH. Thus ⊢S(⋀i≤k□δS,mσGi)→□δS,mσH. But δS,m+1((⋀i≤k□σGi)→□σH)=(⋀i≤k□δS,mσGi)→□δS,mσH.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proof of Claim (iii): By induction on the complexity of A.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Claim (iv): S admits the rule of disjunction. S is closed under δS by (ii) for m=0; the result follows by 5.1.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Now suppose that ⊢SA0∨⋁1≤i≤k□j(i)Ai for some j(1),…,j(n)>#A0. Let m=#A0. ⊢SδS,m(A0∨⋁1≤i≤k□j(i)Ai) by (ii). Now δS,mA0=A0 by (iii); since j(i)>m by assumption, δS,m□j(i)Ai=□mδS,0□□j(i)−m−1Ai. Thus ⊢SA0∨⋁1≤i≤k□mδS,0□□j(i)−m−1Ai. There are two subcases.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Subcase 1: ⊢S□j(i)−m−1Ai for no i. Thus for all i, δS,0□□j(i)−m−1Ai=⊥, so ⊢SA0∨⋁1≤i≤k□m⊥. But ⊢S¬□m⊥, so ⊢SA0.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Subcase 2: ⊢S□j(i)−m−1Ai for some i. By repeated application of (iv), ⊢SAi.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proposition 6.2 If S is the closure of {¬□i⊥:i>0} under some □-introduction rules then S provides the alternative rule of disjunction.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proposition 6.3 If S is the closure of {¬□i⊥:i>0} under some □-introduction rules including RM then S admits the rule of margins.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proof: Suppose ⊢SA→□A. By RM, ⊢S□iA→□i+1A for all i, so ⊢SA→□iA and ⊢S¬A∨□iA for all i, so ⊢S¬A or ⊢SA by 6.2.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proposition 6.4 If S is the closure of {¬□i⊥:i>0} under some □-introduction rules including RM and RN then S admits the MacIntosh rule.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proof: Suppose ⊢SA→□A. By 6.3, either ⊢SA or ⊢S¬A. If ⊢SA, then ⊢S¬□¬A→A. If ⊢S¬A, then ⊢S□¬A by RN, so ⊢S¬□¬A→A.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
The next proposition shows that 6.3 and 6.4 would be false if the qualification about RM were omitted.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proposition 6.5 There is a set of □-introduction rules including RN under which the closure of {¬□i⊥:i>0} admits neither the rule of margins nor the MacIntosh rule.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Proof: Let S be the closure of {¬□i⊥:i>0} under the □-introduction rules RN and ⊩□¬⊤→□(⊥∨p). The weakness of S makes the latter rule quite different from ⊩□⊥→□p, since S is highly sensitive to syntactic differences between truth-functionally equivalent wff. The proof will exploit this fact; the strategy is to show that if S admits the MacIntosh rule then ⊢S◇⊤, but that the latter is impossible. By the second rule, ⊢S□¬⊤→□(⊥∨□¬⊤), so ⊢S(⊥∨□¬⊤)→□(⊥∨□¬⊤). Suppose that S provides the MacIntosh rule. Then ⊢S¬□¬(⊥∨□¬⊤)→(⊥∨□¬⊤). By the proof of 6.1, S is closed under δS,0, i.e. δS, so ⊢SδS(¬□¬(⊥∨□¬⊤)→(⊥∨□¬⊤)), i.e. ⊢S¬δS□¬(⊥∨□¬⊤)→(⊥∨δS□¬⊤). Now δS□¬⊤=⊥, for otherwise ⊢S¬⊤, which is impossible since the result of deleting all occurrences of □ in a theorem of S is a theorem of PC; hence ⊢SδS□¬(⊥∨□¬⊤). Thus δS□¬(⊥∨□¬⊤)≠⊥, so ⊢S¬(⊥∨□¬⊤) by definition of δS; thus ⊢S¬□¬⊤. Define a mapping η by:
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

It is easy to show by induction on the length of proofs that if ⊢SA then ⊢PCηA. Thus since ⊢S¬□¬⊤, ⊢PCη¬□¬⊤; but ¬⊤≠□i⊥ (⊥ is primitive), so η□¬⊤=⊤, so η¬□¬⊤=¬⊤; thus ⊢S¬⊤, which is impossible. Thus S does not provide the MacIntosh rule. Since the argument from 6.3 to 6.4 used only RN, S does not provide the rule of margins either.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
The next proposition shows that 6.4 would be false if the qualification about RN were omitted.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proposition 6.6 The closure of {¬□i⊥:i>0} under RM does not provide the MacIntosh rule.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Proof: Let the system be S. Put ν□A=⊥ for all A, and let ν commute with the other operators. It is easy to show by induction on the length of proofs in S that if ⊢SA then ⊢PCνA. Thus we cannot have ⊢S¬□¬⊥→⊥; but ⊢S⊥→□⊥.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Examples like those in 6.5 and 6.6 can be given to show the need for the qualifications to the propositions below. There is room for further investigation in this area. For example, the system S in the proof of 6.5 does not provide the rule RE, since not ⊢S□⊥≡□¬⊤. Is there a set of □-introduction rules including RN and RE under which the closure of {¬□i⊥:i>0} does not provide both the rule of margins and the MacIntosh rule? In any case, some results are still obtainable when RM is weakened to RE.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proposition 6.7 If S is the closure of {¬□i⊥:i>0} under some □-introduction rules including RE then S admits the rule p≡□p⊩p,¬p.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proof: Suppose that S admits RE and ⊢SA≡□A. By RE, ⊢S□iA≡□i+1A for all i, so for all i ⊢SA≡□iA and ⊢S¬A∨□iA, so ⊢S¬A or ⊢SA by 6.2.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proposition 6.8 If S is the closure of {¬□i⊥:i>0} under some □-introduction rules including RE and RN then S admits the rule p≡□p⊩◇p≡p.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proof: From 6.7 as 6.4 was proved from 6.3.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proposition 6.9 The closure of {¬□⊥} under some □-introduction rules including RE is the closure of {¬□i⊥:i>0} under those rules.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proof: It suffices to show that if S admits RE and ⊢S¬□⊥ and ⊢S¬□i⊥ then ⊢S¬□i+1⊥. But if ⊢S¬□i⊥ then ⊢S⊥≡□i⊥, so by RE ⊢S□⊥≡□i+1⊥, so ⊢S¬□i+1⊥ iff ⊢S¬□⊥.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Proposition 6.10 If ℒ is the closure of the D schema □A→◇A under some □-introduction rules including RM, then there is a set of □-introduction rules including those rules under which ℒ is the closure of {¬□i⊥:i>0}.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Proof: It suffices to show that {¬□i⊥:i>0} is a consequence of D by RM and that D is a consequence of {¬□i⊥:i>0} by RM and the □-introduction rule ⊩(□p∧□¬p)→□⊥. The latter is trivial. For the former, suppose that S admits RM and contains D. Since ⊢S⊥→¬⊥, ⊢S□⊥→□¬⊥ by RM; but ⊢S□⊥→¬□¬⊥ by D, so ⊢S¬□⊥. The result follows by 6.9.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Proposition 6.9 allows {¬□i⊥:i>0} to be replaced by {¬□⊥} in propositions 6.3, 6.4, 6.6, 6.7 and 6.8 (recall that any theory providing RM also provides RE). Similarly, proposition 6.10 allows {¬□i⊥:i>0} to be replaced by the D schema (i.e. the set of its instances) in propositions 6.3, and 6.4; it also gives modified versions of 6.1 and 6.2 in which S is the closure of the D schema under some □-introduction rules including RM.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
We now turn to the T schema. Mappings δS,m* will be used that stand to the δS,m mappings as δS* stands to δS (thus δS,0*=δS*):
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Proposition 6.11 Let S be axiomatized by all PC theorems and the T schema with MP and a set of □-introduction rules including RE. If ⊢SA0∨⋁1≤i≤k□j(i)Ai for some j(1),…,j(n)>#A0, then ⊢SAi for some i (0≤i≤n).
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proof: The strategy is a variant of that used for 6.1.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Claim (i): If ⊢SA then ⊢SδS,0*A. Since δS,0*=δS*, the argument is as for 5.5 (where RN was not used at the relevant points).
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Claim (ii): For all m, if ⊢SA then ⊢SδS,m*A. We show this by induction on the length of proofs, assuming (i).
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Basis. PC theorems are unproblematic. For the T axiom, δS,m+1*(□A→A)=(δS,m+1*A∧□δS,m*A)→δS,m+1*A.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Induction step. MP is unproblematic. It suffices to show that if a □-introduction rule Y⊩(⋀i≤k□Gi)→□H is used in the axiomatization of S, σ is a substitution, and both ⊢SσB and ⊢SδS,m*σB for all B∈Y, then ⊢SδS,m+1*((⋀i≤k□σGi)→□σH), i.e. ⊢S(⋀i≤k(δS,m+1*σGi∧□δS,m*σGi))→(δS,m+1*σH∧□δS,m*σH). Thus it suffices to prove ⊢S(⋀i≤kδS,m+1*σGi)→δS,m+1*σH and ⊢S(⋀i≤k□δS,m*σGi)→□δS,m*σH. The former can be proved by an argument like one in the proof of 4.12 (with δS,m+1* in place of τυ), the latter by one as in the proof of 6.1.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Claim (iii): For all m, if #A≤m then ⊢SA≡δS,m*A. Proof by induction on the complexity of A. The only interesting case is the induction step for □. Suppose that #□A≤m+1, so #A≤m. By the induction hypothesis, ⊢SA≡δS,m*A. By RE, ⊢S□A≡□δS,m*A. By T, ⊢S□A→A; again by the induction hypothesis, ⊢SA≡δS,m+1*A, so ⊢S□A→δS,m+1*A. Thus ⊢S□A≡(δS,m+1*A∧□δS,m*A), i.e. ⊢S□A≡δS,m+1*□A.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

Now suppose that ⊢SA0∨⋁1≤i≤k□j(i)Ai for some j(1),…,j(n)>#A0. Let m=#A0. Thus ⊢SδS,m*(A0∨⋁1≤i≤k□j(i)Ai) by (i) and (ii). Now ⊢SA0≡δS,m*A0 by (iii). Since j(i)>m, it is also easy to prove that ⊢SδS,m*□j(i)Ai→□mδS,0*□□j(i)−m−1Ai. Thus ⊢SA0∨⋁1≤i≤k□mδS,0*□□j(i)−m−1Ai. The rest is as for 6.1, with T in place of (iv).
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proposition 6.12 If S is the closure of the T schema under some □-introduction rules including RE then S admits the alternative rule of disjunction.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proposition 6.13 If S is the closure of the T schema under some □-introduction rules including RE then S admits the rule of margins.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proof: Suppose that ⊢SA→□A. By T, ⊢S□A→A, so ⊢SA≡□A. The proof then proceeds as for proposition 6.7, by appeal to 6.12 rather than to 6.2.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proposition 6.14 If S is the closure of T under some □-introduction rules including RE and RN then S admits the MacIntosh rule.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems
Proof: As for 6.4, by appeal to 6.13 rather than to 6.3.
Some admissible rules in nonnormal modal systems

If one considers the set of all □-introduction rules, propositions 6.4 and 6.14 say that KD and KT respectively provide the MacIntosh rule. These results were proved syntactically, as requested by Chellas and Segerberg.
