The alternative rule of disjunction produces a failure of a certain kind of compactness. Where X and Y are sets of formulae and S is a modal system, put X⊩SY iff for every uniform substitution s, if ⊢Ss(A) for all A∈X then ⊢Ss(B) for some B∈Y. ⊩S is an abstract consequence relation in that it is reflexive and admits thinning on the right and left and a cut rule; moreover, if X⊩SY then s(X)⊩Ss(Y) for any uniform substitution s. The rule of necessitation for S can be expressed as {p}⊩S{□p}, and the Lemmon–Scott rule of disjunction for a fixed n as {□p1∨…∨□pn}⊩S{p1,…,pn}. The alternative rule for n=1 is {p∨□jq:j≥0}⊩S{p,q}. If S is a consistent normal system and provides the alternative rule (and so for n=1), ⊩S fails to be compact in that although {p∨□jq:j≥0}⊩S{p,q}, there is no finite subset X of {p∨□jq:j≥0} such that X⊩S{p,q}. For otherwise {p∨□jq:k≥j≥0}⊩S{p,q} for some k; substituting ∼(q&□q&…&□kq) (or just ∼□kq if S extends KT) for p, one concludes that since ⊢S∼(q&□q&…&□kq)∨□jq for k≥j≥0, either ⊢S∼(q&□q&…&□kq) or ⊢Sq, which are both impossible by the consistency and normality of S.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

One does not necessarily restore compactness by restricting the conclusion of ⊩S to a single formula. For example, if S= KD, KDG1, KDB, KT, KTG1, or KTB, {p∨□j(◊q&◊∼q):j≥0}⊩S{p}: for {p∨□j(◊q&◊∼q):j≥0}⊩S{p,◊q&◊∼q} by the alternative rule, and the second formula in the conclusion can be omitted as none of the systems in question has any theorem of the form ◊A&◊∼A (consider a one-world reflexive frame). Now if {p∨□j(◊q&◊∼q):k≥j≥0}⊩S{p} for some k, one concludes from the previous paragraph that ⊢S∼(◊q&◊∼q&□(◊q&◊∼q)&…&□k(◊q&◊∼q)), which is not the case for any of the systems (consider a two-world frame in which both worlds are accessible from both worlds). Thus for S= KD, KDG1, KDB, KT, KTG1, or KTB, ⊩S cannot be axiomatized for single-formula conclusions. One cannot provide axioms in the language of propositional modal logic and rules of inference with finitely many premises such that X⊩S{A} iff A can be inferred from X and those axioms by a finite number of applications of the rules of inference, for any such axiomatization would yield a compact consequence relation.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

Although the alternative rule makes ⊩S noncompact for the systems covered by the theorem, examination of the proof shows it to establish that each system admits a finitary strengthening of the alternative rule. For S= KD, KDG1, KDB, KT, KTG1, KTB, if ⊢SA0∨□j1A1∨…∨□jnAn then ⊢SAi for some i, where ji=#A0+#Ai+1. This can be reduced to ji=#A0+1 for S= KD, KT. For KD, one has ji=#A0+#A1+…+#Ai−1+i. These systems admit parallel finitary strengthenings of the weak rule: put A0=p&∼p, so #A0=0. For systems providing the Lemmon–Scott rule, it is another finitary strengthening of the weak rule.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic
Problem Do the alternative and weak rules have finitary strengthenings in terms of #A0,…,#An for every normal system that provides them?
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

The difference between the finitary strengthenings of the rules for KD! and those for the other systems is not merely an artifact of the proof. ⊢KD!□∼p∨□p, but neither ⊢KD!∼p nor ⊢KD!p, contrary to the finitary strengthening of the weak rule for the other systems given above. KD! also violates the finitary strengthenings of the alternative rule for the other systems. There is a related difference over what might be called the homogeneous alternative rule of disjunction: if ⊢SA0∨□jA1∨…∨□jAn for all j (≥0) then ⊢SAi for some i (0≤i≤n), another strengthening of the alternative rule. KD! does not provide the homogeneous alternative rule, since ⊢KD!q∨□j∼p∨□jp for all j. In contrast, KD, KDG1, KDB, KT, KTG1, and KTB do provide the homogeneous alternative rule. The proof of the theorem for these systems can easily be adapted to show that if ⊢SA0∨□j1A1∨…∨□jnAn for some j1,…,jn where ji≥#A0+#Ai+1 then ⊢SAi for some i (where the inequality is strict, the truth value of Ai in the bottom copy of ⟨Wi,R1,Vi⟩ is protected by a deeper pile of other copies than necessary). Thus if j=max⁡{#A0+#A1+1,…,#A0+#An+1} and ⊢SA0∨□jA1∨…∨□jAn then ⊢SAi for some i, so that S provides the homogeneous alternative rule. Similarly, say that S provides the homogeneous weak rule of disjunction just in case if ⊢S□jA1∨…∨□jAn for all j then ⊢SAi for some i; this rule is intermediate in strength between the weak rule and the Lemmon–Scott rule. By reasoning like that above, KD, KDG1, KDB, KT, KTG1, and KTB provide the homogeneous weak rule (put A0=p&∼p), but KD! does not.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

KD! also constitutes a counterexample to the natural extension of Lemmon and Scott’s semantic characterization of their rule to the weak rule. They show ([6], p. 45) that a consistent normal system provides the rule of disjunction iff its canonical frame ⟨W,R⟩ (the frame of its canonical model) is left-directed, in the sense that for any x1,…,xn∈W there is a y∈W such that yRx1,…,yRxn. One might correspondingly suppose that a normal system provides the weak rule iff its canonical frame is ancestrally left-directed, in the sense that for any x1,…,xn∈W there is a y∈W such that yRj1x1,…,yRjnxn for some j1,…,jn (≥0). This condition seems to stand to the Lemmon–Scott condition just as the weak rule stands to the Lemmon–Scott rule. One can indeed show that if the canonical frame of a normal system is ancestrally left-directed, then the system provides the weak rule of disjunction. However, the converse fails. Since the sets {□j∼p:j≥0} and {□jp:j≥0} are both consistent in KD!, they have maximal consistent extensions x1 and x2∈W respectively, where ⟨W,R⟩ is the canonical frame for KD!. Suppose that yRj1x1 and yRj2x2 for some y∈W. Then ◊j1□j2∼p∈y since □j2∼p∈x1, and ◊j2□j1p∈y since □j1p∈x2. Thus {◊j1□j2∼p,◊j2□j1p} should be a consistent set in KD!. But it is not, for ⊢KD!◊j1□j2∼p↔∼□j1+j2p and ⊢KD!◊j2□j1p↔□j1+j2p. Thus no such y exists. The canonical frame for KD! is not ancestrally left-directed, even though KD! provides the weak rule.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

Although the frame of the canonical model for KD! is not ancestrally left-directed, KD! can be characterized by a model whose frame is ancestrally left-directed. For let A0,A1,A2,… be an enumeration of the consistent formulae in KD! (where the set of propositional variables is taken to be countable). By an argument like that in the proof of the theorem, one can show that {A0,◊j1A1,◊j2A2,…} is consistent in KD!, where ji=#A0+#A1+…+#Ai−1+i. Thus it has a maximal consistent extension x. The submodel of the canonical model of KD! generated by x characterizes KD!: a formula is consistent in KD! iff it holds at some world in this submodel (however, a set of formulas may be consistent in KD! without all holding together at any world in the submodel, by the argument of the previous paragraph). The frame ⟨W,R⟩ of any generated submodel is ancestrally left-directed, since the generating world has the ancestral of R to any world in W. A similar argument can be given for KD, KDG1, KDB, KT, KTG1, and KTB, with ji=#A0+#Ai+1. However, in the absence of general finitary equivalents of the infinitary rules of disjunction there remains:
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic
Problem Find semantic characterizations of the infinitary rules of disjunction.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic
An important consequence of the alternative rule is:
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic
Corollary 2 The following are equivalent for S= KD, KDG1, KDB, KT, KTG1, KTB, and KD!:
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

Proof: (a) ⇒ (b). For any normal S, if ⊢SA→□A then ⊢S□iA→□i+1A for all i, and hence ⊢SA→□iA, i.e. ⊢S∼A∨□iA, for any i. If S provides the alternative rule of disjunction, ⊢S∼A or ⊢SA. (b) ⇒ (a). S is normal. (c) ⇔ (b). This is like (a) ⇔ (b), for (c) is equivalent to ⊢S∼A→□∼A and (b) is symmetric between A and ∼A.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

If ⊢S∼A or ⊢SA whenever ⊢SA→□A, let us say that S provides the rule of margins (the margin between the truth of A and its necessity). Any normal system providing the alternative rule also provides the rule of margins. Thus, for example, no consistent extension of K4 provides the alternative rule, since it would have ⊢S∼□p or ⊢S□p, leading to inconsistency (in the latter case by another application of the rule). More generally, no modality entails its own necessitation in any consistent normal system providing the alternative rule of disjunction.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

The equivalence of (a) and (c) in Corollary 2 follows from the rule of margins, but not conversely. If S extends KB, (a) and (c) are equivalent (if ⊢S◊A→A then ⊢S□◊A→□A, and ⊢KBA→□◊A), so they are equivalent in KB4, which does not provide the rule of margins (in contrast, (a) and (c) are not equivalent in K4, for ⊢K4□p→□□p but not ⊢K4◊□p→□p). The equivalence of (a) and (c) will not be treated as a rule of disjunction.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

Corollary 2 is weaker than the theorem. A normal system can provide the rule of margins without providing the alternative rule (even for n=1). A counterexample is the system KT ∨ KDB, where ⊢KT∨KDBA iff ⊢KTA and ⊢KDBA. KT ∨ KDB is complete with respect to models that are either reflexive or both serial and convergent. If ⊢KT∨KDBA→□A then ⊢KTA→□A and ⊢KDBA→□A; by Corollary 2, ⊢KT∼A or ⊢KTA and ⊢KDB∼A or ⊢KDBA. If either ⊢KT∼A and ⊢KDBA or ⊢KTA and ⊢KDB∼A, KTB would be inconsistent. Thus either ⊢KT∼A and ⊢KDB∼A or ⊢KTA and ⊢KDBA, so ⊢KT∨KDB∼A or ⊢KT∨KDBA. However, KT ∨ KDB does not provide even the weak rule. For ⊢KT□i(□p→p)∨□j(p→□◊p) and ⊢KDB□i(□p→p)∨□j(p→□◊p) for all i and j, but neither ⊢KT∨KDB□p→p nor ⊢KT∨KDBp→□◊p.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

Nevertheless, the rule of margins has many of the consequences of the alternative rule. If S is normal and provides the marginal rule, it extends KD, and if it is consistent, it does not extend K4 or KE.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

The rule of margins signals a kind of expressive incompleteness in the systems which provide it. Suppose that □* is a (perhaps complex) operator in a normal modal system S, where □*A is to be interpreted as the infinite conjunction A&□A&□□A&…. Thus S should satisfy at least three conditions: (i) if ⊢SA then ⊢S□*A; (ii) ⊢S□*p→p; (iii) ⊢S□*p→□□*p. If S provides the rule of margins, either ⊢S□*p or ⊢S∼□*p by (iii). If the former, ⊢Sp by (ii) and S is inconsistent. If the latter, ⊢S∼□*(p∨∼p) by substitution; but ⊢S□*(p∨∼p) by (i), and S is again inconsistent. Thus a consistent normal system providing the rule of margins cannot express the ancestral of its own necessity operator. If an operator for the ancestral is introduced, the new system will not provide the rule of margins.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

Now for the application. Some things are clearly heaps, some are clearly not heaps, and borderline cases are neither clearly heaps nor clearly not heaps (‘clearly’ could be taken epistemologically, semantically, or ontologically). □A can be read as ‘It is clearly the case that A’. That A is a borderline case may be expressed as ∼□A&∼□∼A. Let S? be an appropriate system of modal logic for this reading. The choice of a classical underlying propositional logic is controversial in the context of vagueness, but it may be motivated by either a supervaluational approach (Fine [3]) or the claim that clarity is an epistemological rather than a semantic or ontological matter (Cargile [2], Campbell [1], Sorensen [7]). Given classical logic, one cannot assert ‘If X is a heap then X is not a borderline case of a heap’ and ‘If X is not a heap then X is not a borderline case of a heap’ without abolishing the borderline cases altogether; rather, p&∼□p will be regarded as a consistent combination (p atomic). To assume that S? is normal is to assume that the clear propositions are closed under logical consequence, but that need not be implausible: if X is genuinely a borderline case of a heap, it surely follows that one cannot deduce from what is clear that X is a heap, nor that it is not. It also seems plausible that if something is clearly the case, then it is the case. That makes S? at least as strong as KT.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

Vagueness is often said to be ubiquitous in natural languages. One development of this idea would be the claim that it is never a matter of logic that all cases of A are clear cases, unless for the trivial reason that it is a matter of logic that A has no cases or that everything is a case of A. In other words, if ⊢S?A→□A then either ⊢S?∼A or ⊢S?A. Thus the rule of margins can be taken to represent the ubiquity of vagueness. It is therefore satisfying that KT provides the rule, since on the present approach it is the minimal logic of clarity.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

The claim formalized in the previous paragraph is not equivalent to the claim ‘It is a matter of logic that A lacks borderline cases only when it is a matter of logic that A has no cases or that everything is a case of A’. The latter would be formalized by the rule that if ⊢S?□∼A∨□A then ⊢S?∼A or ⊢S?A. This rule is a special case of the Lemmon–Scott rule of disjunction and is therefore possessed by systems such as K, K4, KD4, and KT4 that provide that rule but not the rule of margins. On the other hand, KD! provides the rule of margins but not the new rule, since ⊢KD!□∼p∨□p but neither ⊢KD!∼p nor ⊢KD!p. However, the new rule follows easily from the rule of margins in extensions of KT, so the latter is the stronger rule in S? and therefore seems a more appropriate representation of the ubiquity of vagueness. The same point applies to the rule that if ⊢S?A→□A and ⊢S?∼A→□∼A then ⊢S?∼A or ⊢S?A, corresponding to the claim that all cases of A are clear cases and all noncases clear noncases only if A is a logical truth or falsehood. This rule is a consequence of both the previous one and the rule of margins and is equivalent to the former in extensions of KT. It says that when A is not a logical truth or falsehood, its truth-conditions are liable to unclarity on at least one side; the rule of margins says that they are liable to unclarity on both sides.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

The ubiquity of vagueness is relative to a language. If □*A is introduced to mean that A and clearly A and clearly clearly A and …, one must expect □*p→□□*p to be a theorem of the new system and the rule of margins to fail, as noted above. This does not mean that KT is the wrong logic for clarity, of course, for what the rule of margins fails in may be a conservative extension of KT. There is no need to deny that precise sentences can be introduced into a so far thoroughly vague language. The rule of margins indicates that (with trivial exceptions) such sentences have not yet been introduced.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

The connection between vagueness and the rule of margins can also be discerned in the proof of the theorem. In the case relevant to the rule, one takes a world at which A holds and a world at which ∼A holds and constructs a sequence of worlds from one to the other, each accessible from its predecessor. The point is that there must be a cut-off point, a last world at which A holds; A&∼□A will hold at that world. This is reminiscent of a sorites argument.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

Assume that S? is a consistent extension of KT and provides the rule of margins. It follows that S? does not extend K4. The failure of what is clear always to be clearly clear is a striking result but one predicted by the epistemic theory of vagueness. (Sorensen [7], pp. 242–243 argues from the epistemic theory of vagueness and the vagueness of knowledge to the failure of the corresponding principle for knowledge.) It is harder to accommodate within the standard apparatus of supervaluations; this may be a version of the problem of higher-order vagueness (perhaps a hierarchy of valuations is required).
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

One way to realize these ideas would be to suppose that A is clear at a world iff it is true at all nearby worlds on some appropriate metric. Perhaps A is clear iff we are very reliably right about it, and reliability is a matter of leaving a margin for error, at least for sentences of the language in question (Williamson [8], pp. 103–108 offers a tentative defense of the epistemic theory along these lines). One would thus consider models ⟨W,R,V⟩ with a metric d defined on W, where uRv iff d(u,v)<k (u,v∈W, k>0). R would therefore be reflexive and symmetric; conversely, every reflexive symmetric relation is induced by some metric in this way (to see this, put d(u,v)=0 iff u=v, d(u,v)=1 iff uRv but not u=v, d(u,v)=2 otherwise; let k=2). Thus KTB would be the strongest system valid for these models. It is satisfying that KTB provides the rule of margins.
An alternative rule of disjunction in modal logic

Of course, KTB is not a plausible logic of clarity once undecidable propositions are taken into account. If Goldbach’s Conjecture (GC) is false, it is clearly false in the relevant sense, for a counterexample can be computed; by contraposition and bivalence, if GC is not clearly false, it is true. The B axiom says that if GC is true it is clearly not clearly false: but then it would be clearly true. The truth of GC should not entail its clear truth, for it might be true yet not even informally provable. The B axiom is implausible in the light of such examples. KT is a better candidate for the strict logic of clarity. However, KTB is the system that emerges when one idealizes away such phenomena and concentrates on what may be the main source of sorites paradoxes. On this view, the impossibility of identifying a cut-off point for A can be explained. The last cases of A are cases of A near cases of ∼A, that is, they are cases of A&∼□A; but A&∼□A has no clear cases, for □(A&∼□A) is a contradiction in any normal extension of KT. Thus nothing is clearly one of the last cases of A.
I thank Lloyd Humberstone for many helpful comments.
[1] Campbell, R., “The sorites paradox,” Philosophical Studies, vol. 26 (1974), pp. 175–191.
[2] Cargile, J., “The sorites paradox,” British Journal for the Philosophy of Science, vol. 20 (1969), pp. 193–202.
[3] Fine, K., “Vagueness, truth and logic,” Synthese, vol. 30 (1975), pp. 265–300.
[4] Hughes, G. E. and M. J. Cresswell, A Companion to Modal Logic, Methuen, London, 1984.
[5] Humberstone, I. L., “A more discriminating approach to modal logic” (abstract), Journal of Symbolic Logic, vol. 51 (1986), pp. 503–504.
[6] Lemmon, E. J. and D. Scott, The “Lemmon Notes”: An Introduction to Modal Logic, edited by K. Segerberg, American Philosophical Quarterly Monograph Series, Blackwell, Oxford, 1977.
[7] Sorensen, R., Blindspots, Clarendon Press, Oxford, 1988.
[8] Williamson, T., Identity and Discrimination, Blackwell, Oxford, 1990.

works.title: Fregean directions
passages: THE QUESTION ‘What is the criterion of identity for directions?’ might be construed as asking either ‘When do lines have the same direction?’ or ‘When are directions identical?’. Frege’s answer ‘When they are parallel’ fits the former question, not the latter, for it specifies a relation other than identity between lines, not directions. Jonathan Lowe thinks the latter question more fundamental, and claims that Frege’s criterion can be reformulated to answer it: ‘When some line with one is parallel to some line with the other’. At p. 147 of Identity and Discrimination I make three points against this view: (a) Lowe’s construal does not permit a principled rejection of an intuitively unacceptable answer to the original question, (b) On pain of circularity, Lowe’s answer uses conceptual resources (‘Of’ as primitive) beyond those of Frege’s, and thus is not a mere reformulation, (c) Lowe’s question seems to make the hopeless demand for something more basic (in some sense) than ‘x=y’. Lowe’s reply ‘One-level versus two-level identity criteria’ (Analysis, this issue) does not address (b) or (c). I shall follow him in discussing only (a).

An intuitively acceptable answer to the question ‘What is the criterion of identity for directions?’ will mention parallelism. Given Frege’s construal, one can explain why: the point is to say when lines have the same direction without mentioning directions. Given Lowe’s construal, no such explanation is possible. Why is it wrong to answer his question ‘When some line has both’? Lowe agrees that directions are identical if and only if some line has both. Indeed, his preferred equivalence entails this new one (the only point here is that someone who uses his equivalence should not reject the new one as false; Lowe seems to have misread the book as claiming more for the entailment). Nor can Lowe accuse the new answer of circularity or total uninformativeness. Yet it is intuitively unacceptable, for it does not mention parallelism. It does not even distinguish directions from lengths, and Lowe rejects it for this reason. However, he leaves it as an unexplained datum that what the identity of directions ‘consists in’ must differ from what the identity of lengths ‘consists in’ (whereas what the identity of cats ‘consists in’ is presumably the same as what the identity of dogs ‘consists in’). He gives no basis of principle on which to reject the claim that each separately ‘consists in’ the existence of a line having both. In contrast, the Fregean approach makes the obvious explanation available. Directions and lengths have different criteria of identity because two lines can have the same direction and different lengths, or vice versa. I continue to find this contrast in explanatory power a good reason for preferring Frege’s approach to Lowe’s.

The closure under a certain rule of the modal system usually called “K4” is shown to be the modal system called “K4” by Sobociński.
A relation between namesakes in modal logic

A modal system S provides double cancellation iff for all sentences A and B, if ⊢SLA≡LB and ⊢SMA≡MB then ⊢SA≡B. It is of course not required that ⊢S((LA≡LB)&(MA≡MB))⊃(A≡B). If S is any modal system, there is a smallest normal extension S+ of S providing double cancellation (terminology as in [1]). For reasons given in [3], the double cancellation rule may be of some philosophical interest. This note extends the results of [3] and [4] on double cancellation in normal systems.
A relation between namesakes in modal logic

The name “K4” is ambiguous. It is now customarily used for the smallest normal system containing the schema LA⊃LLA; this practice is followed here. Sobociński used the same name for the smallest system containing KT4 (= S4) and the schemata A⊃(MLA⊃LA) and MLA≡LMA ([2]); this normal system is here referred to as K4Sob. The relation to be established between these namesakes is that K4+=K4Sob; it will also be shown that K4Sob is the only normal extension of K4 providing double cancellation in which there is not modal collapse. This extends the results of [3], in which it was shown that KD4!+=K4Sob, where KD4! is the smallest normal system containing the formula MT (T being a constant tautology) and the schema LLA≡LA, and [4], in which it is shown that KW+ is inconsistent, where KW is “provability logic”, the smallest normal system containing L(LA⊃A)⊃LA, an extension of K4.
A relation between namesakes in modal logic

Proof. Let S be any normal extension of K4Sob. Theorem. The normal extensions of K4 providing double cancellation are K4Sob, 𝑇𝑟𝑖𝑣 and the inconsistent system.

Proof. Any normal extension of K4 providing double cancellation is one of the three mentioned systems by Lemmas E and F. K4Sob provides double cancellation by Lemma E. 𝑇𝑟𝑖𝑣 and the inconsistent system provide it trivially.

works.title: Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT
passages: Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT

The main result of this paper is that KT (=T) is closed under a cancellation principle (if LA is provably equivalent to LB and MA is provably equivalent to MB then A is provably equivalent to B). This result extends to KTG1, but it does not extend to modal systems associated with the provability interpretation of L, such as KW (=G) and KT4Grz (=S4Grz). Following Williamson, these results are applied to philosophical concerns about the proper form for theories of meaning, via the interpretation of L as some kind of verifiability. The cancellation principle can then be read as saying that verifiability conditions and falsifiability conditions jointly determine truth conditions.
Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT

A modal logic S has the single cancellation property just in case A↔B is a thesis of S whenever LA↔LB is, where L is the necessity operator. S has the double cancellation property just in case A↔B is a thesis of S whenever both LA↔LB and MA↔MB are, where M is the possibility operator. The main result of this note is that KT (=T), the smallest normal system to contain the T axiom Lp→p, has the double (but not the single) cancellation property. Although these properties are mathematically quite natural, there is also a philosophical reason for investigating them, which it may be worthwhile to mention.
Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT

One can give a nonstandard interpretation of a modal logic S by reading L as an operator expressive of some kind of verifiability rather than of necessity. One could then say that formulas A and B have the same verifiability conditions according to S if and only if LA↔LB is a thesis of S. By the redundancy property of truth, one can also say that A and B have the same truth conditions according to S if and only if A↔B is a thesis of S. Thus S has the single cancellation property just in case formulas with the same verifiability conditions (according to S) have the same truth conditions (according to S). More briefly: the single cancellation property expresses the claim that verifiability conditions determine truth conditions. In the same vein, A and B would have the same falsifiability conditions according to S if and only if L∼A↔L∼B were a thesis of S, given that falsification is verification of the contradictory; if M is equivalent to ∼L∼ and the underlying propositional logic is classical, L∼A↔L∼B is equivalent in S to MA↔MB. Thus S has the double cancellation property just in case formulas with both the same verifiability conditions and the same falsifiability conditions (according to S) have the same truth conditions (according to S). More briefly: the double cancellation property expresses the claim that verifiability and falsifiability conditions jointly determine truth conditions. It would follow that the potentialities of linguistically formulated propositions to be true (or false) could not transcend the capacities of relevant subjects to recognize them as true (or as false). Questions of truth and falsity would supervene on questions of verification and falsification. Some would call this a form of antirealism; however, it should be noted that these claims do not by themselves equate truth with verifiability, for a modal system can have either cancellation property without having p↔Lp as a thesis (“modal collapse”). Supervenience does not entail reduction. In any case, cancellation rules in modal logic can be used to express various conceptions according to which epistemic features of propositions determine their content (this philosophical background is elaborated, with references, in Williamson [4]). One can then investigate the logics of verifiability which permit such conceptions. That is, which modal systems are closed under the corresponding cancellation rules?
Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT

Williamson [4] began such an investigation. There, as here, only normal systems are considered (see [2] for relevant background). This restriction corresponds to nontrivial philosophical assumptions: that the underlying propositional logic is classical, that ∼L∼ is equivalent to M, and that verifiability obeys some significant closure conditions. [4] defended these assumptions; its arguments will not be repeated here. It is also shown in [4] that, in any normal system interpreted as above, verifiability conditions determine truth conditions if and only if falsifiability conditions do.
Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT

Some known results about the cancellation properties may be mentioned. From [3] one can gather that K (the smallest normal system) and KD (the smallest normal system containing the D axiom Lp→Mp) have the single and therefore the double cancellation property, but that no normal system which includes the T axiom but does not suffer modal collapse by also including p→Lp has the single cancellation property. In [4] it is proved that the smallest normal system with the double cancellation property which includes both Lp↔LLp and Lp→Mp is KT4 (=S4) +p→(MLp→Lp)+LMp↔MLp. Both KT4 and KT5 (=S5) lack the double cancellation property. The question thus arises of whether any familiar modal system has the double cancellation property without having the single one. Since KT lacks the single cancellation property, the following result answers that question in the affirmative.
Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT
Fact If LA↔LB∈KT and MA↔MB∈KT, then A↔B∈KT.
Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT

Proof: Suppose that LA↔LB and MA↔MB∈KT but A↔B∉KT. It can be assumed without loss of generality that A→B∉KT. Since KT is complete for reflexive models, there is a model ⟨W,R,V⟩ (where W is a set of “worlds”, R a binary accessibility relation on them, and V a valuation on the frame ⟨W,R⟩) such that R is reflexive and for some w∈W, V(A,w)=1 and V(B,w)=0. Choose elements w(0),w(1),w(2),… such that w(0)=w, w(i)∉W for i>0, and w(i)=w(j) only if i=j. Let W∼=W∪{w(1),w(2),…}. For x,y∈W∼, put xR∼y iff either xRy or x=y or for some i, x=w(i+1) and y=w(i). Let V∼ be the unique valuation on ⟨W∼,R∼⟩ such that, if x∈W, V∼(C,x)=V(C,x) for all wff’s C, and if x∉W but x∈W∼, V∼(C,x)=V(C,w) for all atomic wff’s C. Thus V∼(A,w)=1 and V∼(B,w)=0.
Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT

The idea of the proof is to show that w(0),w(1),w(2),… form a tail down which A takes alternating values, so that it always “knows” whether it is an odd or an even number of worlds below w(0)—which is impossible, for the complexity of A turns out to impose an upper bound on how far up the tail it can “see”, while the tail itself is homogeneous.
Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT

It will first be proved by induction on i that if i is even then V∼(A,w(i))=1 and V∼(B,w(i))=0, while if i is odd then V∼(A,w(i))=0 and V∼(B,w(i))=1. We already have the basis i=0, since w(0)=w. Suppose, for the inductive step, that i is even, V∼(A,w(i))=1, and V∼(B,w(i))=0. For x∈W∼, w(i+1)R∼x iff either x=w(i+1) or x=w(i). Suppose that V∼(A,w(i+1))=1. Then w(i+1)R∼x would imply V∼(A,x)=1, giving V∼(LA,w(i+1))=1. Since R∼ is reflexive, ⟨W∼,R∼,V∼⟩ is a model of KT, so by hypothesis V∼(LA↔LB,w(i+1))=1; thus V∼(LB,w(i+1))=1, which is absurd, since w(i+1)R∼w(i) and V∼(B,w(i))=0. Thus V∼(A,w(i+1))=0. Similarly, suppose that V∼(B,w(i+1))=0. Then w(i+1)R∼x would imply V∼(B,x)=0, giving V∼(MB,w(i+1))=0. Since ⟨W∼,R∼,V∼⟩ is a model of KT, V∼(MA↔MB,w(i+1))=1; thus V∼(MA,w(i+1))=0, which is absurd, since w(i+1)R∼w(i) and V∼(A,w(i))=1. By a symmetric argument, if i is odd, V∼(A,w(i))=0, and V∼(B,w(i))=1, then V∼(A,w(i+1))=1 and V∼(B,w(i+1))=0. This completes the induction.
Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT

Now define the modal depth |C| of a wff C in the usual way: |C|=0 if C is atomic; |∼C|=|C|; |C&D|=max⁡{|C|,|D|}; |LC|=|C|+1. It will be proved by induction on the complexity of C that for all i and j, if |C|≤i and |C|≤j then V∼(C,w(i))=V∼(C,w(j)). For the basis C is atomic, but then by definition of V∼, V∼(C,w(i))=V(C,w)=V∼(C,w(j)). Suppose that all wff’s less complex than C obey the hypothesis, and |C|≤i and |C|≤j. Case (a): C=∼D. Easy. Case (b): C=D&E. Since |D|≤|C|≤i, |D|≤|C|≤j, |E|≤|C|≤i, and |E|≤|C|≤j, by the induction hypothesis V∼(D,w(i))=V∼(D,w(j)) and V∼(E,w(i))=V∼(E,w(j)), so V∼(D&E,w(i))=V∼(D&E,w(j)). Case (c): C=LD. Since |C|=|D|+1, 0<i and 0<j. By construction of R∼, V∼(LD,w(i))=1 iff V∼(D,w(i))=V∼(D,w(i−1))=1, and V∼(LD,w(j))=1 iff V∼(D,w(j))=V∼(D,w(j−1))=1. Now |D|=|C|−1≤i−1 and |D|≤j−1, so by the induction hypothesis V∼(D,w(i−1))=V∼(D,w(j−1)) and V∼(D,w(i))=V∼(D,w(j)), so V∼(LD,w(i))=1 iff V∼(LD,w(j))=1. This completes the induction
Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT
The contradiction is now obvious. Let |A|≤2i. By the former induction, V∼(A,w(2i))=1 and V∼(A,w(2i+1))=0. By the latter, V∼(A,w(2i))=V∼(A,w(2i+1)).
Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT

Naturally, the proof extends to any system complete for a class of models closed under the construction just given (that of ⟨W∼,R∼,V∼⟩ out of ⟨W,R,V⟩).1 Consider for instance the system KTG1, which results from the addition of the G1 axiom MLp→LMp to KT. It can be shown to be complete for the class of models ⟨W,R,V⟩ such that R is reflexive and convergent, in the sense that for any w,x,y∈W, if wRx and wRy then both xRz and yRz for some z∈W. It is not hard to show that, in the construction above, if R is reflexive and convergent then so is R∼. Thus if LA↔LB and MA↔MB∈KTG1, then A↔B∈KTG1.
Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT

What is the philosophical importance of these results? Suppose that KT (or, for that matter, KTG1) is held to be the correct logic for some notion of verifiability—perhaps one based on a concept of knowledge that does not satisfy the claim “If you know, you know that you know”. It follows that, on such a view, verifiability conditions and falsifiability conditions jointly determine truth conditions, while either set of conditions alone would not.
Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT

Finally, it may be of interest to compare KT with the modal system KW in respect of the double cancellation property, since KW is associated with the reading of L as a different kind of verifiability: provability in a given formal system (cf. Boolos [1], where KW is called G). The property would then express the claim that provability and refutability conditions jointly determine truth conditions. KW is the smallest normal system to contain the W axiom L(Lp→p)→Lp. Let S be any extension of KW with the double cancellation property, and let t be any thesis of KW. Now MMt↔M(Mt&L∼Mt)∈KW because Mp↔M(p&L∼p)∈KW and LMt↔L(Mt&L∼Mt)∈KW because LMp→L∼t∈KW (cf. [1], p. 31). By double cancellation, Mt↔(Mt&L∼Mt)∈S, so Mt→L∼Mt∈S. But MMt→Mt∈KW since Lp→LLp∈KW ([1], p. 30) and L∼Mt→∼MMt∈KW, so MMt→∼MMt∈S, so ∼MMt∈S. Since ∼MM∼t∈KW, MMt↔MM∼t∈S. Moreover, LMt↔LM∼t∈KW. By double cancellation again, Mt↔M∼t∈S. Consequently, Lt↔L∼t∈S. By a third double cancellation, t↔∼t∈S. In other words, no consistent extension of KW has the double cancellation property; it follows that no consistent extension of KW has the single cancellation property either. This result illustrates the inability of a radical interpreter, who can recognize only formal provability and refutability in a mathematical language, to make sense of its sentences.
Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT

The last point does not depend on the failure of provability in a formal system to guarantee truth. For if L is reinterpreted as ‘provable and true’, the corresponding modal system is KT4Grz (=S4Grz), which results from the addition of the Grz axiom L(L(p→Lp)→p)→p to KT4 ([1], pp. 159–167). Now the smallest normal system with the double cancellation property which includes KT4 is KT4 +p→(MLp→Lp)+LMp↔MLp; since Grz is a thesis of this system, the closure of KT4Grz under double cancellation is not the contradictory system but KT4 +p→(MLp→Lp)+LMp↔MLp (this follows from results in [4]). However, p→(MLp→Lp) is not a thesis of KT4Grz ([1], p. 166), so KT4Grz is not closed under double cancellation. One could not rehabilitate the claim that provability and refutability conditions jointly determine truth conditions in mathematics merely by restricting proof to true propositions and refutation to false ones.
Verification, falsification, and cancellation in KT
In summary, if the determination of truth conditions by verifiability and falsifiability conditions has a chance, it may lie with a view on which verification is neither transparent nor formal.
I would like to thank Lloyd Humberstone and the referee for comments on an earlier draft.

A more delicate analysis of the proof shows that it is not necessary to be able to hang an infinite tail from the world w; the proof can easily be adapted to the case in which one can hang only finite tails of arbitrary length from w. ↩︎
[1] Boolos, G., The Unprovability of Consistency, Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, 1979.
[2] Hughes, G. E. and M. J. Cresswell, A Companion to Modal Logic, Methuen, London, 1984.
[3] Lemmon, E. J. and D. S. Scott, The “Lemmon Notes”: An Introduction to Modal Logic, edited by K. Segerberg, Blackwell, Oxford, 1977.
[4] Williamson, T., “Assertion, denial and some cancellation rules in modal logic,” Journal of Philosophical Logic, vol. 17 (1988), pp. 299–318.

works.title: Two incomplete anti-realist modal epistemic logics
passages: Two incomplete anti-realist modal epistemic logics

Many phrases have been used to express what are sometimes called anti-realist conceptions of truth: ‘verifiability’, ‘knowability’, ‘rational acceptability’, ‘warranted assertability’. In spite of their obvious differences, all four of these phrases have a common form; each is a cognitive attitude modified by ‘-ability’. They speak of the possibility of verification, knowledge, rational acceptance or warranted assertion. Schematically, it seems to be claimed that it is true that A if and only if it is possible that it is E’d that A, where ‘E’ is to be replaced by some cognitive verb and ‘A’ by any indicative sentence of the class to which the anti-realist conception is being claimed to apply. Since truth is redundant as a sentential operator, this boils down to the following thesis, where ‘p’ is a propositional variable and ‘M’ expresses the appropriate kind of possibility:
Two incomplete anti-realist modal epistemic logics
Two incomplete anti-realist modal epistemic logics

(*) also formalizes views such as Putnam’s: ‘To claim a statement is true is to claim it could be justified’ [11, p. 56]. It is no doubt a crude model for anti-realism, but one has to start somewhere; by seeing how and why more sophisticated versions of anti-realism differ from (*) one should be able to understand them better too. Moreover, if an anti-realist rejects the equation of truth with, say, warranted assertibility, arguing that truth is rather to be identified with the possibility of getting into a position in which one’s warrant to assert somehow cannot be overturned, the form of (*) is preserved, for truth is still being identified with the possibility of something. The arguments below require no more; nothing else will be assumed about E. The aim of this paper is not primarily to evaluate the philosophical plausibility of (*) under some interpretation, but to discuss systems of propositional modal logic with an added operator E in which it is a thesis, although some results about the latter will naturally provide material for the former task.2 The area also has mathematical interest; in particular, (*) seems to say that the possibility operator M has a right inverse.
Two incomplete anti-realist modal epistemic logics

Consider a language 𝕃 whose primitive vocabulary consists of a denumerable set Atom of propositional variables p,q,r,…, three monadic sentential operators ¬ (negation), M and E, the dyadic & (conjunction) and parentheses. L (necessity) abbreviates ¬M¬ in the metalanguage; ∨, → and ↔ (disjunction and the material conditional and biconditional) are used similarly. The set Wff of well-formed formulae of 𝕃 is defined in the usual way. The concept of a normal modal logic (cf. [9]) has an obvious extension to 𝕃: a subset S of Wff is a normal E-logic iff S contains L(p→q)→(Lp→Lq) and all truth-functional tautologies and is closed under the rules of modus ponens (MP), uniform substitution (US) and necessitation (Nec). By analogy with modal logic, “K” is the smallest normal E-logic, “KT” is the smallest normal E-logic containing the T axiom Lp→p, “KT4” (or “S4”) is the smallest normal E-logic containing it and the S4 axiom Lp→LLp, and so on.3 A normal E-logic collapses iff it contains Mp↔p.
Two incomplete anti-realist modal epistemic logics

The philosophical motivation for interest in (*) requires M to be interpreted as some kind of genuine possibility, and therefore L as some kind of genuine necessity, although perhaps of a restricted sort. It seems reasonable to assume that a necessary consequence of something necessary is itself necessary and that the necessity of a logical truth is itself a logical truth, which suggests that attention should be confined to normal E-logics. US is of course justified by the treatment of p,q,r,… as variables, a wff A of 𝕃 being valid on the intended interpretation iff every substitution instance of A in an interpreted language of some kind has an appropriate kind of logical truth, for every substitution instance of a substitution instance of A is itself a substitution instance of A. The requirement that the underlying propositional logic be classical is a substantive one, for some anti-realists reject classical in favour of intuitionist logic; however, the attempt to combine anti-realism with classical logic is sufficiently common for investigation of its consequences to be worthwhile.4 Thus the concern is with normal E-logics containing (*). Note that (*) is thereby subject to Nec; this seems reasonable, for anti-realists advance readings of (*) in saying what it is for a statement to be true, not just which statements happen to be true. The focus will further be narrowed to normal E-logics containing the T axiom Lp→p, and therefore, equivalently, p→Mp: what is necessary is actual, and what is actual is possible. That is scarcely controversial. Some versions of anti-realism may seem to violate this requirement, for example by claiming that it is true that A iff it is possible to verify that A under epistemically ideal conditions, which suggests a limitation of the possible to the epistemically ideal, thereby excluding the actual. However, these versions can be regimented into line with T by building the restriction into the interpretation of E rather than of M. Again, it might be suggested that ‘It is possible to E that A’ is not equivalent to ‘It is possible that it is E’d that A’, and that the notion of possibility involved in the former is the ‘can’ of ability, which, Anthony Kenny has argued, obeys neither p→Mp nor the thesis M(p∨q)→(Mp∨Mq) of all normal logics ([10, pp. 122–144], and [2]). In both of these cases the problem can be traced to the intuition that one can X only if one has a reliable ability to X. But this condition too can be built into the interpretation of E rather than of M: to E that A might be (in some appropriate sense) to verify that A in a reliable or locally reproducible way. Thus the use of a normal logic with the T axiom does not beg this particular philosophical question. Other interpretations for which the T axiom fails are some on which LA says that A is provable in a given formal system, as in the Gödelian modal logic KW (= G; cf. [1]); however, even granted a formal system in which E is expressible, (*) then equates the truth of a proposition with the formal consistency of the claim that it is cognized, not a principle likely to attract many anti-realists. In any case, if (*) holds for an operator M which obeys “K” and E satisfies the principle Ep→p, then (*) holds for an operator M′ which obeys “KT”, since we can put M′p=p∨Mp.

Finally, collapsing systems should be excluded, for no interesting kind of possibility is logically equivalent to actuality; moreover, if p↔Mp is a thesis of a normal E-logic containing (*), so by US is Ep↔MEp, and therefore by (*) Ep↔p, which would trivialize (*). Thus, since only extensions of “T” are under consideration, Mp→p must not be a thesis.

Given the desiderata of the previous paragraph, an anti-realist system may be defined as a normal E-logic containing (*) and T, and a nontrivial anti-realist system as a noncollapsing one. There are exactly two trivial anti-realist systems: the inconsistent system and the system of classical propositional logic with M and E as redundant operators. If “KT”* (“KT” plus (*)) does not collapse, it is the smallest nontrivial anti-realist system. If it does collapse, there are no nontrivial anti-realist systems. The main result of this paper is the existence of nontrivial anti-realist systems. However, some facts about all nontrivial anti-realist systems will first be listed and briefly discussed.

The usual semantic notions must first be adapted to the language 𝕃 with the new operator E. Interesting questions concern the notion of a frame. As usual, a frame is a pair ⟨W,R⟩, where W is a nonempty set and R a relation on W2. A point of some philosophical significance can be extracted from the proof of Theorem 1. Intuitively, the feature of frames which it exploits to make trouble for anti-realist logic is that they permit world-propositions—propositions true at exactly one world. Now if world-propositions are problematic for the anti-realist, so presumably are worlds, and the anti-realist will wish to put the point in terms which do not presuppose the possible worlds framework. That, however, can be done, since a world-proposition can be recharacterized as a maximally specific consistent proposition. The argument can then be reproduced in an object language with propositional quantifiers, concluding that for the anti-realist no maximally specific propositions are contingently false, as follows. Let A be a maximally specific proposition. Thus for any proposition B, either A entails B or A entails ¬B. In particular, either A entails EA or A entails ¬EA. But if A entails ¬EA then EA is inconsistent (since it entails A), so MEA is inconsistent, so by (*) A is inconsistent. Thus if A is consistent, it entails EA. But then MA entails MEA, and so A. Thus if A is possibly true, it is actually true. So no maximally specific propositions are contingently false. The argument does not immediately rule out contingently true maximally specific propositions, since although the fact that MA entails A means that M¬A entails M¬MA in a normal system, the anti-realist has already been seen to reject the Brouwerian inference from M¬MA to ¬A. In any case, the argument gives a sort of formal vindication to the widespread sense that the notion of a nonactual possible world is anti-realistically suspect. It does not follow, of course, that anti-realists should reject the use of formal possible worlds model theory in proving results about modal logic, for they can regard it as a purely algebraic device; a model ⟨W,R,V⟩ does not really assign truth-values to all propositions at each member of W, but only to those propositions expressible in the language (relative to an assignment of propositions to the propositional variables), and the set of all sentences of the object language true at a given world may not itself be equivalent to a single sentence of that language. What the anti-realist should not do is to regard the possible worlds semantics as having philosophically explanatory force—an independently plausible conclusion.

Theorem 5 opens the way to neighbourhood semantics in the sense of Segerberg [13] for some anti-realist systems. In fact, Kit Fine [personal communication] has used neighbourhood semantics to give an independent proof of the result that “KT”*C is a conservative extension of KT (of which Theorem 4 is an obvious corollary). Defining the degree of a formula as the degree of nesting of E in it (irrespective of occurrences of M), Fine constructs a sequence of neighbourhood models M(0),M(1),M(2),… such that each substitution instance of (*) of degree ≤n is true throughout M(n); a limit model M(∞) can then be constructed such that if A is of degree ≤n then A is true at a world in M(n) iff it is true at that world in M(∞). Since the part of M(0) which handles E-free wff can be any KT model, it follows that any consistent set of wff in KT has a “KT”* model; the neighborhood semantics automatically yields the substitution of equivalents for E.

Theorems 3 and 5 yield a choice between hyperintensional and merely intensional nontrivial anti-realist systems. This in turn suggests a choice between two kinds of explanation for the failure of E(p&q)→Ep from an anti-realist standpoint. On the hyperintensional view, exemplified by “KT”*, the principle fails because E is ‘too intensional’. For instance, its failure might be traced to the point that an answer to the question ‘Is it the case that p and q?’ is not explicitly an answer to the question ‘Is it the case that p?’ Here the emphasis is on occurrent linguistic or intellectual acts. On the alternative, merely intensional view, exemplified by “KT”*C, E(p&q)→Ep fails because E is ‘not intensional enough’. For instance, its failure might be traced to the possibility of a situation in which the information that p and q is accessible even though the information that p is not accessible, because the information that p and q is accessible only in a form in which it is not articulated as a conjunction, or as that conjunction; the consequence p becomes buried. Both the fine-grained and the coarse-grained alternatives seem to merit further investigation.
Two incomplete anti-realist modal epistemic logics

A particularly interesting version of the fine-grained explanation goes as follows (its fine-grainedness will emerge in the discussion); I owe it to Kit Fine. Suppose that cognition of whatever kind E represents comes in levels of increasing self-reflectiveness; such a hierarchy might be independently motivated by reference to epistemic cousins of the semantic paradoxes (cf. e.g. Burge [3] and [4]). What is cognized at a given level includes both what is cognized at a lower level and the results of reflection on that lower-level cognition. Cognition at a level i may be represented as Ei. It does satisfy the conjunction principle: we have Ei(p&q)→Eip for every level i. As just noted, we also have Eip→Ejp whenever i≤j. Moreover, we have an anti-realist axiom schema A↔MEiA at each level, where i is higher than the level of any operator which appears in A. The unsubscripted use of E can then be explained as context-relative, much as in some treatments of the epistemic paradoxes: the implicit level of E in the context EA is the lowest one higher than the level of any operator in A. An explanation for the failure of E(A&B)→EA is then forthcoming, since B may have operators of a higher level than any in A, so that A&B also does. In particular, if A contains no epistemic operators, E(A&¬EA)→EA will be understood as E2(A&¬E1A)→E1A, which can fail since although E2(A&¬E1A) yields E2A, E2A does not yield E1A. Just such a substitution in E(p&q)→Ep was used at (b) above to show its failure in nontrivial anti-realist systems.8

The use of propositional variables complicates the picture, since there is no limit to the level of the propositions which may be substituted for them. If they are assigned fixed numerical levels at all, then some propositional variable p will be assigned a level i no lower than that of some other propositional variable q, in which case E(p&q)→Ep will be read as Ei(p&q)→Eip and thus come out valid. Evidently, the requirement should be that an unsubscripted wff A is valid iff every subscription of it is valid, where a subscription of A is any wff which results from assigning arbitrary levels to the propositional variables and then subscripting each occurrence of E in A by the rule given in the previous paragraph (thus E(p&q)→(Ep∨Eq) should come out valid).

For in such a system S, if MA↔MB∈S, then by substitution of equivalents EMA↔EMB∈S, so by (**) A↔B∈S; but by T, M(Mp→p)↔M(p→p)∈S, so (Mp→p)↔(p→p)∈S, so Mp→p∈S. The use of the term ‘anti-realism’ for an epistemic conception of truth is loosely based on that of Michael Dummett (although the framework of classical logic is not Dummettian); his anti-realist with respect to the past claims, for example, that “The only notion of truth for past-tense statements which we could have acquired … is that which coincides with the justifiability of assertions of such statements” [5, p. 363]. The interpretation of (*) as an account of truth exploits the redundant truth operator, but this is not a problematic move for Dummett’s anti-realist [5, p. 234]. Of course, if E is interpreted as a nonepistemic operator then (*) does not express a form of anti-realism: a realist who thought that the actual world was the only possible one might assert (*), reading E as L or M. Such unintended readings can hardly be ruled out by formal means alone. Just as modal provability logics are ones which it is interesting but not compulsory to interpret in terms of provability, so anti-realist logics are ones which it is interesting but not compulsory to interpret in terms of anti-realism.

A weaker philosophical doctrine, perhaps associated with the verification principle of the logical positivists, characterizes what it is to have some truth value or other, rather than what it is to have a given truth value, in epistemic terms. It might be formalized analogously to (*) by the schema (p∨¬p)↔(MEp∨ME¬p). It can be modelled in any extension of KD by taking E as the redundant operator, but would be of more interest in the context of an intuitionist background logic. However, it may seem strange to give an epistemic account of a disjunction without offering epistemic accounts of its disjuncts. ↩︎
Double quotation marks are used to distinguish E-logics from the corresponding modal logics in a language without E; thus LEp→Ep is a thesis of “KT” but not of KT. ↩︎
One point where a restriction to intuitionist logic would make a difference is at (b) below, since the inference from ¬(p&¬Ep) to p→Ep is not intuitionistically valid (cf. [17]). ↩︎

Although Edgington does not discuss the converse principle ME@p→@p, it is presumably valid on the intended interpretation, since Ep→p yields ME@p→M@p and M@p→@p is valid in the logic of actuality. Thus she could assert @p↔ME@p. ↩︎
This frame has been extensively used by Hughes and Cresswell; cf. [9, Chapter 7]. Note that they use 0 rather than ⟨⟩ as the initial world, and allow it to be followed only by positive integers. ↩︎

The easiest such extension is one on which no constraints associated with E are imposed on frames, just as none were on models as defined above, in order not to jeopardize the required lemma that a finite distinguishable model for a normal system is based on a frame for that system. ↩︎
