works.title: Equivocation and existence
passages: In this paper I want to connect two much-disputed questions:
Is it possible for two groups to employ unequivocally conflicting logics?
Is it possible to have properties without existing?

The connection is roughly as follows. Two groups who answer ‘Yes’ and ‘No’ respectively to question (2) may at least seem to employ conflicting logics. For one group may say ‘It is a basic principle of logic that having properties entails existence, just as it is a basic principle of logic that identity entails having the same properties’, while the other group says ‘Since Madame Bovary and Lady Jane Grey have the property of being pitied, not to mention that of being self-identical, in spite of not (now) existing, it is not a principle of logic, basic or otherwise, that having properties entails existence’. In view of the controversy around question (1), we are obliged to ask whether this is really an unequivocal conflict: do both groups mean the same by the word ‘existence’? In a more cautious formulation: are they using it with the same extension but conflicting beliefs about what that extension contains, or are they using it with different extensions and perhaps no conflicting beliefs?

In section I a style of argument is sketched to show that at least some apparent conflicts of logic are real ones. This style of argument does not show the apparent conflict of logic over (2) to be real, and section III gives prima facie reasons to think that it is indeed merely apparent, so that there are senses of ‘existence’ in which it obeys the proposed logical principle and senses in which it does not. A pragmatic question then arises as to which of these ‘existence’ concepts is the most useful. If we use ‘existence’ in a sense obedient to the proposed logical principle, the style of argument from section I secures us from threats of further equivocation (section II), whereas if we use ‘existence’ in a sense not so obedient we lose that security. Section IV argues that we therefore have good reason to use ‘existence’ in the former sense, which allows us to raise basic questions of ontology in an unequivocal way. Some of the resultant disputes will be transpositions of disputes about (2)—these will not therefore have been anodynely dissolved—for purported counter-examples to the principle about ‘existence’ become purported examples of ‘existence’ in a sense which undisputedly obeys that principle (section V). Nevertheless, an unequivocal conflict of ontology may be an improvement on an equivocal conflict of logic.

If some principle strikes one as so compellingly obvious that one cannot imagine how it could reasonably be denied, and one interprets another person’s utterance as a denial of it, then one has a prima facie reason to believe that one’s interpretation may be wrong. Moreover, one’s basic principles of logic are likely to strike one as compellingly obvious in the relevant sense. So much is scarcely in dispute. More has been claimed, however: that the reason to doubt one’s interpretation is indefeasible, even that it is conclusive. Is it possible to have good reason to believe, all things considered, that someone is denying some of one’s basic logical principles? Even if it is not, is it possible that someone is denying some of one’s basic logical principles?1 This paper is concerned with the epistemological problem, not the ontological one. It is not concerned to ask what constitutes our convergent or divergent interpretations of the terms at issue (in virtue of what do we mean this rather than that by ‘exist’?). Rather it asks: what reason have the parties to an apparent conflict of logic to believe that they are not merely talking past each other, because of some equivocation, given their prima facie evidence to the contrary?

The case of negation can be used to illustrate a technique for arguing that an apparent conflict is a real one. Consider the difference between classical and intuitionist logic. The classical logician accepts the law of double negation elimination (DNE, that the negation of the negation of A entails A); the intuitionist logician rejects it. This dispute has often been said to turn on a divergence between their understandings of negation.2 The suggestion is that each is correct in their use of their own ‘negation’, so that one could have a language with two ‘negations’, one behaving classically and one intuitionistically (‘a fusion of horizons’?). It is not as well known as it should be that this suggestion is provably false. For two operators in the same language which obey the laws common to both classical and intuitionist ‘negation’ are provably equivalent, so that one obeys double negation elimination if and only if the other does; the dispute between classical and intuitionist logic is real, not merely verbal.3

It is worth going into a little more detail. The parties to the dispute need to know whether they are talking past each other when they seem to disagree about DNE. Can they agree on a characterization of negation (−) in terms which they are not equally likely to understand in different senses? For example, it would not help to define −A as A→⊥ (where ⊥ is an absurd proposition), since classical and intuitionist logicians are just as likely to diverge over their understandings of → as they are over their understandings of −. However, in both classical and intuitionist logic ‘negation’ obeys the laws of Reductio Ad Absurdum (RAA) and Ex Falso Quodlibet (EFQ). Why should they not agree to characterize negation as the operator which obeys RAA and EFQ? The immediate problem concerns uniqueness; perhaps several non-equivalent operators obey RAA and EFQ. That apparent possibility can be ruled out as follows. A monadic sentential operator O obeys RAA if and only if the following schema is valid, where X and Y are sets of assumptions and ⊢ is deducibility:
It obeys EFQ if and only if this schema is valid:

Now suppose that the operators O1 and O2 both obey RAA and EFQ. By EFQ for O1 we have A,O1A⊢A and A,O1A⊢O2A, so by RAA for O2 we have O1A⊢O2A; similarly, we have O2A⊢O1A. Thus O1 and O2 are equivalent (as a corollary, DNE for O1 is equivalent to DNE for O2). By agreeing to characterize negation (up to logical equivalence) as the operator which obeys RAA and EFQ, classical and intuitionist logicians can come to a principled rejection of the idea that they are talking past each other.

Of course, a sceptic might wonder whether both sides mean the same by the deducibility symbol ⊢, and indeed not every characterization that one of them made of it would be acceptable to the other. Strictly speaking, the arguments below do not require this doubt to be resolved, but it does seem to be expressive of desperation rather than insight. As a matter of fact, both classical and intuitionist logicians treat X⊢A as meaning that you are committed to A in making the set of assumptions X. It would otherwise be unclear that they could recognize each other as engaged in reasoning at all; to speak of classical and intuitionist logic would be to equivocate on the world ‘logic’. Suppose that there were distinct but equally legitimate ‘deducibility’ relations, one classical and one intuitionist, and that you discovered your beliefs to have a certain consequence in the sense of one but not in the sense of the other; should you accept that consequence or not? Or if the classical ‘deducibility’ relation were applicable only to ‘classical beliefs’ and the intuitionist one only to ‘intuitionist beliefs’, which would a conjunction of a ‘classical belief’ and an ‘intuitionist belief’ be? These are not promising lines of thought, and will be pursued no further here; ⊢ will provisionally be treated as unequivocal.
Two points do need to be noted.

(a) Even if we know just which inferences in a given language its speakers are prepared to accept, we cannot thereby conclusively determine just which inference schemata they are committed to, in the relevant sense of ‘schemata’. For a schema also has instances in extensions of their language; commitment to the schema requires them to accept these further instances. This notion of a schema was at work in the uniqueness proof; for example, EFQ for classical negation O1 was taken to have the instance A,O1A⊢O2A, where O2 is intuitionist negation, so that O2A is not a sentence of the original classical language. We certainly have dynamic commitments of this kind to inference schemata: my commitment to Modus Ponens is not simply a belief that the expressive powers of English are too limited to allow the formulation of a genuine counter-example. What does follow is that even if we come across speakers whose reasoning in their own language fits the schemata standardly associated with intuitionism, it remains at least a theoretical possibility that they are not committed to those schemata. However, this possibility is by no means untestable: behavioural dispositions bear on it just as they do on commitment to the infinitely many instances of a schema within a single language; it is just that the relevant exercises of them are displayed only when the language is enlarged. We can examine the dispositions of purported intuitionists and classical logicians: the uniqueness result is applicable to those who manifest commitment to EFQ and RAA.4

(b) What if classical logicians are mistaken in supposing EFQ and RAA to apply to their ‘negation’, or if intuitionists are making a similar mistake? The possibility seems a remote one, but two remarks on it are worth making. First, by definition it fails to rescue the claim that, properly interpreted, both parties are in the right. Second, it does not arise if the parties define negation (up to logical equivalence) as that operator which obeys EFQ and RAA—unless there is no such operator, which seems an even remoter possibility. Such stipulations will be at issue below.

The argument for the unequivocality of negation can be extended (given the use of classical or intuitionist logic) to the other standard logical constants, conjunction, disjunction, the material conditional, the quantifiers (indeed, one might regard the possibility of giving such an argument as a criterion of a logical constant). For present purposes the most relevant case is that of identity. Consider a dispute over, say, the identity of indiscernibles. Suppose that both parties accept the standard logical laws for identity: Reflexivity and Leibniz’s Law (the indiscernibility of identicals). Are they talking past each other, or do they mean the same by = or ‘is identical with’? They can agree to characterize identity (up to logical equivalence) as the (binary) reflexive relation which obeys Leibniz’s Law, if they can show that all reflexive relations which satisfy Leibniz’s Law are logically equivalent; but they can show this. For suppose that R1 and R2 are such relations. Thus we have ⊢∀xR2xx; Leibniz’s Law for R1 gives ⊢∀x∀y(R1xy→(R2xx→R2xy)), whence uncontroversial logic gives ⊢∀x∀y(R1xy→R2xy). We have ⊢∀x∀y(R2xy→R1xy) similarly, and thus ⊢∀x∀y(R1xy↔R2xy) (so the indiscernibility of x and y is sufficient for R1xy if and only if it is sufficient for R2xy).5 Given classical logic, identity disputes do not turn on equivocation in the sign for identity. Remarks parallel to (a) and (b) above again apply. Note how strained it would be in this case to claim that the dispute turns on an equivocation in ⊢.

Does the form of argument just exhibited apply to the concept of existence? On some views, I have already assumed a positive answer (for classical or intuitionist logic) by assuming that it applies to the quantifiers, for these views treat existence as a second-level concept to be identified with the existential quantifier. On the other views, there is a first-level concept of existence, but it is to be defined in terms of the existential quantifier by the formula ∃yx=y. However, it is unhelpful to take such views for granted when handling a dispute (over (2)) one party to which may hold that some things do not exist; for on that view, the quantifier ‘some’ has existential force only when implicitly or explicitly restricted to existing things. To be fair to such a view we can use quantifier-free formulae and a primitive existence predicate E!.6

What quantifier-free logical principles might govern E!? The obvious candidate is the principle queried in (2), that having properties entails existence. However, the concept of a property is too sensitive to metaphysical pressure to bear much weight in logic. Consider the similar case of Leibniz’s Law, which is sometimes formulated as the principle that identity entails having the same properties. On some views, a predicate does not stand for a property unless it ‘cuts nature at its joints’. Thus someone might claim not to be violating Leibniz’s Law in asserting that Cicero was Tully but Cicero was eloquent and Tully wasn’t, on the grounds that the line between eloquence and non-eloquence is not one of nature’s joints. Since we do not want Leibniz’s Law to be as toothless as that, we formulate it in terms of predicates rather than properties (where of course not every sentence involving ‘Cicero’ ascribes a predicate to him, as at least quotational contexts show). For similar reasons, what I shall call the Existence Principle (EP) is formulated in terms of predicates. It is the schema

where ‘t’ may be replaced by any singular term (closed or open) and ‘Ft’ by any subject-predicate formula with the corresponding subject term.7 If the existence predicate were defined in terms of the existential quantifier, EP would be equivalent (given the standard laws for identity) to the classical rule of Existential Introduction, a rule that some ‘Free Logics’ accept and others reject.8 Now if terms denoting no existent are allowed then E!t is not always a tautology (consider ‘God exists’), but if EP is not to make it one, the negation of E!t must not itself be of the form Ft, so that a distinction is required between sentential negation and predicate negation; t is not the subject term of every formula in which it appears. Such a distinction has been worked out in detail by Robert Stalnaker.9

Proponents of EP will deny that it is possible to have properties without existing; they will also deny that there are things which don’t exist, since they will infer ‘x exists’ from ‘x is a thing’. Conversely, opponents of EP hold that at least in some cases it is logically possible for t to be F without existing. Those who are prepared to quantify over a domain of things which is large enough to include t will allow a good (non-substitutional) sense in which something can be F without existing. Those who are prepared to quantify over a domain of properties which is large enough to include that of being F will allow a good (non-substitutional) sense in which t can have a property without existing. Those who are prepared to do both will allow a good sense in which something can have a property without existing.

Now consider an ontological dispute between two proponents of EP, in particular, an ontological dispute of the kind which can be expressed by means of a singular term. For example, one of them says ‘The number 7 exists’ or ‘God exists’, the other ‘It is not the case that the number 7 exists’ or ‘It is not the case that God exists’. Have they good reason to believe that they are not talking past each other, by equivocating on the word ‘exists’? Following the pattern of the previous section, one can argue that they have. For let the ‘existence’ predicates of the two be F1 and F2, and suppose that each is right in supposing his or her own ‘existence’ predicate to obey EP. Then since F1 obeys EP, we have F2t⊢F1t, and since F2 obeys it, we have F1t⊢F2t; thus the two ‘existence’ predicates are logically equivalent.10 Furthermore the argument shows that (up to logical equivalence) at most one predicate obeys EP; thus both parties can agree to define the ‘existence’ predicate as that which obeys EP, so neither need doubt that the other’s ‘existence’ predicate as so defined obeys EP. Note how strained it would be in this case, as in the earlier ones, to claim that there must be an equivocation on ⊢. In brief, for its proponents EP grounds a common understanding of ‘existence’ and permits genuine disagreement about what exists, just as Leibniz’s Law (with Reflexivity) grounds a common understanding of ‘identity’ and permits genuine disagreement about what is identical with what.

Consider a dispute between a proponent and an opponent of EP, either about EP itself or about some specific issue of ontology. Have they good reason to believe that they are not talking past each other, by equivocating on the word ‘exists’? They certainly do not have the reason that the two proponents of EP had, for they cannot agree to define the ‘existence’ predicate as that which obeys EP. At the same time, they have a stronger reason than any in the previous case to believe that they are equivocating, since their beliefs about the logic of ‘exists’ are surely more fundamental to their understanding of it than are their beliefs about its extension (at least so far as concerns non-paradigmatic cases such as God and the number 7—oneself and the earth may be another matter).

It need hardly be added that there are indeed both proponents and opponents of EP, whether or not it is really with respect to the same predicate. Speaking for myself, I maintain that my ‘existence’ predicate obeys EP. Terence Parsons and Nathan Salmon, for example, would maintain that their ‘existence’ predicate or predicates does or do not obey EP.11 Moreover, enough technical work has been done on both sides to make it clear that both views can be made formally self-consistent. At least the appearance, if not the reality, of a dispute is real.

Is what one party asserts really what the other denies? Both are likely to claim that they are using their words—in particular, the word ‘exist’—in their everyday senses; but even if no unconscious philosophically motivated semantic change has occurred, the word ‘exist’ may have more than one everyday sense; these senses may vary in relative salience from one idiolect to another. It is certainly not clear that ordinary usage returns unequivocal answers to questions such as (2). For part of what needs to be explained is how some intelligent people can find it a blindingly obvious piece of common sense that what doesn’t exist just isn’t there to have properties, while others can find it a blindingly obvious piece of common sense that the dead have the property of being dead and therefore don’t exist, or that fictional characters have the property of being fictional characters and therefore don’t exist. We can be sure that ‘exist’ will not turn out to have two wholly unrelated senses, in the way that ‘bank’ has, but may it not turn out to have senses as different as those of ‘true’ in ‘true statement’ and ‘true friend’?

It would be implausible as well as depressing to suppose that it is the rule rather than the exception for a philosophical dispute to turn on mutual misunderstanding. If the misunderstandings were accidental, philosophy would be less difficult than it actually is; if essential, it would satisfy a kind of incommensurability thesis whose applications elsewhere are increasingly discredited. However, we have already seen that there is a widely applicable method of arguing that a philosophical dispute does not turn on mutual misunderstanding; the rules of the game have not been rigged in advance to favour the opposite claim. The question is what, if anything, can replace that method in cases, such as the present one, where it does not apply. If we can find no replacement, any remaining belief in the non-equivocality of the dispute over EP would be little better than blind faith: for although there may well be an initial presumption that we mean the same by same-sounding words, a given instance of such a presumption hardly deserves to survive the failure to find evidence in its favour, if we have looked in earnest.

It should be remembered, in assessing evidence for and against the homophonic translation of ‘exist’, that our situation is not that of the radical interpreter, who initially lacks all semantic knowledge of the alien language with which he or she is faced. Philosophical disputes are conducted against the background of a shared natural language, or at least, this one is. We have been given, not a general reason for doubting that we ever understand what others say, but a particular reason for doubting that our present interpretation of certain key words in a philosophical dispute is that which our interlocutor intends. To resolve such a doubt, we need a way of fixing the interpretation of those words in terms of that very large part of the background language whose interpretation is not, for present purposes, in doubt; there is no question of trying to rule out the sceptical possibility that our interlocutor’s interpretation of every expression of our apparently common language is wholly other than ours. At the same time, it will not suffice merely to define a key word in terms of an accepted synonym (‘to exist’ means to be) or other expressions so closely tied to the key word that any divergence in its interpretation is likely to extend to a divergence in theirs. This criterion is clearly not a precise one, but that is only to be expected, for the task is to assess the plausibility of a perfectly genuine doubt (do we mean the same by ‘exist’?) -not to exclude definitively the hyperbolical doubts of an hypothetical sceptic—and plausibility is not a precise matter.

It does not seem likely that the proponent and the opponent of EP will share other assumptions about the logic of ‘exist’ of a kind that would allow them to agree on a unique characterization of it (up to logical equivalence) in terms of its logical properties. In particular, it has already been seen that an attempt to define ‘exists’ in terms of the existential quantifier would be unlikely to help, since the opponent of EP would probably need to use ‘exists’ or the equivalent in specifying the appropriate domain of quantification. Nor does semantic ascent seem to help: for example, few opponents of EP will be prepared to accept that ‘t exists’ is true if and only if ‘t’ designates, unless ‘designates’ is understood as ‘designates an existent’. The two parties might try to test for equivocation in the way that one does for non-logical predicates. For instance, they might try to give each other examples of things that satisfy the predicate ‘exists’ (‘To exist is to do what that stone is doing’). However, even if this method does not fail through fortuitous differences in ontology, the opponents of EP will be compelled also to give examples of things that do not satisfy the predicate ‘exists’, in order to distinguish it from what they conceive to be less restrictive predicates such as ‘is a thing’ and ‘is self-identical’; but the proponents of EP will view this attempt to point out particular things that do not satisfy ‘exists’ precisely as good evidence that the term is being used in a different sense.

For both parties, the doubt as to whether the dispute might turn on an equivocation must remain a somewhat abstract one, until they can find a non-homophonic translation of the other’s use of ‘exists’ into their own terms, a translation that makes better sense of what the other is saying and perhaps even wholly dispels the appearance of disagreement. Such translations would both confirm the doubt and enable something to be done about it. For instance, the opponent of EP may well be able to translate the proponent’s use of ‘exists’ by ‘is an object’ or by ‘is self-identical’.12 On such a translation, EP says that a subject of predicates is an object, or that it is self-identical, or something of the kind: principles whose acceptance by the proponent of EP its original opponent need have no difficulty in understanding and may even share. The converse translation is harder, since the diversity of ways of rejecting EP produces a corresponding diversity of translations. In some cases, the proponent of EP may well be able to translate the opponent’s use of ‘exists’ by ‘is causally efficacious’ or ‘has spatio-temporal location’. On such a translation, EP says that a subject of predicates is causally efficacious, or that it has spatio-temporal location, or something of the kind: principles whose rejection by the opponent of EP its original proponent need have no difficulty in understanding and may even share. There will be subtler cases too: an opponent of EP may hold that while both the null set and the person who would have resulted from the union of this sperm and this egg have the property of self-identity, the former ‘exists’ but the latter does not, perhaps because the latter contingently lacks causal efficacy or spatio-temporal location. Further exploration of such a philosopher’s position might suggest a more complex translation scheme for this case. In general, which scheme works, if any, will depend on which proponents and which opponents of EP are in question. Nevertheless, even in their crude state, the non-homophonic schemes promise to enable each party to make more sense of what the other is saying than do their homophonic alternatives. In so doing, they already constitute an argument in favour of the view that what seemed to be a stark clash of intuitions was not what it seemed.

In the worst case, we have a proponent and an opponent of EP at least one of whom cannot find a satisfactory non-homophonic translation of the other’s use of ‘exists’. It still does not follow that the homophonic translation is correct, nor even that it should provisionally be assumed to be correct. For it is perfectly possible that the proponent does not mean by any expression what the opponent means by ‘exists’, and/or that the opponent does not mean by any expression what the proponent means by ‘exists’. Moreover, in such circumstances it could still be fruitful—more fruitful than to persist with the homophonic scheme—for both parties to think of the opponent’s use of ‘exists’ as more restrictive than the proponent’s. That is, if E!p is the proponent’s ‘existence’ predicate and E!o is the opponent’s, it might be agreed that the truth of E!pt is necessary but not sufficient for the truth of E!ot. It would not, of course, follow that the proponent’s acceptance of E!pt is necessary but not sufficient for the opponent’s acceptance of E!ot. For the proponent might reject E!pt, and therefore E!ot, in a particular case where the opponent accepted E!ot, and therefore E!pt, because of some adventitious ontological dispute between them, independent of EP (for example, ‘t’ might be ‘God’, the proponent an atheist and the opponent a theist). To return to the argument, if we have E!ot⊢E!pt without E!pt⊢E!ot, it is at least a live possibility that we have Ft⊢E!pt without Ft⊢E!ot, and thus that the proponents are right that E!p obeys EP while the opponents are right that E!o does not. In any case, the argument for the equivocality thesis need not show both parties to be right: it need only show them both to be intelligible.

In this section I have sketched a case for the claim that parties to a dispute over EP are characteristically using ‘exists’ in different and non-equivalent senses. I take the case to be not decisive, but promising.13

Suppose that the argument of the previous section is correct in the most satisfying way: not only does the sense in which proponents of EP use ‘exists’ differ from the sense in which opponents use it, but the former sense makes EP valid and the latter makes it invalid. Is the dispute over EP therefore a purely verbal one, to be determined by considerations of stylistic convenience? It must be remembered that the situation is not perfectly symmetrical. We have already seen that two proponents of EP (for their own use of ‘exists’) have good reason to believe themselves to mean the same by ‘exists’; in contrast, two opponents of EP (for their own use of ‘exists’) have no such reason to believe themselves to mean the same by ‘exists’. Roughly speaking, there is only one sense of ‘exists’ in which it obeys EP, but many in which it does not. Thus agreement to use ‘exists’ in a sense obedient to EP, unlike agreement to use it in a sense disobedient to EP, provides a background against which parties to the agreement can go on to discuss their disagreements on fundamental issues of ontology without threat of equivocation on the word ‘exists’. The latter agreement cannot defuse the threat of equivocation constituted by such fundamental disagreements. Call those who accept EP for their own use of ‘exists’ EPers, and those who reject it non-EPers. Although non-EPers do not have disagreement over EP itself as an additional reason to fear equivocation amongst themselves, some of the arguments of the previous section apply, as obstacles to their attempts to defuse the threat of equivocation when they disagree with each other on fundamental issues of ontology.

Suppose that one non-EPer says ‘To exist it is necessary and sufficient to cause or to be caused’ while another says ‘To exist it is necessary and sufficient to perceive or to be perceived’; what reason have they to think that they mean the same by ‘exists’? Disagreement over the satisfaction conditions for a predicate does not automatically overturn the initial presumption that members of a speech community mean the same by it, of course, but this initial presumption is a feeble thing indeed if it can survive critical reflection only by default. It may be reasonable for non-EPers to believe, prior to seeking evidence, that they mean the same by ‘exists’, but it does not follow that this belief remains reasonable for them after they have tried and failed to find evidence for it (should they therefore refuse to look?). Perhaps the non-EPers will be able to confirm the belief by discovering substantive agreement amongst themselves as to the extension of ‘exists’. The trouble with this method is that, to the extent that it rules out the possibility of equivocation, it does so by limiting the room for ontological disagreement. In this sense, the question ‘What exists?’ may be a more radical one for EPers than for non-EPers, since the former can agree on its sense (by means of EP) without making non-logical assumptions as to its answer.

One might therefore ask, what is the most metaphysically interesting sense of ‘exists’? The non-EPer Terence Parsons raises the question ‘Why Should anyone Care Whether God Exists?’ and finds no reason why someone should care whether the God whom they worship is an ‘existent’ or a ‘non-existent’ God; one is reminded of the line that Robert Nozick quotes, ‘God is so perfect he doesn’t need to exist’.14 A notion of ‘non-existence’ with so little impact on a thing’s other properties is not of much metaphysical interest. No doubt many non-EPers would avoid such extravagances. Nevertheless, it seems to me that the deepest notion of ‘non-existence’, because the most radical, is the EPers’ one, on which if it is not the case that God exists then it is not the case that God has any kind of property whatsoever (not that of being worshipped, nor that of being God, nor even that of being self-identical), and thus not the case that God has any kind of being at all, however exiguous. It is also the notion that makes the prospect of one’s own death—as the end of one’s existence—most vertiginously absolute.

In the remainder of this essay the word ‘existence’ will be used in the postulated sense in which it obeys EP, and which the non-EPer may take to be something like that of self-identity. This terminological readjustment is far from dissolving all the philosophical problems. For the non-EPer’s characteristic arguments can be reinterpreted as attempts, not to refute EP, but to exhibit by its means the bizarre variety of existents in the EPer’s sense. It is a matter of no great import whether the non-EPer’s intention is to discourage the EPer from so using the word ‘existence’; the point is that when the EPer asks ‘What exists?’ a genuine metaphysical question is being raised, to which the non-EPer’s arguments indicate substantive and surprising answers. The EPer’s characteristic (but not compulsory) response is to argue that EP does not have the consequences the non-EPer claims it to have.

Consider, for example, the argument ‘Casanova is famous, therefore Casanova exists’. It seems to be a straightforward application of EP, yet to hold out hope for, quite literally, survival after death. Since both premiss and conclusion are to be read as present-tensed, someone might propose to restrict EP to eternal sentences. That sounds ad hoc, and does not seem to go to the heart of the problem (it does not help with the intuitively similar argument ‘Vulcan is famous, therefore Vulcan exists’, where ‘Vulcan’ may purport to name either a god or a planet). Nor is the premiss simply to be denied; there is a perfectly good sense in which it does not just seem to be the case that Casanova is famous, but is the case. Furthermore, ‘Casanova is famous’ has every appearance of being a subject-predicate sentence with ‘Casanova’ as its subject term. Must one therefore conclude that EP leads to a pathetically etiolated concept of existence, on which Casanova does still exist, perhaps only in virtue of being self-identical? At this point the EPer may reply with an analysis of ‘Casanova is famous’ on which its logical form is not what its surface form suggests (a supporting argument: ‘Rogue elephants are famous’ does not entail ‘At least one rogue elephant is famous’). For instance, it may be proposed that the ‘logical subject’ of ‘Casanova is famous’ is not Casanova himself but a certain property which only he could instantiate, but which can exist even when he does not; the claim will not of course be that this property is itself famous—for it is indeed deeply obscure—but rather that it has an as yet unspecified second-order property of, as one might say, bearing fame.

The argument cannot be pursued here. Instead, I want to give a final application of the ideas about non-equivocality from section I. Much of the controversy over EP concerns apparently relational expressions such as ‘seeks’, ‘envies’ and ‘worships’. Is ‘Cecil envies Casanova, therefore Casanova exists’ an instance of EP? For purposes of argument I am quite prepared to accept that these transitive verbs really are relational expressions. A further question remains: does EP license inferences of the form Rst⊢E!t? Can Rst be bracketed as (Rs)t and Rs treated as an instance of F?

It is technically possible to give a negative answer. I have already appealed to Stalnaker’s predicate notation in regimenting for EP; it allows one to draw a sharp line between instances of Ft and instances of Rst. To obtain a substitution instance of Ft one must substitute a monadic predicate for F, and the only complex monadic predicates in his notation have the form x̂ø, where x is a variable, ˆ a special variable-binding device and ø a formula. Thus the nearest substitution instances of Ft to Rst is x̂(Rsx)t, which one might read as: t is such that s is R to it. Intuitively, the idea is that a syntactically non-ambiguous sentence cannot be an instance of both Ft and Rst because instances of the former have exactly two immediate constituents while instances of the latter have exactly three. (An anti-instrumentalist line on syntax therefore seems to be required.) Now x̂(Rsx)t⊢E!t is a special case of EP, since x̂(Rsx) is an instance of F. In order to derive Rst⊢E!t, it would therefore be enough to have Rst⊢x̂(Rsx)t. This is a special case of Abstraction: the inference from ø to x̂ø′t, where ø′ results from replacing occurrences of t in ø by x, subject to the usual constraints about variable-binding. Abstraction is not a universally valid rule: it fails for quotational contexts, for example (‘Kinnock’ contains seven letters, but Kinnock is not such that ‘he’ contains seven letters). More interestingly, its rejection has already been suggested for negative formulae, in order to block the inference from −E!t (‘It is not the case that Casanova exists’) to E!t (‘Casanova exists’), for x̂(−E!x)t (‘Casanova is such that he does not exist’) entails E!t by EP, so −E!t had better not entail x̂(−E!x)t. An EPer might reject Abstraction for relational as well as negative formulae, and thus block unwanted arguments involving transitive verbs (presumably, −Ft and Rst would still entail x̂(−Fx)t and x̂(Rsx)t respectively in the presence of the extra existential premiss E!t, but that premiss is just the conclusion desired in the present case).15
It is thus possible consistently to accept EP while rejecting the following generalization of it, which will be called EP+:

(R is an n-adic predicate). On the other hand, it is possible consistently to accept EP+; there are other ways of blocking the unwanted arguments involving transitive verbs (for instance, an extension of the technique alluded to in connection with ‘Casanova is famous’). Now consider two logicians, one of whom accepts EP+ and therefore EP and the other of whom accepts EP but rejects EP+. Does their dispute turn on equivocation over the ‘existence’ predicate? It does not. For an earlier argument showed that any two predicates which obey EP are logically equivalent, so that one obeys EP+ if and only if the other does. To at least this extent the dispute is genuine: our two logicians cannot both be right.

Baruch Brody, Peter Carruthers, Graeme Forbes, Richard Grandy, Eli Hirsch, Lloyd Humberstone, William Lyons, Adam Morton, Norton Nelkin and Nathan Salmon have helped me with comments on earlier versions of these ideas. I have not had space to respond to all their points.

Two standard references: W. V. O. Quine, The Philosophy of Logic (Englewood Cliffs, N.J.: Prentice-Hall, 1970): 80–9; A. Morton, ‘Denying the Doctrine and Changing the Subject’, Journal of Philosophy 70 (1973): 503–11. ↩︎
Mappings between intuitionistic logic and the modal system S4 are often invoked at this point. ↩︎

Cf. J. H. Harris, ‘What’s So Logical about the “Logical” Axioms?’, Studia Logica 41 (1982): 159–71 (where the result is also proved for other standard logical constants). The main idea goes back to N. D. Belnap, ‘Tonk, Plonk and Plink’, Analysis 22 (1962): 130–4, reprinted in P. F. Strawson (ed.), Philosophical Logic (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1967): 132–7; he credits it to H. Hiz. It is discussed in W. D. Hart, ‘Prior and Belnap’, Theoria 48 (1982): 127–38, and I. L. Humberstone, ‘Unique Characterization of Connectives’ (abstract), Journal of Symbolic Logic 49 (1984): 1426–7; cp. also T. J. Smiley, ‘The Independence of Connectives’, Journal of Symbolic Logic 27 (1962): 426–35. ↩︎

In some respects an open-ended schema is more like a sentence with an initial second-order universal quantifier than a first-order schema restricted to instances in a single language. However, there is no analogy to the application of sentential operators to schema, or to second-order existential quantification. ↩︎

The argument can be found in W. V. Quine, ‘Reply to Professor Marcus’, Synthese 13 (1961): 323–30, reprinted in The Ways of Paradox (New York: Random House, 1966): 175–82, and The Philosophy of Logic (op. cit.): 62–3. G. H. Merrill, ‘On the Uniqueness of the Identity Relation’, Analysis 39 (1979): 133–6, replying to Quine, ignores the possibility that speakers can be committed to a version of Leibniz’s Law whose instances are not confined to their own language (cp. (a) above), but so do many of Quine’s writings on identity and indiscernibility. Note that (contra Hart, op. cit.) this uniqueness property is weaker than implicit definability in the sense of Beth. For if identity were implicitly definable in terms of the rest of the vocabulary in a first-order language, it would be explicitly definable (by Beth’s Theorem), which in general it is not. The difference comes about as follows. Where R is a binary predicate, let X(R,L) be the set of sentences which contains exactly ∀xRxx and every instance of Leibniz’s Law (with R in place of identity) for the language L. Let L1, L2 and L1,2 be the results of adding the sets of binary predicates {R1}, {R2} and {R1,R2} respectively to a language L. Then the uniqueness property in the text is that X(R1,L1,2),X(R2,L1,2)⊢∀x∀y(R1xy↔R2xy), whereas implicit definability requires that X(R1,L1),X(R2,L2)⊢∀x∀y(R1xy↔R2xy). The same difference arises for the ancestral of a relation, which can be uniquely characterized but not implicitly defined by a first-order schema. ↩︎

Cf. e.g. G. E. Moore, ‘Is Existence a Predicate?’, Aristotelian Society supplementary volume 15 (1936): 175–88, J. L. Mackie, ‘The Riddle of Existence’, Aristotelian Society supplementary volume 50 (1976): 247–67, S. L. Read, ‘“Exists” is a Predicate’, Mind 89 (1980): 412–7, E. Bencivenga, ‘Again on Existence as a Predicate’, Philosophical Studies 37 (1980): 125–38, C. J. F. Williams, What is Existence? (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1981), B. Miller, ‘Negative Existential Propositions’, and C. J. F. Williams, ‘Reply to Miller’, Analysis 42 (1982): 181–8 and 189–90 respectively. ↩︎

For a technical study cf. K. Fine, ‘Model Theory for Modal Logic—Part III: Existence and Predication’, Journal of Philosophical Logic 10 (1981): 293–307, where something virtually equivalent to the Principle is called the Falsehood Principle. It is discussed in G. Forbes, The Metaphysics of Modality (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1985). In ‘Free and Classical counterparts: response to Lewis’, Analysis 47 (1987): 147–52, Forbes seems to deny in effect that EP is logically valid, on the grounds that it is philosophically controversial: but could not the same be said of the Law of Excluded Middle? I formulate EP in this way in order to emphasize that its applicability to a language does not require the presence of any other logical constants. It is intended to be at least as strong as ⊢□∀x□(Fx→E!x) on most interpretations. For other recent discussion, see many of the essays in R. Haller (ed.), Non-existence and Predication, i.e. Grazer Philosophische Studien 25/26 (1985/6). ↩︎
For an informal introduction to the subject of Free Logic cf. K. Lambert, ‘On the Philosophical Foundation of Free Logic’, Inquiry 24 (1981): 147–203. ↩︎

I assume that F1t⊣⊢F2t yields the intersubstitutability of F1t and F2t in modal contexts. Thus A⊢B will require the truth of A to be sufficient for the truth of B in all worlds, not just the actual world, otherwise (as Lloyd Humberstone points out) one might have E!t⊣⊢@E!t without ⊢□(E!t↔@E!t), where @ is the ‘actually’ operator. ↩︎
T. Parsons, Nonexistent Objects (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1980); N. U. Salmon, ‘Existence’ (forthcoming). ↩︎

The most that is being claimed for the translation, in this and subsequent cases, is logical equivalence (‘mean the same’ will henceforth be used in that sense). Thus it would not be enough for the opponents of EP to object that ‘exists’ and ‘is self-identical’ (a predicate I assume both parties to use in the same sense) are not intuitively synonymous; a reason would have to be given for thinking that they are not logically equivalent. ↩︎

Meinong is an interesting case in point. Standardly translated, his view is that Trafalgar Square has existence, a geometrical square has subsistence but not existence, and the round square has neither. Which of these notions is closer to what you mean by ‘existence’? Cp. K. Lambert, Meinong and the Principle of Independence (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1983): 13–15. ↩︎
Parsons, op. cit.: 212–7 (compare 217–9 on ‘Might I Be a Nonexistent Object?’). The line quoted by Nozick is at Philosophical Explanations (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1981): 125. ↩︎

Note that the equivalence of the EPer’s concept of existence with the concept of self-identity (x̂(x=x)) requires only the equivalence of E!t with x̂(x=x)t, not with t=t; when Abstraction is rejected, t=t may not entail x̂(x=x)t. ↩︎

works.title: Bivalence and subjunctive conditionals
passages: ABSTRACT. Writers such as Stalnaker and Dummett have argued that specific features of subjunctive conditional statements undermine the principle of bivalence. This paper is concerned with rebutting such claims. 1. It is shown how subjective conditionals pose a prima facie threat to bivalence, and how this threat can be dissolved by a distinction between the results of negating a subjective conditional and of negating its consequent. To make this distinction is to side with Lewis against Stalnaker in a dispute about possible worlds semantics for such conditionals, and reasons are given for doing so. 2. These arguments are extended to answer Dummett’s claim that behaviourist and phenomenalist analyses in terms of subjunctive conditions violate bivalence. This answer is shown to be compatible with the principle that hypothetical statements are true only in virtue of categorical facts.

Robert Stalnaker has argued that subjunctive conditional statements violate the principle of bivalence, which says that, of necessity, every well-defined statement is either true or false. In a different way, Michael Dummett has argued that certain statements, analyzed in terms of subjunctive conditionals, violate bivalence. This paper aims to show how, if we are careful to negate subjunctive conditionals correctly, we can answer both arguments.

Had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, would it have been gold? Apparently, to answer “Yes” is to say that had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, it would have been gold; to answer “No” is to say that had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, it would not have been gold (and therefore would have been silver). Not only have we no reason to say either of these things, but it is hard to take seriously the supposition that one or other of them is, unbeknownst to us, true. Can subjunctive conditionals then fail to be either true or false, thereby falsifying the principle of bivalence?

There is an obvious way of dealing with this threat, as follows. The answer “Yes” to the original question is obviously unacceptable. To answer “no” is to deny that, had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, it would have been gold. That is to assert that it is not the case that, had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, it would have been gold. The argument does not require that there be a more idiomatic reformulation of this rather cumbersome assertion, but if one is required, a good candidate would be the assertion that, had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, it might not have been gold. However, none of this is to assert that, had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, it would not have been gold. For there is no reason why negating a subjunctive conditional should be equivalent to negating its consequent, although it is plausible that it is equivalent to changing “would” to “might” and then negating the consequent. We can also, of course, assert the triviality that, had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, it would have been either gold or not gold – for there is no reason why this conditional with a disjunctive consequent should entail the disjunction of unattractive conditionals, that either had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, it would have been gold or had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, it would not have been gold. Of these assertions, only the one to which the answer “No” does not commit us (had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, it would have been gold) is unacceptable. Hence we can reasonably answer “No”. But if it is not the case that had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere it would have been gold, then the statement “Had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, it would have been gold” is false; since it is false, it is bivalent. In other words, the apparent threat to the principle of bivalence is diagnosed as resulting from a confusion between the scopes of negation and subjunctive conditional operator.

Such a treatment is suggested by the work of David Lewis on counterfactuals.1 Stalnaker has championed a rival view on which the above treatment would fail. Before we examine the bearing of their debate on the issue of bivalence, however, it is worth formalizing the original dilemma; for in doing so we shall uncover an unexpectedly elaborate network of assumptions about subjunctive conditionals that are of use in subsequent discussion.

Let us write the subjunctive conditional with antecedent P and consequent Q as P□→Q. ‘−’, ‘∨’ and ‘&’ are negation, disjunction and conjunction respectively. G is the statement that there is nothing but a gold sphere, S the statement that there is nothing but a silver sphere. Thus the queried statement is (G∨S)□→G. What needs to be explained first is why we find each of (G∨S)□→G and (G∨S)□→−G a silly supposition. Clearly, it is crucial that we regard the case as being symmetrical between G and S; not only do we know of no reason why the solitary sphere should be gold rather than silver or vice versa, we believe that there is no reason to be known. In other words, we take the actual world to be neutral between G and S. This assumption can be formulated as follows. Let A be any statement made up entirely of G, S and the above logical operators, and let A(G//S) be the result of interchanging G and S throughout A (for example, if A is (G∨S)□→G, then A(G//S) is (S∨G)□→S). Then we can endorse the following schema:
A is true (in the actual world) if and only if A(G//S) is true (in the actual world).

This symmetry does not yield a dilemma unless G and S are incompatible, for otherwise the supposition that the solitary sphere would be gold would not entail that it would not be silver, and thus would not produce an asymmetric preference for gold over silver. Thus we assume:

Finally, the antecedent of the supposition – that there is nothing but a gold or silver sphere – must be possible, otherwise its impossibility would be a sufficient explanation of our unhappiness with both (G∨S)□→G and (G∨S)□→−G. So we assume:

If the reader is not convinced of (a)–(c), there are several classic and less far-fetched examples which can plausibly be taken to have the same structure, to which the argument below can be applied. For example, Goodman uses “Jones is in South Carolina” and “Jones is in North Carolina” in place of G and S.2 Similarly, Lewis considers “If Bizet and Verdi were compatriots, Bizet would be Italian”; thus we could take G as “Bizet and Verdi are both Italian” and S as “Bizet and Verdi are both French”.3

In order to construct a plausible argument from (a)–(c) to the conclusion that neither (G∨S)□→G nor (G∨S)□→−G is true, the following elementary assumptions about the logic of subjunctive conditionals are required. We state the schemata informally in order to avoid irrelevant commitment to particular formal systems.
If Q1,…,Qn logically entail R, then P□→Q1,…,P□→Qn logically entail P□→R.
If P and Q are logically equivalent, then P□→R and Q□→R are logically equivalent.
If P□→Q is true and P is possible, then Q is possible.

(I)–(IV) all seem to be intuitively persuasive, and the corresponding formal inference rules are certainly validated by various standard semantics for counterfactuals and modal operators.4 (I)–(III) could all be restricted to the case when the antecedent P is possible, but there is no obvious reason to do so.

We can now argue that (G∨S)□→G is not true, as follows. Suppose, for a contradiction, that (G∨S)□→G is true. Then, by (a), (S∨G)□→S is also true. Hence, by (II), (G∨S)□→S is true. Thus, by (I), (G∨S)□→(G&S) is true. (IV) then requires that if G∨S is possible, so is G&S, which contradicts (b) and (c). Then (G∨S)□→G is not true. By symmetrical reasoning, (G∨S)□→S is not true. Furthermore, suppose for a contradiction that (G∨S)□→−G is true. By (III), (G∨S)□→(G∨S) is true. By (I), (G∨S)□→S is therefore true (for −G and G∨S entail S); but we have already seen that is is not. Thus (G∨S)□→−G is not true either. By symmetrical reasoning, (G∨S)□→−S is not true. Note that all of (a)–(c) and (I)–(IV) were used in this reasoning.

By the previous paragraph, none of the statements (G∨S)□→G, (G∨S)□→S, (G∨S)□→−G and (G∨S)□→−S is true. Thus, for the defender of bivalence, all four are false. For them, the following assertions are therefore true: −((G∨S)□→G), −((G∨S)□→S), −((G∨S)□→−G) and −((G∨S)□→−S). This is precisely to formalize the treatment of the case informally proposed at the beginning. The scope of the negations is obviously crucial, since if −((G∨S)□→G) entailed (G∨S)□→−G, the treatment would involve a contradiction. Note also that (G∨S)□→(G∨−G) and (G∨S)□→(S∨−S) can be unproblematically asserted; indeed, they can be shown to be true on the basis of (I) and (III) given classical logic.

These considerations can also be modeled within Lewis’s possible worlds semantics for counterfactuals.5 Roughly speaking, when P is possible Lewis defines P□→Q to be true at a world w if and only if P&Q is true at a world w′ such that P&−Q is not true at any world which is as similar to w as w′ is. It follows that −(P□→Q) and P□→−Q are by no means equivalent. If the most similar worlds to w at which P is true include some at which Q is true and some at which it is not, or if for every world at which P&Q is true there is a world more similar to W at which P&−Q is true and vice versa, then −(P□→Q) will be true and P□→−Q false at w; either of these cases could be used to model the symmetry of G and S (taking P as G∨S and Q as G). Lewis treats the remaining case of a counterfactual with an impossible antecedent as vacuously true, so in this case too −(P□→Q) and P□→−Q are not equivalent: the former is false and the latter true. Note also that any counterfactual of the form P□→(Q∨−Q) will be trivially true. Finally, it is not hard to check that Lewis’s semantics validates all of (I)–(IV), when they are formulated in the obvious way.

So far, everything has run smoothly for the defender of bivalence. However, Stalnaker has criticized Lewis’s system on precisely the point which is being used to defend bivalence, the distinction between −(P□→Q) and P□→−Q; Stalnaker argues that “the normal way to contradict a counterfactual is to contradict the consequent, keeping the same antecedent”.6 His argument turns not on any technical feature of Lewis’s system but on the sheer appearance of contradiction in saying things like “Had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, it would have been either gold or not gold, but it is not the case that, had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, it would have been gold, nor is it the case that, had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, it would not have been gold”. Lewis himself admits that there is an appearance of contradiction.7

Stalnaker’s possible worlds semantics for counterfactuals virtually obliterates the distinction between −(P□→Q) and P□→−Q; it is the main point on which he differs from Lewis, and – unfortunately for the defender of bivalence – it is one on which Stalnaker seems to be closer to our ordinary use of language. Technically, Stalnaker makes P□→Q true at a world w if and only if Q is true at f(P,w), which can be thought of as the most similar world to w at which P is true.8 −(P□→Q) and P□→−Q are equivalent because each is true at w if and only if Q is false at f(P,w). There is just one exception – if P is true at no world, Stalnaker takes f(P,w) as an “absurd world” at which every statement is true; thus (Q&−Q)□→Q and (Q&−Q)□→−Q are both true, and therefore are not contradictories.9 We could, however, just as easily stipulate that if P is impossible, f(P,w) is w itself. We have no firm intuitions about counterfactuals with impossible antecedents for this to violate, and it would make −(P□→Q) and P□→−Q equivalent in all cases.

Not only would Stalnaker’s semantics render self-contradictory the way of defending bivalence which we have suggested: it poses a direct threat to bivalence itself. This comes about as follows. It is not very plausible to assume that for every statement P and possible world w there is a unique world which is the most similar to w at which P is true; for example, the assumption seems to fail when P is G∨S and w is the actual world: if there is a world which is the most similar to the actual world of those in which there is nothing but a gold or silver sphere, is the sphere in that world gold or silver? Hence the function f(P,w) does not seem to be well defined. This may look like a reason for preferring Lewis’s system – which does not require uniqueness – to Stalnaker’s.10 However, then P□→−Q would cease to be the contradictory of P□→Q. So Stalnaker, while agreeing that the structure of possible worlds does not single out a unique function f(P,w), argues that we should treat this as a case of vagueness, i.e., it is indeterminate which function “f(P,w)” should be since there are many determinate functions which do the job equally well. Each such function gives an admissible bivalent valuation of counterfactual statements. Since it would be arbitrary to choose one of these valuations rather than another, Stalnaker combines them by Bas van Fraassen’s method of supervaluations: P will be true at w on the supervaluation if and only if it is true at w on each admissible bivalent valuation; P will be false at w on the supervaluation if and only if it is false at w on each admissible bivalent valuation; P will be neither true nor false at w on the supervaluation otherwise. Thus bivalence will not hold in general for counterfactuals.11 Consider again our example. Let w be the actual world. Then, to avoid an implausible asymmetry, Stalnaker will allow that one admissible valuation will use a function f such that f(G∨S,w) is a world at which G is true, while another admissible valuation will use a function f′ such that f′(G∨S,w) is a world at which S is true.12 On the former valuation, (G∨S)□→G will be true at w; on the latter, it will be false at w (given (b)). Hence, on the final supervaluation, (G∨S)□→G will be neither true nor false at w, the actual world. Similarly, the supervaluation will make (G∨S)□→−G neither true nor false. In general, P□→Q counts as neither true nor false when and only when P□→−Q does, for the biconditional −(P□→Q)≡(P□→−Q) remains logically valid (the impact of supervaluation is on the semantics, not the logic, of counterfactuals). Similarly, ((G∨S)□→G)∨((G∨S)□→−G) is true on the supervaluation, even though neither disjunct is.

Thus if one allows −(P□→Q) and P□→−Q to be equivalent, a very natural line of thought leads to the abandonment of bivalence for such statements. Conversely, the defender of bivalence should not allow them to be equivalent, and thus must deal with Stalnaker’s arguments that they are. Lewis’s own reply to Stalnaker is that a natural and elegant analysis of conditionals of the form “If it had been that P, it might have been that Q” is as −(P□→−Q), but that if P□→−Q were equivalent to −(P□→Q), this analysis would make the “might” conditional equivalent to the corresponding “would” conditional, which would surely be wrong. Thus Lewis challenges Stalnaker to produce an analysis of “might” conditionals.13 Stalnaker, however, has produced such an analysis, which there is not space to evaluate here.14 Rather, I shall make some critical remarks about Stalnaker’s arguments for the equivalence of −(P□→Q) and P□→−Q, and then give some arguments for their non-equivalence.

Stalnaker has certainly adduced evidence that we tend to treat the denial of P□→Q as though it were equivalent to the assertion of P□→−Q, but he does not show that this is not a fallacy that we tend to commit, rather than something constitutive of the truth conditions of our thoughts and sentences.15 For the upholder of bivalence can explain why we should tend to confuse −(P□→Q) with P□→−Q. It is not just that human beings have a well-documented general tendency to make scope confusions; in this particular case something more interesting can be said. The natural English negation (“not”) attaches to a verb; since the main connective of a conditional in English (“if … then –”) does not contain a verb, we naturally attach the “not” to the main verb of the consequent, thereby making the confusion to be explained. The point of using the sentential operator “It is not the case that …” to negate conditionals is precisely that the main verb “is” falls outside the scope of “if … then –”, but we seek to avoid such constructions because they are so cumbersome.16 Thus Stalnaker’s appeal to linguistic intuition cannot prevent his opponent from distinguishing between −(P□→Q) and P□→−Q.
However, the defender of bivalence would like to have some independent arguments for making this distinction. I shall suggest two. First, consider the following principle:

We can show that anyone who thinks that −(P□→Q) is always equivalent to P□→−Q is committed to (V), given classical logic and the uncontroversail principle (I) above, as follows. Assume −((P□→Q)∨(P□→R)). This is equivalent to −(P□→Q)&−(P□→R), which by hypothesis is equivalent to (P□→−Q)&(P□→−R). Since −Q and −R entail −(Q∨R), (P□→−Q)&(P□→−R) entails P□→−(Q∨R) by (I). The latter is equivalent to −(P□→(Q∨R)) by hypothesis. Contrapositively, P□→(Q∨R) entails (P□→Q)∨(P□→R). As we should expect, Stalnaker’s system (but not Lewis’s) validates (V). However, (V) is not a very plausible principle. For example, it takes us from the trivial premise that, had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, there would have been nothing but a gold or silver sphere (which follows from (III)) to the implausible conclusion that either, had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, it would have been gold or, had there been nothing but a gold or silver sphere, it would have been silver. Stalnaker will say that the disjunction can be true even though neither disjunct is, but that reply is inadequate, for the disjunction itself is implausible. Moreover, the sense that (V) is implausible certainly does not depend on a prior commitment to bivalence, for Michael Dummett, who is no friend of bivalence, has objected to (V) – his example is that “If Fidel Castro were to meet President Carter he would either insult him or speak politely to him” does not entail “Either if Fidel Castro were to meet President Carter he would insult him or if Fidel Castro were to meet President Carter he would speak politely to him”.18

A second argument against the equivalence of −(P□→Q) and P□→−Q is as follows. It is not incoherent to deny determinism; after all, we do not know it to be true, and perhaps have scientific evidence that it is false. Yet the most natural articulation of an indeterministic account of the world would become self-contradictory were −(P□→Q) deemed equivalent to P□→−Q. For example, suppose that a certain apparatus was not switched on at noon. Surely a respectable scientific theory can entail that nothing about the apparatus and its surroundings at noon determined whether, had it been switched on, it would have emitted a particle. The only natural way to express this entailment in terms of subjunctive conditionals is as the negation of the disjunction of P□→Q and P□→−Q, where P is “The apparatus is switched on at noon” and Q is “The apparatus emits a particle”. If P□→−Q were equivalent to −(P□→Q), this would be a contradiction; given that it is not a contradiction, P□→−Q is not equivalent to −(P□→Q).19 Note that it would be unsatisfying to substitute for −((P□→Q)∨(P□→−Q)) some metalinguistic comment on the semantic status of (P□→Q) and (P□→−Q) (for example, that neither is true on the supervaluation), for in an important sense the scientific theory is talking about the apparatus itself, not about our talk about it. Nor could the denial of (P□→Q)∨(P□→−Q) be replaced by the mere refusal to assert it, for our aim is to express what the theory does say, not what it does not.

Thus there are good reasons to reject Stalnaker’s semantics for counterfactuals, so his argument against bivalence for them fails. Now observe that the second of the above arguments (unlike the first) remains valid when the background logic is taken to be intuitionistic. For the crucial point was that it should be consistent to assert −((P□→Q)∨(P□→−Q)), which the equivalence of −(P□→Q) and P□→−Q would rule out. Intuitionistically, if −(P□→Q) is equivalent to P□→−Q then −((P□→Q)∨(P□→−Q)) is equivalent to −((P□→Q)∨−(P□→Q)), which is intuitionistically inconsistent, for any statement of the form −(R∨−R) is as inconsistent intuitionistically as it is classically. Thus an upholder of bivalence who uses the distinction between −(P□→Q) and P□→−Q to defend themselves against an intuitionist opponent cannot simply on those grounds be accused of begging the question against the intuitionist. This point is of some importance to the second half of the paper, in which we consider a line of argument against bivalence, again turning on subjunctive conditionals, which Michael Dummett has proposed.

Another well-known line of argument against the principle of bivalence has been advanced by Michael Dummett, in which subjunctive conditionals again figure largely.20 It is, of course, only one front in a complex assault on the realist doctrine – that the truth of sentences of our language can transcend our ability to recognize them as true – on which Dummett takes classical logic and semantics to rely.21 However, I shall not say much about this background. For there are local ways of resisting this element of Dummett’s attack on bivalence which do not raise every global issue. In particular, it has just been seen that to distinguish between −(P□→Q) and P□→−Q is not tantamount to assuming realism; indeed, Dummett himself does not deny that such a distinction can be drawn.22 Hence, in what follows, that result of the previous section may legitimately be applied.

Dummett’s primary concern is with statements which someone wishes to analyze reductively in terms of subjunctive conditionals. For example, a phenomenalist might begin by analysing the material-object statement “a is ϕ” as “If a had been in circumstances C, a would have appeared ϕly”. Similarly, a behaviourist might begin by analyzing the psychological statement “a is ϕ” as “If a had been in circumstances C, a would have acted ϕly”. I shall not ask whether such analyses are in fact correct, but only whether they have the consequences which Dummett claims them to have; in each case, the antecedent and consequent certainly require further analysis, but that should not affect the overall conditional form.

To reconstruct Dummett’s argument, consider a class of statements which are to be analyzed as subjunctive conditionals: if R is in the class, its analysis will be A(R)□→C(R). If the class is closed under negation, −R will be analyzed as A(−R)□→C(−R). Since we understand −R by understanding R and negation, A(−R)□→C(−R) must somehow be composed from the material in A(R)□→C(R) and negation, and the only promising solution is to take A(R) as A(−R) and −C(R) as C(−R); thus −R is analyzed as A(R)□→−C(R). To call R false is, we may for present purposes assume, to call −R true. Thus R is bivalent if and only if either A(R)□→C(R) is true or A(R)□→−C(R) is true. Dummett argues that we often have no reason to accept the latter disjunction, and thus no reason to suppose that R is bivalent. In particular, he suggests that an hypothetical statement can be true only if categorical facts make it true, and that it is implausible that there should always be either categorical facts to make A(R)□→C(R) true or categorical facts to make A(R)□→−C(R) true. Most poignantly, the very facts (such as Jones’s bravery or cowardice) which seem to have the best chance of deciding between A(R)□→C(R) (“Had Jones been in danger, he would have acted bravely”) and A(R)□→−C(R) (“Had Jones been in danger, he would not have acted bravely”), are those like R (“Jones is brave”), and are therefore excluded by the analysis itself as being, despite appearances, not really categorical. I shall not develop Dummett’s argument on this last point, since I do not propose to criticize it and I have already accepted its conclusion – that it is not always the case that either A(R)□→C(R) or A(R)□→−C(R) is true. If that conclusion is false, subjunctive conditionals a fortiori do not undermine bivalence.

Given our previous discussion, the obvious reply to Dummett’s argument is as follows. The negation of A(R)□→C(R) is by definition −(A(R)□→C(R)), and no reason has been given to suppose this equivalent to A(R)□→−C(R); we have already seen how they could have been confused with each other in spite of not being equivalent. This confusion led us mistakenly to suppose that the bivalence of R required either A(R)□→C(R) or A(R)□→−C(R) to be true (Dummett calls this “strong bivalence”), which is indeed implausible; that bivalence loses its air of implausibility once we see that it requires only either A(R)□→C(R) or −(A(R)□→C(R) to be true (“weak bivalence”).23 Cases in which it is genuinely indeterminate what would have happened can now all be described consistently with the principle of bivalence after the following pattern. It is not the case that had Jones been in danger he would have acted bravely; it is not the case that had Jones been in danger, he would not have acted bravely – trivially, of course, had Jones been in danger, he would have either acted bravely or not acted bravely. In symbols −(A(R)□→C(R)), −(A(R)□→−C(R)) and A(R)□→(C(R)∨−C(R)) are true. A(R)□→C(R) and A(R)□→−C(R) are bivalent, because they are false. Thus the principle of bivalence is not threatened for the subjunctive conditionals themselves. R, however, has been mishandled. For the negation of the analysis of R (−(A(R)□→C(R))) is not equivalent to the analysis of the negation of R (A(R)□→−C(R)): the scheme of analysis is internally inconsistent and must be revised. More generally, the class of statements to be analyzed as individual subjunctive conditionals (not just as truth functions of subjunctive conditionals) must not be closed under negation (I assume that if any subjunctive conditional were the negation of A(R)□→C(R), it would be A(R)□→−C(R)).

Thus reductionists have two alternatives. (i) They can take the apparent negation of R to be its real negation. They must then analyze the apparent negation of R as the negation of the analysis of R. If they analyze R as a subjunctive conditional, they must analyze −R not as a subjunctive conditional but as the negation of one. Since they have been given no reason to deny that either A(R)□→C(R) or −(A(R)□→C(R)) is true, they can assume R to be bivalent. (ii) They can take the apparent negation of R (nR) not to be its real negation. Hence they can still analyze R as A(R)□→C(R) and nR as A(R)□→−C(R), but since the falsity of R will not require the truth of nR, they can assume R to be bivalent.

How does Dummett reply to this objection? He sometimes suggests that we might be able to recognize the falsity of R as directly depending on the truth of A(R)□→−C(R) without considering what the negation of R is.24 Now we can grasp that a statement might be false independently of whether it has a true negation, in a case in which it has no negation, or at least not one which there are the means to express, i.e., if the statement was made in some limited system of signs. But we have no reason to deny that A(R)□→C(R), the analysis of R, does have a negation, −(A(R)□→C(R)), which we would not be justified in calling the negation of R unless (at least) −(A(R)□→C(R)) is true if and only if A(R)□→C(R), therefore R, is false. Of course, our identification of a statement as the negation of R may depend on our prior grasp of what it takes for R to be false, and if we had an overwhelming intuition that R is false if and only if A(R)□→−C(R) is true, we should have to take −(A(R)□→C(R)) as equivalent to A(R)□→−C(R). I ignore this line of argument having no such intuition myself.

Dummett has considered positions for reductionists which resemble (i) and (ii), but his objections to them are unsatisfactory. He rejects (i) on the grounds that “it is plain that” in the cases with which they are concerned, reductionists will analyze all statements, positive and negative, in a given class into statements of the form P□→Q; but plainness, like or unlike beauty, is in the eye of the beholder.25 Dummett rejects (ii) on the grounds that it is integral to a realist account of the class of statements which includes R that it should be closed under negation; but this requires an account of realism in which its acceptance for a given class of statements requires the application of a highly specific style of truth-conditional semantics to them; therefore the rejection of realism in this sense does not entail the rejection of bivalence for the given class.26

Whether or not reductionists accept the principle of bivalence, they are unlikely to feel bound by Dummett’s twin demands – that the given statements should all be analyzed into the form P□→Q, and that as a class they should be closed under negation. For they can argue as follows. The second demand has no obvious rationale except that the class should be closed under standard truth-functional operations; hence it should also be closed under disjunction – if the second demand is legitimate. Thus if R and S are in the class, so is R∨S, and their analyses, if the first demand is legitimate, will be A(R)□→C(R), A(S)□→C(S) and A(R∨S)□→C(R∨S) respectively. Since we understand R∨S by understanding R, S, and disjunction, then A(R∨S)□→C(R∨S) must somehow be composed from the material in A(R)□→C(R), A(S)□→C(S) and disjunction. We can assume A(R) and A(S) to be identical since this can only simplify the problem which I am about to argue to be insoluble. In particular, A(R) and A(S) have already been assumed to coincide when S is −R. The only promising solution is to take A(R) (=A(S)) as A(R∨S) and C(R)∨C(S) as C(R∨S); thus R∨S is analyzed as A(R)□→(C(R)∨C(S)) (this is merely to transpose the argument for the analysis of −R as A(R)□→−C(R) from negation to disjunction). But then the problem arises that the analysis of a disjunction is not equivalent to the disjunction of the analyses of its disjuncts. For, as we saw, Dummett himself admits that the inference from P□→(Q∨R) to (P□→Q)∨(P□→R) ((V) above) is not generally valid (although its converse is), and his counterexample involves just the kind of conditionals which might occur in a behaviourist analysis of psychological statements (c.f. Fidel Castro). Indeed, Dummett’s critique of bivalence gives him good reason to reject (V), for a statement such as “Jones is acting bravely” is not itself supposed to be the source of the threat to bivalence, so that we can assert “Had Jones been in danger, he would have either acted bravely or not acted bravely”, from which (V) would allow us to infer what Dummett thinks we should not assert “Either had Jones been in danger he would have acted bravely or had Jones been in danger he would not have acted bravely”.27 Thus even reductionists who reject the principle of bivalence for statements in the given class should either deny that it is closed under disjunction or analyze disjunctions whose disjuncts are analyzed as subjunctive conditionals as disjunctions of subjunctive conditionals, not as individual subjunctive conditionals with disjunctive consequents. If at least one of these alternatives is acceptable for disjunction, why should the corresponding alternative ((i) or (ii)) not be acceptable for negation? But then the motive for rejecting the principle of bivalence disappears.

Dummett has one line of attack left. Consider the following plausible principle: a subjunctive conditional statement can be true or false only in virtue of categorical facts – that is, only if non-conditional facts make it true or make it false.28 The principle is less than crystalline, but can be clarified as much as present purposes demand; it could be denied, but I shall not deny it, preferring to resolve the tension between it and the assertion of bivalence for subjunctive conditionals that Dummett claims to discern. He presses the question: why suppose that there must be either categorical facts to make P□→Q true or categorical facts to make it false? For if his opponent has no right to suppose this, then they also have no right, given the above principle, to suppose that P□→Q must be either true or false.

My answer to Dummett’s question, relying on classical logic, ultimately defends bivalence. This does not beg the question against him, for Dummett’s aim is to bring to the surface internal tensions within the position of reductionists who say subjunctive conditionals are either made true by categorical facts or made false by them. If reductionists can resolve these purported tensions in their own position by use of the logic of that position, then Dummett’s strategy fails.

Reductionists can defend themselves as follows. Either there are categorical facts to make P□→Q true or there are not (by the law of excluded middle). If there are, well and good. If there are not, then P□→Q is made false (and −(P□→Q) true) by the absence of such facts. Of course, “the absence of categorical facts to make P□→Q true” need not denote an entity of a queer kind, an absence – it merely indicates that the statement “There are no categorical facts to make P□→Q true” figures in the explanans of “P□→Q is false”.29 For Dummett’s principle about conditionals and categoricals would lose its immediate claim to assent if it had to be read as ontologically committed to such things as facts. The above account certainly suggests that the explanation of the truth of a subjunctive conditional will differ in kind from the explanation of the falsity of one, but this should not occasion surprise. We already know that the explanation of the truth of an existential statement will differ quite similarly in kind from the explanation of the falsity of one; a particular F which is G can make “Some F is G” true (indeed, this is a paradigm of a non-trivial explanation of the truth of a statement, which Dummett’s principle requires), whereas only the absence of Fs which are G may make it false.30 Thus the negative account of what makes a subjunctive conditional false merely exploits an apparatus to which anyone who recognizes the legitimacy of Dummett’s question will already be committed. It does not create new difficulties.

Now Dummett will doubtless have objections to the principle of bivalence for the underlying categorical statements, but we have seen that they will run along quite different lines from any which we have considered here; for example, how does our ability to conceive, of any particular categorical statement of some kind, that it is false give us the ability to conceive that all categorical statements of that kind are false? Our point has been that the non-existence of a right answer to questions about which of several possibilities would have been realized in a counterfactual situation poses no autonomous threat to the principle of bivalence.

0. The technical parts of this paper concern the effect of some non-standard rules of proof on normal modal logics. There is also a philosophical motive for investigating this topic, which it is as well to explain first.
