(A) and (B) are deliberately schematic. In particular, the discussion will apply to a variety of epistemological concepts, each of which can be used as a reading for ‘assertibility’. The assertibility of a sentence might be a descriptive matter (Quine’s dispositions to assent), or it might have prescriptive overtones (Dewey and Dummett’s warranted assertions). It might require conclusive proof, or only defeasible evidence. (A) and (B) could also be rephrased in a less linguistic mode, as concerning the relation between the truth-conditions of thoughts and the conditions under which they can be verified, accepted or confirmed. They clearly have something to do with philosophical disputes about ‘verificationism’ and ‘anti-realism’. On the face of it, (A) seems to be the natural destination of certain arguments summarized in the slogan ‘Meaning cannot transcend use’ and (B) an absurdly strong form of verificationism; any difficulty in holding (A) without (B) would therefore constitute a prima facie objection to those arguments. A better understanding of the logical relations between (A) and (B) might throw some light on this confusing area.

(B) obviously entails (A); identity is a special case of determination, provided that (as here) the latter is taken in a logical rather than a causal sense. (A) does not obviously entail (B); after all, someone who holds that falsity-conditions determine truth-conditions is not thereby committed to holding that falsity-conditions are truth-conditions. If (A) does not entail (B), there is a philosophical position to be considered on which (A) is asserted and (B) denied; it would offer a non-trivial explanation of how sentences get their truth-conditions, without doing so at the expense of an implausibly verificationist consequence.1 That might be a good way of reconciling realist and anti-realist insights. On the other hand, if (A) does in some non-obvious way entail (B), then anyone who wishes to deny the verificationism of the latter faces the task of saying what beyond assertibility-conditions determines truth-conditions, if they are determinate at all. There would be the prospect of non-trivial connections between semantics and metaphysics, for it looks as though semantic premises might entail (A), while (B) might entail metaphysical conclusions.

Section 1 shows that on a variety of assumptions (A) does entail (B). The assumptions have some prima facie plausibility, but their detailed evaluation is not attempted here; it will be sensitive to the notion of assertibility at issue. Section 2 is technical; it investigates a rule of proof in modal logic corresponding to (A). Section 3 discusses the proposal that someone who wants to avoid (B) but thinks that epistemological facts do determine truth-conditions might replace (A) by:

Assertibility-conditions and deniability-conditions together determine truth-conditions.
Assertion, denial and some cancellation rules in modal logic
Section 4 is technical; it investigates a rule of proof in modal logic corresponding to (A’). Section 5 concludes that (A’) is not in a much stronger position philosophically than (A).
Assertion, denial and some cancellation rules in modal logic

1. Consider a language L of whose (indicative) sentences (A) is true. L will be assumed to contain the usual truth-functional connectives, satisfying classical propositional logic; since some anti-realists reject classical logic, the scope of this assumption can itself be regarded as under test. It will also be assumed that a concept of assertibility is represented in L by an operator (not a predicate) L with the sense ‘it is assertible that’. For present purposes, assertibility-conditions and truth-conditions can be thought of as classes of possible situations in which a sentence may be uttered; such situations will be called contexts.2 The use of an assertibility operator in the object language will be defended at the end of Section 1.
Assertion, denial and some cancellation rules in modal logic

The gist of (A) is that two sentences with the same assertibility-conditions have the same truth-conditions. A quick argument from (A) to (B) then goes as follows: it is assertible that A if and only if it is assertible that it is assertible that A; therefore A and LA have the same assertibility-conditions; therefore, by (A), they have the same truth-conditions; since the truth-condition of LA is the assertibility-condition of A, the assertibility-condition of A is its truth-condition, which gives (B). More formally, (A) corresponds to the L-cancellation property, that for any sentences A and B of L, if LA↔LB is true in all contexts then so is A↔B. (B) corresponds to the L-collapse property, that for any sentence A of L, A↔LA is true in all contexts. The assumption used above in moving from the former to the latter is a kind of S4 biconditional, that for any sentence A of L, LA↔LLA is true in all contexts; it has considerable intuitive plausibility, and by itself does not require assertibility to be either necessary or sufficient for truth. The idea is that warrants for assertion must be recognizable to speakers, for otherwise such warrants could not play the role required of them in governing the speakers’ use of the language; but then speakers can reflect that a warrant to assert that it is assertible (in their context) that A gives them a warrant to assert that A; conversely, they can reflect that a warrant to assert that A gives them a warrant to assert that it is assertible (in their context) that A. Nevertheless, this equivalence can itself be regarded as under test. Note that the argument did not appeal to any laws of truth-functional logic for L at all.3
Assertion, denial and some cancellation rules in modal logic

Different assumptions about L can be used to construct another argument from (A) to (B). It may seem reasonable to assume that the assertibility of a conjunction entails the assertibility of its conjuncts and that if a sentence is assertible, it is not also assertible (in the same context) that the sentence is not assertible, nor is the negation of the sentence assertible. Thus for any sentences A and B of L, L(A&B)→(LA&LB), LA→−L−LA and LA→−L−A (that is, LA→MLA and LA→MA) are true in all contexts. In contrast to the previous case, the S4 principle LA→LLA is not assumed. By the first assumption we have L(A&−LA)→(LA&L−LA) and L(A&−A)→(LA&L−A), whose consequents the second and third assumptions respectively make inconsistent. Thus L(A&−LA) and L(A&−A) are true in no contexts, and so L(A&−LA)↔L(A&−A) in all. By L-cancellation, (A&−LA)↔(A&−A) and so A→LA are true in all contexts. As a special case we have −A→L−A; combining this with the third assumption gives LA→A. Thus A↔LA is true in all contexts.4 (A) again yields (B).

Although the arguments above require L and the truth-functional operators to be present in L, this is less of a restriction than it might appear. All that is really required is that these operators can coherently be added to any language, for then — given the extra assumptions — it follows that if (A) is true of all languages, so is (B). Of course, it has not been ruled out that the sentences of a restricted language (one not containing L, for instance) should obey (A) but not (B), even if the extra assumptions hold in all languages: but the ambitions of the literature on realism and anti-realism call for readings of (A) and (B) on which they aspire to characterize all languages, rather than merely distinguishing some from others. For instance, the claim ‘Meaning cannot transcend use’ is not intended to state a contingent fact about English.

This is not the place to decide whether one should use the conditional ‘If (A) then (B)’ for a Modus Ponens or for a Modus Tollens (the latter looks more promising); that may partly depend on which concept of assertibility is at issue. The present point is just that it is much harder than one might imagine to combine (A) with the negation of (B).

2. The discussion above can be set in the context of normal modal logics.5 The syntax is standard: sentential variables p, q, r, …, the usual truth-functions, including the contradiction ⊥ and the tautology ⊤, L, and M abbreviating −L−. For present purposes, a normal modal logic can be defined simply as a set of formulae that contains all truth-functional tautologies and the formula L(p→q)→(Lp→Lq) and is closed under the rules of Modus Ponens, Necessitation and Uniform Substitution; thus the logic is identified with the set of its theorems.6 This formal language L′ should not be confused with the language L of Section 1. L may contain all sorts of compositional devices not definable from the resources of L′ (L and the truth-functions). Rather L′ can be thought of as a meta-language for L, with the atomic sentential variables of the former ranging over all sentences of the latter. On one such interpretation, a formula of L′ will be valid if and only if the result of uniform substitution of sentences of L for its variables always yields a sentence of L true in all contexts (note that the truth-functional operators and L are therefore thought of as in common between L and L′). Thus the rule of Uniform Substitution takes valid formulae of L′ to valid formulae of L′. Upper-case italic letters are used as meta-linguistic variables ranging over sentences of L′. The standard notation for rules of proof is used, on which Necessitation becomes: A/LA.

That the valid sentences of L′ are closed under Necessitation and that L(p→q)→(Lp→Lq) is a valid sentence, on this interpretation, are substantive assumptions. Their plausibility will, of course, depend on which concept of assertibility is at issue. There might indeed be a decisive objective to them if they amounted to the assumption that the set of sentences of L assertible in a given context is closed under logical consequence, for then membership of such a set would characteristically not be a decidable property and it may be essential to the philosophical motivation for (A) that assertibility in a given context is a decidable property (otherwise it might lack the right connection with the use of language). However, all that is really being assumed is that the set of valid sentences of L′ is closed under logical consequence, and membership of this set may well be a decidable property even if membership in the set of assertible sentences of L is not. It will turn out that the most relevant modal logics for present purposes are indeed decidable; trivially, where (B) is true of the sentences of L, so that p↔Lp is valid in L′ (modal collapse), validity in L′ reduces to truth-functional validity and is therefore decidable.7 Thus the use of normal systems may not involve too damaging an idealization.

Just as p↔Lp is valid on the above interpretation if (B) is true of the sentences of L, so the following rule of proof L↔C holds in L′ if (A) is true of the sentences of L: if LA↔LB is valid, so is A↔B. For if LA↔LB is valid, then LA′↔LB′ is true in all contexts for any sentences A′ and B′ of L resulting from A and B respectively by uniform substitution of sentences of L for their variables, so by (A) A′↔B′ is always true in all contexts, so A↔B is valid (note that the converse argument from the validity-preservingness of L↔C to the satisfaction of (A) by sentences of L is not valid without extra assumptions, since a particular sentence LA′↔LB′ of L might be true in all contexts for reasons dependent on the content of A′ and B′, so that no sentence LA↔LB of L′ of which it was a substitution-instance would be valid). Obviously, L↔C no more says that any sentence (LA↔LB)→(A↔B) is valid than the rule of Necessitation says that any sentence A→LA is valid. Questions about the rule independent of the original interpretation, but with consequences for it, now suggest themselves. What is the effect of L↔C on normal modal logics?

It is obvious that L,M→C is derivable from L→C and from M→C, that L↔C is derivable from L→C and M↔C from M→C, that L↔C is interderivable with M↔C and that L→C is interderivable with M→C. L→C follows from L↔C because in any normal system LA↔L(A&B) follows from LA→LB. To complete the chain of equivalences it is sufficient to show that L→C is derivable from L,M→C. So suppose that LA→LB∈S (a normal modal system). Evidently LA→L(A→B)∈S. Now −M(A→B)→(LA&L−B) is in any normal system, so −M(A→B)→(LB&L−B)∈S, so −M(A→B)→−MA∈S, so MA→M(A→B)∈S. Thus, given L,M→C, A→(A→B)∈S, so A→B∈S. Thus all five of the above rules are equivalent. To revert to the interpretation above: M↔C says in effect that deniability-conditions determine truth-conditions; L→C might be compared with the intuitionist semantics for the conditional, which allows one to assert a conditional when one has seen the assertibility of its antecedent to guarantee the assertibility of its consequent.9

In Section 1, it was in effect observed (N. 4) that the addition of L↔C to any normal system containing Lp→p and L(p&q)→(Lp&Lq) causes modal collapse; since any normal system contains the latter formula, the addition of L↔C to any normal system that includes the system T (KT) causes modal collapse. Similarly, it was observed that the addition of L↔C to any normal system containing Lp↔LLp has the same effect. Not all normal systems collapse under L↔C, however. For instance K, the smallest normal system, is closed under L↔C. For suppose that A↔B∉K. Since K is complete with respect to the class of all models, there is a world x in some model at which A↔B does not hold. The model can be extended by the addition of a world y, accessible from no world and from which only x is accessible, so that LA and LB hold at y if and only if A and B respectively hold at x. Thus LA↔LB does not hold at y, and so is not in K. Contraposing, if LA↔LB∈K then A↔B∈K.10 This argument also shows the closure under L↔C of the system D, which results from the addition of M⊤ to K, for D is complete with respect to the class of serial models (those in which from every world at least one world is accessible) and the extended model will be in this class if the original one is. A quirkier system closed under L↔C results from the addition of p↔LLp to K: for if LA↔LB is a theorem, so is L(LA↔LB), therefore LLA↔LLB and therefore A↔B. None of these systems contains p↔Lp (in the last case, consider models with two worlds, each accessible from the other but not from itself).

Two somewhat better-known rules of proof can be derived from L↔C: they are MA/A and LA/A. For in any normal system S, if MA∈S then L−A→L⊥∈S, so if S is closed under L↔C and therefore under L→C then −A→⊥∈S, and therefore A∈S. Similarly, if LA∈S then L⊤→LA, giving ⊤→A∈S and therefore A∈S by L→C. Both of these rules are weaker than L→C. This is obvious for LA/A, under which all systems that include T are closed, whereas L↔C has been seen to cause modal collapse in them. The rule of proof MA/A must of course be distinguished from the schema MA→A; the former says that if MA is a thesis then so is A, not that MA entails A. The addition of MA/A also causes any normal system that includes T to collapse, since it contains the thesis M(p→Lp), but the consistent system which results from the addition of L⊥ to K is vacuously closed under this rule, not having any theorem of the form MA, whereas the addition of L↔C would make it inconsistent, since L⊤↔L⊥ is a theorem.11

Finally, a general connection can be made between L↔C and the standard semantics, where a model (W,R,V) consists of a set of worlds W, an accessibility relation R and a valuation V, a formula A holds at a world iff V(A,x)=T and a characteristic model for a system is one such that the formulae holding at all worlds in the model are precisely the theorems of the system:

FACT. A normal modal logic S is closed under L↔C iff it has a characteristic model (W,R,V) in which ∀x∈W∃y∈W∀z∈W(yRz⇔z=x)

Proof. Suppose that S has such a characteristic model (W,R,V) and that LA↔LB∈S. Let x∈W, and choose y∈W such that ∀z∈W(yRz⇔z=x). Thus V(LA,y)=V(A,x) and V(LB,y)=V(B,x), so V(A↔B,x)=V(LA↔LB,y)=T. Thus A↔B holds at each world in W, so A↔B∈S.

Conversely, suppose that S is closed under L↔C. Let (W,R,V) be the canonical model (whose worlds are maximal S-consistent sets of formulae) for S, which is always characteristic.12 Let x∈W. Consider the set X={MA:A∈x}∪{LB:B∈x}. Suppose that X is S-inconsistent. Thus there are A1,…,Ap,B1,…,Bq∈x such that (LB1&…&LBq)→−(MA1&…&MAp)∈S; since S is normal L(B1&…&Bq)→L(−A1∨…∨−Ap)∈S. By L→C, and so by L↔C, (B1&…&Bq)→(−A1∨…∨−Ap)∈S, contradicting the S-consistency of x. Thus X is S-consistent. Let y∈W be a maximal S-consistent extension of X. By the definition of R for the canonical model, yRx because {MA:A∈x}⊆y; yRz requires z=x because if B∈x, LB∈y so B∈z, so x⊆z, so z=x.

3. The following principle is at least plausible:
Assertion, denial and some cancellation rules in modal logic
It is assertible that it is assertible that A if and only if it is assertible that A.

However, (C) was seen in Section 1 to yield the equivalence of (A) with (B). There is thus a problem for those who feel that (A) has the right end of the stick and (B) the wrong one. An obvious move for them to make, and one that has been proposed in the literature, is to treat denial on a par with assertion, and to hold that truth-conditions are determined only by assertibility-conditions and deniability-conditions together, as in (A’).13 This feature is already built into Quine’s model of radical translation, on which the native speakers’ assent and dissent behaviour have equal status.14 In less linguistic terms, a version of (A’) would say that the content of a thought is determined by the conditions for its falsification (disconfirmation, rejection) as well as those for its verification (confirmation, acceptance). The truth-conditions of ‘It is assertible that A’ could then be distinguished from those of A, even on the assumption (C) that they have the same assertibility-conditions, for when there is no evidence either for or against A, ‘It is assertible that A’ is deniable while A is not. Of course, this shows only that one quick argument from (A) and (C) to (B) cannot immediately be transformed into an argument from (A’) and (C) to (B); it does not rule out the possibility of a different argument from (A’) and (C) to (B), for (A’) says that identity in assertibility- and deniability-conditions is sufficient for identity in truth-conditions, not that it is necessary. The acceptance of (A’) and (C) does turn out to be consistent with the rejection of (B), but more work will be needed to show this.
Assertion, denial and some cancellation rules in modal logic

The denial of a sentence is, of course, equivalent to the assertion of its negation. It has been objected that to put denial on a par with assertion in determining truth-conditions is to treat negative sentences as semantically unstructured, and thereby to flout an obvious constraint of compositionality: for the meaning of −A should be exhibited as a function of the meaning of A.15 This point might be well taken if the denial of a sentence could be expressed only as the assertion of its negation. However, Quine’s model of radical translation suggests otherwise: assent and dissent are conceived symmetrically (saying ‘Yes’ or ‘No’, shaking or nodding one’s head). For the purposes of (B), assertion and denial should be treated as equally basic speech acts, with the equivalence between the denial of a sentence and the assertion of its negation defining negation rather than denial.

Within the context of normal systems, the recourse to denial in determining truth-conditions fails to have its intended effect; (A’) and (C) cannot be satisfied together in a normal system without violating the logic of defeasible assertibility, either by not making a tautology assertible or by making truth a consequence of assertibility. However, there are other concepts of assertibility on which Lp→p is acceptable as a theorem; for instance, one might read L as ‘There is conclusive evidence that’, or (in the case of mathematical language) as ‘It is informally provable that’. Another possible reading would be ‘It is implicitly known that’, where implicit knowledge had the requisite closure properties. Thus the possibility remains open for someone to adopt a concept of assertibility obedient to S4, and then endorse (A’), and thus L,M↔C. The presence of the formula p↔(Lp∨(Mp&−MLp)) in S4 + L,M↔C is of particular interest. For, on the earlier interpretation, it means that truth, although not equivalent to assertibility, is at least definable in terms of assertibility and deniability: it says, in effect, that a formula is true if and only if either it is assertible or its assertibility but not the formula itself is deniable. It remains to be seen whether there are any concepts of assertion and denial for which this rather bizarre equivalence is plausible. Clearly, (A’) is a consequence of any such definition of truth in terms of assertibility and deniability. More formally: any normal system is closed under L,M↔C if it has a theorem of the form p↔A, where A is a modal function of Lp and Mp (just as it will be closed under L↔C and M↔C if A is a modal function either of Lp or of Mp). On the other hand, a normal system can be closed under L,M↔C even if it has no such theorem. The systems K and D are examples. For if they had such a theorem, so would S5, which would therefore be closed under L,M↔C, which it is not — indeed S5 collapses under L,M↔C, since S4 + L,M↔C, and therefore S5 + L,M↔C, contains the theorem p→(LMp→Lp) and S5 contains p→LMp. Yet K and D are closed under L,M↔C, for they are closed under L↔C.
Assertion, denial and some cancellation rules in modal logic

5. Is there any concept of assertibility for which S4 + L,M↔C is a plausible system? One might attempt to model some sort of speculative interpretation on the characteristic two world frame. Suppose, for instance, that we could make sense of the phrases ‘the world of reality’ and ‘the world of appearance’ in such a way that sentences of the language L not containing L could be said to hold or to fail to hold at these worlds. Then one might stipulate that LA holds at the world of appearance if and only if A holds at the world of appearance, but that LA holds at the world of reality if and only if A holds at both the world of reality and the world of appearance, with standard clauses for the logical constants. One might read L as ‘it is evident that’, understood as a factive. Perhaps there is some limited domain in which this interpretation would be a useful one, but taken generally it seems both fanciful and crude.
Assertion, denial and some cancellation rules in modal logic

Does any concept we actually employ validate S4 + L,M↔C? If L is read as something like ‘it is informally provable that’, at least S4 is arguably validated: but many additional theorems of S4 + L,M↔C are not. Consider the theorem L(−p→L(p→Lp)), for instance: on this reading, it says that it is informally provable that if p is false then it is informally provable that p is informally provable if true; but no such informal proof seems to be generally forthcoming. Again, the theorem LMp∨L−Lp is read as making the not generally plausible assertion that either it is informally provable that p is not informally disprovable or it is informally provable that p is not informally provable.
Assertion, denial and some cancellation rules in modal logic

No concept of assertibility that I know of validates S4 + L,M↔C. The retreat from (A) to (A’) therefore does not by itself meet the objections to (A) in a philosophically satisfying manner. The discussion in this paper has of course been based on a number of simplifying assumptions, which may need to be called into question. Of these, the appeal to the concept of truth-conditions is perhaps the least significant, for although there obviously are conceptions of truth which many tempted by (A) or by (A’) would regard as suspect, they are not required by the preceding discussion. For just as the identity of A and B in assertibility-conditions amounted to the validity of LA↔LB, so their identity in truth-conditions amounted to the validity of A↔B, where it was not essential that the notion of validity should itself be explained in terms of some controversial notion of truth. In effect, the operative notion of truth was that of a redundant sentential operator, representing the identity truth-function. More deserving of controversy are the closure assumptions about assertibility (the use of normal logics), the treatment of assertibility as though it did not come in degrees, even the appeal to classical logic. A claim often made at this point is that the truth-condition of a sentence is determined by its compositional structure as well as by its assertibility- and deniability-conditions; that may be so, but as a bare claim it hardly comes to grips with the problem for it does not explain what determines the effect of a compositional device other than the conditions for the assertion and denial of the sentences which serve as its arguments and values. In any case, if a more true-to-life model does imply a relation between assertibility and truth essentially different from the results above, it should at least be illuminating to discover what the crucially misleading simplifications were, and why.
It will be proved that S4 + L,M↔C is Sobociński’s K4. In order to show that S4 + L,M↔C includes Sobociński’s system, we can start by showing the former to contain p→(MLp→Lp):
We can now show S4 + L,M↔ also to contain p→(LMp→Lp):
It is now straightforward to show that S4 + L,M↔C contains the remaining axiom of Sobociński’s system, LMp↔MLp:

Thus S4 + L,M↔C includes Sobociński’s system. In order to prove the converse, it suffices to show that his system, which includes S4, is closed under L,M↔C. We first show it to contain p↔(Lp∨(Mp&−MLp)):
Sobociński’s system can now be shown to be closed under L,M↔C, as follows:
This completes the proof that S4 + L,M↔C (and therefore K + M⊤ + Lp↔LLp + L,M↔C) is equivalent to Sobociński’s system.

Two alternative axiomatizations of this system may be noted. First, it is equivalent to K + p↔(Lp∨(Mp&−MLp)). For the latter formula has been seen to be contained in it, and in turn to ensure closure under L,M↔C. Thus it remains only to show that K + p↔(Lp∨(Mp&−MLp)) contains the characteristic S4 axioms. Lp→p is obvious. For Lp→LLp, substitute p&−Lp for p; the result simplifies to M(p&−Lp)→(p&−Lp), which yields Lp→L(p→Lp). Second, the system is equivalent to T + p→(MLp→Lp) + p→(LMp→Lp); this follows without difficulty from what has been established so far.
For a recent discussion bearing on this point see Peacocke [8]. ↩︎

In this sense, the truth-condition of a sentence is the set of possible situations in which it can be truly uttered; it is not the set of situations with respect to which the sentence, as uttered in a fixed context, is true. The sophistications of two-dimensional modal logic will be avoided. The assertibility-condition of a sentence is, correspondingly, something like the set of possible situations in which its assertive utterance is warranted. ↩︎
Arguments of this kind are proposed in Brandom [2], following Dummett [3] at pp. 450–451. ↩︎

The second and third assumptions are of course consequences of the validity of LA→A. Given the first assumption, the argument therefore applies to any truth-entailing concept of assertibility, such as provability in mathematics. Its application is clearly more general than that, however. ↩︎

The rewards of a finer-grained approach are illustrated in Humberstone [6], which distinguishes between the derivability of a rule in a system and the mere closure of the system under the rule. Interesting questions could be raised in these terms about the rules discussed in this paper, but they go beyond its scope. ↩︎
For some relevant results see Lemmon and Scott [7], pp. 81–85. ↩︎

works.title: On the paradox of knowability
passages: Dorothy Edgington has recently helped an argument of Fitch’s against verificationism to emerge from ill-merited obscurity.1 Roughly speaking, the argument shows that not obviously silly forms of verificationism entail obviously silly forms of it. Edgington treats the argument as a paradox because she holds that we must retain some form of verificationism in order to do justice to certain considerations about what it is to grasp a concept, considerations which seem to owe something to Michael Dummett. She ingeniously proposes a modification of the verificationist schema that blocks Fitch’s argument. I shall argue that if there is a way of reading the modified schema as a not obviously silly form of verificationism, it has not yet been revealed.
A not obviously silly form of verificationism says, roughly, that all truths are knowable. It can be formalized by the schema:

where ‘◇’ and ‘K’ abbreviate ‘it is possible that’ and ‘it is at some time known that’ respectively.2 An obviously silly form of verificationism says that all truths are known. It can be formalized by the schema:

By substituting ‘p&−Kp’ for ‘p’, Fitch showed that schema (1) entails schema (2), given principles of classical modal and epistemic logic that neither Edgington nor I dispute. If it is an unknown truth that p, it is an unknowable truth that it is an unknown truth that p.

According to Edgington, the trouble with (1) is that it conflates the situation s in which p with the situation s+ in which it is known that, in s, p. For the crucial substitution ‘p&−Kp’ for ‘p’, the idea is that there is no reason why it should not be known in s+ that, in s, it is an unknown truth that p. Contradiction results only if one puts s=s+, when it would be known in s that, in s, it is an unknown truth that p.3 Thus, Edgington’s preferred form of verificationism can be expressed by the schema:

In (3), the quantifiers range over situations, which should be thought of as nonspecific possibilities; Edgington uses situations rather than possible worlds in order to avoid making the knowledge in (3) involve the infinite amount of detail that the specification of a possible world would require. One can make (3) comparable to (1) and (2) by restricting ‘s’ to actual situations and using the ‘actually’ operator ‘A’, in the sense of ‘in some actual situation’. The result is:
(4) is a sub-schema of (1).4 Fitch’s argument does not reduce (4) to any obviously silly form of verificationism.

In one respect, (4) is a surprisingly weak form of verificationism. For, as Edgington notes, ‘Ap’ always entails ‘□Ap’, where ‘□’ abbreviates ‘it is necessary that’. Thus, the only knowledge that (4) requires is of necessary truths. One might expect a robust form of verificationism to insist that at least some contingent truths are knowable. Of course, although the truths that (4) requires to be knowable are all necessary, they need not all be a priori. Actually to know the necessary truth that it actually snowed in 1985 is just as a posteriori a business as actually to know the contingent truth that it snowed in 1985. However, Edgington’s defence of (4) depends on the possibility of non-actual knowledge about what is actually the case, and what could constitute such knowledge remains to be seen.

Indeed, it is hard enough to see what could constitute even non-actual thought about what is actually the case, let alone knowledge. For, as Edgington notes, if people had non-actually had thoughts which they could have expressed by saying something of the form ‘It is actually the case that p’, they would not have been expressing thoughts of the requisite kind, since their use of ‘actually’ would refer rigidly to their own situation, not to ours. In the same way, at seven o’clock I shall not be able to express the thought that it is now (six o’clock) raining in the words ‘It is now raining’, since my use then of the word ‘now’ will refer rigidly to seven o’clock, not to six o’clock. This temporal analogy suggests a further problem. How is one to think at seven o’clock the thought that one could have expressed at six o’clock in the words ‘It is now raining’? It will not do to think at seven o’clock the thought that one could express at seven o’clock in the words ‘It is raining at six o’clock’ (‘is’ tenseless). For one can express the latter thought in the same words at six o’clock, when they notoriously express a different thought from that which the words ‘It is now raining’ express; at six o’clock, one may not know that it is six o’clock. The only apparent way in which one might think at seven o’clock the thought that one could have expressed at six o’clock in the words ‘It is now raining’ is by remembering six o’clock; given the right context, such a thought could be expressed in the words ‘It was then raining’. However, this analogy offers no comfort to Edgington, for the memory link between the later thought and the earlier time requires there to be a causal link between events at the two times; in contrast there can be no causal link between the non-actual and the actual. In this respect, non-actual thought about the actual differs crucially from non-present thought about the present.5

More generally, the problem concerns thought and knowledge about counterfactual situations. We can raise it without use of the ‘actually’ operator by focusing on the quantificational version of Edgington’s verificationism. In schema (3), the situation variable ‘s’ occurs inside the knowledge operator ‘K’. The person who knows that, in s, p must somehow have specified the situation s. Moreover, they must have done so in the right sort of way, for it cannot be assumed that every way of specifying s will permit their knowledge to be described by means of the de re construction. Four ways of specifying a situation will be considered: (i) by necessary and sufficient conditions, (ii) by counterfactuals, (iii) by space-time co-ordinates, and (iv) by ostension. It will be argued that, on the one hand, whenever s may be specified in way (i) or (ii) in the knowledge that, in s, p, this knowledge requires no more than knowledge of a trivial logical truth, while, on the other hand, (iii) and (iv) do not yield non-actual knowledge of the actual. Thus, none of (i)-(iv) yields nontrivial non-actual knowledge of the actual. In the absence of some further way of specifying situations, Edgington can differentiate her position from obviously silly forms of verificationism only by making it too weak to be a form of verificationism at all.

These claims may sound implausibly strong. Surely we can have knowledge of counterfactual situations in the form ‘If s were to obtain, it would be the case that p’; surely such knowledge requires more than knowledge of a trivial logical truth. Both points are correct, but they are no objection to the argument, which—following schema (3)—concerns knowledge in the form ‘In s, p’. The two forms are not equivalent, for ‘In s, p’, unlike ‘If s were to obtain, it would be the case that p’ (for most values of ‘s’ and ‘p’), is necessarily true, if true at all. This view needs to be established as a preliminary to consideration of (i)-(iv).

What is it for something to be the case in a situation? Edgington thinks of situations as like possible worlds, but as not completely specific. Thus, the truth value of a proposition in a given situation does not itself vary from situation to situation, just as the truth value of a proposition in a given possible world does not itself vary from world to world. ‘In s, p’ is therefore necessarily true, if true at all. Edgington also requires this result for her quantifier and operator formulations (such as (3) and (4) respectively) to mesh with each other. Her operator formulations concern knowledge only of propositions of the form Ap, which are necessarily true, if true at all; since she takes them to be restatements of her quantifier formulations, the latter should also concern knowledge only of propositions with this property. There is a deeper reason for this result. Verificationists hold not just that all truths of a particular kind—those of the form ‘If s were to obtain, it would be the case that p’, for example—happen to be knowable; they hold that all truths are knowable, because of what truth is. Edgington seeks to vindicate this idea by arguing that a truth can be known ‘from’ a situation other than that (or those) in which it is located. (3) has that effect only if the truth which ‘p’ expresses in s is the same as the truth which ‘In s, p’ expresses in s+. The only way that I can see of making out such a claim is in terms of a trivial equivalence between ‘In s, p’ and ‘In s+, in s, p’, that is, in terms of the claim that ‘In s+’ is redundant as applied to ‘In s, p’—which can be so only if the latter holds no contingency for ‘In s+’ to fasten on. Thus Edgington’s project requires ‘In s, p’ to be necessarily true, if true at all. It is now easy to argue that what ‘In s, p’ amounts to is ‘Necessarily, if s obtains then p’ (in an operator formulation). The latter clearly entails the former. For the converse, note that ‘In s, p’ entails the material conditional ‘If s obtains then p’, whence ‘Necessarily, in s, p’ entails ‘Necessarily, if s obtains then p’; since ‘In s, p’ entails the former, it also entails the latter.

With the locution ‘In s, p’ thus clarified, the various ways of specifying situations can be considered. In what follows, s is any situation in which p; by the previous paragraph, necessarily, if s obtains then p. What (3) requires is a situation s+ in which it is known that, in s, p.

Assume first that, in knowing that in s, p, one can specify s in way (i). Thus, for some value of ‘q’, necessarily, s obtains if and only if q: moreover, the knowledge that, necessarily, if q then p counts as knowledge that, in s, p. Now it is easy to show that, necessarily, s obtains if and only if both p and q. Thus the condition that both p and q specifies s in way (i) just as well as the condition that q does. It would therefore be quite ad hoc not to permit its use in de re knowledge about s, since the latter condition may be so used. Hence the knowledge that, necessarily, if both p and q then r counts as knowledge that, in s, r. In particular, the knowledge that, necessarily, if both p and q then p counts as knowledge that, in s, p. Thus, given the assumption about (i), the knowledge that, in s, p requires no more than knowledge of a trivial logical truth.

Similarly, assume that, in knowing that, in s, p, one can specify s in way (ii). Part of what is meant by saying that s is specified by a counterfactual is that, for some value of ‘q’, s would obtain if q. However, that by itself would not specify s uniquely, for whenever s obtains, so do other situations which stand to it as genus to species; what is required is for s to be the most specific situation which would obtain if q. Thus the assumption is that, in some situation s+, s is the most specific situation which would obtain if q, and the knowledge that if q then it would be the case that p counts as the knowledge that, in s, p (note that s may not be specifiable as the most specific situation which would obtain if q in a situation other than s+). Now it is certainly true in s+ that if q then it would be the case that p, for s would obtain if q and, necessarily, if s obtains then p. By standard counterfactual reasoning (which both the Stalnaker and Lewis semantics validate), it follows that what would be the case if q is just what would be the case if both p and q; in other words, the counterfactual statements ‘It would be the case that r if q’ and ‘It would be the case that r if both p and q’ have the same truth value at s+. Therefore, since s is the most specific situation which would obtain if q, it is the most specific situation which would obtain if both p and q. Thus, in s+, the condition that both p and q specifies s in way (ii) just as well as the condition that q does. It would therefore be quite ad hoc not to permit its use in de re knowledge about s, since the latter condition may be so used. Hence the knowledge that if both p and q then it would be the case that r, counts as knowledge that, in s, r. In particular, the knowledge that if both p and q then it would be the case that p, counts as knowledge that, in s, p. Thus, given the assumption about (ii), the knowledge that, in s, p requires no more than knowledge of a trivial logical truth.

No such arguments can be made for ways (iii) and (iv), since they do not specify s by a condition into which the conjunct that p can be built. For the same reason, however, they do not permit knowledge of counterfactual situations. ‘The situation in the Balkans in 1913’ or ‘this situation’, as used in actual situations, refer (if at all) to actual situations. As Edgington admits, it is obvious that not all actual truths are actually known. It is thus wholly unclear that (3) can be interpreted as a not obviously silly form of verificationism. If it permits the use of either (i) or (ii) in the knowledge at issue, its demands are too weak to be verificationist. If it permits the use only of (iii) and (iv), its demands are too strong not to be obviously silly. The onus is on anyone who defends (3) as a not obviously silly form of verificationism to give some account, which avoids these twin dangers, of how situations may and may not be specified in knowledge about them. Until that has been done, (3) should be treated as uninterpreted formalism.

Given these problems in reading Edgington’s quantified formulations, it might be better to concentrate on those, such as (4), which use operators instead. However, (4) is equally problematic, and for the same sort of reason. If (4) is not to collapse into the obviously silly schema Ap→AKAp, non-actual knowledge that actually p is required. A fortiori, non-actual thought that actually p is required. How would such thought be conceptualized? The proponent of (4) faces a dilemma. Either non-actual thinkers of the thought that actually p have the concept which we express by ‘actually’, or they do not (in the sense in which the English word ‘actually’ expresses different concepts in different worlds). If they do, they can think about an absolutely specific counterfactual world—the actual one—and that is quite implausible; Edgington herself says ‘Knowledge of counterfactual situations is never of one specific possible world’ (p. 564). If they do not, what relation is required between their thinking and our sentence ‘Actually p’ for the latter to characterize the former (as by hypothesis it does)? For, on this horn of the dilemma, it is possible to think that it is actually the case that p without having the concept of what is actually the case. It is certainly not enough that their thought should be necessarily equivalent to the thought that actually p, for the latter thought is a necessary truth (given that it is true), and thus necessarily equivalent to any tautology; (4) is not a form of verificationism if its truth requires only the possibility that someone knows a tautology.

It might be thought that Edgington’s replacement of possible worlds by actual situations would allow her to accept the first horn of the dilemma. If our concept of what is actually the case refers to a non-specific actual situation, might it not be available to the non-actual thinker? This objection rests on a technical mistake. The move from worlds to situations affects the semantics of modal language, not its logic. The same inferences are validated, but in a different way. Now, in a standard logic for the actuality operator A, the inference from −Ap to A−p and its converse are valid; moreover, if q follows from p1,…,pn, then Aq follows from Ap1,…,Apn. Suppose that non-actual thinkers have the concept A (which they of course cannot express by ‘actually’); then they can hypothesize a situation at which all instances of the schema ‘p↔Ap’ are true. It follows from what has been said about the logic of A that they have specified a consistent and complete counterfactual situation—the actual one. In other words, the notion of a complete world is built into the technical concept of actuality to which Edgington appeals. Nor is it clear how a different concept of actuality, more apt to her purposes, could be introduced. For ‘the actual world’ means this world; the ostension succeeds because it takes place in a single world. In contrast, one could not say ‘Let “the actual situation” mean this situation’, for the ostension takes place in many situations of varying degrees of specificity simultaneously, and therefore fails. Situations differ from worlds precisely in not being mutually exclusive. The onus is on anyone who defends (4) as a not obviously silly form of verificationism to give some account of the nonstandard sense in which they are using the ‘actually’ operator. Until that has been done, (4) should be treated as uninterpreted formalism.

How else might a verificationist escape from Fitch’s argument? One way would be to substitute intuitionistic for classical logic.6 It may even be the only way. If so, that would confirm the connection between the logical and metaphysical issues which Michael Dummett has argued to exist. It is also a blow to the hope, or fear, that verificationism might come at no significant cost to logic. Conversely, to the extent that we are more likely to be mistaken in our theory of meaning than in our logic, we have further reason to reject any form of verificationism so far proposed.
I thank Simon Blackburn for helpful comments.
‘The Paradox of Knowability’, Mind, 1985, pp. 557–68; cf. G. N. Schlesinger, The Range of Epistemic Logic, Aberdeen, Aberdeen University Press, 1985, pp. 103–6. ↩︎

Known by whom? Obviously, the problem does not arise if the relevant knowers include a necessarily existent and omniscient one. One can think of the knowers as human or mildly superhuman beings. Neither Edgington’s discussion nor mine depends on a particular answer. Likewise, I follow Edgington in using the concept of knowledge, although verificationism may be better formulated in terms of a weaker cognitive relation; this choice too is not crucial for the main issue. Edgington characterizes the possibility for which ‘◇’ stands as ‘logical’. I should prefer the term ‘metaphysical’. For ‘◇’ is presumably the dual of ‘□’, and Edgington allows the inference from Ap to □Ap, where ‘A’ is the ‘actually’ operator (op. cit., p. 567); now, given that Italy actually won the World Cup in 1982, it may be metaphysically necessary that it actually did, but it does not seem to be logically necessary (one cannot work out who actually won the World Cup by logic alone). ↩︎
Strictly, it must also be known that s obtains. ↩︎
Edgington notes that (4) can be given the same generality as (3) by means of a ‘fixedly’ operator. ↩︎
Edgington makes extensive use of analogies between modal and temporal arguments. ↩︎

works.title: On knowledge of the unknowable
passages: If it is an unknown truth that p, it is an unknowable truth that it is an unknown truth that p (cf F. B. Fitch, ‘A logical analysis of some value concepts’, The Journal of Symbolic Logic 28, 1963, pp. 135–42, at p. 138). It follows, by classical logic, that if all truths are knowable then all truths are known. This hardish fact makes life difficult for the verificationist who wishes to assert that all truths are knowable, but to deny that all truths are known. He might try rejecting classical logic (cf. my ‘Intuitionism disproved?’, Analysis 42.4, October, 1982, pp. 203–7). Dorothy Edgington has recently suggested a different way out (cf. ‘The paradox of knowability’, Mind 94, 1985, pp. 557–68). She admits that there are unknowable truths in the sense of Fitch’s argument, but interestingly revises the verificationist principle, to give it this form: if, in a situation s, it is a truth that p, then there is a possible situation s′ in which it is known that, in s, p. Although the truth (for some values of ‘p’) that, in s, it is an unknown truth that p cannot be known in s, it might be known in some possible situation other than s. I have argued elsewhere that this account faces difficulties of principle in explaining how the knower in s′ can pick out the situation s in thought with adequate specificity (cf. ‘On the paradox of knowability’, Mind forthcoming). I waive those objections here, to examine Edgington’s application of her principle to a particular case of knowledge in one situation that something is an unknown truth in another. I shall argue that her account does not generalize to the full range of cases which it needs to cover.

Suppose that, in the actual situation s, it is an unknown truth that it rained last night. Nevertheless, someone could have known that it rained last night. How would this provide knowledge that, in s, it is an unknown truth that it rained last night? According to Edgington, ‘the possible knower that it rained last night has to know that it still would have rained, had neither he nor anyone else noticed. And any possible knower that it rained does, or at least can, know this’ (p. 567). Such an account obviously does not apply to cases in which the corresponding counterfactual is false, but, Edgington says,
If there are truths which fail to satisfy the principle
p would still have been true, had no one known that p,
that I am in pain, for example, then they satisfy the principle,
If p, then someone knows that p
and, a fortiori, they satisfy [the verificationist principle] (ibid., my numbering).

Evidently, the above account of knowledge that, in s, it is an unknown truth that p presupposes that it is knowable that p (in the ordinary sense, in which Edgington concedes that not all truths are knowable). It therefore does not cover a case of the following kind. Let ‘p’ abbreviate a description of all the neurophysiological events which ever actually take place in any brain, conjoined with the proposition that no other neurophysiological events take place in any brain. It is an unknown truth that p. However, it does not even seem knowable by creatures such as us that p, for such knowledge would have to be recorded in a brain by different states from those which record actual knowledge, making it false that p. Thus Edgington’s account does not show how there could be knowledge that, in s, p, for this value of ‘p’. This limitation noted, one can look at those cases where it is known in some situation s′ that p.

Suppose that (1) is known in s′ to be true by someone who also knows that p. Edgington’s argument requires this to constitute knowledge that, in s, it is an unknown truth that p. Now clearly, in s′, (1) could not tell one that it would still have been true that p in s, unless s would or might have obtained, had no one known that p; otherwise, its being true that p in s would not be a necessary condition for the truth of (1). For the truth of a counterfactual does not require its consequent to be true in all possible situations in which its antecedent is, but only in those which are most similar to the situation at which the counterfactual is being evaluated, for some appropriate respect of similarity. Thus Edgington’s argument requires the following counterfactual not to hold in s′:
s would not have obtained, had no one known that p

For this reason, s′ should be chosen so as to differ as little as possible from s, given that it is known that p in s′ but not in s (and that (1) is known in s′ but not in s — this may force further, unwanted differences between s′ and s). Even when s′ is chosen in this way, however, (3) often will hold in s′. For example, suppose that in s a flower bloomed on this spot at time t (= p), where t is a past time at which there were no relevant thinking beings. It is an unknown truth in s that p. Nevertheless, it could have been known that p; in some s′, human beings evolve earlier and see a flower here at t. Their counterfactual thought (1), that a flower would still have bloomed here at t had no one known that it did, is true. However, it is true simply because the flower would still have bloomed here, had they not gone for a walk in the forest that day; for situations of that kind, in which the general evolution of the human race up to t is more or less the same as in s′, are the most relevantly similar ones to s′ in which the antecedent of (1) is true. In other words, (3) holds in s′, for, in s, the human race has not even begun to evolve at t. Hence, as argued above, knowledge in s′ of (1) does not give knowledge of actuality. Note that it is not even clearly true in s′ that a flower would have bloomed here at t had the human race not evolved until it did in s; the most relevantly similar situations to s′ in which it does evolve later might be ones in which the absence of human beings altered the ecology of the area in such a way that a flower did not bloom here at t.

Thus, even if someone can know both (1) and that p, Edgington’s account of knowledge that, in s, it is an unknown truth that p breaks down for some cases. Her other line of argument in the quoted passage is intended to apply when (1) is false. There is thus another lacuna: what if (1) were true but unknowable, or at least not knowable by whoever knew that p (in the sense in which Edgington concedes that not all truths are knowable)? However, instead of pressing this point, I shall examine Edgington’s claim that if (1) is false then (2) is true, in which case the verificationist has no problem.

Note first that the difficulty arises when (1) is false in s′, the situation which would have obtained had it been known that p. If the falsehood of (1) entails the truth of (2), then presumably what follows is that (2) is true in s′, which is no surprise since the consequent of (2) is true by hypothesis in s′; but since the truth of (2) in s′ does not seem to rule out the possibility that it is an unknown truth in s that p, no way seems to have been provided of knowing either in s′ or in s that, in s, it is an unknown truth that p. Thus the revised verificationist principle is still under threat. Note that it would be irrelevant to try to argue to the truth of (2) in s from the falsity of (1) in s, for, by hypothesis, both the antecedent and the consequent of (1) are true in s. Thus it would have to be claimed that the falsity of (1) in s′ entails the truth of (2) in s. But there is no reason why such an entailment should hold. For example, suppose that it is an unknown truth in s that exactly n lists of a hundred or more items were completed in Carthage from its foundation to its destruction (= p; I assume that 100<n). The corresponding s′ is presumably a situation in which a list of all the n relevant lists, including itself, is completed just as Carthage is about to be destroyed. Let s″ be a situation as relevantly similar to s′ as is compatible with its not being known in s″ that p; s″ is presumably a situation in which the list of lists is not completed, and no lists are completed which were not completed in s′. Thus at most n−1 relevant lists are completed in s″, so in s″ it is not the case that p. Hence, by the choice of s″, (1) is false in s′. Nevertheless, (2) is not true in s — the Carthaginians did not actually make such a list of lists. In this example, it might be claimed that a modified version of Edgington’s argument would go through, in which s′ would be chosen as a situation in which the list of lists is completed and contains n+1 items including itself; in s′, it would not be the case that p, but it would be known that it would have been the case that p had it not been known that exactly n+1 relevant lists were completed; this might be claimed to be knowledge of s. However, such a move is ad hoc: there is no longer any general way of finding a situation s′ of the right sort, nor any reason to think that there is any such situation. Moreover, there are more recalcitrant examples. Suppose that our best physical theory tells us that one can know what state a ?-particle is in only by interacting with it in ways which unpredictably change its state. Suppose also that it is an unknown truth in s that ?-particle z is in state k (= p). Then (1) is not true in the corresponding s′, but (2) is not true in s. Of course, a verificationist might deny that there can be unknown truths in cases of this kind: such a claim represents, however, a sharp increase in the price to be paid for the dubious advantages of verificationism. Certainly, there is no reason to regard the falsity of (1) in the relevant situation as any general guarantee of the actual truth of (2).

Edgington has offered a model of non-actual knowledge that, in the actual situation, it is an unknown truth at p. I have argued that, even if one accepts the model for the simple examples which she gives, it seems to break down for more complicated ones. Nor is there any obvious prospect of adapting the model to these cases.

The model therefore provides no reason to think that the revised verificationist principle, which requires such knowledge, is universally true. Edgington also discusses weaker forms of verificationism, in which the concept of knowledge is replaced by that of reasonable belief, or of evidence; the arguments of this paper apply just as much to them. If revised verificationism lacks independent plausibility, Edgington would probably wish to rest her defence of it on an appeal to considerations about our grasp of concepts (p. 557). It would be interesting to have a detailed account of what it is about such considerations in virtue of which they lead to revised verificationism rather than to the fundamentalist principle, in the sense in which Edgington rejects it, that all truths are knowable.

works.title: Invertible definitions
passages: Introduction A concept of informational equivalence between relations is explicated to generalize some suggestions by Geach. It is shown that two relations are informationally equivalent if and only if each can be defined in terms of the other without the use of quantifiers. It is shown that there is a general method for listing the j-place relations informationally equivalent to an arbitrary given i-place relation if and only if i≤j. The equivalence classes of the relation of informational equivalence are characterized as the invariants of the group of invertible quantifier-free definitions, for i=j.

Quantifier-free definition is contrasted with general first-order definition by means of an example of two first-order interdefinable relations which are not interdefined by any pair of mutually inverse first-order definitions.

1 Geach ([3], pp. xi–xii, 25–26, 33, 52) has suggested that one property or relation may be so closely connected to another that to have the concept of either is to have the concept of both. For example, to know what is red is to know what is not red, and to know what is to the left of what is to know what is to the right of what. If a relation is the same as its contradictory and its converse in this respect, it is presumably also, by transitivity, the same as the contradictory of its converse in the same respect. Since Geach claims to refute some theories of concept acquisition and possession on the basis of their neglect of this equivalence relation, a formal characterization of it would seem desirable, so that a general principle covering his remarks can be stated and tested.

Geach’s suggestion is plausible if concepts are thought of as discriminative capacities. For vividness, imagine an ω-sequence of labeled objects to which we have no direct access, but about which we can gather information via a robot (the discriminative capacity). Suppose that we can use the robot to discover whether the object with a given label is red (when the instruction ‘Red’ is input, followed by the label, the robot moves along the line until it finds the object with that label, and on its return flashes a light if and only if that object was red): then ipso facto we can use the robot to discover whether the object with a given label is not red (similarly with ‘red’ and ‘not red’ reversed). ‘Red’ and ‘not red’ correspond to the same discriminative capacity. Again, suppose that for any labels a and b we can use the robot to discover whether the object labeled a is to the left of the object labeled b, by inputting the instruction ‘Left’, followed by a followed by b: then for any labels a and b we can use the robot to discover whether the object labeled a is to the right of the object labeled b, by inputting the instruction ‘Left’, followed by b followed by a (similarly with ‘left’ and ‘right’ reversed). ‘Left’ and ‘right’ correspond to the same discriminative capacity.

To generalize these examples, we need to define a relation—call it informational equivalence—which applies to pairs of converses and contradictories, such that a philosopher (whom I shall call “Geach”) might plausibly claim that if R is informationally equivalent to S then to have the concept of R is to have the concept of S. Here are some desiderata for the definition of informational equivalence1:

(i) Geach’s suggestion would become unnecessarily tendentious if we made first-order interdefinability entail informational equivalence. For consider the first-order interdefinable predicates Fx and Fx≡(∃yFy&∃y¬Fy). In the example above, let the domain of quantification be the set of all objects in the ω-sequence, F be true of all and only the red ones and “Red” be the robot’s only instruction. Suppose that, unknown to us, all the objects are red. Then, by means of the robot, we shall discover that ∃yFy is true, but we shall never discover that ∃y¬Fy is false, so we shall never know the extension of Fx≡(∃yFy&∃y¬Fy). Since we can use the robot to discover the extension of one property but not of the other in a finite way, it is not arbitrary to rule that they are not informationally equivalent. Moreover, even for a finite domain, we could know the extension of one over a proper subset of the domain without knowing the extension of the other. (For a generalization of (i), cf. (iii).)

(ii) However, Geach would lose one of his examples if we made the informational equivalence of two i-place relations entail that the extension of each could be recovered from the extension of the other over every set of i-tuples. For consider the singleton set {(x,y)}. If one is told only that (x,y) is not in the extension of to the left of, one cannot tell whether it is in the extension of to the right of (x may be on top of y). What we can make the informational equivalence of two i-place relations entail is that for every set of individuals, the extension of each relation could be recovered from the extension of the other over every set of i-tuples of members of that set. For example, if one is told the extension of to the left of over a set {(x,x),(x,y),(y,x),(y,y)}, one can deduce the extension of to the right of over that set.

(iii) Consider the predicates Fx and Fx≡P, where P is a closed formula whose truth value is contingent. Although in any given world Fx≡P is extensionally equivalent either to ¬Fx or to Fx itself, we should not treat Fx and Fx≡P as informationally equivalent, since one cannot tell how to determine the extension of one from that of the other if one does not happen to know the truth value of P.

(iv) We should allow an i-place relation to be informationally equivalent to a j-place relation even when i≠j. For example, suppose that Rxy is defined by Gx&Gy, so that Gx is logically equivalent to Rxx. Then, for any set, if we knew the extension of Gx over that set we could deduce the extension of Rxy over all ordered pairs of members of that set and vice versa.

We shall treat an i-place relation as a function from possible worlds to sets of i-tuples (a property is a one-place relation). Some relations in an intuitive sense (such as serial ordering) may not naturally correspond to a particular set of i-tuples in given circumstances; however, since possible worlds figure in the mathematics below only as indices, they can be regarded as including arbitrary stipulations for the extensions of such indeterminate relations (different stipulations will give different worlds). In any case, the results below can be interpreted in a more syntactic fashion, so that they are not as different as they look from the work of Beth and his successors on definability (see [4]). Think of the possible worlds as the models of a first-order theory T. Given an ordering of the variables of the language, each open formula in which at most the first i variables are free determines a function from models to sets of i-tuples in the obvious way. Two open formulas determine the same function if and only if they are satisfied by the same sequences in all models of T, hence if and only if they are provably equivalent in T; such relations can thus be thought of as the elements of a Lindenbaum algebra (cf. [2]). Since the definitions with which we shall be concerned are first-order, for each result below a corresponding result can be stated in syntactic terms.

Now we can define a sense in which R and G from desideratum (iv) necessarily determine each other’s extensions as follows. For any n, suppose that the sequences (x0,…,xn−1) and (y0,…,yn−1) are alike with respect to R, in the sense that (xi,xj) is in the extension of R when and only when (yi,yj) is, for i,j<n; then (x0,…,xn−1) and (y0,…,yn−1) are alike with respect to G, in the sense that xi is in the extension of G when and only when yi is, for i<n. In virtue of this entailment we can say that R determines G. Similarly, the converse entailment holds, and in virtue of it we can say that G determines R. This definition can be generalized; if we then say that two relations are informationally equivalent if and only if each determines the other, it turns out that we meet all four desiderata. Note that, in order to meet desideratum (iii), we allow x0,…,xn−1 to be drawn from one world and y0,…,yn−1 from another: that is, the informational equivalence of two relations requires that the way in which one determines the other to be invariant over possible worlds, for the receiver of information may not know which possible world it is in. Before we give the general definition we require some technical apparatus.

P(X) is the power set of X. Card (X) is the cardinality of X. X×Y is the Cartesian product of X and Y. YX is the set of functions from X to Y. i and j are finite ordinals, identified with natural numbers (thus 2={0,1}, etc.). The variables w,w′, etc., range over a class whose elements are called the possible worlds. For each, w, Dw is a set whose elements are called the individuals in w. An i-place relation R is treated as a function taking each w to a subset Rw of Dwi. ei is the identity function on i and 1i is the identity function on the class of all i-place relations. If f and g are functions, fg is g followed by f, 𝑑𝑜𝑚(f) is the domain of f and 𝑟𝑎𝑛(f) its range. The variable I can range over all sets, but in cases of interest is a finite ordinal.
If R and S are i- and j-place relations respectively, R determines S iff:

Determination is obviously reflexive and transitive. Since {f:f∈Ii&xf∈Dwi−Rw}=Ii−{f:f∈Ii&xf∈Rw}, R determines ¬R. Since {f:f∈I2&xf∈R̆w}={g:g∈I2&∃h∈{f:f∈I2&xf∈Rw}(g(0)=h(1)&g(1)=h(0))}, R determines its converse R̆. Thus the definition captures Geach’s examples.

The proposal is to generalize Geach’s original suggestion to all pairs of relations which are informationally equivalent in the sense of determining each other. We shall now show that one relation determines another if and only if the latter can be defined in terms of the former by use only of variables (that is, the permutation and identification of arguments) and truth functions. Hence the proposed generalization is in effect to all pairs of relations which are first-order interdefinable without the use of quantifiers. Although desideratum (i) is thereby met, Geach’s suggestion may seem to be threatened when it is thus generalized. In order to know what it is for x to love y, does one really need to know what it is for x to love y if and only if z does not love itself? The condition hardly seems to be necessary if one thinks of the subject’s ability to manifest understanding verbally: but Geach’s original examples are already under threat at this level, since it seems that a child could master the predicate ‘is red’ without having mastered a sign for negation. Geach’s claim is best defended for discriminative capacities, at which level the proposed generalization is not obviously wrong. We commend this issue to the reader, and turn to the proof that mutual determination and quantifier-free interdefinability are equivalent.
We now require a formal representation of definitions which use only truth functions and variables. Let A⊆P(ji). Define a function MA taking subsets of Dwi to subsets of Dwj, for all w, by:

Note that MA is implicitly relativized to i and j; in practice this causes no confusion. A function M taking i-place relations to j-place relations is an i,j-satisfaction function iff for some A⊆P(ji), for all R and w, M(R)w=MA(Rw). If R is i-place, think of each f∈ji as taking variables from ‘MA(R)x0…xj−1’ to give p(f)=‘Rxf(0)…xf(i−1)’; think of each X⊆ji as the conjunction c(X) of p(f) for each f∈X and ¬p(f) for each f∈ji−X; think of each A⊆P(ji) as the disjunction of c(X) for each X∈A. Thus A codes a definition of MA(Rw) which uses only truth functions and variables, in disjunctive normal form. Conversely, any definition which uses only truth functions and variables can be coded in this way. For example, A={X:X⊆ii&ei∉X} codes negation on i-place relations and if a∈22 is given by a(0)=1, a(1)=0, A={X:X⊆22&a∈X} codes conversion.
We now show that mutual determination and interdefinability by satisfaction functions are equivalent.
Proposition 1 If R is i-place and S j-place, R determines S iff for some i,j-satisfaction function M, M(R)=S.

These definitions would also allow certain privileged relations to be used as fixed parameters. For instance, if one treated identity as a logical constant one might be interested in the equivalence relation which holds between R and S iff each is definable in terms of the other using only truth functions, variables, and identity: in other words, when {R,=} collectively determines S and {S,=} collectively determines R.
Proposition 2 If R is i-place and S is j-place, R determines S and S determines R iff for some i,j-satisfaction function M and some j,i-satisfaction function N, M(R)=S and N(S)=R.

Since satisfaction functions make the generalization of Geach’s idea more perspicuous, we list some of their elementary properties. We first show the coding of i,j-satisfaction functions by subsets of P(ji) to be unique except for small domains.
Proposition 3 If A,B⊆P(ji), MA=MB and for some w either j≤𝑐𝑎𝑟𝑑(Dw) or i=0 or both i<𝑐𝑎𝑟𝑑(Dw) and i=1, then A=B.

Proof: Let I⊆ji. For j≤𝑐𝑎𝑟𝑑(Dw), choose x∈Dwj to be 1-1; for i=0 choose any x∈Dwj; for 1<𝑐𝑎𝑟𝑑(Dw) and i=1, take a,b∈Dw (a≠b) and define x∈Dwj by: for k∈j, if the function g∈ji such that g(0)=k is in I, let x(k)=a, otherwise let x(k)=b. In all cases, let Rw={y:y∈Dwi&∃g∈I(y=xg)}. Hence for f∈ji, xf∈Rw iff for some g∈I, xf=xg. Thus if f∈I, xf∈Rw. Conversely, let xf∈Rw: if x is 1-1, xf=xg (g∈I) entails f=g, so f∈I; if i=0, g∈I entails f=g, so f∈I; for 1<𝑐𝑎𝑟𝑑(Dw) and i=1, xf=xg (g∈I) entails that f∈I iff g∈I by the choice of x, so f∈I. Thus {f:f∈ji&xf∈Rw}=I. But MA(Rw)=MB(Rw), so {f:f∈ji&xf∈Rw}∈A iff {f:f∈ji&xf∈Rw}∈B, so I∈A iff I∈B. Since I was arbitrary, A=B.
