works.title: The contingent a priori : has it anything to do with indexicals?
passages: ‘CAN some contingent truths be known a priori?’: when this question is raised in modern philosophy – as, following Kripke, it often has been – it generally introduces a discussion of certain examples which seem to turn on indexical or indexical-like words (Nathan Salmon lists most of the important work on the topic at pp. 77-8 of Reference and Essence, Blackwell 1982; I have also been helped by Graeme Forbes’s typescript ‘States of Affairs, Bedeutung and the Contingent A Priori’, 1985, and subsequent correspondence). Sometimes the indexicality is quite obvious, as in ‘I am here now’, sometimes it appears only on analysis, as in ‘If anyone uniquely invented the zip, Julius did’, where by stipulation ‘Julius’ rigidly designates the inventor of the zip (if there is one), for the rigidity of ‘Julius’ can be expressed by means of the ‘actually’ operator, which is at least formally analogous to an indexical (cf. Martin Davies Meaning, Quantification, Necessity, Routledge 1981, pp. 230-8 on the similar metre rod example). Moreover, this indexicality has been exploited in a well known argument that what is known a priori can be contingent only in a superficial way (Gareth Evans ‘Reference and Contingency’ Monist 62 (1979) pp. 161-89; technical details are omitted, since deep and superficial contingency coincide for sentences, such as those considered below, without ‘actually’ or similar operators). The purpose of this note is to argue that there are deeply contingent a priori truths which in no way turn on indexicals. I do not deny that there are also contingent a priori truths which do turn on indexicals, but we are unlikely to get clear on the contingent a priori in general if we take it to be essentially tied up with indexicals when in fact it is not.
There is at least one believer

To keep (1) free of indexicals, the verb in it should be read tenselessly. A believer is anyone who has beliefs. For the moment, I assume (1) to be a contingent truth: I show later how it can be modified to meet someone who thinks that at least one believer – God – necessarily exists. Now since it is impossible to believe (1) falsely, it seems that one can know (1) a priori. Note that (1) is contingent in the deep sense in which Evans suggests that a contingent a priori truth would be persistently puzzling (technically, possible worlds semantics can evaluate (1) as false even with respect to a world which it is treating as actual): if there is a paradox about the contingent a priori, it has not been dissolved by Evans.
However, it might be replied that, although (1) does not contain indexicals, one can know (1) a priori only if one infers it from the vaguely Cartesian proposition:

Therefore, it might be continued, one’s knowledge of (1) is a priori only if one’s knowledge of (2) is a priori. Moreover, since (2) entails (1), (1) is contingent only if (2) is contingent. Thus, the objection would go, (1) is contingent a priori only if (2) is contingent a priori, and (2) does involve an indexical. At this point, the objection could be rounded off either by a mild moral or by a severe one. The mild moral would concede that (2) is a contingent a priori truth, but claim that this turns on its indexicality, that I could not know the truth of what results from replacing ‘I am’ in (2) by ‘N.N. is’ (where ‘N.N.’ is my name); thus the link between the contingent a priori and indexicals would remain. Note that this mild moral would not help Evans, for (1) and (2) remain deeply contingent a priori truths in his sense. The severe moral (which is inconsistent with the mild one) would deny that (2) can be known a priori at all, and consequently that (1) can be known a priori either, on the grounds that (2) can be known only by a posteriori introspection, observation of one’s own behaviour or the like. This severe moral would help Evans, since neither (1) nor (2), however deeply contingent, would be a priori.
I shall answer both lines of objection by denying that one can know (1) a priori only by inferring it from (2). Consider the following method for forming beliefs:
Given a valid deduction from the premise that someone believes that P to the conclusion that P, believe that P

It is logically necessary (and, therefore, a priori) that any belief which one forms by use of (M) is true. Since (M) is an absolutely reliable method for forming true beliefs, any reasonable theory of knowledge should count a belief that P which has been formed by use of (M) as a case of knowledge that P. Moreover, since one can know a priori that (M) is absolutely reliable, the knowledge which it gives should be a priori (note also that (M) appeals only to ratiocination). In other words, if one comes to believe that P by use of (M), one knows a priori that P.
Now replace ‘P’ in (M) by (1). In order to apply (M) here, one needs a valid deduction to the conclusion (1) from the premise:
Someone believes that there is at least one believer

Such an inference is, of course, trivially valid. Now the crucial point is that (M) does not require us to derive a priori knowledge of (1) from a priori knowledge of (3). If it did, we should be in difficulties. For a priori knowledge of (3) might in turn have to be derived from a priori knowledge of:
I believe that there is at least one believer

But the attempt to derive a priori knowledge of (1) from a priori knowledge of (4) (via (3)) is open to just the same objections as were levelled against the attempt to derive it directly from a priori knowledge of (2); in both cases, the indexical ‘I’ would be crucial. Fortunately, (M) avoids these problems. For it gives the valid deduction from (3) to (1) as by itself a sufficient reason to believe (1); (4) is irrelevant. Thus one can come to believe (1) by use of (M): so, by the conclusion of the previous paragraph, one can know the contingent truth (1) a priori. This way of coming to know (1) did not exploit indexical or indexical-like words at any point.
(1) can be modified to accommodate a religious believer. Consider:
There is at least one fallible believer

One is fallible, in the required sense, if and only if not all of one’s beliefs are true. Presumably, it is possible that no believer other than God exists and impossible that God is fallible: hence (1′) is a contingent truth. In order to use (M) to gain a priori knowledge of (1′), one needs a valid deduction to the conclusion (1′) from the premise:
Someone believes that there is at least one fallible believer

Here is such a deduction: suppose that (3′) is true; consider any x who believes that there is at least one fallible believer; either x is fallible or x is not fallible; if x is fallible, x is a fallible believer, so (1′) follows by existential introduction; if x is not fallible, all of x’s beliefs are true, so x’s belief in (1′) is true; either way, (1′) is true. Thus one can come to believe (1′) by use of (M): so, by the conclusion of the previous paragraph but one, one can know the contingent truth (1′) a priori. This way of coming to know (1′) did not exploit indexical or indexical-like words at any point. Incidentally, the reader might care to imagine the following situation: there are (up to now) no believers except for a necessarily not fallible one, who is now in the act of coming to know (1′) a priori.

Intuitively, (1) is a much less puzzling case of the contingent a priori than, for example, ‘If anyone uniquely invented the zip, Julius did’. With the latter, a linguistic stipulation seems to summon substantive knowledge out of thin air, and Evans’s deflationary tactics are apposite. In contrast, (1) is the kind of proposition which we should expect, for good Kantian reasons, to be contingent a priori; those reasons are articulated in (M).

In arguing that (M) gives a priori knowledge, I appealed to our grasp of the concept of the a priori, but not to any formal definition. This was because it is very hard to find a non-trivial definition of the a priori which does not clearly deviate in extension from the concept to be defined. Indeed, traditional definitions seem not to apply to any necessary truths, let alone contingent ones. For example, Kant himself, in the Critique of Pure Reason, defines knowledge to be a priori if it is ‘absolutely independent of all experience’ (B3, Kemp Smith’s translation). Is our mathematical knowledge absolutely independent of such experiences as checking through a proof we had written out some time before, or listening to a teacher tell us that our answer to an exercise was correct? (cf. Paul Teller ‘Computer Proof’ Journal of Philosophy 77, 1980, pp. 797-803; Michael Detlefsen and Mark Luker ‘The Four Color Theorem and Mathematical Proof’ ibid. pp. 803-20; Philip Kitcher The Nature of Mathematical Knowledge, (Oxford University Press 1983)). Tamara Horowitz (‘A Priori Truth’ Journal of Philosophy 82, 1985, pp. 225-39) has recently given a new definition, on the basis of which she accepts examples of the contingent a priori similar to (1) (ibid. p. 233). Roughly, Horowitz defines a truth p to be a priori if and only if everyone necessarily has enough experience to know that p whenever they exist and have the concepts in p and p is true. However, this condition seems to be neither sufficient nor necessary for a truth to be a priori. For let p be the proposition that no one has the concept of a joke; since anyone who has the concepts in p has the concept of a joke, the truth of p is incompatible with anyone’s having the concepts in p; thus Horowitz’s conditional is vacuously satisfied, since its antecedent is self-contradictory; hence had p been true, as it could have been, it would have met the condition – but it would not have been a priori, for it is impossible to know that p. Conversely, someone could have the concepts in a mathematical truth p without in Horowitz’s sense having enough experience to know that p, because they did not have all the concepts in any proof of p, even though such proofs existed; hence p would fail the condition – but it would still be a priori (for Horowitz, mathematical truths are paradigms of the a priori). Similar examples to the latter also suggest that Philip Kitcher’s definition (op. cit. p. 24) does not give a necessary condition for a priori knowledge, although it may give a sufficient one (if so, it could be used to defend the claim that (M) yields a priori knowledge – in Kitcher’s terminology, the use of (M) could be an a priori warrant). I certainly know of no definition of the a priori which is plausible enough to be relied on as a test of whether a given truth is a priori.

However, to claim that (M) guarantees a priori knowledge is in effect to lay down the following condition as sufficient for P to be knowable a priori: it is impossible to believe falsely that P (I assume bivalence). One then naturally wonders whether this condition is not also necessary.

works.title: Realism and the burden of proof
passages: Realism and the burden of proof

Realism, as I shall use the term, is the principle that a language can express true propositions which its speakers cannot, even in principle, verify as true. Anti-realism is the negation of this principle. In brief, anti-realism asserts, and realism denies, that truth entails verifiability. Hilary Putnam has recently advanced arguments which, if sound, would refute realism. This paper concludes that they are not sound (parts III and IV). More generally, it examines some rather delicate issues about the dialectical logic of the debate between realism and anti-realism (part II). Still more generally, it concerns the nature of philosophical argument (part I).

Arguments against a theory T are of two kinds.1 Roughly, the weak kind aim to show that T need not be true, the strong kind that T cannot be true. On one, we are not obliged to believe T; on the other, we are obliged not to believe T. Typically, the former claim that some T’, incompatible with T, is possible, the latter that T is not possible.2 The former tend to attack sufficient conditions for T, the latter, necessary conditions.

However, these ways of drawing the distinction can mislead. For they suggest a continuum of arguments, from those assigning T a probability of less than one to those assigning it a probability of zero (as it were). Such gradations, though certainly possible, conceal a deeper dichotomy. For epistemic probability – in the loosest sense – must be assessed from a point of view. Take, say, an argument against vulgar phenomenalism, showing it to have consequences repugnant to common sense (Russell’s unsupported tablecloth) yet fully consonant with that theory. From the common sense point of view, the theory becomes much less probable: from the theory’s own point of view, it remains as probable as before. So arguments against T divide over their intended audience, some aimed at those uncommitted to T, some at those committed to it. Both say ‘No’: the former to the question ‘Should I adopt T?’, the latter to the question ‘Should I retain T?’. However, advertence to intention makes the distinction extrinsic: different philosophers could intend the same argument for different audiences. The crucial distinction concerns different kinds of dialectical validity and is intrinsic: some arguments use premises plausible to a ‘neutral’ party but not mandatory on T, others use only premises mandatory on T (I prefer ‘mandatory on T’ to ‘entailed by T’, to include propositions not entailed by T but which T tells us to adopt in certain conditions, described in terms of T, which do in fact occur). The first discourage us from entering T, but only the second encourage us to leave it (whether ‘encourage’ becomes ‘force’ is another matter).

Now if an argument of the first sort is valid, the so-called neutral party is miscalled. For the argument makes essential use of premises not mandatory on T but plausible to that party. Since its conclusion contradicts T, given T (and so any premises that are mandatory on T) those supposedly plausible premises are false. Thus the argument has simply made explicit an already implicit disagreement between T and the ‘neutral’ view. That is still a bad result for T if we were already more strongly inclined to the ‘neutral’ view than to T, before we recognized their conflict, for we now have reason to reject the latter on the basis of the former rather than vice versa. Otherwise, we merely oppose T from the standpoint of another theory, without reason to start there rather than at T. Since this antecedent bias is the condition for such arguments to be effective, I shall speak of the ‘ordinary’ rather than the ‘neutral’ view, opposing it to the theoretical view, that of T.

Here too a continuum underlies the dichotomy. For neither the pure ordinary man nor the pure theoretician inhabits mundane reality: who would listen to an argument against a theory they had no inclination to accept or to reject? What fanatic cannot be caught off guard by pre-theoretical instinct? In practice, argument is often fruitful because ad hominem, exploiting the embryo of theory in the common man, the vestiges of common sense in the theoretician. Sometimes even agreement is reached. However, amongst those primarily responsive to the dictates of theory, the opposite phenomenon is more common: polarization. Each side, to preserve its ruling idea in consistency, expels the traces of its antithesis that threatened it with contradiction. So this dichotomy of points of view is not arbitrarily imposed on a continuum, but represents its inherent tendency to tear and shrivel towards opposite poles. In contrast, the previous continuum – of degrees of conclusiveness – tends to concentrate on its centre: most philosophical arguments end up classified as of some but not much force.

So opponents of T must decide whether to appeal to proponents of T or to those of some other theory they hope to show incompatible with T. Common sense might be such another theory, though I do not myself believe that common sense, or anything else, is both pretheoretically privileged and theoretically potent. When common sense purports to state an obvious fact inconsistent with some philosophical theory (‘this is a table’), that theory, if of any merit, can redescribe the ‘fact’ as consistent with itself, leaving common sense, except in so far as it is ‘the metaphysics of the stone age’, unable to choose between the descriptions. However, I need not invoke this suggestion, for whether the anti-realist arguments I shall discuss appeal only to pre-given common sense will emerge clearly enough.

Certainly the only quite satisfying argument against a theory is one aimed at the theoretician, valid on the theory’s own terms: a reductio ad absurdum. Anything less is unsatisfying both logically – because dependent on extra premises – and humanly – because our opponent rejects it and consensus is not achieved. Perhaps Hegel more than any other great philosopher took this point to heart, and a programme that the introduction to the Phenomenology suggests, to watch at least one of each pair of serious, conflicting theories fail on its own terms, must be completed if philosophy is to achieve perfect rationality. Few would suppose Hegel to have executed this task, many would suspect it of being impossible: but in so far as it is, philosophy must learn to live with an approximation, more or less rough, to perfect rationality. If two theories, neither in a privileged relation to common sense, are both consistent on their own terms, but inconsistent with each other, how do we choose between them?3

Moreover, this hard necessary condition for the ideal may not be sufficient. For even had one seen one of each conflicting pair of theories fail on its own terms, how could one know that one had? One would need a census of all theories, to check them off: what could provide that but a theory or part of one, and how would that be established? So this method seems to yield only negative results. A theory can be refuted, but not established, on its own terms. One might use the slogan, ‘If you think you’ve got problems, you have got problems’: for if you think you have problems, if you had no problems that false belief would itself be a problem. The corresponding slogan, ‘If you think you’ve no problems, you have no problems’, is mere whistling in the dark: if you think you have no problems, if you had problems that false belief would itself be a problem. Perhaps Popper’s asymmetry between verification and falsification has some truth on this informal understanding.4

Hegel’s answer is that a theory’s failure on its own terms is not a merely negative result, because it has been seen to fail in a specific way.5 This seems inadequate, for a specific contradiction, though a positive fact, is not a positive theory. A diagnosis of why the old theory had failed in the way it did might yield a new theory – but the diagnosis itself could only be made on the basis of theory, and so would not yield the presuppositionless theory for which we long. Greater attention to the role of developing self-consciousness in the dialectic might facilitate the links between the stages, if each is the turning of awareness on its predecessor, but what could rule out the possibility of a true theory lying altogether outside the progression, leaving the dialectic to stumble from error to error, ever far from the truth?

So far I have spoken of philosophical argument in general, and in pessimistic tone. A theory consistent on its own terms may always be contradicted by another theory, consistent on its own terms. Might not realism and anti-realism be two such theories? However, the specific content of anti-realism complicates matters. It says that truth must be verifiable. So, by its own lights, it must if true be verifiable. So, absolutely, it must if true be verifiable. What might seem stalemate, neither realism nor anti-realism able to refute the other, is defeat for anti-realism: in failing to falsify realism it fails to verify itself, and so falsifies itself.6 For of what interest is an anti-realism that makes no claim to truth? If a stipulation rather than a proposition, it can simply be rejected.

Can so neat an argument be valid? Sometimes such arguments are accused of neglecting the vital distinction between object and metalanguage: a principle stated in the metalanguage about sentences of the object language has (it is said) been illicitly applied to a sentence of the metalanguage. This criticism is perverse. Anti-realism is not an empirical doctrine about what happens to be expressible in some particular language – which might contain only decidable sentences – but a philosophical one about what is expressible in any possible language. Indeed, the only grounds for asserting anti-realism for the sentences of a powerful, prima facie realist natural language such as English are general philosophical ones, applicable to any possible language. So on the only plausible or philosophical version of anti-realism, a theorem in the metametalanguage will say that all sentences of the metalanguage are, if true, verifiable; since a theorem in the metalanguage says that all sentences of the object language are, if true, verifiable, anti-realism comes to the conclusion that it is verifiable that all sentences of the object language are, if true, verifiable. If realism has survived anti-realist attacks more or less unscathed, it will consistently deny that all sentences of a particular object language such as English are verifiable. Since anti-realism cannot, by hypothesis, refute this denial, it cannot verify that all sentences of the object language are, if true, verifiable. Hence anti-realism is falsified: it cannot escape up a hierarchy of metalanguages.

Could anti-realism have refuted realism on its own understanding of ‘refute’ but not on the realist understanding? Then, on its own terms, anti-realism would be verified. Philosophers would make short work of their opponents if they were allowed to tailor the concept of refutation to their own needs. But one does not win a war by redefining ‘victory’.7 To show that realist premises led through anti-realist logic to contradiction would be trivial; anti-realist premises certainly lead through realist logic to contradiction.8 If a grey area remains, assume that nothing that anyone could reasonably call a self-refutation of realism exists, for the interesting question is: what then?

Could anti-realists continue to assert the existence of a self-refutation of realism, while always admitting that it had not yet been found? On most anti-realist logics they could not: for, constructively speaking, one may assert that an F exists only if one has an example, or at least a method guaranteed to produce one within a finite time. But here a self-refutation of realism is not even in the offing. Such optimistic anti-realism refutes itself – unless so optimistic in estimating its prospects of refuting realism as to incur the strictures of the previous paragraph, by redefining ‘guarantee’. Let S be a situation where no method of producing a self-refutation of realism is known. Granted that anti-realism is not warrantedly assertible in S, it may not have refuted itself in S. It has done so only if the impossibility of a self-refutation of realism is warrantedly assertible in S: but it may not be. Clearly, the mere present absence of a self-refutation of realism yields no general method for refuting any future putative self-refutation of realism.9 Those with anti-realist instincts should be agnostic in S. I claim that the actual situation is such an S.

However, if philosophical investigation continues to fail to find a self-refutation of realism for long enough, any reasonable anti-realism must admit that the inductive evidence that realism does not refute itself is increasingly good, hence that the inductive evidence against anti-realism is increasingly good. Of course, the inductive evidence against a theory cannot be equated, even quantitatively, with the inductive evidence against one of its consequences: but as the latter mounts, so in the long run must the former. Thus anti-realism would refute itself by degrees.

Could anti-realism challenge this use of induction? It cannot adopt Popper’s anti-inductivism, for on Popper’s view a true empirical generalization is in no sense verifiable. Could it say that an hypothesis whose only evidence is inductive must be false? So extreme a view could make little sense of the use of empirical statements in natural languages. Could it allow that some hypotheses are projectible, but that ‘any purported reductio ad absurdum of realism is fallacious’, like ‘any emerald is grue’, is not one of them? As special pleading, this could not be taken seriously, but it might be based on a general principle: that inductive evidence never has any weight for philosophical hypotheses, say. But that is implausible: most philosophers, for instance, would take the sheer failure to find a convincing translation of material object language into sense datum language as evidence that none exists, over and above any general argument against phenomenalism. Thus if realism is internally coherent, certain forms of anti-realism could always consistently deny the existence of any evidence that this was so, but probably at the cost of viewing evidence in a way so extreme or ad hoc as to be intellectually disreputable. In short, anti-realists would have to be cranks: the self-refutation of realism their Godot. Given that no proof that realism is internally coherent is likely to be valid on any anti-realist terms, the realist should hope for an inductive self-refutation of anti-realism.

Hilary Putnam has endorsed a self-refutation argument against Logical Positivism.10 However, he sees it as threatening only an anti-realism that would have all verification criterial11 – that is, certifiable by institutionalized norms. He seems to assume that it leaves open a form of anti-realism on which truth must be verifiable, but in a looser, less formal way. Though one cannot anticipate the conversation of mankind, this leaves anti-realism with a heavy task. For if the realist cannot be driven into contradiction, or even uncontroversially bizarre conclusions, he has not been refuted even in this looser, less formal way – nor, therefore, has anti-realism been verified in that way. Could Putnam regard the consistent realist as the philosophical equivalent of the consistent Nazi,12 with a conceptual scheme that we can see to be irrational on the basis of the conceptual scheme we have adopted, even though it is so ‘warped’ that it cannot be brought to recognize its own irrationality? At present, such a ‘we’ cannot be defined without begging the question: realists are not yet pariahs. I doubt if Putnam even hopes to inspire his reader to drive them into the wilderness. Such a line would become plausible only if realism had to reject evidently valid13 arguments against itself. Putnam’s arguments for the incoherence of realism have much to do.

Anti-realism fails unless it can find internal incoherence in realism. However, the failure of anti-realism would not be the success of realism. For it leaves open extreme, perhaps Wittgensteinian, views on which all abstract philosophical theses are meaningless. Such a view might itself be self-refuting if it said that all abstract philosophical theses are meaningless, since that too is an abstract philosophical thesis. However, it could avoid self-refutation by calling each abstract philosophical thesis meaningless individually, while refusing to assert (or deny) it collectively, or it could confine the charge of meaninglessness to certain philosophical theses, including realism and anti-realism. But realism survives such diversity of possible opinion, for it can regard itself as an unverifiable truth (though perhaps supported by good evidence).
Any satisfying attack on realism – and therefore, as Section II claimed, any satisfying defence of anti-realism – would show its incoherence on its own terms. Is this how Putnam argues?

The target of ‘Realism and Reason’14 is ‘metaphysical realism’, a view on which the terms of the reference relation, words and things, are radically distinct. Putnam takes it to entail that a false theory could be verified.15

Is, then, metaphysical realism (verifiability does not entail truth) the converse of ordinary realism (truth does not entail verifiability)?16 No: the word ‘verification’ is being used differently. In our sense, verification, where it occurs, is conclusive. In Putnam’s, verification is the best operational status a theory can hope for, which may not be conclusive. If P is verifiable but not true in Putnam’s sense, −P is true but not verifiable in ours, for if −P were verifiable in our sense, P would not have the best operational status it could hope for, hence would not be verifiable in Putnam’s sense. Thus metaphysical realism implies ordinary realism. However, ordinary realism does not imply metaphysical realism. For instance, to say that arithmetic has unprovable truths is not to say that it has disprovable truths, to say that we cannot have conclusive evidence for a theory is not to say that we can have good evidence against it. So even had Putnam refuted metaphysical realism, he would not thereby have refuted ordinary realism. But the points made below will not turn on which realism is at issue.

Putnam argues that, given a supposedly false theory verifiable in his sense, one can always define a new ‘reference’ relation making the theory true, such that the realist cannot say in virtue of what his reference relation, not Putnam’s, is correct. Yet on Putnam’s relation, ‘cat’ might refer to a set of entities with which, the metaphysical realist wants to say, we have no causal connection. Aware of this, Putnam remarks:
Notice that a ‘causal’ theory of reference is not (would not be) of any help here: for how ‘causes’ can uniquely refer is as much of a puzzle as how ‘cat’ can, on the metaphysical realist picture.17

This is very strange. The metaphysical realist picture is accused of internal incoherence because it cannot explain how words refer uniquely; it offers an explanation, in causal terms, of how they do, which is failed for assuming that the words it uses refer uniquely. Now if this is the demand that the realist use only words whose unique reference he has already explained, it is blatantly absurd. For when he begins to speak, by hypothesis he cannot already have explained how his first words refer uniquely: he would have to remain forever silent.18 The ‘theory’ that language is meaningful at all could be dismissed on the same grounds, any explanation it gave of how language means being accused of begging the question, by assuming that the language of the explanation was meaningful.

Interpret Putnam more charitably, then, as accusing the realist of using the assumption that ‘cause’ refers uniquely to explain how ‘cat’ refers uniquely, whereas what must be explained is how any word can refer uniquely. But does the realist explanation assume that ‘cause’ refers uniquely, except in the sense just discussed? For a causal theory of reference uses ‘cause’, but need not mention it (and might be true even of a language with no word for ‘cause’19). The realist explanation need include no premise that ‘cause’ refers uniquely. Let R be some causal relation. Consider the argument:
For any x and y, x refers to y if and only if x bears the relation R to y.
‘Cat’ bears the relation R uniquely to the set (or whatever) of cats.
Therefore: ‘Cat’ refers uniquely to the set (…) of cats.

For the realist, this is a perfectly good, if skeletal, explanation of how ‘cat’ refers uniquely, which does not refer to the word ‘cause’. Putnam might object20 that it is useless because the reference of ‘R’, and therefore of ‘the set of cats’, is indeterminate too. But to do so would be profoundly to misconceive the dialectical situation. Realism is accused of failing on its own terms, of making explanatory demands on itself that it cannot meet. Hence the pertinent question is whether the explanation is good on realist terms. To object that it fails on anti-realist terms because, on them, ‘R’ is indeterminate, is quite beside the point. It merely shows that the realist cannot convince the anti-realist that he can refer uniquely. But he was not trying to convince the anti-realist, he was trying to explain to himself how he could do something that he already assumed he could do: in that, he succeeded. He avoids internal incoherence, and in doing so returns that threat to anti-realism.

Putnam’s argument about reference parallels scepticism about perception. Imagine an upholder of a causal theory of knowledge challenged on his knowledge of the external world: ‘How do you know that a table is before you?’. He may, indeed must, quite legitimately assume that a table is before him in explaining the causal production of his belief that a table is before him and therefore how he knows that a table is before him. To accuse one who assumes that P in explaining how they know that P of begging the question is sheer error (so in further explaining how one knows that one knows, one may assume that one knows, and so on). Such an explanation will not convince a sceptic who doubts that P, that P is known, but it does precisely what was asked of it: answer the question ‘how do you know that P?’ The sceptic, who has failed to show internal incoherence in his opponent’s position, accuses him of begging the question by not having shown internal incoherence in the sceptic’s position. The sophistry is transparent.

Now the metaphysical realist, in using ‘cause’, presupposes its unique reference. So that too is a fact that he would want to explain; though he will not be surprised if the realization of the reference relation turns out to be rather different for ‘cat’ and for ‘cause’.21 Suppose that he can explain, on a causal theory, thus using ‘cause’, how ‘cause’ refers uniquely: this is quite legitimate on realist terms, and they are what count. The realist offers a virtuous regress: each explanation can be followed – not preceded – by another, explaining how the terms used in the first refer uniquely. Indeed, the regress is likely to be infinite only for the rather trivial reason that the reference of the object language word for ‘reference’ can be discussed only in a metalanguage: radically new concepts will hardly need to be introduced after the first few stages.
Arguments so schematic22 point to nothing that the realist needs to and cannot on his own terms explain. Realism remains internally coherent.

So far I have accepted without demur Putnam’s implicit assumption that realism is obliged on its own terms to explain how words can refer uniquely. This seems to rest on a principle of sufficient reason: all semantic phenomena are so and not otherwise in virtue of some reason. Might a realist deny this? Realism satisfying such a principle is certainly more attractive than realism that does not, but if – what I do not believe – realism turned out unable to satisfy the principle, the alternative to a realism flouting it would be anti-realism: need the latter be more attractive? At present, though, the demand that realism explain its own claims on its own terms is reasonable.
Hartry Field encapsulates a similar point:

The reason why accounts of truth and primitive reference are needed is not to tack our conceptual scheme on to reality from the outside; the reason, rather, is that without such accounts our conceptual scheme breaks down from the inside.23

However, I have associated the need for such accounts with general demands on explanation rather than with the physicalism Field advocates24 (which is no part of my conceptual scheme). Whether such accounts are finally given in causal terms and of truth and primitive reference or in other terms and of other concepts does not matter here (for definiteness, I will continue to speak of causal theories, but without assuming anything specific to causality). I am not concerned to show in detail how the realist is to explain his claims, only that the very general considerations Putnam adduces do not show that he cannot.25

To take another case: the realist wants to show how speakers can give truth-conditions such that the law of excluded middle holds even for undecidable sentences. He may quite legitimately use the law of excluded middle in explaining why it holds for our language (roughly: the explanation of why ‘sv−s’ is true assumes that Pv−P); and a corresponding explanation of why the law holds in the metalanguage can be given in the metametalanguage. Clearly this does not prove the law: but it does undercut any attempted disproof. Nor is it trivial: the law will not hold in the object language simply because it holds in the metalanguage: the metalogic used for intuitionist logic is often classical.26

Putnam has a further explanatory task for realism.27 Suppose that reference is a certain causal relation R: what makes that so? Now had the realist identified reference with a general causal relation S such that, as a matter of scientific fact, R plays the causal role of S in this world, he could, non-trivially, have explained why x refers to y if and only if Rxy. But Putnam can assume R to be what fundamentally corresponds to reference (in that case, S). Thus the realist is saying that necessarily x refers to y if and only if Rxy, or:

Putnam will then ask: what makes (A0) so? Here explanation does seem to come to an end. Putnam says that (A0) would be ‘a kind of primitive, surd, metaphysical truth’.28 He contrasts it with the Kripkean example:

This latter ‘metaphysical necessity’ ‘is explained by mundane chemistry and mundane facts about speakers’ intentions to refer’,30 whereas these intentions would signify only in virtue of, and so could not explain, (A0).

This too is very strange. Water would have been H2O regardless of what intentions speakers had had in respect of ‘water’, or any other word (except on the crudest anti-realism of all, that cannot even distinguish between use and mention). These intentions are irrelevant to explaining (B0). Perhaps Putnam was thinking of:
Speakers’ intentions might be relevant to explaining (B1), but it corresponds to:
not to (A0); (A0) corresponds to (B0), not to (B1).

Now (B0) has an odd status, for while ‘mundane facts about speakers’ intentions’ are unnecessary to its explanation, ‘mundane chemistry’ is insufficient. For neither ‘water’ nor any roughly intertranslatable term is even part of the technical vocabulary of chemical theory: hence such theory alone cannot possibly explain (B0) (anyone who thinks that (B0) is a tautology or triviality can think the same of (A0): neither would call for explanation). For, familiarly, to explain something under one description is not to explain it under another: (A0) and (B0) are explicable only in a theory describing the identity as they do. Similarly, the technical vocabulary of the causal theory in which R appears will hardly include ‘refer’. This is, of course, a case of the problem of ‘bridge laws’ and their status in science: a theory cast in purely non-observational terms (as high-level theories are) cannot explain their link with observation as such.31 This is no mere technical hitch in the philosophy of science, but an eruption of profound difficulties about subjectivity and objectivity. For a theory explaining (A0) or (B0) would have satisfyingly to relate (relatively) objective reality (R, H2O) and its subjective appearance (as reference, water) to us: but to know what such a theory could be like would be almost to have solved the mind-body problem. This is no place for such an attempt. Fortunately, the present point is just the fallaciousness of Putnam’s attempted disanalogy between (A0) and (B0). One may not know what to say about either, but it has not been shown that what must be said about one cannot be said about the other. If (B0) is acceptable metaphysics, why should not (A0) be?
The apparent inexplicability of (A0) is no objection to realism. Putnam could instead ask for an explanation of (A1). Now (B1) is presumably to be explained by (B0) and:
Similarly, (A1) is presumably to be explained by (A0) and:

(this blurring of the distinction between object and metalanguage is harmless). (A2) in turn should be explained. Is this the place for Putnam’s objection, that (A2) could only be explained in terms of speakers’ intentions, which themselves signify only in virtue of (A2), making any explanation of it impossible? If the realist were to make reference require a formulated intention, he might be vulnerable to that charge: but he would also have begun an obviously vicious regress, since the formulation could refer to the words only by another formulated intention, and so on. Instead, the realist should take R as giving the causal basis on which any relevant intentions supervene,32 so that (A2) would hold simply in virtue of the word ‘reference’ having R to the reference relation: and Section III has already defended explanations like that.33

Even without the difficulty of relating different levels of appearance, the idea of explaining (A0) or (B0) is obscure. Putnam could seem to give a straightforward explanation of (B0) only by misrepresenting it as contingent while calling it necessary. Given that (A0) and (B0) are not contingent – I have no wish to challenge the necessity of true identity statements34 – they are not contingent on anything: so what could explain them? Only necessary truths can explain a necessary truth, lest its generality be missed. To ‘explain’ why either an explosion occurs at spatio-temporal location x or one does not by explaining why an explosion occurs at x and then applying the ‘or’ introduction rule, is at best obtuse. For the occurrence of an explosion is contingent, so at least some of the premises used to explain it must have been contingent, since what necessary premises entail is itself necessary (nor has probabilistic explanation from necessary premises any chance here): but the disjunction would have been true even had those premises been false. (Note that it concerns a decidable matter, so that anti-realist worries about the law of excluded middle do not apply here.) Whether or not such a deduction counts as an explanation, it is certainly not a good one. In practice, if asked why either an explosion occurs at x or one does not, one might say something like: it couldn’t have been otherwise. This could be construed either as a rejection of the question, or as an explanation of P by deduction from □P; either course would be applicable to (A0) and (B0), still yielding no asymmetry between them. One who asks why reference is R may not feel much enlightenment on being told that reference is necessarily R: but neither may one who asks why water is H2O on being told that water is necessarily H2O. Again, some proofs in mathematics seem to explain why their (necessary) conclusions are true: but is the resemblance to standard forms of explanation deep or superficial? If, for instance, to explain something is to give the causes or intentions behind it, explanation in mathematics is but pretence. Anyway, (A0) and (B0) cannot hope for mathematical lucidity. The problems set for realism seem rather to be problems for our concept of explanation (which was not itself used in defining realism).
However, (B0), though necessary, is closely related to a contingent truth:
H2O is what appears to us in the way we actually associate with water.

Another liquid, with the same phenomenal qualities as water, could have predominated instead in our environment, as we are often reminded. This contingent truth presumably has a straightforward explanation: someone might claim that this is what defuses (B0). The parallel for (A0) is:
R is what appears to us in the way we actually associate with reference.

Could another relation, with the same ‘phenomenal’ qualities as reference, have predominated instead in our environment? That sounds incoherent: assume that it is, for otherwise the symmetry between (A0) and (B0), which I have been defending for other respects, remains here too.

The reconstructed argument parallels Kripke’s celebrated attack on mind-brain identity:35 only pain can appear as pain, just as only reference can appear as reference. The argument against (A0) would be, roughly, that whereas the real contingency of (B3) explains the apparent contingency of (B0), (A3) is not really contingent, so that no corresponding explanation of the apparent contingency of (A0) can be given: hence (A0) must be assumed at most contingently true; as an identity it is, if true, necessarily true; hence it is false. Now whatever one thinks of Kripke’s original argument, this imitation uses the concept of appearance uncritically. For what does the apparent contingency of (A0) come to? To imagine (A0) false one can only imagine that philosophical discussion finds irremediable divergences between reference and R. In the same sense one can imagine that somebody will find a proof of 0=1 in Peano arithmetic. In neither case does one know how to fill in the picture: being able to imagine in this sense that P is no evidence that P is really possible. One could imagine speakers saying ‘a refers to b’ where a obviously was not R to b, and ‘a does not refer to b’ where a obviously was R to b: but one cannot then assume that they would mean by ‘reference’ what we mean by it; reference is not a phenomenological notion like pain.
The argument has become so general that it threatens any philosophical analysis whatsoever. For instance, Putnam wants to say something like:
Truth is what rational discussion would ultimately converge on.

One can as easily imagine rational discussion turning against (C) as against (A0): Putnam would rightly deny that this sense of ‘imagine’ is strong enough for the contingency of (C) to follow, so he cannot argue in this way against (A0).36 As for some strong Humean sense of ‘imagine’ in which the imaginable is somehow fully imaginable and therefore possible: to imagine an argument would already be to possess it, to imagine (A0) false would anticipate the future of philosophy. In Humphrey Lyttleton’s words: ‘If I knew where Jazz was going I’d be there already’.

The Kripke argument cannot be paralleled. Could one still argue that realism must and cannot explain (A3)? Now the necessity of (A3) adds to (A0) only that nothing but reference could have played the role which reference plays in our lives. In itself, this is quite unpuzzling, for that is just the kind of concept that reference is: concerned with the role, not what plays it, with form, not with matter. Without attempting more precision, one can easily explain the difference: ‘water’ is a term of embryonic chemistry, ‘reference’ of embryonic philosophy. The only question is whether this generality of reference is compatible with the specifically causal nature of the relation R. But if causality is understood as realizable by different specific relations in different universes, the difficulty disappears. Whether or not such an understanding is correct for the everyday English usage of ‘cause’, it is what the causal theory needs. So the long search for a disanalogy between (A0) and (B0) has found that ‘reference’ is a more abstract word that ‘water’. In philosophy, as in mathematics, the price of following the argument where it leads is sometimes to find oneself back where one started.

Neither a disproof of realism nor a disproof of the possibility of such a disproof has emerged. How many philosophers since – and before – Berkeley must have felt that at last they had the fallacy of realism ‘formulated, sprawling on a pin’? ‘Metaphysics is the finding of bad reasons for what we believe upon instinct, but to find these reasons is no less an instinct.’ Must the purging of fallacy lie deeper in us than its commission?
Thanks are due to Peter Lipton for comments on an earlier draft of this paper.

By ‘theory’ I mean something like a principled point of view: this includes both scientific and philosophical theories, but not every deductively closed set of sentences. A ‘principled point of view’ must include at least criteria for assessing relevant arguments. ↩︎

A falsified prediction is a problem for a scientific theory on its own terms, even though it can be blamed on over-idealization of the initial conditions; a more suitable idealization must still be found. Vulgar relativists – and realists – often imagine that a theory cannot be threatened by observations interpreted on its own terms. ↩︎

Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit, tr. A. V. Miller (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1977), paragraph 79; cf. Meaning and the Moral Sciences (London: Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1978)—henceforth Putnam 1978—p. 130: ‘Metaphysical realism collapsed at a particular point …. And the point at which it collapsed tells us something’. ↩︎

Though on some interpretations (not mine) of this result anti-realism would be meaningless, not false. Note that ‘verify’ and ‘falsify’ must be taken in a strong sense: if they meant merely ‘confirm’ and ‘disconfirm’, anti-realism would be reduced to the innocuous proposition that every truth is confirmable to some degree; certainly, any truth could be confirmed by an oracle found inductively to be reliable. This is not to say that all verification and falsification must be absolutely conclusive. ↩︎

This remark applies equally to realism: but I am elucidating, not redefining, ‘refute’. Someone said that the English always play the game but reserve the right to change the rules: realism is not yet reduced to claiming a stiff upper lip in defeat as the truest victory; perhaps it would seem less brash if it were. ↩︎
Intuitionist mathematics has conclusions of the form ¬∀x(Fxv¬Fx). Cf. M. A. E. Dummett, Elements of Intuitionism (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1977), p. 84. ↩︎
Cf. ibid. pp. 12-26 for the intuitionist interpretation of the quantifiers used here. Note that the next paragraph does not depend on it. ↩︎
Reason Truth and History (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1981)—henceforth Putnam 1981—pp. 105–13. ↩︎
Note that what Putnam calls ‘internal realism’ has nothing to do with what I call ‘ordinary realism’. ↩︎

Even had the realist given an infinite series of explanations E0, E1, E2, …, each Ei+1 preceding Ei and explaining how the words of Ei refer uniquely, he could still be asked for an explanation—Eω—of how any of the words in the Eis refer uniquely, and so on through all the ordinals. ↩︎

If a causal theory assumes that x refers to whatever stands in the causal relation R to x only if speakers intend that x refers to whatever stands in the causal relation R to x, this will be in a sense in which intentions need not be articulated, even on prompting: a causal theory should not assume itself to be believed by ordinary speakers. ↩︎

Might Putnam’s objection be that the word ‘cause’ could not be causally related to anything so nebulous as causality itself? That is not my reading of him. Moreover, that objection would not be decisive: if the word ‘tiger’ can be causally related to the species tiger via particular tigers, why cannot the word ‘cause’ be causally related to the relation causality via particular cases of causation? In any case, the objection is specific to causal theories of reference; the essential points of this paper still apply if the realist explicates reference in terms of some concept more general than that of causality, while the objection lapses. ↩︎

Not all Putnam’s arguments are so schematic: more detailed ones can be found in many of the papers in his Realism and Reason: Philosophical Papers, Volume 3 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1983). For present purposes, however, these add only epicycles. Further criticisms of Putnam’s anti-realist arguments can be found in: Michael Devitt, ‘Realism and the Renegade Putnam: A Critical Study of Meaning and the Moral Sciences’, Noûs 17 (1983) pp. 291–301, and Realism and Truth (Oxford: Blackwell, 1984); John Koethe, ‘Putnam’s Argument Against Realism’, Philosophical Review 88 (1979) pp. 92–9; David Lewis, ‘New Work for a Theory of Universals’, Australasian Journal of Philosophy 61 (1983) pp. 343–77, and ‘Putnam’s Paradox’, Australasian Journal of Philosophy 62 (1984) pp. 221–36; G. H. Merrill, ‘The Model Theoretic Argument Against Realism’, Philosophy of Science 47 (1980) pp. 69–81; Raimo Tuomela, ‘Putnam’s Realisms’, Theoria 45 (1979) pp. 114–26. ↩︎
‘Tarski’s Theory of Truth’, Journal of Philosophy LXIX (1972) pp. 347–75, at p. 373 (his emphasis). ↩︎

I except that trivial sense—cf. Noam Chomsky, Language and Mind (New York: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, enlarged edition 1972), p. 98—in which any concept in an irreducible explanation may come to be called ‘physical’, but Field’s physicalism, which he contrasts with mechanism and vitalism (op. cit. p. 357), amounts to more than this. ↩︎

Peter Lipton points out to me that the fallacy could be stated in Hempel’s terminology as the confusion of explanation-seeking and reason-seeking why questions; cf. Aspects of Scientific Explanation (New York: The Free Press, 1965) pp. 334–5. ↩︎
Of course, the inference from (i) True⁡(s)↔P,
(iv) Pv−P to (v) True⁡(‘sv−s’) is trivial: the point is that (iv) does not explain how (i)–(iii) are possible for undecidable s. ↩︎
Impurities cloud the issue: let us do Putnam the favour of pretending that water is pure H2O. ↩︎
The point stands if observationality is a matter of degree, not of kind. ↩︎

Again, with the caveat that the realist need not be embarrassed if R relates ‘cat’ and ‘reference’ to their referents in somewhat different ways. ↩︎

works.title: Criteria of identity and the Axiom of Choice
passages: Criteria of identity and the Axiom of Choice

At times, even the best philosophical theories must resort to Procrustean techniques. A frequent occasion is the attempt to confer respectability on some class of entities by giving them that obscure privilege, a “criterion of identity”.1 For such a thing is, minimally, a relation that meets certain formal constraints, which the only obvious candidate may fail: it must be hacked into the shape appropriate to a criterion of identity, if the search for one is not to be given up altogether. Many theories of personal identity face such problems, whose logical structure this paper analyzes and generalizes.
Criteria of identity and the Axiom of Choice

Identity, that relation which each thing has only to itself, is probably clearer than any concepts in terms of which one might seek to explain it. However, although one should not expect an analysis of the bare relation x=y, given a function f one might in suitable circumstances have the right to expect an analysis of the relation f(x)=f(y). For, unless f is one-one, the latter relation between x and y is not itself identity. Thus one might be able to reach a nontrivial conclusion of the form:

Here the things whose identity the criterion is for—the f(x)s—are in principle distinct from the things it relates—the xs (the variables ‘x’ and ‘y’ range over the arguments, but not necessarily the values, of f). In certain cases, (1) assumes philosophical interest. Frege gave a paradigmatic example: let ‘x’ and ‘y’ range over lines, f(x) be the direction of x, and R the relation of parallelism; then (1) states the criterion of identity for directions (74–79). For it seems that, if we could not think of directions as the direction of lines, then we could not think of them at all, that our thought about directions depends on a conceptually prior grasp of what it is for two lines to be parallel. I do not seek to clarify these familiar notions; I merely note their prevalence. On another interpretation of (1), ‘x’ and ‘y’ range over sets, f(x) is the cardinality of x, and R is the relation of one-one correspondence; then (1) states the criterion of identity for cardinal numbers (not quite as Frege conceived them). Or ‘x’ and ‘y’ can range over spatiotemporal locations, f(x) can be the table (if any) at x, and R some physical relation such that (1) states a criterion of identity for tables. This case seems to differ in rationale from the first two, since in it x is more, not less, abstract than f(x), but such differences will not affect the analysis below. Again, ‘x’ and ‘y’ can range over particular experiences, f(x) can be the subject of x, and R some physical or psychological relation such that (1) states a criterion of identity for subjects of experience.
Criteria of identity and the Axiom of Choice

Since identity is an equivalence relation (it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive), (1) requires R to be an equivalence relation too. In fact, without further information about f, that is all that (1) requires of R, since one can easily show that if R is an equivalence relation, there is a function f that makes (1) true. However, such an R can sometimes be hard to find. For example, let ‘x’ and ‘y’ range over color samples and f(x) be the perceived color of x. It is tempting to take R as the relation of indistinguishability (in color): but, since the indistinguishability of x from y and of y from z does not entail the indistinguishability of x from z, this relation is formally ruled out as a candidate for R, because it is not transitive. If ‘x’ and ‘y’ range over person-stages and f(x) is the person of whom x is a stage, otherwise promising interpretations of R have difficulty with the person who, when old, remembers being middle-aged and, when middle-aged, remembers being young, but, when old, does not remember being young, or with the results of supposed personal fission or fusion. Again, if f(x) is a physical magnitude of which (for whatever reason) one is trying to give an operational definition, the test for the identity of f(x) and f(y) is likely to give a positive result when x and y differ by sufficiently little (otherwise our measuring instruments would have to be infinitely precise): since the sum of many little differences is not itself little, the favored candidate for R will not be transitive.2 In some of these cases, however, the unsuccessful candidate relation S, in spite of its formal ineligibility, may still seem to us central to the identity of f(x)s; then we must somehow exhibit an R, to make (1) true, as a modification of S. In other words: given a relation S, which is not an equivalence relation, how can we best approximate it by an equivalence relation R, thus preserving as much as possible of the original intuition [which could be stated by putting ‘S’ for ‘R’ in (1)]?
Criteria of identity and the Axiom of Choice

Beneath the philosophical task of understanding the identity conditions of certain entities lies the logical task of defining a clear sense in which an equivalence relation R can approximate a relation S, which is not itself an equivalence relation. We cannot insist that S be both necessary and sufficient for R, but we do have an obvious pair of fall-back positions: either that S be sufficient for R but not necessary, or that it be necessary but not sufficient. For neither of the following formulas by itself requires S to be an equivalence relation, given that R is:

By accepting (2) or (3) [and (1)], we preserve one or other half of the oversimple intuition that S is the criterion of identity for f(x)s.
Criteria of identity and the Axiom of Choice

In (2) and (3), ‘S’ should be regarded as a constant and ‘R’ as a variable; for we are seeking conditions on equivalence relations R in terms of S which will make (1) plausible. For this, (2) or (3) alone would be too weak. For we could satisfy (2) by taking R to be the tautologous relation and (3) by taking it to be identity, and neither of these equivalence relations is likely to be a plausible criterion of identity for f(x)s. In either case, we should expect to be able to find a closer approximation to S.3 We say that R approximates S at least as well as R′ does if and only if whenever R′ and S agree, so do R and S:

Criteria of identity and the Axiom of Choice

R approximates S better than R’ does if and only if R approximates S at least as well as R’ does and R’ does not approximate S at least as well as R does. When S is fixed, both of these second-order relations are obviously transitive; approximating S better than is irreflexive and asymmetric; approximating S at least as well as is reflexive, and one can show that if each of R and R’ approximates S at least as well as the other does, then R and R’ are equivalent: for simplicity, I shall assume that equivalent relations are identical, so that approximating S at least as well as is antisymmetric. Given a notion of an eligible candidate, two promising constraints on R come immediately to hand, a weak one and a strong one. The weak constraint (which resembles Pareto optimality) is that no eligible candidate should approximate S better than R does; the strong constraint is that R should approximate S better than any other eligible candidate does. We have in turn two possible definitions of an eligible candidate R to hand: either as an equivalence relation that obeys (2) or as an equivalence relation that obeys (3). To use a mathematical analogy: we can choose either the greatest lower bound or the least upper bound. Of course, our choice is likely to be determined by philosophical considerations: S will sometimes be plausible as a sufficient condition for f(x)=f(y), sometimes as a necessary condition, rarely as both. The two cases will be treated in turn.
Criteria of identity and the Axiom of Choice

(A) Suppose that Sxy is plausible as a sufficient condition for f(x)=f(y). For example, let S be a relation on person-stages x and y of an unrivaled and very high degree of the right sort of psychological resemblance and continuity: S will fail to be transitive (consider a person who changes gradually); it will be plausible as a sufficient, but not as a necessary, condition for personal identity. The standard move at this point is—if one still regards S as the key to personal identity—to take as a criterion of identity the ancestral of S: x and y are stages of the same person if and only if there is a finite chain beginning with x and ending with y, each member of which has S to the next.4 A few details aside, we can use the preceding analysis to show that this is in fact the general solution for this case. Since we are taking Sxy as sufficient for f(x)=f(y), we define an A-eligible candidate as an equivalence relation R that obeys (2). The relation in (4) of approximating S at least as well as, restricted to A-eligible candidates, can then be shown to be equivalent simply to the extensional inclusion of R in R′. Thus R obeys the weak A-constraint if and only if R is an equivalence relation that includes S and does not properly include any equivalence relation that also includes S; R obeys the strong A-constraint if and only if R is an equivalence relation that includes S and is included in every equivalence relation that includes S. We now define in terms of S a relation that uniquely obeys the strong A-constraint; a fortiori, it also uniquely obeys the weak A-constraint. When S is reflexive and symmetric, the defined relation will simply be its ancestral. We recursively define a relation Si for each natural number i, and then define R in terms of them, as follows:

It is elementary to check that: R is an equivalence relation; R obeys (2); if R′ is an equivalence relation that obeys (2), R′ includes R. Thus R obeys the strong A-constraint; it does so uniquely because if R′ obeys the strong A-constraint, R and R′ include each other and so are identical. Thus if we seek a criterion of identity for f(x)s which makes Sxy sufficient and as near as it can be to necessary for f(x)=f(y), our desiderata unambiguously single out R, as defined above. The second case is more difficult. For in case (A) we seek the smallest equivalence relation that includes S, that is, the intersection of all equivalence relations that include S, and the intersection of a set of equivalence relations is itself an equivalence relation; in case (B) we seek the largest equivalence relation that is included in S, that is, the union of all equivalence relations that are included in S, and the union of a set of equivalence relations need not itself be an equivalence relation.
Criteria of identity and the Axiom of Choice

(B) Suppose that Sxy is plausible as a necessary condition for f(x)=f(y). For example, let S be a sort of physical or psychological connectedness which a stage of either of the results of an hypothetical case of personal fission has to a stage of the person when about to undergo the fission but not to a stage of the other result: S will thus fail to be transitive; it will be plausible as a necessary, but not as a sufficient, condition for personal identity.5 Or again, let S be indistinguishability in color, as a relation on color samples: S will fail to be transitive; it will be plausible as a necessary, but not as a sufficient, condition for identity of perceived color.6 The same can be said of operational definitions of physical magnitudes, where S will be a relation of indistinguishability by our measuring instruments. Suppose that we still regard S as the key to the identity of f(x)s, and take Sxy as necessary for f(x)=f(y). Consequently, we define a B-eligible candidate as an equivalence relation R that obeys (3). The relation in (4) of approximating S at least as well as, restricted to eligible candidates, can then be shown to be equivalent simply to the inclusion of R′ in R. Thus R obeys the weak B-constraint if and only if R is an equivalence relation that is included in S and is not properly included in any equivalence relation that is also included in S; R obeys the strong B-constraint if and only if R is an equivalence relation which is included in S and which includes every equivalence relation that is included in S. We must now ask whether at least one relation obeys the weak or strong B-constraint and, if so, whether more than one does.
Criteria of identity and the Axiom of Choice

We may assume S to be reflexive; for otherwise there will be no B-eligible candidates [if R is reflexive and obeys (3), S is reflexive]. We may also assume S to be symmetric; for an equivalence relation is included in S if and only if it is included in the symmetric relation Sxy&Syx. If Sxy is not already reflexive and symmetric, we replace it by the reflexive and symmetric relation x=y∨(Sxy&Syx). In all the examples above, S was reflexive and symmetric. Thus we may further assume S not to be transitive; for otherwise it would be an equivalence relation, in which case our problem would not arise, since (in the absence of any other obstacle) S could itself be taken as the criterion of identity for f(x)s.
Criteria of identity and the Axiom of Choice

The position now turns out to be as follows.7 We can show that no relation obeys the strong B-constraint. If we assume the Axiom of Choice [that for any set X of nonempty sets, there is a function f such that for every x∈X, f(x)∈x], we can show that several nonequivalent relations obey the weak B-constraint. If we do not assume the Axiom of Choice, we cannot in general show that any relation obeys the weak B-constraint, although we may be able to show this for particular values of S: for the assumption that, for every reflexive symmetric relation S, some relation obeys the weak B-constraint in respect of S is actually equivalent to the Axiom of Choice.8 What is the philosophical significance of these results?
Criteria of identity and the Axiom of Choice

The Axiom of Choice, though once controversial, is now for most working mathematicians an element of their normal equipment, if not a frequently used one.9 I take this to be a sensible attitude. However, I shall not argue for the plausibility of the Axiom here. Those who reject it are in the following position. If they wish to treat S as a necessary and as nearly as possible sufficient condition for the identity of f(x)s (whatever they happen to be), then they are assuming that the relation f(x)=f(y) obeys the weak B-constraint in respect of S. Since they reject the Axiom of Choice, they will allow that in some formally analogous cases no relation obeys the weak B-constraint in respect of S: they are therefore under some obligation to explain why, in the case at issue, they think that there is such a relation. Sometimes, we may simply be told that there is such a relation because f(x)=f(y) is it; but then the motive for seeking a criterion for the identity of f(x)s becomes obscure, if we have this independent grasp of the relation f(x)=f(y). If any interesting explanation of the identity of f(x)s in terms of xs is to be given, we seem to require an argument in terms of xs, not of f(x)s, for the existence of a relation obeying the weak B-constraint in respect of S. If the set of xs is countable, such an argument can be given; for the existence of a choice function for subsets of a countable set can be proved without appeal to the Axiom of Choice, and so the use of the Axiom in proving the existence of a relation obeying the weak B-constraint was unnecessary in this case. If the xs are empirical items, however, it may in turn be hard to prove the existence of a one-one correspondence between xs and natural numbers without appeal to the Axiom of Choice. The progress of the argument will depend upon the details of the individual case, but clearly, those who take approach (B) to the identity of f(x)s and refuse to use the Axiom of Choice have a good deal of work to do. For they face the apparently live possibility that their concept of f(x)s is incoherent, in that no relation meets what is demanded of the criterion of identity for f(x)s.
Criteria of identity and the Axiom of Choice

The application of either the Axiom of Choice or the above substitutes for it requires us to treat relations as in some sense set-theoretic entities, such as sets of ordered pairs. This raises a problem: a criterion of identity is usually expected to work for all possible worlds, not just the actual one; now the existence of a set plausibly requires the existence of its members, but then the set of ordered pairs that works as a criterion of identity for one world will not work for another, since it will not relate objects that exist in the latter world but not in the former. To overcome this problem, one could think of a relation as being realized by different sets of ordered pairs in different worlds, and, as it were, apply the set-theoretic arguments to each world separately. However, that would leave two further problems unsolved: first, it would not give us any help with transworld identities; secondly, since more than one set of ordered pairs would obey the weak B-constraint in respect of S in any world where S failed to be transitive, some kind of transworld Axiom of Choice would be required to form a complete relation by choosing one appropriate set of ordered pairs from each world (for this reason, we cannot dispense with the Axiom in the case of personal identity merely on the grounds that only finitely many fissions and fusions will occur: for even excluding possible worlds in which infinitely many occur, some form of Choice is generally required to choose one member from each of an infinite collection of finite sets). A bolder approach would be to apply the Axiom directly to a class of ordered pairs of possible individuals and worlds. Having noted but not solved these problems, I shall assume for the sake of argument that relations are either extensional entities to which the Axiom of Choice can be applied or intensional entities to which some plausible, intensional variant of the Axiom of Choice can be applied.
Criteria of identity and the Axiom of Choice

Given an extensional or intensional version of the Axiom of Choice, several nonequivalent relations obey the weak B-constraint in respect of any given reflexive, symmetric, nontransitive relation S, and no relation obeys the strong B-constraint in respect of S. Thus if the identity of f(x)s is determined only as such that S is a necessary and as nearly as possible sufficient condition for it, then the identity of f(x)s is indeterminate [unless there is a better way than (4) of measuring the approximation of one relation by another]. Less ontologically: if we try to specify f(x)=f(y) as the relation that obeys the strong B-constraint in respect of S, we fail because there is no such relation; if we try to specify f(x)=f(y) as the relation that obeys the weak B-constraint in respect of S, we fail because there are many such relations. We can even prove something stronger. Let T be any equivalence relation for which S is necessary: then some relation R for which T is sufficient obeys the weak B-constraint in respect of S. That is: we can make any (positive) judgments of identity we like among f(x)s, providing that they are consistent with the principle that Sxy is necessary for f(x)=f(y), and some criterion of identity for f(x)s, with apparently as much claim to be correct as any has, will make those judgments come out true. Since the discussion has been rather abstract, let us apply it to particular cases.
Criteria of identity and the Axiom of Choice

Suppose we are seeking a criterion of identity for perceived color. If the perceived color of x and the perceived color of y are identical, we cannot perceptually distinguish x from y in respect of color: so the (perceptual) indistinguishability (in color) of x and y is necessary for the identity of the perceived colors of x and y. Conversely, we should not want our criterion of identity for perceived colors to give rise to cases where x and y were deemed to have distinct perceived colors, but anything that is deemed to have the same perceived color as x is indistinguishable from anything that is deemed to have the same perceived color as y (in particular, x is indistinguishable from y). For then the distinction between the perceived colors of x and y would seem to have no perceptual basis: we should not be talking of perceived color. So we demand that our criterion of identity for perceived colors not give rise to cases of that anomalous kind. This demand, however, is simply equivalent to the demand that the equivalence relation of having the same perceived color (R) should obey the weak B-constraint in respect of indistinguishability (S) (for in the above case the criterion of identity that was like ours except that it identified the perceived colors of x and y would be an equivalence relation that would be included in S and would properly include our criterion of identity, so the latter would not obey the weak B-constraint; conversely, if an eligible candidate R did not obey the weak B-constraint, it would by definition be properly included in an equivalence relation R’ which was in turn included in S, and the cases where R’xy held and Rxy did not would be anomalous). Now S is a reflexive, symmetric, nontransitive relation; so the previously mentioned results apply. Several nonequivalent relations obey the weak B-constraint; none obeys the strong one. We have several possible criteria of identity to choose among. To see the extent of the choice, consider any three color samples a, b, and c for which transitivity breaks down: a is indistinguishable from b and b from c but not a from c. Define two relations on color samples, as follows:

T′xy if and only if x=y∨(x=b&y=c)∨(x=c&y=b)
